<meta>The text continues the analysis of Neoplatonic theories of perception, specifically transitioning from a general commentary on Theophrastus to the specific views of Priscian of Lydia regarding how the senses interact with the "transparent medium."</meta>

### ON THEOPHRASTUS

The <term>forms</term> <note>original: "Species"; here referring to the sensory images or "forms" of things that travel from an object to the eye.</note> of things, which are essentially their shapes, are images of divine things. They act formally and, in a sense, spiritually upon the formal and spiritual part of us—specifically upon the instrument of sense, which is the living being itself. Such action leads directly and specifically to sensation. However, when the action of the soul (which I mentioned shortly before) is added to this, the purely physical and material action either hinders it, does not help it, or is insufficient for the actual effect of sensing. Because such a soul contains all sensible things within its own body through their underlying causes, it looks into all sensible things through a kind of internal sense, using this as both an instrument and a cause at once. Conversely, because the principles of sensible things are not located within *our* human bodies, our sense is forced to look outward. From this, it is clear that this Priscianus is a Platonist. For what he touches upon regarding the sensation of the celestial soul comes from Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Proclus. Indeed, throughout the preceding and following passages, it is clear that he is a Platonist and a diligent follower of Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus was a Syrian Neoplatonist who influenced later philosophy with a mix of logic and mysticism.</note>.

### OF PRISCIANUS

<insert>But</insert> what exactly is seeing, or hearing, or smelling? And are all the senses produced through a certain medium? Just as sight occurs through the <term>transparent medium</term> <note>original: "diaphanum"; the clear substance, like air or water, that allows light to pass through.</note>—that is, a medium that is clear and passable for the eyes—or do certain senses instead touch the things to be sensed without any medium? Likewise, what exactly is this transparent medium?

I believe, for my part, that vision is achieved neither through a simple reception from external things (as if it were shaped by the things being sensed through some flow coming from them), nor by an emission from the eyes (as if some physical body were sent out to touch the things sensed). Nor do colors move the transparent medium as if they were shaping it, and the transparent medium then moves the sight in a similar way. Rather, I believe the <term>forms</term> <note>original: "species"</note> themselves possess an active power. Through this power, each form acts upon that which is most exposed to such an experience—not merely by touching it, but also acting upon things at a distance, provided that the distance is commensurate: both for the object to act and for the sense organ, in turn, to receive. For since a natural, physical form is contained within something and circumscribed by a specific place, it does not act upon just anything placed anywhere. It acts only upon that which is at a distance according to a proportion that is measured both against the effective power of the agents and the power of the receivers, which is suited and exposed to this action. And again, this corresponds to the measure of the experience itself. The visible object acts upon the instrument of sight from a certain interval, which is balanced both to the one seeing and to the thing being seen.

<summary>This page discusses the Neoplatonic theory of perception, arguing that vision and other senses do not work through physical "flows" or emissions, but through the active power of forms acting across a balanced distance.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as the formal dedication and introduction to Marsilio Ficino’s collection of Neoplatonic translations. It follows the table of contents and introduces the primary text of the volume: Iamblichus’s "On the Mysteries." Ficino addresses Giovanni de' Medici, the future Pope Leo X, establishing a connection between ancient "pagan" wisdom and the high offices of the Christian Church.</meta>

# Marsilio Ficino the Florentine humbly commends himself to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Giovanni de' Medici, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.

When I had decided to write a letter to you to congratulate you on the cardinal's dignity recently conferred upon you, and was considering to whom I might best give it to deliver to you—someone who would make our congratulation much more pleasing—I suddenly betook myself to the Academy <note>The Platonic Academy of Florence, a circle of scholars led by Ficino under Medici patronage.</note>, hoping that at least in its innermost shrines some greeter most acceptable to you would not be lacking. There, by a certain divine fate, I first encountered Iamblichus, known among the Academics by the nickname "the Divine," and a great priest there. To him I said, "Greetings, Iamblichus, great priest. In your presence (as you see), I am about to congratulate Giovanni de' Medici, a new prelate of the Christian religion; I pray you, if I ask what is right, that you will make our congratulation—which would otherwise be meager—fuller with your divine words and mysteries." He nodded to my prayers, and with this sentiment he comes to you: "Giovanni, great priest, a Great Priest <note original: "Magnus ille sacerdos">Ficino is playfully equating the young Cardinal Giovanni with the 'great priest' Iamblichus.</note> comes to you." Therefore, receive such a greeter joyfully, and after the first greeting, after the letter has been read, listen more attentively (if it please you) to what that divine man says. For he promised that he would speak things worthy of both his persona and yours alike, and that he would express to you in brief what the Egyptian and Assyrian priests felt concerning religion and divine matters.

### SUMMARY OF THE BOOK OF IAMBLICHUS.

Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note>, who is called "the Philosopher" among the Platonists because of his excellence, sent a long letter to Anebo, an Egyptian priest, full of various and weighty questions regarding all parts of philosophy, especially concerning God, and <term>angels</term>, <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "dæmonésq;"; in this context, these are not evil spirits but intermediary beings between gods and humans.</note>, and souls; concerning providence, fate, prophecies, magic, miracles, sacrifices, and vows. Iamblichus, his pupil, answered all of Porphyry's questions. However, he introduces Abammon, an Egyptian priest, as the one responding to Porphyry on behalf of his student Anebo, to whom Porphyry had sent the letter. Of this entire inquiry and surely divine response, I have translated almost every thought rather than every word <note original: "non verba, sed sensum traduxi">A common Renaissance translation philosophy: "sense-for-sense" rather than "word-for-word."</note>, as if I were still too occupied with Plotinus. Thus, it should not be thought strange if the speech seems disconnected in places, especially among the very beginnings of the disputation where the loss of words is slighter. Henceforth, the context of the words will appear more continuous. I was, however, forced at times to intersperse some words of my own for the sake of continuity or understanding. Moreover, the reason for this swifter edition was Pierleoni <note>Piero Leoni of Spoleto, a famous physician and friend of Ficino.</note>, a man most desirous of all secrets. Truly, what I wonder at most is this: he always seems to strive for those things which he already possesses. For by a certain divinity of character, he attains the secrets of the philosophers, both Greek and barbarian, even before they are read.

<summary>In this preface, Marsilio Ficino dedicates his translation of Iamblichus to Cardinal Giovanni de' Medici, framing the ancient Neoplatonic text as a "divine" greeting suitable for a high-ranking churchman. He explains his translation method—focusing on meaning over literal wording—and acknowledges the influence of his friend Piero Leoni.</summary>

# IAMBLICHUS ON THE MYSTERIES. On the knowledge of divine things 1

<sig>a iii</sig>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Æ' featuring a classical figure in armor and a helmet, set within an ornate square frame with floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

<margin>A large curly brace on the left spans the first seven lines of the text block.</margin>
Egyptian writers, believing that all discoveries originated with Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes; here referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage thought to be the father of all philosophy and magic</note>, dedicated their books to Mercury. Mercury is the source of wisdom and eloquence. Pythagoras, Plato, Democritus, Eudoxus, and many others visited the Egyptian priests. The teachings of this book belong to the Assyrians and Egyptians and are drawn from the "columns of Mercury" <note>Legendary pillars upon which Hermes was said to have inscribed the sum of all human knowledge</note>. Pythagoras and Plato learned their philosophy from these columns of Mercury in Egypt. The columns of Mercury are filled with sacred doctrines. Before any use of reason, there exists a naturally implanted notion of the gods. Indeed, there is a certain "touch" of divinity that is better than mere knowledge; from this, the natural desire for the good is ignited, along with our capacity for reasoning and judgment. This essential knowledge of divine things, which is perpetual in the soul, is not actually the kind of "knowledge" through which we enjoy God. For in ordinary knowledge there is "otherness" <note>A logical gap or distinction between the person knowing and the object being known</note>, but here there is a certain essential and simple contact. We cannot reach Unity <term>Unity: The Neoplatonic "One," the absolute source of all existence which transcends even being itself</term> except through a most unified state and a unity of the mind which stands above the usual properties of the soul and the mind. The Unity of the gods unites souls to itself from eternity through their own internal unities, in a proximity so precise and effective that it appears to be a continuous connection. The divine intellect gives being to the soul through its own essential act of understanding. Therefore, the very being of the soul is a kind of understanding—specifically an understanding of God, upon whom it depends. Our very being consists in knowing God, because the highest part of the soul's being is its intellect, in which "to be" and "to understand divine things" are the same perpetual act. From that primary being, the wandering powers of the soul are derived. After the gods, we rank demons, heroes, and pure souls; these three orders are the attendants of the gods. We cannot reach these attendants—demons, heroes, and pure souls—solely through the discursive paths of human reason. Instead, it is necessary to rise up to essential and eternal intelligence.

<margin>A small curved mark or brace in the right margin next to the first three lines of the second paragraph.</margin>
Just as the gods are always reached through an innate notion, so too the divine attendants are first reached when the soul sets aside its "mobile" mode of cognition (the changing way we think about the world), which belongs to the rational power formed by the intellect and intelligence, which they call the "acquired intellect." For the primary knowledge resides in the active intellect. Since knowledge occurs through a process of alignment, it follows that we reach the eternal and unchanging "least things" <note original: "minima sempiterna">Referring to the fundamental, indivisible, and eternal principles of reality</note> through a notion that is itself eternal, unchanging, and simple. The knowledge by which we understand "separate substances" <note>Entities that exist without physical bodies, such as the gods or pure intellects</note> is of a different kind than the knowledge by which we know other things.

->The knowledge of divine things was always in the soul through simple intuition.<-

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of how the human mind can know divine, incorporeal beings. It transitions from the introductory concepts of "divine touch" to a technical discussion of the nature of separate substances (immaterial beings) and how they differ from material things.</meta>

-># IAMBLICHUS.<-

...or touch. Some believe they can grasp separate <term>substances</term> <note>Separate substances are "incorporeal" beings that exist independently of matter, such as gods, angels, or pure intellects</note> through a method of opposition—namely, that material things are mobile, bound to a location, capable of being acted upon, and so forth; therefore, separate substances are immobile, and so forth. In this way, one certainly learns what they are *not*. However, what they truly *are* is acquired through an "adequacy of cognition"—a matching of our knowledge to that which is naturally present in the soul through the intellect. This is attained in our rational power through a certain study, yet not so much by the work of comparison and conjecture as by the labor of separation and purification <note>The Neoplatonic idea that the soul must "purify" itself from sensory distractions to see higher truths</note>. There was also a method of logical division: namely, that the gods are either temporal or eternal. They are not temporal; therefore, they are eternal. Yet even this method, because of its own "mobility" <note>Referring to the step-by-step movement of logical reasoning</note>, does not suit those things which are immobile.

### On the properties of each of the higher beings.

<margin>s</margin>If any composition <note>The way a thing is "put together" from different parts or traits</note> exists within separate and separable substances, it does not come from a <term>genus</term> <note>A general category</note> that is indeterminate in itself and a <term>difference</term> <note>The specific trait that defines a species</note> that limits it. For those substances are complete <term>species</term> in every way, existing in a defined and finished state of <term>actuality</term> <note>Latin: "actu." In philosophy, being "in act" means being fully realized and active, rather than just having the potential to be</note>. If separable substances, being simple, do not differ from one another through specific differences under the same genus, then they do not differ through individual differences under the same species. Each one is, therefore, like a single genus or species existing by itself. They differ by their own nature and by the order of their ranks, and because they relate to the **First** <note>The "First" refers to the supreme, unified source of all existence—the Neoplatonic "One"</note> in different ways.

Intellects do not agree or differ among themselves by genus or any specific differences—for they are most simple—but rather insofar as they relate to the **First** by the same or different reasons. Some are arranged in the prior ranks of perfection, others in the subsequent ones. The differences between things in their actions and their ways of being acted upon must always be traced back to differences in their powers <note>original: "iurium," likely a variant of "virium" meaning powers or forces</note>, and these to differences in their essences. We must not stop at the secondary effects, but proceed to the prior causes. 

In the higher substances, and even in our soul, there is no passive motion <note>Movement caused by an outside force</note>; instead, the whole is an effective act. The movement of the soul, by which it moves itself, is not divided into a "mover" and a "moved," or "moving" and "being moved," but is an essential act that proceeds through time. Accidents <note>Properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, like being "tall" or "sitting"</note> belong to composite things and forms that exist within a subject; they do not suit immaterial forms. Whatever exists in separable forms is essence and essential traits of a certain superior and equal lot. No accident or consequence is found there. Movements and actions differ because of the differences in natures, not the other way around. 

If we say there is only one genus of separate things, we throw theology <note>The study of divine and immaterial things</note> into confusion. Separable substances do not belong to one single genus in which they are distinguished by differences; rather, they are distinguished by themselves and by the order of their ranks. Insofar as they relate to the **First** through different degrees of perfection, they nevertheless agree...

<summary>This page argues that divine, immaterial substances cannot be understood through standard Aristotelian logic or material comparisons, but rather through a process of spiritual purification. It establishes that these higher beings differ not by category or "accidents," but by their degree of perfection and proximity to the supreme source (the First).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of divine beings. The previous page established that we know these beings not through logic or comparison, but through a purification of the soul. Here, the author begins to define the specific hierarchy and "properties" (essential characteristics) of the Gods, Demons, Heroes, and Souls.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES.
iii

...more closely related to one another are those things which, in a similar fashion, refer back to the first and the last. The Good is twofold: that which is above <term>essence</term> <note>In this Neoplatonic context, "essence" or "being" refers to the first level of defined reality; that which is "above essence" is the ultimate, indescribable Source or "The One"</note>, and that which is according to essence. Essence is the property of all the gods. However, the Good itself is above essence; it is called the cause of good—namely, the principle of essential good. Accordingly, the ranks of the gods are distinguished among themselves according to the degrees of their essence. In the lowest rational souls, essential good is not present as it is in the gods; rather, they possess a participation in the good according to intellectual beauty, and this is present in them immovably.

->On the order of the higher beings.<-

<margin>a</margin> Our souls are counted among the classes of divine beings. <term>Heroes</term> <note>Not just "brave people," but a specific class of semi-divine mediator spirits in ancient philosophy</note> are greater than men; therefore, <term>demons</term> <note>original: "dæmones." These are not "demons" in the modern sense of evil spirits, but "daimons"—intermediary spirits who act as messengers and guides between gods and humans</note> are much greater still. The first of the divine beings is the Good itself, followed by the gods. The last are the particular rational souls. Between these two are two intermediaries: namely, the heroes, who are close to the souls, and the demons, who are close to the gods—just as air and water exist between fire and earth. Although heroes excel us in power, virtue, beauty, and greatness, they are nonetheless very much in harmony with our soul and its life. Demons are superior to heroes; they are the ministers of the gods, acting like subordinates to the master-architects in the "crafting of the world" <note>Referring to the *demiurge* or the divine work of shaping the physical universe</note>. What is ineffable and hidden in the gods, the demons express and make manifest. The demons and heroes adapt the universal, simple, and immobile gifts of the gods for the use of inferior beings; they reconcile all things and are the authors of the harmonic consent and mutual compassion of all things. They transmit divine things to us, and likewise lead our affairs back to the divine. Furthermore, they distribute the degrees of the gifts from the higher beings and manage the preparation of those who receive them. Different classes of divine beings differ from one another by a three-fold mode of properties: namely, in regard to their essences, their powers, and their actions. The property of the gods is unity, remaining within themselves, being the immobile cause of motions, and possessing an eminent providence that has nothing in common with those things for which it provides; this property is preserved in them according to their essence, their power, and their action. The property of souls is an inclination toward the "many" <note>The physical world of diverse, changing things</note>, motion, and a connection with the gods; they receive things from others and are filled with vital motion, harmonizing everywhere with all things—partly with those that are stable and partly with those that are flowing—tempering all things in and through themselves. This property is preserved in them according to their essence, their power, and their action. The properties of demons are to contain within themselves the gifts of the gods in a manner lower than the gods, yet to contain the conditions of lower things under a divine "idea" and "reason." This means that while their nature is multiplied, it is mixed in a unified way; though it is also distinct, it remains unmixed. Finally, it moves, yet remains stable...

<summary>This page outlines the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being, placing Heroes and Demons as vital intermediaries between the perfect, unified Gods and the multi-faceted, moving human Souls. It defines the "Double Good" and explains that while Gods remain unified and separate from the world, Demons and Heroes translate their divine gifts into terms that lower beings can receive.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of divine beings. The previous page established the intermediaries between the One and the soul. This page specifically distinguishes the characteristics and actions of demons and heroes compared to the gods and human souls.</meta>

IAMBLICHUS.

...spiritually. Heroes, on the contrary, possess unity, identity, stability, and excellence, despite the conditions of multiplicity, motion, and mixture. <term>Demons</term> <note>original: "dæmones." Not evil spirits, but intermediary beings</note> and <term>heroes</term> <note>Semi-divine beings positioned between humans and gods</note> are closest to the extremes: the former to the gods, the latter to souls. The primary differences between demons and heroes are as follows: heroes sometimes decline more toward particular and moving things than demons. These two intermediaries—namely, demons and heroes—are composed of the properties of the extremes (that is, of gods and souls), but in demons there is more of the divine, whereas in heroes there is more of the human.

## How the actions of the superior beings are distinguished among themselves.

<margin>d</margin> Gods hold the highest rank of beings, souls the lowest. Gods can do all things, united in a single moment; souls, by contrast, can neither do all things, nor act in a single moment, nor act as a united whole. Gods act and care for all things without <term>inclination</term> <note>Meaning they act without being emotionally "pulled" or changed by the things they care for</note>.
<margin>ti.</margin> Souls act with a certain inclination and turning. Gods are the primary causes. Souls depend perpetually on the will of those gods. Gods, with the swiftest vigor, grasp their innermost ends together with their principles. Souls proceed from one thing to another, from the imperfect toward the perfect. Gods cannot be encompassed by any measure or form. Souls are held back and overcome by inclination, habit, and will. They are touched by a desire for and familiarity with inferior things, and from this, they contract certain qualities.

## On the intellect and the soul.

<margin>i</margin> <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "Intellectus." In Neoplatonism, this is the "Nous" or Divine Mind, the level of reality containing the eternal forms</note>, the craftsman of all things, is always present most fully to all gods through a single act remaining within itself. The soul is a participant in intellect, but in a way that is more divisible and multiform, adapted for governing; it naturally provides for inanimate things, being affected now by one shape, now by another. Likewise, order and beauty itself (or the cause of both) are present to the gods from higher causes; but for the soul, order and intellectual beauty are present as something received. Likewise, in the gods, there is a measure powerful over all things. The soul, however, is determined by that measure and acts through it upon specific things. Demons and heroes, as intermediaries between gods and souls, relate to the extremes and to themselves in a fitting proportion; they are composed of the properties of both souls and gods, which we described above. If, therefore, you wish to grasp the nature of the gods, think of the properties of the lowest rational soul and attribute the opposite perfections to the gods. If it pleases you to define the nature of a demon, compose it from both, while attributing more of the divine. Finally, if you seek the nature of a hero, compose it from both, but bringing in more of the conditions of the soul. He critiques <term>Porphyry</term> <note>Porphyry was Iamblichus's teacher; Iamblichus wrote this text ("On the Mysteries") as a response to Porphyry's skeptical questions about religion and magic</note>...
<meta>catchword: ...for treating as separate</meta>

<summary>This page defines the hierarchical ladder of existence, distinguishing Gods as unified, effortless causes, while Souls are gradual and subject to change. It positions Demons and Heroes as the "connective tissue" of the universe, blending divine and human traits in different proportions.</summary>

While the previous page distinguished gods, demons, and souls by their capacity for action and their relationship to time, this page argues that these beings should not be defined by the physical bodies (ethereal, aerial, or terrestrial) they govern. It establishes the Neoplatonic principle that the higher contains the lower, and that the divine is essentially omnipresent and independent of material constraints.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES.
<sig>a iiii</sig>
<meta>Catchword/marginal mark 'm' at bottom left. Hand-drawn mark in right margin near second paragraph.</meta>

...separated by their <term>relationships</term> <note>original: "habitudines," referring to the specific way a higher being relates to or "holds" a lower one</note> to the bodies that distinguish them: namely, gods by their relationship to ethereal bodies, <term>demons</term> <note>original: "dæmones." Intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demonic" in the modern sense</note> to aerial bodies, and souls to terrestrial ones. For obviously, prior things and causes should not be defined by later things and their effects. Incorporeal substances are not contained within bodies, but rather they lead them from the outside; they give something to the bodies but receive nothing from them. Therefore, they are neither changed along with them, nor are they divided according to the distribution of those bodies. For they are not "dispositions" of bodies or material forms, but are self-subsisting and separable; indeed, they are already separate and exist before the bodies. These separate and separable substances do not turn out as they are because they chose a certain lot or province, or were assigned one; rather, it is the reverse. Whatever kind of life and form the soul brought forth into act within itself before entering the body, it is allotted a corresponding organic body and a consequent nature, which is then subjected to the perfection of the soul's own life. The <term>rational soul</term> <note>The human soul capable of reason, as opposed to the animal or vegetative soul</note> comes into a body that is already living, but only imperfectly so. Divine things naturally generate their entire work, distinct within themselves, before they bring it forth. In those beings which possess the nature of a universal principle, the lower things are produced within the higher: bodily things within incorporeal things, and created works within their creators. In these higher beings, they are contained and directed in a circular manner. Therefore, the celestial orbits are brought back to the orbit of the celestial souls. Indeed, the souls of the worlds—that is, of the spheres and the stars—as they enter into their own <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "intellectum." The higher realm of pure thought/being</note>, are completely grasped by it and are first generated within it. The particular intellect is contained within the universal intellect, and that in turn within higher things likewise. Since, therefore, subsequent things are always turned back toward the first things, and the higher things lead the lower as if they were <term>exemplars</term> <note>The perfect "blueprints" or models of things</note>, it is certain that essence and form are produced from the higher and are present to the lower; all things are first produced among the better things that follow them. Therefore, order and measure in the following things depend on those higher ones, and not the other way around; thus, the properties of the higher should not be assigned based on the lower. Consequently, an incorporeal essence cannot be distinguished by bodily qualities, with which it has nothing in common.

<margin>squiggle mark</margin> Divine principles grant to their works not only their essence, but their entire distinction and formal order. An essence that is present to bodies non-locally is not distinguished by physical locations; and that which is not confined by the particular boundaries of its subjects is not at all contained by the parts of the world in a particular way. An incorporeal nature is suddenly present wherever it wills, with nothing anywhere prohibiting it.

# IAMBLICHUS.

...a certain creative power <note>original: "uirtus opifex"</note>, and a participation in the forms <note>original: "specierū participatio"</note> is diffused through all things. Finally, unless these things were divine, the power of sacrifice <note>original: "sacrificii uirtus"</note>—which consists of a certain communion of the gods with humans—would be removed from everywhere. The gods contain all things for this reason most of all: because they are themselves contained by nothing. Since earthly things are created and exist by the gift of divine beings, whenever they are rendered more ready for the divine, they suddenly obtain the gods who exist there: even here, before the specific natures of earthly things. Furthermore, since in any god whatever the power is infinite, and the nature is indivisible and incomprehensible, they cannot rightly be confined to certain specific places. Likewise, there would be no true union of universal providence among the gods unless all were equally present everywhere. It is also said that some gods are "of the air" while others are "of the water," not because they exist only there, but because they rule there most especially. Priests used to call upon "earthly" and "subterranean" gods, who are certainly called such not because they are only there (for they are all everywhere), but because some act most powerfully in one place or another. For even the soul of any star is everywhere, although it acts more in that specific place. In statues, a certain divine illumination <note>original: "illustratio"</note> is received.

### On providence and how the gods are everywhere:

<margin>q</margin>When the gods are said to specifically "obtain" various parts of the world, or cities, temples, and statues, understand that their essence and power—which is active everywhere within itself—illustrates this or that thing most especially. And just as light remains within itself, without mixing or dividing itself, yet illuminates different things in various places, so do the gods. Just as the light of the sun is a single continuous whole everywhere, and can neither be divided into parts, nor enclosed anywhere, nor separated from its own source, nor is it mixed with the air even though it is present. Indeed, while it leaves nothing behind, the heat of the light is nonetheless left by the source of the heat; in this same way, the light of each god, as an indivisible whole, is intimately present to the whole world, even though it grants its power to a certain part that is most specially adapted to it. Meanwhile, it somehow fills all things because of its perfect power and its utterly immense causal excellence. Hence it perfects all things and unites the furthest extremes with one another through the middle, encompassing all things within itself and reflecting itself back upon itself, entirely united to itself. This is the very gift that the world also imitates through its circular motion, and by a certain connection and reconciliation of parts, which transfers elements into other elements in turn and sends the power of the higher things down to the lower. He who accepts this manifest statue <note>The author uses "statue" here metaphorically to mean the visible, ordered cosmos as a physical representation of the divine</note> of the gods, which is entirely united everywhere, ought to be altogether careful that he says nothing <unclear>alien to</unclear> <note>original: "sis aliena." The ink blot obscures the full sentence, but the catchword suggests a warning against speaking of the gods in a way that suggests they are "alien" or "separated" from the world they govern.</note>

...to perceive them as alien is to think of them as being locally (if I may put it that way) separate. For if there is no communion between the world and the divine powers <note>original: "numina"</note> in terms of essence, power, and action; and no shared distribution or fellowship, then certainly no co-extension or shared distribution according to place—and the defining quantity as far as that is concerned—can be thought of as mutual comprehension or mixing of species or genus. But those things which differ entirely from each other admit no reciprocal distribution, mixture, or comprehension at all. When the distribution of divine powers occurs through different regions of the world, understand that different regions receive the gifts of the gods in different ways according to their own specific properties. Considering this, the art of sacred works <note>original: "ars sacrorum operum," referring to theurgy</note> uses specific invocations which seem appropriate to that kind of distribution and the property of the divine powers. Any part of the world receives something from any god, for every god is present in their entirety to every part of the world. But different parts receive from them in different ways: the Ether <note>the high, pure air of the heavens</note> receives in an ethereal manner, while the Air receives in an airy manner. For by certain materials and invocations, the gifts of the gods are naturally attracted.

### That everything divine is free from passions.

<margin>n</margin>The divine powers superior to us have nothing within them that can suffer <term>passible: the capacity to be affected, changed, or moved by external forces or emotions</term>, and they do not possess this "impassibility" (so to speak) as an acquired virtue, but by their very nature. Not even the soul, which is the lowest of the divine things, has anything within it that can suffer—I speak here of the soul that is pure and free from bodies—for it is not even touched by the disturbance of pleasure, which is merely a restoration to a natural state. Since its life is supernatural and unbegotten, it is without any dissolving pain, as it exists outside of every body and the nature divided around the body, and outside the harmony that descends into the body from the soul's primary harmony. Nor does it require the sensations that precede passions. For it is not contained by a body, nor is it forced to perceive bodies through external instruments. Indeed, since it is an indivisible and uniform essence <note>original: "essentia"</note>, remaining incorporeal according to itself and having no communication with the body, it naturally admits no passions of division, alteration, or any change whatsoever.

<margin>a</margin>The soul does not suffer even while it is present in the body, nor do the "seminal reasons" <term>seminal reasons: the underlying formative principles or "blueprints" that organize matter</term> which it grants to the body suffer anything. For these are simple and uniform forms <note>original: "species"</note>, which undergo no disturbance or departure from themselves...

...perceiving. Passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to being "passive" or "affected" by external forces, including emotions and physical sensations.</note>, of whatever kind they may be in a living creature, are not in the soul, of whatever kind that may be, but in the body; for the body, under the governance of the soul, possesses a certain quality through which it both suffers and acts. And the soul does not only acquire this impassibility <note>The state of being unable to suffer or be changed by outside forces.</note> through choice, but possesses it by its very nature, which is significantly superior to bodies. Daemons and heroes are impassible and everlasting. For they always follow the gods in preserving the order of the world; where there is passion, perpetual order is not maintained. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who often raised critical questions about traditional religion.</note> suspected that the daemons who rule the world were in some way passible because of the things offered to them in sacred rites. Iamblichus denies this because where there is perpetual order, there is no passion, which an incorporeal essence cannot receive through eternal things. Perhaps, however, he would concede that the lowest and evil daemons, those deprived of divine governance, are touched by effective passions—not indeed in their soul, but in a body constituted in such a way by the presence of a soul. Just as nature makes manifest things from hidden principles <note>original: "rationibus"</note>, so the Priest <note>Referring to the "theurgist" or practitioner of divine ritual.</note> employs manifest things to signify hidden ones. The Priest often performs many actions to create something similar and appropriate to divine things, so that through this kinship he might attract something from the divinity. Meanwhile, he also performs many things to purify the soul and turn away evils from us. Daemons, who are superior to us, receive no natural utility from us; for they either do not lack anything, or they themselves abundantly provide for themselves everywhere. Indeed, they never suffer any change from corporeal things. There are within us certain beginnings of disturbances, which, if they are restrained too violently and suddenly from the start, eventually burst forth more sharply, like a compressed flame or suppressed laughter; <margin>n</margin> therefore, they should be corrected more gently. Heraclitus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher known for his doctrines of change and the unity of opposites.</note> notes that sacrifices are medicines because they purge the soul from the diseases contracted in this generation <note>i.e., this earthly life or the process of being born into a body.</note>. Porphyry suspected that not only daemons but even the gods were touched by some passion, since they are "moved" during invocations. The will for the good in God and the gods is more excellent than goodness itself, and therefore freer than our own choice-based life regarding the good. And so, the gods are not moved to provide good to men because they are invoked. Rather, they spontaneously provoke us toward the good, and they meet us of their own accord when we have turned to them in invocation, showing and bestowing something. Men indeed think they are free to ask. So be it; therefore, the gods are even freer to give. Because of their free will for the good and their eternal and perfect action, the gods do good to all as soon as they have turned toward them through invocation. The soul, arriving at the contemplation of divine things during supplications, transforms its former life which was subject to passions...

->**On the wrath of the gods.**<-

<margin>q</margin> **When** we turn away from the beneficent care of the gods, as if from the light of the sun, we are immediately in darkness, and God is said to be angry with us. Therefore, to appease the wrath of the gods is to return to them by supplicating. Such appeasement brings no passion to God; rather, it frees the soul from its previous passions. Gods and divine daemons <note>In ancient philosophy, "daemons" were not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or guides between humans and gods.</note>, when humbly adored and worshiped, repel many evils that would otherwise happen naturally.

---

->**On the necessity and liberty of the gods.**<-

<margin>n</margin> **It is necessary** for the gods to be as they are, not by a necessity imposed from the outside, but by a natural necessity that is optimal for them, and therefore it is most voluntary; they would never wish to be otherwise if an option were proposed. Porphyry <note>A significant Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of traditional religious practices.</note> and many philosophers say that gods are indeed pure intellects, while daemons are intellects or some animated participations of intellect. But Iamblichus <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who defended ritual and theurgy; the primary author of this work.</note> objects that the property of daemons is not correctly established in this way; for souls are also animated intellects and certain participations of intellect itself. Nor, on the other hand, is the property of the gods correctly established; for the gods preside over pure intellects.

---

->**On the difference between gods and daemons among the Greeks, and those most devoted.**<-

Porphyry and others suspect<insert>n</insert> <note>original: "suspicantur". Nor do they depart from themselves, but staying within themselves, they are present, inclined toward the intention of those praying. Indeed, it is fitting to supplicate most humbly; recognizing our <unclear>nothingness</unclear> if we are compared to the higher beings causes us to supplicate most greatly and be <unclear>joined</unclear> to them entirely, and through constant habit, we may <unclear>become</unclear> <unclear>similar</unclear> <unclear>appropriately</unclear>

->IAMBLICHUS<-

<warning>Heavy ink staining and bleed-through in the lower half of the page.</warning>

But to me, those prayers sent from the heavens, in which a divine power resides, are indeed beneficial; this is in opposition to Porphyry, who thinks that we should specifically worship the worldly gods because they possess senses. Likewise, while Porphyry thinks supplications <note>original: *supplicationes*; humble prayers or petitions</note> are not at all fitting for the purity of divine minds, Iamblichus believes they are fitting because of the "inner sense" <note>An intuitive or spiritual perception that connects the human to the divine.</note> that resides in prayers, especially those that are divinely inspired. Pure intellects know sensible things <note>Objects perceived by the physical senses.</note> without the use of senses.

### Again on supplications.

Porphyry says that certain material things are used in prayers, and therefore they are used only for those gods who are "animates" <note>original: *animalia*; here meaning beings that possess a soul and sensory life, as opposed to pure intellects.</note>. Iamblichus responds that within these material things, beyond their physical qualities, there also lie hidden incorporeal and divine principles <note>original: *rationes*</note>, forms, and measures, through which the things used are made compatible with the gods. Indeed, whenever something is offered that is in any way consistent with and similar to the gods, the gods are immediately present; they are joined to it, they offer their gifts, and they hear the prayers. A small degree of harmony between our earthly things and the gods is sufficient for us to draw something from them. For they are always most ready for this because of their natural goodness and wondrous power. Indeed, a powerful cause acts upon matter even if it is only slightly prepared. Porphyry distinguishes Daemons from gods by the fact that the former are incorporeal, while the latter are corporeal; Iamblichus says, however, that their substances and properties cannot be distinguished by these traits alone.

### On the difference between gods and daemons, and on celestial beings.

The celestial gods can be called "incorporeal" because no hindrance from physical bodies affects their more excellent action and the happiness of their life. But insofar as the gods tend toward the "One" itself <note>The ultimate, indivisible source of all existence in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>, their bodies voluntarily strive toward the same; they do not "contain" souls, but are most excellently "contained" by them. The celestial body is the most closely related of all physical things to the incorporeal, because of its simple, undivided, and constant nature, and its single action—that is, its revolution <note>original: *circuitum*; the circular motion of the stars and planets.</note>—and its innate life and light. In the heavens, there is no composition of soul and body into a single "third nature" <note>Like the way a human is a mix of body and soul.</note>; rather, the body is drawn entirely toward the nature of the soul and is, as it were, a certain visible soul. Perhaps the heaven is light itself, without matter and without dimension. For dimension appears there only because of light's ample presence. From this, the first <unclear>is the soul</unclear> of heaven, accommodating itself to the eyes and to perishable things, and around <unclear>it is</unclear> the revolution of the soul. Light is the intellect of that same soul. Just as in the lowest body form becomes material, so in the highest, matter becomes "formal" and the body becomes soul-like <note>original: *animale*</note> rather than the soul becoming "body-like"—if indeed there is any matter in heaven at all. Just as the highest air becomes fiery, so the celestial fire becomes soul-like. That intellectual soul turns in—

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous folio regarding how divine and celestial influences interact with the material world. The text transitions from discussing the "inner sense" of prayer to how the celestial bodies (the planets and stars) broadcast their "virtues" or powers down to Earth. It addresses the problem of evil or harm—specifically why certain planets like Saturn or Mars are considered "malefic" in astrology—by explaining that the harm originates in the receiver's material weakness, not in the divine source.</meta>

<header>ON THE MYSTERIES</header>
<sig>d</sig>
<page-num>4</page-num>

...the intellect is made boniform <note>original: *boniformis*; literally "good-formed," meaning the intellect takes on the shape or nature of the Good itself</note>. Celestial living beings <note>original: *animalia*; referring to the stars and planets as animate entities with souls</note> can be called incorporeal. All celestial beings are good and beneficial, looking only toward the Good itself, and in this eternal intuition, they act. Inestimable powers <term>virtues; from the Latin *virtutes*, meaning inherent powers or medicinal/spiritual potencies</term> are discovered, both inherent in the celestial beings and in their bodies, and descending through emanations <note>original: *defluxus*; literally "outflows" or "down-flowings"</note> into all things without hindrance down to the lowest depths, shared both by individuals and by species. They are everywhere immutable, even though they rule over changeable matter, preserving the process of generation in a certain perpetual order and always acting beneficially. 

Accordingly, when the celestial flow enters into matter full of discords, a result occurs that is dissonant to us. Temporal things receive eternal things in a temporal way. Bodies receive incorporeal things in a bodily way. These material things receive the immaterial powers of the heavens in a changeable and disordered manner. Just as those things which exist in the divine world are not themselves shaped, even though they are received as "shapes" in the heavens, so too celestial things are not evil, even though they are received here as evil. All the powers of the celestial beings descend from that source as good; however, they are changed in this mixture of opposites. 

Therefore, the quality that causes harm on earth is something different from that which had traveled here from the heavens. First, that which is given is one thing in the giver and another outside of them—even if the giver remains unchanged—and furthermore, the gift is diminished. Second, while it is received in a lowlier subject, it becomes lowlier itself. Third, it is received in a different way because of the different nature of the receiver. Fourth, it is received according to the different qualities that are captured equally by the same subject. Fifth, as the subject undergoes change <note>original: *patiens*; referring to the philosophical concept of "suffering" or being acted upon by an external force</note>, the quality itself suffers. Sixth, from all the things contained within the subject, a different final result emerges. 

Celestial influences extend into material things. The power of Saturn is indeed "holding" <note>original: *contentiva*; the power to bind or contain</note>, while the power of Mars is "moving" <note>original: *motrix*</note>. The former often harms "by accident" when it is received by colder matter, and the latter when it is received by hotter matter. Likewise, the former hurts when it is received through a process of freezing <note>original: *congelatio*</note>, and the latter through scorching heat—which happens according to the disposition of the matter. That is, when the matter is not hot enough and is meanwhile too dense, or when the matter is inherently too hot and too fine. Although the light and color of the sun may seem to offend a weak eye, they are nonetheless necessary for life. Similarly, all celestial influences arrive as beneficial, whether the subject's own purity receives them as they are, or its weakness cannot easily tolerate the efficacy of the higher things. 

All movements contribute to the whole universe and to the necessary parts of the universe, even if meanwhile, among the smallest particles under this motion, one might be hurt by another, or such particles cannot easily sustain the motion of the whole. It is just as in a dance <note>original: *in chorea*; a choral dance</note>: while individuals dance harmoniously and agree in their gestures with one another and with the whole group, a finger or a foot may be strained or bumped. And if anything weak enters into the movement, it is cast down.

---

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of celestial beings and their governance of the material world. <header>IAMBLICHUS</header>

...of intelligence, and of a will quite effective and perpetual. And therefore they rule without labor, which is clearly apparent from the always constant order. To those thus disposed, the gods are joined as separate beings rather than to bodies. The governance concerning the heavens cannot distract the gods from the intention of intelligence, since they rule all the more powerfully and easily the more attentively they speculate there. For from this proceeds also that. The same would also happen to our living beings, if they contemplated their own cause, from which comes also the faculty of growth <note>original: *uegetandi facultas*; in the Aristotelian/Neoplatonic tradition, this refers to the "vegetative soul" responsible for basic life functions like growth and nutrition</note>.

### Confirmation of the Above

<margin>m</margin> The divine Mind <note>original: *Mens*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the *Nous* or the realm of pure Intellect</note> produces the souls of the celestial gods through its Ideas and, through those souls, produces the celestial bodies, and keeps both joined to itself forever. Mundane gods <note>original: *Dii mundani*; the gods who reside within the cosmos or "world"</note>, who are also called intellectual species, are united among themselves, both because they all look upon the same exemplar in which the intelligible species exist, and because that exemplar flourishes everywhere as a whole in any mundane god. Neither space nor diverse subjects prevent any incorporeal essence from being present everywhere within one another. Mundane gods are in one another and in their own ideas, both because they are from the One and are referred back to the One, and because the divine unity prevailing everywhere unites them, and because they proceed among themselves and are converted <note>original: *conuertuntur*; a technical term in Neoplatonism where a being "turns back" toward its divine source</note>, and receive from one another. In natural composites, unity is accidental <note>original: *aduētitiæ*; literally "adventitious," meaning it comes from the outside and is not part of the thing's core essence</note>, depending on higher things and overcome by multiplicity. In separable forms, unity surpasses multiplicity, and in the gods it surpasses it to such an extent that their being is a certain unity—I say "certain," because the first principle is simplicity/unity itself. Since, therefore, unity prevails so much within the gods from the inside, it deservedly overflows from the prior ones into those that follow. Thus, these [lower gods] consist in the unity of those [higher gods], by which unity, as if by a common thing for all, they are all one in a certain act, just as bodies among themselves are one by a certain material potentiality. Celestial gods are inwardly united to the invisible gods, both because celestial souls are outside of bodies, and because the superior gods (that is, the Ideas) have infinite unity, insofar as all are in each, through which unity they unite the following gods to themselves and among each other. For since all gods are defined by unity, one common unity is spread into all, through which they are one in the act of all things, from one toward one absolute object, and principle, and end, at the same point and moment.

->On providence, and on the gods and demons.<-

<margin>d</margin> Their providence is universal, while that of demons is particular. The first God gives all things to all; the following gods bestow some things to all. Demons and souls [give] only to some, and only some things. There are invisible gods, and there are visible gods in heaven; there are also demons. Indeed, the gods conspicuous in heaven exist in that very union with the hidden gods. But demons are far distant from them, as if from contemplators...

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...more readily occupied with pure things in their activity. Therefore, they are far removed even from the visible gods. Likewise, the essence of both types of gods—their power and providence—is universal, extending through all things. The nature of **demons**, however, is a particular providence concerning certain things and regions. Furthermore, the gods so greatly transcend their bodies, and their bodies are so obedient to them, that they are said to be "separated" from those bodies. **Demons**, by contrast, are more affected by and joined to bodies. Likewise, the gods are the **architects**, while the demons are the **ministers**. Demons are hidden from the senses; the gods are hidden even from human reason. Even if the gods should happen to appear upon the earth, they remain superior to the demons of the air. For a change of location or office does not change the divine nature. Finally, the gods are free from those powers that flow into <term>generation</term> <note>original: "generationem"; the process of physical birth and becoming in the material world</note>. Demons, however, are by no means free from them.

He <note>The author, writing as Abammon the Teacher</note> refutes the arguments that **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre, a 3rd-century philosopher who wrote a letter questioning the efficacy and morality of religious rituals</note> had brought forward from history: namely, that many things are done toward the gods as if they were **passible** <note>original: "passibiles"; meaning subject to passions, emotions, or being "acted upon" by external forces</note>. He argues this because the law of sacred rites commands one to be free from passions during sacrifices. This law was given divinely, even by the first father of the world, from whom all **symbols** in sacrifices—signifying something most hidden—also originate. Finally, those things that are performed according to rite in sacred ceremonies have a divine cause so remote from passion that even reason cannot reach it. 

The common crowd <note>original: "vulgus"</note> cannot grasp the reason for ceremonies that have been divinely instituted. Nevertheless, they try to assign a reason. By assigning reasons based on their own passions, they attribute passions to the gods. The crowd uses gestures of veneration toward powerful people and offers gifts to the gods in the same way. But they do this toward men because of their own passions and the passions of their superiors. They assume that similar passions exist in the gods as those found in powerful men, and that such things are offered to the gods because of similar passions in the subjects and worshipers. But in truth, ceremonies divinely instituted are not driven by any passion, but rather by admiration, veneration, and a steadfast intelligence and joy that is entirely like them.

### ***How Demons, Heroes, and Souls Differ***

<margin>8</margin>
In the gods, there are generative and creative powers; there are also **vivific** <note>original: "uiuificæ"; life-giving</note> powers, which are contained more sublimely in the higher beings. The former are spread more widely than the latter. The latter are defined by the former. **Demons** begin after a long progression of these powers, where they are already derived into many divisions. **Heroes** are defined by the second type—that is, the life-giving powers—before they reach the lowest level. For at their lowest level, **souls** begin. Therefore, the office of **demons** is the creative work regarding worldly natures, to carry out and perfect everything down to the individual parts, and to bind souls to bodies. The office of **heroes**, however, is to give life, to reason, and to guard souls, and to lead them to...

...to release from bodies. The duty of **demons** <note>original: "Dæmonum"</note> is broader than that of **heroes**. The former work more concerning the universe as a whole, while the latter work more concerning souls. We do not say that souls are created [by them], but that they receive something from demons and heroes, and additionally provide many things from themselves, beginning their own duty near the end of the divine works. This is not because divine things do not act further, but because souls are admitted at the furthest edges of divine duties. Likewise, the soul is able to bring forth such various forms of living from itself that, according to their suitability, it may inhabit the individual regions of the world. It is also able to meet with whomever it wishes, and again return into itself, and join itself as much to the gods as to inferior beings, insofar as it brings forth the divine principles <note>original: "rationes"</note> as an inferior being. And although it is often joined to the gods through demons and heroes, it can also join itself to the gods through its own intermediary means, by which it differs from them. Sometimes the soul reconciles itself to divine things through other harmonies of its essence and actions, different from those by which demons join themselves to the higher beings. And even if the soul does not maintain such a consistent course of life, yet often, illuminated by the benevolent will of the gods, it transcends the **demons** toward an **angelic life** rather than an animal one. Although the soul may seem to exhibit all principles and whole forms <note>original: "species"; here meaning the archetypal patterns of reality</note> within itself, it is nevertheless always determined according to some single thing—that is, one specific form. Meanwhile, based on preceding causes, it coordinates itself now to some things and now to others, moving itself.

### When the various divinities appear and act differently.

All the higher beings <note>original: "superi"</note>, when invoked, come into view, but some appear under different forms and powers than others. The souls of the stars also move the sight in certain new ways. The visions of the **gods** appear uniform and most simple; those of **archangels** are somewhat less uniform or simple. Those of **angels** are even less so. The visions of **demons** are varied; those of the **principalities** <note>original: "principatuum"</note> are more varied, yet in a wonderful order of variety. Those of **heroes** are somewhat similar to these, while those of the **archons** <note>original: "principes"; distinct from "principatus," these are often seen as lower or more material rulers</note> are quite varied and poorly ordered. The visions of particular souls, naturally, take on every kind of form. For since the higher beings are diverse in their natures and actions, and since they appear to each person in their own way, they deservedly encounter people in different manners. The **gods** come into view as entirely salutary; **archangels** are both terrifying and gentle at the same time. **Angels** are milder. **Demons** are to be feared. **Heroes** are to be revered, though less so. **Principalities** are stunning; **archons** are harmful and hostile. **Souls** are similar to heroes, though inferior. The images of the **gods** appear completely unchanging in size, form, shape, and action. Those of archangels and angels are progressively less unchanging, though close to the gods. The images of demons are indeed changeable in size and form; for they appear differently at different times, yet they are recognized as the same. Those of principalities are unchanging, while those of heroes...

...nearly just as the rulers of demons, the lives of **souls** <note>original: "animarum"</note> vary in many ways, being far more changeable than those of demons. **Gods** appear with a certain quietness and order. **Archangels** appear with the same, but they add a sense of efficacy to these qualities. **Angels**, naturally, add an ordered and moderated motion to that same quietness and order. **Demons** appear with a disturbance that oversteps order. **Principalities** <note>original: "principatus"; refers to a rank of celestial administrators</note> appear with stability and constancy within themselves. **Heroes** appear with motion and haste. **Rulers** <note>original: "principes"; likely refers to planetary or worldly governors</note> appear with tumult. **Souls** appear much like heroes, but with less stability and order.

To a **god**, there occurs an inestimable, incomparable, and admirable beauty, delighting beyond measure. The beauty of **archangels** and **angels** is similar, but gradually unequal. **Demons** and the spirits of **heroes**, when appearing by themselves, have beauty in determined forms; but the former possess it according to the principles of their essence, while the latter according to an act of fortitude. The beauty of **principalities** is primary and innate, while that of **rulers** is artificial, adorned, and labored. The beauty of **souls** consists of certain determined principles <note>original: "rationibus"</note>, but these are more divided than in the form of heroes, though still contained under one appearance.

The actions and effects of the **gods** are swifter than the intellect can grasp; yet, meanwhile, they remain utterly stable. The speed of **archangels** is in some way mixed with effective actions. The speed of **angels** is accompanied by motion, and they do not have the power to complete a task at the very moment it is commanded. The actions of **demons** appear swifter than they actually are in effect and truth. **Heroes** proceed magnificently toward an action, yet they perform more slowly than demons. **Principalities** come to action with authority and command. The effort of **rulers** indeed has much outward show <note>original: "emphasim"; refers here to an impressive appearance that lacks substance</note>, but it falls short in its effect. The actions of **souls** are more mobile than those of heroes, but weaker.

The magnitude of the **gods** when they appear seems to occupy the whole sky, and when they advance, it is thought that even the earth cannot support them. When **archangels** appear, certain parts of the world are moved, and a divided light precedes them; they themselves, according to the magnitude of their dominion, display a magnitude of light and form. The **angelic** form and light are both smaller and more divided. The magnitude and form of **demons** are more divided and smaller still. The **heroic** appearance is again narrower, though of a magnanimous aspect. **Principalities** appear very grand and vast, while **rulers** appear inflated, proud, and insolent. The images of **souls** are unequal and smaller than those of heroes. Finally, each one, according to the greatness of their power and the breadth of their command, displays a magnitude of form and light.

The sights of the **gods** meet us as exceptionally bright, shining to the highest degree, wonderfully distinct in their splendor, and clearer than they are in reality. Those of **archangels** are true and perfect. The images of **angels** maintain the same appearance, except...

...and they fall short of the fullness of knowledge in the distinction of their recognition. The diminished and, as it were, fleeting natures of **demons** <note>original: "Dæmonum exilia & quasi caduca"</note>. The slighter natures of **heroes**. Heroic fire has things similar to these, but not equal. The fire of **principalities** is excellently bright, while that of **princes** has something opaque. The fire of **souls** is greatly divided, multiform, and mixed from many natures of the world.

The fire of the **Gods** is entirely stable to the sight. That of **archangels** partakes in that stability. That of **angels** is moved in a stable manner. That of **demons** is unstable. That of **heroes** is more rapid. That of **principalities** arrives quietly. That of **princes**, however, is tumultuous. The fire of **souls** is changed by many motions. The **Gods** purge souls most perfectly. **Archangels** recall them upward. **Angels** only loose them from the chains of matter. **Demons** draw them toward nature. **Heroes** lead them to the care of sensible resources <note>original: "sensibiliũ opum"</note>. **Principalities** exhibit the leadership of worldly affairs. **Princes**, indeed, display a devotion to material things. **Souls**, when they appear, struggle and draw one into generation <note>meaning the cycle of physical birth and material existence</note>. Whatever is pure and firm in the image occurring to us, attribute it to the higher ranks. That pre-shining quality which remains firmly within itself, attribute to the **Gods**. That which shines and remains, yet as if in another, attribute to **archangels**. That which remains in another, to **angels**. Again, that which is mobile, wandering, and full of foreign natures, attribute everywhere to the inferior orders. **Demons** have mixed within themselves the vapors of the world, and they are carried unstably alongside or near the motion of the world. With **heroes**, generative compositions of spirits are mixed, around which they too are moved. **Principalities** remain in the same way, showing the worldly nature they possess. **Princes** are full of material fluids. **Souls** are filled with superfluous stains and foreign spirits; with these, as often as they appear, each of these ranks reveals itself. **Gods** consume matter suddenly. **Archangels** do so little by little. **Angels** loose from it and recall to the sublime. **Demons** diligently adorn it. **Heroes** adapt themselves to it in appropriate ways...

...everywhere vigorously and fittingly caring for [the soul's] measures. **Principalities** <term>Principalities: Celestial governors who oversee broad regions of the cosmos and the laws of nature</term> stand over it, pre-eminent, and in this way they reveal themselves. **Princes** <note>original: "principes"</note> show themselves to be thoroughly filled with matter. **Pure souls** <note>original: "Aiæ puræ"</note> indeed come separately from matter. But **impure souls** show themselves to us as enwrapped in matter. Furthermore, different beings exhibit different gifts to us. The **Gods**, when present, give health to the body, virtue to the soul, and purity to the mind. They recall all our faculties to their own proper principles. Whatever in us is cold and death-bearing they destroy; they foster heat, making it more effective for life. They also cause all things of the soul and mind to agree and be measured by these same divine standards; they pour out a light of intelligible harmony. 

What is not a body, they show as if it were a body to the eyes of the soul itself, through the physical eyes. **Archangels** perform the same actions. But they are not as sufficient or permanent, nor do they act so far beyond our human proportion. **Angels** distribute goods that are more particular and divided; they perform an effect that is significantly deficient in vigor compared to that innermost divine source. 

**Demons**, by their presence, weigh down the body, afflict it with diseases, or punish it in other ways. They also drag souls toward nature; they do not depart from bodies and the senses associated with them. Even those who strive toward celestial or divine fire, these demons detain around the lower regions, nor do they release them from the bonds of **fate** <term>Fate: In this context, the deterministic laws of the physical world that bind the unpurified soul</term>. **Heroes** do other things similar to demons, but they have this unique quality: they rouse us to certain noble and great works. 

**Principalities**, when appearing, bestow worldly goods and supply all the necessities of this life. **Princes** provide material and earthly goods. When **souls** appear, if they are pure souls established in the angelic order, they recall us upward; they provide health to the spirit and a sacred hope, along with the sacred gifts for which one hopes. **Impure souls** twist us down toward generation <note>The cycle of physical birth and death</note>; they frustrate hope by taking away its fruits, and they fill the onlookers with passions that bind the soul to the body.

The order which each being holds is also designated in their appearance. The **Gods** show gods or angels standing around them. **Archangels** display angels either running before them, standing around them, or following them, or some other crowd of angels surrounding them like a bodyguard. **Angels** display works suitable to their specific order. **Good demons** bring into view their handiwork and the goods which they bestow. **Avenging demons** <note>original: "dæmones ultores"</note> show the various forms of punishments. Other demons, however depraved they may be, appear surrounded by deadly and voracious wild beasts. 

**Principalities** demonstrate certain provinces of the world along with themselves. **Princes** bring into view the condition of matter—wandering and lacking order. A **soul** that is whole, not held in any particular form, shows a fire without a certain shape around the entire world, by which the nature of the **World Soul** <note>The soul of the universe, which connects the divine and material realms</note> is signified as undivided, one, and bound to no specific form. A **purified soul** shows a fiery figure—a pure fire and a gleaming light that is simultaneously stable. Such a soul follows along with a sublime leader, rejoicing with good will; and thus in its works...

But the whole air does not become more refined, nor does it become so unsuitable for the priests that they cannot endure it. Under the **principalities**, a revolution of many forms runs around them, which is difficult to endure, and a worldly volume <note>original: "volumen... mundanum," perhaps referring to a cosmic scroll or a swirling mass</note> of this kind surrounds them. Around the **princes**, however, it is terrestrial, yet there is neither a light of world-transcending subtlety nor of the highest elements. When **souls** appear, the visible air is more akin to them, and being adapted to them, it receives their description.

The dispositions of the souls of those invoking the beings report an exceeding perfection, action, divine love, and incredible joy when the **Gods** meet them. With **archangels**, they receive an intellectual contemplation that is exceedingly pure and an immutable power. With **angels**, they receive a rational cognition and virtue set in the highest order. With **demons**, they receive an appetite for generation; and with **heroes**, they receive similar things and, moreover, an interest in civic governance. <meta>This page continues Iamblichus's explanation of the different spiritual ranks. Having previously described the physical appearance of these entities, he now transitions into the specific types of gifts or "goods" they provide to humans and addresses a philosophical disagreement with Porphyry regarding whether spirits "boast" or tell the truth about themselves.</meta>

<header>->ON THE MYSTERIES<-</header>

...[souls] of a mundane or material nature act with the spirit of nature and the fulfillment of fated works. To **souls** <note>original: "animis"</note> belong the appetite for generation and the zeal for caring for bodies. The appearance of the **Gods** strengthens truth, power, and actions to the highest degree and provides the most ample goods. The gifts of **archangels** are similar, but more particular, offering knowledge and power not in a general sense, but for a specific purpose, place, time, and manner. Those of **angels** are even more specific and determined. **Demons** do not provide goods for the soul, but for the body and corporeal matters, as far as the worldly order allows. The gifts of **heroes** <note>original: "heroū"</note> relate to the worldly or earthly republic <note>original: "r. p." refers to the "res publica," the public affairs or social order of the world.</note>. The **principalities** <term>Principalities: High-ranking celestial beings (Archons) who govern the physical elements and the administration of the world.</term> provide worldly benefits and all the comforts of life provided by princes; the lower orders provide a greater abundance of material things. **Souls** appear in a truly familiar encounter to provide those things which contribute to human life.

Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyre was a philosopher who wrote a "Letter to Anebo" questioning the validity of Egyptian and Chaldean religious rituals. This entire book is Iamblichus’s response to him.</note> related an opinion which claims it is common to all—gods, angels, demons, and all superior beings—that when they appear, they show themselves off, boast wonderfully, and project an imaginary likeness of themselves. Iamblichus refutes both parts of this. A **God**, an **angel**, or a **good demon** teaches a person when they appear what their essence truly and really is, speaking nothing more nor less than the truth. For just as light naturally and constantly follows the sun, so truth follows God and his attendants <note>original: "pedissequos"</note>—especially since they are perfect and full, and neither need nor are able to claim for themselves more than what they are.

When errors are made in **theurgy** <term>Theurgy: Ritual practices ("god-working") intended to invoke divine presence or achieve union with the divine.</term> (that is, the divine-making and priestly faculty), then it is not the good spirits we desire who meet us, but rather inferior and evil ones under the pretext of being good. For evil spirits often transform themselves into the likeness of good ones; they come boastfully and claim for themselves more than what they are. Indeed, wherever a corrupt beginning arises, a great deal of falsehood proceeds from that perversity. Priests <note>original: "sacerdotes"</note> must examine the appearances of spirits by the rule of the whole order and remember that boastful arrogance is in no way a property of true and good spirits. They must take care that they never stray from the sacred rite. And if, in an error of appearance, some insolent beings suddenly arrive, it is not right to judge the whole common nature and condition of the divine beings based on them. For it is a sacrilege <note>original: "nephas"</note> to change things that have been proven in sacred rites through many ages and laborious effort by judging them rashly based on a few sudden occurrences.

Even if false spirits lie, the good spirits are truth-telling and legitimate when in the presence of the **fire** <note>In theurgy, the "fire" often refers to the intellectual or divine fire that purifies the soul and reveals the true nature of spiritual entities.</note>. For in every genus, the primary beings begin from themselves; they provide for themselves what they exhibit to others, and this exists in their essence, life, and motion. Likewise, the superior beings, exhibiting truth to all, first speak truly of themselves and reveal their very essence especially to those who contemplate them. Therefore, they demonstrate the fire—which is to be seen in its own proper form—to the priests in the proper rite. For it is not the nature of heat to make things cold, or of light to darken and hide, nor for anything that acts through its very essence to ever do the opposite of that essence.
