<sig>r</sig>
<meta>catchword: intelligentiam</meta>

[of] its nature: but only in the manner of a mirror-image <note>original: "idoli specularis"</note> does it vainly draw the mind of the viewer; and it deceives while it pretends to be something, of whose nature it possesses nothing. It is therefore a cause of falsehood, which in no way belongs to any true essence. Therefore, neither the gods nor their followers <note>Referring to the ranks of angels, demons, and heroes who follow the gods.</note>—who are not meager and empty, but reveal natural and true images of themselves—[send such things]. They do not send mirror-like images (as I said) which are vain, for why would they be sent? Certainly not to demonstrate their essence and power, for those images fall short of the total nature of that essence. Nor are they sent for the utility of those who see them. For what utility can come from a lie combined with deception? Finally, they do not send them because it is in their nature to project such a phantom from themselves. Since their essence is firm, consisting in itself, and is thus the cause of other essences and of truth, it in no way sends into another any fallacious and deceptive imitation of itself—something that claims to be something while having nothing of its true nature. 

Therefore, neither the gods nor their followers transform their nature into any false images, nor do they produce these from themselves into another; rather, they illuminate and demonstrate true forms of themselves in the true characters <note>original: "moribus," referring to the disposition or moral state of the soul.</note> of the soul. 

<note>Note this similar point: that in the blessed homeland <note>The celestial realm or the state of the soul after death.</note> the blessed mind sees the divine essence not through an image created by it which is entirely deficient, but through that same essence: just as one who sees light through light, in the light. It is not like one who perceives heat through light, or who sees a body in a mirror. Separate substances <note>Purely spiritual beings without physical bodies.</note> have no genus in common. Likewise, gods, angels, and good demons do not appear in a phantastic <term>Phantastic: Relating to the "phantasia" or the imagination; here used to mean an illusory or deceptive image.</term> manner, but in their own proper and true way. Evil spirits, however, appear in a phantastic and deceptive manner; nor is it proper to judge the way good spirits form the soul by their presence based on the conditions under which these evil ones appear to us.</note>

Porphyry says that the knowledge of divine things is indeed a sacred matter, while ignorance is profane. Iamblichus approves of this, because since the gods act upon beings through intelligence, we deservedly please and are approved by the gods through our intelligence of those beings. However, he places religious operation <note>Theurgy: the practice of rituals intended to invoke the presence of the gods.</note> before intelligence, as it alone is effective for acquiring the **deific union** of the soul with God. So great is the virtue of sacred rites rightly performed for God, that even if you are ignorant of these rites, yet you observe them piously, they have no less efficacy. For it is not intelligence that joins the practitioners of sacrifice to God; otherwise, philosophers would be the ones to achieve deific union.

### Concerning the virtue of the sacraments.

<margin>o</margin> The decent observance of the precepts and divine works, which exceed all intelligence, and the wonderful power of symbols and sacraments known to the gods alone, provides for us the **deific union**. When we labor in sacred rites, we do not perform [them] by...

# ->ON THE MYSTERIES<-

<note>In the original manuscript, horizontal ink lines have been drawn through the first six lines of the following paragraph, suggesting a deletion or a disputed passage.</note>

[un]derstanding; otherwise the sacrament <note>original: "sacramento"</note> and its intellectual action would be something belonging to us and provided by us. On the contrary, even when we do not understand, these rituals perform their own work by themselves; the power of the gods to which these rites refer recognizes its own ineffable images through itself, rather than being awakened by our own intellects. For universal causes are not moved by particular effects; thus, divine things are not primarily moved to act by our thoughts. However, it is necessary for understanding, a good disposition, and purity of heart to precede the ritual as certain necessary occasions. 

But what principally stirs the divine will are the divine sacraments themselves. Thus, divine things are awakened by themselves and do not receive the beginning of their action from any external source. Do not think, therefore, that the entire authority of a ritual’s efficacy lies within us, nor that their true work is completed by the truth of our understanding, or that these things should be measured by our own errors. For it is not necessary that if we know the properties of a certain class of things, we will immediately achieve the truth of their operation.

Without knowledge, an effective unity with the divine never arrives; yet knowledge and unity are not entirely the same thing. For this reason, divine purity is not achieved through correct knowledge (just as bodily health is not achieved through medical theory), but rather this unity is a purity that is both united and purified above knowledge—that is, through a power superior to knowledge. Therefore, no other human quality contributes anything to the final goal of divine actions. Conclude this opinion of Iamblichus—writing as the Egyptian priest—against the Assyrian <note>Referring to the philosopher Porphyry, who prioritized intellectual study over ritual practice.</note>: just as in agriculture, medicine, the making of images, or human procreation, a person appropriately prepares the matter; but when a superior and universal power applies the "form"—as happens in sacrifice when symbols and *synthemata* <note>original: "synthemata," meaning divine tokens or "signatures" placed in the natural world by the gods.</note> (that is, sacred signs) and sacraments are used—the priest provides certain material things arranged in a beautiful order, but God impresses the effective power upon the sacraments.

## What Prophecy Is and From Where It Comes:

<margin>u</margin>Prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium"</note> itself is brought about neither by human art, nor by nature, nor by natural logic or the movements of animals. It is not produced in any way other than being eternally sent down to us from the divine. This entire prophetic faculty is referred back to the gods, and all its authority consists in them; thus it is handed down and signaled through divine works. It possesses divine visions and contemplations endowed with true knowledge. All other things are subjected as instruments to this gift of prophecy sent from the divine—whether they pertain to the soul, the body, or the nature of the universe. Indeed, physical locations and such things are required for prophecy only as the "matter" or setting; it is not fitting to believe prophecy arises without a cause—that is, from things that have no foreknowledge in themselves. Instead, one should contemplate prophecy as something derived from the gods, who hold within themselves the limits of all knowledge. This prophecy is distributed throughout the whole world and throughout all the distinct natures in the world; thus, the cause of prophecy is primary and most universal, possessing in itself whatever it exhibits to those who participate in it.

# IAMBLICHUS

...principally offering truth, which is necessary for prophecy <note>original: "vaticinio"; the art of foretelling the future through divine inspiration</note> and, above all, essence, containing within itself the cause of all things that come to be. From this cause, the perpetual consequence of foretelling necessarily proceeds. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who often questioned the mechanisms of the divine</note> says that when we sleep, we sometimes foresee the future through a present thing, without any awareness of our current state, even if we are not at all moved into ecstasy <note>A state of being "outside oneself" or in a trance</note>. I think he means to suggest that this happens not so much by an external divine influence flowing in, but from the very nature of the soul and mind. Iamblichus, however, argues that dreams which arise from human causes—whether through our physical nature, or through our emotions, thoughts, and daily actions—reach the truth only very rarely and obscurely, and more often than not, they hit upon the truth only by mere chance.

->On Dreams.<-

Dreams are sometimes stirred within us by innate understandings and reasons, or by the imaginations and cares of the day. While these occasionally touch upon the truth, they are mostly deceptive. Such dreams originate from human principles and happen to those who are fully sleeping and possess no spark of wakefulness. But dreams sent by the divine do not happen in this way; instead, they come either between waking and sleep, or between sleep and waking, or even during wakefulness itself. In these moments, short voices are heard, advising on what should be done; and sometimes a certain spirit—neither corporeal <note>having a physical body</note> nor touchable—surrounds those lying down. This spirit is not seen with the eyes, but is perceived by another kind of sense and awareness that is felt in a shared agreement <note>original: "consensu"; a harmonious perception</note> as it enters with a certain force. It surrounds the person on all sides without physical contact, and wonderfully drives away the passions of the soul and body. At other times, a pure and quiet light shines, by which the eyes are closed while the soul remains open. But the other senses remain awake and perceive how the gods reveal themselves in that light; they hear what the gods say and see what they do with continuous awareness. This whole experience is discerned more perfectly when the physical sight also sees, and the strengthened intellect follows what is happening, and those who watch are moved in a similar way. Such great differences as we have described are not of human origin. They occur when our "sleep" is actually a heaviness of the head, or a closing of the eyes, or a state between wakefulness and sleep, or a sudden awakening, or even wakefulness itself. All these states are divine and suitable for receiving the gods; they are sent from the divine. Indeed, such experiences serve as the precursors or parts of a divine apparition. Dreams proceeding from human and visible causes suffer from two defects: they happen to those who are completely asleep, and we do not then distinctly or fully notice either what occurs or our own state in that moment. But when dreams are divinely mixed, we are not truly asleep; we grasp and notice things more clearly than we are accustomed to when awake. Therefore, prophecy is most especially found in dreams of this kind. The soul has a double life: one lived together with the body, and the other separable from every body. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the soul's ability to transcend its physical bonds during sleep, moving from the general nature of divine dreams to specific historical examples of divine intervention and prophecy.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES,

Our life is mostly shared with the body, except for those times when we are completely separated from it—either because we are understanding things through the intellect or thinking with pure reason. However, in sleep, we can be entirely released, as if from chains that had been placed upon the soul, and we then make use of a life that is separated from the realm of becoming <note>original: "generatione"; the world of physical birth and decay</note>. When the soul is loosened from the body in sleep, that aspect of life which remains within itself—which is separable, separated, and either intellectual or even divine—immediately awakens within us and acts according to its own nature. Since the intellect contemplates true being and the soul contains within itself the <term>seminal reasons</term> <note>original: "rationes seminales"; the formative, seed-like patterns or blueprints of all things in the universe</note> of all things that are created, it rightly foreknows the future, organized within those preceding reasons which encompass the cause of what is to come.

We have spoken of the foretelling of the soul as it returns to itself in a state similar to sleep. I say "in itself," meaning it returns to its seminal and intellectual reasons, though up to this point, it still does so under a form belonging to its present life—that is, the form of this particular life and action. But if it soon unfolds the universal form of its reasons and thoughts, as it once lived, it will then bring back foretelling that pertains more to the universal condition of worldly affairs, within which it can also see various particular things. Furthermore, if through such a universal form it is joined to the very minds of the gods, it will see not only what belongs to the higher world, but also what belongs to this one; through those divine minds, it will understand things more absolutely, as if through their primary causes. In this state, not only will thought be perfected, but the imagination will also hold pure images of both physical and divine things.

Because the patterns of all created things exist within the soul’s power—both their effects and the knowledge of them—and because these patterns depend on the reasons that exist within the gods, the soul, when joined to the gods, activates these patterns into a state of action. This results in a most expansive kind of knowledge, functioning under the mode of divine providence. Through this, the soul considers the past and the future and all temporal things, their actions and experiences, and the remedies and cures for the diseases and vices of the soul. It also perceives the decrees of laws and the arts necessary for the human race. Thus, in the temple of <term>Aesculapius</term> <note>The Greco-Roman god of medicine and healing</note>, dreams are received through which diseases are cured, and the very art of medicine was established through divine dreams. The army of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note>, when it was about to perish from disease, escaped the danger through remedies shown in a dream by the god Dionysus. King Lysander was besieging the city of Aphytis and was ordered in a dream by Ammon <note>An Egyptian deity often identified with Zeus or Jupiter</note> to lift the siege. Many similar things happen daily that are beyond human speech and reason.

# IAMBLICHUS

...so that they even use their senses. Yet, in the meantime, they are not in possession of human reason. Iamblichus says that souls who are truly foretelling and inspired <note>original: "afflatos"; literally "breathed upon" by the divine</note>, even when they seem to be sleeping, are not sleeping; and when they seem to be awake, they are not properly awake, nor do they use their senses in the manner of humans. Souls divinely inspired and stirred have their own life completely submersed in the god who inspires them. Therefore, whether they submit themselves as a vehicle or as an instrument, they have set aside their former mode of life and have either exchanged their own life for a divine life, or they conduct their life entirely toward God. Thus, they neither use their senses, nor are they awake in the way those with alert senses are, nor do they foretell or move by any human impulse or habit, nor do they notice their own state, nor do they produce any knowledge or action of their own; rather, everything is performed there under a divine form and action.

<margin>Many miracles are performed by the prophets.</margin>
<margin>¶</margin>
That those who are divinely inspired do not live [a normal life] at that time is evident from the biological <note>original: "animalis"; referring to the life shared with animals, based on breath and sensation rather than intellect</note> life itself. For many, when fire is brought near them, are not burned—the god within them repelling the fire as he inspires them—or if they are burned, they do not feel it. Neither do they perceive stabbings, or scrapings, or any other torments. Likewise, it is clear that their actions are not human, since they walk through pathless places, and are carried through fire untouched, and cross rivers in a miraculous way, just as the priestess herself does in Castabala <note>An ancient city in Cilicia; its priestesses of Artemis Perasia were famous for walking barefoot over hot coals without injury</note>. Through these things, it is clear that they live neither a human life nor a biological one burning with senses and impulse, but a divine one, as if their soul were at rest and God were there in place of the soul, moving them like a more excellent soul.

There are various types of those divinely inspired, partly due to the variety of the gods (who inspire in different ways), and partly due to the difference in the modes of inspiration. These modes are as follows: either the god himself occupies us, or we devote ourselves to him and become entirely his, or we perform a common action with the god. Likewise, we may come to possess either the lowest divine powers, the middle, or the highest. Sometimes it is the bare presence of the god; sometimes, beyond presence, a communion <note>original: "communio"; a sharing or fellowship</note> occurs; occasionally, beyond this, a union is achieved. Again, regarding the inspiration, either the soul alone is possessed, or the body also becomes a participant in some way, or the shared biological being <term>animal commune</term> <note>the composite of body and soul acting together</note> is equally possessed. According to these different levels of divinity, there are signs, effects, and works of the inspired. According to the aforementioned diversity of the inspirers and the inspiration, some of the inspired are moved in their whole body or in certain limbs, while others, conversely, remain at rest. Likewise, they perform dances and harmonious songs, or the opposite. Again, their body seems either to grow tall or wide, or to be carried through the air, or the opposite. Also, they produce voices that are either even and continuous, or uneven and interrupted by silence. And then—

...they relax entirely, then they exert themselves. The inspired person is free from his own action and possesses God in place of a soul. The greatest sign of divine inspiration <term>afflatio; literally "a breathing upon"</term> is that the one who <margin>power</margin> brings down and introduces the deity <term>numen; the divine presence or will</term> perceives the spirit descending, sees how great and what kind it is, and is mystically taught and guided by it. Indeed, even the one who receives the deity sees a certain appearance of fire before the reception. Sometimes this is even seen by those present, either as the god arrives or departs. From this sign, those skilled in these matters most truly discern the power of the deity, its order, the truths it speaks, and what it may accomplish. But those who introduce spirits secretly without such visions—as if hiding in darkness—are blind. Nor do they understand what they are doing, except for some small signs in the body of the inspired person himself.

   Therefore, since the excellence of the divine fire and a certain appearance of light shines from without upon the one possessed, it fills him entirely and dominates him from within. It embraces him on all sides so that he cannot perform any action of his own. What sense, perception, or personal awareness can there be in a mind receiving the divine fire? What human motion, passion, distortion, imagination, or "alienation" of the mind <note>original: "alienatio"; the state of being "beside oneself"</note> can exist, as some suspect?

   **Porphyry** <note>A Phoenician Neoplatonist philosopher and critic of theurgy</note> defines divine inspiration as follows: "a motion of the mind along with demonic <note>original: "dæmonica"; in this context, referring to intermediate spirits rather than evil entities</note> inspiration."

   **Iamblichus** <note>The author, a Syrian Neoplatonist defending the divine nature of these rites</note> says that in a soul divinely inspired, neither the human mind nor human thought is carried along, if it is truly contained by the divine. Nor is it the inspiration of demons, but of the gods. Nor, again, should it be defined as a "departure" or "alienation." For these terms signify a fall for the worse; rather, it should be called a "reduction" and "restoration" for the better.

   Inspiration is therefore nothing other than the soul being entirely occupied and contained by the god. From this, "ecstasy" <term>extasis; literally "standing outside oneself"</term> follows later—that is, a kind of departure or alienation—as an accidental consequence of the inspiration.

   **Plato**, in the *Phaedrus*, says that the ancients called prophecy "mania" <note>original: "manian"; meaning madness or divine frenzy</note>. This is because only those seized by divine fury truly prophesy. Later people, however, by adding the letter 'r', called it "mantia" <note>original: "mantiam"; the Greek word for divination</note>. Likewise, priests, sibyls, and prophets, as long as they are "prudent" <note>meaning they rely on their own human reason and caution</note>, predict very little, or obscurely, or nothing at all. But when they are seized by God, they truly prophesy. Hence, among many nations, they have foreseen dangers looming from heaven, warned the people, and appeased divine **Nemesis** <note>The goddess of divine retribution and balance</note> through sacrifices. He also says that prophecy made by art <note>learned skills like reading bird flight or tea leaves</note> is called "conjectural estimation," and it is of no importance if compared with divine inspiration and prophecy.

->r<-

...but that it is entirely the act of God himself, depending simply upon God. I speak of an act <term>actus; an actualization or operation</term> performed by God in the mind or soul simply, as if in instruments devoid of any motion of their own. Thus true foreknowledge is granted; however, if motions from the body or soul, or any such quality, are meanwhile inserted or come before, the visions are seen to be confounded. Nor will there be true prophecies, nor is divine inspiration <term>afflatio; a "breathing upon"</term> legitimate there where anything human is mixed in. 

There were generally three opinions concerning divine inspiration and prophecy. The first referred its cause to the soul. The second to the body. The third to the composite <note>The "composite" refers to the union of soul and body together as a single entity</note>. The first places it in that state where the whole soul is drawn back into its own divine part, or into the mind; or when its action has become more vehement or fuller; or when thought has become sharp and most swift in motion; or when the mind has grown hot. The second places its cause in the body, when it possesses a certain complexion <note>In ancient medicine, a "complexion" is the specific balance of humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual</note>—specifically either a melancholic <note>A temperament associated with black bile, which ancient philosophers like Aristotle often linked to both madness and exceptional genius</note> or a tempered one—or a certain elemental quality, or even a special quality, or a certain spirit. The third says its cause is a certain proportion by which the body and soul are joined together. 

Iamblichus says that it is not the work of the soul or the body or the composite, nor does it have its cause in them. For that prophetic inspiration acts, both in foretelling and in effecting, beyond all custom of human nature. Moreover, man, or anything belonging to man, cannot progress beyond his own limits toward divine limits. Nor can superior things be generated by inferior ones. Therefore, the cause of this is solely divinity itself: namely, when lights descend from the gods into us and spirits are handed down by them. Then an absolute mastery and power from that source is present to us, encompassing all things that are in us and entirely driving out our own perception and motion. It brings forth speeches through the human indeed, but not with the human's own thought; rather, it pronounces them through the mouth of one raving <note>original: "furentis"; describing the "divine frenzy" or mania, a state of being "outside oneself"</note> and placed outside of himself. This occurs while everything in us serves the deity <term>numen; divine presence or will</term> entirely and yields to the sole dominant divine action. 

Porphyry says that music brings passions to the soul and likewise calms them, and that different sounds suit different souls and characters. Likewise, it changes the complexions and affections of the body; it moves madness and restrains madness. Iamblichus concedes these things. But he denies that these are the causes of divine inspiration, since they are human—partly natural, partly artificial—and have nothing divine in themselves. Porphyry seems to suspect this when he says that some are inspired when they hear flutes <note>original: "tybias"; these were double-piped reed instruments common in ecstatic religious rites</note>, or cymbals, or drums, while others are moved by other melodies. These correspond to various orders of the gods...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the causes of divine inspiration. # ON THE MYSTERIES

In the world, there are various types of motions, specific ones belonging to specific things. From these, in turn, various melodies flow forth. These melodies correspond, through their respective movements, to certain gods in a defined order—the gods who are themselves the original principles of motion. Since these gods are present everywhere and impart their gifts most especially to those things that belong to them, they are particularly present in the melodies that most closely correspond to them. Insinuating themselves into our spirits—which are moved by these melodies—they take possession of the person, quickly filling them entirely with their own essence and power. The cause of this inspiration <term>afflatio; literally a "breathing-upon" or divine influence</term> is not so much a "passion" <note>In this context, a "passion" refers to a state of being acted upon or an emotional reaction</note> excited in the human being through music, but rather the intrinsic correspondence of the music itself to the god, to which the god is naturally present. 

Things that come to our sight are too imagery-based and refer more to the realm of the intellect. Things that come to the senses lower than hearing are too material. However, things that come to the sense of hearing are intermediate and suitable for the soul; once they have worked their way into the spirit through movement, emotion, and meaning, they powerfully affect the soul on one hand and the body on the other. Hence the whole person, according to the properties of the melodies, becomes a vessel <term>susceptaculum; a container or receptacle</term> for this or that deity. Those who are inspired behave differently in their movement, their stillness, and their other states, primarily according to the diversity of the deities by whom they are inspired, rather than because of the differences in the music. 

For the effect of the sound has already ceased here once the god acts. The soul, in the intelligible world <note>original: "mundo intelligibili"—the realm of pure thought and forms in Platonic philosophy</note>, once heard divine harmony; it remembers this harmony here when it hears melodies that bear a trace of the divine. Upon remembering, the soul is then powerfully moved by it, if the soul is among those that especially contemplated the Idea of Harmony itself in their true homeland <note>The "homeland" refers to the divine realm from which the soul originated before birth</note>. Having been made familiar with God by such an affection, the soul is then inspired by a certain singular presence of the divine. From this, it performs wonders. Therefore, the cause of this inspiration and wonder is not a "passion" brought on by sounds, nor the nature of the soul being composed of harmony, but rather a likeness to God and the presence of God.

One must also say much less that inspiration consists in this: that certain superfluities hardened within the soul and body are purged through music and the inspiration itself. The power of prophecy <term>vaticinium; the gift of foretelling</term> does not come from a certain physical temperament. For the gifts of God are not breathed out in various ways according to physical variety. Indeed, the divine gift is impassible <note>original: "impatibile"—meaning it cannot be affected, changed, or harmed by external, material forces</note> and is given through God's own action, above the power of nature. Neither water, nor air, nor any other physical thing provides prophecy; rather, it is the sacred rites performed around these things—or even more, the purification of the mind along with the purification of its vehicle <note>The "vehicle" (vehiculum) refers to the "astral body" or subtle spirit that serves as the intermediary between the immaterial soul and the physical body</note> and an intent focus upon God—that receives the divine power, which is everywhere and always most ready. When an inspired mind speaks and acts above and against the custom of nature, the cause of such inspiration is not natural—neither from our body, nor the quality of a place, nor from the celestial disposition at a person's birth or during their work—but these things happen because of the presence of God. Hence, the various types of inspired people do not follow the natural variations within us...

# IAMBLICHUS

But there are different species, both of the inspiring spirits and of the modes by which we participate in divine presences. Therefore, when people are divinely inspired—some remaining quiet, others being driven to excitement, some seeking out mountains and deserts, and others behaving in various ways—this does not proceed from the differences of natural causes within us, nor from locations, nor from the music they may have recently heard or are currently hearing. Instead, it arises from the various properties of the gods by whom the inspired are governed, and from the various modes of inspiration. Porphyry <note>Porphyry was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose "Letter to Anebo" prompted this response from Iamblichus</note> brings forward three oracles from among many: one at Colophon, where prophecy came by drinking water; another at Delphi, where the prophetess prophesied while sitting at the mouth of a cave; and a third at Branchidae, where they prophesied by drawing vapor from the water. Each of these acts upon itself with effects and works according to the mode of its own nature. Therefore, the spirits themselves, which depend upon the gods, rouse and excite men; in this very act, they exceed all natural and human motion, and this action of theirs is in no way similar to the customary actions known to man.

There was in Colophon <note>An ancient Greek city in Ionia, home to a famous oracle of Apollo at Claros</note> a subterranean place in which there was a spring. The priest, therefore, would sacrifice on appointed nights. Afterward, he would taste the water. Finally, he would prophesy there, having been made invisible to those present. It might seem to someone that a divine spirit passed through the water into the priest. However, it is not actually so. For the divine does not pass through the things that participate in it according to physical distance or division; rather, it encompasses from the outside and illuminates and fills the water from within with a certain power contributing to prophecy—namely, a purifying <gloss>purgatoria</gloss> power. Thus, when the priest drinks, it purifies the "luminous spirit" <term>luminousum spiritum; in Neoplatonism, this is the "vehicle of the soul" that mediates between the physical body and the higher intellect</term> implanted within us and adapts it to the god; by this purification and adaptation, we are able to receive the god. But there exists, moreover, another presence of the god beyond the power infused into the water, a presence that is prior, and from above, and which illuminates from around and from within. This presence is absent from no one, provided they can reach it through congruence. Thus, the god is present suddenly and uses the prophet as an instrument <note>The idea that the prophet is a passive "flute" or "tool" played by the divine</note>; meanwhile, the prophet is neither in control of himself, nor does he notice what he speaks. Indeed, he is even ignorant of where he is, so that after the response, he scarcely recovers his own self. Furthermore, before drinking the water, he abstains from food for a day and a night, and withdraws himself to certain sacred rites inaccessible to the common people. Therefore, on account of this sequestration from human affairs, he renders himself sincere and fit for receiving the god. From these things, it is gathered that a person is prepared for the god here in two ways: one through the purifying water made such by the god, which purifies the spirit; the other through sobriety, solitude, the separation of the mind from the body, and the directing of the intent toward the god. The Sibyl in Delphi <note>The Pythia, the priestess of Apollo at the Delphic Oracle</note> used to receive the god in two ways: either through a certain thin and fiery spirit <note>original: "spiritum... tenuem, igneúmq;" referring to the geological vapors believed to rise from the earth at Delphi</note> which broke out somewhere from the mouth of a certain cave, or by sitting in the inner sanctuary <term>adyto; the "un-enterable" most sacred chamber of the temple</term> upon a bronze seat having three or four feet—which was dedicated to the god—and in both instances she exposed herself to the divine spirit...

by the divine spirit, whence she was illuminated by a ray of divine fire. Thus, sometimes a great deal of fire, flying out all at once from the cavern, is poured around her on all sides and fills her with divine splendor. Sometimes, while she clings to the seat sacred to the god, through which she is adjusted to the god, she is adapted to the stable <term>prophecy</term><note>original: uaticinio; the art or practice of a prophet</note> of the god. In both ways, the Sibyl becomes entirely possessed by the god, whereby the god is suddenly present. Yet, in the meantime, the god remains separate, existing as something other than the fire, the spirit, the seat itself, and all the equipment of that place, whether artificial or natural. 

The prophetic woman among the **Branchidae** <note>The Branchidae were the hereditary priests of the Temple of Apollo at Didyma, near Miletus</note> also either sits upon a chariot-axle <note>original: 'in axe', likely referring to a specific ritual seat or the cosmic axis represented in the temple</note>, or holds in her hand a rod given by some god, or dips her feet or the hem of her robe in water, or draws in vapor from certain water; in these ways, she is filled with divine splendor. Having obtained the god, she prophesies. For from all these things she becomes adapted to the god, whom she receives from without. 

But that the prophecy does not arise from any corporeal power, nor from the soul’s own nature, nor from the instruments of the locations, but rather from the presence of the god coming from without, is clear from this: that the priestess herself, before delivering many oracles, performs the sacrifices according to the rites, observes <term>sanctity</term><note>original: ſanctimoniã; a state of ritual purity</note>, washes, and abstains entirely from food for three days. She lives in seclusion, and already begins to be gradually illuminated and to rejoice wonderfully. Through these things, it is clear that the god is summoned from without so that he may arrive, and that he does indeed arrive from the outside. Even before the priestess comes to the place of the water, she is in a certain way inspired; and in the place itself, while a certain spirit <note>original: ſpiritus; here meaning a sacred breath or vapor</note> flies out from the water of the spring, it is established that the god is something else besides these things, separated from them all: the cause of the place, the spring, and the entirety of the prophecy. 

The power that inspires prophecy in us is free from places and times. Otherwise, it could not express all places and times at once. For if it were inseparably attached to the nature of places or materials, or if it proceeded according to a motion determined by number, it would not be able to foreknow those things which are everywhere and always, nor would it be everywhere and always equally present. But if it is free from these things—as those things which happen in time are surpassed by higher things—it is not contained by a location; it is present to all waters wherever they may be, and it is present to all things that happen in time simultaneously on every side. Thus, in one moment, it grasps the truth of all things because of its essence, which is entirely separate and surpasses all. 

The divine power, the origin of prophecy, is everywhere whole and always whole. That power is not from the body, nor from the soul addicted to the body, but from those who are absolute—that is, from the angels and the god who are everywhere. This power is present to all, yet separate from all corporeal things. It is not grasped by a location, or a body, or a soul that is tied to any particular species. Rather, this prophetic power belongs to the god; it is separate from all things, and therefore it is present everywhere all at once to those capable of participating in it, illuminating them from without and filling all things, running through all the elements. It leaves no living thing nor any nature behind to which it does not—according to that thing’s capacity—imprint something of itself, contributing to the <term>presage</term><note>original: præſagiũ; a foreboding or prophetic feeling</note>. Yet, for this very reason, it is able to fill all things equally because it is equally free from all.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of divine inspiration. While the previous page described the physical and ritual settings of famous oracles like Delphi and the Branchidae, this page shifts to a philosophical critique of "private" divination and the mechanics of how the divine light interacts with the human mind, specifically distinguishing between holy prophecy and demonic deception.</meta>

-># IAMBLICHUS<-

Porphyry, in addition to the publicly celebrated prophecies, mentions a certain private type: specifically those who profess that they will attract spirits for the purpose of prophecy through certain **magical symbols** <term>characters</term><note>original: characteres; these are not alphabetic letters, but esoteric sigils or signs believed to compel or invite spiritual entities.</note>, a practice which Iamblichus rejects. He argues that because these practitioners entirely neglect religion and holiness, trusting only in these symbols, they are unable to obtain the actual presence of any god or good deity.

True prophecies are usually granted through such divine presence, but these people are mistaken; though they use symbols appropriate to the gods and focus their minds, they only receive a certain meager and obscure imaginary appearance from the higher beings. And because they neglect holiness in the process, they fall under the power of **evil demons** <note>original: malorum dæmonum; in this Neoplatonic context, 'demons' are intermediary spirits that can be either helpful or, as described here, deceptive and malicious.</note> who lie and deceive. Whatever tiny bit of signs or appearances they might obtain from the gods, these demons pervert and confuse. But those who are granted the true presence of the gods receive a true and unchangeable foreknowledge, which cannot be disrupted by evil spirits. For just as when the sun comes, the darkness cannot endure its presence but suddenly flees away without hindering the sun at all, so when the power of the gods shines from every side—filling all things with good—every disturbance that usually happens through evil spirits finds no place and is suddenly destroyed. For when good deities are fully present, evil spirits vanish; they can neither move themselves nor darken the divine splendor.

He condemns those who neglect all contemplation and religious holiness, trusting only in symbols, by which they hope they will "enclose" the very substance of some god whose presence allows them to prophesy. Porphyry also disapproved of their confidence. He also reports that, besides these, there are others in whom the **imagination** <term>phantasia</term><note>original: phantasia; a technical term for the faculty of the soul that receives and processes mental images and divine visions.</note> is sometimes stirred. This happens when they employ certain objects, even if they are otherwise of sound mind, while they are in a state of **divine frenzy** <note>original: furentes; a state of trance or ecstatic possession common in ancient ritual.</note> with imagination during sacred rites. Specifically, this occurs when they have hidden in the dark, or drunk certain potions, or used specific chants or ritual constructions. Then, in their frenzy, they imagine hidden and future things—some seeing them in water, others on a wall, others under the open sky (that is, in the clear air), others in the sun, and others in the stars.

This divine light enters the imagination specifically; if we see anything marvelous externally, it is through the vision that follows the imagination. The gods move the soul either through their presence alone—without a middle-man—whenever they find it prepared, or they pour a certain light from themselves into the **ethereal vehicle of the soul** <note>original: æthereum animæ uehiculum; in Neoplatonism, this is a subtle, light-like body that serves as the interface between the immaterial soul and the physical world.</note>, by which the images are moved in the imagination just as the gods wish. In both cases, the divinity is never "enclosed" within the ritual. When those things suitable for prophecy are employed, the attention of the mind and the thought perceive what is happening, even when the divine light does not properly reach these things, namely the...

...rational powers, but meanwhile the imagination rages, set apart, because it is incited from above beyond human custom. It sometimes holds the man who is to receive a prophecy in darkness. For nothing in these states obstructed the coming light. Sometimes <insert>~~they hold him~~</insert> in light when they prepare him, so that there may be a greater likeness to the divine light; and then that light is received in the light of the sun, or the moon, or a clear night, or in water prepared as a transparent medium <term>diaphanon</term><note>original: diaphanon; a Greek-derived term used here to describe a scrying medium like a bowl of water.</note>, or on a wall prepared with sacred **characters** <term>sigils</term><note>original: charecteribus; these are not letters, but esoteric symbols believed to hold spiritual power.</note>. For here, because of the solidity of the surface, that which is once received from the divine is retained for a longer time. 

Furthermore, they bring forward certain things related to the gods to be introduced, and they provide the one about to divine with potions, and certain compositions, and songs or incantations suitable for preparing the recipient <note>literally the 'receptacle'</note> and accommodating the presence and appearance of the gods—specifically, so that their hidden light may be revealed somewhere to the senses. However, this always happens according to the will of the gods, whether the light is drawn from the ether, the air, the sun, the moon, or another celestial sphere. 

As far as it pleases the gods, who give freely and act as the primary authors, they move the imagination; through the imagination, they sometimes move the senses toward suitable objects, and sometimes they work through the senses directly. Magic images made from solid material keep their power for a longer time. The higher beings give gifts to those who are prepared, not only through natural means, but through the intellect and free will of the gods themselves. 

The gods also give portents of the future in **entrails** <term>extis</term><note>original: extis; refers to extispicy, the ancient practice of divining the future by inspecting the internal organs of sacrificed animals.</note>, in birds, and in new wonders among the stars. From these, human cleverness interprets outcomes by the proportion of the signs to what is coming—just as one might interpret the fall of a man from the fall of a bird, or a failure from a defect in the limbs of the entrails, or their dejection from something falling meagerly. The gods imprint signs of the future in things through the ministry of universal nature and specific natures, or by the obedience of **demons** <note>original: dæmonum; in the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary spirits that act as messengers between gods and humans, not necessarily 'demons' in the modern evil sense.</note> who serve the gods and rule over the elements, animals, and all similar things, which act easily according to the will of the gods. 

And if they declare the will of a notable god and future events symbolically, it is as Heraclitus said <note>Heraclitus famously stated that the Oracle 'neither speaks nor conceals, but gives a sign.'</note>. Meanwhile, they represent the method of their divine craftsmanship. For just as they make things through firm images and prefigure events, so they also work through new portents and signs of every kind; meanwhile, they sharpen our own keenness through these same causes and occasions. 

The internal organs in portents are transformed against nature within animals by the animal's own soul, by the demon presiding over them, and by the motion of the air and the sky. This happens beyond the laws of nature and according to the will of the gods in order to warn men. That this is done by divine power is clear, because often certain principal organs necessary for life are not found in the animals at all. These are suddenly taken away by a miracle, even though it is certain they could not have been missing a moment before. In interpreting **auguries** <term>bird signs</term>, birds are miraculously moved by their own soul, by a presiding spirit, and by the motion of the air and the sky. From that sky, a power descends through the whole air, shaping it and moving it toward...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of theurgical divination, transitioning from the physical mediums of light and water to the cosmic mechanisms of the "World-Animal" and the nature of divine providence. It specifically addresses how the gods can remain transcendent while still providing signs through birds, stars, and even humble materials like flour.</meta>

-># IAMBLICHUS<-

...their opinion for the production of signs. I speak of an opinion pre-signified and decreed from the beginning: thus birds often cast themselves down, or strike themselves, or otherwise kill themselves while they contribute to signaling. This they do not do of their own accord, but because they are drawn by divine power. Certain flames like stars, produced by divine power, are sometimes very easily formed in the air as signs of future things at the command of the celestial gods. The upper air is ignited there, which is most easily guided and shaped—especially by the gods—into fire. Meanwhile, certain influences of the celestial bodies descend into this air, leading to the creation and movement of such stars, which are similar to the celestial lights in their power and motion.

The **World-Animal** <note>original: Mundanum animal; the Neoplatonic concept that the entire universe is a single, living, interconnected organism.</note> is so united with itself that its members feel together with one another <note>this is the concept of cosmic 'sympathy' or *sympatheia*</note>. Even those parts that seem remote from each other are moved together as if they were close, just like the limbs of the same animal. And this union and sympathy allows the gods to show signs to humans, first through the heavens, and then through the air. The gods do not act immediately, but through intermediate instruments—namely, spirits <term>daemons</term>, souls, natures, and everything depending on them—they produce signs for humans, beginning from a single principle. 

And from there, they spread a motion descending from themselves wherever they wish. Therefore, without being restricted by or bound to things that are born and die, they rule over each of these. Just as in craftsmanship and providence, so too in showing signs: their intellect is not turned away toward our affairs. Rather, while the divine intellect remains within itself, it turns all signs and prophecy toward itself; it perceives these things as proceeding from its own nature.

All prophets confess that they obtain prophecy through gods or spirits, because no one can see the future except those who are the causes and masters of future things, through whom others may also see. **Porphyry** <note>a philosopher who wrote a famous letter questioning the mechanics and morality of Egyptian and Chaldean rituals</note> wonders why the gods would serve humans so much that some prophets even predict using flour <note>original: præ farina; referring to aleuromancy, an ancient method of divination using meal or flour</note>. **Iamblichus** responds that the gods do not perform this out of servitude, but through an abundance of power and goodness. 

And since they contain all things in themselves, while they remain within themselves without turning toward lower things, they bestow gifts and signs upon them according to their degree of preparation—just as the sun gives light to transparent things and to eyes. And this is how it works: because we see humans taking care of subjects by turning toward their tasks and being distracted by various things—being drawn away from themselves and working hard—we similarly suspect that the gods provide in this way. 

On the contrary: insofar as they are turned toward themselves and their own single form—which is the cause of lower things—to that extent they act, move, and rule all things. They are not distracted by various tasks, but from a single principle and a simple command, they set all things in motion in a certain independent succession; they themselves do not bend toward their subjects. Instead, by their very state and most fully, they make all future things similar to themselves. God supplies various modes of prophecy; not indeed being distracted himself, but by an undivided command and a simple form, he suggests them all. He suggests different modes at different times, not being varied through time himself, but with an eternal and identical stroke of mind and will, he inspires them all, even though they unfold at different times.

...tion. Nor is divine power confined or distracted by these omens, but embracing all signs within its single form, it expresses them from itself while remaining fixed within itself, handing everything down through a single act of will. So great is the abundance of providence in showing us signs that it provides indications of the future even in pebbles, rods, wood, stones, grain, and flour. In these instances, it wonderfully appears to grant a soul to the inanimate, motion to the motionless, and a certain intelligence to those lacking reason, as if these objects seem to know the future they portend to us. And just as God often speaks wisdom through foolish men—declaring that it is not the man speaking there, but God—so He portends the future through even the most lowly things, being Himself utterly superior to them and instructing our intellect through all things. God reveals certain higher knowledge through the lowest things that lack their own knowledge, whereby He testifies that He far exceeds nature. While He offers various signs, He is not constrained by them nor distracted by them; instead, standing in His single and indivisible form, He encompasses all signs there. From that place, with a single and simple nod, He unfolds all things and provides us everywhere with evidence of things past, present, and future.

->No work of any efficacy occurs in sacred rites except through the power, and indeed the presence, of some divinity.<-

In religion, no work of any miraculous efficacy can be performed unless one of the higher beings is present as an observer and fulfiller of the work. Indeed, the gods conduct perfect works, angels the intermediate, and spirits <term>daemons; in this Neoplatonic context, these are intermediary spirits, not "demons" in the modern evil sense</term> the third. Human nature can neither undertake a rational argument nor a prayer concerning the gods without the gods themselves, much less be able to perform divine works without them. For human nature is so weak and dull that it has no remedy for its own nothingness except for a certain portion of divine light descending from above, without which nothing divine is done by us. Just as those who believe they can create a soul from inanimate things or a mind from the mindless are deceived, so too are those who believe they can perform divine things from non-divine things, or the proper works of the gods—such as prophecies, miracles, and similar things like apparitions and purifications—without the gods.

->The divinities, when invoked, are present to us, not by compulsion but by their own will.<-

It is acknowledged that the efficacy of religious works is perfected by the presence of gods, angels, and spirits <term>daemons</term>. <meta>This page continues the defense of theurgy and divine inspiration from the previous page's discussion on sacred rites. It specifically addresses the philosophical debate between Iamblichus and Porphyry regarding whether prophecy and miracles originate from the human soul or from a truly divine source.</meta>

# IAMBLICHVS.

...to be drawn to these things by a certain necessity of invocation. Iamblichus denies that any necessity is imposed, whether by man or by the world, upon the deities; since they are immaterial, they do not receive an order that is added from elsewhere. Likewise, invocation and sacred operation move the priests toward the deities through a certain assimilation and a kind of familiarity: no violence is inflicted upon the priests, let alone upon the deities. God and the entire chorus of deities joined to God are above all necessity coming from the outside.

Prophecy is perfected while the priest performs sacred rites; no passion <note>original: *passio* — here meaning a state of being "acted upon" or a passive reception of external influence, rather than an emotion</note> falls upon the priest or the diviner when they are divinely inspired. Much less does it fall upon the deities, who do not glide into minds unless they are empty of passion. Nor should it be said that the prophetic mind is a middle instrument and an effective agent of divine things, or that the priest who invokes is the effective cause <term>effective cause|the primary agent or force that produces an effect</term> of divine works. On the contrary, God is all and can do all; He fills all things with Himself. Human nature, however, has no efficacy in these matters. Indeed, compared to divinity, it is like a game <note>original: *ludus* — a reference to the Platonic idea that human affairs are merely a "plaything" or trivial compared to the divine</note>—we laugh at those who say that God is present to some by a certain chance through the power of a celestial configuration at their birth. For it is not fitting for unbegotten and universal causes to be enslaved to anyone through birth, or its cycle, or through external causes. 

Some people, because they were unwilling to burden God with cares and did not perceive any mode of creation or providence beyond that which occurs through human anxiety, denied that the gods act or provide. Similarly, those who do not see the excellent way in which the gods are present without labor or change to themselves would deny that gods take part in prophecies and miracles. Yet the mode of action that is proper to the gods through all these things is known only to the gods themselves. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who wrote a "Letter to Anebo" questioning the validity of theurgical practices</note> says that divine works, such as prophecies and miracles, are sometimes certain "passions" of the soul stirred up from small sparks, and that the soul can imagine, speak, and do these things by its own virtue. Iamblichus says that a divine work is neither done by chance, since it is ordered, nor by man, who is far inferior. For it is necessary that a divine work be done by divinity. Therefore, all works similar to divinity do not sprout from human nature, but from divine nature.

**Works of miracles and prophecy are not performed by any power of the stars, the body, or the soul, but by the pure and free power of God.**

The human soul is both confined within a single species and too much overshadowed by the decaying body. Therefore, it has no effective power for divine work. If ever we seem [to do] some such thing in some way...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that prophecy and miracles are the results of pure divine power rather than human effort, astrological alignment, or the soul's own imagination. He specifically refutes Porphyry's skeptical view that such phenomena are merely psychological states of the soul.</summary>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

...to be able to do so; we only act by divine illumination flowing from above, through which we are seen to be participants in divine action. If divine works were performed by the soul through the soul's own nature and its own power, the soul would be the master of virtue and wisdom, or indeed every soul would do such things. But in truth, not every soul does this, and even a soul that seems perfect is still imperfect compared to divine things. Therefore, it is not the soul, but divinity itself that is the cause of divine works. Otherwise, religion would not be necessary for us; <unclear>without</unclear> God and <unclear>through</unclear> worship we would be masters of divine works if they <unclear>acted</unclear> by their own power. Finally, if the soul performed divine acts by its own power, it would either do <unclear>everything</unclear>, or at least those things which possess the soul's own virtue and perfection—namely, knowledge, art, wisdom, and the character traits acquired through wisdom. But in fact, it is not such wise people who do these things, but rather those who are inspired and drawn out of themselves.

Porphyry <note>original: *Porphyrius* — a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a critical letter to Anebo questioning the mechanics of theurgy</note> had proposed three views concerning divine works. First, that for these the soul is an instrumental cause; second, that the soul is sometimes the principal cause <term>principal cause|the primary agent that produces an effect by its own power</term>. Third, that the soul can be an equal co-cause, such that from it and the divine spirit, some third kind of substance or subsistence is formed.

Iamblichus <note>The author/persona defending the sacred rites</note> says that whenever one thing is made from many, those many things must be related and changeable, so that by being in another they are thus mixed into one—just as the four elements are mixed into a fifth thing, or as many souls might yield to one whole (perhaps the vegetative, sensitive, and motive faculties in us yield to the intellectual and are reduced into its action), or perhaps from all these a vital harmony results in the body, or perhaps souls in their homeland <note>original: *patria* — referring to the celestial or intelligible realm where souls originate</note> breathe together into one Idea of all souls. But divinity, being as if <unclear>exempt</unclear> from all things, does not merge into one. The third option [Porphyry’s] is impossible, especially with the soul, which has already fallen from its high state; and because divinity, being so vastly different, does not fall into a mixture. And since divinity is immutable, it is not changed into something else common to both.

It was said previously that divine forms are stirred up in the soul by tiny sparks; let it be so, but these would not be translated into simply divine forms if they were merely bodily and natural. Finally, where it is said that the soul joins with divinity into a third thing, the soul is made equal to God, and it is granted that God is changed there and receives something from the soul, just as the soul is changed and receives something from God. This is absurd, especially because from this it is admitted that the gods, like elements, would merge in their effects into one form made in time out of eternal things, and they would be contained in the temporal. When it is said that from the soul and God, or from the gods in turn, some temporal thing is made, we ask whether something results beyond the parts coming together or not; if it does not result...

c iii

<summary>This page argues that divine miracles and prophecy are caused solely by divinity, not the human soul. Iamblichus refutes Porphyry's suggestion that the soul and God could merge into a "third" substance, calling such an idea absurd and degrading to the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s systematic refutation of Porphyry’s theories regarding the soul's role in theurgy. While the previous page dismissed the soul as the primary agent of divine works, this page specifically addresses—and rejects—the idea that the soul or material objects can "create" or "summon" daemons (intermediary spirits) through natural or sympathetic means.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS:

Then no true union will occur, nor a true oneness, just as it is in a craft where the work depends solely on the art; if eternal things fall from their stable state so that something temporal <term>temporal|referring to things bound by time and subject to change, unlike the eternal</term> is created, they would cease to be eternal. For unless they are changed, a "third thing" does not result. Indeed, it is utterly absurd to claim that something made through a temporal generation is itself eternal. Nor is it proper to suggest it is temporal, lest the eternal be made a servant to the temporal. Neither is it right to suggest that this "third thing" is dissolvable if it is made from eternal things. And yet, by the nature of a new generation, it would seem to be dissolvable. Therefore, that opinion is absurd.

Porphyry <note>original: *Porphyrius* — a younger contemporary and critic of Iamblichus</note> says that the soul sometimes generates a power and a daemonic essence <term>daemonic essence|the nature of a "daemon," a spirit that acts as a bridge between the divine and the human</term> that imagines the future through such motions. He claims the soul "generates" this when it brings together certain materials that possess such powers within themselves—specifically materials taken from living creatures.

Iamblichus denies that daemons are generated or destroyed. For he denies that daemons—who are superior to both bodies and the soul—can be generated by the soul from bodily powers. He also denies that the actions of a particular soul, enclosed within a body, can result in essences that exist independently outside of that soul. He denies that the powers of bodies, which are entirely devoted to matter, can be released from them to generate daemons.

Furthermore, he asks what power it is that releases these material forces from matter and fuses them back together to generate a daemon. In such a case, this power would already seem to be "daemonic," and thus the daemon would exist even before it is supposedly "generated." A soul cannot be generated from things lacking a soul and the power of prophecy—especially a soul that foretells the future. Something more excellent cannot be procreated from something inferior. No essence or substance can be established from the motions of the soul and bodily powers, which are themselves neither substances nor essences.

Likewise, none of those things produced through generation possesses anything greater than what was given to it by its principal generating cause. Since, therefore, neither the body nor the soul possesses the power of prophecy <note>original: *uaticinium* — the gift of seeing the future or divine will</note> by themselves, the soul cannot procreate a prophesying daemon from its own motions or from bodies.

Perhaps someone might say that daemons are not generated by us, but that they preside over living beings in a certain order; and so, when materials from animals dedicated to a specific daemon are applied at the right time, that daemon is drawn here to such things as if through sympathy <term>sympathy|the philosophical idea that parts of the universe are interconnected and "feel" or react to one another</term>. 

Iamblichus says that daemons who are so affected by sympathy cannot prophesy the truth. For true prophecy does not belong to a nature that is "passible" <term>passible|capable of being acted upon or changed by external forces</term> or enclosed by any body, place, or time. Instead, it must be independent of all these things, so that it may look upon things that have happened in any place or time with equal and simple clarity.

<meta>catchword: Concerning the soul</meta>

<summary>Iamblichus refutes the idea that humans can create or "generate" spirits (daemons) through ritual materials or soul-power, arguing that the superior cannot be created by the inferior. He concludes that true prophecy must come from a source that is independent of physical "sympathy" or material constraints.</summary>

### On divine and human dreams.

Porphyry <note>original: *Porphyrius* — a philosopher and student of Plotinus who questioned the reality of theurgy</note> claims that the forewarnings found in dreams come partly from within ourselves and partly from an external source. Iamblichus <note>original: *Iamblichus* — the defender of traditional priestly wisdom and theurgy</note> argues that they come solely from the outside. His reasoning is that we often study and perform various actions to "hunt" for these premonitions, yet they are not granted to us; conversely, they are often given to those who are not seeking them at all. If the effect of dreams arose from our own nature or human choice, it would occur when we provided the conditions for it. Instead, it is sent by the gods according to their own will—specifically when and how they wish—to demonstrate the future out of a kind of benevolence. An Orphic hymn <note>original: *Orphicus hymnus* — sacred poems attributed to the legendary figure Orpheus, often used in mystery traditions</note> declares the same thing. 

Porphyry says the cause of prophecy <term>prophecy|original: *vaticinii*, the act of foretelling future events through divine inspiration</term> is a certain "passion" <term>passion|original: *passionem*, here meaning a state where the soul is "passive" or acted upon by a force, rather than its active rational self</term> of the soul. Iamblichus denies this, saying that passion is by its very nature unstable, disordered, and agitated. Prophecy, however, ought to be entirely stable and ordered. Therefore, it cannot reside in passion. Furthermore, when the soul is wise and constant, acting according to its more excellent powers—namely the intellectual and rational ones—it does not see the future. How then would it achieve this when it suffers according to disordered and agitated movements? Additionally, passion has nothing to do with the contemplation of true reality but instead brings about an obstruction. 

Moreover, if things in the world were composed of "passions," then a passion might reach them through a certain similarity. But since things are established and governed by "reasons" <term>reasons|original: *rationibus*, likely referring to the *Logoi* or rational principles that structure the cosmos</term> and "forms" <note>original: *speciebus*</note>, a foreknowledge of them is certainly something else entirely, foreign to all passions. Again, passion perceives only the present. Since prophecy also reaches the future, it does not involve passion.

Porphyry says that prophecy is a certain passion arising in the imagination <note>original: *phantasiæ*</note>, either from our own thoughts, from the instinct of our bodily nature, or occurring by chance, just as it happens that the "frenzied" <note>original: *phreneticis*</note> prophesy. As evidence for this, he points out that in the state of prophecy, the imagination acts vehemently while the senses are meanwhile occupied and restrained. He also notes that fumigations <term>fumigations|the ritual burning of incense or herbs</term> are used by those about to divine, presumably to affect the imagination. Similarly, invocations are used to incite this same condition. Finally, he notes that not everyone is fit for this, but rather the young and the more "simple-minded" are most suitable.

Iamblichus argues that the "occupation" or shutting down of the senses is actually a sign that no *human* imagination is present at that time. Vapors are used to create a harmony <note>original: *congruitatem*</note> with God, not to affect the soul of the observer. Invocations do not stir up thoughts or bodily passions within us; for those remain unknown to us and are known only to God who is invoked. He argues that only the simpler-minded are exposed to the divine spirit coming from the outside. Regarding Porphyry's claim that prophecy is a passion of the imagination—the kind that often happens to the melancholic or the senseless who speak as oracles—he is misusing <note>original: *abuti* — the text breaks off here as the author begins to refute the comparison between divine prophecy and mental illness</note>

<summary>This page records the philosophical debate over whether prophetic dreams and visions are psychological products of the human mind or external gifts from the gods. Iamblichus refutes Porphyry’s "internalist" view, arguing that the stability of prophecy cannot come from the unstable human imagination or emotions.</summary>

L iiij
<meta>catchword: and firm</meta>

...ordered by the divine gift of prophecy, while he compares the alienation <note>original: *alienationem* — a state of being "outside" oneself, often used to describe both madness and religious ecstasy</note> caused by the divine for the better to the alienation resulting for the worse from diseases, drunkenness, or madness. Alienation of the soul arising from our own passions <term>passions|original: *passionibus*, meaning internal emotions or bodily urges that "act upon" the soul</term> is an accident that casts the soul down below the human state; but that which is produced by God lifts man above his human nature and joins him to the Divine. The former makes him unstable and plunges him entirely into matter; the latter makes him constant, a master of order, and releases him from the material world.

In no way should it be said that divine inspiration <term>divine inspiration|original: *afflationem divinam*, literally a 'divine breathing-upon'</term> has anything in common with the alienation caused by the humors <note>original: *humoribus* — the bodily fluids like bile or phlegm which ancient doctors believed caused mental illness when out of balance</note>, drunkenness, or madness. For these states are distant from God beyond what can even be imagined. Therefore, such insanity is just as distant from divine inspiration; they have nothing similar or in common. Alienation caused by bodily factors is a corruption of the mind resulting from weakness. However, that which is divinely produced is the salvation of the soul, resulting from a fullness of power. In the former case, when the soul attempts its own operations, it produces them in a perverse and turbulent way.

In the latter case, however, while the soul is vacant from its own life and intelligence, it exposes itself to a superior power to be used. Ultimately, just as divine things are distant from the lowest natural things, so are the actions and effects of the divine distant from the effects of nature. Therefore, the alienation induced by the divine has nothing in common with that which occurs humanly. When you think of the divine sort, you must separate it entirely from all the defects and accidents of the human sort. Furthermore, when you consider the sacred sobriety and vigilance received from the divine, do not compare it with the sobriety of ordinary men. In both cases, remove from the soul any imagination of divine origin that is in any way similar to those imaginations stirred up by the humors or similar causes. Likewise, do not think the ambiguous human state—poised between a sober mind and an alienated one—is similar to the state of the sacred soul, which gazes upon God with a single intuition. Nor should you believe that the most certain intuitions of divine things are like imaginations stirred up by the craft of sorcery. For the things we imagine when enchanted <note>original: *fascinati* — those under the influence of a spell or 'fascination'</note> have no truth of action or essence beyond the mere images themselves. Indeed, the end of such magic is not to simply create something real, but to project images only until they appear to be real.

It must not be thought that the divine prophet <term>prophet|original: *vatem*, a divinely inspired seer or poet</term> stumbles upon the truth by chance, as the insane sometimes do, nor even by some natural passion, as animals often suffer from certain parts and forces of the world when they sense something future beginning to happen—already occurring in the air, as it were, before it happens on the earth. By "suffering" <note>original: *patiendo* — being affected by an external physical force</note> in this way, they sometimes foresee future earthquakes and storms; this is especially true of animals that are either easily affected or possess acute perception. For foreknowledge arising either by chance or by such a physical passion is rare, disordered, discontinuous, and entirely obscure. Divine prophecy, however, maintains the continuous order of the universe...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that divine prophecy is a superior, stable state of the soul granted by God, which must not be confused with medical insanity, drunkenness, or the natural instincts of animals. He emphasizes that while human madness is a "weakness," divine ecstasy is a "fullness of power" that elevates the human above their mortal limits.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s defense of divine inspiration against Porphyry’s skeptical inquiries. The previous page discussed how the soul, when filled with God, is saved and empowered, contrasting this with medical or alcoholic mania. This page completes that thought by arguing that true prophecy is a divine gift, not a natural human faculty.</meta>
