...and beholds connected things with firm reason. If any innate faculty for perceiving the future exists within us, it is not for that reason true prophecy: for such a faculty is not always truthful, but only occasionally, and not in all people, but only in some. True prophecy <term>prophecy|original: *vaticinium*, the art of the seer or prophet</term>, however, is truthful both always and in all instances. Likewise, foreknowledge achieved by art <note>original: *prenotio arte facta* — referring to technical divination like reading entrails or bird flight, rather than direct inspiration</note> hunts for the future from signs that are not entirely reliable, because they do not always have the outcome joined to themselves. But the effect achieved by divine providence beholds things from their causes with a firm, present, and utterly continuous gaze, connecting all mutable and temporal things—even those distant from one another—anticipating future events as if they were already present. 

Someone might say that the future can be predicted from four gifts joined together: namely, from the certain nature of a man, from the art applied to him, from the common sympathy <note>original: *compassione* — the Stoic and Neoplatonic idea that all parts of the universe are "breathing together" and interconnected like a single living organism</note> of things among themselves as if they were parts of the same animal, and from that disposition of bodies by which some provide signs to others. But in truth, when signs are clearly perceived through the meeting of these factors, this perception does have something similar to prophecy, and the universe holds traces of prophecy everywhere, though not everywhere are they clear. Yet just as the image of the Good itself <note>A reference to Plato's "Form of the Good," which Iamblichus argues leaves an imprint on all of creation</note> reflects God in all things, so there is some trace of prophecy in all things. 

Nevertheless, the one divine species of prophecy must not be defined by these images sent down into the realm of generation, and much less by the imaginings of those who are delirious. For all these things are deceptive. Prophecy itself must be defined by a single principle and a single order, and by one divine species and one intelligible and immutable truth. Conversely, every mutable perception must be separated from it as something indefinite, which in no way befits the gods or divine things. Whenever we perform a work natural to us, the seeds <term>seeds|original: *semina*, the latent potentials or "reasons" implanted by nature</term> and preparations for it are certainly granted from the beginning by nature itself, which is the cause of such a work. Therefore, no preparations or seeds have been given by nature—either universal or human—for that prophecy which is above nature and human custom. For nature lacks intellect. Nor is it the principal author of the things that happen, especially insofar as nature is within us; rather, prophecy is more than intellectual, reaching the very causes of events. In one sudden intuition, it embraces the order of the universe. A work of this kind is the property of God acting within us, while we are then vacant <note>original: *vacantibus* — a state of stillness or "holy leisure" where the human mind stops its own noise to hear the divine</note> from our own activity. 

If some presentiment <term>presentiment|original: *præfagium*, a "pre-feeling" or hunch</term> falls upon us by the instinct of nature or is performed by art, it can certainly have a preparation and aptitude in our nature; but this presentiment is very narrow and obscure, and susceptible to "more or less." True divine prophecy is most ample and certain; it possesses a single and stable—that is, the highest—degree everywhere. Therefore, it could not have been implanted in us by nature. <margin>Porphyry</margin>

<summary>Iamblichus argues that true prophecy is an immutable divine gift that sees the future through its causes, distinguishing it from natural hunches or technical divination which are unreliable and rooted in human biology.</summary>

# IAMBLICHUS

<note>The manuscript contains heavy ink staining, underlining, and strike-throughs in several places, particularly in the lower half of the page, which interfere with the legibility of certain words and phrases.</note>

...[Porphyry] conjectured that a certain affection of our nature, either bodily or animal, contributes chiefly to prophecy <term>prophecy|original: *vaticinium*, the inspired art of the seer</term>, based on the fact that those who summoned prophecy into a human being carried certain small stones and herbs, and tied sacred knots, and again untied those that were bound. They also changed the conditions presented to those who had received such things from them, turning bad circumstances into better ones. But Iamblichus redirects observations and effects of this kind into a different conjecture: namely, that the inspiration of prophecy comes from outside, from another source, and from above. For such things, being agreeable to certain deities, accommodate us to receive that inspiration when they are applied to us.

Porphyry says that the art should not be despised which, at certain times, makes idols <term>idols|original: *idola*, here referring to theurgical statues or talismans constructed to house divine power</term> of the gods under the opportune influences of the stars; immediately, there appear things similar in some way to the gods, and possessing a similar efficacy. Iamblichus, however, says that these idols are held in low esteem by the priests who have clearly seen the true forms <note>original: *species* — the actual divine essences or appearances</note> of the gods. Nor can any excellent good be found in that which sprouts from matter and the forms within it, and from the forces of such forms combined with human art. For what is made by man is inferior to man, and what is made in this way, such as an idol, is a kind of shadow—appearing rather than truly existing—and vanishing almost as soon as it is made. Nor is it produced by the craft of a maker who manufactures true essences, but rather by an imitative craft that produces only images of essences. 

Indeed, God the maker of the world <note>original: *mundi opifex* — the Demiurge or Creator</note> does not manufacture all things through celestial motions, nor through particular matter, nor through powers divided in such a way; rather, he effects worlds by intellects, by wills, by immaterial forms, and by the eternal soul—both supramundane <note>above the physical world</note> and mundane. <unclear>A maker, indeed, of this kind</unclear> of idols is said to work through the stars: yet not in the same way that God creates the stars, as perhaps it might seem. For since there are innumera<unclear>ble</unclear> powers in the celestial gods, the lowest of all is the natural power. <unclear>Under that</unclear> natural power of the celestial gods are the generative "seed-reasons" <term>seed-reasons|original: *rationes seminales*, the formative principles or "codes" that guide the growth and development of physical things in the material world</term> for the purpose of formation; then there are certain other immobile reasons preceding the seed-reasons in that same coordination of forms. Therefore, the authority of both these types of reasons precedes all generation; afterwards, there are qualities, forces, motions in the celestial bodies, and from these, the "effluxes" <note>original: *defluxus* — the celestial "flow" or influence streaming down from the stars to the earth</note> that dominate the entire ordering of mundane things according to these reasons. The lowest power of the heavens, which he calls the force for the generation of earthly things, leads this process. 

Many arts, such as medicine, gymnastics, and agriculture—whichever, that is, communicate in their operation with the operation of nature—use qualities and forces transmitted to lower things through celestial effluxes. And even from an idol that has been made, the maker himself draws some portion of generative power from celestial effluxes, however small and weak it may be. For he does not use the actual motions of the heavens <unclear>nothing</unclear>

<summary>Iamblichus argues that prophecy and theurgy are divine gifts from above, rather than natural human faculties or material effects. He contrasts the weak, imitative "idols" created by human astrological art with the true, essential creation of the Divine Demiurge.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 4, where Iamblichus begins to dismantle Porphyry’s fascination with the technical creation of theurgical statues. While the previous page established that true prophecy comes from a divine source rather than physical objects, this page critiques the specific "art" of making "idols" or talismans, which Iamblichus views as a pale, unstable imitation of divine reality.</meta>

### ON THE MYSTERIES

By those very powers which are in them, or by powers naturally founded around celestial motions, this art cannot reach the gods themselves. Instead, it is occupied with certain powers that have flowed down from the nature of the heavens to the very end, falling to the lowest place of the world. The maker indeed uses a certain art, but it is not one that is pious and divine <note>Iamblichus distinguishes between "theurgy" (divine work) and "goetia" or mere artificial magic.</note>. These lowest powers of the heavens, conspiring around certain particular matter, are able to transmute, transfigure, and transform it in various ways. Furthermore, they undertake the transposition of those powers which are in particular things from some objects into others. 

When someone manufactures idols <term>idols|original: *idola*, here referring to man-made talismans or statues intended to capture divine influence</term> of this kind from many materials and under celestial influences, then the variety of celestial actions on one hand, and the gathered material powers on the other, indeed produce something. But this action degenerates far not only from divine workmanship, but also from natural production. For Nature performs its own work with a single, continuous course and simple action. Therefore, this manufacture of idols is an artificial mingling concerning the furthest outflow <note>original: *defluxum*, the "leavings" or lowest energetic remnants of the stars</note> of the heavens, and concerning those things which are moved and recede from celestial nature at the very end. 

Since man is a better being, procreated from better origins, he ought not to devote himself to the manufacture of idols. These things are not truly alive, but are merely inflated with a certain outward show of life. Nor are they held together by an internal and true harmony, but by an external and feigned one, destined to remain for only a short time. They do not possess anything true or legitimate, since they are fashioned solely by human art. Truly, only that which is simple and uniform in action or composition prevails within them. 

And therefore they are greatly deficient, because they are heaped together from qualities that are far diverse and contrary, and they do not have any perfect power. Because a multitude of such outflows is caught from many sources and mixed into something external, it is utterly meager and weak. Nor do these idols have any stability; rather, they vanish more quickly than the images that appear in mirrors. For when incense <term>incense|original: *subfumigatio*, the ritual act of burning substances to create vapors</term> is brought near with exhaling vapors, they are immediately composed; but when the vapor spreads and pours itself through the entire air, they are suddenly dissolved. 

This manufacture of idols for such marvels is entirely unworthy of a seeker of truth. For he who contrives these things—whether he delights in them while recognizing their utility—becomes like them; or if he worships them as gods, he is guilty of a crime unspeakable in word and deed. Nor does any divine light shine into a soul occupied with the dark phantasms of idols. Porphyry says that the makers of idols observe the course of the heavens during their manufacture, saying in what specific <unclear>state</unclear> of the heavens the course runs—

<meta>This page continues the critique of "idol-making" or talismanic magic, where Iamblichus argues that man-made objects cannot capture true divinity. It transitions from the physical mechanics of statues to the nature of spiritual entities, moving into a new section regarding Chaldean and Egyptian mysteries about the priesthood and the nature of demons.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

...with you, and with which things or persons occurring together true prophecies will come forth, or false ones. Likewise, regarding those things that happen there: whether they are meaningful, effective, or on the contrary, empty of significance and efficacy. Although they construct idols <term>idols|original: *idola*; here referring to man-made talismans or statues intended to capture celestial influence</term> from chosen materials by observing the stars, these nevertheless have nothing divine in themselves. For the materials that are moved here from the heavens are the last in the order of generation and are subject to the furthest outflows <note>original: *defluxus*; the weakest, most diluted remnants of celestial power reaching the earth.</note> from heaven. Indeed, such phantasms <term>phantasms|original: *phantasmata*; unstable, illusory images or appearances.</term> are so easily changed that, at the slightest nod, they are either inert or, on the contrary, prophetic—whether meaningful or effective. Certainly, such easy passivity and rapid changeability declare that they possess nothing of divine power. There are no powers in materials that are the "elements" of demons, nor can demons be generated from particular physical bodies; rather, these bodies are generated and guarded by the demons. Nor can man, by his own machines, create the very forms of demons; on the contrary, we ourselves are formed according to the body by demons. It must not be thought that some multitude or composition flows together from the joining of elements that possesses a power proper to demons in itself. For the daemon <note>The translator uses "daemon" to distinguish these spiritual beings from the modern concept of "demons" as purely evil; here they are intermediaries in the cosmic hierarchy.</note> is himself simple, uniform, and self-subsisting; he gathers diverse elements into one and generates composites from them, and whatever perseverance exists in them, he himself grants. Nor is it proper to call idols "demons." For the author of idols is one thing, and the daemon—the great leader of daemons—is another; the very substance of daemons is different from the phantasms of idols. Regarding this, you also, Porphyry, confess that neither God nor any daemon is drawn down from above. Therefore, this manufacture of idols, since it is void of both God and daemon, brings about neither prophecy nor any sacred work.

Although Porphyry does not approve of this opinion, he nevertheless records it while consulting the Egyptian <note>The "Egyptian" here refers to the persona Iamblichus adopts (Abammon) to answer Porphyry's skeptical letter.</note> on this matter. ...the good beings are purified through sacrifices; by dwelling with them and through this holy association, they drive away depravity and passion far from the participants. By their radiance, they keep those dark spirits at bay. For evil spirits flee like shadows before the sun when the light of the gods enters; they can no longer disturb the pious sacrificer, who has been liberated from all wickedness, perversity, and passion. 

However, those who are destructive and who insolently infringe upon the holy rites, contrary to established ritual and order, are unable to reach the gods due to the weakness of their actions and their lack of power. Instead, due to certain defilements, they are barred from the gods and matched with evil spirits. They are filled with the foul breath of these spirits and emerge as the worst of men—namely, profane, dissolute, and unjust. Their desires are unlike those of the gods, and they are in all respects most like the wicked demons with whom they constantly associate. Thus, being full of passions and depravity, they draw evil spirits to themselves through their natural affinity. Once possessed by these spirits, they are incited to every form of iniquity, where each reinforces the other in a cycle—like a circle joining its beginning to its end, creating a self-sustaining loop of corruption.

Thus far the Chaldeans <note>Iamblichus frequently cites the "Chaldean Oracles" or traditional Babylonian wisdom as his primary authority on theurgy.</note>. When the profane handle sacred rites improperly, the outcome is thwarted; for in place of the gods, other entities are celebrated, and evil spirits insinuate themselves where good spirits should be. Therefore, their errors should not be mentioned when discussing legitimate sacred rites, nor should what happens to them be taken as a rule. Just as sacrilege is the opposite of divine worship, so those possessed by evil demons—the authors of excess and deception—are the opposites of legitimate priests. From the true priest, every evil spirit, depravity, and passion is far removed; instead, the presence of good deities is near, and they are filled with truth from above by the divine fire <term>divine fire|original: *ignis divinus*; in Neoplatonism, this is the purifying, intellectual energy that descends from the highest divine realms during a ritual.</term>. 

To these priests, evil spirits offer no obstacle to the goods of the soul. They are not influenced by the "smoke" of pride or soft flattery, nor are they deceived by incense offerings <note>original: *subfumigatione*; refers to the use of vapors or smoke in lower magic to attract or feed lower spirits.</note> or disturbed by any external force. But all these evils are instantly dispersed and vanish like a lightning strike when a good deity is present. To such people comes a true prophecy, incomparable to any other, which must be pursued with the sanctity we have described. 

For only in this way is unshaken truth in prophecy and absolute virtue in the soul acquired. By these two means, the priest ascends to the intelligible fire <term>intelligible fire|original: *ignis intelligibilis*; the highest level of divine reality, representing the realm of pure thought and being.</term>, which should be the ultimate goal of all sacred rites and sacrifices. You have been too reckless, O Porphyry <note>Iamblichus is writing this book as a response to a letter from his fellow philosopher Porphyry, who had expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of ritual.</note>, in thinking that the opinions of those who claim all...

### Invocations and the commands of men against spirits.

**P**orphyry <note>A philosopher and student of Plotinus who questioned the logic of religious rituals.</note> wonders why we invoke spirits sometimes with supplication, as if they were our superiors, and at other times with commands, as if they were our inferiors. Iamblichus <note>The author of this work, defending the "divine way" of theurgy.</note> distinguishes the matter in this way: The Gods, certainly—and all beings superior to our own nature—grant what is appropriate to worthy souls through their fullness of goodness, their will for the good, and a certain kindness. They cherish the religious as their own offspring, nurslings, and disciples, and they take pity on those who struggle.

Furthermore, there are certain middle classes of divine beings <note>original: "numinum"</note> who are overseers and presiding officials of discernment and judgment; they consult on what is fitting to do and what to avoid. They help with just actions and call us back from the unjust, often justly turning back the injuries that wicked men attempt to inflict upon others, so that those men suffer what they themselves were striving to do.

There is, again, another class of spirits surrounding us that is undiscriminating and unreflective; it has been allotted a single power in number because of its specific distribution from the individual parts of the universe. Thus, one spirit is dedicated to only one task. For just as a sword only cuts and performs no other action, so it is with the spirits distributed throughout the world due to the necessity of their partial nature. This one only divides; that one only collects the things that are being made or generated.

Therefore, because each of these hidden spirits has been allotted a different power, they each perform only that for which they were ordained. If anyone, therefore, taking those things which are contributed to the whole in a distributed order, should deflect them elsewhere and do something as if by a transgression <note>acting outside the natural cosmic order</note>, the result that follows is the loss of the one who uses the power badly. 

But let us return to the question. To answer the inquiry: violent orders and commands are directed toward spirits that neither use their own reason <note>original: "propria rone" / ratione</note> nor possess the principle of judgment and discernment. For since our thought possesses a nature of reasoning and discerning the condition in which things exist, and since it encompasses many powers of life within itself, it is accustomed to command spirits that do not use reason and are determined toward only a single action. 

Therefore, we invoke them as superiors, since they attempt to draw from the universal world containing us those things that contribute to the whole, toward certain things contained in particular and divided parts. We command them, in turn, as inferiors, because our intellectual nature <note>original: "natura noſtra intellectualis"</note> is more excellent than that which lacks intellect, even if those spirits [possess] a wider [sphere of action] in the world...

<summary>Iamblichus explains the hierarchy of theurgy, justifying why humans pray to higher gods but command lower, non-rational spirits based on the superiority of human intellect over specialized cosmic forces.</summary>

...possesses the power of action. Likewise, there is a dual role in the priest, or rather a twofold character <note>original: "figura," referring to the persona or role the priest adopts during a ritual</note>: one human, the other divine. The divine character he puts on through the sacred rites <note>original: "sacramentis"</note> in which the divine power lies hidden. This power lifts the soul upward toward divinity and joins it with God. Therefore, by applying the divine character to his soul, and clothed in it, he can—under the guise of God—command spirits of that kind as their superior. Even so, as a human being, he is accustomed to pray, invoking them as superiors insofar as he calls upon powers from the universe.

But this is the truest resolution of the question: a certain communion of consenting benevolence and a bond of indissoluble unity contains the entire fulfillment of the sacred rites, so that this effect is divine and exceeds every limit of human capability. Therefore, we must remove all human limitation from this. The priest does not summon them as if they were distant, nor does he delegate a task to be performed by someone separate—as men are accustomed to doing among themselves. On the contrary, a single and identical action of divine fire <note>Iamblichus uses "divine fire" as a metaphor for the pure, transformative energy of the gods.</note> shines forth and acts of its own accord—ready, present, and acting from itself. It does so in the same way through all things at once, both those things which are passed down to others and those which can receive something from it.

Therefore, the divine works completed in the sacred rites are not accomplished through the opposition of one thing to another as in the world of change; nor are they transformed through the distinction between the one calling or moving and the one being called and moved, as human things usually are. Instead, they are fulfilled through identity, union, and consensus. Once all discrepancy is removed, that which acts and that by whose power it is acted upon are a single, simple, and common thing everywhere.

Porphyry <note>The student of Plotinus who wrote "Letter to Anebo," questioning the logic of religious rituals.</note> asks why the higher beings often command their followers to be just, yet sometimes, when entreated, they inflict injury. Iamblichus <note>The author, a Neoplatonist philosopher defending "theurgy" or divine work.</note> responds that they do not inflict injuries, but rather just punishments—and if they were to act unjustly, they would not be gods, but wicked spirits <note>original: "dæmones improbos"</note>. The Gods do not look upon only a single part of this life, but upon the whole; and not just this life, but the entire life of the soul from age to age. Thus, they often punish in a following life for merits or faults contracted in a previous one, whether they are asked to punish or not. Meanwhile, we, who see nothing beyond the present, believe that adversity sometimes happens to us without merit.

Yet we often suffer in this life what we have already inflicted in another, and what we do now, we shall one day suffer. Furthermore, many sins of men are hidden from us but are not at all hidden from the gods. Likewise, we define justice as each person doing his own duty according to the current laws of the fatherland. But the Gods define it much more broadly, looking toward the total order of the universe, and especially toward that principle by which the judgment of souls is carried out for their benefit. And so great is the difference between divine judgment [and human judgment...]

# IAMBLICHUS

...concerning justice itself and our own nature, which is such that we cannot fully grasp it. Now indeed, the gods themselves weigh what is just in one way when looking at a single soul, and in another way when looking at the entire kinship <term>kinship: original "cognationem," referring to the interconnectedness of all souls in the Neoplatonic hierarchy</term> of souls. For if a communion of the same nature exists among souls—both those living in a body and those situated outside the body—it creates a certain embrace that is the same and common to all, according to the total life of the world and the worldly order. Therefore, it is necessary that the execution of judgment be demanded from the whole—that is, from the universal order—and required by the necessity of souls among themselves. This is especially true where the magnitude of crimes committed by a single soul exceeds the punishment that follows what is expected. The gods, therefore, never inflict punishments unless they are just, even when they are not prayed to. Since they possess goodness according to their very essence, they cannot be the cause of evil or injustice. But if someone should perhaps argue from the curses <note>original: "imprecationibus," referring to rituals intended to bring harm to others</note> made to the powers above that certain adversities happen to people unjustly, we will be compelled to seek out other causes besides the gods and the good spirits. If we happen not to find them, we still ought not to suspect anything of the gods that is unworthy of their divine nature, nor of that certain knowledge concerning the goodness of the gods that is innate in our intellects. In this belief, without a doubt, all Greeks and barbarians agree. Accordingly, since there are different kinds of evils, and they are discordant, they must be referred not to one cause, but to several different causes.

If what we were saying about idols <note>original: "idolis," here meaning phantasms or deceptive images created by lower spirits to mislead humans</note> and wicked demons is true, then a manifold origin of evils certainly arises from this. For they simulate the presence of the gods and of good demons. Therefore, they command their worshiper to be just, so that they themselves might appear good, just like the gods. However, because they are evil by nature, when asked to inflict evil, they do so willingly, and they lead us toward unjust acts. These are entirely the ones who lie and deceive in oracles and who advise and perform shameful things. The gods and good demons, however, never deceive, nor do they contribute to iniquities. Furthermore, the nature of evil demons is inconsistent within itself, unstable and at odds with itself, persuading one thing at one time and another at another. But the nature of those who are superior is consistent with itself and always preserves the same course in action. The physical parts of the world are not devoid of excellence <note>original: "uirtute," meaning power or inherent quality</note>; indeed, just as they are larger, more beautiful, and more perfect than our bodies, so they have greater powers and actions. Therefore, every single one of them has distinct powers separately and produces different actions. Likewise, by a certain relationship with each other, they can accomplish many more things. Moreover, from the whole parts of the world, a certain multi-faceted action descends into the smaller parts. It descends very easily because of the similarity of their powers—insofar as, clearly, the powers that follow step-by-step correspond to those that precede them. Especially where par...

# CONCERNING THE MYSTERIES

### [PART 4]

...the one who suffers <note>original: "patiens," the recipient of an action</note> is furthermore adapted to the one who acts. Therefore, due to the necessities of the body, certain evil and destructive things happen to specific parts of the world, even though these same things are healthy for the whole and in harmony with the universal order. Although they are meanwhile harmful to individual parts—either because those parts cannot withstand the actions of the whole, or because of a mixture occurring in the lower realms and the weakness natural to the lowest things, or because the parts are not in proportion to one another. Furthermore, besides the body of the world itself, the nature of the world can accomplish many things. For the concord of similar things and the discord of dissimilar things produce many effects; even more is produced through the union into a single whole living thing. Whatever powers are active in the world act one way in wholes and another way in parts, due to the inherent weakness of the parts which are distributed and divided to the furthest extent.

Friendship, love, and strife <note>These are likely references to the elemental forces of Philia and Neikos described by the philosopher Empedocles</note> within the whole are "actions," but within the parts they are experienced as "passions" <term>passions: original "passiones," meaning things that are undergone or suffered rather than actively willed</term>. Likewise, the forms <term>forms: original "species," the ideal archetypes or blueprints in the divine mind</term> and pure reasons that exist in the divine intellect participate in a certain material deficiency when they enter the nature of the universe, and finally reach a state of formlessness in individual things. What is united in the whole becomes discordant in the parts. Moreover, certain parts are destroyed so that the whole, constituted according to nature, may be preserved; certain parts are crushed and pressed down, while the wholes from which they arise remain free from such suffering.

When a sorcerer <term>sorcerer: original "veneficus," one who uses charms or natural "medicines" for magic</term> by his prayers brings down some calamity from above—specifically by using certain natural and physical powers of the universe for this purpose—the "transmission" <term>transmission: original "traditio," the flow of energy or influence from higher to lower realms</term> of such an action comes from above without any choice or inherent wickedness. Although the evildoer, by using this very thing, deflects that transmission toward things that are entirely contrary and evil, the transmission and action descending from above is moved by a certain sympathy <note>original: "compassione," referring to the Greek "sympatheia," the idea that all parts of the cosmos are interconnected like a single organism</note> because of the likeness between opposing forces. 

The sorcerer, however, by his own choice, draws what has been handed down toward evil against what is just. Yet the transmission itself follows the single harmony of the world, so that even things that are most distant work together. If someone, discovering this, strives to unfairly direct certain strong parts of the whole against other parts, the universe is not the cause of such injury; rather, it is human abuse, which oversteps the order of the universe and perverts what is lawful. 

Therefore, the gods do not bring evil upon us, but rather the natural forces and bodies that depend on the divine. And these forces do not send down their influence as evil, but as good and healthy flows for the world. However, those who receive them transform them through their own internal mixture and perversity, so that what was given in one state is received in an opposite, harmful condition.

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's discussion on how universal forces affect individual parts of the world. It specifically addresses the paradox of how a divine, harmonious cosmos can result in "illicit" human behavior, such as unlawful lust, by distinguishing between universal law and individual corruption.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS

By hidden causes we are incited to intercourse that is not lawful according to human laws, though perhaps it is lawful according to the laws of the world—that is, when a necessary birth must result for mankind. For indeed, the instinct for love <note>original: "venerem," referring to Venus/sexual desire</note> in the world as a whole tends toward friendship and harmony; but in the individual parts, it becomes more violent. This is because these parts, due to their own constitution, are too easily and mutually affected both by each other and by the whole. Finally, that which descends from heaven for a good purpose is here often turned toward evil.

The world is a single living being <note>Iamblichus uses the Neoplatonic concept of the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, where the universe is a conscious organism</note> in which the parts, though distant in location, are nevertheless drawn toward each other because of their shared nature. And yet, that very unifying force of the world and the common cause of the mixing of all things draws the parts toward one another by its very nature. This kind of attraction and desire can be increased beyond the natural order by a certain **Art** <note>This refers to theurgy or "magic," the practical application of spiritual knowledge</note>.

The unifying force infused in all things is indeed good, and is everywhere the cause of fulfillment, community, harmony, mutual love, and a worldly union which is created and exists by the command of the governing power. However, in the individual parts—because of their distance from one another and from the whole, and because of their weak and needy nature—this force creates a mutual coming together through **shared suffering** <term>shared suffering: original "compassio," meaning a sympathetic reaction or "feeling-with" that occurs between different parts of the cosmos</term>. From this, a sharper desire is born in many people.

Therefore, the **Art** [of sorcery], detecting this binding force scattered everywhere in nature, contracts it from all sides, collects it, and directs it toward a single point. In this way, by its own devices, it renders unbridled that desire for necessary union which is naturally moderate. It does this by applying matter that contributes especially to procreation, and by mixing together different natural powers. By this mixing, it rules and brings about sexual unions for procreation at its own will.

Furthermore, since there are powers in herbs and stones that can both dissolve and bind, and since there are much greater powers in the larger things of nature, a drive toward intercourse can certainly be intensified by using such things. Indeed, love can be ignited and attraction created by these things even without the help of the Art.

We have found that **wicked spirits** <term>spirits: original "dæmones," which in this context are lower spiritual entities that mediate between gods and men</term> have great power over procreation and earthly human affairs. Therefore, it should not seem surprising that a burning desire for illicit intercourse is frequently ignited in us by them. Certain souls can also contribute to this: both those living in a body (which possesses a miraculous power of attraction) and those freed from the body but still wrapped in a turbulent and moist spirit <note>Iamblichus refers to "restless" souls or ghosts that remain near the physical realm</note>, wandering near the places of procreation and committing such acts.

Therefore, let no one blame the gods, or the spirits who follow them, as the causes of unlawful love and intercourse. Instead, blame either our own depraved natural instincts, or the art of sorcery, or evil spirits, or souls that have not yet been purified.

<header>ON THE MYSTERIES</header>

<sig>d ii</sig>

### On sacrifices: from where they derive their power and what they contribute.

The question is asked by what logic sacrifices are both fitting for the gods above and beneficial to men, and what effect they have in the world. Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who often questioned the efficacy of physical rituals.</note> says that not only prophets, but also **hypophetae**—that is, all priests who deliver a prophecy received from others <note>original: "hypophetas ideſt oes ſacerdotes." An interpreter of oracles or one who assists in the sanctuary.</note>—must abstain from animals <note>This refers to a vegetarian diet or abstaining from meat before a ritual.</note>, lest the gods be contaminated by the vapors exhaling from them.

To this opinion, however, the common saying is contrary: namely, that the gods are especially soothed by the smell of roasted meat <note>original: "nidoribus," the heavy smoke and scent of animal fat being burned.</note> as if it were food, and are thus "caught" or attracted. Iamblichus condemns both views—namely, that the gods are either stained by the smells of meat or ensnared and baited by them. 

The **World Soul** <note>The animating principle of the entire universe.</note> and the celestial beings, by the fact that they are present to their bodies without receiving passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to being affected or changed by external physical forces.</note> from them, are not distracted from their higher intellects. Individual souls, however, suffer both. He would err greatly who attributed similar defects to the higher souls, for the condition of universal things and particular things, or of principles and effects, is not equal. 

Indeed, eating bodies that were once joined to a soul undoubtedly brings a burden and pollution upon us; it creates a leaning in our soul through which it may melt into and succumb to pleasures, and it produces many other diseases in the soul. But the vapor exhaling from animals and the sacred incense, when the rite is properly performed, does no harm to the gods, the worldly beings, or the universal causes. For the vapor does not contain or order the higher beings to itself; rather, it is contained by them, and is coordinated with the universe just as it is with the gods. Therefore, in this way, it can be harmoniously adapted to the higher beings through their own command. 

The religious, therefore, abstain from animals, but not because the gods could be defiled by animal vapors. For the power of the gods—before any material thing can even touch it—disperses that matter without even coming into contact with it. Not only do the gods destroy and delete these bodily things from a distance before they can approach, but even the celestial bodies themselves do not receive any material element into themselves. They neither admit anything foreign nor lose anything of their own. 

Furthermore, the vapors of earthly things, having progressed barely five **stadia** <note>A Greek unit of distance; five stadia is roughly 3,000 feet or 900 meters. The author argues that earthly pollution is physically incapable of reaching the heavens.</note>, flow back down; they do not infect or nourish the material and revolving body of the heavens. That heavenly body has no power within itself for change, nor does it have anything contrary to itself; it is not moved away from the center or toward the center, but must either remain at rest or revolve. 

The bodies below the moon, therefore, since they are composed of conflicting powers and movements, are entirely transmutable and are carried either upward or downward. They have nothing in common with the heaven—neither nature, nor power, nor action. Therefore, neither vapor nor anything else from them reaches the heaven, which is entirely separate from them. And rightly, the unbegotten...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that sacrifices do not feed or "stain" the gods, as the divine and celestial realms are physically and ontologically separate from the shifting, "transmutable" matter of the earthly (sublunar) world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s counter-argument against Porphyry’s skepticism regarding religious rituals. While the previous page discussed the physical qualities of sacrificial vapors, this section moves into the metaphysical distinction between the divine nature and human nature, specifically addressing why material offerings can have spiritual effects.</meta>

<header>IAMBLICHUS</header>

they undergo no change from things subject to generation <note>The realm of "generation" refers to the physical world of birth, decay, and constant change.</note>. Can the nature of the gods, then, be defiled by such vapors—a nature which repels material vapors with a single strike (as it were)? Such things are not harmful to the beings above, but to us; for these things, being divisible, material, and kin to us, have something in common with us in terms of **suffering** <note>original: "passione." In this philosophical context, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> or action. But against celestial and divine beings—which are placed in a different category of essence, endowed with different natures and powers, and are utterly transcending—such vapors are unable to act or communicate in any way.

->What the logic of sacrifices is... and their utility.<-

<margin>p</margin> Porphyry thinks that sacrifices are offered for a twofold reason: so that we might honor the gods with such gifts, as we often do for our elders, and also so that we might return thanks for the good things received from the divine, rendering good things for good. Iamblichus says that a cause of this kind is drawn from common human custom among men, and does not suit the nature of the gods, which vastly exceeds human ways. Indeed, such modes and declarations of sacrifice do not fully demonstrate the great efficacy of these rituals. I speak of an efficacy without which we are not liberated from plague, famine, or scarcity, nor do we obtain timely rains; rather, it is through this efficacy that we also attain the purification and perfection of our souls, and gain freedom from this realm of **generation** <note>The cycle of reincarnation and physical existence.</note>. Therefore, one will not much approve of these modes from your assignment <note>Iamblichus is addressing Porphyry directly.</note>, as if you had assigned a worthy cause for their effects. And if by chance one did approve of them, he would certainly accept them only in the second place, as consequences and as things fitted in a secondary way to the first and most ancient causes of such works. We therefore desire the logic by which sacrifices have the efficacy to bring things about, and from where they are joined to the primary gods—the causes and principles of those things which are done.

Someone might say that because the world is a single living creature <note>The concept of the *Anima Mundi* or "World Soul," where the entire universe is viewed as a single, interconnected organism.</note> and has one and the same life everywhere, it therefore moves similar things through the communion of similar forces, or even the distance of dissimilar ones, or certainly a certain fitness of the agent toward the patient. This occurs while it runs according to a single **sympathy** <note>original: "compassionem." Not "pity" in the modern sense, but "co-suffering" or "shared feeling," where a change in one part of the universe is felt in another.</note> even from the most remote thing to the most remote, as if these things were also close at hand. For even among these things themselves, the communion of life is an equal distribution of this kind. He truly speaks the truth, and that which necessarily follows regarding sacrifices. However, the true mode of sacrifices is not shown in this way. For the very essence of the gods is placed neither in nature nor in natural necessities, by which an obligation would coexist out of natural passions, or [be spread] throughout all nature...

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s response to Porphyry. Having previously argued that the gods are not affected or "defiled" by the physical vapors of sacrifices, he now moves to explain how material objects—like animals or specific numbers—serve as links to the divine through a system of "correspondences" or "friendships" between the earthly and the heavenly realms.</meta>

<header>IAMBLICHUS</header>

is moved by extended powers. Yet beyond these things, it remains determined according to itself, having nothing in common with them—neither in essence, nor in power, nor in action and **suffering** <note>original: "passione." In this context, "passion" refers to the capacity to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> simultaneously. To the previous explanation, some add that there is a certain harmony in lower things with those above, which contributes to the efficacy of sacrifices. For example: in the crocodile, the **hexagonal number** <note>original: "hexagonarius numerus." Likely referring to the number six, which was traditionally associated with the Sun in Neopythagorean numerology.</note> corresponds with the Sun. Likewise, in the dog and the **dog-headed baboon** <note>original: "cynocephalo." This animal was sacred to the Egyptian god Thoth and associated with the Moon.</note>, certain physical ratios and powers are shared with the Moon. So too in other cases, certain material species—such as the colors, figures, and forms found in sacred animals—might suit one of the higher beings; or even a specific limb of an animal, such as the heart of a rooster. Other similar natural things used in sacrifices may also be the causes of miraculous works.

From the explanation of causes given above, one does not find the **divine cause** <note>The "divine cause" is the highest level of reality, existing entirely beyond the physical world.</note> (which is entirely supernatural and is not moved by natural motions). Instead, a certain natural power contained within matter and bodies is identified; thus, it is stirred up by bodily motions and material things, and again it is calmed—naturally, I say, and alongside those things which pertain to nature. Indeed, if any such result follows from the sacrifices, it is joined to the preceding causes as a **necessary condition** <note>original: "concausa sine qua non." A cause without which the effect cannot happen, even if it isn't the primary driver.</note> for the work to occur.

It is better, therefore, to say that the miraculous effects of sacrifices proceed from a cause rooted in a certain "friendship," accommodation, and conciliating relationship—much like that of craftsmen to their works, or parents to their offspring. When, therefore, guided by this common principle, we take some animal (or another living thing born of the earth) that sincerely and exactly preserves the will and purpose of its creator, we then—through such an object—move the specific creative cause that is set over this mixed nature. 

Because there are many such causes—some presiding intimately and without a mediator (such as **daemons** <note>original: "demonia." In Iamblichus' philosophy, daemons are intermediate spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil.</note>), while others are ordered higher than these (such as the divine causes in their proper sequence), and one most ancient cause presides over them all—it is certain that in a **perfect sacrifice**, all these causes are moved in their proper order. According to the rank each has been allotted, they are familiarly accommodated to the sacrifice by a kindred condition and (so to speak) are **appropriated** to it. 

If, however, the sacrifice is imperfect, it only ascends to a certain level but does not transcend further. This is why many people believe that sacrifices are only made to "good daemons," and many others believe they reach only the lowest powers of the gods. Still others think they reach only the worldly or earthly powers of daemons or gods. While these people are indeed explaining a *part* of what happens in sacrifices, they remain ignorant of their total power and all the benefits that extend deep into every level of the divine. We, however, admit all these things while simultaneously comprehending the underlying natural principles.

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s defense of theurgy and sacrifice. Building on the previous page's discussion of animal correspondences (like the dog and the moon), he now explains the hierarchical connection between earthly rituals and the higher demiurgic powers, while explicitly refuting the idea that divine beings require physical nourishment from sacrifices.</meta>

<header>IAMBLICHUS</header>

Indeed, those things which—as if in a single living creature—are moved together according to an aptitude, or a **sympathy** <note>original: "compassionem." In Neoplatonic philosophy, "sympathy" refers to the "hidden strings" or connections that link all parts of the universe together like a single organism.</note>, or a reactive **impulse** <note>original: "repassionem." This refers to the way one part of the universe reacts when another part is acted upon.</note>, we accept simply as subjects following and serving the effective cause appearing in sacrifices. But we accept demons and the divine powers surrounding the earth and the world as those appointed next to our own rank. However, we judge that the most powerful causes of effective sacrifices belong to the most perfect and **demiurgic powers** <term>demiurgic: Relating to the "Demiurge" or the "Creator of the world," the craftsman-like power that shapes the physical universe.</term>. Since those highest demiurgic powers embrace all causes in order within themselves, we believe that all efficient causes are moved together with them at once by a single stroke.

->Since in a perfect sacrifice there are moved together with<-
the highest and demiurgic causes those causes following in order, then from all these a common benefit results for the whole of creation. Sometimes this benefit occurs through cities, peoples, and all kinds of nations, or through larger or smaller boundaries. At other times, blessings reach households or each individual man, as the higher beings grant them abundantly with a beneficent will—not displaying their distribution through a **passion** <note>original: "passione." Here, "passion" refers to an emotional state or an external force that changes one's mind; Iamblichus argues the gods give gifts because it is their nature, not because they are "moved" by the ritual.</note>, but judging with an impassive mind that gifts should be given according to suitability, intimacy, and kinship. A certain inner friendship that contains all things brings about this binding through an ineffable communion.

These things are certainly more true and participate more in the essence and power of the gods than what you suspect: namely, that the higher beings are primarily enticed by the odors of animals in a sacrifice. For if demons are enveloped in some body—which some think is nourished by sacrifices—that body is surely immutable, impassive, and luminous, nor is it in need; thus, nothing flows out from it and nothing is necessary to flow in. And even if something were necessary, why would it need to flow in through sacrifices? Since the world and the air within it have an inexhaustible exhalation from the earth surrounding them everywhere. 

Furthermore, if the bodies of demons were to waste away, sacrifices would not restore them in an equal portion, nor would they preserve the natural balance between excess and defect for the demons, nor keep a similar proportion. Finally, since the **Creator of the world** <note>original: "mundi faber." Literally the "World-Smith" or "World-Maker."</note> has provided abundant and prepared nourishment for all earthly and marine animals, would he have left those beings superior to man without nourishment? And when he has decreed that the daily food of other living things be provided copiously through their own efforts, why would he want an external nourishment to be provided by men for demons alone? And if by chance we were to neglect such nutrition, the bodies of the higher beings would surely burn out and perish. Therefore, if we were the ones nourishing the demons, even the [generation]...

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus's argument against the critics of theurgy (sacred ritual). He specifically addresses the misconception that gods or spirits "feed" on the smoke and vapors of sacrifices. Instead, he explains that the fire of the ritual acts as a purifying force that elevates the human soul and the ritual offerings from the material realm to the divine, immaterial realm.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES.

d iiii

...[if we fed] them, and we were superior to them. But the truth is quite the opposite. For they nourish us. Indeed, superior things everywhere nourish inferior things, just as celestial things nourish terrestrial things. The soul is perfected and nourished by the intellect, and the soul in turn perfects nature. Furthermore, the offering of sacrifices through fire consumes the matter. It transforms that matter entirely into itself, rather than making itself like the matter; it leads it back to the divine, celestial, and immaterial fire, and in no way does it decline downward toward matter and the realm of **generation** <term>generation: In Platonic thought, this refers to the physical world of change, birth, and decay, as opposed to the eternal, unchanging realm of the divine.</term>. For if the exhalation of vapors from sacrifices were intended to be material nourishment, it would be necessary for the matter to remain intact. In that way, a more abundant influx of nourishment would reach those who were to receive it. But in reality, the whole of the matter is burned and consumed, and it is thoroughly transformed into the very purity and subtlety of fire. This signifies the exact opposite of what you [Porphyry] claimed. 

For the higher beings are free from **passions** <note>original: "passionis expertes." In Neoplatonic philosophy, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or changed by something external, which would be impossible for a perfect, divine being.</note>, since it pleases them that matter be dispersed and consumed by fire. They make us free from passions and make whatever is in us similar to the gods, just as fire makes all hard and opaque things similar to subtle and shining bodies. It elevates us through sacrifices and their consumption by fire toward the gods, just as fire elevates toward fire, leading heavy and hard things upward to the divine and celestial realms. 

The **corporeal vehicle** <term>corporeal vehicle: The "astral body" or "spirit-shell" that was believed to mediate between the immaterial soul and the physical world.</term> provided for the demons does not come from matter, nor from the elements, nor from any body known to us. Therefore, nourishment for demons cannot come from elemental essence, as that is entirely foreign to them. Rather, just as the gods use lightning-fire to divide and separate from matter whatever is immaterial by essence but bound to matter—rendering the **passible** <note>original: "passibilibus." This describes things that can be affected or altered by physical forces.</note> things impassible—so too our fire, imitating the action of divine fire, destroys whatever material it finds in the sacrifice. It purifies the things brought to it, releases them from the bonds of matter, and, through the purity of its nature, makes them fit for communion with the gods. 

In the same way, it releases us from the bonds of generation, assimilates us to the gods, makes us fit for the friendship of the gods, and lifts our material nature toward an immaterial nature. This general reasoning regarding sacrifice is, I believe, sufficient for those who are clever and able to wisely investigate the specific nature of each sacrifice based on this common rule. Nevertheless, showing indulgence toward those with slower wits, we shall add some specific points, bringing clearer matters to light. The very first principle for all these things is one that explains the context of sacrifices as being linked in sequence to the divine order. We posit that some gods are material, while others are immaterial. The material gods are those who encompass matter within themselves and organize it. The immaterial gods are those who are entirely and utterly separate from matter. Therefore, according to the **priestly art** <term>priestly art: Also known as theurgy (literally "god-working"), the practice of using rituals and symbols to achieve union with the divine.</term>, it is proper to begin sacrifices with the material gods; for otherwise one cannot ascend to the immaterial gods...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that sacrificial fire does not feed the gods but rather purifies matter and the human soul, transforming them into a divine, immaterial state. He concludes by distinguishing between material and immaterial gods, noting that ritual must begin with the material to reach the immaterial.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s defense of theurgy and ritual practice. Having previously discussed how divine fire purifies material offerings, he now explains the distinction between immaterial gods and those who oversee the material realm, and why different types of sacrifice are necessary for each.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS.

The way upward is open. These beings, therefore, have a certain communion with matter insofar as they preside over it and dwell upon it. These same beings also rule over those things which occur within the realm of matter: such as division, the impact of percussion and its reaction, change, **generation** <term>generation: The process of physical birth and becoming in the material world, often contrasted with the eternal "Being" of the divine realm.</term>, decay, and all material bodies. If anyone, therefore, wishes to worship these beings rightly, he ought to offer a worship that is excessive in accordance with their nature and their rank—offering, I say, material worship to material beings. For in this way, we are led toward them in their entirety through all that we are, and we shall offer a kinship in worship that is appropriate to them. Therefore, bodies deprived of life, the slaughter of animals and the destruction of bodies, multiform change, decay, and the general casting away of preceding matter are appropriate for the material gods. This is not for their own sake, but for the sake of the matter over which they preside. For even if they are most highly separated from matter, they are nonetheless simultaneously present to it. And even if they contain matter within an immaterial power, they nevertheless exist together with it. Indeed, things governed are not alien to their governors, nor are things adorned alien to their adorners. Furthermore, the things supplied are easily adapted as instruments to those who use them, according to their proper proportions. Wherefore, while it is alien to immaterial gods to employ matter in sacrifices, it is entirely consistent for all the material gods.

Above all, it is worthwhile to consider the dual state of our own life. At certain times, we become entirely soul, positioned outside the body and elevated by the mind; then, together with the entirely immaterial gods, we are raised up through the sublime heights. At other times, however, we are bound to the earthly body and are corporeal, being gripped by matter. Similarly, there will be a twofold method of divine worship. One will be simple, incorporeal, and pure from all **generation** <note>original: "generatione." Again referring to the realm of physical change and corruption.</note>, which is suitable for pure souls. The other, however, is full of bodies and material action, which is appropriate for souls that are not yet pure, nor yet purged of all generation. 

There are, therefore, two species of sacrifice. The purest sacrifices are those of men who are most highly purified. This happens rarely to one person, or to very few indeed, as **Heraclitus** <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535 – c. 475 BC) was a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his views on the ever-changing nature of the universe.</note> says. But material sacrifices, and those involving change, are appropriate for souls still occupied by the body. For cities and communities not yet purged of their physical and corporeal connection, if you do not grant these kinds of sacrifices, you will wander away from both the immaterial and the material goods alike. For the former [the immaterial gods] cannot receive such things, while to the latter [the material gods], men do not offer what is proper and consistent. Added to this is the fact that each person ought to care for their own essence according to what they are, not according to what they are not. It is not right, therefore, to transgress this proper measure and nature of the worshiper. Indeed, I judge that the specifically adapted bond between the men who perform the service and the powers who are served will select a mode of worship suitable to itself. For a bond of this kind, tempered in an immaterial way...

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s explanation of ritual logic. While the previous page established that material gods oversee material matter, this page argues that because humans possess both a physical body and an immaterial soul, we must employ different modes of worship—corporeal rituals for bodily needs and immaterial contemplation for the soul’s higher aspirations.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

The soul chooses the **immaterial** <term>immaterial: Existing without physical substance; in Neoplatonism, this refers to the higher realm of pure intellect and divinity.</term> insofar as it is joined to purely incorporeal things by its own purely incorporeal powers. A union of this sort, being bodily adapted to bodies, chooses a form of worship similar to the essences that preside over bodies. Often, for the necessary use of the body, we make vows and perform some work toward the gods who govern the body and the good **demons** <term>demons: From the Greek 'daimones,' these are not 'evil' spirits in this context, but intermediary beings who bridge the gap between gods and humanity.</term>, namely while we strive to purge the body of certain stains and ancient filth, or to release it from diseases, and to bring health, or to remove heaviness and sluggishness, and to bring lightness and efficacy, or to procure some other good for the body. 

In such cases, therefore, we shall not treat the body rightly through some intellectual or incorporeal reasoning. For the body is not so constituted as to be able to be cured in those ways; rather, when it obtains things related to itself, then the body is cured and purged by bodies. There will be, therefore, a rite of sacrificing for such a purpose that is necessarily corporeal. In this way, it will purge the superfluities of the body, fill what is lacking according to necessity, and reduce whatever has been disordered back to proportion and order. 

We often sacrifice by asking the higher beings for things suited to human life, namely those things which are either necessary for food or pertain to those things which we desire for the sake of the body. What then will come to us from the gods themselves, who are completely separated from all human **generation** <term>generation: The cycle of birth, death, and physical becoming in the material world.</term>? Will they confer something to drive away poverty or sterility, or to bring abundance, or lead to other necessities of life? Surely nothing. They are absolved from all such things and do not handle gifts of this sort. 

But if someone should say that those immaterial gods contain within themselves completely immaterial gods, and that they embrace their gifts according to one **primary cause** <note>original: "unam causam primam"</note>, he would certainly be saying that a certain abundance of divine gift descends from that place to the realms below. But it must be granted to no one to say that those gods, in handling these things, actually perform human life and actions themselves. For the dispensation of things of this kind, which exist here, is divided and particular, and is carried out with a certain turning toward these material things; it is not entirely separated from bodies, nor can it admit a pure and sincere government and prefecture. 

Therefore, the mode of sacrificing appropriate for such things is one which has commerce with bodies and generation, not one which is completely separated from matter and the body. For he who is entirely pure transcends such things, nor does he have a proportion to them. But he who uses bodies and their powers is most closely related to all such things, being able to supply certain prosperous things for life, and to avoid adversities threatening us, and to provide a moderate temperament for the human race. The vast crowd of men is subject to universal nature and is governed by natural powers, and proceeds downward to complete the works of nature...

<meta>Continuing the previous discussion, Iamblichus now categorizes the various types of human souls and the corresponding levels of the divine hierarchy, explaining that the "style" of worship must match the nature of the deity being invoked.</meta>

### IAMBLICHUS:

...and takes up the dispensation of fate and the order of fatal works, exercising practical reason solely concerning natural things. A very few, relying on the supernatural power of the mind, depart from nature and betake themselves to the separate and unmixed **intellect** <term>intellect: In this context, the "intellect" (Latin: *intellectus*) refers to the highest part of the soul that can perceive divine truths directly, without needing physical senses.</term>. As a result, they become superior to natural powers. 

Some, however, hold a middle ground between pure intellect and nature; of these, some follow each in turn, while others lead a life that is a mixture of both. Others still are released from the lower things and transfer themselves to the better. 

Therefore, those who are governed by universal nature, and who lead a life enslaved to their own nature and enjoy only the powers of nature, will practice a form of worship suitable to nature and congruent with bodies moved by nature. For this purpose, they will choose specific locations, qualities of the air, matter, the powers of matter, bodies, the qualities and habits of bodies, appropriate movements, and the changes of those things involved in **generation** <term>generation: The process of physical things coming into being and passing away; the material world of change.</term>, as well as similar elements in other parts of divine worship and the rite of sacrifice.

But those who live by the mind alone, released from the bonds of nature, will meditate upon an intellectual standard of worship that is free from bodies in every part of their religion. 

Those who lead a middle life between intellect and nature will also follow a middle religion, and according to the differences within that middle life, they will seek out different modes of worship through intermediary means. For they will either deal with each in turn, or they will shift from one to the other, or they will touch upon lower things so that through them they may attain the higher, thinking they cannot otherwise reach those more sublime heights.

In the genus of divine essences and powers, some indeed have the soul and nature subject to them—namely, serving their handiwork as far as they wish. Others, however, are entirely separate from soul and nature; I do not mean only from the **mundane** <term>mundane: From the Latin 'mundus' (world). These are gods who operate within the physical universe, rather than those who exist purely beyond it.</term> and generative soul, but even from the divine soul and its nature. Finally, others hold the middle and reconcile the connection between these extremes, either through a single indissoluble bond, or through the exuberant transmission of the greater beings, or through the unimpeded reception of the lesser, or through the bound consensus of both.

When we worship the gods who rule over the soul and nature, it is not out of place to offer them natural powers and to consecrate the bodies ruled by nature to such masters. For all the works of nature both obey them and contribute something to their administration. But when we desire to venerate gods who are far removed and collected in their own unity, we ought to venerate them with honors entirely absolute from matter. Indeed, to these are owed intellectual gifts: an incorporeal life, perfect virtue, consummate wisdom, and the duties pertaining to them. 

But to the **middle gods** <note>original: "mediis diis"</note>, the leaders of middle goods, intermediate things are appropriate, as we have said. Starting, therefore, from another principle—namely from the world, the distribution of the mundane gods, and the four elements in the world—from the common strength according to the measures of the elements, from the circumference of the circle...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 29 regarding the levels of the soul and the appropriate forms of worship for each. Iamblichus is arguing that because humans are physical beings within a physical world, their religious rites must usually account for the material and "mundane" (world-based) powers, rather than being purely intellectual.</meta>

# ON THE MYSTERIES

With these centers revolved in their proper order, we find a clear and easy path to the truth of **sacrifices** <term>sacrifices: In this context, sacrifice (Latin: *sacrificia*) refers not just to animal offerings, but to the entire ritual process of "making sacred" and connecting the human to the divine.</term>. For if we exist within the world and are contained within it as parts—born from it first, perfected by its collective powers, composed of its four elements, and possessing a certain portion of life and nature from it—then we certainly must not overlook the world and the **mundane** <term>mundane: From the Latin *mundanus*, meaning "belonging to the world" or "cosmic," rather than its modern meaning of "boring" or "ordinary."</term> orders in our divine worship. 

Let us suppose, then, that around every part of the world there is a certain body, as we can see; and moreover, that there are incorporeal powers distributed in an orderly fashion within those bodies. The law of sacred rites, therefore, rightly distributes "like to like" and proceeds from the highest things to the lowest through all the intermediaries. It applies bodies to things of the body and incorporeal things to the incorporeal, giving to each its own proper due. 

However, if a religious person attains a **super-mundane** <term>super-mundane: Divine powers or states of being that exist "above" or "beyond" the physical universe and its laws.</term> divinity—though this happens only very rarely—that person alone, placed apart from bodies and matter, naturally follows a form of worship that is also super-mundane, united with the super-mundane gods. But because such a state is barely achieved by a single person at the very peak of the priesthood, it is not suitable to establish it as a common law for everyone at the beginning or middle stages of religion. For these people still perform a form of worship that is, in some way, bodily.

Every expert in the priesthood will therefore admit that worship offered to the powers above must be neither partial nor imperfect, but fitting and whole. Since all the powers underlying the gods are set in motion and precede them like forerunners and ceremonial processions before the gods themselves arrive and descend to earth, it follows that whoever does not distribute to all what is fitting, or fails to honor each with its specific due, will fail to attain the presence of the gods themselves. 

But he who makes all the divinities favorable to himself by offering to each what is pleasing and most similar to them, will certainly not be disappointed in the outcome; rather, he receives the divine choir in a complete and full presence. Since this is the case, the religious rite should not be simple or composed of only a few elements, but multiform, consisting of every **harmony** <term>harmony: The Neoplatonic idea that the universe is tuned like a musical instrument; ritual must match this "tuning" to be effective.</term> and constituted from all the things in the world. 

If the divine power being called upon in the priesthood were something simple and of only one order, then a simple mode of sacrifice would suffice. But in truth, no one knows the sheer multitude of powers that are stirred up when the gods descend and move, except for those priests who have experienced it through the "work" itself <note>The "work" refers to *theurgy*, or "god-working," the ritual practice of invoking the divine.</note>. Only they know what constitutes the perfect fullness of worship, and how much the outcome fails us if even a few things are omitted. Just as in a musical harmony, if one string is broken, the whole suddenly sounds out of tune; so too, if even one divinity is bypassed, the religion as a whole does not reach its desired end, for the sacred work loses its structure due to this one deficiency...

# ON THE MYSTERIES I

...and does not possess its full integrity. When the divine powers are about to descend openly to our senses, a manifest loss occurs for us if we overlook any of the higher beings and leave them unhonored. Similarly, when they come secretly during a **sacred rite** <note>original: *opere sacro*, referring to theurgic rituals where the presence of the gods is felt internally or through signs rather than physical appearance</note>, it is dangerous if you grant honors to one but do not honor another according to their proper dignity and rank. For he who defrauds any being of its own proper honor throws the entire work of religion into confusion by dismantling a single, unified arrangement. It is not, as some might think, that only the act of receiving the god is made imperfect; rather, the entire structure of the rite perishes. 

But what of this? Does not the very summit of holiness itself return to the one supreme Principle and the unified Beginning of the entire multitude of divinities? And in that Principle, does it not worship all divine essences and powers together? Undoubtedly. However, such a summit of realization arrives very late and only to a very few; we should consider ourselves fortunate if such a thing happens to us even at the very end of our lives. 

The present discussion does not set down laws for a man of that caliber—for such a person is superior to any law—but rather it establishes these laws of sacred rites for those who stand in need of some law. The **multitude of divinities** <term>multitude of divinities: The hierarchy of gods, angels, demons, and heroes that Neoplatonists believed governed different aspects of the universe.</term> is like a world unto itself, having many orders that all breathe together into a single, unified order. In the same way, sacrifices must possess a specific number and order that likewise breathe together into one system, so that individual rites correspond rightly to individual gods. 

Furthermore, the things around us and within us are multiple; they should not correspond to the divine causes of our affairs from only one part, but should respond harmoniously from all parts to the supreme leaders. Therefore, religious observance works in various ways around us and within us. It either perfects us as if by growth, or it prunes away what is unnecessary, or it cleanses us, or it brings order to what is chaotic, or it separates us further from **mortal error** <note>The state of being "lost" in the physical world and forgetting one's divine origin</note>. Finally, it reconciles all things to the whole of the heavenly powers through a shared intimacy. 

When both meet as one—the divine causes from above and the human preparations from below—then absolute religion accomplishes everything and brings back immense blessings from the sacrifices. Truly, the abundance of power in the highest causes of the universe is such that, just as it surpasses lower things in every other respect, it also vastly surpasses them in the very magnitude of its presence. Thus, the causes of all things are most present to all things, so that the power of each cause is present everywhere, in its entirety, and always, free from any hindrance. 

By this reasoning, the very first principles of all things shine through even to the lowest levels. Immaterial principles are present in a "material-less" way within material things. Let no one wonder if we say there is a certain kind of **matter** <term>matter: While often seen as "heavy" or "evil" in other philosophies, Iamblichus argues that physical matter can be purified to act as a vessel for divine presence.</term> that is pure and divine. For since matter itself was created by the **Craftsman and Father** <note>original: *opifice patreque*, referring to the Demiurge or Creator of the universe</note> of all, it has rightly acquired a certain perfection of its own that makes it fit to receive the gods. Furthermore, nothing prevents...
