# ON THE MYSTERIES
## 21

...nothing prevents the higher beings from shedding their light upon the lower ones. Therefore, they do not allow matter to be entirely devoid of the influence of the higher powers. For this reason, whatever part of matter is perfect, pure, and **god-shaped** <term>god-shaped: In Latin *deiforme*, describing matter that has been prepared or naturally possesses a structure capable of reflecting or receiving divine energy</term> is not unsuitable for receiving the gods. Since it was necessary that even earthly things should by no means be excluded from divine communion, the earth itself received a certain divine portion sufficient to host the gods. 

The wisdom of sacred rites, having contemplated these truths and having carefully found suitable **receptacles** <note>original: *susceptacula*, referring to objects like statues or talismans that "catch" or hold divine presence</note> for each of the gods according to their harmony, often combines stones, herbs, animals, spices, and other similar things that are sacred, perfect, and god-shaped. From all these, it builds a pure and complete vessel. For it is not right to despise all matter, but only that which is alien to the gods. One should choose that which is proper to them, as it is capable of harmonizing with and contributing to the "buildings" of the gods, the foundations of statues, and the works of sacrifice. For in no other way can earthly places and the humans living here obtain any possession or portion of the divine, unless such a foundation is first established.

One must believe the secret teachings which testify that, from the gods themselves through blessed visions, a certain kind of matter was handed down. This matter is therefore **naturally related** <note>original: *cognata*, meaning it shares a common essence or "kinship" with the divine source</note> to those very gods who handed it down. Consequently, the sacrifice of such matter rouses the gods to reveal themselves, immediately calls them to our understanding, receives them when they are present, and demonstrates them perfectly. 

Anyone can see these same truths in the way divinity is distributed according to location, and from the specialized authority that is divided among individual things. This is evident in whatever has obtained such roles across various orders, whether greater or lesser. For it is well known to the gods who govern certain places that a sacrifice consisting of the very things that grow there is highly appropriate; what is governed is pleasing to the governors, and what belongs to them is pleasing to them. To creators, their own works are always especially dear. And those who first give life to things hold such things as most acceptable. 

Therefore, whether it be certain animals, plants, or other things dispensed by the powers above, they have simultaneously received a role under those powers and procure for us an indivisible communion with the higher beings. Some of these, as long as they are preserved and held, increase the familiar affinity of the holders toward the gods—specifically those things which, by remaining whole, preserve the power of communion between humans and gods. Such are certain animals among the **Egyptians** <note>Iamblichus often cites Egyptian religion as the purest form of theurgy, where animals were seen as symbols or "receptacles" of specific divine attributes</note> and, everywhere, the "sacred man." Other things, however, when slaughtered and burned, create a clearer affinity, because their resolution into the principle of the primary elements makes them more closely related to the causes of the higher powers.

# IAMBLICHUS 1

...and according to a more sacred rite. For everywhere, the more that appropriateness and **familiarity** <note>original: *familiaritas*, suggesting a close, kinship-like bond between the practitioner and the divine</note> are perfected, the more perfect are the goods that descend to us from there. Nor are these merely the inventions of men, nor have they gained their authority from human customs; rather, God himself, rightly called upon during sacred rites, is the author of such laws, around whom many gods and angels revolve. Under him, throughout whatever nations exist on earth, some **divinity** <term>divinity: *numen*, a term for a divine power or presence that presides over a specific place or function</term> has been allotted a common prefecture and province. 

From that same source, a specific divinity has been assigned to each individual temple. Likewise, of the sacred rites we perform for the gods, some god is the overseer and governor. Those performed for angels have an angel as overseer; those for **demons** <note>In the Platonic sense, *daemones* are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil beings</note>, a demon; and in other matters, in the same way according to their own kind, a perfect being has been allotted a kindred prefecture. Since, therefore, we conduct sacrifices under the gaze and authority of these divine powers, we must revere the laws of divine holiness and the legitimate sacrifices, and therefore hope for success in them because we sacrifice under the sovereignty of the spirits and gods. 

In the meantime, we must take the greatest care not to offer anything to the higher beings that is either unworthy or alien to them. Finally, we briefly advise that we should diligently look around at every single thing within us and around us, as well as the things in the world—likewise the gods, angels, and demons distributed among the nations. In this way, we should similarly offer a friendly sacrifice to each. For by this method alone is the holiness and religion worthy of each divinity preserved. 

**Votive offering**, **adoration**, and **prayer** <note>original: *votum*, *adoratio*, *oratio*</note> complete every work of sacrifice; they contribute above all to the whole of religion and forge a sacred, indissoluble communion for souls with the gods. Of this, there are truly three species: 

1. The first gathers us together and provides us with contact and knowledge of the divine. 
2. The second binds a consenting communion to the divine and calls down gifts sent from above, even as we speak and understand them to be the fulfillers of our entire work. 
3. The third completes an **ineffable unity** <term>ineffable unity: a state of mystical oneness that cannot be described in words</term>, placing our entire authority within the gods and perfectly situating and confirming our soul within them. 

Now, indeed, within these three boundaries by which all divine things are measured, prayer forges a friendship for us with the gods and brings us a threefold sacred benefit from them. One pertains to illustration or enlightenment; another to the common execution of works; and another to a perfect fullness from the **divine fire**. Likewise, adoration and its power sometimes precede the sacrifices themselves, sometimes are inserted into the middle of the sacrifices, and sometimes complete the end of the sacrificing. Indeed, no work in the sacred rites is ever accomplished without the supplications of adoration. Finally, adoration—when practiced for a very long time—nourishes and perfects our **intellect** and makes the soul much more spacious for receiving the divine.

...reveals to men. It accustoms them to receive the splendors of divine light. Gradually, it perfects those qualities within us that allow us to reach the **deities** <term>deities: *numina*, the plural of numen, referring to divine powers or presences</term>, until it leads us to the very summit. Furthermore, it gradually draws back our human habits of thought and introduces divine ways; it creates a persuasion, a communion, and a friendship that is perpetual and far from any interruption. It increases divine love, kindles that which is divine within the soul, elevates it, and purges whatever is contrary or adverse to the mind. From the very **ethereal and splendid spirit** <note>original: *spiritu æthereo*, the "astral body" or subtle vehicle of the soul in Neoplatonic thought</note> that surrounds the soul, it shakes off whatever leans toward the realm of birth and generation. It even provides good hope and perfects our faith regarding the light. Finally (to speak briefly), for those who pray frequently, the power of adoration makes them familiar interlocutors and disciples of the gods.

Since adoration is of such a nature, and has such a connection with sacrifices, it is clear that the goal of sacrifices shares in a contact with the **Creator** <note>original: *opificii*, referring to the Demiurge or the divine "Workman" who crafts the universe</note>. For through these works, one is adapted to the gods. Therefore, the good derived from it is as great as that which is sent from the primary causes and creative acts to the human race. From this, the power of adoration appears again as something that leads us back, perfects us, and fulfills us; it shows how it is effective in creating union and holding a common bond with the gods. In this way, adoration and sacrifice mutually confirm each other and bestow upon one another the power of the wonderful effects of religion. From this, it appears that the priestly discipline and its operation possess a **harmony** <note>original: *conspirationem*, literally a 'breathing together,' implying that every part of the ritual works in unison like a living organism</note> among their parts no less than an animal has among its limbs, nor can any part of it complete its work without all the other parts.

### On the sacrifices of animals.

**Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a philosopher who wrote a critical letter to the Egyptian priest Anebo, which prompted this response from Iamblichus</note> wonders why it is necessary, by the law of sacred things, for one who is about to inspect divine things not to touch a dead body at that time, yet divine invocations and achievements are frequently performed through the bodies of dead animals. **Iamblichus** <note>The presumed author of this text, defending the traditional Egyptian and Platonic view of theurgy</note> solves the problem in this way: the prophets command the spectator of divine things not to touch a dead body that has not been made sacred. But they permit touching that which is **consecrated** <note>original: *consecratur*, implying the animal has been ritually dedicated to a god</note>. Furthermore, they forbid even looking at or touching human bodies which the soul has already left. For a certain trace, image, or demonstration of divine life is extinguished in the human body by death. But no religious law forbids touching the dead bodies of other animals, since they did not participate in a more divine life while alive. Furthermore, as much as we rise toward the immaterial gods, it is helpful not to have touched such a body. But as much as we strive to approach the material gods, touching is frequent...

For we are accustomed to call upon the gods of this kind through animals—specifically, those gods who preside over such animals, especially those who govern them closely and, as it were, through a kindred condition. Likewise, for men who are confined in matter, bodies deprived of life bring a certain stain; that is to say, the non-living brings a stain to the living, the filthy to the pure, and that which lacks a "habit" <note>original: *habitum*, referring to a stable state of being or soul-disposition</note> to one who possesses it. To one who possesses a mortal body, death brings the potential for dying because of a certain common relationship between these states. But to a **spirit** <note>original: *dæmoni*, referring to a benevolent intermediary spirit, not a malevolent entity</note> that is entirely incorporeal and impassible <note>meaning incapable of suffering or being affected by external physical forces</note>, such bodies do not hinder them at all. For such a spirit stands far above all things that are subject to decay.

### Concerning divination through animals.

<margin>¶ q</margin> When divination is performed through the bodies of sacred animals and their **entrails** <note>original: *extorum*, the practice of reading the liver or organs, known as haruspicy</note>, one should not think that the gods themselves approach these things—that is, the universal providers coming down to a divided, particular, material, and proportional care over individual animals. Instead, it is **spirits** <note>original: *dæmones*</note>, and these are highly divided and specific ones, distributed to each individual species of animal, having obtained the immediate care and prefecture over those animals. For these spirits have obtained a leadership that is not entirely sufficient or free from matter. Therefore, they are appropriately accustomed to touching such instruments. 

To this end, therefore, so that we may obtain this kind of divination from these spirits through animals, it is necessary to prepare for them a **seat** <note>original: *sedem*, a ritual "receptacle" or place for a spirit to dwell</note> through which they can move among men and interact with us. This seat must be incorporeal, so that the incorporeal spirits may be present to us through it. This seat will therefore be the **soul** of such animals, now released from the body. Insofar as this soul is itself in some way separated from the body, it is suited to the spirits, and it is suited to us because of a certain kinship of life. 

Therefore, acting as a middle-ground, it serves its presiding spirit by suggesting the prophecy to the man and declaring the spirit’s commands, and it reconciles us with that spirit. The soul that uses such divination does not only hear or receive the prophecy; it also contributes no small amount from itself toward its execution and the works pertaining to it. For this soul is moved and cooperates, and at the same time foresees through a certain **sympathetic necessity** <note>original: *copatiente necessitate*, referring to the Neoplatonic concept of "sympathy" where parts of the universe resonate with one another</note>. 

But this kind of divination is very far removed from the divine and true kind. It is concerned with small and brief matters—things that are placed in a divided nature, and whatever is now carried along together in the realm of generation <note>the physical world of birth and change</note>. Since these things exhibit motions from themselves and inflict various **passions** <note>meaning "influences" or "effects"</note> upon those things naturally disposed to "suffer" them in sympathy, such a prophecy arises through this **sympathy** <note>original: *compassionem*</note>. However, a perfect foreknowledge cannot occur through sympathy. For that which is unclean and muta-

### How the conjurers used to threaten the spirits.

Porphyry <note>A philosopher who wrote a famous letter questioning these Egyptian practices</note> relates that priests were accustomed to use certain violent threats against the powers, such as: "Unless you do this, or if you do something against it, I will shatter the heavens," or "I will reveal the secrets of Isis," or "I will divulge the secret hidden in the abyss." Or "I will stop the *Baris*" <note>original: *bari*, the sacred Egyptian boat of the sun</note>, or "I will scatter the limbs of Osiris to Typhon" <note>referring to the myth where the god Osiris is dismembered by his brother Set, known in Greek as Typhon</note>, and other similar things. Iamblichus adds that the cursers were not accustomed to direct threats of this kind—as Porphyry thinks—toward the Sun, the Moon, and the other celestial bodies. Instead, there is a certain kind of power in the world that is highly divided, undiscerning, and thoughtless. It receives "reason" <note>original: *rationem*, implying an instruction or formula</note> from another and hears the spoken word, but it lacks any intelligence of its own. It discerns neither truth from falsehood, nor the possible from the impossible. Therefore, this class [of spirits], when provoked by threats, is immediately stirred and stunned, because it is naturally agitated by vehement words, and it is led and drawn along by a certain dull and unstable fantasy <note>an image-forming faculty of the mind that reacts without logic</note>.

Furthermore, the priest often commands and threatens the worldly powers not by human virtue, but by the divine power of the ineffable **sacraments** <note>original: *sacramentorum*, here meaning sacred theurgic rites</note>. At that moment, the priest is established in the order of the higher gods, and for that reason, he uses commands and threats proper to a higher nature. He does not do this as if he were truly going to perform what he asserts, but to declare how much power he has obtained through his union with the gods—a power acquired from the knowledge and possession of ineffable symbols or signs which we call **sacraments**. Likewise, the **spirits** <note>original: *dæmones*, referring to intermediary entities</note> distributed through provinces and regions, who guard the parts of the world, have such great care for the parts entrusted to them that they cannot tolerate even a word contrary to that order and arrangement. They zealously guard the perpetual and unchangeable preservation of worldly things. Indeed, they received this immutable order because the order of the gods remains immobile within them. Therefore, in the very essence of their being—whether they are spirits of the upper air or distributed around the earth—they cannot even listen to the idea of being attacked by threats.

Hence, the **spirits** studiously look after the guarding of the ineffable and secret mysteries. They do so with such great observance because they understand that the order and arrangement of the universe is contained especially in such mysteries. To the extent that these deities are designated allegorically through these words...

...governed, and the worldly orders. For this reason, the parts of the world remain in their proper order because the benevolent power of Osiris <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife and rebirth, representing the stabilizing principle of the universe</note> remains pure and untouched, and is not mixed with contrary tumult and error. Furthermore, the very life of all things remains always pure and incorruptible insofar as the life-giving and beautiful "reasons" <note>original: *rationes*; here referring to the divine blueprints or formative principles</note> which are hidden within Isis <note>The goddess of magic and motherhood, seen here as the container of divine forms</note> persist in that same place. While the world is driven from that source, these principles themselves do not descend into this body that is manifest to our eyes. 

And yet, all things remain immobile and simultaneously everlasting—specifically through the succession of generation—since no one can ever stop the course of the sun. Moreover, they persist whole because those things which are hidden in the abyss <note>original: *abysso*, meaning the primordial, unmanifested depth</note>—that is, the profound depths—are never revealed. In these hidden things, therefore, the universe and all things within it find their salvation. This is because those things which are naturally secret are preserved as secrets; thus, the most hidden essence of the gods never undergoes a contrary fate, nor is it mixed with its opposites. 

I say that the earth-dwelling demons <note>term: <term>demons</term> (original: *dæmones*); in this context, these are not "evil" spirits in the modern sense, but intermediary beings that mediate between gods and men</note> cannot endure to hear these secrets spoken or even listen to them, being affected differently and profaned by the words. Therefore, against demons of this kind, the use of such authoritative words has some power. However, no one ever threatens the gods themselves. Nor are such commanding prayers established toward them. For this reason, the Chaldean <note>Priests of ancient Babylon, famous for their "Chaldean Oracles," whom Iamblichus considers the masters of pure theology</note> priests—among whom the speech directed to the gods is judged and decreed as pure—never use threats. But the Egyptians, who mix demonic formulas with divine sacraments, sometimes turn themselves to threats of this kind.

## Exposition of the symbols of Egyptian theology.

<margin>i</margin> The Egyptians, imitating the very nature of the universe and the creative handiwork of the gods, display certain images of mystical and hidden notions by creating symbols. Just as nature expresses hidden principles in apparent forms as if through symbols, and the gods explain the truth of "Ideas" <note>The perfect, eternal patterns of things in the divine mind</note> through manifest images. 

Since they perceive that all higher things delight in being represented by lower things, and moreover desire to be filled with goodness from those higher powers—insofar as they may imitate them to the best of their ability—the Egyptians rightly offer a mode of acting suitable to the higher beings. They do this when they introduce hidden mysteries into manifest symbols. In interpreting these, you must **let go of the mere words and receive the deeper meanings.** 

Therefore, when they name "mud" <note>original: *lutum*; in Egyptian and Neoplatonic thought, this represents "prime matter" or the fertile substance from which the world is shaped</note> in their sacred rites, understand this to mean the body of the world and its matter, as well as the generative power inserted into it—which is simultaneously stirred and flowing—or even the principal cause, placed as a sort of foundation for the elements and the elemental powers. Since it is of this nature, God himself—the author of generation and of all the powers of nature...

...of all things that are implanted in the elements, as he is the cause who surpasses all these things; he is immaterial, undivided, immobile, and unbegotten <note>original: *ingenitus*; meaning he was not created by another but exists eternally</note>, being entirely from himself and entirely within himself. He clearly precedes all these things and leads them, encompassing all things within himself; and because he encompasses all things and grants a worldly nature to all from his own essence, he shines out from them. But because he surpasses all things, he shines forth as one separated from all worldly things, proceeding alone by himself through the sublime.

This is also confirmed by the symbol that follows, where God is depicted sitting upon a water lily <note>original: *loton aquaticam*; refers to the Egyptian lotus, a symbol of the sun and creation</note>. This signifies that God, in his sovereignty, exceeds the "mud" of the material world and does not touch it while governing, but instead holds a sovereignty that is purely intellectual and <term>empyrean</term> <note>pertaining to the highest, most refined part of heaven, often associated with pure light and divine fire</note>. For all things in the lotus are round—both the fruit and the leaves—which signifies the circular activity of the Mind <note>original: *mentis*; the Neoplatonic *Nous* or divine intellect which moves in perfect circles</note> as it acts through the same things in the same way. God himself remains within himself above even this action, surpassing such sovereignty; he is holy and venerable, resting entirely in himself, which is signified by the act of sitting.

Accordingly, where they introduce God as the **pilot** of a ship, they signify his sovereignty as the governor of the world. For just as a pilot, though separated from the ship and the rudder, moves, rules, and directs the ship with a single effortless movement, so God himself rules the world from above, providing the primary causes of motion from the first principles of nature.

Since all parts of the heavens, the celestial animals <note>referring to the constellations of the Zodiac</note>, the entire motion of the universe, and time itself—according to which the world moves—receive powers descending from the sun (some mixed within them, others surpassing any mixture), the symbolic mode of expression brings these forward. It uses words to describe the sun as being figured according to the celestial animals, and as changing its forms in turn through the hours. Yet, it simultaneously demonstrates his immutable and total transmission throughout the whole world. But because those things which look up to him are carried in different ways around the indivisible transmission of God, they receive multiform powers from the sun according to the diversity of their own natures and motions.

Therefore, symbolic tradition maintains that one God enters through a multitude of gifts, and that one power of God is present through multiform powers. For this reason, he says that the One and the same remains consistent, but asserts that the changes of forms and transfigurations result in those who receive them. Thus, he is said to change according to the animals and the seasons, as if such mutations vary around God himself, when in fact they vary according to the different recipients of God. The Egyptians use such symbols not only for the gods themselves...

### On Divine Names.

<margin>p</margin> Porphyry <note>A Phoenician Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus who wrote a letter questioning the validity of Egyptian theurgy</note> asks why priests use certain names that signify nothing to us. Iamblichus responds that all such names signify something among the gods, although in some cases the meaning is unknown to us; nevertheless, there are certain known names whose interpretation we have received from a divine source. In general, however, the manner of signification in these names is ineffable <note>original: *ineffabilem*; meaning it cannot be expressed in ordinary human language</note>. It does not function according to human imaginations, but according to the intellect which is divine within us—or rather, in a simpler and more excellent way, according to the intellect united with the gods. Therefore, we must remove from divine names all human fabrications, <term>discursive reasonings</term> <note>logical, step-by-step thinking, as opposed to direct intellectual intuition</note>, and natural resemblances of the voice itself which are born from things found in nature. Just as the symbolic character of the divine likeness is in itself intellectual and divine, so we must assume and accept this same quality in all these names. Furthermore, that which remains hidden from us here is precisely what is most to be venerated in them; for it is too excellent to be divided into our finite knowledge. Now truly, in those divine names for which we have received an explanation from a divine source, we possess the entire knowledge of their essence, power, and divine order encompassed within the name itself. We also hold a mystical and ineffable image, and at the same time, we preserve the whole image of the gods in the soul. Through these names, we lift the soul up to the gods and, once elevated, we join it to them as much as we are able.

Furthermore, it is asked why we prefer "barbaric" <note>original: *barbara*; in this context, it refers to non-Greek languages, particularly the ancient and "sacred" languages of the East</note> names over others among divine names. It is clearly because the gods have approved the entire speech of sacred nations—such as the Egyptians and Assyrians—as being most fitting for sacred rites. For this reason, we believe that common expressions and ways of speaking should be applied to the speech and prayer akin to the gods, especially that mode of speaking which was the oldest and the first to exist. And because they received these proper names from a divine source, when they mixed them with their own language as something familiar, tempering them with a voice agreeable to those names, they handed them down to us to be preserved forever. And so we must thereafter duly preserve the rule of tradition itself. For if anything else is fitting for the gods, it is the eternal and immutable, which is most akin to the gods above all else. Among these points, Porphyry says that he who hears the sound of divine names looks to what is signified, and therefore the concept itself—which remains the same everywhere—would suffice, regardless of the specific word used. Iamblichus responds in this way: It is not as you think; for if the names...

...if they were established by human agreement and compact, it would make no difference to exchange some for others. But if they were adapted to the nature of things, those which most agree with this nature are also most dear to the gods. From this it is clearly evident that the language of the sacred nations is rationally preferred over others. For names do not preserve exactly the same meaning when translated into another language. Rather, there are certain properties unique to each nation which cannot be expressed in another's tongue by a single word. Furthermore, even if we could interpret the properties of meanings through another language, they do not preserve the same power when changed. Moreover, "barbaric" <note>original: *barbara*; in this context, the term refers to non-Greek languages, specifically Egyptian and Assyrian, which Iamblichus considers more ancient and sacred</note> names have much emphasis—that is, an efficacy in demonstration and in reaching the soul. They also possess a concise brevity. Because of all these things, they are most fitting to the higher beings, with the least amount of ambiguity, variety, and multitude of words.

Therefore, cast aside those suspicions falling away from the truth, by which you suspect that the Egyptian language is applied there only because the invoker is Egyptian, or that it was simply the use of the Egyptian tongue that was then called upon. Instead, consider that since the Egyptians were the first of all to be allotted the presence and participation of the gods, the gods especially approve when called upon by the Egyptian rite. Nor should it be said that these barbaric, obscure names of the divine are some kind of devices of <term>prestigiators</term> <note>original: *praestigiatorum*; meaning illusionists or stage magicians who use trickery</note> and sorcerers. For in what way would those things which are most closely joined to the gods—and which join us to them as well, having power nearly equal to the higher beings—be fantastic fictions, without which no work is accomplished in the sacred rites?

Neither are such veils and coverings produced through our own passions, attributed to the divine from common report. For we do not assign these expressions to them by starting from what we ourselves suffer; rather, fittingly, we attribute to them expressions according to nature, starting from the properties of the gods themselves. Nor do we hold contrary notions about the divine—that is, contrary to how it truly is—but rather as nature itself holds, and as the first people attained the truth about it. Those who handed down to us the laws concerning the holiness of religion—we persevere in them. For if anything else in sacred laws and rites pleases God, stability itself pleases Him most and is especially fitting. It is necessary, therefore, always to keep the ancient rites of adoration intact as sacred, neither taking anything away nor adding anything from elsewhere. For this has recently become a cause for almost everything—both names and prayers—to be weakened, because through this very transgression and desire for innovation, they are always being changed, and they do not cease to be changed.

For the Greeks are by nature lovers of new things and are carried headlong in every direction; like a ship lacking ballast, they have no stability, nor do they preserve what they have received from others. But even this quickly...

->The Opinion of the Egyptians Concerning God and the Gods.<-

<margin>q</margin> Next, Porphyry <note>the philosopher to whom this book is addressed</note> asks what the Egyptians believe the first cause to be: whether it is intellect or something above intellect. Likewise, whether it is one thing alone or one along with something else, or several others. Again, whether it is incorporeal or perhaps corporeal. Furthermore, whether it is the same as the creator of the world <note>original: *opifice mundi*; a reference to the Demiurge or craftsman of the universe</note> or superior to the creator, and whether all things have flowed forth from one or from many. And whether they want the first foundation to be entirely unformed matter <note>original: *materiam prorfus informẽ*</note>, or specific types of bodies; and whether matter itself is ungenerated or created. To this, Iamblichus responded thus: Indeed, first of all, I will tell you why the sacred and ancient writers of the Egyptians thought various things about these matters. Moreover, why the wise men of this age do not speak of these things in the same way. For since there are many essences in the universe, and they differ among themselves in many ways, it is only right that many principles have been handed down concerning them, having different ranks, and different principles by different priests. Indeed, all the universal principles are as Seleucus <note>an ancient historian of Egyptian affairs</note> relates. Hermes <note>original: *Mercurius*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage-god associated with the Egyptian Thoth</note> himself handed them down in twenty thousand volumes, or as Meneteus <note>likely Manetho, the famous Egyptian priest and historian</note> records, he handed them down in thirty thousand volumes—and likewise in six thousand five hundred and twenty-five—and in these he demonstrated all things perfectly. Yet other ancients have introduced various principles specific to particular essences here and there. It is necessary, therefore, to declare the truth briefly about all these things and first regarding what you asked first. The first God is before being <note>original: *ante ens*</note> and alone, the father of the first god <note>referring to a hierarchy where the absolute One precedes the first manifested divinity</note>, whom he begets while remaining in his own solitary unity, and this is above the intelligible <note>original: *super intelligibile*; beyond the reach of human or divine intellect</note>. He is the exemplar of that god, who is called father of himself, son of himself, father to the one, and truly good God. For he is greater and first, the source of all things, and the root of those things which are first understood and which understand—that is, the Ideas. From this One, also, the self-sufficient god unfolded himself. And therefore he is called self-sufficient, father of himself, and prince of himself. For this is the principle, the god of gods, a unity from the One, above essence <note>original: *super essentiam*</note>, the principle of essence. For from him comes essence; for this reason, he is named the father of essence. For he himself is the super-existent being, the principle of intelligible things. These are the most ancient principles of the empyrean <note>original: *empiũ*; referring to the highest, most fiery heavens</note> gods, which Hermes places before the ethereal, supreme, and celestial gods...

...books: composing one hundred books on the empyrean realms <note>the highest part of heaven, believed by ancient cosmologists to be composed of fire or pure light</note>, as many on the ethereal realms, and a thousand on the celestial realms. According to another order, however, he places the god Emeph <note>likely a corruption of the Egyptian 'Kneph' or 'Kmeph,' a creator deity</note> before the celestial gods as their leader, whom he says is an intellect thinking itself and turning all thoughts into itself. Before this one, he places the indivisible One, which he calls the first model, or the expression, or the image; this he calls Icthon <note>another name derived from Hermetic tradition, representing the first manifestation of the divine</note>. In this is the first thinking subject and the first object of thought, which is worshiped in silence alone. Besides these, other leaders preside over the crafting of visible things. For the craftsman-intellect <note>original: *opifex intellectus*; the Demiurge or divine worker who shapes the world</note>, who is both the master of truth and wisdom—insofar as he moves forward into the process of generation and brings the hidden power of concealed principles into the light—is called Amun in the Egyptian language. However, insofar as he accomplishes all things without falsehood and with craftsmanship alongside truth, he is named Phtha <note>the Egyptian god Ptah</note>; the Greeks, indeed, call him Vulcan <note>the Roman name for Hephaestus, the god of fire and smithing</note>, considering only his craftsmanship. Insofar as he is the bringer of good, he is called Osiris, and he has other names according to his different powers and actions. There is also among them another sovereignty over all the elements placed within the realm of generation, and over their virtues, of which four are masculine and four are feminine. This sovereignty they attribute to the Sun. Likewise, another sovereignty over all nature involved in generation is attributed to the Moon. **Marsilio.** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Renaissance philosopher who translated this text, adds his own summary here</note> You can arrange these in an order consistent with Proclus <note>a later Greek Neoplatonist whose complex hierarchies Ficino used to explain Iamblichus</note> in this way: First is the One itself, above being and above the whole intelligible realm. Second is the "one-being," or the unity of being, in which its unity is placed before its being; it can also be called the "intelligible intellect" and the "father of itself." Third is the intellect that is both intelligible and intellectual at once, both the unity of intellect and the expression, the first Icthon. Fourth is the intellectual intellect, now unfolded, the leader of the celestial gods, Emeph. Fifth is the craftsman-intellect, the immediate leader of the worldly craftsmen (who are the celestial, empyrean, and ethereal gods); this is perhaps the intellect of the World Soul, which is named Amun, Phtha, Vulcan, and Osiris. **Iamblichus.** Dividing the heavens into two parts, or four, or twelve, or thirty-six, or doubles of these, or in any other way whatever, they also establish sovereignties over these, either fewer or more. Again, they place one leader before these, and thus the Egyptian treatise on principles, proceeding from the highest down to the last, descends from the One into the multitude. That is to say, an indefinite nature everywhere governed by the One, by God, is held together under a certain defined limit by His command. Especially, indeed, by that Unity which is the exalted cause of all things. Furthermore, God produced matter from "materiality" <note>original: *materialitate*; the abstract essence or potential for matter that exists within the divine before the physical world is created</note>, namely...

...from the derivative essentiality <note>the fundamental nature of being</note> which the Craftsman <note>original: *opifex*; the Demiurge or divine creator who shapes the universe</note>, taking as a vital force, used to form simple and impassive spheres. However, He took the final part of this essence for the creation of bodies that are subject to birth and decay. With these distinctions made, the doubts you say you conceived while reading the Egyptian books are easily solved. For those books which are circulated under the title of Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom many Egyptian-Greek philosophical texts were attributed</note> contain Mercurial opinions, even if they often speak in the style of Greek philosophers. This is because they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men who were not unskilled in philosophy.

I would truly wish that whoever touches upon the primary causes of worldly things would also declare the ultimate principles. Likewise, I wish that whoever treats the planets, the zodiac, the decans <note>subdivisions of the zodiac signs used in ancient astrology</note>, the horoscopes, and the stars as powerful leaders, would hand down the specific distributions of those principles. Therefore, the doctrines found in the *Salemeschoiniaka* <note>original: *salaminiacis*; a reference to ancient Egyptian astrological texts</note> are very brief and contain only a part of the Mercurial arrangements. Similarly, those matters treated concerning the appearances or disappearances of stars, or the waxing and waning of the moon, hold their assignment of causes in the lowest place among the Egyptians. Indeed, the Egyptians do not believe that all things are merely natural; rather, they distinguish between the intellectual life, the animal life, and nature itself. This applies not only to the world at large but also to human beings. Since they have placed intellect and reason—which exist independently—in charge, they judge that whatever happens does so according to their rule. They assert that the Craftsman is the first and chief father of all things involved in the process of generation <note>the cycle of birth, life, and death in the material world</note>. They also recognize the vital power, both that which is in the heavens and that which exists above the heavens.

Likewise, they place pure intellect above the world, with one indivisible intellect presiding over the whole world, and another distributed through all the celestial circles.

Now truly, they are not accustomed to contemplate these things with empty words and naked reason alone; rather, they advise and teach that our nature can progress toward higher, more universal realms, rising above fate toward God himself, the Craftsman of the world. In this state, the soul carries no matter with it, nor anything else besides the observation of the proper timing. They teach that we attain this through sacred works <note>referring to theurgy, or rituals intended to invoke the presence of the divine</note>, and simultaneously bring it about. Mercury himself handed down this path to us. The prophet Bitys <note>the OCR reads "prophetabitis," likely a corruption of "propheta Bitys," a legendary figure said to have interpreted Hermes' writings for King Ammon</note> revealed the description of this journey to King Ammon, having found it inscribed in sacred letters within the inner sanctuaries of the temple in the city of Sais <note>original: *Sayn*; an ancient capital in the Nile Delta</note> in Egypt. The name of God runs through the entire universe. There are also many other orders of teachings concerning these same things. For this reason, you do not seem to me to be right in reducing all Egyptian teachings to natural causes alone. For among them, there are many things involving many different essences, as well as super-worldly powers which they have worshiped with religious principles and sanctity.

### On free will and how we are released from fate.

Following this, Porphyry asserts that many Egyptians also subjected our very will to the movement of the stars. Iamblichus responds based on the Mercurial teachings <note>original: *mercurialibus sententiis*; referring to the teachings of Hermes Trismegistus</note> in this manner: that man has two souls, as the Mercurial writings teach. One indeed is from the first Intelligible <note>the realm of pure, divine thought above the physical world</note>, and shares in the power of the Creator <note>original: *opifex*; the Demiurge or divine craftsman of the universe</note> himself. The other, however, is instilled in us from the circuit of the heavenly bodies, into which the soul that contemplates divine things also enters.

The soul, therefore, descending into us from the worlds, follows the circuits of those worlds. But the soul which comes from the Intelligible is present in an intellectual way and towers over the circuit of generation <note>original: *genesicū circuitum*; the cycle of birth, death, and physical change</note>. Through this higher soul, we are both released from fate and ascend to the intelligible gods. We possess a religion that tends toward eternal things; therefore, one should not think—as you were doubting—that all things are bound by the unbreakable chains of necessity, which they call fate.

For the soul has a principle proper to itself, by which it may betake itself to the Intelligible, and depart from those things which are born <note>the physical realm</note>, and approach Being itself and the Divine. Nor, again, do we apply fate to the gods, whom we worship in temples with sacrifices and statues as those who release us from fate. The gods themselves dissolve fate. However, the lowest natures descending from them, which are already entangled in the generation and the body of the world, carry out the decrees of fate.

Rightly, therefore, we offer every act of holiness to the gods, so that they alone, ruling over necessity through intellectual persuasion, might dissolve the evils threatening us from fate. For not everything is bound within the nature of fate; rather, there is another principle of the soul, more excellent than nature and generation <note>the physical process of coming-into-being</note>, through which we can be joined to the gods, surpass the worldly order, and participate in the eternal life and activity of the super-celestial gods.

Through this principle, therefore, we are able to exempt ourselves from fate. For when the more excellent parts of us are active, and the soul is recalled to its own more excellent nature, then it is utterly separated from those things which bind it to the world of birth and decay, and it moves away from inferior things. It exchanges one life for another and places itself into a different order, while altogether deserting the prior order.

What then? Is it not possible to release oneself from fate through the gods who move in circuits <note>the planetary gods</note>, and yet meanwhile consider those same gods the leaders and authors of fates, binding lives completely with unbreakable chains? Perhaps, indeed, nothing prevents this from being so. For since the gods embrace many essences and powers within themselves, what prevents them from possessing other differences and even contradictions that are beyond our estimation?

Indeed, it is also permitted to say this: that in each of the gods, even the visible ones, there are certain intelligible principles of essence, through which the soul’s escape and freedom from the world of generation may occur. If, however, one [distinguishes] two orders of gods...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that humans possess a dual soul: one part bound to the stars and fate, and another divine part capable of transcending the physical world. He explains that while the gods manage the laws of fate, they also provide the means for the soul to escape these laws through religious devotion and intellectual ascent.</summary>

<header>IAMBLICHUS</header>

...does not admit [it] to the duty of release. Namely, regarding both the mundane <note>original: *mundanos*; gods associated with the physical world and the stars</note> and the supramundane <note>original: *super mundanos*; gods who exist above and beyond the physical universe</note> gods; at the very least, through the supramundane gods, a release will eventually occur. But these matters are declared more carefully in the treatise on the gods: which gods specifically are the ones who lead us back upward, and how they recall us, by what powers they do so, by what reasoning they dissolve fate, and through which specific "returns" <note>the soul’s journey back to its source</note> established by sacred operation; and what is the order of mundane nature, and in what way perfected intellectual action rules over this order. 

Wherefore, regarding what you brought forward from the verses of Homer—namely, that "the gods are flexible" <note>Referring to *Iliad* 9.497, suggesting gods can be swayed by prayer</note>—we deem it a sacrilege to say so. For the holy works of religion have long since been defined by pure and intellectual laws, and by a greater order and power, lesser things are dissolved. Insofar as we are translated into a better lot, to that extent we depart from the lesser forces. Nor does anything happen because of this that is contrary to the rule established from the beginning, as if the gods are "bent" or changed because of a sacrifice or worship performed at a later time. Rather, from the first descent, God sent the soul down according to its own condition, so that it might return to Him again. Nor do the ascent and descent of souls conflict with one another. For just as in the intellectual universe, "generation" <note>the process of becoming or being born</note> exists together with "essence"—indeed, this whole is rightly connected—so too in the disposition of souls, their care concerning physical birth agrees with their release from it.

### On one’s own personal daemon.

After these things, Porphyry asked many questions about each person's personal daemon <note>original: *daemone*; a guardian spirit or guiding genius assigned to a person at birth</note>. Iamblichus responds to these as follows: The treatise on the daemon proper to each individual is twofold. One part is indeed sacred, or deific <note>divine-making</note>. The other is technical <note>original: *artificiosus*; related to the "art" or craft of astrology</note>. The former invokes the daemon from celestial causes. The latter from the circuits involved in generation <note>the cycles of physical birth and the zodiac</note>. The former does not make use of the exploration of an individual’s birth chart <note>original: *geniturae*</note>; the latter explores such things diligently. The former is universal and above nature; the latter more specifically worships and cares for the daemon according to nature. 

Since these things are so, it seems absurd to me that you have transferred a more perfect form of worship to a merely human level, and focused your questions solely on this. Furthermore, where you seek or worship the daemon only by a natural way, you seem to have grasped only a tiny part of such a path. For those who investigate and work technically regarding nature are accustomed to call upon the daemon in an orderly fashion from the "decans" <note>original: *decanis*; the 36 rulers of the 10-degree segments of the zodiac</note>, that is, the "doers." And from the dispensers of influences: the images of heaven, the stars, the sun, and the moon. Likewise from the poles and all the elements and the world. 

But you, choosing incorrectly the smallest part of these—namely, the "lord of the birth figure" <note>the dominant planet in a person's astrological chart</note>—bring in questions only about this, and in this area you examine this one premise: in what way the lord of the chart grants the daemon. And according to what kind of life or power, or influences, it flows from him into us. In this, you linger entirely in the exploration of the birth chart, inves[tigating]...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that the gods are not "swayed" by prayer but rather the soul aligns itself with higher divine laws to escape fate. He also distinguishes between a high, sacred understanding of the personal guardian spirit (daemon) and a lower, technical astrological approach.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between human souls, fate, and the divine. Iamblichus is responding to Porphyry's skeptical questions about whether a personal guardian spirit (daemon) can actually help a person escape their astrological destiny (fate).</meta>

...doubting whether the daemon exists or not, and whether the lord of the birth chart <note>original: *figurae*; refers to the astrological "figure" or horoscope at the moment of birth</note> can be found, or perhaps cannot. You finally assert that a person would be blessed who, having found the figure of his birth, has thus escaped the decrees of fate. Thus, you say, he has clearly observed his own daemon. To me, however, these things seem to contradict each other and to fall away from the truth. For if the daemon is assigned to us by the very figure of our birth, and we have recognized him from that source, how exactly shall we flee the decrees of fate through the knowledge of a daemon who was himself bound to us by fate? And even if, as you affirm, we can drive away necessities through the daemon, how is this possible when these things were destined for us by fate along with the daemon?

->On the judgments of astrologers and the daemon.<-

**P**orphyry says that if anyone should know the figure of their birth and the lord of that figure, they would find their own daemon, and through him be released from the fate of birth. But he adds that it is impossible to know that figure or to find this daemon, and that the rules of astronomy and astrology are incomprehensible and uncertain, as witnessed by Chaeremon <note>An Egyptian priest and Stoic philosopher who wrote on astrology</note>. Iamblichus says that the daemon is neither known nor assigned from that birth chart and its demonic influence. Otherwise, he would not release us from the fate of birth. Instead, the daemon is given from a more ancient and higher principle—namely, from the superior gods—and at the very moment the soul first leans toward sensible things before conception. We are released from fate not so much through the daemon as through the worship of a higher divinity. Truly, those statements of Porphyry not only disagree with themselves but also with the truth. For the daemon is not assigned to each person entirely from the specific figure of birth; rather, there is a more ancient origin for this. Likewise, if only this specific daemon were recognized, he who knew the daemon of genesis <note>original: *genesicum dæmonem*; the spirit associated with the physical process of birth</note> would not be happy for that reason. And who indeed would take him as a guide to escape the decrees of fate? If he was assigned for the very purpose of fulfilling those decrees, then you are altogether overlooking the most important questions regarding the essence and order of the daemon. You only touch upon the final points regarding where he descends from.

You claim, furthermore, that innumerable rules of astrology are circulated, as well as doubts concerning the birth-horoscope. From this, it would appear that no certain knowledge can be held regarding these things. But I, on the contrary, judge first that a most certain truth regarding the stars can indeed be held through divine prophecy <note>original: *uaticinium*; referring to divinely inspired insight rather than just calculation</note>. We do not entirely need the counting of rules or artificial predictions. Furthermore, I add that you do not demonstrate such knowledge to be completely impossible as far as it pertains to the mathematical science <note>original: *mathematicam scientiam*; in this context, the technical study of astrology</note>, simply because diverse opinions are held among practitioners, or because Chaeremon or someone else contradicts it more profoundly. For in this way, in every science and art alike, we would be forced to say that no science exists because of conflicting opinions. But surely, everywhere, not only do false things disagree with each other, but false things also disagree with the true, so that truth may be found everywhere beyond what is false. Porphyry says the rules...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that the personal daemon is not merely a product of one's birth chart (fate) but comes from a higher divine source, allowing humans to transcend their astrological destiny through worship.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Iamblichus’s rebuttal to Porphyry regarding the "personal daemon" or guardian spirit. Porphyry had questioned whether such a spirit could be identified through astrology to help a person escape their fate. Iamblichus argues that while astrology has some basis in truth, it is limited, and the true guardian spirit is found through divine means rather than mathematical charts.</meta>

# IAMBLICHUS:

...that these things cannot be comprehended even by astronomy, let alone astrology, and that there are many disagreements among them and many who challenge them. Iamblichus responds that divine prophecy <note>original: *vaticinium*; refers to divine inspiration or theurgy rather than technical fortune-telling</note> can teach the nature and effects of the stars without the need for technical art. Astronomy and the other arts were once given by the gods, but over a long time, they have become confused by human opinions and retain very little of divinity or truth. In astronomy, there is some truth, though little of it is clear, which is seen through the effects of the stars upon one another arising from their measurements in the heavens, just as was said before regarding the eclipses of the sun and moon and the aspects 
<margin>1</margin> of the planets. The rules and measurements of their size, distances, progressions, comets, and similar things—observed long ago among the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians, famous in antiquity for their advanced astronomical observations</note> and among us—testify that the science of astronomy is true. Porphyry says that the lord of the birth chart <note>original: *dominus figurae*; the planet that holds the most power in a person's horoscope</note>, or whether there are multiple lords, cannot be grasped even by the judgment of astronomers and astrologers, but that one's own daemon must be sought from that source. Iamblichus says that astrologers provide rules—some providing five, others fewer, others more—for finding or discerning the lords of the charts. I do not say, however, that these rules are actually held, found, or discerned, but rather that they are thought to be so, and are handed down by them contrary to what Porphyry says. What is to prevent the lord of the chart and the daemon from being found only with difficulty through astrology, yet very easily through divine prophecy and sacrifices? Nor should it be thought that the daemon is assigned by the lord of the chart alone. For there are more principles to this, and more ancient ones. We cannot find our own daemon through human arts, but through divine ones. Each person's own daemon is not distributed from some particular element or disposition of the heavens, but from the entire disposition of the world, when the soul descends while the daemon is ruling and assigning a certain executor of the life which the soul has chosen. This daemon reconciles the soul to the body and cares for the life communicated to the body. It directs the soul's own life and provides the principles for its constant thought; we do such things as the daemon brings to our minds, and it governs us to the extent that, having been perfected by sacred rites, we might exchange the daemon for the Lord <note>original: *dominum*; likely referring to a higher divine union or God, moving beyond the intermediary spirit</note>. Then the daemon, yielding to God, either ceases its work or leads the soul toward Him. A person's lot is assigned to the soul while it descends from the whole body of the world and life as it then relates to her, and that lot is led and fulfilled by a certain daemon. Therefore, it is impossible to judge events with certainty when we cannot comprehend the convergence of all causes, unless we attain it through divine inspiration.

### From where the personal daemon comes, what it does, and whether it is unique.

The personal daemon is not assigned from one part of the heaven or the elements, but rather from the whole world, and from the multiform life within it, and from the
<sig>p i</sig> multiform bodies through which the soul passes as it descends into genera-

# ON THE MYSTERIES.

...is properly distinguished and determined as a certain lot <note>original: *sors*; refers to the "allotment" of one's destiny or guardian spirit, a concept famously described in Plato’s Myth of Er</note> within us, distributed according to its own proper prefecture. This daemon was certainly present in the exemplar <note>The "exemplar" refers to the divine or ideal realm of Forms that exists before physical creation</note> before the souls fell into the realm of generation <note>original: *generationem*; the process of being born into a physical body</note>. As soon as the soul receives this spirit as its leader, the daemon immediately stands by it, fulfilling the succession of its lives. This daemon, as I have said, binds the soul to the body as it descends. He himself cares for the common "animal" <note>In this context, the "animal" refers to the composite being of body and soul together</note> of that person. He directs the soul’s own life, and whatever we reason, he provides the principles for that reasoning; we act in such a way as he brings to our mind. He governs us until, through the purification of sacred works <note>original: *sacris opibus*; refers to theurgy, the ritual practices intended to unite the practitioner with the divine</note>, we take up a God as our leader instead of a daemon. After this, the daemon yields to the God in such a way that he either becomes quiet in the God’s presence or assists the God in that same leadership.

Next, you asked whether several daemons are present to each individual, with different spirits governing different parts of the human being. To this we respond that the daemon does not merely preside over some specific part of us, but is present to the whole and leads the whole at once, just as he has been assigned by the universal orders that exist in the world. You conjectured that many daemons might be present to us according to the number of our parts. Furthermore, you suggested that even within the body itself there might be different daemons—one caring for health, another for beauty, and others for some specific habit among these—and that one spirit might preside over these equally in the body. In this way, you thought that one daemon might rule the body, another the soul, and another the mind. 

However, it is better to conjecture that the body, the soul, and the intellect are all governed by the same single daemon. Therefore, do not divide them so as to suggest there is one daemon for the body, another for the soul, and another for the intellect. For it is absurd to believe that the living being is one, yet to think that the spirit presiding over that being is multiform. Indeed, those things which hold the position of leadership are everywhere simpler than the things they rule. It is even more absurd if many ruling daemons were like disjointed parts of a spirit, not fused into one but separated from each other. You even introduce a sense of conflict among them, as if some of the ruling daemons were good and others were evil. Yet evil spirits never hold the lot of a prefecture <note>original: *præfecturæ*; an official office or position of authority</note>, nor are they distributed with equal authority or in the same number as an opposition to the good spirits.

After this, you suspect that the personal daemon is actually a certain part of the soul—namely the intellect—and that a person is **blessed** <gloss>that is, happy</gloss> <note>original: *ευδαιμον* (eudaimon); the Greek term for having a "good daemon" or being in a state of flourishing</note> if they possess a wise intellect. If this were the case, there would no longer be any order of being more excellent than man presiding over man. Instead, among the divided parts of the soul, the higher part would simply rule over the lower. However, in that case, all parts would be of the same kind; none would rule as an absolute power over its subjects. 

After this, you suggest that the worship of the daemon is directed toward several entities—partly as if toward two daemons, and partly toward three. But it is a sin to divide the causes that preside over us, or to fail to reduce that prefecture to a single unity. Indeed, unity dominates in all things. Now, concerning those who assign the spirit according to the body...

<summary>Iamblichus argues that each person has a single, unified guardian spirit (daemon) that governs the whole person—body, soul, and mind—rather than multiple spirits for different parts. He rejects the idea that the "daemon" is simply a person's own intellect, asserting it is a superior external guide assigned before birth.</summary>

->IAMBLICHUS<-

...and divides the administration of the body, he reduces its leadership into a very narrow part of the same. Therefore, it is not fitting to consider religious worship toward the <term>daemon</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, a "daemon" is not an evil demon, but a protective intermediary spirit that links humans to the divine</note> as being divided in such a way, since the very opinion upon which it is founded wavers in its weakness. There is, therefore, one proper daemon as a governor for each of us. Furthermore, it is not right to believe there is one identical daemon common to all men; or rather, that there is one common daemon within himself, but joined to each person by a unique condition. For the very division of matter according to each species, and the very "otherness" of things, does not admit of an incorporeal identity and sameness within itself.

### Invocation of the daemon.

<margin>q</margin> You ask next why we are accustomed to call upon the daemon with a certain common invocation among all people, since clearly the invocation is performed through the one Lord of the daemons <note>original: *deum dominum unum daemonum*; likely referring to a high deity like Zeus or a cosmic governor who oversees the distribution of guardian spirits</note>, who from the beginning defined for each their own daemon, and who in sacrifices reveals to each their own spirit according to his own will. For always, in the order of sacred operations <note>original: *sacrarum operationum*; a reference to "theurgy," or ritual practices intended to invoke the gods</note>, the lower powers are called through the superior divinities. Therefore, among the daemons, there is a certain leader of those who hold the primacy over the realm of <term>generation</term> <note>The cycle of birth, death, and physical existence</note>, and he sends down to each person their own daemon. When the daemon proper to each is present, he then reveals the worship appropriate to himself, and makes known his own name and his own specific mode of invocation. And this is the fitting order of the daemons. For one order is related to those who invoke; another proceeds from more ancient causes; and another is completed by a conspiracy <note>original: *conspiratione*; used here in the sense of "breathing together" or harmonious cooperation</note> among them, contributing commonly to the same end. Do not, therefore, judge divine invocations to be similar to human ones, nor compare the unutterable <note>original: *ineffabiles*</note> to the utterable, nor compare those things which surpass every limit and every indeterminate mode to human commands and orders, whether these be defined or entirely indefinite. For the things that exist among us have nothing in common with the whole genus of those beings who exceed us according to the entire order, and who surpass our whole essence and nature. Indeed, from this point, the greatest errors often befall men: when, out of human weakness, one tries to reason something regarding the dominations of daemons, and compares great, momentous, and perfect things to those that are small, worthless, and divided.

### On happiness.

<margin>s</margin> Do you suspect that perhaps some other path to <term>beatitude</term> <note>Blessedness or supreme happiness</note> lies hidden besides divine worship, and do you ask what this path might especially be? But truly, if the essence and perfection of all good things are contained in the gods, and if the primary power and the first principle of all goods are there, then deservedly only we priests—and whoever has similarly surrendered themselves to the higher powers and achieved a lawful union with them...

<header>ON THE MYSTERIES.</header>

...having attained these things, we zealously pursue the principle and end of all goods. In this state, surely, the contemplation of truth is present, as well as the perfection of **intellectual science** <note>original: *intellectualis scientiæ*; in Neoplatonism, this refers to "noetic" knowledge—the direct, intuitive grasp of divine truths rather than step-by-step reasoning</note>. And together with God and knowledge, there also follows a turning toward ourselves and a recognition of our own nature. Truly, you suspect in vain that perhaps the religious man depends on human opinions and favors. For what leisure can there be for a soul devoted to the gods to listen to human praise?

### That Religion is True.

But neither are you right to doubt what follows—fearing perhaps that the religious man himself is deceived—where you say the soul often imagines great things out of chance circumstances. For what beginning can there be for figments of the imagination among things that truly exist? Is it not the **imaginative power** <term>phantastica</term> <note>The faculty of "phantasia" or imagination was often viewed by Neoplatonists as a lower power that could produce deceptive images, whereas the higher Intellect perceives reality directly</note> within us that fashions and transforms idols? And when the intellectual life acts perfectly, no imagination arises. Does not truth itself exist according to its essence among the gods, together with them? Is not that truth which is founded upon the harmony of intelligible things even more real? Therefore, such things are spread by you and others in vain. Furthermore, when you and others slander religious men as if they were sorcerers, empty, and boastful, you depart further from the truth. For just as in other arts, so also in religion there are those who falsely profess it. Such a profession departs further from religion than anything else; for evil is more contrary to the good than it is to that which is merely "not good."

### Concerning natural, artificial, and divine foreknowledge.

If any natural aptitude is implanted in us for the **foretelling of the future** <note>original: *præsagium*; a presentiment or "pre-sense" of what is to come</note>—just as animals possess a natural foreknowledge of earthquakes, storms, and cold—such a pre-knowledge does not seem to possess anything venerable. For such a natural foretelling follows from a sharpness of the senses, or a shared feeling, or some other agitation of natural powers. Nor does it seem that such a presence is particularly honorable if one predicts through the discourse of reason or the observation of preceding signs—just as doctors are accustomed to foresee a fever by the contraction of the pulse and by shivering. For such things proceed from a human, suspect, and corporeal condition. Therefore, only that prophecy which arrives by divine means truly exhibits the divine life to us, since it possesses both foresight and divine understandings. It renders us truly divine and brings to us a legitimate good; for the most blessed intelligence of the gods is filled abundantly with all goods. Perhaps you will suspect that prophets inspired by the divine foresee the future, yet are not happy because of it? For they can foresee, yet not know the futur[e]...

### The Way to Happiness.

¶ You asked then what the way to happiness is, and in what thing happiness itself consists. Listen then to this: man is himself an **intellect** <note>original: *intellectus*; refers to the higher, intuitive part of the mind capable of direct perception of truth</note> capable of contemplation; he was once joined to the contemplation of the gods. But afterward, he entered another soul, fitted and tempered to the human form, and because of this, he is bound in the chain of necessity and fate. It is fitting, therefore, to consider by what reasoning he might be released from such chains. There is no solution except the knowledge of the gods themselves. For the "idea" or essence of happiness is to know the **Good** itself. Just as the essence of evils is the forgetting of the good and a fallacy concerning evil, that higher knowledge meets together with the divine. But this forgetfulness and deception is inseparable from that which is perishable. Likewise, that knowledge rightly measures the essences of intelligible things through the sacred ways of holiness. But this soul, falling from its principles and being repulsed, casts itself down to measure the material world. The former, again, is the recognition of one's own parent; the latter is a departure, a state of being far removed and forgotten by God the Father, who is above all and self-sufficient. The former preserves the true life, calling it back to the Father; the latter leads man, the prince of creation, down to that which never remains the same and is turned in a perpetual flux. Let this be your first path to happiness: possessing the intellectual fullness of **divine union** <note>original: *unionis divinæ*; the goal of theurgy, where the soul is unified with the divine source</note> within souls. The sacred and deifying tradition of happiness is called the gate to the Creator-God of all, or the place, the <unclear>courts and</unclear> hall, of the Good. It possesses its first power through the chaste and sober holiness of the soul, which is far more useful than the sober chastity of the body. Then follows the adaptation of thought to the participation and vision of the Good, and simultaneously the expulsion of contraries. Thirdly, it exhibits union with the gods, the givers of all goods. Afterward, specifically and properly, it extends to the parts of the world, and to the di...

<header>ON THE MYSTERIES</header>

...to the divine powers diffused throughout the parts of the world, then it joins the soul to the whole **Craftsman** <term>Craftsman: original *opifex*, the Latin equivalent of the Greek *Demiurge*, the divine "Architect" or creator of the material world</term>. It offers agreement with Him from every side, and places the soul outside of all matter, now joined with the sole eternal universe. For example: in that power of the Craftsman which is self-generated, self-moving, sustaining all things entirely, elevating, and intellectual, and which similarly adorns all things. Likewise, being called back to the intelligible truth—which is perfected through itself and is both the perfecter and the maker—the soul is fitted to the other powers of the Craftsman-God, step by step, according to the property of each. This is done so that in their actions, their understandings, and their creative faculties, the purified and sacred soul may be perfectly strengthened. And then, finally, he places the soul within God, the complete Craftsman.

### Conclusion on Religion and Happiness among the Egyptians.

<margin>a</margin>
And here, among the Egyptians, is the end of the religious and sacred elevation. They believe the Divine Good itself to be one thing—namely, the God who is understood beforehand—while the Human Good is another: specifically, union with that same Lord. This is as the prophet **Bytis** <note>Bytis is a legendary Egyptian priest mentioned in Hermetic literature as having translated the secrets of Hermes</note> explained from the **Books of Mercury** <note>original: *libris mercurialibus*; these refer to the "Hermetica," sacred texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, whom the Romans identified with the god Mercury</note>. Therefore, this part of the path has not been overlooked by the Egyptians, as you suspect, but has been duly handed down to us as it pertains to sanctity. Nor do the priests disturb the divine intellect regarding trivial matters, but rather regarding those things which pertain to the purification, release, and salvation of the soul; they do not meditate on difficult things that are useless to men. On the contrary, they focus on the most useful matters of the soul. Nor do the priests hallucinate, clouded by some deceitful and seductive **daemon** <term>daemon: in this context, a lesser spirit or supernatural being that could be either helpful or deceptive, distinct from the higher gods</term>; for they entirely transcend the deceptive and demonic nature in all things and ascend to the intellectual and divine nature. Now that these matters have been treated, I beseech the gods to grant me and you the true guardianship and observance of the intellects, which shall never fail at any time, and to provide the truth for everlasting eternity. May they make us masters of the more perfect understandings concerning the gods, in which the most blessed end of all good things is set before us, as well as all the authority and foundation of friendship and mutual harmony between us.
