<header>PROCLUS</header>

### Excerpts by Marsilio Ficino from the Greek commentaries of Proclus on the first *Alcibiades* of Plato.

The most important and firmest principle of the Platonic dialogues and of all philosophy is considered to be the **knowledge of our own nature** <term>knowledge of our own nature: original *naturae nostrae cognitionem*; the famous Delphic command "Know Thyself" interpreted as the starting point for understanding the universe</term>. For once this is rightly known, we will be able to know more absolutely the good that is consistent with us, and the evil that is at odds with us. It is so arranged by nature that just as the essences of things differ among themselves, so too do the perfections proper to those things. Therefore, so that we may find what the perfection of our nature is and how it is obtained, we must first of all recognize our own essence. This indeed is the goal proposed in the *Alcibiades* and is the end of the entire doctrine of Plato.

When we consider the essences of things, we must investigate whether the essence of a thing is among those which are **individual** <note>original: *individuae*; here meaning "indivisible" or "singular," referring to purely intellectual or divine things</note>, or of the kind that are divided around bodies, or those placed in the middle. Likewise, we must ask whether the essence is eternal, or existing throughout all time, or if it comes to be in some specific part of time. Again, whether it is simple and existing before composition, or whether it is composite—perhaps composed with insoluble bonds, or able to be resolved back into the elements from which it is composed. And if we consider each thing in this way, we will then be able more easily to judge what its good might be. For it is certain that for an entirely indivisible essence, the good is eternal; but for a divisible essence, the good is also involved in time and motion. Finally, for a **middle essence** <term>middle essence: refers to the Soul, which Neoplatonists believed occupied a middle ground between the eternal, indivisible Intellect and the temporal, divisible physical world</term>, its perfection is weighed according to the measure of its own substance; for such a perfection requires time, but "first time," which can be aptly measured into bodily circuits.

Indeed, we are ignorant of ourselves, because we are occupied by **forgetfulness of birth** <note>original: *oblivione genesica*; the Neoplatonic idea that the soul loses its memory of the divine realm upon entering a physical body</note> and struck by the disturbance of life among rational forms. Meanwhile, we think we know many things of which we are ignorant, because we possess the **reasons of things** <note>original: *rerum rationes*; the innate "logoi" or blueprints of reality that the soul carries within itself</note> as innate to our essence. There are three types of **conversion** <term>conversion: original *conversio* (Greek *epistrophe*); the process of a being turning its attention or motion toward a specific level of reality</term>. For whatever is converted is either turned toward something worse than itself while slipping from its own perfection; or it rises toward something better through the vigor of its own life and natural action; or it is reflected back toward itself through a knowledge harmonious with itself, which is the middle type of motion. Conversion toward the worse is a kind of suffering for the soul, which casts off its wings and is placed in forgetfulness both of itself and of higher things. But conversion both toward itself and toward the better belongs not only to souls but also to the divine beings themselves, as **Parmenides** <note>Parmenides: a pre-Socratic philosopher who is the subject of one of Plato’s most difficult and influential metaphysical dialogues</note> himself teaches us.

Plato signifies in the preface, among other things, that the soul studious of truth produces cognitions harmonious with the things to be known. It does not produce an immutable knowledge of mutable things, nor an ambiguous and wavering knowledge of necessary and stable things. But as he taught **Socrates** in the *Republic*, knowledge should be simple and

->uniform<-

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s translation and commentary on the Neoplatonic philosopher Proclus. While the previous page established that self-knowledge is the foundation of philosophy, this page explores the different levels of human knowledge and introduces the "Order of Love" (Eros) as a mediating force that connects the human soul to the divine. It draws heavily on Plato’s dialogues, specifically the *Timaeus*, *Cratylus*, and *Symposium*.</meta>

<header>ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.</header>

...to know all intellectual things joined together by a uniform intellectual power. But through scientific and cogitative knowledge, by the unfolding of species and the composition of **principles** <note>original: *rationes*; in this context, it refers to the "Logoi" or the rational blueprints of things</note>, one contemplates the intermediate reasons of things. Third, by a power of the senses that turns away from truth, one judges sensible things through their own appropriate cognitive instruments. Finally, by the power of the imagination, one apprehends the images of sensible things. 

Now, in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the creation of the universe</note>, when distinguishing the types of knowledge by a certain proportion to the things to be known, he commands us to judge beings by intelligence and reason; however, those things which are not truly beings, but are constantly becoming and perishing, are to be judged by opinion and sense. He states that the principles of those things which truly exist are fixed and absolute, while the principles of things flowing in the realm of "generation" <note>the physical world of change and birth</note> are imaginary and contingent. For everywhere, principles and discourses imitate the very things they explain. 

Furthermore, Socrates says in the *Cratylus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the origin of names and language</note> that concerning eternal things, names touch more closely upon the nature of the thing; but concerning changeable things, the names themselves often change and are based more on convention. 

Among the other gods, different properties exist everywhere. For some are the craftsmen of the universe and the creators of the species of beings, giving substance to the world's adornment. Others propagate life and bring forth various vital energies. Others still preserve the unchanging order of the king and guard the indissoluble connection of all things. Finally, others, having been allotted different powers, preserve all things through their own particular beneficence. 

In a similar way, the entire **order of Love** <term>order of Love: original *amatorius ordo*; the Neoplatonic concept of Eros as a cosmic force that draws the soul back to the Divine</term> is the cause of "conversion" <note>the process of the soul turning away from the material world and back toward its divine source</note> for all things toward divine beauty and form. It leads all things that follow back to that beauty, joining them to it, and strengthening them once they are joined. It then fills the things that follow from that source, radiating the gifts of divine light proceeding from there through all things. 

For this reason, it is taught in the *Symposium* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the nature of Love</note> that Love is a great **spirit** <note>original: *dæmonem*; not an evil "demon," but a *daimon*, a mediating spiritual being that bridges the gap between gods and humans</note>. This is because Love, the first of all such things, demonstrates this mediating power in himself. He stands in the middle between the object of desire and the one who desires, and is the cause of the turning of later things back toward earlier things. 

Therefore, the entire "amatory cohort," stationed in the vestibule of the Cause of Beauty, calls all things to it. It creates a middle passage between that which is lovable and those things which are recalled by love. Because of this, Love reveals in himself the pattern of the entire "daemonic" or spiritual order, holding this middle position among divine things which the spirits hold between the divine and the mortal. 

Since, therefore, every amatory cohort possesses this property among the gods, we conceive of its single and hidden summit as being joined to the first and intelligible beauty among the supreme gods. Its middle progression shines with an intellectual character among the "supramundane" <note>existing above the physical world</note> gods. Its third progression is distributed in many ways around the world, producing many orders and powers from itself and distributing these gifts to the different parts of the world. After the unique and first principle of Love, and after the tripartite substance [proceeding] from there...

# PROCLUS:

...now a varied crowd of **Loves** <note>original: *amorum*; referring to the different levels of Eros or desire for the divine</note> shines forth. From this source, choirs of angels [shine] with the splendor of love. Even the throngs of demons, full of this god, follow the gods, having been called back toward intelligible beauty. The army of heroes, together with demons and angels, revel wildly around beauty. Finally, all things are stirred up, revived, flourish again, and grow warm around the influx of beauty itself. Indeed, the souls of men, touched by such inspiration and naturally known to God, are moved constantly around beauty and descend into the province of **generation** <note>original: *generationis*; the physical world of birth, death, and change</note> to provide a benefit to more imperfect souls, and to provide for those things that seem to need salvation. The gods themselves and the attendants of the gods, remaining in their own proper state, do good to those who follow them and turn them toward themselves; but the souls of men, having fallen downward and touching the realm of generation, display the beneficial providence of the gods to the best of their ability. 

Therefore, just as some souls, established according to one god or another, purely oversee the falling provinces and the souls wandering here—and some indeed benefit the more imperfect through prophecy, others through expiations and sacrifices, others through divine methods of healing—so also the souls that have chosen the "amatory life" <note>a life dedicated to the pursuit of Beauty</note> are moved by the presiding god of beauties toward the care of gifted souls. From the beauty appearing to the senses, they are led back to divine beauty, calling their beloved ones together with themselves. But those souls which, due to a perverse education, fall away from the celestial gift—though they have otherwise obtained an amatory nature—falling into the images of beauty, they admire and love bodily forms because of their ignorance of true beauty, being ignorant of their own nature. For just as with **Plotinus** <note>the 3rd-century philosopher who systematized Neoplatonism</note>, the downward flow of the mind creates cunning, and a fallen portion of wisdom creates the **sophistical art** <note>deceptive or superficial wisdom</note>, so also the gift of love, falling into an impure vessel, creates an intemperate and tyrannical life.

## A superior cause acts upon a work before and after an inferior one, and acts together with it and is more present to the work.

<margin>q</margin> Things that are more perfect everywhere, and which have the character of an exemplar <note>an original pattern or blueprint</note>, utterly encompass the actions of [their] images. So much so that inferior things are nowhere present to anything to which more perfect things have not also, much earlier, handed over something from themselves. He who is the **One** itself <note>original: *ipsum unum*; the ultimate, transcendent source of all existence in Neoplatonism</note> also encompasses other things through all the orders of things, and acts before them, after them, and together with them.

## Evil demons also appear in sacred rites and deceive under the pretext of good things.

<margin>c</margin> We find it ready at hand in expiations and sacred rites that something from the inferior realms everywhere puts on an image of perfection, through which it may entice souls not yet perfected to itself and divert them from higher things. Therefore, just as in physical contemplation the "sophistical life" is an impediment to divine...

...and drawing that weaker part away from the contemplation of true beings toward the imagination familiar with falling things; thus, in the "elevation of love," the crowd of popular lovers acts as an impediment, pretending to be a true lover and twisting the soul of the youth away from heavenly goods toward the earthly and dark. Similarly, in all the most holy purifications and sacred rites, before the god himself is openly present, certain spirits of earthly demons rush to meet us; these strange sights disturb those being purified and perfected, turning them away from pure goods toward **matter**. For this reason, the gods command that you should not look upon them until you have shielded your eyes with the power of the sacred rite. For thus say the divine oracles: <note>likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles</note> "It is not profitable for you to look upon them before you have purified and consecrated your body. Since they, by soothing the souls, everywhere turn them away from the sacrifices." Just as in the sacred rites the divine first appears only when we have driven out all this demonic influence that drags souls toward matter, so too the divine lover meets the beloved only after the rejection of popular lovers. Likewise, just as the good spirit of each person guards them from childhood and examines all their actions and words, providing for them even before their parents and remaining present after their parents as a constant governor of their whole life—and after death is our guide to the judges—in the same way, Socrates conducts himself toward **Alcibiades** <note>the famous Athenian statesman and student of Socrates</note>. Finally, just as the good spirit is present to us, mostly hidden, providing for us secretly and counseling us in silence, and correcting us ineffably, so Socrates acts toward Alcibiades.

->**The Intellect in us is always active by illuminating, yet we do not always notice it.**<-

For then the Intellect shines upon us; then it speaks as if with us; then it communicates its voice to us, though it was previously present in silence.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s commentary on Plato’s "First Alcibiades." Previously, Proclus described how a divine lover like Socrates serves as a protective guide, mirroring the role of a "good spirit" (daemon). He now transitions into a metaphysical explanation of why Socrates holds this role, comparing the relationship between Socrates and Alcibiades to the relationship between the Intellect and the Soul.</meta>

# PROCLUS

...man as himself, and now man as a governor, not simply as a man or a charioteer. In general, that which is **unparticipated** differs from that which is **participated** <term>In Neoplatonism, an "unparticipated" principle is a higher, pure source that remains distinct and transcendent, while a "participated" principle is the version of that quality that actually enters into and mixes with lower things</term>. Furthermore, that which exists according to itself differs from that which is already considered together with something else. And finally, that which is transcendent differs from that which has been assigned a shared rank with another. 

Since, therefore, Alcibiades is understood in two ways—both as soul simply, and as a soul using a body—in the sense that he is simply a certain soul, Socrates stands in the place of **Intellect** toward him. But in the sense that he is a soul using a body, Socrates plays the part of a **good spirit** <note>original: *boni daemonis*; a guardian spirit or guiding divinity</note>. And he himself is both a spirit (in relation to the man) and an intellect (in relation to the soul). Indeed, when we consider the intermediary nature of spirits, we place them between gods and men. But when we consider the Intellect, we suspend the soul from the Intellect itself as its highest point, and the body from the soul. You have, in fact, one division in the *Symposium* <note>referring to Plato's dialogue on love</note>, where it is taught that spirits exist as a medium between gods and men; you have another in the *Timaeus* stating that the soul holds the middle place between the Intellect and the body. Therefore, the same entity is both Intellect and spirit: toward the soul it is considered Intellect, but toward the human soul it is considered a spirit.

->How the god Love is neither the first nor the last, and how in divine things there are the Good, the Wise, and the Beautiful, as well as Faith, Truth, and Love.<-

<margin>a</margin> We ought to place Love, the master, neither among the first of beings nor among the last. Not among the first, because the **Beloved** <note>original: *amabile*; the object worthy of love</note> is superior to Love itself. Not among the last, because the lover is a participant in love. It is necessary, therefore, to establish Love between the Beloved and the lover, and to assert that it is posterior to **Beauty** itself, but prior to all those things that love. 

Where, then, did Love originate from the beginning? In what way does it proceed through the universe, and with what "unities" did it come forth? Since there are three substances among the intelligible and hidden gods: the first is marked by the **Good**—meaning it understands the Good itself from within itself—where, as the sacred oracles teach, the paternal unity resides. The second is designated by the **Wise**, where the first intelligence flourishes. The third is defined by the **Beautiful**, where the most beautiful of intelligible things exists, as the *Timaeus* says. Surely, three unities also exist according to these intelligible causes; they consist uniformly in the intelligible realm according to their cause, but they shine forth first in that ineffable order of the gods as **Faith**, **Truth**, and **Love**. 

**Faith** establishes all things in the Good. **Truth** unfolds all knowledge in existing things. Finally, **Love** turns all things back and gathers them into the nature of Beauty itself. Truly, a trinity of this kind proceeds from here through all the [orders of the gods]...

### ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.

...orders and irradiates all things toward the intelligible itself, in union. In another way, however, he declares himself through other orders, everywhere folding his powers into God and his specific properties. In one place, indeed, he exists ineffably, unknowingly, and uniquely. In another, by the principle of containment and connection. In another, as if perfecting and forming; here again, intellectually and paternally. There, he is entirely moving, life-giving, and effective. In that place, as if impressing and assimilating; there, absolutely, deeply, and purely. In that other place, already multiplied and divided. Therefore, **Love** descends from the higher intelligible realms <term>intelligible realms: the highest level of reality in Neoplatonism, consisting of pure ideas or truths that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</term> down to the worldly things, calling all things together toward divine beauty. **Truth** also proceeds <margin>p</margin> through all things, illuminating everything with forms of knowledge; **Faith** proceeds through the universe, establishing all things individually in the Good. Here, the divine oracles teach that all things are governed by these three—Love, Truth, and Faith—and consist in them <note>This "trinity" of Love, Truth, and Faith is a central concept in Proclus’s philosophy, acting as the three links that bind the soul to the divine</note>. For this reason, the gods command those who sacrifice to join themselves to God through a trinity of this kind. The intelligible beings themselves, because of their inestimable unity, do not need the medium of Love. But where there is both a unity of beings and a distinction, there Love exists; for he is the binder and reconciler of those things which are after him and those which are above him. He is the one who turns following things toward the prior, and is the leader-back and perfecter of the imperfect.

**Providence** runs through individual things down to the very smallest, and yet remains unattached to any.

<margin>q</margin> Those who are more diligent in assigning reasons to the King <note>original: *rege*; likely referring to the supreme "One" or the Demiurge who rules the cosmos</note> hand down these two most powerful elements of divine and spirit-like providence:

First, that providence proceeds from above through all things down to the very last, and does not omit even the smallest thing from sharing in itself. Second, that it receives absolutely nothing from the things it governs, nor is it filled by their nature, nor is it mixed with them anywhere. For it is not because it preserves and disposes all things that it is therefore mixed with the things it governs. For the nature of the divine and of the spirits <note>original: *daemonum*; intermediary beings between gods and humans</note> is not subject to the "passions" or emotions of individual souls. Nor, however, while it separately towers over the things that follow it, does it therefore leave anything among the lower things disordered or uncultivated. On the contrary, for this very reason, it adorns all things fittingly and remains free from the things it dispenses. For it is equally beneficent and pure, the adorner of all, and meanwhile remains unhindered by the things it has cultivated. It runs through all things, especially because it is nowhere restrained. Furthermore, even divine men provide for lower things most diligently and at the same time tranquilly. What, then, must be said about the gods themselves and the good spirits? Are they not present to all things yet free from all things? Filling all things with themselves, they are mixed with nothing anywhere; running through the universe, they have nowhere surrendered their own life. Shall we not confess that the gods love their own offspring? Just as the poets imagine that **Jupiter** loves a girl, and even **Venus** herself. Naturally, because love of this kind is a provider, a preserver, a perfecter, and a contain...

# PROCLVS

...uniter, divinely loved. Meanwhile, he is both beneficent and sincere, and uninvolved with external things through any habit. Tell me, please, from where did such a privilege of love come to the souls of men on their journey to the divine, unless it first existed in the gods themselves? For whatever good and health-giving thing belongs to souls has a cause determined by the gods. Wherefore Plato proves that the archetypes <note>original: *exemplaria* — the perfect, divine blueprints of things found in the physical world</note> of all virtues and bodily goods—such as health, strength, justice, and temperance—precede us in the presence of God. How much more, then, shall we confess that the principal cause of the gift of love exists among the gods. Indeed, since this affection of love, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the soul, beauty, and rhetoric</note>, is granted as a certain divine gift. Therefore, the gods love gods; the elder indeed love the lesser by the gift of providence, while in turn the lesser love the greater by a certain duty of conversion <note>original: *conuersionis* — the Neoplatonic concept of 'epistrophe', where the soul turns back toward its divine source</note>. To perfect what is lower and to provide for inferior things belongs also to souls, insofar as they are souls; for they descend for this very reason: for the providence of things that can be generated and for the care of mortals. But to provide in such a way that you, the provider, are not mixed with those you govern, nor affected like one enslaved, nor receive anything from them, is characteristic of the gods and good spirits <term>dæmonum: here referring to 'daimones', intermediary spirits that bridge the gap between gods and humans, not malevolent demons</term>; and whenever this happens to human souls, it happens by divine or spiritual bounty. Priests are accustomed in the holiest sacrifices, either through words or through things shown to the eyes, to lead those present into admiration and awe <note>original: *stuporēm* — a state of being overwhelmed by the presence of the divine</note>. For awe is accustomed to expose the soul to God. Socrates would never have lived a life of love so correctly had he not chosen it by the breath of a spirit <note>A reference to Socrates's *daimonion*, a private divine sign or voice that guided his actions</note> and held to that choice.

->Amor is the middle between the lovable and the lover; it is a great spirit binding all things together, and whatever things desire, it—as the medium—couples them first to the object of desire.<-

<margin>8</margin> Therefore, the sacred oracles <note>original: *Acra eloquia*, likely a typo for *Sacra eloquia*</note> declare this love of the Lord to be that which binds all things together, residing in all things; it holily connects all things and joins us to the ranks of the spirits. Diotima <note>The wise woman in Plato's *Symposium* who instructs Socrates on the nature of Love</note> called this a "great spirit," since it fills every middle space between those who desire and that which is desired. That which is to be loved claims the first rank for itself. The lover, however, takes the third rank from the beloved. Finally, Love occupies the middle between both, gathering and binding together the desirer and the desired into one, and filling the lower with the better.

Now, among the intelligible and hidden gods, Love unites the intelligible intellect to the first and secret beauty through a life that is better than intelligence itself. Therefore, the theologian of the Greeks <note>Usually a reference to Orpheus, the legendary poet-prophet</note> himself calls that Love "blind." In those things that are outside the intelligible realms, it does not yet illuminate the indissoluble bond, perfected for all things by him. For the bond...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Love (Eros) as a unifying force that connects the different levels of reality. It transitions from the previous page's focus on the divine origin of love to its specific functions across the hierarchy of existence: gods, spirits, and human souls.</meta>

-># ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT<-

it is a certain union, but one that contains much distinction within that unity. For this reason, the sacred scriptures <note>original: *eloquā sacra* — likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles, which were highly regarded by Neoplatonists</note> are accustomed to call the uniter by the fire of this love. For proceeding from the intelligible intellect, it binds all subsequent things to each other and to that source.

It therefore reconciles all the gods to intelligible beauty, then joins the spirits to the gods, and finally joins us to the spirits and the gods. In the gods, Love exists in the first degree; in the spirits <term>dæmonibus: 'daimones' or intermediary spirits, not to be confused with modern concepts of evil demons</term> in the second; and in individual souls in the third degree, through a certain procession stemming from the first principles. Again, in the gods, it exists above essence, for the entire race of gods is of that nature. In spirits, however, it exists through their essence. Finally, in souls, it exists through the effect of illumination. And this threefold order seems similar to the threefold power of the Intellect. For one Intellect is "imparticipable" <note>original: *imparticipabilis* — a philosophical term for a source that remains pure and distinct from the things that derive from it</note>, absolute and set apart from all particular kinds. Another is "participated," of which the souls of the gods share as something better than themselves. Yet another is infused by this into souls, and this is truly the perfection of the souls themselves. Plato himself indicates these three aspects of the Intellect in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the cosmos</note>. Therefore, understand that the love implanted in the gods is consistent with the imparticipable Intellect; for it is absolute, both in itself and in all things that receive from it and are illuminated by it. Compare the spirit-like <note>original: *dæmonicum*</note> love to the participated Intellect. For it is also essential and perfect in itself, like a pre-participated intellect dwelling most closely within souls. Finally, you must assign the third kind of love—the one infused into souls by illumination—to the Intellect received according to habit <note>original: *secundum habitū* — a state or disposition of the soul</note>. Not without reason do we consider Love to be joined to the entire intellectual difference. For in the intelligible Intellect, Love holds the first and hidden substance. For if it came forth from there, it is also established there through that substance. And it seems to me that Plato found this god in the works of Orpheus <note>The legendary poet and prophet whose hymns formed the basis of Orphic mystery traditions</note>, where the same being is called both Love and a Great Spirit, and Plato himself seems to have been satisfied with this hymn. Justly, then, does Diotima <note>The priestess in Plato’s *Symposium* who teaches Socrates about the nature of Love</note> call Love a "Great Spirit" <note>original: *magnum dæmonem*</note>. And Socrates, where he disputes concerning love, also disputes concerning spirits.

This essence is more intellectual for those who possess a greater and more perfect substance, but less intellectual and rather more "rational" for those who possess the middle rank. Those of the third and last rank of the spirit-order have a more varied and rational na—

# PROCLUS:

...and material nature. Established in such a substance, they are divided among the gods in equal measure, acting as ministers to the gods. For they respond and serve in one way to the gods who are entirely absolute <note>original: *absolutis* — referring to the "hypercosmic" gods who exist beyond the physical universe</note>, who begin and lead all things before the world existed; but they serve in another way to the mundane gods <note>Gods who oversee the physical cosmos</note> who immediately preside over parts of the world, and who are distributed according to the twelve celestial gods. These spirits are distributed according to all the properties of the mundane gods. For every mundane god commands a certain order of spirits, to which he imparts his own power because they are close to him. 

For the <term>Demiurge: the "Craftsman" god who fashioned the universe</term> grants a creative power; an unchanging god provides an unpollutable faculty; a perfecter likewise provides a perfecting power. And around each god is an innumerable multitude of spirits, which bear the same names as their divine leaders. Indeed, they are pleased when they are called Apollos, Mercuries, or Jupiters, since they express the properties of their own gods within themselves. Accordingly, through these spirits, mortal things obtain divine influences; thus plants and animals are created, some reflecting the images of one god, some of another. To these, the spirits grant the gifts of their leaders from close at hand, while the gods, presiding from above the spirits, do so more eminently.

Therefore, the lowest things sympathize with the highest in their experiences. For the marks of the first things are found in the last, and the causes of the last are contained in the first. Indeed, the middle ranks of spirits fill all things and connect them at once, holding the union of all things together; while they participate in the gods, they are in turn participated in by transient things. If anyone should say that the Craftsman of the universe established the fabric of the whole order within the spirits, he will not wander from the truth. Since even Diotima <note>The wise woman in Plato's *Symposium* who explains the nature of Love to Socrates</note> attributed this order to them—connecting divine and mortal things, drawing down the flowing fluids from above, referring all following things back to the gods, and finally filling the universe according to the connection of this very mediation.

### *He refutes two opinions: one saying there are no other spirits besides our souls released from a more solid body; and the second, the view of Amelius, who thinks that spirits are some kind of straying gods.*

Therefore, we shall not accept those who say that spirits are our souls, having fulfilled their state and moved into another. For it is not fitting to equate a spirit considered by "habit" <note>original: *habitu* — here meaning a temporary condition or acquired state of the soul</note> with one that is a spirit by its very essence; nor is it fitting to establish the eternal mediation of all mundane things from a manifold life that changes itself. For that spiritual guardianship itself stands always in the same way, keeping the whole universe continuous. The soul, however, does not retain its order in this way, as Socrates says in the *Re-*

Nor will we again approve of those who think some of the gods are spirits, as if they were "erratic" or wandering gods, as Amelius <note>Amelius Gentilianus, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> thinks. ### On familiar spirits. Likewise, he counts five kinds of spirits and their various duties.

Since therefore spirits are established in the middle, as we said, the first and highest among them are divine spirits; they frequently appear as gods because of their excellent similarity to the gods. Truly, the first member of any order reflects the form of the order above it. For the <term>Intellect: the divine mind or *nous*</term> presents itself as if it were a god, and the oldest part of souls is intellectual in nature. Therefore, the highest genus of spirits, being next to the gods, is uniform and divine. 

The second after these are spirits already endowed with an "intellectual" property, presiding over the ascents and descents [of souls], and declaring and handing down the works of the gods to all. 

The third are the spirits who distribute the effects of divine souls into the things that follow them; they complete the bond of those who receive the divine flow, and from there, the flow descends to them. 

The fourth transmit the effective powers of universal natures into "generable" things <note>Things that are born and subject to change, as opposed to eternal things</note>, and they inspire life, order, and rational principles, as well as the whole production of mortal things into particular natures. 

The fifth are in a way "corporeal" <note>Physical or body-like</note>, and they bind together the outer limits of bodies.

For in what way could eternal bodies ever harmonize with those that are falling and transient? How could the causes agree with the effects, unless a middle ground of this kind joined them together? For a nature of this middle kind rules over the well-being of bodies and provides for all natural abundances. Most of their number are occupied with matter; they contain and weave together the powers descending from above—from celestial matter into physical matter—and they thereafter guard it and preserve the variety and the "painting" <note>original: *picturam* — referring to the diverse appearances and characteristics of physical forms</note> of forms within it.

### The five offices of spirits; the first spirits join souls to their own gods.

Since therefore spirits are many and multiform, as Diotima says, the highest indeed join the souls proceeding from the Father <note>The Demiurge or Creator</note> to the gods who are their leaders. For every god leads spirits first, and then particular souls. Just as the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe</note> says, the god who is the maker of these things sowed some souls in the sun, others in the moon, and others in other gods.

# PROCLUS

Indeed, there are divine spirits who have obtained souls according to their essence and join them to their own leaders <note>Original: "ducibus"; these are the "leader-gods" who head various ranks of the divine hierarchy</note>. And every soul, even if it revolves around its own god, needs the benefit of such a spirit. For spirits manage the ascents and descents of souls, and it is through them that the choices of life are distributed to souls. 

Truly, those most perfect souls who live their lives in the world of <term>Generation: the physical world of birth, change, and death</term> without being entangled in its commerce, have chosen a life consistent with their own god. Thus, they live according to a divine spirit, who joined them to their own god while they were still dwelling among the higher beings. It was for this reason that the Egyptian priest admired Plotinus <note>A reference to a story in Porphyry’s *Life of Plotinus* where an Egyptian priest tried to evoke Plotinus’s guardian spirit in a temple, only to find it was a god, not a lower spirit</note>, as he was governed by a certain divine spirit. Therefore, concerning souls who live their life here as if they are soon to return to the heights, the spirit here is the same as the one above. However, concerning less perfect souls, the spirit that is theirs by essence is one thing, while the one that accompanies their newly manifest life is another.

---

->A spirit is defined in three ways: by **essence**, by **comparison**, or by a certain **disposition**.<-

---

<margin>8</margin>
If these points are correctly established, no one should now agree with those who say our rational soul is a spirit. For a spirit is something other than a human, as Diotima <note>The priestess from Plato's *Symposium* who describes spirits as the "interpreters" between gods and men</note> teaches, placing spirits between gods and men. This is also what Socrates himself signifies when he distinguishes between a human cause and a spiritual cause, saying: "It was not a human cause, but a spiritual obstacle <note>Original: "daemonicum obstaculum"; the *daimonion* or "divine sign" that Socrates claimed spoke to him</note> that held me back." Since a human is a soul using a body, the spirit and the rational soul should not be thought of as the same thing. 

Now, this is also manifest where Plato, in the *Timaeus*, says that the spirit is the faculty of reason established within us. However, we must only accept this in the sense of a certain **comparison**. For a spirit by essence is one thing, a spirit by comparison another, and a spirit by disposition or habit yet another. 

Everywhere, it is the custom to call "spirit" that which stands immediately above an inferior thing in a certain spiritual order. By this usage, Jupiter <note>Original: "Iuppiter," referring to Zeus</note> in the works of Orpheus called his father Saturn <note>Original: "Saturnum," referring to Cronus</note> a spirit; and Plato himself in the *Timaeus* called those gods who manage the immediate work of generation "spirits," where he says: "To speak of other spirits and to bring their generation into the light is a task greater than human genius can bear." 

A spirit by **comparison** is of this sort: namely, one that provides for each thing immediately, even if it is a god, or even if it is inferior to a god. But a soul is called a spirit by a certain **disposition** when, through some marvelous similarity to the spiritual genus, it produces actions that exceed the human level and suspends its entire life from that spirit.

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT
<note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE"</note>

By this reasoning, I believe Socrates, in the *Republic*, called those souls **spirits** <note>original: "daemonas"</note> who have lived their lives well and have been transferred to a better lot, now dwelling in more venerable places. Finally, the spirit itself, according to its essence, is not called a "spirit" because of its relationship to what follows it, nor because of some similarity to another, but it has obtained this property through itself; it is distinguished in its existence by its own powers and different modes of action. Indeed, in the *Timaeus*, the rational soul is called an "animal spirit." We, however, are investigating the spirit of the human being himself—not the spirit of the living creature <note>original: "animalis"; referring to the composite of soul and body</note>, but the one who directs the rational soul, and who is not merely its instrument. This is the one who eventually leads the soul, once freed from the living creature, to the judges. As Socrates asserts in the *Phaedo*, when the living creature no longer exists, the spirit leads each person to the judge—specifically, the spirit who had been allotted to that person while they were still living. For if the spirit found the person while living, and brings them to judgment after death, it clearly found more than just the animal body. Indeed, starting from above and commanding from there, it governs our entire constitution.

->Those who argue against the spirit being either a working part of the soul, or a part set over it.<-

<margin>8</margin> But those people are also not to be approved of who, having dismissed the rational soul, say the spirit is simply that which works within the soul—as if, in those living according to reason, reason itself were the spirit; but in those living by anger, the "irascible" <note>the part of the soul associated with spiritedness or anger</note> part were the spirit; and in those living by desire, the "concupiscible" <term>Concupiscible: the part of the soul traditionally associated with physical appetites and desires</term> part were the spirit. Nor should we listen to those who say the spirit is that which, in our life, presides most closely over whatever is active—as if reason presided over the angry, or the power of anger presided over the lustful. To begin with, to say that spirits are parts of the human soul belongs to those who admire human life too much, and who do not approve of Socrates in the *Republic*, who arranges the heroic and human race after the gods and spirits. He rebukes the poets for introducing heroes as being no better than men, but enslaved to similar passions. Therefore, Socrates, in rebuking such things, would be far removed from the opinion that spirits—who are superior to heroes—should be placed among the parts and powers of the soul. For from these ideas it would follow that the spirit, which is better by its essence, would receive inferior things inside itself to be complete. Furthermore, changes in lifestyle would bring about various changes in the spirits. For a greedy man is often changed into an ambitious life; an ambitious man into a state of living by right opinion; and this man into a state endowed with knowledge. The spirit would therefore be first one thing, then another. For the active part itself in the soul exists as one thing at one time and another at another. If, therefore, either this working part or the part presiding closely over it were the spirit, then without a doubt, the spirits would change alongside the changes in human life; and indeed, within the same life, there would be many

### PROCLUS.

The same soul will not obtain different spirits <note>original: "daemones"</note>, which could in no way happen. For a soul never changes its spirit’s leadership within the same course of life. Instead, the same spirit governs us from our very birth until we stand before the judge of life. As Socrates asserts in the *Phaedo* <note>The *Phaedo* is Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul</note>.

A spirit is not a particular intellect, but a substance differing from the intellect, placed within the breadth <note>original: "latitudine"; referring to a specific rank or "level" in the Neoplatonic hierarchy</note> of souls.

***

**T**herefore, those who think that a particular intellect is the same as the spirit <note>original: "daemonem"</note> allotted to us do not seem to me to be correct in confusing an intellectual property with the substance of a spirit. For all spirits are contained within the breadth of souls and exist after the divine souls. The intellectual order, however, is something other than the soul; they have not obtained the same essence, or power, or the same action. Furthermore, souls enjoy the intellect only when they have finally turned toward it, received light from there, and joined their own action to it. However, they possess the leadership of a spirit through their whole life, their whole way of living, and through all things that proceed either from fate or providence. For it is the spirit itself that rules our entire life, fulfills the choices we made before birth, and bestows the gifts of fate and the rewards of the leaders of the gods of fate. Moreover, it suggests and measures out the illuminations from providence. Indeed, we, as souls, depend on the intellect alone, but as souls using a body, we also need a spirit. Therefore, Plato called the intellect the "helmsman" of the soul in the *Phaedrus*, but called the spirit the "observer" and "caretaker" of men throughout his works. Yet no one, considering rightly, will find any other single providence close to us pertaining to all things except for the spirit's providence and care. For the intellect is participated in by the rational soul (as we have said), but by no means by the body; nature is participated in by the body, but not at all by the intellect. The rational soul rules over anger and desire, but it has no command over accidental things. The spirit alone moves all things and governs everything. It cultivates and arranges all our affairs. Indeed, it perfects our reason, tempers our disturbances, inspires our nature, holds the body together, provides for accidental events, fulfills the decrees of fate, and grants the gifts of providence. Each spirit stands over a universe, a rector holding the rudders of the whole life for those things within us and around us.

->Three things regarding the spirit of Socrates: first, that it is also a god; second, that it appears through a voice; third, that it calls back rather than calls forward.<-

**CONCERNING** the spirit of Socrates, three things must be considered by us. First, that it is called a "god," as is clear here and in the *Apology*. Second, that it gave a voice to Socrates as a sign, which appears in the *Theages* and the *Phaedrus*. Third, that it would call Socrates back <note>original: "revocabat"; this refers to the famous "Socratic Sign" which Socrates claimed only told him what *not* to do, never what to do</note>, not call him forward...

# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.
<meta>catchword: and; signature: 4</meta>

...as the *Apology* <note>original: "apologia"; referring to Plato’s *Apology of Socrates*, where the philosopher defends his life and mentions his "divine sign"</note> testifies. Among the principle of divine souls—those which have chosen an intellectual life—the spirits <note>original: "daemones"; in Neoplatonic thought, a *daimon* is a protective spirit or lesser deity that bridges the gap between humans and the high gods</note> are divine, being the highest in the genus of spirits. Indeed, they are participants in the gods before all others; for just as there is a spirit in a god, so too in spirits there is a god. But in the former, the substance is divine, while the proportion <note>original: "proportio"; refers to the mathematical or metaphysical relationship between different levels of existence</note> is spirit-like. In these spirits, however, the property is spirit-like, while the proportion declares a divine essence. For they so excel other spirits that they frequently appear as gods. Rightly, therefore, Socrates calls his spirit both "spirit" and "god," as if it were the highest from the order of spirits. Wherefore the perfected Socrates, governed by a spirit and directing himself toward the norm of such a spirit of his... accordingly, as far as that voice of the spirit is concerned, pay attention. Socrates indeed first enjoyed the inspiration of the spirit through intelligence and the knowledge of separate things <note>referring to the Platonic "Forms" or "Ideas" which exist separately from physical matter</note>, which assiduously called him back to divine love. Secondly, it also directed its providence toward inferior things in the affairs of life; and according to that action of the spirit, he received light proceeding from there, not only through intelligence or thought nor by the powers of opinion alone, but also by the breath <note>original: "spiritu"</note> itself, while that spiritual inspiration suddenly proceeded through his whole life and already moved the senses themselves. For it is established that when the same action hangs over us from above, the reason enjoys the bestowed gift in one way, the imagination in another, and the sense in yet another; and each of those things within us is moved and acted upon by the spirit according to its own specific condition. Therefore, the voice did not fall upon Socrates passively from the outside, but was an inspiration proceeding from the innermost parts through the whole soul, and advancing even to the instruments of the senses, it finally emerged as a voice—that is to say, coming into notice not so much by any physical sense as by a "con-sense" <note>original: "consenfu"; a shared internal perception or harmony between the soul and the senses</note>. For such illuminations from good spirits and gods are accustomed to happen in this way.

->Other spirits ordered under other gods have various duties among each other.<-

<margin>q</margin> What has been said concerning the spirit of Socrates—namely, that it "calls back" <note>original: "reuocare"; refers to the fact that Socrates' spirit only warned him *not* to do things</note> and does not "provoke" <note>original: "prouocare"; to urge forward or incite</note>—is not a benefit common to all our spirits. Therefore, the character of Socrates, full of charity toward men in common and spontaneously ready for benefits, did not lack spiritual exhortation. Nevertheless, the spirit discouraged him whenever he approached his discipline either unseasonably or with those unfit for it. Namely, he stood in need of a bridle rather than spurs. Furthermore, some spirits possess a purging and uncontaminable power, others a generative one, others a perfecting one, others a craft-making one, and they are divided entirely according to the properties and powers of the gods under whom they are ordered. Now, according to their substance, individuals act as patrons for their clients toward a blessed life; some moving us toward the care of inferior things, others withdrawing us from external actions.

# PROCLUS. 1

It seems, therefore, that Socrates’ spirit <note>original: "daemon"; in this context, Proclus refers to a protective spiritual entity that acts as a link between the divine and the human</note> attained a purifying property and became the cause of an untainted life, ordained under the power of Apollo <note>The Greek god of light, prophecy, and purification</note> who presides over universal purification through a single, uniform virtue. By this virtue, the spirit separates Socrates from excessive commerce with the common crowd and draws him back into the inner sanctuary of the soul, toward actions set apart from lower things. Indeed, just as in the Orphic mysteries <note>Ancient Greek religious traditions attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus</note> Apollo presides over Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>, calling him back from his progression into the "Titanic multitude" <note>In Neoplatonism, this refers to the soul's fragmentation or scattering into the material world, symbolized by the Titans tearing Dionysus apart</note>, so too does the spirit of Socrates, who is an attendant of Apollo. For our intellect is the offspring of the Apollonian divinity.

To know the substances <note>the fundamental "being" or "essence" of a thing</note> of the gods and of souls belongs to a perfectly purified intellect. Commonly, however, we recognize their powers through their actions, and through these powers, we divine their essences.

<margin>i</margin> Among these matters, Socrates promises Alcibiades <note>Referring to Plato's dialogue *Alcibiades I*</note> that it is not the substance of the spirit that will be known, but its power. For the divine Iamblichus <note>A highly influential Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD)</note> says that the substances of spirits, and generally of all beings superior to us, are very difficult for us to contemplate unless we possess a perfectly purified intellect. Since even the essence of the soul is not easy for everyone to grasp, only Timaeus <note>The narrator of Plato’s *Timaeus*</note> declared its entire essence. For its nature is entirely divine and requires a long exposition to be explained, as Socrates says in the *Phaedrus*. It is easy, however, to explain the powers of the divinities; for from their actions, of which those very forces are the immediate "mothers," we perceive those powers. For power is the medium between action and essence, produced by the essence and producing the action. Furthermore, power itself has the greatest familiarity with spirits. Everywhere, the spirit holds the middle position like a "power." In the realm of intelligible things <note>the highest reality, accessible only to the mind</note>, it joins the Father and the Intellect. For power exists simultaneously with the Father, while the Intellect exists from the Father. In intellectual things, however, power joins actions with essences; for action is the offspring of power, but essence gives birth to powers from itself. Spirits, therefore, which are the mediators between us and the gods, are properly designated by the name "Power," as they possess the middle ground everywhere. For true essence and true being exist within the gods. Power, duly ministering to the gods, has its place in the spirits. Finally, action and effect, having progressed outward through their power, are found in us.

<margin>o</margin> The knowledge of future contingent things <note>events that might or might not happen</note> is certain and necessary among the higher beings: so says the divine Iamblichus, and that leader of ours <note>likely referring to Proclus's teacher or a revered authority like Syrianus</note>, and they ask and resolve it thus:

<meta>This page continues Proclus's commentary on the nature of spiritual guardians, moving from their role in purifying the soul to the philosophical mechanics of how they possess knowledge that exceeds human capacity.</meta>

## ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT

...or rather to divide the objects of knowledge according to the differences of the knowers. Thus, that which is eternal and divine by its very essence knows all things in an eternal and divine way; that which is human knows in a human way; that which is truly indivisible knows without division, or it anticipates those things which are divided. That which is eternal knows even temporal things beyond the constraints of time. That which is rational knows rational things rationally as well. From these points, it is clear that the gods and spirits <note>original: "daemones"</note> know indefinite things definitely, and unstable things in a stable and firm manner. Do we not see that many things unknown to those below us are, in the meantime, known to us? For irrational beings <note>original: "Inrationalia"; referring to animals or the lower parts of the soul</note> cannot grasp the nature of the universal itself, whereas we are able to gather it. Why then do we wonder any further that the higher beings <note>original: "superos"</note> firmly comprehend those things which we only guess at through ambiguous and deceptive knowledge? For our weakness is not the judge of their power, just as the irrational creature below us has no judgment over our reason; why should any irrational part within us or outside of us move our intelligence? Why should it not be absurd for a speculative reach toward the future to be found in some places, but for a stable, determined, and certain knowledge to be found nowhere? For the very nature of things cannot take its beginning from the imperfect, the impure, or things mixed with their opposite; if the guessing of the future shares in ignorance and is not constant, where then is the knowledge of the future itself and in its own right? Where is that pure source, from which that which comes after and desires it has received its substance, if not among the higher beings?

->May the higher beings counsel us well, even if they foresee that we will not obey them.<-

<margin>a</margin>
Pythian Apollo <note>Apollo in his role as the source of the Oracle at Delphi</note> answered Laius <note>The King of Thebes and father of Oedipus</note>, advising him not to beget a son; otherwise, he would be subjected to the violence of the spirits. He foresaw, meanwhile, that Laius would not obey the oracle. But Phoebus <note>Another name for Apollo, meaning "the Bright One"</note>, being good, set before him the choice of a better life. And Laius, indeed, did not err in the god's sight, but because of his own ignorance, he was ensnared by future dangers. Indeed, all actions of virtuous men tend toward their own innermost depths. Therefore, if one has acted beneficently and divinely, he already has his end established in his own proper action, even if nothing further is perfected outside of it. In a similar way, the spirits often work around us. Hence, divine things frequently seem to encounter and run ahead of lower beings, while in the meantime they do not depart from their own seats; but while they remain in themselves, they seem to draw near because of the readiness of the one looking up to them. For both in the invocations of the gods and in encounters that happen spontaneously, divinity itself seems to approach us in a certain way, though it is we, evidently, who have set out toward it.

PROCLUS.

...among the Pythagoreans <note>The followers of Pythagoras, the Greek philosopher and mathematician known for his belief in the transmigration of souls and the importance of discipline.</note> it was a custom to judge those who came to them by signs fixed in the body, determining whether they were fit for a higher life or not. For Nature herself, who fashions bodies for souls, provides them with suitable instruments and displays the images of the souls within their bodies, through which those skilled in this art <note>This refers to physiognomy, the ancient practice of judging a person's character or soul from their physical appearance.</note> can detect the natural disposition of the souls.

### A dialectical rule concerning necessary and contingent propositions.

Those skilled in logic <note>original: "dialecticis"</note> are accustomed to say that even if one has used ten thousand necessary propositions but a single contingent one <note>A "necessary" proposition must be true (e.g., 2+2=4), whereas a "contingent" one might be true or false depending on circumstances (e.g., "it is raining"). In logic, a conclusion is only as strong as its weakest premise.</note> has intervened, the conclusion will turn out to be entirely like the weaker part. Similarly, if the object we are to know has anything of a material or unstable nature mixed into it, this undoubtedly results in our knowledge of it being indefinite and ambiguous. For knowledge of unstable things is not safe from refutation; rather, such things are barely grasped through a kind of approximation. Such is the nature of natural power, for everywhere that which is imperfect, being akin to matter, is most easily changed. 

Self-sufficiency <note>original: "Ipsa per se sufficientia"; often termed 'autarkeia' in Greek philosophy.</note> belongs primarily to the gods; for the gods are good, and are certain "super-essential" goodnesses <note>In Neoplatonism, "super-essential" refers to realities that exist above the level of ordinary being or essence.</note> and the fullness of all beings. Through them, self-sufficiency belongs to all other things: to intellects, divine souls, spirits <note>original: "daemonibus"</note>, and us. However, these other things are self-sufficient through a kind of participation, whereas the gods are self-sufficient by their very essence. For this reason, common and unchanging opinion identifies happiness <note>original: "beatitudine"</note> with self-sufficiency; for those to whom it belongs to be well, it is also fitting that they have enough within themselves.

<margin>The rational soul comes from the first creator of the world; the irrational soul from the younger gods. Therefore, the former is nobler than the latter.</margin>
<margin>2</margin>

We say that the rational soul within us is nobler than the irrational soul, because the first Creator of the world <note>original: "primus mundi opifex"; referring to the Demiurge or supreme craftsman in Plato's dialogue, the *Timaeus*.</note> produced the former, while the younger gods <note>original: "dii iuuenes"; the secondary deities who, in Platonic cosmology, create the mortal parts of the soul and the physical body.</note> brought forth the latter. Indeed, the nobility of human families is an image of this very nobility of spirit, yet human nobility has an element of lowliness mixed in and is subject to change. However, the stable and eternal nobility of souls is derived from the gods, around whom the Fates <note>original: "fatae"</note> are said to dwell, and from the divine powers under which they were ordered. For those souls are nobler which are the attendants <note>original: "pedissequae"</note> of the higher gods, depending on greater powers according to the distribution arranged throughout the universe. I assert the same regarding cities. For from above, according to the lots...

...while powerful differences descend all the way to souls. And we say that some gods are of fire, others of ether, others of the heavens, and lastly, some of the earth. Likewise, some souls come from the solar sphere, others from the sphere of Mercury, and others from the lunar sphere. And this distribution of souls according to their places is such that one can truly boast in it. It is not a nobility based on earthly parents and cities.

<margin>Perfections received</margin>The perfections of the soul were brought toward the more sublime gods and spirits <gloss>which are around them</gloss>, and they are very near to them.

<margin>Socrates</margin>Among these things, Socrates points out the differences between the good spirits <note>original: "daemonum." In Neoplatonic philosophy, a "daemon" is not an evil entity, but a guiding spirit or intermediary between gods and humans.</note> who preside over us according to their essence, and the powers they have been allotted in the world. Likewise, the perfections of souls are subject to the more powerful spirits, are preserved by them, and are guided everywhere as is beneficial; however, their imperfections are subject to lower spirits. For just as souls are fated to be near the gods according to their worth, so too are they rightly ordered under the spirits. And just as the Father and Architect of the world <note>This refers to the Demiurge, the divine craftsman who, in Platonic thought, shapes the material world based on eternal forms.</note> is said to have appointed gods as leaders, so he has appointed spirits as caretakers over souls. Therefore, Socrates calls the spirit and god appointed over him his "guardian." Clearly asserting to Alcibiades <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and student of Socrates; the subject of the Platonic dialogue this text comments upon.</note> that this alone is the true guardian of a human being. This guardian is the author of happiness <note>original: "beatitudinis"</note> because of its wonderful power, which surely no human can achieve for us.

The order of things requires that, after the primary Cause of Ideas <note>The "Ideal Cause" refers to the eternal, perfect blueprints (Forms) of all things.</note>, there be things that participate <insert>once through the Ideas</insert> and are entirely stable; then come things that are ordered yet always changeable.

<margin>Love</margin>Love <note>The original "Mor" is an abbreviation for "Amor."</note> that depends on bodily beauty is changeable, since that beauty is also changeable. It is indeed wrong for an effect to exceed the condition of its causes in any way or to turn out better than them. For even where causes are ordered, disordered effects are often born; where causes are stable, the outcomes are often shifting; where they are determined, they frequently happen to be indefinite. Therefore, it is even more certain that effects lacking order and stability arise from causes that themselves lack order and stability.

The sequence of the universe descends from above through these kinds of steps to the lowest extremes, which at last are such that they can be changed and claim a natural mutation for themselves. Just as with justice: one thing is the "Just Itself"—justice in its primary form <note>The abstract Form of Justice, which is perfect and unchanging.</note>—which is not just by participation; while another thing is the primary participant in that justice, which is always participating in it. Finally, there is that which participates at some times, but at other times falls away from participation.

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic exploration of the hierarchy of being. Having established that souls are ordered under spirits (daemons) according to their merit, the text now explains how divine Qualities or "Forms" must flow downward into the world, and how "Opportunity" (the right time) acts as a bridge between the divine and the human, illustrated by the relationship between Socrates and Alcibiades.</meta>

# PROCLUS.

For it was not right for Justice itself to remain sterile, bestowing absolutely nothing of its own essential nature upon anything else; indeed, none of the primary things are of such a kind. Rather, sterility itself belongs only to matter, as it is the lowest of all things. Furthermore, it was not right that what was first to be shared by others should be shared directly by those things which only participate in it occasionally. For from that which stands as entirely simple and immutable, this thing which is composite and changeable is certainly too far removed; therefore, it requires a certain middle link <note>The "middle link" refers to the Neoplatonic concept of "mediators"—intermediate stages of reality that connect the perfect, unchanging divine realm with our messy, changing world.</note> to make contact with that higher source. Nor again was it proper for that which is shared by things capable of being eternally illuminated to stop its gift at those things alone, lest this very thing—which is always suspended from its principles—be the final end in the universe. Therefore, it is necessary to establish a threefold order, as we have said, not only concerning Justice <note>original: "iustum." This refers to the eternal Form or Idea of Justice.</note>, but concerning the Beautiful, the Equal, the Similar, and finally all the **Forms** <term>species: the eternal, perfect blueprints of reality in Platonic thought</term> of things.

<margin>q</margin>Just as the gods bestow benefits by applying cures for diseases—that is, the sins of the soul—and providing fruits at the appropriate seasons, so too do divine men seek the right opportunity for teaching. However, the gods determine the measures of these opportunities themselves through their intellectual and divine form, whereas men pursue them through knowledge. There are also those among men who hunt for these opportunities through the inspiration of a guardian spirit <note>original: "dæmonica." This refers to the *daimon*, a guiding spirit or protective genius.</note>. For the presence and familiarity of good spirits has a primary power within us to infallibly seize the right opportunity everywhere, which is what happened to Socrates. Now, just as a place is properly destined for every body by nature itself, so too do different parts of time suit different actions. And just as certain cycles of the whole world are the causes of fertility or sterility in animals and plants, so too does one time suit one action, and another time suit another, for the completion of this or that deed. Such a time is the "opportunity" <note>This translates the Greek concept of *Kairos*—not just chronological time, but the "perfect moment" for action.</note> of any action, bringing the good and the goal both to those who act and to the results. For this reason, the **Pythagoreans** also named the First Cause itself, from which good is present to all things, "Opportunity" <note>original: "oportunitatem"</note>, since it grants to all things that they might be perfect. By such an occasion, Socrates, relying on his guardian spirit, was brought to **Alcibiades** <note>Alcibiades was a brilliant but volatile Athenian statesman and student of Socrates; Proclus is explaining why Socrates chose a specific moment to approach him.</note>, coming to him to say certain things just when Alcibiades was also thinking of going to him to ask those same things. For in this way, all things are fitted together in turn, and thus the communion of goods is perfected everywhere for all, while the perfecting causes are most ready to hand them down.

-># OF THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT<-
->51<-
->g iii<-

Those things that are ready to receive participation are awakened; they, in turn, extend a perfecting power. These things have received from nature a potential for suitability. For potential is twofold: one belongs to the **agent** <term>agent: the active force that gives or initiates an action</term>, the other to the **patient** <term>patient: the passive receiver or subject that undergoes an action</term>. The former is the mother of action, while the latter is the vessel for perfection. Now, it is necessary that what is to act must be overflowing within itself and so ready for action that even if there were nothing to receive it, it would still be perfect in itself and moved of its own accord to give. Likewise, that which is to undergo an action must yearn for participation and move itself toward that perfecting power; even if that power is not present, it should still be stretched out toward participation through its highest degree of suitability.

Since there are two kinds of causes—some being immobile and present to everyone everywhere, and others being mobile and present to those being perfected at some times, but distant at others—certainly intelligible things <note>referring to higher spiritual or mental realities that exist beyond the physical world</note> are present similarly everywhere, bestowing their gifts upon everyone always in the same way. However, sensible things <note>objects and forces we can perceive with our five senses</note> may be present to those participating in them or absent by turns, just as the sun is now present and fills everything with light, and then departs. When things are thus, when the suitability for some immobile cause is present in the one who will participate, then that cause is also present, and the work of the efficient cause is completed. 

In such matters, only the unsuitability of the subjects usually prevents these gifts. Since those things which are to bestow gifts always do so, and are always everywhere in the same way, whatever has become suitable immediately becomes a sharer of the cause. But when something is prepared for one of the mobile causes, even if it is ready, often that which was to be bestowed is absent. For this cause must arrive at the right time, since it requires a specific place to give.

In every way, as we have said, it is necessary for these two things to precede all sharing of goods: the perfecting power of the giver and the completed suitability of the receiver. The perfection of the bestower must meet with the preparation of the receiver, and together with such a meeting, the efficient cause itself is carried above the patient according to its essence. Such a meeting is not accidental; nor does something orderly usually arise from disordered or uncoordinated things, like things that happen to flow together by chance. Instead, it is necessary for such a "breathing together" to occur in some places through nature, and in others through the intellect. 

Likewise, in some places it comes from a certain **daemonic** <term>daemon: a guiding spirit or intermediary between the divine realm and the human world</term> cause, and elsewhere from a divine one. Truly, under this condition, **Socrates** met with **Alcibiades** <note>Alcibiades was a brilliant but volatile Athenian statesman; Socrates' attempt to guide his soul is a central theme in Plato's writings.</note> at the opportune moment. A "good spirit" <note>original: "bonus daemon"</note> was the cause of this timely meeting, determining the opportunity for Socrates to encounter him. For opportunity itself, beginning from above among the divine, proceeds all the way to the lowest things; and some opportunities...

# PROCLUS

...unity is determined by the gods. Another kind of unity is demonic <note>In the Platonic sense, "demonic" refers to *daemons*, intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil beings</note>; another is fated; and yet another is fortuitous. For as the saying goes, Fortune and Opportunity govern all human affairs.

### You pursue here, above all else, the images of those things which you saw more intently in your homeland.

<margin>a</margin>Our souls wander here among the images of those things which they had seen in their first state <note>The "first state" or "homeland" refers to the celestial realm where the soul resided before being born into a physical body</note>, and they are more deeply affected by those images whose original patterns they had contemplated more attentively there. For some souls are suited to different spectacles than others. Therefore, different souls dwell upon different images, for they love the likenesses of those things which they had gazed upon in that higher place.

<margin>•</margin>Indeed, those who were once attendants of the great Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis"</note> above, and lived together with him—within the order that holds the rank of leader among the twelve princes of the universe <note>A reference to the twelve Olympian gods who govern the celestial spheres</note>—these souls, having arrived here, surely seek out a commanding way of life according to the character of their god. Yet they are ignorant of what is truly imperial, and instead they pursue the mere appearance of leadership among these earthly images. If they happen upon wise teachers, this inclination leads them toward salvation through a certain return to the heavens. If, however, they linger too long among these images, they decline into tyranny. On this matter, Socrates says in the *Republic* that souls recently arrived from the heavens most often choose lives of power. For since they were moving among the celestial gods only a short time before and witnessed their power dominating all things, they themselves also affect a life similar to theirs, ruling over others. Very many abuse this inclination, while only a very few use it rightly. Plato ranks the best kind of life as the **contemplative** <term>contemplative: a life devoted to philosophy and the study of divine truths</term>. The second is the **ambitious** life. The third is the **voluptuous** or **greedy** life. Souls coming from heaven who have been most rightly educated choose the contemplative life. Those also coming from heaven, but who were poorly educated, choose the ambitious life; the rest, coming from the earth, choose the remaining types.

### It is a natural belief in all people that the gods know the secrets of souls.

<margin>•</margin>All men naturally address their innermost thoughts, passions, and desires to the gods, being persuaded by certain "immutable anticipations" <note>original: "anticipatiões" - the Platonic/Stoic concept of *prolepsis*, or innate ideas that every human is born with</note> that divinity itself knows all things, even the hidden impulses of the soul. Certainly, every bond and community formed by reason requires the presence of God. For what else unites the many and gathers together those things that were scattered, if not divinity?

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic commentary on the soul's journey.
