# ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT
<note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE". In this Platonic context, a "daemon" refers to an intermediary spirit or guiding genius that connects the human and divine, rather than an "evil" entity.</note>
g iiii

### God, through His providence, confirms our free will.

<margin>d</margin>The gods set before souls various types of lives, and after the souls have made their choice, the gods determine by a fixed lot whatever is necessary for the life that was chosen. In this way, our freedom of choice is contained within the middle of Providence; it is moved and determined by it, and revolves within it. These matters are clearly described in the *Republic* <note>original: "re. pu." refers to Plato's Republic, specifically the Myth of Er in Book X</note>, where the prophet sets the lives before the souls, having received the lots from the knees of Lachesis <note>Lachesis is one of the three Fates; she measures the thread of life and represents the past</note>, and cries out to the souls, "O souls of a day," and so forth. Indeed, the presentation is made by Lachesis through the intermediary of the prophet. However, the choice concerning the lives proposed there belongs to the souls themselves. Now, the prophet there, anticipating all the soul's choices within himself, finally casts the lots. Thus, the very thing that seems unstable and undefined is always grasped beforehand—stably and orderly—according to a single limit within those higher and more perfect realms.

### Three teachings of Plato.

<margin>e</margin>From the words of Plato we gather three things here: first, that being evil is to be judged as entirely worse than not existing at all; second, that the separation of the soul from the body frees us from the evils found in this falling region <note>The "falling" or "perishable" region refers to the physical, material world subject to decay</note>, and from the obstacles which here hinder the achievement of a fitting end. Third, that the soul’s own desires have the greatest power over the forms of life it takes, and we are not such beings as are formed and moved solely by external things. For we produce the choices from within our own selves, and through those choices, we live our lives.

### The Higher Beings hold with certainty those things which are uncertain in reality.

<margin>f</margin>From this you will receive a wondrous teaching: namely, that those things which are more excellent and uniform always anticipate the lesser things. Yet, the lesser things can never equal the power of the superior. Likewise, the knowledge of the higher beings firmly encompasses the actions of the lesser within itself. However, the knowledge of the inferior can never fully grasp the entire action of the superior. That which is higher receives nothing from the lesser into itself, just as the heavens do not receive any suffering or change from the things below them. Nor does the Immovable Cause <note>The "Immovable Cause" or "Unmoved Mover" refers to the ultimate divine source of all motion</note> admit anything of the world into itself because of the movement of worldly things. Nor do eternal things admit anything into themselves from things acting in time. Finally, this necessitates that while the divine knows all things, it does not undergo any change, even when it knows that which is subject to change.

# PROCLUS
<note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was one of the last major Greek philosophers of late antiquity, known for his systematic "Neoplatonic" interpretations of Plato’s works.</note>

### Double argumentation through negation and affirmation: the former resolves, the latter composes, and both agree with the very nature of the soul.

---

<margin>

</margin>
Alcibiades <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and student of Socrates; here, Proclus refers to the dialogue where Socrates questions Alcibiades' knowledge.</note> is unable to assign a time in which he thought he was ignorant of those things about which he now deliberates; certainly, he neither sought those things at any time, nor did he ever learn them from teachers. But if he neither sought them nor received them from others, then surely he neither learned nor discovered them. If he neither learned nor discovered them, he rightly does not know them; if he does not know them, he is not a good judge in matters where he cannot assign a time when he thought himself to be ignorant. You see, surely, how if the dispute is conducted in this way, we proceed sometimes by **composition** and sometimes by **resolution**: speaking through affirmation in composition, and through negation in resolution.

This very composition and resolution entirely suits the nature of the soul. Indeed, the soul slips down from more perfect things to lesser things through the "composition" of reasons and the "adding on" of certain foreign garments <note>original: "indumentorũ". Neoplatonists used the metaphor of "garments" or "tunics" to describe the layers of materiality and emotion the soul takes on as it descends from the divine realm into a physical body.</note>, until it is imprisoned in this thick and solid bond. Conversely, however, it rises again to the heights through "resolution" and the casting off of those things which disagree with its very nature, until—emerging naked, as the sacred words <note>This likely refers to "the Chaldean Oracles" or other mystical texts Proclus considered authoritative.</note> hand down—it may be joined with forms entirely separated from <term>matter</term> <note>In this philosophy, "matter" is the lowest level of reality, devoid of form or spirit.</note>. Therefore, argumentation proceeding through affirmation descends from more perfect things to less perfect ones. You shall proceed, in turn, through negation.

->**The Good itself, though it surpasses intellectual essence, nevertheless extends itself down to the very lowest things.**<-

<margin>

</margin>
The Good itself <note>original: "Ipsum bonum". In Neoplatonism, "The Good" or "The One" is the ultimate, indescribable source of all reality, existing above even the gods or the intellect.</note>, as if standing within itself above intellectual nature, descends (if it is right to say so) even to the last things, illuminating all, preserving all, adorning all, and meanwhile turning all back toward itself. First, it is present to those things that truly exist; second, to divine souls; third, to the spirits <note>original: "numinibus". These are the intermediate deities or guiding powers.</note> presiding over the human race; fourth, to our souls; and thereafter to animals and plants, and to all bodies. Finally, even in formless matter—the lowest dregs of things—the Good itself performs its own duty for all things, secretly and ineffably, before any order is established. All things participate in it everywhere, each in a different way according to its own order, and as far as each is naturally fit, they bring back "the good" from there. Some do so more weakly, others more effectively; some more uniformly. Those in a divisible condition do so more [variably]; those above do so eternally, while the others do so changeably. For just as more divine things have an indivisible essence, so they possess an undivided and united good. But those things which have departed further from the principles, being now placed in a certain distance and division, acquire their own good [in parts]. For this reason, such things, in a certain assembly striving toward the same goal and with mutual...

-> 53 <-

...they deeply stand in need of a **harmony** <note>original: "conspiratione," literally a "breathing together." In this Neoplatonic context, it refers to the internal agreement or "symphony" that binds diverse parts into a single whole.</note>. Since each individual thing does not possess self-sufficiency—which is the hallmark of the Good—it must at least supply the deficiency of its nature through mutual communion. In this way, it may strengthen the weakness caused by its division through this "breathing together." For this reason, individual men, who are weak when standing alone, gather together for common counsel, thus coupling their divided minds with one another and striving to ignite a single light from many sparks. Indeed, a multitude never appears to provide for its own common good unless it is ordered around some single prevailing principle. One may observe this across the entire order of things: namely, that a multitude is everywhere born alongside a "one," and must be brought back to that totally absolute unity through a related "one." The divine Good has therefore implanted a desire for itself in all things, so that through this desire it might be able to bestow its benefits upon us.

<margin>Mercury is the author of discovery and learning for us.</margin>
**Mercury**, as the messenger of Jove <note>Proclus uses the Roman names Mercury and Jove/Jupiter for the Greek Hermes and Zeus. Hermes is the "messenger" who translates the divine will into language the soul can understand.</note>, unfolds the paternal will to our souls and thus offers us **learning**; and again, as the author of inquiry, he grants **discovery** to his students. Now, when learning comes into our souls from the powers above, it is superior to discovery. But when it comes from our equals—such as men awakening the cognitive power within us—it is inferior to discovery. **Discovery**, therefore, is a middle ground, suited to the nature of the soul which is "self-moving." Through discovery, that power within us that lives and operates by itself is most clearly revealed. Learning, however, works in two ways: in its better sense, it fills the soul from its higher causes; in its lesser sense, it awakens the vital force within us from things outside ourselves, through a condition that is moved by something else. That a certain knowledge of things is born in us even from the powers above is often enough declared by the gods themselves through their manifest presence and explanations, showing to souls the order of the universe, running ahead like guides on the journey toward the divine, and hanging torches like beacons to mark the path.

<margin>Because of the notions of things innate to us, we think we know everything.</margin>
Our souls are weighed down by a **double ignorance**: they think they know many things because of the notions of things implanted in them from the beginning, yet they are ignorant because of forgetfulness. He who is weighed down by this double ignorance seeks nothing further, just as the wise man himself does not seek. In this respect, he is in a way similar to the wise man—just as **matter** is similar to God through a certain "dissimilar similarity." <note>This "dissimilar similarity" is a famous Neoplatonic paradox. Both God (the One) and Prime Matter are "without form," but God is above form while Matter is below it.</note> As someone rightly hands down: for just as matter is formless, so is God; and both are deeply infinite and unknown.

# PROCLUS.

Even if all these things correspond to God according to what is better, they belong to matter according to what is worse.

->**The soul becomes like the mind through acquired knowledge; through a twofold ignorance, it becomes like matter.**<-

<margin>a</margin> The soul, through knowledge itself, turns out to be like the intellect <note>original: "intellectui," referring to the higher Mind or *Nous* in Neoplatonic thought.</note> by grasping the object of knowledge in its very act, just as the intellect grasps the intelligible. However, through a "double ignorance" <note>A Platonic concept where one not only lacks knowledge but is unaware of that lack, mistakenly believing they possess truth.</note> it becomes like matter. For just as matter seems to possess all things, though in truth it possesses nothing, so too the soul suffering from double ignorance seems to itself to possess what it does not. Consequently, there is a twofold cognition of souls. One is indistinct, occurring through simple and naked intelligence. The other is articulated, possessing certain knowledge and free of ambiguity. For we seem, as he says <note>A reference to Plato, likely the *Meno* or *Phaedrus*, regarding the theory of Recollection.</note>, to know all things as if through a dream, yet to be ignorant of those same things while awake. This is because we possess the rational principles <note>original: "rationes," or the *logoi*—the inner blueprints of reality.</note> through our very essence, and we breathe forth their cognitions from within; yet, in terms of active production, we do not possess them sufficiently. Therefore, time does not precede the notion of the species <note>The "species" or Forms are the eternal patterns of things.</note> which is implanted and constant within us by essence; for we have had this from eternity. But time does precede the knowledge that is brought about through the production and distinction of those rational principles. Thus, we are able to assign the specific time when we first received this knowledge. For I know that I learned what a circle is at one time, and learned the nature of the species of justice at another, and similarly with other things of which we possess knowledge in act. Therefore, regarding the thing itself—or the matter which we recollect—we do not fully recall the time. But for the act of recollection itself, there is certainly a determined time.

### The seven ages of man, congruent with the seven planets.

<margin>a</margin> The order of the human ages follows the order of the universe. The first age follows the power of the Moon; for then we live according to the nutritive and vegetative faculty. The second age follows Mercury, when we practice the study of letters, the lute <note>original: "cytharæ," the kithara or lyre.</note>, wrestling, and similar games. The third age is of Venus, when the limbs swell with seed and we are immediately incited to procreation. The fourth is the Solar age, for then vigor reigns, the perfection of age hastens on, and it is the middle of life. The fifth is the Martian age <note>The age of Mars.</note>, in which we strive for power and victories. <margin>1</margin> The sixth is the Jovian age <note>The age of Jupiter (Jove).</note>, which desires prudence and an active, civic life. The seventh is the Saturnian age, in which it is natural to cease from procreation, to separate oneself from bodily things, and to transfer oneself to another, incorporeal life. The higher things are everywhere...

# ON THE SOUL AND THE GUARDIAN SPIRIT.
### c

Higher forms of knowledge uniquely and more excellently embrace the cognitions of lower things. For whatever the sense perceives under material conditions, the imagination perceives immaterially. What mere opinion reckons without a cause, scientific knowledge <note>original: "scientia," referring to *episteme*, or knowledge derived from first principles rather than simple observation.</note> understands through its cause; and so on, higher things always contain within themselves, through absolute eminence, the entire cognition suitable for inferior things. Therefore, the guardian spirit <note>original: "daemonem," referring to the personal tutelary spirit or "daimon" assigned to an individual in Neoplatonism, acting as a link between the human and the divine.</note> appointed over us is ignorant of nothing within us—neither the movements of the soul, nor our natural capacity, nor accidental changes. Instead, he surveys and governs all things uniquely. In this universe, all the ends of everything arranged within it lead toward the very end of the world. For so that the world might be perfect, as Timaeus <note>A reference to the speaker in Plato’s *Timaeus*, who describes the world as a "living being" containing all other living beings, divine and mortal.</note> says, all living things were brought forth, both the divine and the perishable. Similarly, in a well-ordered city, the ends of all parts serve the end of civic expertise. Furthermore, just as each thing within the realm of generation <note>The physical world of birth, death, and change.</note> possesses its being according to a single species <note>The specific "form" or "type" that defines what a thing is.</note> and is therefore not infinite, the Intelligible <note>The realm of pure Mind and the eternal Forms that serve as the blueprints for reality.</note> itself is "all things," since it contains the causes of all sensible things. In the same way, any private artisan is largely ignorant, being skilled only in his specific craft; however, the statesman is absolutely prudent. He knows both his own end and the ends of others, and he directs the other arts toward the single life of the city.

->*Through the harmony reigning in heaven, the higher powers temper all other things harmonically.*<-

<margin>c</margin>
Heaven is full of concord and the suitability of its motions. Next, the divinities superior to us are participants in the harmony that precedes them from heaven. After these, the well-ordered life of humans takes on a consonance of character and a suitability of actions; from there, the gift of these same superior beings descends even to the brutes and the plants. For these, too, are naturally participants in harmony. The higher powers contain and perfect all mundane things by a harmonic principle, accommodating them to one another and to the world. Indeed, they harmonize the body with the Intellect by means of the soul through harmonic reason. They relate the realm of change <note>original: "generationem," the physical world of becoming.</note> to the constant circuit of Sameness <note>original: "identitatis," a reference to the celestial motion of the "Same" (the fixed stars) from Plato's *Timaeus*.</note> by means of the circuit assigned to Difference <note>original: "alteritati," referring to the motion of the "Other" or "Different," associated with the wandering planetary spheres.</note> (if I may put it that way). Finally, they bind earth to fire through intermediate links. Furthermore, they cultivate every soul with harmonic principles. They join every body everywhere with similar measures, and they perform every movement everywhere with musical measures. Therefore, the musical disposition within us is a gift of the Muses, although it is the lowest image of them. For the artistic and contemplative dispositions within us have gods as their presiding guardians and derive their origin from them.

# PROCLUS.

->He who is ignorant of the final cause is ignorant of every cause.<-

<margin>i</margin>Ignorance of the final cause <note>The "final cause" refers to the purpose or goal for which a thing exists (teleology).</note> regarding any matter ensures that the other causes pertaining to it are similarly ignored. Since the end [goal] is the first, chief, and most powerful of causes—for it is for the sake of this end that both the efficient causes act and the things produced are brought into being. For this reason, Timaeus <note>The main speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name.</note> considers such a cause to be held as the best among the wise. In the *Sophist*, Plato teaches that there is a twofold depravity of the soul. One of these is ignorance, which falls within the reason; the other is discord, where the irrational part of the soul rebels against the rational. Such discord is the disease of the soul, while ignorance is its deformity. For since reason holds the rank of the "form" <note>original: "speciei," referring to the defining essence or blueprint.</note> within the entire soul, the depravity of reason is deservedly called the soul's ugliness, just as the virtue of reason is the soul's beauty. Indeed, ignorance occurs because of the dominance of irrational power, while knowledge arises through the command of the rational. This deformity of the soul happens when reason is overcome—namely, when it produces its own actions in a way that is uncoordinated, incongruous, ineffective, and inept for its goal. In cultivating the soul, one must remove impediments and move the soul deeply toward the contemplation of reality. For the knowledge of truth is innate within us, but we are prevented from directing our soul toward it because of the passions arising from the realm of generation <note>The physical world of birth and decay.</note> that stand in our way. These passions—I mean forgetfulness, mere opinion, false imaginations, and immoderate appetites—must be expelled; then the mind must be turned back into itself, and thus it suddenly enjoys the truth.

---

->The end of war is justice. The end of peace is friendship, which is more desirable than justice.<-

<margin>b</margin>The end [goal] of war is indeed justice. But the end of peace is something even more excellent: namely, friendship and union. For the goal of all virtue, as the Pythagoreans teach and Aristotle confirms, is that once everyone has become friends, we no longer require justice—specifically, when "mine and not mine" <note>A reference to the abolition of private interest or property in favor of common bond.</note> has been removed. Even if all people were just, there would still be a need for friendship to gather them together. That injustice is the origin of wars is declared by war itself, which material forms <note>In Neoplatonism, "material forms" are the physical qualities (like heat or cold) that occupy matter and compete with one another.</note> wage against one another. For heat fights against cold, not when they are separated by location, but when one strives to occupy the place of the other. Since a form requires its "seat" [in matter], it deservedly resists that which comes from the outside and tries to thrust it from its place; for this reason, the rational principles <note>original: "rationes," referring to the *logoi* or divine blueprints.</note> implanted in nature run together without rebellion. For each of these principles consists within itself. But material forms, since they cannot remain apart from matter, deservedly contend among themselves for a common lodging. This is because matter cannot receive two contrary forms at once without confusion.

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.

## How the soul, in descending, is variously clothed, and again is purified and returns in its turn.

<margin>d</margin>
The descent of the soul into the body has indeed separated it from the divine souls, from whom it was once filled with intelligence, power, and purity.
->Indeed, it has joined it to generation <note>The realm of birth, death, and physical change.</note>, nature, and material things<-
from which it was imbued with forgetfulness, error, and ignorance. For as the soul descends toward birth, multiform lives and various "garments" <note>This refers to the "neoplatonic vehicles" or layers of energy the soul acquires as it passes through the celestial spheres.</note> are added to it, drawing it into a perishable composition and obstructing the contemplation of "separate things" <note>Refers to divine realities that exist independently of matter.</note>. It is necessary, therefore, to lead the soul from here back to that ever-watchful, upright nature by cutting away the secondary and tertiary powers that grew upon it during its descent—just as one must scrape the seaweed, rocks, and shells from the sea-god Glaucus <note>A reference to Plato’s *Republic* (Book X), where the soul is compared to the sea-god Glaucus, whose original form is obscured by the debris of the ocean.</note>. One must restrain the impulses that carry the soul outward. One must remember again the essence of separate things and the divine nature from which the descent began, and toward which it is proper for all life to strive.

->The soul is self-moving by its own nature. The body is moved from without. But through their<-
->mutual exchange, each takes on the condition of the other.<-

<margin>a</margin>
The soul is, by its very essence, self-moving; yet, when joined to the body, it somehow becomes "moved from without" as well. For just as the soul’s presence gives the body a final trace of the ability to move itself, so too does the soul, because of its companionship with the body, take on the mark of being moved by external forces. Because of its self-moving power, the soul is fertile and prone to discovery; it gives birth to rational thoughts and sciences. But because of this condition of being moved from without, it frequently needs to be "awakened" by others. Indeed, more perfect souls are prompter in discovery, while imperfect souls require more external assistance. The former are more "self-moving" and share less in the lower nature. The latter move themselves less, suffering the lot of the body. Nevertheless, when even these souls make progress—rising, as it were, from the body and collecting themselves back from matter—they immediately become more fertile and inventive regarding those things in which they were previously sterile and uncertain. That earlier state was due to the clumsy sloth of a life in contact with matter and the foul numbness contracted from the realm of generation. We, therefore, observing the "mean" <note>The middle path or balanced perspective in philosophical inquiry.</note>, assign the causes of the rational nature and its condition, pertaining especially to its more imperfect and more perfect habits. We judge such paths to be the way toward their perfection. Whoever assigns reasons for these things but fails to observe this "mean"—either rising too high or sinking too low—wanders far from the truth of the soul. For we do not approve of those who...

PROCLUS

...they say <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "dicunt" (they say).</note> that the soul, having fallen into a moist body <note>In Neoplatonism, "moisture" symbolizes the heavy, material world of "generation" that weighs down the soul's fiery nature.</note> and being hindered by its obstacle, is from the very beginning irrational; however, as the moisture gradually evaporates due to innate heat and becomes more balanced, the soul's power of prudence grows strong. This mode of perfection must be judged as corporeal and material, for it assumes that the perfection of the soul arises from the tempering of the physical body. But the soul possesses its entire substance before the elements and the whole of generation; it is a certain kind of life, mixed neither with the body nor with nature. Nor, again, do we agree with those who think the soul is a part of the divine essence, and that this part is entirely unlike the whole <note>Meaning it does not share the limitations of the whole material creature</note>, and always perfect. They claim that tumult and disturbances only surround that which is "the animal" within us. For those who say these things imagine the soul to be always perfect, always knowing, never in need of <term>reminiscence</term> <note>The Platonic theory that "learning" is actually the soul "remembering" knowledge it possessed before birth.</note>, always free from passion, and never depraved. Yet <term>Timaeus</term> <note>The narrator of Plato’s dialogue of the same name.</note> says the essence of our soul was not constituted from the primary classes of being at all, as the superior souls were, but was composed from the second and third. And <term>Socrates</term> says in the <term>Phaedrus</term> that our powers are mixed with the opposite of good and are full of mutual dissension. For this reason, sometimes the better parts and sometimes the worse parts are accustomed to prevail. What more? Does he not say himself that our <term>charioteer</term> <note>original: "aurigam"; Plato’s metaphor for the rational part of the soul that must guide the two horses of spirit and appetite.</note> is also sometimes depraved, writing clearly that many souls limp due to the depravity of the <term>charioteer</term> himself? Many, likewise, lose more of their wings. But indeed, the <term>charioteering</term> power <note>original: "aurigaria"</note> within us is more ancient. This is that which remembers divine things and uses the secondary and tertiary powers as servants. This we are plainly taught in the <term>Phaedrus</term>.

Indeed, as we have said, we must preserve the proper measures of the soul, assigning reasons for the soul's perfection and progress that are derived neither from corporeal things nor solely from divine things, so that we may be true interpreters of <term>Plato</term>. We should not twist the philosopher's words to fit our own opinion. Since, therefore, the soul is at one time imperfect and then again perfected, and suffers forgetfulness of divine things and then remembers them again, it is certain that time also contributes to its perfection. For in what way could it be transferred from imprudence to prudence, and from depravity into virtue, unless it effected these changes through time? Every change is enacted within a span of time. Let these things be said generally regarding the perfection of souls. From this, we must accept that he who knows what is just must have at some point passed from ignorance into the knowledge of it, and does not always have the rational principle of justice ready at hand—unlike those beings superior to us. For we are born imperfect from the beginning. Nor, again, purely because of the change of the body...

<header>ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT. <note>original: "DE ANIMA ET DAEMONE"</note></header>

...also that the knowledge of the just reaches us. For our essence is not corporeal, nor is it composed of material things. It is necessary that all changes of the soul be measured by time. Whence also **Aristotle** <note>The author is likely referencing Aristotle’s *Physics* or *De Anima* regarding the relationship between movement, time, and the soul's states.</note> places a temporal measurement upon the soul's change according to its **activity** and **habit** <note>In Greek philosophy, "habit" (*hexis*) refers to a stable disposition or state of being, while "activity" (*energeia*) is the expression of that state.</note> and their opposites. Therefore, it is doubted by no one that the soul, when joined to the body and passing from depravity and ignorance into their opposites, requires an interval of time. Some, however, think that the soul itself, remaining apart in itself, does not need time to act, but rather that time is created from the soul itself; this, however, I believe requires some explanation. For time is twofold: one kind is born together with natural life and the corporeal movement of the universe; the other truly proceeds through **incorporeal life**. This latter time measures the circuits of even the divine souls. In turn, it completes the actions of our own souls even when they are separated from the body; whereas the second kind of time, which is extended alongside natural life, measures the life we lead in company with the body. It does not, however, measure the life of the soul living by itself in any way. 

Nevertheless, there is some knowledge within us that exists before all time. Other knowledge is formed within time. **Socrates**, therefore, looking at knowledge expressed through activity, inquires what time existed before this knowledge. **Alcibiades**, however, possessing at least that knowledge placed in his **essence**—because of which he thinks he knows even what he does not know—is unable to assign a time when he first received it, for we have possessed this from eternity <note>original: "ab æuo"</note>. Wherefore, if one speaks of one kind of knowledge and the other of another, both are true: namely, that time preceded knowledge, and that one cannot readily identify a time which one could claim preceded knowledge. For before knowledge that is not yet fully formed, there is no time; but before knowledge that is perfected in activity, time did exist.

### Many levels by which we ascend from the multitude to the One through contemplation.

<margin>through</margin>
**Plato** and **Pythagoras** command us to flee the **multitude** <note>In Neoplatonism, "the multitude" refers to the chaotic, fragmented world of the senses and many desires, which stands in opposition to "the One" or the simple truth.</note>, so that we may pursue the simplest truth. Indeed, we must flee the multitude of the "exterior people," who distract and deceive us in many ways, but much more must we flee the multitude of the "interior people" <note>This refers to the inner "crowd" of conflicting thoughts, passions, and sensory images within a person's own mind.</note>; for these distract and deceive us far more. Therefore, first flee the varied multitude of the passions. Second, flee the senses. Third, flee the imaginations. Fourth, flee independent opinions. For every multitude already mentioned is so diverse within itself that some parts are contrary to others in every respect. Whence it is better to betake oneself to the **sciences** <note>Here "sciences" (*scientiae*) refers to organized, certain knowledge, such as mathematics or logic, which Neoplatonists used as a bridge from the physical world to the divine.</note>. Within these, the multitude no longer possesses any contrariety. For even if passions are contrary to passions, senses to senses, imaginations to imaginations, and opinions to opinions, yet no science is contrary to another science.

### PROCLUS.

...is found. In this multitude of propositions and notions, therefore, let us gather them into one and connect the whole number of sciences by a certain single bond. For they are so far from being contrary to one another that one notion serves another, and all the lower sciences serve the superior one, having their origins from them. Here, moreover, it is necessary to move from the many sciences that presuppose one [higher science] toward that very "one" which presupposes nothing further, and to refer all things rightly to this first principle. 

After science and the study of it, it is now expedient to lay aside compositions, divisions, and multiform discourses <note>Discursive thought (dianoia) involves step-by-step reasoning, which Proclus argues must eventually be surpassed for direct intellectual intuition.</note>, and to ascend from there to the intellectual life and its simple intuitions and perceptions. For science is not the highest peak of cognition. Rather, above it is **intellect**; I do not mean only the intellect that is separated from the soul, but also the very illumination of the soul infused from that source, of which **Aristotle** also says that it is the intellect by which we know the terms <note>original: "intellectum esse, quo terminos cognoscimus." Referring to the primary, indemonstrable principles of logic.</note>. And **Timaeus** <note>The speaker in Plato's dialogue of the same name.</note> says this very thing never occurs in any other thing except in the soul. 

Ascending, therefore, to this intellect, let us contemplate the intelligible essence together with it, observing the indivisible and simple genera of beings with indivisible and simple perceptions. But after the venerable intellect, it is finally right to stir up the highest existence of the soul (if I may call it that), through which we are **one** and under which our multitude is united. For just as through our intellect we touch the divine intellect, so also through our own unity—the "one" within us—we may reach the **first One** <note>In Neoplatonism, "The One" is the supreme, transcendent source of all reality.</note>, from which union is instilled in all things. It is possible to reach it as if touching the **flower of our essence** <note>original: "essentiae nostrae florem." A mystical term for the highest, most refined part of the soul that can experience union with the Divine.</note>. 

Indeed, through our own unity we are most greatly joined to the divine. For "like" can everywhere be comprehended by "like": things known by science, things intelligible by intellect, and the most unified measures of beings by the unity of the soul. Now, this unity through which we act is the summit of our actions; through this, we are made divine. This happens when, fleeing all multitude, we take refuge in our own unity and are made "one," acting in a uniform manner. 

Hitherto we have advised that multitude must be fled by proceeding through the degrees of cognition in order. Next, let us proceed similarly through the degrees of the "knowable" <note>The "knowable" (cognobilium) refers to the objects of knowledge, moving from the physical to the metaphysical.</note> to prove the same thing. Flee all **sensible things**; for they are crowded together, divisible, and utterly changeable. Therefore, they cannot be held by pure knowledge. From these, therefore, transfer yourself to the incorporeal essence. For every sensible thing has only an accidental unity; it is dispersed through itself and full of infinity. Because of this, its "good" is partible, accidental, and distant from itself, departing and residing in an alien seat. When truly ascending...

He emphasizes that the highest form of union with the divine is achieved through the "flower of the soul," which mirrors the unity of the First Principle.</summary>

# ON THE SOUL AND THE DAEMON.
<page-num>57</page-num>
<sig>h</sig>

...once you have arrived there and have been placed among incorporeal things, you will behold that soul-like <note>original: "animalem." In this context, it refers to the nature of the *anima* (soul), not "animal" in the modern sense.</note> order, which moves above bodies, acting of itself and through itself, possessing its own substance in and from itself. You will see it multiplied, yet anticipating within itself a certain appearance of essence that is to be divided among physical bodies. There, truly, you will see many relationships of reasons <note>original: "rationum," likely referring to the *logoi* or formative principles that govern the physical world.</note>, various proportions, and many bonds. Likewise, you will see certain wholes, and parts, and soul-circles, and a multiform variety of powers. Furthermore, you will see that the perfection of souls is not eternal, nor does it exist entirely all at once, but it is unfolded in time and exists within discursive movements. For such is the nature of the soul. But after the multiplicity belonging to souls, take yourself to the **intellect** and the intellectual realms, so that you may possess the unity of things. There indeed be a contemplator of that nature. Behold a nature remaining in eternity <note>original: "æuo," referring to *Aion*, or nontemporal eternity, as opposed to *tempus* (linear time).</note>, a vigorous life, and an awake intelligence to which nothing of life is lacking, which does not require the cycles of time for its perfection. When you have inspected these things, and seen by how great an interval they are better than souls, seek next whether there is some multiplicity there and—since the intellect is one—whether it is also universal. Likewise, since it is uniform, ask whether it is additionally multiform. You will indeed find it to be so. When, therefore, you have seen that intellectual multiplicity—though it is entirely indivisible and united—lead yourself back again to another principle. And above intellectual essences, consider their units <note>original: "unitates." These are the *Henads*, the highest divine principles in Neoplatonism that bridge the gap between the One and the many.</note>. And finally, consider the **Unity** absolute from all things. Having progressed this far, you will have left behind all multiplicity and reached the very fountain of the **Good** itself. Since it is clear through these things that the perfection of the soul is prepared precisely by our fleeing from all multiplicity—both external and internal, and even the multiplicity of the universe itself—we can also conclude here that our souls do not merely gather knowledge from sensible things <note>Things perceived by the five senses.</note>, nor do they find the "whole" and the "one" by starting from particular and divided things. Instead, the soul brings forth learning from its innermost depths and corrects what is imperfect in apparent things. For it is not fitting to think that those things which truly are not <note>Referring to the material world, which in Platonic thought is a shadow of true reality and thus "is not" in a final sense.</note> are the primary causes of the knowledge existing in the soul. And those things which disagree among themselves, and which require the soul’s reasons and arguments and are ambiguous, cannot precede a knowledge that remains always in the same way. Nor can reasons that change in various ways generate something that stands as one. Nor can indeterminate things be the causes of determinate intelligence. Therefore, it is not fitting to receive the truth of eternal things from the "many." Nor should we seek the judgment and distinction of universals from sensible things. Nor should we seek the judgment and sentence of good things from things lacking reason. Rather, it is necessary for the soul to enter into itself.

...being, there to investigate the true and the good, and the true reasons of all things. For the essence of the soul itself is full of these. However, they lie hidden because of the forgetfulness of birth <note>original: "oblivione genesica." In Neoplatonic thought, entering the physical world of change (*genesis*) causes the soul to forget its divine origins.</note>. Therefore, the soul seeks the truth by looking at outward things, while all the while possessing it within its own essence; it explores the "good" outside itself, having deserted its own self.

From here, therefore, everyone ought to begin the knowledge of themselves. For if we distract our gaze among a multitude of men, we will never discern that one Form <term>species: In this context, the Platonic "Form" or "Idea"—the perfect, singular blueprint of "Humanity" that exists beyond individual people.</term> of them, obscured as it is by the multitude, the division, the discord, and the manifold change of those who participate in that Form. But if we turn our sharp focus into ourselves, here indeed we behold the human Form as one, both in reason and in nature, removed from all disturbance. 

Rightly, then, does Socrates separate the soul far from the sight of the multitude when it is about to learn what a human being truly is; he refutes those opinions which act as obstacles to this contemplation. For the multitude is an obstacle to the soul's turning back into itself and to the knowledge of the one Form. For here, variety overshadows the one. Otherness obscures identity. Dissimilarity darkens similarity. For around matter, the Forms are confused, and better things are mixed with the worse.

---

## The life properly natural to the soul is not in an earthly body, but in a sublime one; therefore, all forms here are sickly and delirious.

No one should wonder if—while we say that what is natural is more frequent than what is against nature, and that the latter is narrow and restricted while the natural is expanded throughout the universe—we nevertheless confess that the majority of men are ignorant and evil, and very few are the opposite. For it is not natural for souls to lead a life together with bodies and to be occupied in the realm of generation <note>original: "generatio." This refers to the physical world of birth, death, and constant change, which Neoplatonists viewed as a lower state of existence.</note>. 

On the contrary, a separate, immaterial, and incorporeal life is more suited to souls. Therefore, when they are occupied in the realm of generation, they become like people inhabiting a plague-ridden region. Whenever they live outside of generation, they are, as Plato says, like those who dwell in the meadows <note>A reference to the "Meadow of Judgment" or the "Plain of Truth" in Platonic myth, where souls find peace and clarity.</note>. Just as one should not wonder that among those inhabiting plague-ridden places very many are sickly while very few preserve their natural health, so too you should not wonder that many souls placed in the realm of generation are subject to passions and are wicked. 

On the contrary, it would be astonishing if souls—bound by these knots, not yet released from such bodies, and surrounded by so much change—were found at any time to be sober, pure, and undisturbed. Is it not a wonder for the soul to live immaterially within material things, and to remain uncontaminated among things that perish...

...to preserve itself [un]sullied anywhere. And when it has already drunk from such cups, it is not lulled to sleep by these potions. For in truth, forgetfulness, error, and ignorance are like a potion that diverts souls into the "region of dissimilarity" <note>original: *in locum dissimilitudinis*. A famous Platonic concept used to describe the material world, where the soul feels "unlike" itself and far from God.</note>. Why then do you wonder that many are like wolves in their way of life, many are like pigs, and many others are surrounded by some other wild beast-like appearance? Since this earthly place is their lodging, and many souls have been lured by poisoned cups because of their immoderate desire. Rather, wonder at this: if any among mortals are found anywhere who are not charmed or even ensnared by such drinks—those who, relying on the gift of Mercury <note>Mercury (Hermes) was the god of reason and the one who provided the antidote (the herb *moly*) to Circe’s transformative potions.</note>, betake themselves to reason and knowledge. For just as you should not wonder if you look into Tartarus and see tortured souls—for that is the place for such things—so also you should not wonder if many souls living in the realm of "becoming" <term>generation: *generatio*; the physical world of birth and change, often viewed by Neoplatonists as a place of confusion for the soul.</term> are disturbed, ignorant, and mindless. For the realm of becoming requires such souls; just as in heaven all are good, and in Tartarus all are wicked, so in the realm of becoming, the majority are indeed depraved, while fewer are upright. For the realm of becoming does not incline toward the better and more divine extremes, but toward the worse.

->The wicked man agrees neither with others nor with himself.<-

the wicked man cannot agree with his own self. For it is necessary that he see the truth in some way because of his rational nature, yet remain largely ignorant and at odds with himself because of his disturbed imagination. Repentance <note>original: *penitentia*. Here meaning the regret or "after-thought" that occurs when the initial impulse of a vice fades.</note> demonstrates this, arriving once the disturbances have subsided. Thus, the intemperate man, because of his intelligence which is kin to the divine, sometimes thinks and speaks of divine things; but because of his desire and disturbed imagination, he wanders far from divine temperance. And since he is always at war with himself, he certainly cannot agree with others.

->Whoever knows something about a matter agrees completely regarding it.<-

It is necessary for those who know something about a matter to be in harmony regarding it. The first cause of this harmony is the determined nature of the things themselves; the second is that the judging faculties of cognition are the same in everyone; the third is that in the "first principles," the intellect is united to itself. Therefore, whatever possesses intelligence is a participant in this union. Knowledge is indeed a certain illumination depending on the intellect, while harmony is an illumination proceeding from unity. For harmony is the union of different things. It is therefore necessary that those who share in the same knowledge agree with one another.

# PROCLUS.

### Each of us is a soul, and this soul possesses within itself all divine and natural forms.

<margin>to produce from itself, and to recognize within itself, all divine and natural forms <note>original: *species*. In Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal blueprints or "Ideas" of all things.</note>.</margin>
**P**lato’s entire purpose in this book is to recall us to the knowledge of ourselves, and to demonstrate that our essence consists of forms and rational principles. Indeed, perfect knowledge of ourselves would be to judge our powers from our essence, and our actions from those powers. However, we possess a more common knowledge of ourselves by knowing the essence of the soul from its powers, and its powers from its actions; indeed, these three flow together within the soul. For its essence is in actuality, and its action exists essentially. This action becomes intellectual according to the act, while the essence becomes kindred to its own perfection.

**T**he soul leads itself by free motion; it provides good for itself, purifies itself, and educates itself, even when it seems to be educated from elsewhere.

<margin>Animals, being deprived of reason, are governed by external impulse and are cared for from the outside—specifically under the condition by which the mover itself moves them, as they are stripped of that faculty by which they might regain their footing and preserve themselves under their own guidance.</margin>
The rational soul, however, because of its characteristic of being self-moving and self-operating by its very nature, can act upon itself, move itself, and provide its own good. Now, purification does not happen to us from external sources, but takes its origin from the innermost parts of the soul. For every evil happens from external things and is foreign to the soul, but good comes from the innermost depths. For the soul is naturally "good-formed" <note>original: *boniformis*. Having the shape or nature of the Good.</note>. And the more perfect it becomes, the more it claims for itself a life that is self-moving. This is because it becomes movable from the outside only due to its connection and interaction with the body. Therefore, whatever it receives from external sources remains placed outside itself, just like sensory objects and those perceived through the imagination. Only those things are truly in the soul which are made by the soul within itself and are produced by it. Thus, it is purified by itself, since reason, beginning from itself, ends in itself. For this reason, it is rightly understood what Socrates says—namely, that among those disputing, the one who truly speaks is the one who responds. If this person is then refuted, and the refuted person is purified, they certainly purify themselves while being purified and liberate themselves from ignorance, applying the refutation to themselves. This is indeed consistent with the nature of the self-moving soul. This saying also confirms that "learning is recollection" <note>original: *disciplinas esse reminiscentias*. The Platonic theory of *anamnesis*, suggesting that we do not "learn" new things, but rather remember truths the soul knew before it was born into a body.</note>. For the fact that those responding speak all things from themselves is the greatest sign of recollection—namely, that souls bring forth reasons and discourses from within themselves, and only need someone to awaken them. They are not like blank tablets <term>tabula rasa: *tabellas uacuas*; a writing tablet with no marks on it, used here to argue against the idea that the mind is born empty.</term> that receive figures from the outside. For they are...

<summary>Proclus argues that the soul is self-moving and contains all universal knowledge within itself, meaning that learning is actually a process of internal "recollection" rather than external instruction. He distinguishes the rational human soul, which can self-purify, from the souls of animals which are driven only by external impulses.</summary>

->**ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT.**<-
<note>original: *daemon*. In this Platonic context, a *daemon* is not a "demon" in the modern sense, but a tutelary spirit or divine intermediary that guides an individual's soul.</note>

...for these [principles] are always inscribed within, and the writer himself is inside. Yet not everyone can read what is inscribed or recognize that they have been written there. Indeed, because of a "beneficent forgetfulness," <note>This "forgetfulness" (*lethe*) is a central Platonic concept; the soul forgets its divine origin upon entering a body so that it may experience the physical world, but must "remember" to find truth.</note> their eye is clouded with filth, and through that very forgetfulness, they have fallen into passions. Therefore, the only task necessary is to remove the obstacle placed in the way. Knowledge brought in from the outside is not required. For souls have within themselves the doors of truth, but they are closed by earthly and material appearances. If, therefore, someone demonstrates things with great diligence, the souls—while incited from elsewhere—produce learned responses from within themselves. By this very fact, they declare that Platonic saying to be true: that the soul knows all things, and needs only something from the outside to incite it to respond.

Furthermore, when someone is being educated, the fact that they purify themselves is the work of a daemonic power. For spirits <note>daemones</note> do not act upon us from the outside, but direct and govern us from within, as if from the stern of a ship. Nor do they purify us as if we were merely bodies receiving motion from an external source. Instead, they care for us as beings who move by our own power. In this way, they provide good things and purge the passions. Socrates, therefore, acting in the role of a good spirit, showed that a youth is refuted <note>Socrates was famous for his "elenchus" or method of questioning which forced students to see their own ignorance.</note> not so much by another as by himself.

### Why the evil and ignorant man is at odds with himself and others; why the good man is in agreement, and those who know are in harmony with one another.

<margin>c</margin> Frequent discord with themselves rightfully happens to many people, because they admit some things from the senses, others from the imagination, others frequently from opinion, some from anger, and many from lust. For such passions are not only stirred in men by their opinions, as the Stoics <term>Stoics: A school of philosophy that taught that destructive emotions resulted from errors in judgment.</term> teach, but also conversely: because of certain passions and impulses, people often change their opinions, frequently bringing back the worst ideas instead of the best. Therefore, receiving multifaceted motions within themselves from many principles and powers—and these being of a lower sort—they undoubtedly have a soul that is distrustful and discordant. But those endowed with knowledge receive all cognition from a single, higher principle. For the Intellect <term>Intellect: *Nous* in Greek; the highest faculty of the soul that perceives truth directly and intuitively.</term> hands down the principles to them. Now indeed, all true judgments are daughters of the Intellect. Since, therefore, they all proceed with simplicity from such a principle, it is right that they are all in harmony with one another.

### Those who think man is composed of soul and body consequently separate the useful from the just; those who believe man is the soul join them together.

<margin>u</margin> Whether the "just" and the "useful" are the same thing is a point where others disagree. The Platonists, however, judge them to be the same. For the Epicureans <term>Epicureans: Philosophers who argued that pleasure and the avoidance of pain are the primary goals of life.</term> and certainly some of the Stoics, placing our ultimate end in what is "according to nature"...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s Neo-Platonic commentary on the nature of the soul. While the previous page discussed the "inscriptions" of truth within the soul and the role of the inner guardian (the daemon), this section contrasts the soul's true nature with the physical body and explores how the soul's focus determines its state of being.</meta>

# PROCLUS:

...to live, as do the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who generally believed that human happiness requires both virtue and external/physical goods.</note> who fulfill our "good" from necessary physical things. They cannot easily confirm that the **just** and the **useful** <note>original: *iustum atque utile*. This was a major debate in ancient philosophy: is doing the "right" thing always "advantageous" for the person doing it?</note> are the same. This is likewise true for anyone who claims that a human being is merely an "animated body," or a composite made of both body and soul. For such a person will flee from wounds and death—even if it means acting unjustly—simply so that the "animal" (the body) might be preserved. This is because they believe the good of any animal is to behave according to its physical nature and to be preserved in that physical state. In their view, therefore, what is **useful** (survival) disagrees with what is **just**.

However, those who place the ultimate goal (the *end*) in the soul alone—not needing any bodily things—and who believe that the human being **is** the soul itself using a body as a tool, these people certainly judge the **just** and the **useful** to be the same. For they place both within the soul, and they understand that the "passions" <note>Physical sensations or sufferings.</note> of the instruments (the body) are separate from the users of those instruments (the soul). The argument proving that the **just** is **useful** proceeds in this way:

->Every **just** thing is **beautiful**;<-
->every **beautiful** thing is **good**;<-
->therefore, every **just** thing is **good**.<-

And since the **good** and the **useful** are the same thing, it follows that every **just** thing is **useful**.

*The soul draws into itself the likeness of the thing to which it adheres; likewise concerning the vehicles of divine souls and our own.*

<margin>a</margin> Souls also draw toward themselves the "forms" <note>original: *species*. In this context, the soul takes on the characteristics or "shape" of what it focuses on.</note> of those things to which they join themselves. Certainly, when they liken themselves to the **Intellect** <note>The higher realm of divine, unchanging truth.</note>, they soon claim for themselves an immutability in their opinions and their life. But when they couple themselves to **Generation** <note>The physical world of constant change, birth, and decay.</note>, they pursue novelty everywhere, and are carried now into these opinions, now into those. In that state, they hardly perceive the stable "reasons" (the internal truths) of the soul.

By this, **Plato** signifies that more noble and gifted souls—those possessing the intelligence of the gods' unstained purity—tend to be occupied with a kind of "apparent purity," which they insert into their own "idol" <note>original: *idolo*. Here, it likely refers to the lower reflection or image of the soul that interacts with the physical world.</note>. This is because the essence of the **divine garments** <note>This refers to the "astral vehicle" (*ochema*) or the subtle body that Neoplatonists believed the soul "wore" as it descended from the heavens.</note> is inviolable and their purity is immaterial. It is indeed necessary for souls to put on these "garments," purifying their own kindred coverings and keeping their "clothes" uncontaminated by the world of Generation, rather than placing all their focus on the purity of their external, physical clothes.

*One science, remaining within itself, fills many without being diminished; from this we conclude the soul is separate from the body.*

<margin>e</margin> It is the work of the same science <note>original: *scientia*. Here meaning a body of knowledge or a branch of learning.</note> to persuade one person and to persuade many. In this Platonic sentiment, a kind of hymn and celebration of **Knowledge** is contained. From this, it becomes clear how great and of what sort each branch of knowledge is: because by imitating the **Intellect** itself, the same knowledge fills each individual and everyone simultaneously with understanding. It is indeed indivisible and remains confident within itself, and meanwhile, it perfects all things that participate in it.

...just like the mind, which indeed hands down from itself to all, and yet again to each one individually. These things certainly judge our essence <term>essence: the fundamental nature of what something is, independent of its physical form</term> to be separate from the body and remaining within itself. For if knowledge—which is our perfection—possesses such a faculty, it is because physical powers diminish themselves when they transmit themselves. Therefore, the soul is similarly present to the entire body and to all its members, although different members participate in it in different ways.

->Someone can be prophetic without knowledge; but a true prophet knows for certain what he proclaims.<-

<margin>ii</margin> If Plato speaks of diviners <note>original: *uaticinatores*; those who predict the future through divine inspiration or signs</note>, he means that such a person foretells what he announces there by opinion, not by knowledge. For certain diviners are not endowed with knowledge, but are carried along by opinion; however, those who are not only diviners but also true prophets <note>original: *uates*; a higher class of inspired poets or seers</note> already possess knowledge, and they hold a knowledge superior to the human kind. He also means that the impulses and motions of more noble souls are somehow stirred up by the higher powers <note>original: *superis*; the celestial or divine beings</note>, precisely because they act even beyond opinion, often even if they operate without [discursive] knowledge.

## **The Good. The Beautiful. The Just. The Super-intelligibly Intelligible. Intellectual Essence. Life. Intellect.**

<margin>i</margin> Among the principles of things, the **Good** itself towers over **Beauty**, and Beauty over **Justice**. For the Good stands above the "intelligibles" <term>intelligibles: the highest realm of reality, consisting of pure ideas that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses</term>, situated in an inaccessible place. Beauty, however, remains hidden within the primary intelligibles. More explicitly, though, it is found at the very end of that order. Finally, Justice remains united in the first rank of the "intellectuals" <term>intellectuals: the level of being just below the intelligibles, associated with the active, thinking Mind</term>. Consequently, it shines forth at the conclusion of the intellectual procession of the gods. Again, the Good itself reigns among the gods, Beauty in the Minds <note>original: *mentibus*</note>, and Justice reigns in souls. For this reason, that which is **just** is also **beautiful**. Yet, not everything beautiful is necessarily **just**; rather, the very cause of beautiful things precedes Justice. Likewise, everything beautiful is **good**, but the source of all good things precedes everything beautiful. Again, the **just** is indeed **good**, being joined to the Good through the mediation of Beauty; but the Good is superior to both. You will find it to be so if you consider even the furthest extremes of things. For the material cause, although...

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s Neo-Platonic commentary on the nature of the soul. Having previously established the soul's separation from the body, he now explores how the soul acts as a "middle point" where divine qualities like Goodness, Justice, and Beauty converge into a single essence.</meta>

# PROCLUS.

...even if something should exist that is base and deformed, it certainly participates in the One, yet it is devoid of form <note>original: *speciei*; in Platonic philosophy, a "Form" or "Idea" is the perfect archetype that gives a thing its recognizable nature</note>. That which is perceivable by the senses, however, possesses traces of beauty, but in no way possesses justice. For this reason, in the *Phaedrus*, Socrates says that among decaying images there is no splendor of justice or temperance. But beauty alone holds this privilege: that it is most clearly visible everywhere and is most desirable. Where, therefore, there is the just, there is the beautiful. Where there is the beautiful, there is the good—whether you choose to look at the primary principles or at the manifestations of those principles extending down to the furthest limits. All things indeed participate in the Good itself, for it is the principle of all things. But only those things which possess some form participate in the Beautiful. Finally, only souls are participants in justice.

Now, however, in the very center of all things—which is the soul—all these qualities are connected to one another: the good, the just, and the beautiful. Indeed, the soul's "good" is its beauty and its justice. The just is also simultaneously both beautiful and good. Likewise, the beautiful is both good and just. And this statement is true not only in this kind of trinity, but also in many other cases. Just as among the first principles Being <term>Being: the most basic state of existing (Latin: *ens*)</term> precedes Life, and Life precedes Mind. Similarly, in the effects of these principles, not every composite that possesses Being also possesses Life, nor is every living thing immediately endowed with a Mind. But, in turn, all things with intelligence also live and exist, and living things also exist by the very fact of their living.

But since there is such a difference through this kind of trinity in the outer limits of creation, they all flow together in the soul, where Being, Life, and Intellect exist simultaneously. Here, Life is both Intellect and Essence. Intellect is likewise both Essence and Life. For there is one simplicity in the soul, a single substance; neither its existing, nor its living, nor its understanding is something added from the outside <note>original: *aduenticiú*; something external or accidental rather than essential to the nature of the thing</note>. Rather, its intellect is essential and living; its life is also intellectual by its very essence. Finally, its essence is intellectual and living. 

Therefore, everywhere everything is present, and from all these things a "one" is formed by a similar logic. Its good prevails through beauty and justice, and the beautiful is both good and just; and again, the just is filled with the good and the beautiful. To be sure, the subject is one, but the definitions <note>original: *ratióes*; the logical descriptions or aspects used to understand a thing</note> are diverse. Here we neither rely on the identity of these three according to their definitions, nor do we think they are separate according to their subject. Instead, we preserve their differing definitions as they relate to one another, while maintaining that the subject is one. For this reason, these qualities concur everywhere through the actions of the soul. Just as the definitions of the virtues are different, yet there is only one composite of them all; it is impossible to be a participant in justice and yet be void of temperance, or to have only these two while lacking the others...

->He proves that every just thing by its own nature is beautiful and good.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' featuring architectural or foliate patterns.</image-desc>
**O**mne just thing we shall confirm to be beautiful by the following reasons: 
since the soul is a certain multiplicity, and in it this part indeed is first, 
that part is middle, and that part is last. 
Come, tell me, when do we say justice is created in it? Is it when the middle 
or the last part attempts to dominate the higher parts? Or rather when the first 
commands the middle, and the middle the last? But if it were the case that 
the worse prevailed over the better, they would no longer be such things by nature. 
For that which is fitting to be named "better" is more honorable by nature. 
If, therefore, it is impossible for the same thing to be naturally better and worse 
at the same time, justice must then be found in the soul when that which is best 
within it holds the command of the entire life; while the middle part, 
being subject to the better, prevails over the last part. For then each part 
of the soul has what is suitable to it: the first indeed reigning, 
the second guarding, and finally the last serving the better. 
Therefore, the "just" itself is by nature a distributor of that which is 
suitable to each part of the soul. It is the cause for each part 
preserving its own duty <note>original: *officii*; meaning its proper function or role</note> and of distributing its own dignity, 
and thus it is the preservation of the whole order. 
Indeed, an order and moderation of this kind, being fitting to nature, is 
naturally beautiful. Justice is therefore the cause of beauty and is itself beautiful. 

Furthermore, the "just" is twofold. One type is found in contracts, 
which preserves arithmetical equality <term>arithmetical equality: a simple 1:1 ratio where everyone receives the exact same amount regardless of status</term>. 
The other, however, is concerned with distribution, 
consisting in geometric equality <term>geometric equality: a proportion where rewards are given based on a person’s merit or value</term>. 
In the first case, it preserves arithmetical equality so that we do not 
defraud a companion in contracts—namely, by receiving more ourselves 
than we have given. In the second case, it distributes unequal things 
to unequals according to the dignity of each, geometric proportion being 
preserved; just as persons differ among themselves, so also should the things 
distributed to those persons differ. And so, every just thing, 
as we have said, is equal...

<meta>This page continues the argument regarding the soul’s internal order. <header>PROCLUS.</header>

Moreover, everything equal is beautiful; for the unequal is disjointed and ugly. Therefore, everything just is beautiful. Furthermore, beauty exists in bodies when form overcomes matter. For matter itself is shapeless and ugly; but when form is overcome by matter, then form is filled with a certain lack of form and ugliness, and becomes as if it were something formless, having been made similar to the underlying nature <note>referring to the chaotic, shapeless nature of raw matter</note> of that which it occupies. If, therefore, that which is intellectual within us in the soul takes the place of form, and the irrational part takes the place of matter—for intellect
<margin>1</margin>and reason are counted in the order of the limit <note>original: *termini*; in Platonic thought, "Limit" provides structure, while the "Unlimited" or "Indefinite" is chaotic</note>, while the irrational is placed in the category of the indefinite—for by nature it is indeterminate and lacks measure—it is necessary that in the soul also beauty shines forth then, when reason indeed reigns, and the modes of life lacking reason are subjected to reason. But justice itself gives command to reason and assigns servitude to the irrational. For it attributes to each what is consistent with itself: to the leading part,
<margin>i</margin>the leadership; to the inferior part, it designates obedience. Just as in the craftsmanship of the world the irrational is subject to us, and the irrational is subjected to the reason implanted in us like a vehicle <note>the "vehicle of the soul" is a Neoplatonic concept of an ethereal body that carries the soul through the heavens</note>. Thus, the just is
<margin>i</margin>naturally beautiful and the cause of the soul's beauty. Likewise, the just is something perfect and defined. For the unjust is judged to be imperfect and indefinite, and it wanders infinitely, never halting its step, overstepping the boundary of justice. Therefore, justice itself imposes measure and limit upon whatever it is present in, and thus makes all things perfect. Since it is such, it deservedly makes the soul beautiful. For beauty naturally follows that which is perfect and measured, just as ugliness
<margin>i</margin>accompanies the unmeasured and the indeterminate. Therefore, the just is by nature beautiful. Finally, the World-Maker <term>Mundi faber: also known as the Demiurge, the divine craftsman who shapes the universe</term> himself adorned this whole universe through justice. For he bound the world with the most beautiful of all bonds, and made it indissoluble because of the power of analogical proportion, which holds it together and makes it friendly to itself in every part. Now, that which is similar to the world—the most beautiful of all visible things—is surely itself also beautiful. Therefore, what is just is necessarily also beautiful.

->### ON THE SOUL AND THE SPIRIT<-
<margin>5</margin>
<margin>62</margin>

and at first sight, it moves souls toward itself. This is confirmed in the *Phaedrus* <note>one of Plato’s dialogues exploring love, beauty, and the immortality of the soul</note>. For in truth, **the beautiful** <note>original: καλὸν (*kalon*)</note>—whether it is so named from the word **to call** <note>original: παρὰ τὸ καλεῖν (*para to kalein*)</note> because it summons souls, or from **to charm** <note>original: παρὰ τὸ κηλεῖν (*para to kelein*)</note> because it soothes those who look upon it—is certainly lovable by its very nature. For this reason, love is said to lead the lover toward the beautiful. 

Whatever is lovable is also **desirable**; for love is a robust and vehement desire for something or someone. And whatever loves, desires that which it lacks. Furthermore, everything desirable is also **good**, whether it is truly good or merely appears to be so. Indeed, many things that are not actually good present themselves to us as objects of pursuit because they offer themselves to those who desire them under the guise of being "good." 

However, it was clearly demonstrated by **Socrates** in the *Meno* <note>a Platonic dialogue concerning whether virtue can be taught</note> that it is impossible for those who recognize the true nature of evil to actually desire it. Therefore, every object of desire is a "good." And if it is primarily desirable, it will also be primarily good. If, however, it is only an *apparent* object of desire, it will be a similar kind of "good." In every case, one must apply the distinction of whether a thing is "apparent" or "real." 

For if something is beautiful and apparent, it is certainly both lovable and desirable, and thus shares in that kind of "good." But if it is beautiful and lovable by its very nature, it is likewise truly good. 

Yet what could possibly be desirable besides this? Could it be **evil**? No, that is impossible; once a thing is known to be harmful, no one would choose it. All things desire the good, and no desire is directed toward evil for its own sake. Nor is desire directed toward anything that is neither good nor evil, for such a thing is only acted upon for the sake of something else, and constitutes no end in itself. Every object of desire is an **end** <note>the goal or purpose of an action</note>. 

Thus, if something evil is desired, it is because it *appears* to be good; it is longed for as a good. And if something not beautiful is loved, it is because it *appears* beautiful; it is loved as a beauty. If, therefore, everything beautiful is lovable, and everything lovable is desirable, and everything desirable is good, it follows that **everything beautiful is good**. 

And conversely: everything good is desirable; the desirable is lovable (since to love is to desire vehemently). Hence, in the *Symposium* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the nature of love</note>, Socrates says that the good is lovable just as the beautiful is. If, I say, every good is desirable, and the desirable in turn is lovable, and the lovable is beautiful, it follows that every good is beautiful. 

Let no one object to us now that the "Good" itself resides above "Beauty," nor that there are two distinct types of things called "lovable." For we are not currently disputing the first principles of the universe <note>a reference to the highest metaphysical levels in Neoplatonism where the 'Good' or 'The One' is above all else</note>, but rather those beauties and goods that exist within ourselves. Therefore, the good that is within us is simultaneously desirable and to be loved. 

Through love, therefore, we acquire and possess it—through love, I say, and an earnest devotion. And if anyone reflects upon themselves, they will clearly see and recognize that this kind of internal good inspires in us a sharper love than the beauties manifested to our physical senses.
