->**Man is a soul using a body as an instrument.**<-
->Therefore, the evils of the body do not<-
->pertain to the soul or to the man,<-
->just as the defects of tools do not pertain<-
->to the craftsman or his art.<-

<margin>f</margin>
Furthermore, most people consider wounds and death to be evils. Yet which of these is truly an evil for us? If indeed it does not pass into the **soul**—which is what we ourselves actually are—then it is not an evil. For the sufferings of the instruments do not change the virtues of those who use them; therefore, a blacksmith does not lose his **art of cutting** <note>original: *artem secandi*</note> just because his saw is blunt at some point. Nor, even if our happiness consisted in the craft of blacksmithing, would I consider the blacksmith unhappy simply because he lacked a saw. Now, just as the soul possesses the body as an instrument, so the body possesses certain instruments through which it moves external things. A defect in these does not harm the good condition of the body; similarly, the sufferings of the body do not pass over into the soul. 

For this reason, even if **death** is an evil of the body, it is nevertheless not an evil of the soul. If, therefore, the beauty of an action resides in the soul, while an evil simultaneously occurs in something else, it has not yet been shown that the same thing is both beautiful and evil at once. One may also distinguish this through **dialectical reasoning** <note>the art of investigating the truth through logical discussion</note>: one thing may be something in itself, while another is so by **accident** <note>original: *secundum accidens*; a philosophical term for a quality that is not essential to the thing's nature</note>. Indeed, a brave action is beautiful in and of itself. If it is ever "evil," it is so only by accident, because it happens that the one acting bravely dies. For let us grant, if you wish, that death is numbered among evils. Therefore, a brave duty is not an evil because of the very fact that it is brave (and thus beautiful), but it is "evil" only by accident. That which is brave is one thing (beautiful), while that which happens is another (the perceived evil). It has not been shown that a thing is evil for the same reason it is beautiful, but rather it is called evil by circumstance due to death. 

Consequently, he is ignorant of the **essence of man** who separates the Good from the Beautiful, placing one in one thing and the other in another—the Good in the body, and the Beautiful in the actions of the soul. But in truth, the human being is the **intellect** itself, an essence segregated from the body, in which whatever is beautiful is also good.

->**How these two differ: namely, "according to itself" and "insofar as it is itself."**<-

<margin>d</margin>Phrases of this kind—namely *according to itself* <note>original: *secundum seipsum*</note> and *insofar as it is itself* <note>original: *qua ipsum*</note>—are distinguished even in the works of **Aristotle**. For that which belongs to something *according to itself* might not belong to it primarily. However, that which is fitting for something *insofar as it is itself* belongs to it primarily and equally, beyond just being a fitting attribute. Therefore, if **Beauty** is the cause of **symmetry** <note>original: *commensuratio*; refers to the harmonious proportion of parts</note> in the soul, and for this very reason is called "beautiful," it ensures that the better part of the soul dominates the worse, perfects us, and purges the soul's deformity. By this very reasoning, it is **Good**—not indeed by accident, but by the very reason it is beautiful. For insofar as it is beautiful, it is symmetrical; and insofar as it is symmetrical, it is also good. For the Good is the measure; certainly, insofar as it is beautiful, it exists also as good. Similarly, the **Ugly**, insofar as it is ugly, is evil. For insofar as it is ugly, it is formless, indeterminate, and disordered, and by this very reasoning, it is evil. Therefore, insofar as it is ugly, it is surely evil. Consequently, the same thing is always both beautiful and good; and conversely, a thing is equally ugly and evil. Keep this rule in mind here, which Aristotle also used later: **If any two things are interchangeable, then their opposites are also interchangeable.** If, therefore, the Beautiful and the Good are interchangeable with each other, then their opposites—namely the Evil and the Ugly—are similarly interchangeable.

### The Work of Proclus on Sacrifice, translated by

<margin>q</margin>Just as lovers proceed by reason from the beauty that appears to the senses toward divine beauty, so too the **ancient priests**, when they considered the certain kinship and **sympathy** <note>original: *compassionem*; in this context, it refers to "natural resonance" or "co-suffering," the idea that objects in the physical world are linked to spiritual forces</note> of some things for others in nature, and of manifest things for hidden powers, they discovered "all things in all things" and established their sacred science. For they recognized the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest things in the highest. In heaven, they found earthly things according to their cause and in a celestial manner; on earth, however, they found heavenly things—but in an earthly manner.

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s treatise "On Sacrifice and Magic." On the previous page, the author established that the soul is distinct from the body. Here, he begins to explain the principle of "sympathy"—the idea that all things in the universe, from stars to plants and stones, are interconnected through a shared divine harmony.</meta>

# PROCLUS:

no. For why else do we think those plants called **heliotropes** <note>original: *heliotropias*; from the Greek for "sun-turner"</note>, which follow the sun, move toward the sun's motion? Or that **selinetropes** <note>original: *selinetropias*; "moon-turners"</note>, which follow the moon, turn toward the moon? Surely all things pray and sing hymns to the leaders of their own particular order—some in an **intellectual** way, others **rationally**, others **naturally**, and still others in a **sensible** <note>meaning: through the physical senses or physical movement</note> way. 

Thus, the sun-follower moves toward the sun in whatever way it can. Indeed, if anyone could hear the vibration <note>original: *pulsationem*; a beating or pulsing</note> made by it in the air as it turns, they would surely perceive it as a kind of sound composed in honor of its king, the sort of song a plant is capable of producing. 

For this reason, one may see the sun and moon upon the earth, though according to their earthly quality. Conversely, in the heavens, one may find all plants, stones, and animals existing according to their celestial nature, possessing an **intellectual life**. The ancients, having contemplated these things, applied certain earthly things to certain celestial ones; through this similarity, they drew divine powers down into the lower realm. Indeed, similarity itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another. 

For if someone should heat hemp or papyrus and then bring it near a lamp, even if it does not touch it, he will see the hemp suddenly catch fire. Though it did not touch the flame, the ignition descends from above to the lower material. Let us therefore compare the heated hemp or papyrus to the "kinship" of lower things to higher ones; its approach to the lamp represents the opportune use of things at the right time, place, and material. The movement of the fire into the hemp represents the presence of **divine light** to that which is capable of receiving it. Finally, the catching fire of the hemp represents the **deification** <note>original: *deificationi*; the process of becoming god-like or being filled with divine power</note> of mortals and the illumination of material things, which are then carried upward like the burning hemp because of their participation in a certain divine seed.

What shall I say of the **Lotus**? Before the sun rises, the Lotus keeps its leaves folded; but as the sun rises, it unfolds them little by little. As the sun reaches the highest point of the heavens, the Lotus expands its leaves to their fullest. But as the sun moves from the midpoint toward its setting, the plant gradually contracts its leaves. It seems that by this expansion and contraction of leaves, the plant honors the sun no less than humans do with the expressions of their faces and the movement of their lips. 

Not only in plants, which have a trace of life, but also in stones, one may observe an imitation and a certain participation in the lights from above. Just as the **helitis** stone <note>a "sun-stone," possibly aventurine or a similar shimmering quartz</note> imitates the solar rays with its golden beams, so the stone called the **eye of heaven** or **eye of the sun** has a shape similar to the pupil of an eye, and a ray flashes out from the center of that pupil. Likewise, the **selenite** stone <note>original: *selenitus*; "moon-stone"</note>, which is the lunar stone, mimics the horned shape of the moon and follows the lunar motion through its own internal change.

This interconnectedness allows practitioners to draw down divine influences by using earthly materials that share a kinship with celestial powers.</summary>

...flame. Then there is the **heliofelenus** <note>original: *heliofelenus*; likely a variation of *helioselenos* or "sun-moon stone," a legendary gem believed to contain the properties of both luminaries</note> stone, which is both solar and lunar; it imitates, in a certain way, the meeting of the sun and the moon, and reflects them in its shape and color. In this way, all things are full of divine things. Earthly things are indeed full of celestial ones, while celestial things are full of those that are above the heavens. Every order of things proceeds down to the very last. For those qualities which are gathered into one above the natural order are thereafter expanded as they descend. There, different souls are arranged under different divine powers <note>original: *numinibus*; referring to the indwelling spirit or power of a deity</note>.

Then there are also many **solar animals**, such as lions and roosters, which participate in a certain solar deity according to their own nature. From this, it is marvelous how much lower things in the same order yield to the higher, even if they do not yield to them in physical size or power. For this reason, they say the rooster is greatly feared by the lion and almost worshipped. We cannot assign a cause for this based on physical matter or the senses, but only from the contemplation of the higher order. For it is clear that the presence of the **solar virtue** <note>the specific spiritual power or essence of the sun</note> suits the rooster more than the lion. This is also apparent from the fact that the rooster applauds the rising sun with certain hymns, as it were, and calls to it when the sun turns toward us from the mid-heaven of the **antipodes** <note>the opposite side of the earth</note>. Sometimes, certain **solar angels** have appeared endowed with such forms; though they themselves are formless, they appear in a form to us, who are ourselves formed creatures.

At times, solar demons have even been seen with the face of a lion. When a rooster was presented to them, they suddenly disappeared. This occurs because things lower in the same order always revere the higher, just as many people, when looking upon the images of divine men, are accustomed by that very sight to fear committing something shameful.

To speak briefly, some things revolve their hearts toward the revolutions of the sun, like the plants we mentioned. Others imitate the shape of solar rays in some way, such as the palm and the date. Others [imitate] the fiery nature of the sun, like the laurel, and others something else. One may truly see the properties that are gathered in the sun distributed everywhere among the things following in the **solar order**—namely, among angels, demons, souls, animals, plants, and stones.

Therefore, the authors of the **ancient priesthood** <note>referring to practitioners of theurgy, a form of ritual magic intended to unite the soul with the divine</note> discovered the worship of higher powers through visible things, while mixing some and purifying others. They mixed many things together because they saw that simple, individual things possessed some property of a deity, but not enough on their own to successfully summon that deity. For this reason, by the very mixing of many things, they attracted celestial influences; and by composing one thing out of many, they made it like that **One** <note>the Neoplatonic "One," the supreme source of all existence</note> which is above the many. They fashioned statues mixed from many materials and collected compound scents, bringing them together into one by the art of **divine symbols** <note>original: *symbola*; physical objects that "contain" a spiritual essence</note>, creating a single thing that exists just as the divine exists according to its essence...

While the division of these powers weakened each one, their mixture restored them to the form of the **archetype** <note>original: *exemplaris ideam*; referring to the Platonic Ideal or original model</note>. Sometimes, however, a single herb or stone suffices for a divine work. For the **thistle** <note>original: *Cnebison*</note> is sufficient for the sudden appearance of some deity; the **laurel** for protection; the **spiny shrub** <note>original: *Raccinum*</note>, **sea onion**, **coral**, **diamond**, and **Jasper** [serve other needs], while the **heart of a mole** is used for prophecy. For purification, one uses **sulfur** and **sea water**.

Therefore, the priests, through the mutual kinship and sympathy <note>original: *compassionémque*; the concept of *sympatheia*, where earthly objects are spiritually linked to celestial ones</note> of things, gathered them into one, and through their natural repulsion, they expelled [harmful things]. They purified with sulfur and **bitumen** <note>original: *asphalto*</note> when necessary, sprinkling sea water. Indeed, sulfur purifies because of the sharpness of its odor, while sea water purifies because of its fiery portion. They also employed animals that were fitting for the worship of the gods, and other similar things.

Because of this, receiving powers from these and similar things, they first recognized the powers of the **daemons** <note>original: *dæmonum*; intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</note>, realizing that they were closely linked to natural things and actions. Through these natural things, to which they are drawn, they summoned the daemons into their presence. Then, they proceeded from the daemons to the very powers and actions of the gods. Part of this was through daemons teaching their students, and part was through their own diligence, interpreting fitting symbols and ascending to the very understanding of the gods. Finally, having set aside natural things and actions, and for the most part the daemons as well, they received themselves into the
->**fellowship of the gods.**<-

### Porphyry on the Occasions, or causes leading us to the Intelligibles. Translated by Marsilio Ficino.

### On the nature of corporeal and incorporeal things.

Every body is in a place. But none of those things which are incorporeal in themselves are in a place. Those things which are incorporeal by their own nature are everywhere, for the very reason that they surpass all body and place; they are not spread out by distance, but exist in a certain indivisible condition. Those things which are incorporeal by their own nature are not present to bodies in a localized way, but are present to them whenever they wish, by turning and inclining toward them, insofar as they naturally turn and lean toward those things. Yet, even when they are not present to bodies by any local condition, they are present to them through a certain relationship.

65

Those things which are incorporeal by nature are certainly not present in bodies through substance or essence. For they do not mix with bodies; nevertheless, from their very inclination, a certain power subsists in them as if in an instant, communicated now to the bodies nearby. Indeed, that very inclination provides a certain secondary power close to the bodies.

### On the nature, the binding, and the releasing of the soul.

The soul is a certain middle point between indivisible essences and the essence that is divisible among physical bodies. The Intellect, however, is an indivisible essence alone. But material qualities and forms are divisible according to the bodies they inhabit. Not everything that acts upon another does so through proximity and touch; even those things which do act through proximity and touch do not use that proximity except by accident. The soul is bound to the body by a certain turning <note>original: *conuersionē*; a Neoplatonic term for the soul’s attention or orientation</note> toward the passions <note>term: *passiones* (passions) — here meaning physical sensations and emotions that "act upon" the soul</note> arising from the body. Conversely, it is released insofar as it suffers nothing from the body. What nature has bound, nature itself also releases. Again, what the soul has united, the soul itself tears apart. Nature indeed binds the body to the soul. But the soul binds itself to the body. For this reason, nature separates the body from the soul, but the soul separates itself from the body.

All things are in all things in a certain way, according to the condition of those things in which they exist.

We do not understand "all things in all things" in a uniform way; rather, the essence of each thing relates to all things according to its own nature: in the intellect, it exists intellectually; in the soul, rationally; in plants, through seeds; in bodies, through images. And in that which is above all these, it exists in a certain way that is beyond the intellect and beyond essence.

In the highest things, there is unity with power; in the lowest, there is multitude with weakness.

Incorporeal substances, when descending, are divided and their powers are multiplied through deficiency as they reach individual things. When ascending, however, they are unified and return at once into one through the abundance of their power.

### On the kinds of life.

A condition of ambiguity exists not only in bodies, but life itself is also spoken of in many ways. For the life of a plant is one thing, that of an animal another. Again, there is the life of an intellectual essence, and finally that of a superior nature. There is the life of the soul and that of the intellect; for even those higher things live, even if none of the things that exist because of them may be granted a life similar to theirs.

Those things which generate sometimes turn toward what they have generated, and sometimes they do not.

Everything that generates by its own essence generates something inferior to itself, and...

Everything that is generated turns back toward its generator by its very nature. Among those things that generate, some do not turn toward their offspring at all. Others, however, are partially turned toward them and partially not. Finally, some turn only toward their offspring and do not, in the meantime, reflect back upon themselves.

### Sense, imagination, memory, and intelligence.

Memory is not a certain preservation of images <gloss>original: ἀπὸ τῶν μελιτηθέντων προβαλλέσθαι ἰδέας προβλήματα; from those things practiced, to project ideas as objects of thought</gloss> but rather it is the very propositions or productions into action of those things which the mind has meditated upon, bringing them recently into actualization.

The soul indeed possesses the reasons <note>term: *rationes* (reasons) — in Neoplatonism, these are the "formative principles" or blueprints of all things held within the soul</note> for everything. It acts according to these reasons, either being prompted from the outside toward such an undertaking, or by turning itself inward toward its own reasons. When it is prompted from the outside, it commits to introducing the senses as if to external things; but when it enters into itself, it reaches toward the intelligences. Therefore, the senses do not exist outside of imagination. Nor, as one might say, do the intelligences, insofar as they belong to a living being. Again, the senses do not exist without the "passion" <note>term: *passio* (passion/affection) — here meaning the physical state of being acted upon by an external stimulus</note> of the sensory instruments. Likewise, intelligences do not exist without imagination, unless there is a corresponding condition: just as a physical shape is a certain consequence for a sensory animal, so a mental image <note>original: *phantasma*</note> is something that follows the intelligence of a soul thinking within a living being.

### The soul is immortal.

The soul is an unextended, immaterial, and immortal essence, possessing life from itself and likewise possessing its existence in life.

### The suffering of the soul and the body is far different.

It is one thing for bodies to suffer <note>original: *pati*; meaning to undergo a change or be acted upon by an external force</note>, and another to suffer within a body. For the suffering of the body occurs with a transformation <note>original: *transmutatione*; a physical change in state</note>. However, the suffering of the soul is a certain adaptation and an affection toward the thing itself, and a certain action. It is in no way similar to the heating or cooling of bodies. For this reason, if the suffering of bodies happens with transformation, it must be said that all incorporeal things are free from suffering. For those things which are separated from matter and bodies in their activity remain the same; but those which approach matter and bodies are not themselves passive, but rather the things in which they appear are the ones that suffer. For when a living being perceives, the soul seems to be like a certain separate harmony <note>original: *armoniæ*</note> that, by itself, moves the tuned strings. The body, however, is like the harmony that exists inseparably within the strings. But the soul <note>original: *animal*; referring to the living composite</note> seems to be the cause of movement because it is "animated" <note>term: *animatum* — literally "souled" or given life</note>. This is similar to a musician being the cause of music because he is harmonious. The bodies, which are struck through sensory suffering, appear similar to the tuned strings. For indeed in that place

...indeed, it does not suffer from separate harmonic things. But the strings—the musician certainly moves them through the harmony that is within himself, yet the strings would not be moved by musical reason even if the musician wished it, unless harmony itself directed it.

### On the differences between incorporeal things.

The very name "incorporeal" <note>original: *incorporeorum*</note> is not assigned according to a commonality of one and the same genus, in the way that "bodies" are named. Rather, it is defined according to the simple absence of body. Therefore, nothing prevents some among them from being essence, while others are not essence; and again, some existing before bodies, while others exist alongside bodies. Likewise, some are separate from bodies, while others are inseparable. Furthermore, some subsist by themselves, while others require other things in order to exist. Finally, some remain the same in their actions and movements, while others are changed in a certain way by their movements and qualities. For they are named according to the negation of what they are not, rather than the presence of what they are.

### The qualities of primary matter as assigned by Plotinus.

According to the ancients, these are the properties of matter: it is indeed incorporeal, for it is distinct from bodies. Moreover, it is void of life; it is neither intellect, nor soul, nor anything living by itself. It is formless, changeable, infinite, and powerless. Therefore, it is not "being," but rather true "non-being," a faint and shifting image. Since its primary state is found in bulk <note>original: *mole*; referring to physical mass or volume</note>, it is inherently powerless. It is a longing for existence, standing but never in a fixed state. Furthermore, it is always appearing within itself—now small, now large, now less, now more, now deficient, now exceeding. It is always becoming, but never remains; yet it is unable to escape, since it is the very lack of all being. For this reason, whatever it promises, it lies about. Even if it appears large, it suddenly turns out small. It is like a sort of game fleeing into non-existence. For its flight does not happen in space, but occurs as it falls away from being. Because of this, the images within it are contained in yet another, inferior image—just as in a mirror, an object located elsewhere appears to be in a different place. The mirror itself seems full, and yet it possesses nothing while appearing to possess everything.

### What undergoes "passion" and what does not.

All "passions" <note>term: *passio* (passion/affection) — in this philosophical context, this refers to the state of being acted upon, changed, or affected by an external force</note> concern those things subject to chance and destruction. For the path toward destruction is the admission of a passion, and it is the nature of that which "suffers" to perish. No incorporeal thing, however, undergoes destruction; rather, among them, things either are or are not. For this reason, none of them undergo passion. For that which is subject to passion ought not to remain as it is, but should be of such a nature that it can be altered and, in the meantime, receive into itself a passion from the qualities of those things that enter and pour into it.

<meta>This page continues the translation of Porphyry’s "Sentences on Intelligible Realities," likely via the Latin translation of the Renaissance philosopher Marsilio Ficino. PORPHYRY:

For alteration does not happen to that which is within from just any source; therefore, matter itself does not suffer. For by its own nature, matter is void of quality, and the forms that enter it and subsequently depart from it do not affect it. Instead, passion <note>original: *passio*; in this philosophical context, it refers to the state of "suffering" an external influence or undergoing a change, rather than emotion.</note> occurs concerning the composite [of matter and form], and the being of the one consists in the composition. For this composite is seen to persist in its existence despite the conflicting forces and qualities of the things entering and <unclear>bringing in</unclear> passion. Therefore, those things whose life comes from external sources and not from themselves can certainly undergo both living and not living. But those things whose very being consists in life must necessarily remain according to life, just as it is consistent with the absence of life not to suffer, insofar as it is an absence of life. Therefore, just as being changed and "suffering" happens to the composite of matter and form—that is, the body—yet does not happen to the matter itself, so living and perishing and suffering in this way is observed in the composite of soul and body. Nevertheless, this does not happen to the soul. For the soul is not something fused together from life and non-life, but consists of life alone, especially since it is a simple essence and the very nature of the soul is a self-moving principle.

### Every intellect contains all forms.

Intellectual essence is so similar in its parts that beings exist in both any particular intellect and in the universal intellect. But in the universal intellect, even particular beings exist in a universal manner; whereas in a particular intellect, even universal things exist simultaneously with particulars, though in a certain particular condition.

### Because the soul is life by its essence, it does not die.

Concerning the essence whose being consists in life, and whose "passions" are certainly a kind of life, even death dwells within a certain kind of life. It does not consist of a total deprivation of life all at once. Because in that realm, passion—or life—is not directed entirely toward not living, even if a certain deprivation <note>original: *orbitas*; meaning bereavement or the loss of a quality</note> occurs there.

### Every incorporeal life, however it may change, remains immortal.

In incorporeal lives, progressions are achieved while the prior states remain firm and stable in themselves. They lose nothing of themselves, nor do they change their substance to provide for lower things. For this reason, the things that subsist from them do not exist through any loss or transformation. Nor is this process like biological generation, which involves death and change. They are therefore unbegotten and incorruptible, and have been made unbegotten and incorruptible according to this very principle.

### How that which is above the intellect is understood.

Concerning that which is superior to the mind, many things are indeed said through the use of intelligence; however, it is actually considered through a certain "emptiness of intelligence," which is an intelligence of a better <note>Porphyry is likely referring to the Neoplatonic "One," which cannot be grasped by logic but only by a higher, non-discursive intuition.</note> kind.

...in a better way, just as regarding a sleeper many things are said through wakefulness, yet through the sleep itself, knowledge and experience of him are obtained: for like is usually known by like, since all knowledge is a certain assimilation toward that very thing which is known.

Non-being, however, is either superior to being, like God, or inferior, with matter. That which is called non-being we either devise ourselves when we are sometimes separated from being itself, or we understand it while we possess being. Therefore, if we are separated from being, we do not understand being itself, nor non-being above being itself, but rather we conceive non-being as a false passion <note>original: "passio"; here meaning an undergoing of change or a state of being affected, rather than emotion.</note>—a state happening to one who departs outside of himself. For just as each person, as they exist—that is, truly and through themselves—can be led back to that non-being superior to being, so by departing from being and from themselves, they are translated to the non-being which is the fall and ruin of being itself.

### Incorporeal substance is wherever it wishes.

The nature of the body in no way prevents that which is in itself incorporeal from being wherever and however it chooses. For just as that which is void of mass <note>original: "moles"; referring to the physical bulk or spatial extension of matter.</note> is incomprehensible to a body and pertains nothing to it, so that which is distended by mass does not become an obstacle to the incorporeal and lies there as if it were non-being. Nor does that which is incorporeal move through local conditions where it wishes by running about; for place exists together with mass. Nor, again, is it coerced by the limits of bodies. For whatever lies in mass in any way can be confined in a narrow space and undergo change through local conditions. But that which is entirely exempt from mass and magnitude cannot be contained by those things which are in mass, and it remains free from local motion. Therefore, it is found there by a certain definite disposition, wherever it is disposed. In the meantime, it exists both everywhere and nowhere at once. For this reason, by a certain definite affection, it is grasped either above the heavens or in some part of the world; yet when it is held in some part of the world, it is not seen with the eyes, but its presence is made manifest to men through its works.

### Incorporeal substance is confined by no body, but produces a presence in the body through which it applies itself to the body.

If an incorporeal thing is ever understood to be in a body, there is no need for it to be shut in as things are enclosed in a vessel; for no body can so contain it within itself, nor can it be held like a bladder draws and contains a liquid or a breath. Rather, it must substitute powers emanating from its own union within itself, by which, descending, it is applied to the body. Thus, its union with the body is fulfilled through a certain ineffable extension of itself. For which reason, it is not something else...

<meta>This page continues the translation of Porphyry’s "Starting Points," focusing on the soul's detachment from the body and the hierarchical relationship between the One (God), Intellect, and Soul. It explores the Neoplatonic paradox of being "everywhere and nowhere."</meta>

# PORPHYRY:

...indeed, binds the body to itself. But it is certainly the soul that binds itself. Therefore, the soul does not dissolve the body itself when it is broken or perishes; rather, the soul unties itself <note>original: "enodat"; literally "to unknot," referring to the soul freeing itself from the physical entanglement of the body.</note> when it turns away from its habitual affection toward the subject.

->Universal causes do not turn toward their effects, but rather they turn their effects toward themselves.<-

No substance through which the universe exists, and which is perfect, turns back toward its own offspring <note>original: "genituram"; referring to the lower levels of reality generated by higher principles.</note>. All perfect substances are instead led back to those things which generated them, and this movement continues all the way down to the worldly body. This body, since it is a completed whole, is led back to the soul—I mean the intellectual soul—and for that reason, it moves in a circle. The soul of the world, in turn, is lifted up toward the **Intellect**. The **Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus"; in Neoplatonism, this is the "Nous," the realm of divine thought and eternal forms.</note> is raised toward the Principle. Thus, all things reach this very point, starting from the furthest extremes, as far as the capacity of each allows; they reach it through an elevation led back to the First. This is usually achieved either from nearby or from afar. These things, therefore, can be said not only to desire God, but also to attain Him according to their strength. 

In particular substances, however—which are capable of falling toward many things—there is a downward inclination toward the realms of generation. For this reason, in these lower things, a "lapse" is said to have occurred, and in them "unfaithfulness" <note>original: "infidelitas"; here meaning a lack of adherence or loyalty to one's divine origin.</note> is condemned. Matter itself contaminates these beings, precisely because they can be deflected toward it. Yet, as long as they remain unerring, they are able to turn themselves back toward the divine. Therefore, perfection follows from the prior causes while preserving those same things turned toward what is higher; whereas a defect turns away from the higher and deflects toward the lower. It causes these beings to love the inferior while, in the meantime, turning away from the superior.

### How God, Intellect, and Soul differ in being "everywhere."

**God** is everywhere because He is nowhere. **Intellect** is everywhere; and because it is nowhere, the **soul** finally is everywhere, because it is and is nowhere. But God indeed is everywhere and nowhere regarding all those things that exist after Him. He belongs to Himself alone, in exactly the way He wills. 

The **Intellect**, however, is "everywhere" within God, but in those things which come after the Intellect, it exists "nowhere" and "everywhere" alike. Finally, the **soul** is in the Intellect and in God, and is similarly everywhere; but in the body, it is everywhere and nowhere at the same time. The **body**, moreover, is in the soul, and in the Intellect, and in God. 

Certainly all things—both beings and non-beings—come from God. And yet, God Himself is not categorized with beings or non-beings, nor does He exist in them. For if He were only "everywhere," He Himself would be all things and would be in all things. But since He is also "nowhere," all things certainly come to be through Him, and they come to be again within Him, because He exists everywhere; yet they remain distinct from Him, because He is nowhere. 

Similarly, the **Intellect**, existing everywhere and nowhere, is the cause of souls and the things following souls; yet it is not the soul itself, nor the things after the soul, nor does it exist in them; because it is clearly not only everywhere regarding those things which are after it, but also nowhere. 

Again, the **soul** is neither the body, nor is it in the body, but is the cause of the body; because while it is "everywhere" through the body, it is simultaneously "nowhere" within the body. Finally, the process of the universe ends in that which is able to be neither everywhere nor nowhere at once, but becomes a partaker of both by certain alternating turns.

ON STARTING POINTS.

## From Porphyry’s *On Abstinence from Animals*, translated by Marsilio Ficino of Florence.

### The soul sleeps in this body.

<margin>a.</margin>
We command abstinence from [eating] animals, not indeed for everyone, but certainly for anyone who intends to contemplate divine things. Such a person is one who has truly observed the charms <note>original: "ueneficia"; literally "sorceries" or "poisonous charms," referring to the distracting and deceptive nature of physical pleasures that trap the soul in the body.</note> of this dwelling place in which we live; furthermore, he recognizes that which is within himself—naturally and perpetually awake—and detects the "sleep" by which he is oppressed here. To this soul, we shall surely provide an education and a way of being nourished that is consistent both with the nature of this physical realm and with its own self-knowledge.

### Happiness is not the knowledge of divine things, but the divine life.

Blessed contemplation for us is not an accumulation of words or a multitude of academic disciplines, as someone might perhaps think; for it is not constructed in that way. Nor does it receive its increase according to the quantity of arguments and words. Otherwise, nothing would prevent those who have gathered all the disciplines together from being happy <note>original: "beatos"; in this context, it refers to "blessedness" or the highest state of human flourishing (eudaimonia).</note>. Yet, in truth, it is not just any discipline that fills one with happy contemplation; even doctrines concerning things that are true never achieve this unless a life translated into the very nature of divine things is present alongside them. 

Indeed, the goal of contemplation is **Being itself**, and to attain the truth in such a way that the internal state of the contemplator—according to the strength of his own nature—melts together into one with that which he contemplates. For the return is not toward something else, but toward his own true self; nor is the "breathing together" <note>original: "cōspiratio"; here meaning a mystical union or harmony.</note> directed at something external, but truly at himself. For he himself is truly the **Intellect** <note>original: "intellectus"; the higher mind or divine reason (Nous).</note>. Therefore, the goal is to live according to the Intellect. To this end, the speeches and disciplines applied from the outside provide us with a purifying condition, yet they are not the actual reason by which our happiness is completed. For if happiness itself consisted in a heap of words and arguments, it would be possible for men who merely hold to their education and certain duties to reach the happy end. But since it is necessary to exchange this life for another, let us say—for the sake of the soul as it purifies itself through words, reasons, and deeds—which speeches and which deeds might best instruct us. Are they not the words and duties by which we are separated from things that move the senses and from the passions of the senses? And finally, let us be led back toward the intellectual life, rising above the imagination and, as much as possible, away from the realm of passion.

### On the soul's descent and ascent.

It is necessary for us—if we are to fly back to those things which are truly our own—to entirely lay aside these things which we have taken on from our mortal nature, along with the lingering affection that sinks down toward them, through which our "descent" occurred. Furthermore, we must remember our blessed and eternal substance, and as we hasten to ascend toward the incorporeal, we must meditate chiefly on two things: first, by what method you may lay aside material and decaying existence...

He emphasizes that the soul must actively "wake up" and shed its physical attachments to return to its eternal origin.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument regarding the soul's ascent. The previous page discussed the nature of the soul's "sleep" within the body; this page describes the specific "path of return" to our original intellectual state by shedding the "garments" of physical sensation and passion.</meta>

.PORPHYRY 30
iiii i

...[we must know] how we might especially return: namely, by returning along the opposite path to that path by which we descended to these things of ours. For we were, and still are, intellectual essences, pure from all sense-perception and living in an irrational nature <note>original: "naturaq; irrationali uiuẽtes"; here Porphyry refers to the soul’s essential state as a pure intellect, which remains even while the soul is currently operating through a lower, irrational physical nature.</note>. However, we have been joined to a sensible nature, partly through the inability of our eternal [self] to turn toward its own intelligible <term>intelligible: that which can be understood by the mind alone, as opposed to the "sensible" which is perceived by the senses</term> [source], and partly through a power that leans toward lower things. For all powers that act through the senses and the body first begin to sprout into effect when the mind <note>original: "animus"; the higher, rational part of the human being.</note> least perseveres in the intelligible realm itself. We are like that depraved earth which, though it has often received wheat, finally yields weeds <note>original: "lolium"; specifically darnel or tares, often used in classical metaphors for undesirable growth appearing in a good field.</note>. And this happens through a certain depravity of the soul, which does not indeed lose its own essence while it sprouts into an irrational seed, but through this very thing the soul is combined with the mortal, while it is pulled from its own into what is foreign.

Therefore, if we ever desire with all our strength to return to our former state, it is necessary to segregate the soul entirely from sense and imagination, and from every irrational condition and passion of this kind that follows, as far as the necessity of nature allows. Indeed, we must rightly arrange and systematically compose those things that pertain to the mind, establishing tranquility and peace from this war concerning the irrational, so that we might not only hear about the intelligible things of the intellect, but also enjoy the great power we have—namely, the contemplation of the mind—and be restored into our incorporeal nature. Thus, living truly through the intellect, and no longer falsely along with natures related to the perishable. Therefore, we must loosen many of our garments—both this visible garment <note>original: "indumentum"; a common Neoplatonic metaphor for the physical body as a "tunic" or "cloak" the soul wears.</note> and those inner robes still applied to us. For we ought not only to avoid vice through its effects, but to root out the effects themselves from the very source. 

A departure from the body can indeed happen with violence, and it can also happen through a certain persuasion; and indeed it is rightly accomplished through a certain thinning out, and as one might say, the forgetting and death of the passions. This is surely the best departure, since it drags nothing with it of that from which the soul itself is torn away; for as we see in things manifest to the senses, whatever is pulled out by violence usually drags something with it—either a part or a trace of itself and of that from which it is uprooted.

->On the release of the soul.<-

The ancient sages diligently avoided everything that could still bind them to the body. Thus the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for their ascetic lifestyle and belief in the transmigration of souls.</note> and similar sages partly withdrew into solitude, and partly lived among the crowds in temples and sacred groves, where they were removed far from all turmoil. Plato, however, chose the Academy as a place to live—a field not only solitary and removed from the city, but also (as it is said) unhealthy. Others indeed did not spare even their eyes, so that they might achieve a deep, uninterrupted, and perpetual contemplation. The philosopher indeed does not drag the soul out of the body by violence...

It cites the ascetic examples of Pythagoras and Plato as models for this philosophical withdrawal.</summary>

# ON ABSTINENCE

...gives; for if he should use force, he will nevertheless remain in that same place from which he was compelled to depart: nor will he think it matters little if, by fattening the body, he has confirmed a harder prison <note>original: "carcerem"; a common Platonic metaphor for the physical body as a jail for the soul.</note> for himself. For he will take care lest the senses and their pleasure, if they grow strong, immerse the soul more deeply into the body. Indeed, if the actions of the senses did not impede the pure action of the mind, what burden would there be in being in the body, provided you suffered very little from the motions that occur through the body? For in what way would you judge, or say that you had suffered, unless you were both suffering and present to those things which you suffered? Let the intellect indeed remain within itself, even if we are least within it; for we who depart from the intellect are already in that place where we have crossed over. Wandering up and down with the zeal of a certain perception's attention, we are already present where that perception itself is performed—not to mention one who descends to the experience of the senses and acts through the irrational faculty. Can he, in the meantime, contemplate the things of the mind with sincerity? Even those who attribute to us two souls <note>A reference to the Platonic theory of a rational and an irrational soul dwelling within one person.</note> do not permit us to have twin attentions simultaneously. Otherwise, they would have created two joined animals. It might be possible for one to be intent on some things while the other does not claim the works of the former for itself. But why then would it be necessary to weaken the bodily passions, and to die to them—meditating on this daily—if we could act according to the intellect while joined to mortals without the mind's inspection, as someone has declared? For "it is the mind that sees, the mind that hears." <note>original: "Intellectus enim uidet intellectus audit"; a famous maxim of the Greek poet-philosopher Epicharmus, often cited by Platonists to show that the senses are mere conduits for the mind.</note> But if you eat luxuriously and swallow the sweetest wine, can you meanwhile dwell upon divine things? Why then are you not frequently in the divine while you cling to human affairs and perform those unions which are not even decent to speak of? For everywhere there are the disturbances of that "child" <note>original: "pueri"; a metaphor for the irrational, impulsive part of the human soul that must be disciplined.</note> who is within us. And because these disturbances are shameful, the contemplator cannot be distracted by them and contemplate at the same time. For where the sense-perception and such awareness are, the <term>intelligible: the realm of pure ideas and spiritual truths that can only be grasped by the mind, not the eyes</term> itself is absent, from which the faculty lacking reason is more greatly excited: and the further away is the intelligence. For it is impossible for someone carried here and there to be here and there at once. For we do not perform our duty with a part of ourselves, but with the whole of our attention.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument regarding the soul's liberation from the body. Having previously discussed the soul's "descent" into a sensory nature, Porphyry now examines the conflict between intellectual contemplation and physical sensation, arguing that the soul cannot truly be in two places at once. This section marks the transition from the general philosophical argument to the specific defense of vegetarianism and asceticism in Book Two.</meta>

# PORPHYRY

The body is struck by external things, and this strike arrives at the point of perception. For perception itself and the turning of attention is the sound itself. It cannot happen that the soul perceives a sound unless it is entirely turned toward that sound and has directed the presiding eye <note>The "eye of the mind" or *intellectus*.</note> toward this very thing.

But when the lack of many things has been removed, and we have been freed from the abundance of those things which are brought into the body, we are lightened of their weight. Then the eye of the soul flashes out from the smoke and the bodily flux; it no longer requires delay or demonstration, because of its natural skill which knows no rest.

Furthermore, the eating of meat contributes very little to health; rather, it hinders it. Since health is maintained by the same means through which it is recovered, and it is recovered through a very sparse diet <note>original: "uictu tenuissimum"; a reference to a light, meager, or "thin" diet typical of ascetic practice.</note> and by abstaining from meat, it follows that health is preserved by these same habits. Even if abstinence from animal flesh contributes less to the strength of a Milo <note>Milo of Croton was a legendary 6th-century BCE wrestler famous for his immense strength and massive consumption of meat.</note>, the philosopher certainly has no need for an increase in raw strength. If he is to be a man of contemplation, and does not give himself over to physical actions or lack of restraint, it is surely fitting to preserve health—not out of a fear of death, but rather so that we are not kept from the good things that come from contemplation. An undisturbed state of soul and a mind focused on that which truly exists <note>A Platonic reference to the world of Forms or the Divine, rather than the changing material world.</note> preserves health most of all. For much vigor overflows to the body from that mental state, as the experience of our own associates has proven. Indeed, it has proven so effective that they expelled the most bitter pains of the joints of the feet and hands—which had forced them to be carried by others for eight whole years—at the same time they cast off their obsession with money, external court business, and turned their zeal entirely toward the divine. Thus, they expelled money, cares, and the disease of the body all at once. From this it appears that a certain habit and state of soul contributes most—indeed, everything—to health; a thin and sparing diet also contributes greatly to the same goal. 

But if it behooves us to freely confess the truth without fear: there is no other way to reach the ultimate goal unless we are eventually attached to God (if it is right to say so) and uprooted from the body and bodily pleasures. Since salvation itself is not gained by the mere hearing of words and theories, but by works, we cannot be joined to God in any other way than through the purest abstinence. This applies not only to any particular lesser god, but much more so to the God who presides over all and exists simply above even incorporeal nature. As much as He is simpler, purer, more self-sufficient, and more remote from matter than all others, so much more must the soul be pure if it is one day to enjoy His presence.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument in Book Two of "On Abstinence from Animal Food." Having established that the philosopher seeks to detach from the physical body, he now moves into a historical and theological defense of bloodless sacrifice. He argues that the earliest and purest forms of worship involved only plants and incense, and that the supreme God requires only the sacrifice of a pure mind and silence.</meta>

<header>->ON OCCASIONS<-</header>

The first sacrificers did not offer animals, but first herbs and flowers, then trees, and they burned aromatics as incense. Those who first began to feed upon animals did so out of a shortage of crops; for previously they were nourished by the fruits of the earth. There are three reasons why one must sacrifice to the gods: to worship them, to give thanks, and to request necessary things from them or to ward off evils. To obtain these things, however, a vow of the mind is sufficient, to which certain small gifts from the crops can be added. But to slaughter animals is a sin <note>original: "nefas"; a term indicating a violation of divine law or a moral abomination.</note>. We too shall certainly dedicate sacred things to the gods, but we shall offer diverse sacrifices, as is fitting. Just as we shall sacrifice to different beings, so to the supreme God himself, who reigns over all—as a certain wise man said <note>Porphyry is likely referring to Apollonius of Tyana, a Neo-Pythagorean philosopher and contemporary of Christ known for his asceticism.</note>—we shall offer nothing perceptible to the senses, neither burning incense nor speaking aloud. For there is nothing material that would not immediately be impure to him who is entirely immaterial. Therefore, neither is spoken language suited to him, nor even the internal word of the mind when it is stained by some passion of the soul; but we shall worship him rightly with pure silence and pure thoughts concerning him.

It is necessary, therefore, that those who have been joined to God and made like unto him should dedicate our own elevation toward God as a sacred victim. This elevation is itself both divine praise and our own salvation. In the contemplation of this God, then, which is free from all passion, this sacrifice is fulfilled. But to his children, who are the <term>intelligible gods</term> <note>In Neoplatonism, "intelligible gods" are divine beings or principles that exist in the realm of Pure Mind (Nous), below the supreme One but above the physical world.</note>, we must now offer praise through speech as well. For a just offering of <term>first fruits</term> <note>original: "primitiae"; the first portion of a harvest dedicated to a deity as an act of gratitude.</note> is made to each of the divinities from those things which they grant, and through which they nourish us and preserve us in our existence, so that we might have the faculty to sacrifice. Therefore, just as farmers bring the first fruits from what they gather—namely sheaves of grain and the fruits of trees—to the divinities, so we shall dedicate to them the first fruits of our intelligence with similar gratitude, giving thanks for those things which they have granted us: namely, the contemplation of the divinities and of their number.

This is especially true since, through their own inspection, they truly nourish us, being present everywhere to us and appearing, and happily breathing upon our salvation. But now, it is a source of regret that many who are even students of philosophy act otherwise; worshipping glory rather than divinity, they revolve around statues, nor do they consider whether or how such things should be approached. They do not seek to learn from those who excel in divine wisdom how far and to what extent one should participate in these things. We, however, shall by no means contend with these people, nor shall we seek to distinguish such things; but we shall greatly imitate the holy ancients, dedicating the first fruits to the divinities from that very contemplation which the powers above have granted us, the use of which is absolutely necessary for our true salvation. Thus, the Pythagoreans, who were occupied with numbers and lines, also dedicated much from these things to the gods: naming one number Pallas, another Diana, another Apollo, another Justice, and another Temperance; and similarly in...

# PORPHYRY

...figures and through such similar sacrifices, they pleased the gods by means of the [Supreme] God <note>original: "à deo"; Porphyry distinguishes between the one high God and the subordinate deities.</note> so that they might call upon each of the gods with their offerings and frequently use their favor for prophecy, or if they needed to examine something. Among the gods, some are within the heavens, whether moving in a certain way as "wanderers" <note>The "errantes" or wandering stars are the planets.</note> or as fixed stars. We must think that their leader is first the sun, then the moon. We can appropriately consecrate fire to them as if it were a relative. And we must observe what the theologian <note>Likely a reference to Orpheus or the ancient authors of sacred hymns.</note> commands. For he says that no living thing <note>original: "animatum"; a being with a soul/breath.</note> should be sacrificed, but only flour, honey, and the fruits and flowers of the earth; for he knows the man who is a true worshiper of piety. To the gods, indeed, no living thing was ever to be sacrificed <gloss>sacrificed</gloss>, but rather to demons and others, whether good or bad. But let us set these matters aside. To me, the clever ideas that most of the Platonists have published seem worth bringing into the open. They hand down this method: the first God, being incorporeal, immobile, and indivisible <note>original: "ipartibilis" (impartibilis); meaning a being that cannot be divided into parts.</note>, contained in nothing—not even in himself—needs nothing external. Nor does the Soul of the World need external things. For it possesses and contains in itself that which is stretched out in three dimensions, and a faculty that moves naturally, and by its own nature it has decreed to move in a well-ordered way, and to move the body of the world according to the highest reason. It has received the body into itself and embraced it, although it is itself incorporeal and free from all passion.

— To the other gods, however—to the world, and the wandering and fixed stars, which consist of soul and body and are visible to the eyes—one must sacrifice with inanimate sacrifices <note>Non-living offerings such as grain, incense, or libations.</note> for the reason we have stated.

### On the kinds of good and evil demons.

There remains the invisible multitude, whom Plato called "un-distinct" <note>original: "in distinctos"; referring to spirits that are not clearly classified or bounded like the celestial gods.</note> demons. Some of these, named by men, have obtained honors equal to the gods and other forms of worship among various peoples. Others, for the most part, are not named, but receive their name and worship secretly, as it were, from certain villages or cities. The rest of the crowd is commonly called by the name "demons." There is a fixed belief among everyone: they will certainly harm the human race if they become angry because they are neglected or do not receive legitimate worship; and again, they will do good to men who have won them over with vows, supplications, sacrifices, and other things that follow. Since, therefore, this opinion about demons is confused and contains much slander against them, it is necessary to distinguish their nature by reason. For perhaps it is necessary, they say, to declare how the error concerning them fell upon men. It should be distinguished in this way:

### ON OPPORTUNITIES
**71**

[They] preside over animals, or over certain fruits, or over other things ordained for their sake, such as rains, temperate winds, serene air, the tempering of the seasons, and everything else that contributes to these. Among us, in turn, they preside over the arts and the disciplines of music, medicine, gymnastics, and similar pursuits. Indeed, it is impossible that those who care for the utility and convenience of things should, on the other hand, inflict harm. Among these are to be numbered the demons whom Plato <note>Porphyry refers to Plato's *Symposium*, where demons are described as intermediaries between the divine and human realms.</note> says transfer and report: human things to the gods, and divine things to men. They carry our prayers to the gods as if to judges, and they lead back the gods' commands and warnings to us, along with the gift of prophecy <note>original: "vaticinio"; the act of foretelling the future or communicating divine will.</note>. 

But whatever souls are not designated to a bound spirit <note>original: "conuincto spiritui"; referring to the "pneuma," a subtle, quasi-physical body that Neoplatonists believed clothed the soul.</note>, but for the most part fall away, these are said to be driven excessively through this spirit when the impulses of anger and lust grow strong. These souls are themselves also demons, but they are rightly called "maleficent" or evildoers. 

Now all these, both the ones we have mentioned and those who differ from them, are invisible and not entirely manifest to human senses, for they are not clothed in a solid body. Moreover, they do not all have a single form, but are marked by many different figures. And the forms that "seal" their spirit-bodies sometimes appear, but at other times do not appear at all. Sometimes, those who are of the worse sort even change their forms. 

Their spirit-body—insofar as it is a corporeal thing—is subject to passion and is dissoluble <note>Unlike the high gods, these demons are not inherently eternal; their subtle bodies can eventually break down.</note>; but because it is bound by the soul in such a way, its form can endure for a long time, though it is not eternal. It is consistent with its nature that something is always flowing out from it and being nourished. The bodies of the good demons consist of proper proportion, just like the bodies of things manifest to us. But the bodies of the malevolent demons are ill-proportioned <note>original: "incocinna"; lacking harmony or elegance.</note>, and they inhabit a place near the earth, being subject to passive affections. 

Therefore, there is no evil that they do not dare to perpetrate. For they have an entirely violent and unhealthy character, being deserted by the guardianship of the better demons; for this reason, they mostly devise and rush forth in vehement and sudden ambushes. And while they carry out their incursions, they partly try to remain hidden, and partly inflict open violence. Wherefore, the sufferings <note>original: "passiones"; can refer to both physical diseases and emotional disturbances.</note> inflicted by them are sharp and swift. The cures and corrections, however, seem to be slower, because they come from the better demons. For every good thing is easy and balanced in its governance; it proceeds in an orderly fashion and does not overstep what is opportune. 

If, therefore, you think of demons in this way, you will never fall into that most absurd opinion that evils happen because of the good ones, or that good things happen because of the evil ones. Nor is the discourse only absurd in that way; but many people, conceiving very bad opinions about the gods...

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from the previous page regarding the nature of "maleficent" or harmful demons. [opi]nions to many people. For this is among the greatest harms inflicted by maleficent demons: namely, while they themselves are the authors of wretched passions and earthly disasters—such as pestilence, famine, earthquakes, scorching heat, fires, and similar things—they meanwhile persuade us that those who are instead the authors of the opposites (that is, of fertility and prosperity) are the ones causing these evils. Thus they try to absolve themselves from being seen as the cause of calamities, and they achieve this through a specific scheme. 

First, they strive to hide their own injustice from us. Then, they bend us toward making supplications and sacrifices suited for the beneficent gods, as if those gods were angry with us. They do these and similar things because they are eager to lead us away from a correct understanding of the gods and draw us toward themselves instead. For they take great delight in all such unjust and discordant actions. 

And by putting on the "faces" of other gods <note>The author suggests that demons "mask" themselves as higher deities to steal the worship intended for the divine.</note>, they take advantage of our ignorance to gather crowds into their company. Because of such lusts, they set human minds on fire with habits and desires for wealth, power, and pleasures. Again, they involve us in new and foreign opinions from which seditions, wars, and other things of the same kind are born. 

What is gravest of all is that they persuade us that such things are caused by the heavenly beings, to the point that they even subject the Greatest God <note>original: "deum maximum"; likely referring to Zeus or the Demiurge, the supreme architect of the universe in Neoplatonic thought.</note> to such accusations, claiming he is the one who throws everything into chaos, turning the world upside down. This error happens not only to unrefined people but also to many dedicated students of philosophy. 

The cause of this error proceeds and is confirmed mutually. For those practicing philosophy who have never separated themselves from the common rabble have fallen into the same errors as the common people; and in turn, the crowds—hearing opinions similar to their own from praised writers—are even more confirmed in this view of the gods. For the artifice of poetry has further excited the suspicions of such men, because it uses a style of speech strongly adapted to produce stupor and a kind of magical attraction. It is easily able to soothe and entice minds, and therefore to bring us to believe in things that are utterly impossible. 

But indeed, one must firmly believe that the good never harms, nor does the evil ever benefit. For it is not the nature of heat (as Plato <note>Porphyry is likely citing Plato’s *Republic* (Book I, 335d), where Socrates argues that it is not the function of the good man or the just to do harm.</note> says) to make things cold, but of its opposite. Thus, it is not the nature of the just to harm; and the divinity itself is by nature the most just of all things. Otherwise, nothing would be divine. 

Should we not, therefore, distinguish this power and lot of the [maleficent] demons from the beneficent ones? For that which is naturally inclined toward opposites is contrary to the beneficent. Indeed, opposites regarding the same thing never occur naturally. Since, therefore, such demons...

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s discourse on the nature of demons from Book 2 of *On Abstinence from Animal Food*. Having previously established that harmful spirits deceive mankind by masking themselves as benevolent gods, he now explains how they utilize sorcery and physical vapors to exert influence, contrasting them with good demons who send warning signs.</meta>

# ON THE OCCASIONS.

## PORPHYRY

In many ways they harm mortal nature, and sometimes in great matters. Surely the good demons <note>original: "dæmones." In this context, Porphyry follows the Neoplatonic view that demons are intermediate spirits between gods and men, categorizing them as either helpful or harmful.</note> never desert their duties in the meantime, but they signify the dangers looming everywhere from the evil ones according to their ability, sometimes showing them in dreams, sometimes through divinely inspired minds, and through many other means. And if anyone could discern the things signified, they would detect and avoid all the machines of the wicked; for these good spirits provide signs to all. But not everyone knows the things signified, just as not everyone is able to read what is written, but only he who has previously learned his letters.

Through the contrary demons, however, all **sorcery** <term>sorcery (veneficium): in Latin, this term refers both to poisoning and to the use of magical "medicines" or spells to cause harm.</term> is effected. For those who inflict evils through sorceries are accustomed to honor these demons and their leader. These demons truly abound in all kinds of shapes and images, and they vigorously deceive with a machine of portents. By their work, the unhappy even <insert>also</insert> devise love-charms and malicious spells; for all intemperance and hope for riches and glory grows strong through them, and especially deception. For lying is characteristic of such demons. They wish to be seen as gods, and the very power presiding over them wishes to be held as the greatest god.

These indeed are the only ones who are delighted by drink offerings and the smoke of meat. For their **spiritual body** <note>Neoplatonists believed demons possessed a "pneumatic" or airy body that could be nourished or "thickened" by physical substances like smoke and blood.</note> is accustomed to grow fat on these; for this body lives on vapors and fumigations and—as is natural—quite variedly; it takes strength through the various odors of blood and meat. Therefore, a wise and temperate man will beware of using such sacrifices, by which he might attract such demons to himself. He will instead strive to perfectly purify his soul, for they never attack a pure soul because of its very dissimilarity to them.

Accordingly, if it happens to be necessary for cities to reconcile these demons to themselves, this use does not pertain to us at all. For in a city, riches and external and bodily advantages are held as good things among citizens, and the opposites as evils, and they care almost nothing for the perfection and purity of the soul. We, however, will not need the advantages that demons bring, as far as possible; but both from the soul and from external things, we will strive with all zeal to be made similar to God himself and those near to him. This is surely completed by tranquility of soul, by a distinct comprehension of the truth of things, and by a life directed entirely toward these goals.

But we must be made dissimilar to wicked men, and to demons, and to everything entirely that rejoices in what is mortal and material. Wherefore, according to those things which **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus was the successor to Aristotle. Porphyry frequently cites his lost work "On Piety" to argue that the earliest and most divine sacrifices consisted of plants and honey, not blood.</note> handed down, we also shall sacrifice, with which the theologians have agreed, knowing clearly that as far as we neglect to purge the soul from **disturbances** <term>disturbances (perturbationes): the Greek *pathē*, referring to passions like anger, lust, and fear that distract the soul from divine contemplation.</term>, so far are we coupled to the wicked power; whence we are deservedly compelled to soothe this power further. [...to esca]pe, as those report who depend on external things and do not yet rule over their passions; by this very condition, they are compelled to repel the onslaught of such power from themselves. Otherwise, they will never be able to find rest from their labors.

## On sacrifices to evil demons, and on abstinence and caution against evil demons.

For this reason, if theologians ever permit the sacrifice of animals to wicked demons for the sake of avoiding the evils they might inflict, they forbid the tasting of such sacrifices. At the same time, they command that before you sacrifice in this way, you must purify the soul through fasting, and especially through abstinence from animal flesh. They believe that the holy purity of the soul acts as a kind of symbol or divine mark <term>character (character): a spiritual seal or "stamp" of identity that distinguishes the soul in the eyes of spiritual beings.</term> by which you are guarded, so that you suffer nothing from those spirits whom you approach while you attempt to win them over through sacrifice. For when your internal state is contrary to that of the spirits to whom you offer sacrifices—that is, when you are purer—you remain unharmed in both body and soul by a divine lot <note>original: "diuini-orte," likely "diuina sorte" (by divine lot/fate).</note>, fortified by pure holiness as if by a citadel. 

For this reason, even to enchanters and sorcerers <term>venefici (veneficiis): literally "poisoners," but in this context referring to those who use magical potions or drugs to influence spirits.</term>, this kind of caution has seemed necessary, as it makes them safer from danger. Yet they can never be entirely safe, for those types of demons are accustomed to address the wicked with wantonness. Therefore, purity and holiness <note>original: "simonia," likely a transcription error for "sanctimonia" (holiness).</note> are not the exclusive property of sorcerers and enchanters, but rather belong to divine men and those who contemplate divine things. Indeed, chastity and abstinence protect their followers everywhere against evil demons by granting them a familiarity with the divine. Thus, if enchanters decided to use these virtues completely, they would certainly never dare to enchant at all, since they would have been called back by this purity from the lusts for whose sake they pollute themselves in their religious rites <note>original: "pietate." Porphyry uses this ironically to describe the "devotion" or religious attention sorcerers give to demons.</note>. 

And so, being full of disturbances and barely refraining even a little from impure foods—and therefore being entirely impure themselves—they pay the penalty for their unjust transgression against the universe. They suffer this partly under the demons whom they themselves provoke, and partly under divine judgment, which looks upon all the works and plans of mortals.

## On true worship, sacrifice, and caution against evil demons.

The divine man, however, will fortify his soul with both divine wisdom and abstinence from those foods that incite passions in men, as well as by his own likeness to God. He will consider the uncontaminated soul to be like a temple of God within this universal temple of God the Father. Furthermore, since every physical body accessible to the senses brings us certain flows of material demons, it is certain that alongside the impurity of nourishment drawn from flesh and blood, there is present within us a demonic power that is friendly to this impurity and easily allures... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "cta pro" suggests the next page begins with a word like "procta" or "prospecta."</note>
