...on account of a very familiar similarity and property. For this reason, all theologians <note>original: "theologi"; in the Neoplatonic context, this refers to ancient sages and divinely inspired philosophers like Hermes Trismegistus or Pythagoras.</note> have rightly applied themselves first of all to abstinence; and the Egyptian <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or the priest Chaeremon, whom Porphyry often cites regarding Egyptian wisdom.</note> revealed these things to us, bringing forth a most natural cause which experience had confirmed. Namely, that a wicked and irrational soul <term>soul (anima): the vital principle that animates the body; in this philosophy, a soul that is too attached to the body becomes "heavy" and "damp."</term> which has left its body by violence, having been stripped of its form, then moves toward that very body and lingers there. From this, the souls of men who have died by violence also linger around their bodies.

This very fact warns us not to exclude the soul from the body by force <note>A common Neoplatonic argument against suicide or violent execution, as the soul remains tethered to the corpse if it does not depart naturally.</note>. Since, therefore, the violent slaughter of living beings compels the souls to love the bodies they have left, nothing prevents the soul from being drawn toward whatever related thing allures it; for which reason many souls have been seen lamenting everywhere. The souls of men lacking burial <note>original: "sepultura"; the ancients believed that without proper burial rites, the soul could not pass to the afterlife and remained a restless ghost.</note> linger around their bodies; these souls indeed sorcerers often abuse to perform their service, compelling the souls by the positioning of the body or by the taking up of some ancient remains. 

When these accounts were discovered by those sages, and they understood the nature of a wicked soul and its kinship to the body, and the pleasure it feels toward the body from which it was torn away, they rightly fled from and condemned the eating of animals. They did this lest they should summon to themselves foreign souls—violently torn away and impure—which are naturally drawn to what is related to them. They also feared being prevented from approaching God "alone and pure" <note>A famous phrase in Plotinian and Porphyrian philosophy: "the flight of the alone to the Alone."</note>, should they be driven away from God by the presence of disturbing demons <term>demons (daemones): in this era, these were not necessarily "evil" in the modern sense, but spirits that occupy the middle ground between humans and gods.</term>. 

Experience has taught theologians in many instances that the nature of a related body is a certain incentive for attracting a soul. For those who desired to instill the souls of prophetic animals into themselves—by swallowing their principal members, such as the hearts of stags, moles, or hawks—immediately received the present soul prophesying in the manner of a god. This soul, along with the internal consumption of its body into the human body, would thrust itself entirely within. 

Rightly, therefore, the philosopher and priest of the God who rules over all, abstains from all animal flesh. Being alone, he strives to approach the "alone God" through himself, provided that no crowd of attending spirits diverts him. By this communion, he himself then understands the nature of things and divines, and he possesses God within himself. From this, he holds the confidence and pledge of eternal life; being entirely translated to God, he now becomes an intimate of Jupiter <note>original: "iouis"; here meaning the Supreme Creator or the Demiurge.</note> in the place of a prophet. 

Accordingly, if any necessity arises, good demons are not lacking to this intimate of divinity, meeting him everywhere—through dreams, signs, and voices—and foretelling the future so that he may learn what is necessary to avoid. For one must only depart from evil and recognize what is best and most venerable in the universe, and realize that the universe, in its entirety, is a good, friendly, and approachable friend. But wickedness and ignorance of divine things compel a man to despise what he does not know, and those...

...to condemn. But among those who are able to hear, nature herself cries out: since she is intellectual, she leads her worshippers deep into sacred mysteries through the intellect. Indeed, the wise man knows that while evil demons <note>original: "dæmones"; in this context, intermediary spirits that can be helpful or malevolent and are often blamed for demanding blood sacrifices.</note> delight in animal sacrifices and portend future events through them, the Gods have no need for such victims. Hence Plato says it is fitting for a good man to perform sacrifices and take part in divine rites, but for the wicked man, laboring over sacrifices is in vain.

### From the third book.
## That souls are sensory and rational, and also immortal.

<margin>i</margin>In the third book, he states that he is presenting the true Pythagorean opinion: namely, that every soul endowed with senses and memory is rational, and possesses both internal and external reason and speech <note>original: "rationem orationemque tum interiorem tum exteriorem"; this refers to the Stoic and Neoplatonic distinction between "logos endiathetos" (thought) and "logos prophorikos" (spoken word).</note> through which animals speak among themselves. It is no wonder that their words are not understood by us, since we hardly understand the speech of many foreign peoples <note>original: "barbarorum"; literally "barbarians," referring to any non-Greek or non-Latin speaker whose language sounded like "bar-bar" to ancient ears.</note>, nor do we think they are speaking so much as making indistinct noises. He adds that if we are to believe the ancients and those who lived in our fathers' time or our own, there are some who say they hear and understand the speech of animals, just as was said of Melampus and Tiresias <note>Famous mythological seers who were said to understand the language of birds.</note> and others of old. More recently, there was Apollonius of Tyana <note>Apollonius of Tyana: a 1st-century philosopher and wonder-worker who was often compared to Pythagoras for his asceticism and alleged miracles.</note>, of whom it is said that while in a gathering of friends, he heard a swallow announcing to others that a donkey laden with wheat had fallen near the city and the wheat was scattered on the ground.

He then contends that animals possess reason, both because they communicate their meanings to each other, and because they care for themselves with diligent skill and provide for future use, and because they learn many things from each other and from humans, and teach each other in turn. He adds that Aristotle, Plato, Empedocles, Democritus, and others who have searched for the truth about animals have found a participation in reason and speech within them. It appears, however, in this diversity—as Aristotle also said—that they differ very little in essence, but rather by the degree of "more or less." Just as most people think the difference between the gods and men lies in this: not according to essence, but according to a perfect or imperfect state of reason; so we believe the nature of reason is common to us and the animals, though differing by "more or less." Aristotle says those animals are "more prudent"—that is, more clever—which excel in the sharpness of their senses. Differences in bodies make the passive soul <term>passive soul (anima passiva): the part of the soul that receives impressions from the physical world and is subject to emotions and sensations.</term> either easily or with difficulty, and grant it a more or less ready use of reason; yet they cannot change the soul according to its essence. ->ON SACRIFICES<-

<image-desc>A small decorative printer's ornament is centered below the header, resembling a stylized leaf or fleur-de-lis.</image-desc>

...neither senses nor passions make them different from one another, nor do they cause perfection to be exceeded. Let it be granted, therefore, that there is a difference of reason in these beings according to "more" or "less"; nevertheless, the rest of the animals are not entirely deprived of reason. Nor, because we understand more than the animals do, should we for that reason deprive them of understanding entirely—just as we do not deny that partridges <note>original: "pdices" (perdices)</note> fly simply because goshawks <note>original: "astures"</note> fly faster. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;One might indeed grant that the soul suffers along with the body, and undergoes changes when the body is affected for good or ill, but the nature of the soul itself is by no means transformed by this. If the soul merely suffers with the body and uses it as an instrument, it will indeed perform many things differently depending on how the instrument is arranged—differently than we do, performing things which we ourselves are unable to do. And while it will suffer alongside a body arranged in a certain way, it will not change its own proper nature. 

Those who say that "brutes" <note>A common historical term for non-human animals, from the Latin "brutus," meaning dull or unreasoning.</note> act rationally by nature do not realize they are actually saying these beings are rational by nature. For if reason were not inherent in us by nature, then our own perfection would not increase according to how we are naturally established; however, that which is divine does not become rational through instruction <note>original: "disciplina"; referring to formal learning or training.</note>. For there was never a time when the divine was not rational, but it both existed and was rational at the same moment. Nor is a being prevented from being rational just because it did not receive reason through instruction—just as in other animals, as in humans, nature itself has taught many things, while instruction has provided others. 

Some have attempted, not without reason, to show that many animals are even more prudent than we are, depending on the places they were allotted. For just as those inhabiting the ether <note>The "pure" upper air where gods and celestial beings were thought to dwell.</note> are rational, so they say are those living nearest to them—that is, in the air. Then those in the water, and then those on the earth, differ among themselves by degrees of reason. For if we measure the dignity of the gods in a certain way and by their locations, so too do we weigh the dignity of animals. 

Socrates, and Rhadamanthus <note>In Greek mythology, a wise judge of the underworld noted for his fairness.</note> before him, used to swear by animals. The Egyptians truly considered certain animals to be gods—whether they actually believed them to be gods, or whether they deliberately painted the forms of the gods with the face of an ox, or the faces of birds and others, so that people would abstain from harming animals no differently than they do humans; or perhaps for some other more secret reason. Similarly, the Greeks placed the horns of a ram upon the statue of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus.</note>, and the horns of a bull upon the statue of Dionysus. But Pan they composed from a man and a goat. They gave wings to the Muses and the Sirens, and they say that Cupid, Mercury, and Jove took on the forms of a bull, an eagle, and a swan. By these things, the ancients testified that animals are to be honored. 

And Socrates was not joking when he said the swans were his "fellow servants." The Tablet <note>likely referring to the Pythagorean doctrines or the *Tabula Cebetis*, which describes the soul's journey.</note> indicates that animals agree with us in having a soul, saying that through the indignation of the gods, souls pass from humans into animals; and when they have passed over, the gods finally take pity. By these and similar things, it is signified that animals are rational—though in most of them reason is imperfect, it is nonetheless not entirely absent.

<meta>This page continues Porphyry’s argument from Book 3 of *On Abstinence from Animal Food*. Having previously discussed how animals share in some degree of reason, he now moves to the ethical consequences: the injustice of killing animals and how a life of minimal harm brings a human closer to the divine nature.</meta>

<header>PORPHYRY.</header>

### It is a sin to kill animals.

It is unjust to kill animals since they are not entirely alien to us. But we, as if we were throughly playful and insolent, frequently kill very many animals everywhere for sport in theaters and in hunts. The result of this behavior is that the wild and cruel force within us has grown more powerful, while humanity and gentleness have ceased. The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who were famous in antiquity for their vegetarianism and belief in the transmigration of souls.</note>, however, practiced gentleness and clemency toward wild beasts as a training ground and specimen for humanity and mercy.

Everything that is inanimate, since it lacks reason and mind, is the opposite of that which possesses a soul along with reason and a certain intelligence. For every animate being possesses a sensory capacity and even a *phantasia* <note>original: "phantasiam" — often translated as "imagination" or "mental representation," the ability to form a mental image of a thing.</note> as a kind of reason. For nature, which does and has made all things for some purpose and toward some end, made the animal sensory—not simply so it would feel and suffer, but so it would perceive what would be advantageous or disadvantageous to it, pursuing the former and fleeing the latter. Sense, therefore, brings knowledge of both to each individual animal. Indeed, those behaviors which follow after sense—namely the pursuit and capture of useful things and the avoidance of harmful things—must be thought not to exist unless the beings possess a certain reasoning, judgment, and memory. And if Strato the Physicist <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 335 – c. 269 BC) who argued that all sensation involves thought.</note> says that sense does nothing without intelligence—since we do not even perceive things present to our senses when we are focused on understanding something else—nevertheless, let it be granted that the sense does not act by the mind for its own action. Yet, when the sense applies itself by acting toward what is its own and what is alien, and places a difference between these two, and follows this while fleeing that, and sagaciously finds the middle ground for following or escaping, we can conclude that reason is present. And these things are indeed the properties of reason, and they are present in all animals—at least those that move forward.

### He who lives content with little and is innocent is like a god.

Since the goal of the soul is to become like God, and God lacks nothing and harms no one, that man is certainly the happiest and most like God who so prepares himself that he requires as little as possible from external things and harms as little as possible. This man, therefore, will feed only on the fruits of the earth, so that he does not harm men and does not harm animals; and as much as it can be done, he will even spare plants and herbs. For the ancients even lamented this very thing: that we have need of the fruits of trees. The cause of this "want" <term>inopia: a state of lack or poverty</term> was created because we were placed in this state of need through the process of generation <note>original: "generationem" — here referring to being born into a physical, material body which has needs like hunger.</note>, and are now farther removed from "plenty" <term>copia: abundance or fullness, often associated with the divine state</term>. Indeed, want seeks its safety from external things. Therefore, he who requires more external things is more closely joined to want, and is thus further separated from the divine. For he who is like God possesses true abundance by that very likeness. The rich man who truly enjoys his riches brings injury to no one; for as long as he brings injury, though he may possess all the money and [occupy] the whole [earth...]

<meta>The catchword "occupet" indicates the first word of the next page: "occupet," likely finishing the thought that even if one occupies the whole world, they are not truly "rich" if they cause harm.</meta>

One who merely occupies the earth must be considered poor, for he is well-acquainted with want. For this reason, the unjust man is profane and polluted by every depravity. This is a vice brought upon us by a certain "fall of the soul" <note>A Neoplatonic concept where the soul loses its divine state by becoming too entangled with physical matter.</note> as it descends into matter and away from the Good. Everything else is therefore nonsense insofar as one falls away from the primary principle. The soul remains in need of all things as long as it does not look up toward that very fullness. However, that which is mortal by its own nature yields, insofar as the soul does not truly know itself. But the person who has already become like God and is content with the smallest things for sustenance enjoys the prosperity of the "Golden Age."

### A certain reason is present even in animals.

Reason is indeed present by nature. However, "right and perfect reason" <note>original: "ratio uero recta perfectaq;" — refers to the Stoic and Platonic ideal of fully developed intellectual virtue.</note> is developed through meditation and teaching. Therefore, a certain participation in the rational faculty belongs to all animals. Yet, one cannot even find a human who has perfectly obtained rectitude and wisdom. Just as there are differences within the faculty of sight itself, or in the act of flying—for goshawks and cicadas do not see in the same way, nor do eagles fly like partridges—so too not every rational being participates equally in sharpness of mind and cunning.

### From the fourth book.
### The ancients abstained from animals.

<margin>d</margin> Dicaearchus the Peripatetic <note>A student of Aristotle who wrote about the history of Greece.</note> says that the ancient Greeks, being born closest to the gods, were the best by nature and lived the best lives, so much so that their race was judged to be "Golden." He adds that they killed no animal. They certainly believed nothing was better for health than to avoid gathering "superfluities" <note>Excessive or unnecessary substances in the body, often blamed for disease in ancient medicine.</note> in the body. Thus, they did not wish to take in nourishment that would overpower their nature, but rather that by which their nature might be made stronger. 

The ancient priests of the Egyptians, who were devoted to the study of wisdom—of whom Chaeremon the Stoic <note>An Egyptian priest and philosopher of the 1st century AD who wrote about Egyptian temple life.</note> treats most diligently—also abstained mostly from animals. Indeed, they even venerated many animals as divine, saying that some were suited to certain gods, such as the hawk, the scarab beetle, the ram, and the crocodile for the Sun. For they understood that the soul of every animal is rational once it has been separated from the body; it possesses a sense of the future, can divine for us, and is capable of all the things a human soul can do when released from the body. Therefore, they did not honor animals without reason, and they restrained themselves from eating them as much as possible.

He notes that they held all things in common, living with mutual charity and abstin[ence]...

cultivated self-restraint and endurance above all things, always intent upon divine worship. They were so strong in spirit that they preferred to be killed rather than deny God. Even in the midst of their very tortures, they were accustomed to smile openly. For this reason, those who were tortured would release their spirits cheerfully, as if they were to receive them back again. For among them, this opinion is firmly held: that souls are immortal and, descending from the thinnest ether, they are joined to bodies by a rush <note>original: "ῥύμῃ" — a Greek term signifying a forceful momentum or natural pressure</note> and a natural instinct. But once they have emigrated from the prison of the body, they exult as if finally free from a long servitude, lifting themselves up through the heights. They abstained both from many types of animals and from all incontinence whatsoever. Finally, from this very way of life—which was most temperate, most studious of the truth, and most devoted to God—many among them could foretell the future. ->The ancient sages despised the present life in hope of the future one.<-

The wise men of India were named "gymnosophists" <note>Literally "naked philosophers" (from the Greek *gymnos* for naked and *sophos* for wise), known for their asceticism and rejection of worldly vanities.</note>. Among them, those who proceeded in the study of religion and wisdom through a certain hereditary succession were called Brahmans; however, those who professed the same by choice alone were called Samaneans <note>original: "samanei" — likely referring to the Shramanas, non-Vedic Indian ascetics including early Buddhists and Jains.</note>. Bardesanes the Babylonian describes their life at length. The Samaneans bore the time of this life as if it were a certain necessary servitude ministering to nature, and they took care to release their souls from the body. Even when they felt the body to be in good health, they would often depart from life even though nothing urged them to it. Thus, their kinsmen considered them blessed in their death, and they wept for those who survived them as being unhappy.

->Sobriety and contemplation join the mind to God.<-

->The Gymnosophists, beyond their other temperance and holiness,<-
->abstained from animals.<-

Indeed, holiness that abstains from mortal things <note>Meaning the eating of animal flesh.</note> contains eternal life. But a fattened body forces the soul to starve as it falls from the happy life. It increases what is mortal in us, while expelling and hindering eternal life; it contaminates us and renders the soul corporeal, turning it aside toward that which is different from itself. Truly, the magnet stone <note>original: "Magnes uero lapis" — the lodestone.</note> transmits a certain "soul" to the iron when it is near it. Thus the iron, which is by nature very heavy, becomes light and is lifted up by the spirit of the magnet, drawing itself toward the magnet. Therefore, if anyone has suspended himself toward God, into the incorporeal and intellectual realm, he should not seek nourishment by which the body is fattened, for that hinders the path to the mind. Instead, he will reduce the body to the smallest and most strictly necessary food. He himself will be nourished by divinity, joined more naturally to God than iron is to the magnet. Indeed, if we did not even require the smallest nutrients, we would be as much happier as we were more immortal. But now, living in this mortal state, we secretly make ourselves (so to speak) even more mortal

# ABSTAINED FROM ANIMALS.

While we increase the body and (as Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he wrote extensively on botany and ethics.</note> says) while the soul, through its innate <note>original: "ἐμφύτῳ" — meaning something implanted or natural to the constitution</note> familiarity, contracts the greatest bond by dwelling with the body and, moreover, devotes itself entirely to it. But would that we had been able to lead a life entirely without food and drink, so that by restraining the outflow <note>The "efflux" or "outflow" refers to the constant physical waste and renewal of the material body which requires food to maintain.</note> of the body, we might immediately be joined to the highest things, in which God also exists as God. 

But why, indeed, do we cry out and lament these things in vain to men who are so blinded that they constantly foster their own evil, yet hate themselves first, and then their true creator? Furthermore, they even hate those who warn and exhort them so that they might one day wake up from their drunkenness <note>Here, "drunkenness" is a philosophical metaphor for being dazed or distracted by worldly pleasures and physical needs.</note>. Democrates <note>Commonly identified as Democritus, the "laughing philosopher" known for his atomic theory and ethical maxims.</note> says that to live imprudently, intemperately, and impiously is not so much to live badly as it is to die for a long time.

->THE END.<-

# IAMBLICHUS:

They receive no change from things that are created. Can the nature of the gods then be defiled by vapors of this kind? For the divine nature drives away material vapors with a single (so to speak) blow. Such things, therefore, are not harmful to the higher beings, but to us; for these divisible and material things, being related to us, have something in common with our family in terms of suffering or action. But against celestial and divine things—which are placed in another kind of essence, endowed with different natures and powers, and completely exceeding us—material vapors cannot act or communicate.

### The reason for sacrifices and their utility.

Porphyry thinks that sacrifices are offered <margin>p</margin> in order to win over the gods with gifts of this kind—as we are often accustomed to do with more powerful men—and also so that we might return thanks for good things received from the divine, giving back good for good. Iamblichus says a cause of this kind is drawn from the common custom of men toward other men and does not fit the nature of the gods, which far exceeds human ways. 

Indeed, such explanations do not fully demonstrate the greatest efficacy of sacrifices. I speak of that efficacy without which we are not freed from plague, famine, or poverty, nor do we obtain timely rains; indeed, it is through this efficacy that we also achieve the <term>purification</term> <note>The Greek 'katharsis,' referring here to the spiritual cleansing of the soul from material influence.</note> and perfection of our souls, and obtain liberty from this <term>province of generation</term> <note>The material world of birth, decay, and constant change.</note>. 

Therefore, a person will not much approve of these modes of sacrifice based on your assignment, Porphyry, as if you had assigned a cause worthy of their effects. And if by chance he does approve, he will certainly accept them only in a secondary place, as being consequent to and arranged in a secondary way after the first and most ancient causes of such works. We desire, therefore, the reason why sacrifices have the power to bring things about, and from what source they are joined to the principal gods who are the causes and principles of what is done.

Someone might say that because the world is one <term>living being</term> <note>The 'Anima Mundi' or World Soul, a concept where the entire universe is treated as a single, interconnected organism.</note>, and has one and the same life everywhere, it possesses a communion of similar powers or even a distance between dissimilar ones—or certainly a certain fitness—to move similar things from the active to the <term>passive</term> <note>In ancient philosophy, 'patient' or 'passive' refers to the thing that receives an action.</note> in the same way. This is because they run through the universe according to a single "sympathy," reaching from the most remote thing to the most remote, as if these were also very close. For among these things there is an equal assignment of the communion of life. 

Truly, this is what he says, and what necessarily follows regarding sacrifices. However, the true mode of sacrifices is not shown in this way. For the essence of the gods is placed neither in nature nor in natural necessities—whereby a bond is stirred up by natural passions—nor is it extended throughout all nature.

<summary>This page explores why the gods are immune to material influence and rejects Porphyry's idea that sacrifices are merely "gifts" or "bribes." Iamblichus argues that sacrifices instead serve to purify the soul and connect the practitioner to the divine essence beyond the material world.</summary>

# MARSILIO Ficino of Florence to the Great-Hearted Lorenzo de' Medici. Greetings.

Synesius, Psellus, Iamblichus, Proclus, and Porphyry—the Platonists—entered your grand home long ago and greeted your noble sons. Up until now, they seem to have done quite well. However, because they left you unsaluted, they have neither acted wisely nor turned out successfully. Recognizing their mistake at last, so that they might be more fortunate, they now revisit your threshold to recognize the father, and in turn, to recognize the sons alongside the father. Thus, they will live more happily from now on. For they recently discovered that not even our own books *On Life* <note>original: "de uita," referring to Ficino's famous three-part treatise on health, longevity, and astral influences.</note> wished to live without your sponsorship. In addition to these five philosophers, Priscian the Lydian and Theophrastus accompany them. Since these two have long wished my <term>well-being</term> <note>The Latin 'valorem' implies both the author's physical health and the "value" or strength of his intellectual work.</note> and have ardently desired it, they approach you eagerly today. They have finally achieved their great wish: that by being safe themselves in your care, they might ensure the safety of my work, which, after God, desires to flourish primarily through you. Greetings above all others, our best patron, and listen happily to such great philosophers conversing in your presence.

# Marsilio Ficino of Florence to the great-hearted Piero de' Medici. Greetings.

Although you read many things daily that are better than mine, I think almost none please you more than ours—if indeed one’s own things usually please most, and those things are most truly one's own which have been possessed the longest. Certainly, "Marsilian" works <note>Ficino refers to his own writings and translations as if they were family heirlooms belonging to the Medici.</note> have been possessed by your family for the longest time. I hope, therefore, that these will always be most dear to you, so that even if I send you "dreams," these too might be held as true by you first, and through you, held as true by others. 

Since I desired that the Platonist Synesius's book *On Dreams* <note>original: "de somniis"</note>, which we recently translated from the Greek, should have authority and trust especially with its first reader and through him with others, I sent it primarily to you. You are now the fourth generation after the great Cosimo <note>Cosimo "the Elder" de' Medici, who originally commissioned Ficino to translate the works of Plato.</note> to read our works, and you will immediately prove these things to everyone by your approval. I have joined the book *On Daemons* <note>original: "de demonibus"</note> by the Platonist Michael Psellus to the book on dreams, and not without reason, since the ancients believe that dreams are sent by <term>daemons</term> <note>In the Platonic tradition, 'daemons' are intermediary spirits—neither purely divine nor purely human—that bridge the gap between gods and men.</note>. Farewell. April 15, 1489.

->SYNESIUS<-

# Synesius on Dreams, translated by Marsilio Ficino of Florence to Piero de’ Medici.

It is an ancient custom, and a most Platonic one, to conceal the weightier mysteries of philosophy under a somewhat lowly pretext, lest by chance those things which were discovered with the greatest labor might perish, or otherwise be defiled if they were openly exposed to the common crowd. Therefore, in this work, we have followed this custom according to our abilities. Whether we have actually achieved that goal, and whether we have treated the other matters of the ancients in an abundant manner, can be judged by those who read these things with a philosophical mind.

### Divination is the best of the pursuits to which humans devote themselves.

If dreams are prophets, and the things seen in dreams present humans with the <term>veils</term> <note>original: "inuolucra," referring to the idea that truth is "wrapped" in allegories or symbols.</note> of future events, they will indeed be wise, but they will not be certain, insofar as the wisdom of dreams consists in that very uncertainty. For the gods have hidden the way of life from humans. Indeed, to obtain the greatest things without labor is a good proper to divinity alone. Among us, however, not only the virtues but also all other excellent things are sought through sweat. Yet <term>divination</term> <note>original: "vaticinium," the art of predicting the future through divine inspiration or omens.</note> will seem to be the greatest of goods. For by its very information—and by the entire faculty of cognition itself—God excels over man, and man over beast. But for God, his own nature is sufficient for knowledge. For man, however, divination brings far more than common knowledge can provide. For the common crowd knows only present things, and merely guesses at the future. But <note>In Homer's Iliad, Calchas is the primary seer for the Greek army at Troy.</note> **Calchas** alone, in the assembly of all the Greeks, knew "the things that are, the things that were, and the things that are soon to come." For this reason, in the works of **Homer**, the affairs of the gods depend on their very "thought," because that thought existed prior and knows more, simply because it is more ancient. I believe he emphasizes "age" in his poems because it happens that one knows more by the benefit of time, since knowledge itself is surely the most honorable thing. 

If anyone, led by other poems, should think that the empire of **Jupiter** <note>Ficino uses the Latin "Iovis" (Jove/Jupiter) to refer to the Greek Zeus, whom Neoplatonists often identified with the "Divine Mind" or Demiurge.</note> consists in the power of his hands because the poet says "he is superior in strength," that person interprets the poem poorly. He does not understand the philosophy within it, which says the gods are nothing other than <term>Minds</term> <note>original: "mentes." In Neoplatonic thought, these are the "Intelligences" that govern the universe.</note>. Thus, regarding the statement that he excels in strength, the poet adds that he is also "prior in birth," since he calls Jupiter the "older mind." But what else is the strength of the Mind itself but **prudence**? Therefore, whoever is a god and is deemed worthy to preside over others, since he is a Mind, he rules by the excellence of his wisdom. Therefore, the phrase "he is more excellent in strength" signifies the same to us as "he knows more things." And for that reason

<header>### ON DREAMS</header>

Therefore, the wise man is also said to be like God, because he strives both to be closer to the divine mind and to exercise himself in the intellect, in which the divine essence consists. By these reasons, let it be demonstrated that their <term>divination</term> <note>original: "uaticinium," the art of predicting the future through divine inspiration or omens.</note>—among those pursuits to which humans apply themselves—is the best.

->In the world, as if in one single animal, some things display signs to others.<-

Now, through all things, all things are signified. Indeed, since all things in the one living world are related, these things are like all-form letters, marked out in the universe just as in a book—partly Phœnician, partly Egyptian, and partly Assyrian. The wise man himself reads these. Truly, the wise man is he who has learned the nature of things; and one person reads some signs, while another reads others; this one more, that one less. Just as one person reads gradually, syllable by syllable, while another reads the whole word at once, and yet another perceives the entire speech in the same way. Thus indeed do the wise foresee future events: some by looking up at the stars, others at flames—whether they are stationary or moving—others searching for the future in the <term>entrails</term> <note>original: "uiſceribus," referring to the practice of haruspicy or organ-reading.</note> of animals, and others in the chirping of birds, observing meanwhile where they fly or where they perch. There are also those who interpret clear signs of the future from voices, and from encounters, or from events happening to another. Since all things are signs for all things, if birds were wise, they would certainly have gathered the art of divination from humans, just as we have accumulated expertise from them. For we encounter them, just as they encounter us: recently or long ago, on the right or on the left.

->Such is the harmony of the world that some things are drawn by others and act in unison.<-

<margin>c</margin>For since this entire universe is <term>sympathetic</term> <note>original: "compatiens," from the Greek 'sympatheia,' meaning to feel or suffer together. This is a core Stoic and Neoplatonic concept where the universe is a single, interconnected organism.</note> with itself and acts in unison, it is necessary that the parts agree harmoniously among themselves, as parts of a single equal whole. It is worth considering whether the lures or the <term>wagtails</term> <note>original: "motacillæ." This likely refers to the *iynx* (wryneck bird), a tool used in ancient "Theurgy" or magic to attract divine influences.</note> of the magi tend toward this. For just as worldly things are signified individually, so they are mutually soothed. Now, the wise man is he who understands the kinship of the worldly parts. For he draws one thing through another, holding present things as if they were pledges of things far distant—namely, voices, materials, and shapes—just as in us, when something suffers internally, another part also suffers in sympathy. Often, an ailment of the finger resonates in the <term>nasal passages</term> <note>original: "emunctorium," literally the organ for clearing waste, like the nose.</note>, while many things between these two parts suffer nothing at all. For both of those are members of one animal, and they have something more closely related between themselves than with the rest. Moreover, this stone or that herb corresponds to some god from the number of worldly gods, to which, as if in sympathy, it yields its nature and is, as it were, enchanted. Just as he who strikes a deep note suddenly moves not the nearest <term>major second</term> <note>original: "sexquioctauam," the 9:8 musical ratio.</note>, but the <term>perfect fourth</term> <note>original: "sexquitertiã," the 4:3 musical ratio.</note>...

<meta>This page continues Synesius of Cyrene's exploration of "universal sympathy"—the idea that all parts of the universe are interconnected like a single living organism—moving from the metaphor of reading nature like a book to the metaphor of musical harmony and the necessity of being "within" the system to understand it.</meta>

...and the sharp note named the <term>Nete</term> <note>original: "netem," the highest note in the ancient Greek musical scale, or lyre.</note>. For these things agree more closely with each other. For just as there is a certain harmony in parts, so also, moreover, is there discord. For this world is not simply one, but one made of many. And in it, there are parts sometimes agreeing with one another, and sometimes disagreeing; yet they do so in such a way that their disagreement leads to the harmony of the whole, just as the structure of a lyre is a certain arrangement of dissonant and consonant tones. Truly, this "oneness from opposites" belongs to harmony, to the lyre, and to the world itself.

->Only that which is connected to the world can be drawn by worldly things.<-

<margin>a</margin>Archimedes the Sicilian used to wish for some location outside the earth, hoping thus that he would be able to balance his weight against the entire earth <note>A reference to Archimedes’ famous boast: "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the world."</note>. For he said that while he was upon it, he had no power against it. In the same way, he who is wise in some matter concerning the nature of the world, if he were placed outside of it, he would no longer have any way to use this wisdom, for he uses it toward the world itself. If the continuity of the world is interrupted, this wisdom is wise in vain, and the signs observed for it lack a soul. But as much as the divine exists outside the world, all that cannot be enchanted or influenced; that which has been sent out is similar to this, caring for nothing, for charms and allurements do not touch the nature of the mind. But that which is passive is soothed by charms and is drawn along. The multitude of things in the world, together with the knowledge of distant things, provides a province and breadth for prophecies and purifications—that is, the multitude of distinct things, but the kinship of those that are united.

Regarding purifications and solemnities—but let the present discourse not disturb anything, giving credit only to civil law—it is safe to receive prophecy, for the truth of the whole system is proven through those things contained within it. As far as the present matter is concerned, it is permitted to select the best path and to be more intensely occupied in its consideration. Meanwhile, we must accept that a certain obscurity is proper to all prophecies, so that no type of divination should be rejected for this very reason, as it is a quality found equally in all of nature's integrity. Now indeed reason has declared that this obscurity is also to be revered; just as there is a secret element in sacred rites, so also oracles are not open to all. Hence also he who gives responses at the <term>Pythia</term> <note>The priestess of Apollo at Delphi.</note> is called <term>Loxias</term> <note>original: "λοξίας," a title for Apollo meaning "The Oblique" or "The Ambiguous."</note>, that is, he is called "oblique" and "twisted." This is because even the "wooden wall," which <term>Phoebus</term> <note>Apollo</note> brought to the Athenians for their safety, the common people would have heard in vain, unless Themistocles had understood the hidden mind of the oracle <note>During the Persian War, the Oracle of Delphi told the Athenians they would be saved by a "wooden wall." Most thought this meant a fence, but Themistocles correctly interpreted it as a fleet of wooden ships.</note>. For this reason, the prophecy of dreams should not be rejected simply because it is obscure, since it holds this obscurity in common with all other oracles.

### Concerning the Intellect, and Reason, and Imagination.

<margin>s</margin>Truly, one must study this [dream-divination] more than all other disciplines, since this is from within us, and is internal, and belongs to each individual soul.

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s philosophical argument regarding how the soul interacts with the cosmos. Having previously discussed the "harmony of the whole" and how the wise man must be "within" the world to understand its signs, he now shifts to the internal mechanics of the human mind—specifically how the soul perceives the "forms" of things through the imagination.</meta>

# ON DREAMS

...properties. For the Intellect contains the forms <note>original: "species," referring to the Platonic "Forms" or ideal archetypes</note> of all things that exist, as ancient philosophy teaches. We can also add this: just as the Intellect possesses the forms of things that *are* (eternal realities), so the soul possesses the forms of things that *come to be* (temporal events). Indeed, the Intellect relates to the soul in the same way that "being" relates to "becoming." Therefore, if we swap these terms—matching the first with the third and the second with the fourth—and exchange them back and forth, we will still be speaking the truth according to the rules of science. Thus it will be demonstrated, as we wish, that the soul possesses the forms of things that are currently happening or coming into existence. 

The soul, then, contains all these forms, but it brings into action first those that are most fitting. It illuminates the imagination <term>phantasia</term> <note>the faculty that bridges the gap between the physical senses and the higher mind</note> like a mirror, and through this mirror, the living being observes the things that remain within the soul. 

Just as we do not notice the actions of the Intellect itself until the "presiding power" <note>likely referring to the faculty of common sense or consciousness</note> announces them to us—and whatever does not reach that power remains hidden from the person—so we do not usually notice the things in the primary soul until their imprints reach the imagination. 

And these imprints seem to exist as a kind of life that has descended somewhat, sinking down by the very property of its nature; yet the powers of sensing are certainly within it. For we see colors, and hear voices, and feel the most intense impact of touch while the physical organs of the body are doing nothing at all. Perhaps there is nothing to prevent this kind of sensing from being more sacred than the physical kind. For through this, we sometimes approach the gods, who warn us, foretell the future, and give us counsel. 

Therefore, if someone finds the gift of dreams to be a treasure, I would not be at all surprised. Nor would I wonder if someone who went to bed knowing nothing of the Muses <note>the goddesses of music, poetry, and the arts</note> should fall among them while sleeping and emerge as a skilled poet—partly speaking and partly hearing. This has even happened in our own generation, and it does not seem entirely unbelievable. 

I will pass over for now the well-known benefits of dreams, such as how people are often freed from traps, or how many times a dream has acted as a physician to drive away illness. But when a dream opens a path to the most perfect contemplation of eternal things for a soul that did not even hope for it or think of it, this is surely the most eminent gift in the order of things. It allows the soul to transcend nature and finally join with the intelligible realm <note>the world of pure thought and divine reality</note>, even for a soul that had wandered so far from there that it no longer remembered its origin.

### On the power of the imagination and the imaginative spirit,

<margin>s</margin> If anyone, however, should think it a great thing to be admitted into the eternal realms, yet does not trust the faculty of imagination...

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s exploration of the soul's internal faculties. Having established that the soul contains the "forms" of things that come to be, he now argues for the superiority of dreams as a divine method of learning, contrasting human instruction with direct divine nourishment, and begins to define the "phantastic spirit" as the primary organ of perception.</meta>

# SYNESIUS

...to be available to us for that blessed commerce <note>original: "commercium," referring to the soul's interaction or exchange with the divine</note>, let one listen to the sacred words <note>original: "eloquia sacra," referring to religious or philosophical teachings</note> which show various paths for this purpose. After the whole order of the narrative, these words provide opportunities from our innermost depths to ascend, through which one is allowed to nourish the inner seed. They say that God has given some the ability to learn the notion of light thoroughly, while others he has made partakers of divine fruit and vigor even in their sleep. Do you not see how the eloquence of teaching is divided here? For it says that one is taught while awake, but another while asleep. But while awake, the teacher is a human; while dreaming, however, God himself makes one a partaker of his own fruit and vigor. It is as if learning were not the same as attaining, for to be nourished by fruits is much more than merely being taught.

Indeed, let this point be taken by us to assert the dignity of the "phantastic life" <note>the life of the imagination and the internal spirit</note> against those who despair of even the smallest part of it. Now, it is no wonder they feel this way because of their superfluous wisdom—those who are well-versed in things that the sacred words reject, where it is taught that sacrifices and the inspection of entrails <note>original: "extorum," referring to the practice of haruspicy or reading animal organs to predict the future</note> are vain and should be shunned. These people, as if they were superior to the common crowd, accept various arts of prediction and approve of such operations, yet they neglect dreams alone. They treat them as something too obvious, in which the ignorant and the wise share equally.

But what if this is exactly why there is greater wisdom here, because it is a more universal gift? Are not other good things—especially those that are the greatest of all—the most common? Nothing among all things seen is more divine than the sun, and nothing is more common than the sun. If, moreover, it is a blessed gift to behold God himself, then perceiving through the imagination <term>phantasia</term> is surely a gift of an older and more personal kind of vision. For this is the "sense of senses," since the phantastic spirit itself is the most universal sensory organ <note>original: "sensorium communissimum," the primary faculty where all sensory data is unified</note> and the first body of the soul. It remains hidden, acting from within, and holds the governing principle of the living being as if from a fortress. For nature constructed the entire framework of the head around it.

Hearing and sight are not themselves senses, but instruments of sense, serving the "common sense" <note>the internal faculty that coordinates the five physical senses</note>. They are like the janitors and doorkeepers of the living being, announcing to the master the external sensations they encounter, which strike the external sensory organs. Meanwhile, the inner sense remains a complete sense in all its parts; for with the whole spirit it hears, with the whole it sees, and it is similarly capable of the rest. It distributes different powers to different parts, each of which is derived from the living being separately. Some are like straight lines flowing out from a center and meeting at the center; they are all one from a common root, yet many in the way they have proceeded outward. Therefore, the sense that occurs through the openly placed instruments is very much part of the living being, even if it is not a "sense" until it returns...

...at the beginning. Moreover, perception occurring without a medium is both closer to the soul and certainly more divine.

## The imagination is more perceptive than the external sense.

<margin>a</margin> But if you, while honoring the bodily senses for the sake of knowledge—since we know best those things we see—reject the imagination <note>original: "phantasiam," referring to the internal faculty that receives and stores images</note> as being less trustworthy than sense, you seem not to notice enough. Not even the eye itself truly shows us everything; it fails to show some things and lies about others, both because of the nature of the things seen and the nature of the organs of sight. Indeed, the same objects appear smaller or larger depending on the distance, and things seen through water appear larger to us, just as an oar appears broken <note>a classic philosophical example of how the senses can be deceived by refraction</note>. To this is added the weakness of the eye itself, for a bleary-eyed person sees things as blurred and indistinguishable. Therefore, whoever suffers from a "sickly" phantastic spirit <note>original: "phantastico languet spiritu"; the "spirit" was thought to be a thin, vaporous substance that carried thoughts and images through the body</note> should not demand clear and distinct visions. You must learn from "secret philosophy" <note>likely referring to Neoplatonic or Hermetic traditions</note> what the disease of this spirit is, the causes for its dullness, and by what means it may be purged, refined, and restored to its natural purity. Once purified by these mysteries, the spirit becomes divine. It escapes external influences before the spirit lets God in; and whoever keeps this spirit pure through a natural way of life uses it as something prepared by God, so that in this way such a gift is most common. For the spirit perceives the state of the soul itself and is not without sympathy for it, just as the earthly body surrounds it. Indeed, the body possesses conditions opposite to the higher states of the soul. But the soul's primary and proper vehicle <note>original: "uehiculum," the "astral body" or "chariot" of the soul that bridges the gap between the physical and the spiritual</note> becomes refined and gains an ethereal condition when the soul is doing well; but when it is doing poorly, the vehicle becomes dull and turns earthly. Truly, this is the space between reason and the irrational nature, between the incorporeal and the corporeal levels; it is the common boundary of both. Through this medium, the divine is joined to the extremes. For this reason, it is difficult for philosophy to grasp its nature.

## The phantastic spirit is the primary vehicle of the soul.

<margin>u</margin> For this spirit claims something for itself as its own, as if from certain neighboring parts of both extremes; things which are so far apart meet in a single nature. Indeed, nature extends the breadth of the "phantastic essence" <note>the substance of the imagination</note> through many lots of things. It descends even to animals which possess no further intellect. In those cases, it is not the vehicle of a more divine soul, but it presides over the lower powers and is the very "reason" of the creature. Much is accomplished through the phantastic faculty in this...

# SYNESIUS

...the living being tastes of essence and acts with propriety; it is purified even in brute creatures, to the extent that something more excellent is introduced. Indeed, entire classes of demons <note>original: "daemonum"; in Neoplatonism, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</note> derive their essence from this kind of life. For these beings are entirely imaginary in their whole existence, formed by the things imagined within. Human beings also perform many activities through this faculty alone—or if through another, they certainly do so more through this one. For we are not accustomed to producing acts of intellect without the imagination, unless perhaps someone briefly reaches the immaterial form <note>referring to pure intellectual intuition without mental images</note>. To transcend the imagination is no less difficult than it is a blessed state. Hence that famous Platonic wish—desirable above all and achieved by few—that mind and wisdom might come to a person even in old age, signifying an intelligence that shines forth without the need for imagination. This is because our preceding and common life is characterized by imagination, or at least by an intellect that makes use of imagination.

The imaginative spirit <note>original: "spiritus phantasticus"</note> stands midway between the eternal and the temporal, and it is in this spirit that we live most of our lives.

Accordingly, this "animal spirit," which the blessed ones <note>likely referring to the authors of the Chaldean Oracles or other sacred Neoplatonic texts</note> have also called the "spiritual soul," becomes a god, an all-formed demon, and an image <note>original: "idolum"; here meaning a phantom or reflected likeness of the soul</note>. In this state, the soul also undergoes its punishments. On this point the oracles also agree, comparing the life of the soul in this state to the visions of those who dream. Furthermore, philosophy proves that preceding lives are a kind of preparation for the lives that follow; thus, the best disposition or habit in souls makes this spirit lighter and wipes away the thickness of a baser condition. By natural pulls, therefore, the spirit is either lifted to the heights because of heat and dryness—symbolized in Plato by the "growing of wings" <note>a reference to the *Phaedrus*</note>, and in Heraclitus by the "dry light" <note>original: "splendor siccus"; from Heraclitus’s maxim that "a dry soul is the wisest and best"</note> which signifies the wise soul—or the spirit becomes thick and damp, whereby it is submerged into the recesses of the earth, hiding by its natural weight and driven into the subterranean region. For this place is most suitable for moist spirits, and there an unhappy life is led, subject to punishments. However, it is possible through time, labor, and other virtues for the purified soul to emerge again; for it runs its course through twin lives <note>the celestial and the terrestrial</note>, and by turns approaches the better and the worse. The soul borrows this kind of spirit from the celestial spheres as it first descends, and mounting this like a small boat <note>original: "cimbam"; a common metaphor for the "vehicle" the soul uses to travel through the heavens</note>, it enters into commerce with the bodily world. Yet it wages a struggle of such a kind that it either brings the spirit along with it, or does not remain with it. Indeed, though it is difficult, it is possible for the soul to be released without following the spirit further—for it is wrong to disbelieve the sacred mysteries. Yet a shameful return to the heavens would occur if souls did not return what was borrowed <note>original: "alienum"; literally "belonging to another," referring to the spirit-vehicle gathered from the planetary spheres</note>, but left scattered around the earth that which they received from above.

And this indeed happens to the unique and fertile one as a gift of God and of the mysteries. For it is arranged by nature that the soul, once implanted in this <term>spiritus (spirit-vehicle)</term>, either exerts an impulse at the same time, or draws it, or perhaps is drawn by it; in any case, it remains joined to it until it ascends again to the place from which it came. For this reason, when the spirit grows heavy due to corruption, it drags down the soul that permitted itself to be weighed down. This is the state in which the sacred oracles <note>original: "eloquia"; likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles, a set of mystical texts highly regarded by Neoplatonists</note> terrify the intellectual seed within us with these words: "Do not decline into the dark world, beneath which lies a bottomless and treacherous depth—a black abyss, filthy on all sides, delighting in a senseless <term>idolum (phantom)</term>." For in what way could a dull and senseless life be beneficial to the mind? Yet, the inferior place is fitting for the "idol"—that is, the phantom—due to such a state of the spirit at that time. For like rejoices in like.

### The imaginative spirit can become purer or more impure, lighter or heavier.

Therefore, if through their union a single thing is made of both, the intellect also, out of a desire for pleasure, sometimes becomes submerged. This is the extreme of all evils: not even to notice the present evil. Those who are oppressed by this do not even attempt to emerge, for the disease has covered them with a very hard callus. And so, since they no longer feel any pain, they understandably do not strive for a cure. For this reason, repentance <note>original: "pœnitentia"</note> possesses a peculiar power that leads one back to the higher realms. Indeed, if one merely endures the present state, one hardly devises a means of flight. Thus, the greatest part of purification is the will. By the gift of the will, both deeds and words stretch out a helping hand. But if the will is removed, the soul lacks its entire purifying mechanism, since the greatest pledge of reconciliation is missing. For this cause, both here and in the hereafter, punishments bring the greatest aid to the order of things, while they oppose pain to pleasures and purge the stupid joy from our soul. Furthermore, those accidents that are said to happen "beyond what is deserved" <note>referring to seemingly unfair misfortunes</note> contribute greatly to rooting out the affection we feel for these fortunes. Certainly, among those who possess a mind, providence is confirmed by such things, whereas those who are out of their minds tend to distrust providence because of them. For no place is left for the soul to escape matter if it encounters no evil here. Therefore, one must consider that the governors of the lower province <note>referring to the planetary or earthly powers that manage the material world</note> have devised "vulgar prosperities" to serve as snares for living beings. Thus, while some might say that souls departing from here encounter the drink of forgetfulness <note>a reference to the river Lethe in classical mythology</note>, for the soul entering this life, a sweet and alluring condition brings the drink of oblivion. When the soul descends to this first life to labor for hire, it willingly becomes a servant for wages... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, continuing the metaphor of the soul's descent into the body as a form of indentured labor.</note>

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s discourse on the soul's entanglement with the material world. <header>SYNESIUS</header>

...strived to fulfill the mystery of universal nature itself, according to the rules ordained by inevitable law. But the soul, fascinated by the gifts of matter, is affected just like those who, though free, are hired for a wage for a set time to work; then, captivated by the beauty of a certain maidservant, they wish to prolong their stay, choosing to serve her harsh master. Indeed, when we are delighted by the profound feeling and external goods related to the body, we seem to agree with the nature of matter that it is beautiful. Matter, however, records our agreement in a <term>secret contract (original: "arcano libello")</term>; and if ever we decide to depart from there as free men, it cries out that we are fugitives, and attempts to call us back, seeking us like runaway slaves while bringing forward the contract. Then indeed, the soul has the greatest need for courage and divine help. For it is no light struggle to renounce one's own confession and pact. It also happens that force is applied, for material avenging punishments are then moved by fate against those who rebel against the laws of fate. 

And this is exactly what is signified by the labors of Hercules and the dangers that the <note>original: "sacra eloquia"; likely referring again to the Chaldean Oracles</note> sacred oracles testify he had to endure—or anyone else who bravely fights for freedom—so that he might lead his spirit to that place where the hands of nature can reach him the least. But if a leap occurs within its boundaries, the soul is confined in a narrow space and requires even more difficult struggles. For then nature does not spare us, as if we appeared already as strangers; and if it despairs of our ascent, it demands punishment for the attempt and offers lives not from both of the <note>Homer describes Zeus as having two jars, one of evils and one of blessings, from which he distributes to men (*Iliad* 24.527).</note> jars which Homer secretly signifies when he says there are two portions of matter, distributing a double condition of fate, from which the good is never pure. Indeed, someone may even suffer a worse, though tempered, lot.

->How useful is the repentance for sins, and how destructive is the love of mortal things.<-

Truly, all lives are engaged in wandering—wandering, I say, where after the first descent, an immediate return does not happen. Consider indeed over how great a distance this spirit conducts business with us. For when the soul is inclined downward, the <note>original: "sacrũ eloquiũ"; the sacred oracle</note> sacred oracle teaches that the spirit also grows heavy and is submerged, until it enters a region that is dark on all sides. But when the soul rises again, the spirit also accompanies it, as far as it is able to follow. However, it is able only until it reaches a completely distant level. Hear now what the oracles teach on this matter: you shall not leave behind this most wretched precipice of matter, but even for the <term>idol (original: "simulacro"; the phantasmal form or shade of the soul)</term> there is a portion in the region that is bright on all sides. This region is directly opposed to the region that is dark on all sides.

...is opposed, even if no one in this place has interpreted it with excessive sharpness: for the <note>original: "eloquium"; referring to the Sacred Oracles, likely the Chaldean Oracles</note> divine word does not seem to suggest that it recalls only the [pure] nature that set out from there back into the <term>spheres (original: "sphæras"); the celestial shells that surround the Earth in ancient cosmology</term>. Rather, it also suggests that if the soul, while descending from on high, contracted anything from the sublime fire or the air into its own <note>original: "naturam simulacralem"; the image-like or "phantastic" nature of the spirit</note> image-like nature before it was clothed in an earthly shell, this very substance of air and supreme fire—so says the word—is recalled to the higher realms along with the better part of the soul. For it is impossible that what is called the most abject matter could signify a divine body.

Now, reason dictates that those things which communicate and contribute toward a single end cannot lack a certain mutual relationship, a joining, and a persistence among themselves—especially those whose regions are neighbors. In this way, fire is closest to the <term>circular body (original: "orbiculari corpori"); the eternal, rotating substance of the heavens</term>, and is not like the earth, which occupies the furthest extremity of things. But if the better elements, by sometimes yielding to the lower, enjoy a certain communion, they fashion an indissoluble body within matter, as if it were formed by that which was permitted to rule during their meeting. Perhaps even the lower elements, if they do not struggle against the acts or actions of the soul but are instead gentle, obedient, and following, might exhibit a middle nature that cannot be dissipated. Under the guidance of the primary soul, these are brought together into the ethereal lot and are raised to the higher realms by a common pull. Even if they do not reach the very summit of the universe, they at least pass beyond the heights of the elements and reach the region that <note>original: "utrinq; lucentem"; likely referring to the border between the physical elements and the pure light of the heavens</note> shines on both sides. For it has, as the word says, a certain portion within itself; that is, it is received into a certain order of the circular body.

But let these words suffice concerning the elements and their lot. One may choose to believe or disbelieve these things; however, it is not permitted to deny that the corporeal essence which set out from the heavens is naturally lifted up from the lowest depths as the soul flies back, and is fitted again to the spheres—that is, it is as if it is poured back into its own true nature.

->The soul possesses a celestial and an airy body, with which it flies back to the heights.<-

<margin>h</margin> Indeed, there are two extreme regions and lots. One is entirely dark on both sides, and the other is shining from every direction; these have been assigned as the extremes of happiness and unhappiness. But how many middle regions do you think exist within the vastness of the world, which are dark on one side but shining on the other? In all of these, the soul lives its life along with this <term>spirit (original: "spiritu"); the pneuma or "astral body" that carries the soul</term>, alternatingly changing its forms, its habits, and its lives. Therefore, when the soul returns to its own noble state, it becomes a storehouse of truth; for it is pure, transparent, and altogether spotless. In that state, it is even a god, and a prophet if it so desires. But when it falls down, it becomes darkened, wandering, and mendacious: for that which is murky within the spirit cannot grasp the clarity of true things. Finally, when it holds the middle ground, it partly wanders, but partly attains...

For in all things, to achieve truth or to err only slightly is divine, or nearly divine. ### On the Region Entirely Bright and Entirely Dark, on the Middle Region, and How the Spirit is Revolved Everywhere.

Hence, one can perceive the order of the living soul in a human from this: whenever the <term>imaginative spirit (original: "phantasticus spiritus")</term> is pure, composed, and alert, it receives true images of things whether awake or asleep. Such a person possesses a pledge by which they can affirm that the very form of their soul has attained a better fate. Furthermore, we can "hunt" for the specific disposition of the animal spirit from the <note>original: "imaginationibus"; the mental images or "phantasies" produced by the mind</note> imaginations it primarily produces and in which it dwells, especially when it is not being struck by anything from the outside. 

Philosophy provides guidance and warning here, urging us to nourish and care for this spirit with the greatest diligence, lest it should ever wander. The best education is always to act according to the power of intuition and perception, so that the primary act of the soul is always entirely intellectual. We should always anticipate and prevent the absurd and rash impulses of the imagination. This is done by turning ourselves toward the best and avoiding commerce with the worse, except as far as absolute necessity compels. 

Intellectual intuition is a power that, more than anything else, separates those things which have become "clotted" or thickened within the spirit. For it subtly thins the spirit beyond what can be expressed and directs it toward God. When the spirit is made fit for this, it draws a divine spirit into commerce with our soul through a kind of knowledge. 

Conversely, when the spirit is constricted by a certain condensation, it becomes too narrow to fill the seats assigned to it by <term>Providence (original: "prouidentia")</term>—those powers that fashioned the human being and placed these seats in the <note>original: "cerebri... uentriculis"; the ventricles of the brain, which ancient and medieval doctors believed were the physical chambers where the soul processed memory, imagination, and reason</note> ventricles of the brain. In such a case, since nature does not tolerate a vacuum, an evil spirit creeps in. Then, indeed, what does the soul not suffer, being constantly weighed down by an accursed evil? For nature has arranged it so that the seats of the spirit are filled either by something better or by something worse. This evil is a punishment for the impious who ignored the divine spirit implanted within them; the good, however, is either the final goal of piety itself or surely very near to that end.

# ON DREAMS
M

### How one may detect the purity of one's spirit, as well as its impurity, 
### and by what method one may purify it.

Since we have resolved to discuss divination occurring through dreams, we must certainly tend to the nature of the imagination <note>original: "phantasticam naturam"; refers to the faculty that produces mental images</note>, lest men despise this practice; rather, they should cultivate it as something greatly beneficial to life. From this discussion, the immediate benefit may seem less apparent, but the more excellent fruit is the restoration of a healthy spirit to the higher realms. Certainly, the sacred gain of the soul is so great that it becomes a kind of religious meditation to strive to render a spirit of this kind fit for divination. Indeed, for this very reason, some—seized by a longing for prophecy—have preferred a sacred and simple table over a gluttonous one, and have loved a pure and entirely unstained bed. It is certainly far from the case that those who spent their time at the <term>Pythian tripod (original: "pythio tripode")</term> <note>The three-legged stool used by the Priestess of Apollo at Delphi to deliver oracles</note> or the bed of <term>Phoebus (original: "phœbeaq; lectica")</term> <note>Another name for Apollo, god of prophecy</note> for the sake of divination, would spend their nights there as witnesses to intemperance; rather, they would both entreat the god and devote themselves more intensely to their vows. For that which is accumulated little by little finally becomes much, and that which is accomplished through another means finally results in something greater, provided that we continue to love God more vehemently and encourage those who did not love Him before toward this love.

->First and foremost, effort must be made that we may have an imaginative spirit that is pure and fit for divination.<-

<margin>n</margin>
Therefore, divination should not be despised, for it leads us to divine things and remains close at hand, being the most excellent power of the soul. Nor is the utility of a soul thus joined to God any less because it has been admitted into divine commerce. For in the meantime, it does not abandon the living being, since it looks around at lower things from a watchtower much more fully than if it were mixed with inferior things. Therefore, remaining unshaken, it will provide images of those things that happen to the living being; and this is what is meant by the <note>original: "descendētem non descendere"</note> **descending without descending**, when the more excellent nature cares for the inferior without being held captive by it. Indeed, I pray that such divination may be present for me and for my children—a gift for which we are not compelled to undertake a long journey, nor to sail beyond our borders, as one must to reach the oracle of <term>Pythian Apollo</term> or <term>Jupiter Ammon</term> <note>The famous oracle of Zeus/Amun in the Libyan desert</note>. Instead, it is enough to give oneself to sleep with "glad hands" <note>original: "lætis manibus"; a poetic way of suggesting a state of ritual purity or joy</note> and after celebrating divine praises. This state is similar to that; and she who is glad beforehand, having put on garments of pure color, makes her vows to <term>Minerva</term> <note>The Roman name for Athena, goddess of wisdom</note>. Thus we shall pray for a dream, just as <term>Homer</term> perhaps prayed for one. Indeed, if one is prepared, the God who is said to be "far off" will be present in an instant—even though he is present everywhere for us when we have performed no such rituals but are merely sleeping—and these things indeed...
