<meta>This page continues Synesius’s argument that dream-divination is the most accessible and "democratic" form of spiritual practice. Having discussed the purification of the spirit in the previous section, he now contrasts dreams with the expensive and cumbersome rituals required by other oracular traditions.</meta>

# SYNESIVS

This entire treatment concerns the mysteries, regarding which no one has ever complained of poverty, as if it would make them less likely to achieve the same results as the wealthy. Most city-states choose their sacred priests from among the most noble and the richest—just as the Athenians choose their ship captains—and in those rites, there is a need for magnificent expenditures and no small fortune. One must import <note>Synesius lists exotic materials required for traditional ritual magic or "external" divination.</note> **Cretan herbs**, **Egyptian feathers**, and **Iberian bone** <note>original: "osq; hibericum"; likely a reference to ivory or whalebone</note>. And, by Jove, there is that "liquid wonder" produced and nourished in the depths of the sea, whether the sun is setting or rising. 

Indeed, such things and many others of that kind are handed down by those who engineer <term>prophecy (original: "vaticinium")</term> <note>The art of foretelling the future through external signs or rituals</note> received from the outside. No private person’s resources are sufficient to supply these needs. A **dream**, however, is seen by those who possess a small estate just as much as those with a large one. The watchman sees them as much as the hired laborer; the citizen no differently than the stranger. In the eyes of God, the herdsman, the slave, and even the madman do not differ from others in their capacity for this prophetic insight. 

Because the condition of this prophecy is so suited to the common people, it is certainly the most **humane**; because it is simple and ready at hand by its very nature, it is highly **philosophical**; because it is not forced, it is undoubtedly **pious**; and because it is present everywhere, it is rightly judged to be the most **divine**. For we are not compelled to employ water, or a rock, or a chasm in the earth <note>References to physical oracles like the Castalian Spring or the Delphic Chasm</note>. 

It is also fitting to praise this path because, for the sake of such prophecy, we are not distracted from even a single business of life, nor do we waste any time. For no one, having abandoned their necessary and present affairs, goes home to bed for a scheduled dream; rather, we use the very time that is necessary for the animal nature to consume for the sake of restoring itself. Since our substance cannot suffice for a perpetual state of wakefulness, this time—I say—is granted to us of its own accord. As the saying goes, it joins a "leisure greater than business" <note>original: "ociũ negocio maius"</note>, combining a necessary state with a desirable one: simply *being* joined with *well-being*. 

On the contrary, regarding those omens that typically arrive through various instruments, we should consider ourselves lucky if they claim only a large part of our lives while allowing some small portion for other uses and actions. If you focus your mind more closely on these matters, you will find it difficult to be assisted by those types of divination. It is not possible for everyone, at any time or place, to obtain the apparatus and furniture required for the administration of sacred rites. Nor is it easy to carry the necessary solemn instruments around with one. 

To pass over other matters, where punishments have recently been accumulated <note>A reference to the increasingly strict Roman laws against certain types of "pagan" divination in Synesius's time</note>, there is a certain heartless burden in carrying these things in the hold of a ship. When other parts of the sacred rites are added to these—namely, the designated men and witnesses (for that is a truer way to put it)—our current age is accustomed to reporting much through the ministers of the law. 

<summary>Synesius argues that dream-divination is superior to other oracles because it is free, requires no expensive exotic materials, and is available to all social classes without interrupting daily work. He contrasts the "humane" nature of dreams with ritualistic divination, which is burdened by heavy equipment and legal risks from government informants.</summary>

-># ON DREAMS<-

...by their works, the sacred rites, now made public, have come into the sight and hearing of the common crowd. For besides the fact that it is dangerous and wretched, I believe it is undoubtedly hateful to God to lean upon these things; for to not wait for someone who is willing, but to move them by force and levers, is nothing other than to inflict violence—something which even the founder of laws himself would not have left unpunished among men. 

Thus, besides all these things which are very difficult for those who search the future in this way, there is also the frequent interruption of the practice itself, and while we wander as exiles, the art itself is omitted. For it is no light task for those wandering everywhere to carry the luggage for such a journey with them <note>Synesius is referring to the heavy and exotic materials—herbs, bones, and specialized tools—required for ritualistic magic or "theurgy," which are difficult to transport compared to the mind's own dreams.</note>. 

In the case of <term>prophecy (original: "vaticinium")</term> <note>The act of foretelling the future or receiving divine messages</note> that comes through a dream, however, each person is their own instrument. So even if they wished to, they could not dismiss such an oracle; it remains with those who stay at home and migrates with those who travel. It serves in the military, handles civil affairs, lives in the country, and engages in trade. Neither do the laws of an envious city forbid this prophecy, nor could they forbid it even if they wanted to. For they have no grounds on which to condemn one who prophesies in this way. After all, how do we do wrong while sleeping? Nor can a tyrant prohibit one from seeing dreams, unless perhaps he banishes sleep far from the city; but it would be the mark of a madman to wish for the impossible, and of an impious man to command things contrary to nature and to God.

### *How useful and desirable prophecy is, especially through dreams.*

<margin>a</margin>To this prophecy, therefore, it is fitting for women and men to approach, the old and the young, the poor and the rich, private citizens and princes, those from the country and those from the city, the refined and the commoners. It rejects no gender, no age, no fortune, and no particular craft. To everyone everywhere, a ready prophet is present—a good and silent counselor, a teacher of the sacred rites, and a disciple. It predicts the good, so that by anticipating its use, one may have a longer-lasting pleasure. It also predicts the bad, so that we may beware of trouble and drive it away. 

Indeed, whatever things nourish the human race—whether they offer the best and most pleasant things, or whether fear brings about foresight and utility—all these are found in dreams. And yet, we are persuaded by no one else to hope in such a way, even though the gift of hoping is so prevalent and healthy in nature that refined <term>sophists (original: "sophistæ")</term> <note>Professional teachers or orators in the Greek tradition</note> declare that men would not have wished to live if they were affected exactly as they were constituted from the beginning. For they would have refused to live, compelled by the difficulties of life, unless **Prometheus** <note>The Titan from Greek mythology who created humanity and gave them fire; here, he is credited with giving humans 'hope' to endure suffering.</note> had inserted hope itself into nature as a remedy for persevering in life. Entrapped by its allurements, men judge what they expect in the future to be more certain than their present state. Hope itself possesses such great power that even when those in chains have the opportunity and fall into it, they are released by hoping for their wishes (so to speak)...

SYNESIUS

...performs a sacrifice, and suddenly he profits twice over. Shortly thereafter he commands a squad, soon he leads an army, conquers, slays, is crowned, hosts banquets, and prepares a table—a **simple** <note>original: "ficulam," literally "of a fig," implying something cheap or modest.</note> one if he wishes, or a **Persian** <note>original: "medicam," referring to the Medes or Persians, synonymous in antiquity with extreme luxury.</note> one if he likes. Meanwhile, he has forgotten his feet <note>He has forgotten his actual physical condition or station in life while lost in the grandeur of the dream.</note> until he is already about to lead the army. 

Yet this is truly the way of one who dreams, even while waking into a dream. For both states are occupied with the same subject, namely, the **imaginative faculty** <note>original: "natura phantastica." In Synesius’s philosophy, the "phantastic spirit" is the mirror of the soul where dreams and visions appear.</note>. Whenever we decide to shape this faculty with images, it brings one particular benefit: it defines our life with joy, flatters the soul with wandering hope, and thus calls us away from the perception of troublesome things.

### An exhortation to obtain the prophecy of dreams, and on the power of imagination.

<margin>q</margin> Indeed, when the **imaginative faculty**, presiding over us in its own duty, awakens hope in us, this happens to those who dream. We hold the promise of a dream like a pledge from God. Wherefore, anyone who eagerly prepares their mind as if to enjoy the grander gifts proposed in a dream reports a double gain: first, because they rejoice before the event itself, and second, because they later use the things they have acquired with knowledge, because they have long meditated on them as being perfectly suited to their life. 

Now, as for that hope which **Pindar** <note>A famous Greek lyric poet known for his odes.</note> praised when speaking of a happy man—saying that "sweet hope, a nurturing nurse, feeds his heart and accompanies him, which most of all rules the swaying mind of mortals everywhere"—one might say that the hope he celebrated is not the deceptive kind that tricks those who are awake (which we fashion for ourselves), but rather that all of this pertains to the appearance of a dream. Pindar's words were intended to celebrate a small portion of dreams.

Therefore, pursuing the **prophecy of dreams** <term>vaticinium somnii</term> <note>The art of foretelling the future through dream interpretation.</note> along with the art, it presents a firmer appearance, so that it does not seem to belong to a baser class. However, **Penelope** in the works of **Homer** <note>In Book 19 of the Odyssey, Penelope describes two gates through which dreams come to men.</note> introduces two gates of dreams, and asserts that half are deceptive, because she did not possess the wisdom of dreams. For if she had possessed the skill to handle these things wisely, she would surely have led all of them through the **gate of horn** <note>In ancient lore, true dreams pass through the Gate of Horn, while false dreams pass through the Gate of Ivory.</note>. She is introduced there being refuted and about to confess her ignorance regarding the vision itself, which she did not believe when she ought to have believed it. "The geese are indeed the suitors," [the dream said]. "I, however, am **Odysseus** <note>The OCR reads "V xiles," a corruption of "Ulixes," the Latin name for Odysseus.</note> the eagle." Yet he [Odysseus] was her companion, and she was talking nonsense to him about the vision. 

I seem to hear Homer saying here that one should not distrust dreams, nor transfer the fault of one's own weakness to the nature of the visions. In his works, not even **Agamemnon** <note>Leader of the Greek forces in the Trojan War.</note> justly accuses his dream of being deceptive when he had poorly received the oracle regarding victory, saying: "I command you to arm the helmeted Achaeans in their breastplates, for now [you shall take the city]..."

...you will capture the most vast city. Agamemnon therefore hastens as if he were suddenly about to storm the city by his own strength, for he misheard—and did not observe—what was actually said by the oracle. For the oracle said that he would indeed conquer if he armed the entire army of the Greeks; but at that time, neither Achilles nor the phalanx of Myrmidons <note>The elite warriors led by Achilles; their absence from the battle due to Achilles' anger led to the Greek losses.</note> went forth into battle, and they were surely the most excellent part of the army.

## How much hope the prophecy of a dream provides us.

<margin>m</margin> I have indeed heaped up many praises, yet I have acted almost foolishly. For I have already said a little while ago that the prophecy of dreams sails with us, dwells with us, fights alongside us, and trades with us, and serves all things to all people. But I have not yet recounted the benefits conferred upon me personally from that source, even though it is in the commerce of **philosophy** <note>original: "philosophiæ," here referring to the pursuit of wisdom and the intellectual life.</note> more than anything else that it is accustomed to communicate with men. Many things that are doubtful while we are awake, it clarifies completely after we have gone to sleep; sometimes it debates with us, and now indeed the dreamer seems to ask questions and learn, and now even to discover. To me indeed, it has often brought books to my side—for it instructed my mind and composed my speech—sometimes describing the day's events, sometimes even changing them; and sometimes, when my whole manner of speaking was foolish and swollen with the novelty of names because of an excessive love for the older and harsher **Attic Greek** <term>Atthis: A reference to the ancient dialect of Athens, which was often imitated by later writers (Atticism) to the point of being overly obscure or pretentious.</term>, this prophecy, through God's help, corrected me. In part it dictated to me, and in part it showed me what was what, soothing and smoothing away certain innate swellings of my speech, expelling the "tumor" of my style and restoring a proper measure. And furthermore, whenever I went hunting, it provided me with strength and gave me strategies against wild beasts that ran with a certain craftiness or lay hidden; sometimes even when I was exhausted and breaking camp, it commanded me to stay, and promised such good fortune that it was a delight to remain in the hunt with eager confidence. When such divination was present, success and fortune were at hand; it clearly showed me the rows of failed catches and the beasts actually captured. To me, my life consists of books and the hunt. Since I have never desired to perform the duties of an embassy—reckoning it no profit to see three **unlucky** <note>original: "nefastos," meaning ill-omened or forbidden. Synesius spent three years on a difficult embassy to Constantinople, which he found miserable.</note> years of one’s life pass by—even then I was helped most of all by this prophecy. For it rendered powerless the plots of **soul-summoning magicians** <note>original: "magorum animascitantium," referring to sorcerers or theurgists who claimed to manipulate spirits or souls.</note> directed against me, sometimes by revealing hidden things, and sometimes by delivering me from all dangers. And so it also arranged my public affairs so that the cities might be governed in the best way. It even reconciled me to the **Great King** <note>Likely a reference to the Emperor Arcadius, whom Synesius addressed during his time in Constantinople.</note> with greater confidence than any of the Greeks had ever enjoyed.

<meta>This page continues Synesius’s philosophical exploration of dreams. After previously discussing the personal and practical benefits he has received from dreams, he now moves into a more metaphysical explanation of why dreams are accessible to everyone and how the soul interacts with divine and worldly images while we sleep.</meta>

<header>SYNESIUS</header>

## Dreams provide us with prophecies in abundance.

<margin>c</margin> While other forms of divination require the care and attention of specific experts, this one is available to all. A good spirit <note>original: "dæmon"; in this context, it refers to a guiding divine presence or "daimon" rather than a malevolent entity.</note> is present to every person, and to those who have meditated while awake to skillfully discover something, a teacher appears in their sleep. So wise a thing is the soul when it takes its leisure from the filth of the external senses, which bring in alien natures from all sides. For the soul possesses many forms, and whatever it is accustomed to receive from the mind once formed, it exhibits these clearly to the internal parts when it is turned inward, and it transmits those things that come from the divine. For to a soul in such a state, the God of the world <note>original: "Deus mundanus"; likely referring to the World Soul or the divine ordering principle of the cosmos.</note> also joins himself entirely, because the nature of the soul itself flowed forth from the same source as he did. These kinds of dreams are therefore considered more divine; they are either entirely or almost completely whole and clear, and they require very little help from the interpreter’s art. But these dreams happen only to those men who live in virtue, whether that virtue is acquired through wisdom or through habit. If they should ever happen by chance to someone else, it is quite rare, though it may occur. However, dreams do not fall into just one small category for everyone; the remaining kind is manifold and very common. This type is entirely hidden, and it is for the sake of this kind that it is necessary to apply an art of interpretation. For it has an origin that is—if I may say so—absurd and monstrous. And since it sprouts from such things, it proceeds as something most obscure. For this is how the matter of dreams stands, as I shall explain.

## The prophecy of dreams is available to everyone.

<margin>a</margin> For all things that are contained within the nature of the universe—whether they exist in the present, were made in the past, or are spoken of as the future (for these too are certain modes of existence)—images flow forth and are constantly emitted from their substance. For if any sensible thing is a form <note>original: "εἶδος" (eidos); referring to the "Form" or "Idea" of a thing in Platonic philosophy.</note>, that is, a species in matter, it is extended together with that matter. We perceive that matter flows outward from the composite object; therefore, reason dictates that the nature of the forms is also derived from the outside through images <note>original: "idola"; these are subtle "films" or likenesses that Neoplatonists believed radiated from objects.</note>, so that on both sides those things involved in the process of "becoming" degenerate from the very dignity of True Being. Truly, of all the images we have mentioned that flow from things everywhere, the **phantastic spirit** <term>spiritus phantasticus: the faculty of the soul that mirrors perceptions and images, acting as a bridge between the physical senses and the higher mind.</term> is certainly the clearest mirror. Otherwise, these images, which wander about and fall away from their stable state—both because of the indefiniteness of their being and because they are recognized by none of the higher beings—would be lost. But as soon as they are ensnared in the animal spirits, which are themselves images but have their seat in nature, they immediately lean upon these and rest within them as if in dwellings. Therefore, regarding those things which have been made, since they have already proceeded into the act of being through...

# ON DREAMS

...clear images <term>idola<gloss>from the Greek 'eidolon,' meaning an image, phantom, or likeness that emanates from an object</gloss></term> are sent forth everywhere, until through the passage of time they finally become weak and small. Those images of things present, however, are far stronger and most manifest, as they still consist of their own substance; but the images of things to come are indefinite and quite indistinct. For these are a kind of preliminary unfolding <note>original: "præuolumina"; Synesius uses a metaphor of a scroll partially unrolling to describe how the future begins to manifest before it actually happens.</note> of things not yet present, a blooming of a nature still imperfect, as if leaping forward and dancing out, like the obscure markings of seeds hidden away. For this reason, an "art" or skill is required for future things, because the images and obscure likenesses that proceed from them are shadowed, unlike the manifest images that come from things already present. Images flow forth from all things, and their mirror and receptacle is the imaginative spirit itself.

<margin>m</margin> The nature of these images is truly miraculous, as they are produced by things that have not yet even occurred. Therefore, something must now be said about this "art"—the method by which it can be acquired. First and foremost, it is best to have prepared the divine spirit in such a way that it becomes worthy for the Intellect and God to be made known to it and to preside over it. Let it no longer be a mere vessel for infinite, random images. The best cultivation of the spirit is two-fold: first, to calm the disturbed motions of the soul through the study of philosophy (for when these motions are stirred, the spirit is occupied like a kingdom in turmoil); and second, through a moderate and balanced diet, to affect the animal nature so that it is as little provoked as possible. One must settle the outermost body so that it does not stir up waves, for the ripple travels all the way to the primary part of the soul. It is necessary to always keep the primary part calm and undisturbed. However, since wishing for this is easy for anyone, but achieving it is more difficult than anything else, and since we desire that dreams be useful to everyone, let us search for a certain limit or rule even among these indefinite things. That is, let us establish an art concerning these <term>idola</term>, or images. They behave in the following manner:

## How we can interpret dreams.

<margin>q</margin><margin>by themselves they signify the city</margin> Those who frequently sail the seas, if they ever encounter a certain rock upon which they climb and from there catch sight of a city, will thereafter signify that same city to themselves whenever they see that same rock. Furthermore, we often guess that army leaders—whom we do not yet see—are about to arrive based on the scouts, because we are accustomed to the leaders always following those same scouts. In the same way, we are accustomed to pre-signify future events everywhere through these images. For the things that come before are the same as the things themselves, and like follows like. Just as it is a pilot’s lack of skill not to recognize the coastline or predict which shores he is approaching when the same rock appears, so too is it with dreams.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of personal observation in interpreting dreams, comparing the dreamer's task to that of a ship's pilot or a weather-watcher. It transitions into a critique of universal dream-interpretation manuals, arguing that the "imaginative spirit" is unique to each individual.</meta>

### SYNESIUS

...and such a pilot lacks the aid of conjectures. So it is with a person who frequently experiences the same vision: unless they have already marked down what specific event it portends for them—whether a passion, a turn of fortune, or an action—they use their life as foolishly as a pilot of that sort uses a ship. We are also accustomed to noting signs of Jove <note>original: "iouia signa"; here referring to atmospheric phenomena like lightning or clouds associated with the god Jupiter/Jove</note> in the surrounding air; for example, looking at the circular area around the moon, we predict that there will be storms because winds have frequently followed such sights. This is what the poet's line refers to: "from this, indeed, the storm is signaled; from that, a circular tranquility." For a broken halo portends winds, while one that vanishes portends calm. Two circles precede a storm; however, a triple circle portends a more violent tempest, especially if it appears black, and even more so if it is broken. So it is in all things: both Aristotle and reason dictate that sense-perception produces memory, memory produces experience and skill, and through this, an "art" <term>art<gloss>from the Latin 'ars,' referring to a systematic craft or branch of knowledge built on observation</gloss></term> is finally established. We ought to proceed in a similar fashion regarding dreams.

->**A common and identical rule for interpreting dreams cannot be applied to all individuals.**<-

Many authors have composed numerous books on the observation of dreams of this kind. However, I laugh at all of these, judging them to be of very little use. For the "imaginative spirit" <note>original: "spiritus phantasticus"; in Synesius's Neoplatonic philosophy, this is a "subtle body" or medium that sits between the physical body and the immaterial soul</note> does not function like this ultimate body of ours—that is, the union of the elements joined together—which can be subject to a universal art and a discourse that follows nature consistently. In the physical body, the same things generally suffer from the same causes, since there is little discrepancy between similar things, and whatever exists in them contrary to nature (such as illness) does not usually remain hidden. Therefore, we do not use a single guiding rule for dreams; I say this because the imaginative spirit itself is not so constituted, but from its very first origin, one spirit differs from another. For one spirit corresponds to one celestial sphere, and another to another, according to which sphere prevails in its tempering. 

Hence that poetic saying: "The most blessed souls flow from heaven to earth," and those are the wealthiest of all, having been allotted inestimable threads of fate. Whosoever are less favored by the "Splendid King" <note>likely referring to the Sun or the Demiurge</note>, and those who come from Jove himself by the thread of powerful necessity—this was also what Plato hinted at secretly and with fear in the *Timaeus*, where he assigned to each soul a star as a companion. But souls, having fallen from their own nature because they preferred to dwell near matter—some less, others more—each used their own "inclination of the scales," as it were, and thus fortunately or unfortunately stained their spirit. The spirit thus inhabits bodies affected in this way, and its whole life is spent in a state of error and disease...

<summary>Synesius argues that dream interpretation must be personal rather than based on universal manuals because the "imaginative spirit" is uniquely shaped by its celestial origins and its descent into matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that dream interpretation is a subjective science. Having previously compared the dreamer to a weather-watcher, the author now explains why universal "dream books" fail: the "spirit" (the medium of dreams) varies from person to person like different qualities of water or mirrors.</meta>

# ON DREAMS

### h 4

...beyond nature, so far as the nobility of the species is concerned, but according to nature as far as it pertains to the animal; for the animal is animated by the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; in this context, it refers to the 'pneuma' or 'imaginative spirit,' a subtle body that mediates between the soul and the physical world</note> when it is so affected. Unless there is an inherent order to the spirit itself, it is regulated by its own state, employing both vice and virtue; for nothing is quite as pliable and changeable as the spirit. In what way, then, in things so unlike each other—whether by nature, by law, or by the passions that result—could the same appearances arise from the same sources? Certainly, it does not happen this way, nor can it. For how could water that is simultaneously turbid and clear, or agitated and calm, be affected in the same way or reflect the same form? But if the turbid condition differs in one person compared to another according to the differences in "colors," and the movements themselves occur in various configurations, then any deviation from a perfectly clear image will be one thing in genus, but diverse in its specific appearance.

Therefore, whether it is Phemonoe <note>A legendary Greek prophetess, said to be the daughter of Apollo and the first to sing in hexameters</note>, or Melampus <note>A famous mythical seer and healer who understood the language of animals</note>, or anyone else who claims to define a common rule for such matters and to order them completely, we shall ask them: can a mirror—whether it be straight or distorted, or made of dissimilar materials—render a similar image of the same object? But those writers did not, from the beginning, philosophize at all regarding the spirit. They think that their own particular spirit, however it may be disposed, is the rule and the test for everyone. I do not deny that some congruence can be found among things that differ in all other respects. However, that which is obscure and dispersed becomes even more obscure; even from the start, the image <note>original: "idōlon"</note> of a pre-existing thing was difficult to know. It is even more difficult to perceive something in every individual mode or character that is exactly like a common vision and perfectly suited to it.

->**Each person should observe their own dreams and the events that follow them.**<-

For these reasons, one should in no way hope that laws for dreams can be established that are equally common to all. Instead, each person ought to treat themselves as the "material of the art" <term>art<gloss>the systematic practice or skill of interpretation</gloss></term>, and can write down in their memory what sort of visions they had and what events they subsequently encountered. For it is not very difficult for a habit <note>original: "habitus"</note> to form around a matter which one meditates upon through use or necessity; for use and necessity suggest the meditation of memory. This is especially true when material is available everywhere. 

In dreams, moreover, nothing is more abundant, and nothing else draws the mind more strongly toward itself. Dreams compel even the foolish to meditate upon them and care for them, to such an extent that it would be shameful for men who have completed a decade since puberty <note>referring to young men in their mid-twenties</note> to still require another prophet, rather than having already accumulated many rules of this art within themselves. It would certainly be worthwhile to commit visions and occurrences to writing individually—both those of waking and of sleep—were it not that civil custom <note>social norms or traditional expectations</note> might find such a novelty...

Having established that the "imaginative spirit" (pneuma) varies between individuals, he now proposes a practical method for mastering this internal landscape: keeping a dream journal.</meta>

...shuddered at the thought. With this permission, we judge that nocturnal records must be joined daily to our journals of the day, so that the actions of both states of human life may be preserved in our commentaries. For reason has posited that a certain life exists within the imagination—at times better than our "middle" <note>Referring to the ordinary, waking life</note> life, and at times worse, depending on how much health or disease the spirit possesses. 

Thus, if we pursue this kind of observation with diligent effort, a skill is gradually built up from which nothing slips the memory. Furthermore, this will be an elegant pastime and an exercise for the mind, as we honor the history of both our waking and sleeping hours. This practice will also contribute to eloquence. For those who care for the training of the tongue, there is, I believe, no invention better suited than this for exercising the faculty of speech in all matters. If the Lemnian Sophist <note>original: "lemnius sophista"; likely Philostratus the Elder, a 3rd-century teacher of rhetoric who advocated for daily writing</note> teaches that daily writings are the best instructors for speaking aptly on every subject—because nothing, however small, should be neglected, but everything both grave and light must be expressed—then why should we not also cultivate nocturnal records for the sake of interpretation?

### *How Varied, Deceptive, and Playful the Imagination Is in Dreams.*

<margin>n</margin>
One might certainly ask how great a task he has undertaken who wishes to match his speech to these visions. In dreams, things that are naturally joined are separated, while those naturally distinct are joined together. Here, there is a need for reason and debate so that a vision which does not seem to occur, may occur <note>i.e., making sense of the nonsensical</note>. It is no light task to translate the monstrous and absurd movements arising in the soul into another mode of expression. When, through the imagination (*phantasia*), things that exist are expelled from their role of being, and things that are nowhere and in no way able to exist naturally are introduced in their place, what method can there be to track an utterly unnameable nature through these internal visions? 

The dream does not show these things in a few forms, nor all at once, nor in a consistent time, even though they occur and extend as they do. For we believe that whatever the soul wishes occurs to it. To express all these things at length and without foolishness is the work of a most perfect orator. This "dream-matter" exults and boasts against the very faculty of discernment, offering something more than simple estimation can carry. For we do not encounter these visions without passion; rather, intense dispositions and affections take hold of us. Great hatreds arise, and those who sleep are often beset by many "benefits" <note>original: "beneficia"; here likely referring to the deceptive allurements or tricks of the dream state</note>. Pleasure, certainly, prevails most strongly then, and this state of life is quite prone to the most alluring enticements—so much so that loves and hates may sprout in the soul that will endure even into the waking state.

He describes the chaotic nature of the imagination in sleep, where the rules of reality are inverted and intense emotions can be birthed that persist into waking life.</summary>

# ON DREAMS
ff

### How wondrous is the variety of the imagination in dreams.

<margin>3</margin>
If anyone intends to speak of things that are not trivial, but rather to complete the discourse for which this work was established—namely, to settle the listener within this very state of being, its opinions, and its perceptions—he will certainly require words that have the power to move. Indeed, in the dream state, a person may simultaneously conquer, fight as a gladiator, fly, or capture; all this is the work of the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note>. But how shall speech capture this? A person sleeps a dream, and in that dream he sees; meanwhile, he "wakes up" while still sleeping, or so he thinks, and while lying there he shakes off sleep. He philosophizes, and knows something of both states regarding the appearing dream—noting that this part is a dream, but that part is twofold. Then he loses faith in the truth of his waking and believes that what is present is real and serious, and that the things appearing to him are living beings. From this, he struggles with all his might against himself, now trying to dismiss the vision, now trying to wake himself up, testing his own reality to uncover the deception. They say indeed that the Aloadae <note>original: "Aloadas"; in Greek mythology, the twin giants Otus and Ephialtes who attempted to storm heaven by piling Mount Ossa on Mount Pelion to reach the gods</note> suffer punishment because they built up the mountains of Thessaly against the gods. But for the sleeper, no law of inevitable judgment ever forbids him from lifting himself high above the earth, more fortunately than Icarus <note>original: "Icaro"; the mythical youth who fell when his waxen wings melted</note>, surpassing eagles in flight, and even flying over the highest celestial spheres. From there, he may look down upon the globe of the earth from a distance—and this vision does not merely signify an inspection of the moon. It is even permitted to debate with the stars and to meet with the hidden gods within the cosmos. For when a thing is most difficult to do in waking life, it becomes easiest there; then the gods appear openly and clearly, and there is no envy or resentment in them. A moment later, the dreamer sits back upon the earth; he has not even moved, but is present there instantly. For nothing is more characteristic of a dream than the way it cuts out the "middle ground" <note>original: "intercipe medium"; skipping the logical or physical steps between two points</note> and does not operate within linear time. Thus, he might immediately speak with little sheep and believe their bleating to be human speech, understanding perfectly what they are "saying." So new and so broad is this material for arguments, and so vast a province for study, if one strives to adapt his speech to dreams. I truly believe that fables <note>original: "fabulas"</note> also received their license and abundance from dreams—those stories in which a peacock speaks, or a fox, or the sea—even if these examples are meager when compared to the absolute freedom of dreams. And though fables are but the smallest part of dreams, they are nonetheless cultivated by the Sophists <note>original: "sophistis"; professional teachers of rhetoric and philosophy</note> and deemed worthy of interpretation. It would be fitting for those who find the beginning of their art in the fable to find its perfection in the dream. This is especially true since the faculty of speech is not exercised in these matters in vain; just as in fables, a deeper meaning <note>original: "profundioris sententiæ"</note> lies hidden within.

->That it is useful for both life and eloquence to record daily what you have dreamed, what you have done, and what has happened to you.<-

Let him spend some time on this, which is indeed the best use of time, for elsewhere...

# SYNESIUS

Divination <note>original: "uaticiniũ" (vaticinium); the art of foretelling the future or interpreting divine signs</note> is acquired through intelligence; that is, the art of gathering signs which we have praised. Indeed, nothing can be more useful than this; nor will the method of speaking be hindered by the great consequence of these matters. To a philosopher, such a treatise will truly be a game and a comfort, providing relief when he relaxes the extreme tension of his mind, just as Scythian archers are accustomed to unstringing their bows. To the rhetorician, however, we shall establish this as the very summit and peak of his demonstrations, for they do not always see the opportunity to exercise their eloquence and vehemence. I speak of men like Miltiades and Cimon <note>famous Athenian generals and statesmen</note>, and even some of no reputation—both the wealthy and the poor—who hold civic life in hatred. Regarding these, I have indeed seen ancient men in the theater arguing sharply, even though they were venerable in the name of philosophy. Each of them (it seemed) had grown a "talent of beard" <note>original: "barbæ talentum"; a humorous way of saying they had grown massive beards to look like wise sages</note>. Yet, the reverence of their profession did not stop them from breaking out into insults and brawls, immodestly waving their hands while arranging their speeches with—as I thought then—sufficient strength. But as they later reported to me, they were neither then, nor had they ever been, truly capable; in fact, they were not so from the beginning of their nature. For how can there be "civility" in a system that grants a prize to the victor for destroying a fellow citizen who simply holds a different opinion on the Republic? Now, indeed, whoever still meditates and struggles with a ninety-year-old fiction <note>likely referring to the tedious, lifelong drills of traditional rhetorical schools</note> only delays the truth with words. They seem to me to entirely misunderstand the very name of "meditation" when they claim to study for the sake of something else; these men have mistaken the preparation for the goal itself, worshipping the path they must walk as if it were the destination. For they have turned meditation into a mere contest. It is as if someone who has exercised his hands vigorously in the wrestling school were to profess himself a master of the Pancratium <note>original: "Pancratiũ"; an ancient Greek "all-powers" combat sport combining wrestling and boxing</note> at the Olympic games. Thus, both a dryness of mind and a flood of words have so occupied men that some seem powerful in speaking, yet have nothing worth saying. However, they ought to have composed themselves as Archilochus and Alcaeus <note>Greek lyric poets known for their raw, personal honesty</note> did; both of them poured out the sweet melody of their voices for the sake of their own lives. Thus, posterity remembers the things in which they took pleasure and the things for which they grieved. They did not pour out vain speeches on fabricated arguments, as this recent breed of "wise men" is accustomed to do, nor did they bestow their goodness upon others like Stesichorus and Homer, who made the heroic race more illustrious through their songs—from which we too have made progress in imitating virtue. Yet those [moderns], as far as it lies in them, seem neglected; we have nothing more to say of them except that they were "vigorous poets." Therefore, whoever desires to be remembered by posterity and trusts that he can commit immortal things to letters, let him follow the method of writing approved by us at present, which lies outside common custom. Let him boldly entrust himself to Time. For Time is a faithful guardian when something is entrusted to it in accordance with God.

# From Michael Psellus on Demons, translated by Marsilio Ficino.

<margin>n</margin>The nature of demons is not without a body. Rather, it possesses a body and is active around physical bodies, which our venerable fathers <note>the early Church Fathers</note> also judged to be true; there are even those who assert that demons appeared to them in their own presence with their specific bodies. Moreover, Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great (c. 330–379), a leading theologian of the early church</note>, the divine inspector of mysteries hidden from us, attributed bodies not only to demons but even to pure angels, describing them as certain thin, airy, and pure spirits. As a witness, he brings forward David <note>King David, traditionally the author of the Psalms</note> saying, "Who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire" <note>Psalm 104:4</note>. This is indeed necessary. For as the divine Paul <note>the Apostle Paul</note> asserts, it is necessary that the ministering spirits who are sent forth have a body by which they move, stand in place, and appear openly; for they knew these ministries could not be completed otherwise than by some kind of body.

If you read anywhere in the scriptures that they are called "incorporeal," I respond that both our people and others are accustomed to calling thicker bodies "corporeal," while they frequently name those thin bodies—which escape sight and touch—as "incorporeal" <note>original: "incorporea"; the author explains that "incorporeal" in old texts often just means "invisible or very fine matter" rather than a total lack of substance</note>. However, the body of an angel is not the same or related to that of a demon. For the angelic body, pouring forth certain rays, cannot be endured by the eyes, vanishing utterly from them. Whether the demonic body was ever such, I do not know how to say. But it seems it was so at some time, since Isaiah names the angel who fell "Lucifer" <note>the Light-bringer</note>; yet now, it exists as something otherwise dark and shadowy.

And if, stripped of its joined light, it is presented to the eyes, it strikes us as something troublesome. The angelic body is indeed entirely devoid of matter, which is why it penetrates and passes through every solid thing. It is even less subject to suffering <term>passionibus: in this context, physical changes, disturbances, or the ability to be acted upon by external force</term> than a ray of the sun. For a ray of the sun, proceeding through or entering transparent and translucent bodies, is detained by earthly and opaque obstacles to such an extent that it undergoes refraction <note>original: "fractione"; literally a breaking or bending of the light</note>, as if it has a kinship to what is bad <note>the physical world was often seen as "lower" or more "fallen" than pure light</note>.

But nothing of these things stands in the way of the angelic body, as it suffers no opposition from anything; for it agrees with none of these in rank or nature. Demonic bodies, however, although invisible due to their thinness, are nevertheless material in a certain way and subject to suffering, especially those that have entered subterranean places. For these have been thickened <note>original: "concreta"; made solid or dense</note> by God so that they may be subject to touch, feel pain when struck, and be burned when approaching fire—so much so that some of them even leave behind a residue of ash. History records that this indeed happened among the Etruscans <note>original: "tuscos"; the ancient people of central Italy</note> of Italy. Nor do I speak of these things as if bringing forth a poetic fable and monsters in the manner of the Cretans and Phoenicians <note>cultures often associated by the Greeks with tall tales and myths</note>. Instead, persuaded by the words of the Savior himself, I affirm these things: that they record demons being tortured by fire, so that

<summary>In this opening to Michael Psellus's treatise, the author argues that angels and demons possess subtle bodies. While angels are made of impenetrable light, demons have denser, "shadowy" bodies that can be physically harmed or even burned by fire.</summary>

# PSELLUS:

<note>The header refers to Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and historian whose work on demonology became a primary source for Renaissance occultists and theologians.</note>

...precisely because they are corporeal <note>possessing a physical, albeit thin, body</note>, they are able to suffer <note>in this context, "to suffer" means to be affected by external physical forces or to feel sensation</note>. For in what way could they suffer if they were incorporeal? For that which is truly incorporeal cannot even be imagined to suffer from a body.

### Six species of demons: how they transform themselves, how they sneak into us, and how they move us.

Indeed, I have received much information about these things from those who have devoted themselves to the study of <unclear>...summoning them to appear; however, I have never seen such a thing, nor do I wish to see demons.</unclear> I was, however, acquainted with someone who led a solitary life in the Chersonese <note>likely the Gallipoli peninsula</note> bordering Greece, named Marcus. He reported that he was of the Mesopotamian <note>original: "Mesopotamium"; the OCR's "sim fluuium" is a likely misreading of this geographic term</note> race, and he had excelled more than anyone else in the worship of demons and had observed their apparitions. At first, he used to despise and detest these things as empty and false; but later he "sang a recantation" <note>original: "palinodiam cecinit"; a Greek idiom for retracting a former opinion</note> and adhered to the true dogmas and our faith. This man revealed many strange and demonic things to us. When I occasionally asked him whether demons could suffer, he replied, "Indeed they do, to such an extent that some demons even cast seed and give rise to certain small animals." Then I said, "It is incredible that demons should have excrement and genital members." He replied, "They do indeed have members, but not like ours. Some kind of excrement does indeed emanate from them." Then he added, "Believe me." But I said, "They would be in great danger if they were nourished in our manner." Marcus said, "They are indeed nourished: some by inhalation, just as the spirit <note>term: spiritus - the vital breath or "pneuma" believed to flow through the body</note> thrives in the arteries and nerves. Others by moisture, but not through a mouth like us; rather like sponges and oysters, sucking up the moisture lying around them. Again, they secrete what is more solid in the moisture. However, not all of them experience this, but only the types of demons closest to matter: the kind of demon that hates light, the water-dwelling, and the subterranean." To this I asked: "Are there many kinds of demons, Marcus?" "Many," he said, "and diverse, both according to their forms and their bodies, so much so that the air above us and around us is full of demons. The land, the sea, and the hidden and deep places are also full of them." I said, "Unless it is a burden, list them." "Generally," he said, "there are six kinds of demons. I do not know whether it is better to divide demons by the places they inhabit, or rather by the fact that the whole race of demons is possessed by a love for the body. I know that the number six is corporeal and worldly. For in that number are the circumstances of physical bodies, and the world is composed through it—or perhaps because this is the first number that composes a scalene triangle <note>a triangle with three unequal sides, used here as a geometric symbol for the imperfection of the material world</note>. I hold that the equilateral triangle <note>a triangle with all sides equal</note> is the property of the divine and celestial, insofar as it is equal to itself and is with difficulty moved toward evil. But the isosceles <note>original: "aequicrurii"; a triangle with two equal sides</note> is the property of the human race, which may wander from its original purpose in one direction, but becomes better through repentance."

### ON DEMONS
#### N ii

The scalene <note>referring to a triangle with unequal sides, a traditional symbol for the "unbalanced" or "imperfect" in Neoplatonic philosophy</note> is truly characteristic of the demonic as something unequal, and in no way approaching the good. Therefore, whether it be in this or another way, he enumerated six types of demons in total. And the first, indeed, he called by a name in the primary barbarian tongue: *Lieliureon* <note>original: "lieliureon"</note>, that is, **fiery**; he said it wanders through the higher air, for every demonic thing is banished from the lunar regions as if something profane is cast out from a temple.

The second type wanders in the air near to us, which is specifically called **airy** by many. The third is **terrestrial**, which dwells mostly upon the earth and opposes earthly things with many schemes and devices. The fourth is **aquatic and marine**, which immerses itself in moisture and gladly lives around lakes and rivers; it destroys many in the waters and stirs up waves and storms in the sea, sinks ships heavy with men, and overwhelms many in the waves. The fifth is **subterranean**, which inhabits caves and crevices beneath the earth; it attacks those who dig wells and mines. It causes cracks in the earth, shakes foundations, and stirs up fire-vomiting winds. The sixth and last is the **light-fleeing** <note>original: "lucifugum"</note>, which is inscrutable and entirely dark, responding violently with cold passions. 

He said that all these types of demons are so disposed that they hate the gods and oppose men; but one is worse than another. For the aquatic, the subterranean, and especially the light-fleeing types are highly malicious and destructive. For these do not merely deprave and harm souls through fantasies and thoughts, but, wandering like wild beasts of the forest, they hasten toward the ruin of men. Thus, the aquatic type suffocates those wandering in the waters and afflicts them with the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> and madness. The airy and terrestrial ones, however, attack by a certain art and calculation, and thus they deceive human minds and bend them toward the foulest, most wicked, and ruinous disturbances. 

Then I asked in what manner and by what actions they achieve these things: whether they rule over us and carry us about like slaves wherever they please? 

They do not rule, he said, but they secretly suggest things to us. For they approach the **phantastic spirit** <note>original: "spiritui... phantastico"; the faculty of the soul responsible for imagination and mental images</note> within us, and since they are themselves spirits, they sound out words of disturbance and pleasure to us. They do not emit a voice by a physical striking or sound, but they instill their speech without sound. 

But in what way, I asked, can they thrust speech into us without a voice? 

Is it any wonder, he asked, if you consider how a person speaking from afar needs a louder shout; but one who has become closer whispers into the listener’s ear. If he could be joined with the spirit of the soul itself, he would need no sound at all; rather, his speech, conceived by the will, would glide into the listener with no sound whatsoever. They say this happens even to souls that have departed the body; for these converse among themselves without noise. In this very way, demons converse with us; secretly, indeed, so that we cannot even tell from where the war is being brought against us.

<summary>This page outlines a hierarchy of six demonic types categorized by their elemental dwelling (fire, air, earth, water, underground, and darkness) and explains that they influence humans not through physical force, but by whispering directly into the "phantastic spirit" or imagination.</summary>

# PSELLUS

...to perceive it. Nor will anyone who has considered the properties of air doubt this. For just as air, when light is present, receives colors and forms and transmits them to those things that are naturally able to receive them—as is seen in mirrors and other reflective objects—so too do demonic bodies receive shapes and colors from their internal **image-making essence** <note>original: "essentia phantastica"; the faculty of the soul that produces mental images</note>. They then transmit whatever forms they wish into our own **animal spirit** <note>original: "spiritu animali"; in medieval physiology, a subtle substance that flowed through the nerves to communicate sensation and movement</note>. In this way, they cause us much trouble by suggesting various plans and pleasures, subtly indicating forms, stirring up memories of delights, and frequently exciting images of passions in those who are both awake and asleep. Indeed, sometimes by tickling the thighs and groins, they incite us to madness and wicked loves, especially if they find **warm and moist humors** <note>referring to the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were thought to determine temperament</note> that are conducive to such things. 

Yet these demons, donning **Pluto’s helmet** <note>original: "plutonis galeam"; a mythological reference to a cap of invisibility, signifying the demons' ability to work unseen</note>, disturb our souls with a certain art and sophisticated fraud. Other types of demons, however, do not devise anything through wisdom or carry out their deeds by cleverness; rather, they are troublesome and highly turbulent, causing harm in the manner of **Charonean spirits** <note>original: "charonei spūs"; referring to the toxic, suffocating vapors found in certain caves or volcanic vents, named after Charon, the ferryman of the underworld</note>. For just as they say this vapor destroys whatever comes near it, whether it be a four-footed beast, a human, or a bird, so too do these dreadful demons suddenly destroy whatever they encounter, agitating bodies, perverting souls, and ruining natural habits. Often they destroy not only men but also some irrational beasts by fire, water, or by casting them over precipices. 

At this point, I asked why these demons would invade irrational beasts. For the **Sacred Scriptures** <note>a reference to the Gospel accounts of the "Gerasene" or "Gadarene" demoniac</note> testify that something of this sort happened to the swine at **Gergesa** <note>original: "gergeſam"; an ancient city on the shore of the Sea of Galilee</note>. To this he replied: since demons are enemies of mankind, it should not seem strange to me that they insult us by harming even irrational beasts—not so much out of a desire to hurt the animals, but out of a greed for **vital heat** <note>original: "caloris uitalis"</note>. 

For because they dwell in the deepest places, which are extremely cold and lacking in moisture, they contract a great deal of dry frigidity. Being thus constricted and forced into narrowness, they crave moist and vital heat. To obtain this, they rush into animals, including those lacking reason, and they flock to baths and pits. They flee the heat of fire and the sun because it is burning and drying, but they love the heat of animals because it is moderate and mixed with a pleasant moisture—especially the human heat, because it is more temperate. For this reason, insinuating themselves into humans, they disturb them greatly by clogging the **channels** <note>original: "meatibus"</note> and filling the spaces where the animal spirit resides. When the animal spirit is struck and condensed by the thickness of the demonic bodies, the human bodies are caused to vibrate and shake, the principal faculties of the mind function poorly, and movements become stupid and erratic. And if the demon that rushes in is **subterranean**, it shakes and destroys the one it has occupied, and the demon even cries out through the person, making use of the victim's own spirit.

<summary>Marcus explains how demons project images into the human mind to incite lust and madness, and describes their physical craving for "vital heat," which drives them to possess both humans and animals, such as the biblical swine of Gergesa.</summary>

ON DEMONS

N iii
<meta>Handwritten number 4 below the signature.</meta>

...spirit as if it were their own instrument. If, however, one of the **light-shunning demons** <note>original: "lucifugorum"; refers to the subterranean or "lucifugous" class of demons who avoid light</note> attaches himself to a person, he brings on a profound sluggishness, suppresses the voice, and renders the possessed person <note>original: "obsessum"</note> as if they were dead. For this genus, being the lowest among the demons, is more "earthy" and exceedingly cold and dry; into whomever it secretly creeps, it blunts and dulls, obscures and destroys all vital force. Since it is entirely devoid of reason and utterly deprived of all intellectual contemplation, led instead by a certain **irrational phantasy** <note>original: "inratiõali quadam phantaſia"; a base form of imagination not governed by logic</note> like the most untamable of beasts, it listens to no arguments and fears no rebukes. Because of this, it is rightly called "mute and deaf" by many; nor does it depart from those it has occupied unless driven out by divine power—specifically through the **prayer and fasting** <note>a reference to the Gospel of Matthew 17:21</note> of the one performing the exorcism.

But I said, "O Marcus, we followers of the physicians are led to believe somewhat more cautious views, asserting that sufferings of this kind are not the effects of demons, but of humors, vapors, and 'winds' <note>referring to *pneuma* or gases in the body</note> that are in a bad state. Therefore, they usually attempt to cure these things with drugs and diet, not with the chants and purifications of sorcerers."

Then he replied, "It is no wonder that the physicians say these things, for they know nothing beyond the senses and have focused only on understanding the physical body. It was perhaps fitting for them to attribute a sleep-inducing heaviness of the head, the constrictions of **black bile** <note>original: "atrae bilis"; the humor associated with melancholy</note>, and the delusions of frenzy to 'bad humors.' These they are accustomed to soothe with baths, potions, evacuations, or plasters. However, 'inspirations' and possessions—by which the one possessed can do nothing through his own intellect, reason, imagination, or sense—are another matter. Rather, it is something else that moves and leads him, and he speaks of things he did not know while occupied and sometimes even **predicts the future** <note>original: "futura nonnunquam prædicit"</note>. In what way, I ask, can we say these things are merely the erratic motions of matter?"

# How demons occupy a man, speak, move, and transform themselves.

I therefore place my faith in Marcus, especially when I recall with you what the divine Gospels hand down to us concerning demons, or what happened to the Corinthian man at the command of Paul, and finally, the many and deeply marvelous things read in the writings of our Fathers concerning demons. It remains, then, to report those things of which I was an observer and at which I was present, so to speak, as an authority. I traveled to **Elasonia** <note>a region in Thessaly, Greece</note> where a certain man, driven by a demon, poured out many oracles to many people. When I met him, I asked from where the faculty of **prophesying** <note>original: "vaticinandi"</note> had come to him. When he was unwilling to reveal it, having at last suffered **Spartan necessity** <note>original: "laconicam paſſus neceſſitatem"; a classical idiom for being forced or compelled, often implying torture or extreme pressure</note>, he finally confessed the truth. He reported that he had been initiated into the works of demons by a certain Aletus...

I have perceived these things, which is why I began to doubt afterwards in this way: by what means a demon disturbing a woman could appear as a woman; and it was doubted, not without reason, whether some of the demons are indeed male and others female, in the manner of mortal animals. Furthermore, how a demon could use an articulated tongue; for it is greatly to be doubted whether some demons speak Greek, others **Chaldean** <note>Referring to the Neo-Babylonian language, often associated in the Renaissance with magic and astrology.</note>, others Persian, and others Syrian. Then, how that demon compressed himself at the threats of that magus and feared the drawn sword; for what can an indivisible and immortal demon suffer from a sword? 

Then Marcus, noticing my doubt, said: "No demon is male or female by its own nature. For passions of this kind belong to **composite beings** <note>Organisms made of different elements and materials, unlike the "simple" or uniform substance of a spirit.</note>, but the bodies of demons are simple, easy to lead and bend, and naturally fit for every configuration. For just as we look up at the clouds and see them offer now the figures of men, now of bears, now of dragons or others, so it is with the bodies of demons. 

But there is this difference: the clouds, driven by external winds, take on various figures. Demons, however, by their own counsel, vary the bodies and forms within themselves as they wish. At one moment they are contracted into a smaller mass, and at another they extend themselves out longer. This is seen to happen to **earthworms** <note>original: "lumbricis"</note> because of their finer substance and ease of movement. And it is not only in size that a diversity occurs to them; they even vary their forms and colors in many ways, for the body of a demon is prepared by nature for both. 

By the same principle that its nature is easily yielding, it is thus transformed into various species of figures. And because it is **aerial** <note>original: "aereum"; the author follows the Neoplatonic idea that demons are composed of the element of air.</note>, it takes on different colors like the air. But the air is indeed colored from the outside. The body of a demon, however, receives the appearance of colors from the internal action of the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiae"; here meaning the power of the spirit to project a mental image onto its own substance.</note>. 

Just as our cheeks grow pale when we are terrified, but redden when we are affected by shame—the soul being affected this way or that—it similarly translates such passions into the body. By the same reasoning, we must think of demons. For these too transmit the appearances of colors into their bodies from within. On account of this, each of the demons transforms its own body into whatever figure it has chosen, and by bringing a certain appearance of color even to the extreme surface of the body, it thus appears as a man, and soon meets one as a woman; it roars in the manner of a lion, leaps like a leopard, or barks like a dog. And sometimes it transforms itself into the form of either vessel <note>Likely referring to the male or female form.</note>. 

And while it changes all such forms in turn, it retains none of them as stable. For the body of demons is not solid, such that it could retain the figures it has received. But just as is accustomed to happen in air and water—namely, whether you pour in color or imprint a figure, it is soon diffused and dissolved—something similar happens to demons. For in them, figure, color, and the appearance of things vanish likewise."

Therefore, it does not change into various forms, since it does not possess the mental images of many things, nor does it possess bodies that are agile in movement or suited for bending. The aquatic and terrestrial demons, holding a middle ground between these others, can indeed change into several forms, but they remain longer in those in which they most delight. For those who live in humid places and lead a softer way of life make themselves look like birds or women. For this reason, people call these 'Naiads,' 'Nereids,' and 'Dryads' of the female sex. Those, however, who dwell in drier places and have somewhat parched bodies—such as those said to be **mountain-dwellers** <note>Greek: ὀρεσκίους (oreskious)</note>—transform themselves into men. Some even show themselves resembling dogs, lions, or other animals in which a masculine character is evident. It is therefore no wonder if a demon visiting women in labor prefers a female form, especially since it is a **deceiver** <note>original: adulterum; in this context, something counterfeit or false.</note> and delights in impure moistures; it assumes a form appropriate to the life it enjoys.

### By what reasoning they might speak Armenian.

Marcus did not explain this, nor was it asked by us. However, I believe it will be clear from this that a specific, unique language of demons cannot be found—even if someone were to claim they preserve the Hebrew language, or Greek, or Syrian, or some other foreign <note>original: "barbaram"; used here in the classical sense to mean any non-Greek/Latin tongue.</note> tongue. For what need is there for a voice among demons who live together without the use of speech? However, just as lower angels preside over various nations, so too do certain demons assist and stay with different peoples. Naturally, they employ the individual languages of those specific nations. For this reason, the demons who live among the Greeks delivered their oracles in **heroic style** <note>original: "heroico stilo"; referring to dactylic hexameter, the formal meter of epic poetry and the Delphic oracle.</note>; among the Chaldeans, they used the Chaldean language, just as among the Egyptians they held their conversations in the Egyptian tongue. Furthermore, demons inhabiting Armenia, if they happen to move elsewhere, use the speech of the natives.

### Why demons fear threats and suffer.

But it is asked why demons fear threats and swords. Certainly, all kinds of demons are full of both audacity and, conversely, timidity—especially those more closely joined to **matter** <note>The author follows the Neoplatonic view that "heavier" or more "material" spirits are more susceptible to physical sensations and fear.</note>. For the aerial ones, being participants in circumspect thought, know how to distinguish whether someone is rebuking or honoring them if they are scolded; nor do they depart from the possessed unless the exorcist is powerful in holiness toward God, and chants the name of God and a **dreadful word** <note>original: "sermonemq; horribilem"; likely referring to a potent formula of adjuration.</note> by divine power. These are indeed the demons closest to matter, fearing lest they be cast down into deeper places and the abyss. Likewise, they fear the angels who hurl them there, specifically whenever someone threatens them with that precipice and brings forth the invocations of the angels appointed for this purpose. Indeed, they fear them greatly.

Yet, because of their ignorance, they do not always distinguish who is threatening them. Thus, if some old woman or a rather proud old man intends such threats in a rustic manner, the demons often depart because they are unable to tell the difference. Therefore, they are also easily subjected to certain superficial things—namely, to nails and hair—by a polluted class of **magicians** <note>original: "magorum"; here used disparagingly for practitioners of "low" or "black" magic.</note>. Likewise, they are bound by lead, wax, and thin thread, and are thrown into confusion by wicked helpers. Thus, **sorcerers** <note>original: "uenefici"; literally "poison-makers," often used for those who deal in harmful charms.</note> and the impious tame these subterranean demons.

However, those who abstain from such wicked ministries mostly worship the aerial demons, taking care lest a subterranean demon intervene. For if any such thing should intervene, besides the fact that it strikes terror, it is also accustomed to throw stones—for it is characteristic of the subterranean kind to throw stones at those they encounter, though with useless strikes. Reason dictates that the aerial demons are bold; yet they bring nothing good, since they are both proud and boastful, and full of the **fantasies of deception** <note>original: "deceptōis phātasias"; the power to create false sensory illusions.</note> and vanities. They pass down many principles, and indeed, these principles were proposed by Manes himself, so that for the God who is the **Maker of Good** <note>original: "bonorum opifici"</note>, a god who is the **Craftsman of Evil** <note>original: "malorum artifex"</note> is established; for the God who is the Lord of celestial things, there is a god who is the lord of the sub-celestial. From this, the wretched Euchetae added a third principle to these. For among them, there is indeed one Father, but two sons—one older and one younger. Thus, there are three principles: but the "super-worldly" things are attributed to the Father, the celestial to the younger son, and the sub-celestial to the elder son as their lords. 

Indeed, this dogma seems to differ in no way from the Greek fables, following that poetic line: *the rewards were distributed in a triple number* <note>A reference to Homer’s Iliad (Book 15), where the world is divided between the brothers Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades.</note>. But among the Euchetae, some worship both sons; for even if they say they are now in disagreement with each other, they nevertheless think both should be adored. Since both are born from the same father, they believe they will be mutually reconciled in the future. Others, however, worship only one—the younger—as he rules over a better and more excellent province. They do not exactly despise the elder, but they observe him with caution, namely so that he does not do them harm. 

The worst among them are entirely separated from the heavenly deity. They welcome only the **Earthly Satan** <note>original: "terrestrem sathanã"</note> within their borders, and they extol him with the highest names, calling him the "first-born" and the one "separated from the father." Likewise, they call him the maker of trees, animals, and all other composite things, yet he is also pestiferous and hostile. But those who introduce these dogmas are blind in both the eyes and ears of their minds. For they do not see from the mutual kinship of things themselves that there is one Author of all, nor do they hear the Holy Scripture teaching this, nor do they consider it with their own reason. For clearly, if there were two makers of things disagreeing with each other, there would not be a single conspiracy and union binding all things together. And if demons promise us riches and glory, they can nevertheless hand nothing over from themselves; for they have no real power, but only bring certain empty visions to their worshippers, entirely varied and unstable, which the impious nonetheless think are divine spectacles.

## How magicians summon and draw out demons.

<margin>Note well</margin>
Sorcery <term>Veneficium: In this context, it refers to "maleficium" or low magic involving potions and material substances.</term> and magic have not received their names in vain, but possess a certain power. For sorcery is an art concerning material and earthly demons. It provokes the apparitions of demons into sight; some it rouses as if from the underworld, while others it draws down from on high. For our discipline <note>Meaning the Christian faith.</note> considers every demon to be evil, having fallen from the angelic state and order due to an excess of pride and vanity. 

However, the Greek <note>Referring to the classical pagan philosophers.</note> opinion judges only a small part of demons to be evil; and they judge this part to be such not by choice, but because they were designated so from the first division of the universe, acting as a tormentor <note>original: "tortoris uicem"</note> against delinquent souls. Therefore, through sorcery, a conjurer <term>praestigiator: a practitioner who uses illusions or "prestidigitation" to deceive the senses.</term> provokes such a portion of demons into an imaginary appearance and presents these images to the spectators. To some, they bring forth certain flowing waters overflowing from the beyond. To others, they promise the breaking of chains, pleasures, and favors. Indeed, they bring such powers of demons to us through certain songs; and in most cases, the demon lies, though in some few things he speaks the truth. 

Magic, however, was seen by the Greeks as a faculty possessing the greatest power. For they hand down that this is the highest part of the priestly art. It brings forth certain sights more often into view, though they falsely present a mask of divinity. For this faculty examines the nature, power, and quality of every thing born under the moon, the power of the elements and their parts—including all animals, plants, seeds, and fruits—as well as stones and herbs. In short, it studies the substance and virtue of every single thing. 

From these materials, magic performs its effects. It creates statues that bring health, equipped with all kinds of symbolic shapes; it also knows other devices that inflict diseases. It understands which things differ from one another and which things agree. The joining of many of these materials brings a "union" to that art, while the distance between them causes separation. Now indeed, among those practitioners, eagles and dragons are said to contribute to health, while cats, dogs, and crows are used to observe watchfulness. Likewise, wax and clay are usually taken by them to be molded into certain parts, as they possess certain properties in their own right. Frequently, they seek to draw down celestial fire to this earth; when they succeed, statues seem to smile and lamps are lit spontaneously. Magic is also heavily equipped with the knowledge of astronomers...
