...possessing much of that faculty, he acts through it. There is also a certain divination using a basin <note>original: "pelui". This refers to lecanomancy, a form of divination using a bowl of water.</note> by which even peasants often prophesy. Just as a certain prediction is made by the *phace* and *pholia* <note>original: "phace atque pholia". These likely refer to specific ancient divination rituals using beans or pulses.</note>, so a certain prediction occurs in the basin, a practice frequent and renowned among the Assyrians. This indeed has a certain affinity with demons that are closely joined to matter. 

Therefore, those who prophesy take a basin full of water, which is suitable for those demons that crawl in the deep. This basin full of water appears, in a way, to breathe on account of the sound it makes; and the water itself poured into the basin does not differ at all in its substance from external waters, but it excels greatly through the power infused into it by incantations. Thus, it is made more fit for receiving the demonic spirit. Indeed, that spirit of the demons is specific and earthly, and it is attracted by material compositions. 

As soon as it glides into the water, it presently gives forth a certain small sound, void of meaning, signaling its arrival <note>original: "remissionem," here suggesting the descent or "letting down" of the spirit into the vessel.</note> to those present. Then, in the now-swelling water, certain thin sounds whisper a kind of prediction of the future. Moreover, a spirit of this kind is found everywhere throughout the earth, since it has been allotted a "solar" rank <note>In Neoplatonic thought, even lower demons were categorized according to celestial hierarchies; "solar" here suggests a specific rank in that order.</note>. This kind of demon emits a thin voice on purpose, so that on account of the indistinct obscurity of the voice, its lies may be less easily detected. 

But can the bodies of demons be struck? Indeed they can, and they feel pain when struck by a solid body. But in what way, since they are spirits, and neither solid nor of a composite nature—and we know that sensation belongs to composite things <note>Philosophically, "composite" things are made of matter and form; pure spirits were often thought to be "simple" and thus unable to feel physical pain.</note>? Truly, in those things that feel, it is not the nerve itself that feels, but the spirit <term>Spiritus: refers to the 'pneuma,' a subtle, vaporous substance that ancient medicine believed carried sensation from the organs to the soul.</term> that is within them. Wherefore, if a nerve is worn down, if it grows cold, or if it suffers anything else, pain occurs—that is to say, by the impact of one spirit upon another. To be sure, a composite body would never feel pain by itself, but only when it partakes in spirit; when deprived of spirit, it is also deprived of sensation. 

Thus, the demonic body is naturally sentient through its whole self; in each of its parts, without any intermediary, it sees, hears, touches, and suffers by being touched. It feels pain when divided, just like solid bodies do. But there is this difference: that solid bodies, when they are divided, are either restored with difficulty or never at all. But the body of demons, when it is cut, is presently recreated within itself and grows back together, just like parts of water or air when something solid falls between them. Indeed, faster than it can be told, the demonic spirit returns into itself. 

Nevertheless, it feels pain in the meantime while it is being divided; for which reason it fears the edge of iron. Noticing this, those who strive to put demons to flight set up spears and swords upright in the places where they do not want the demons to approach. They also devise other means, sometimes repelling them with opposing passions, and sometimes soothing them with a certain agreeable affection.

<meta>This page serves as the dedicatory preface by Marsilio Ficino to his friend Philippo Valori. It transitions from the previous discussion of Michael Psellus’s work on demons to Ficino’s broader project of reconciling Platonic and Aristotelian thought regarding the soul. Ficino mentions his collaboration with other famous Renaissance humanists like Pico della Mirandola and Angelo Poliziano.</meta>

<header>ON DEMONS</header>

# ON DEMONS

### MARSILIO FICINO the Florentine sends his warmest greetings to the noble and high-minded PHILIPPO VALORI. <note>original: "P. S. D." stands for "Plurimam Salutem Dicit," a formal Latin greeting.</note>

He who commands "know thyself" seems to advise us to know the soul; for since the soul is the medicine of things <note>original: "medicina rerū." Ficino frequently viewed philosophy and the study of the soul as a form of spiritual healing.</note>, it is certainly everything. Therefore, once the soul is known, we shall easily come to know all things. Thus, in order to first pursue the soul—through which I might attain all other things—I have long and studiously applied myself to the great philosophers, not those of the common sort, but the most excellent. However, while I anxiously questioned the Platonists on one side and the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> on the other, their answers seemed to disagree with one another; at first, I despaired that I would ever fulfill my wish. But not long after, Themistius gave me the best hope by affirming that such great philosophers do not actually disagree in their opinions, but only in their words—and that the opinion of Plato, Aristotle, and Theophrastus regarding the soul is the same, despite being expressed in different terms. Finally, by a certain divine chance, I happened upon a book by Theophrastus "On the Soul," <note>This refers to the "Paraphrase of Theophrastus’s On the Soul" by the Neoplatonist Priscianus Lydus.</note> explained briefly but diligently by a certain Priscianus Lydus, following the same reasoning by which Plutarch and Iamblichus, distinguished Platonists and Peripatetics, had explained the Aristotelian view on the soul. When I realized in reading these works that the Platonists and Peripatetics were in accord, I held almost everything my mind sought. And so that others might also have this book as soon as possible, I have translated it from the Greek language into Latin. Furthermore, I have added certain brief expositions devised by myself during the course of reading and translating. Yet I did not think I should labor too much or wander too far in this matter at present; for Giovanni Pico della Mirandola—a truly "admirable" man <note>original: "mirandus." Ficino is making a pun on Pico's surname, Mirandula.</note>—is already working on this to the highest degree, where he most diligently discusses the minds of all philosophers on every subject, and demonstrates that Plato and Aristotle are wonderfully in agreement regarding the soul. I decided that this book should be dedicated to you above all, my dear Valori. For you, like me, have long and vehemently desired this harmony of philosophers on this subject. Our Medici patrons, to whom we are accustomed to give—or rather, to return—everything, will undoubtedly agree that this one little gift among many be dedicated to my Valori, who is the dearest friend of the Medici house and always the most ready helper in the production of Platonic works. Although I found only a single Greek manuscript, and a faulty and mutilated one at that, read it with confidence and offer it to others to read; for I have strived most diligently to correct and repair it. And our friend Angelo Poliziano, a man of the sharpest judgment and great learning, has approved this diligence of ours.

->Farewell, and may you read with happiness and offer it to others to read. Farewell.<-

<header>PSELLUS</header>

## The interpretation of Priscianus Lydus on the work of Theophrastus "On Sensation," translated and explained by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine. How the instrument of sense becomes similar to the things perceived.

### Chapter One. MARSILIO’S [COMMENTS].

<margin>a</margin> To this end, so that sensation may occur, its instrument <note>The sense organ or the "spiritus" (a subtle vapor in the body).</note> must become like the things being perceived. This is not in a material or natural bodily form, but in a certain immaterial "species" <note>original: "specie," meaning a mental form or image</note> and principle that is purely representative. The form of a sensible object, being extended [in space], is not sufficient for sensation; for the act of perceiving happens suddenly, all at once and as a whole, which can then be comprehended.

### PRISCIANUS’S [TEXT].

It is Theophrastus's next purpose to discuss sensation. Since Aristotle thinks that the instruments of the senses, when moved by sensible things, are made similar to them through a certain "passion" <note>original: "passione," meaning a state of being acted upon by an external force</note>, Theophrastus rightly investigates what kind of similarity this is by nature. For it seems absurd that in the instruments of the senses—and much more so in the soul itself—any actual likeness to colors, liquids, flavors, sounds, forms, or shapes should be created. Therefore, he also says that this kind of similarity is prepared according to species and principles without matter. We must discuss, then, whether the species falls upon us from the outside, what kind it is, and where exactly it appears; and whether a species extended and divisible around a body is enough for knowledge, if indeed such a species falls in a scattered way. For all knowledge consists of a certain gathering into one, and an indivisible grasping of the whole thing to be known.

### Chapter 2. That which perceives already possesses an immaterial image <note>original: "spem," a common abbreviation for "speciem"</note> of the thing it perceives, which represents it. But before it possesses it, the instrument of sense must be moved and acted upon by the sensible object.

### MARSILIO’S [COMMENTS].

<margin>q</margin>
<margin>while the living being's substance</margin> Insofar as the substance of the soul accommodates itself by a certain inclination to the "spirit" <note>the "spiritus," a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</note>, which is the instrument of sense, the power of perceiving that lay hidden in the soul is unfolded into action. This power, thus unfolded, joins together as one part with such a body to complete the living being. Therefore, the substance of the soul is more separate [from matter], while this power of sensing is more joined to the body and does not act without it. Fantasy—that is, the imagination—affects the spirit in various ways with its sharper movements, and through the spirit, the rest of the body; for fantasy directs its gaze inward toward its own images. "Sensus" <note>External sensation</note>, however, is directed toward external things, and it does not perceive the physical impact on the instrument or the image that contributes to the sensing; rather, through these two things, it perceives the objects that are outside. Therefore, in its acts, it does not alter the spirit, for its action is not limited to internal things, but to external ones.

### PRISCIANUS’S [TEXT].

It is necessary, therefore, that what knows acts according to the image of the thing to be known and carries its character. This is called "assimilation." However, the "passion" <note>the physical sensation</note> happens in the instrument of sensing...

<summary>Ficino and Priscianus Lydus discuss how humans perceive the world, arguing that sensation requires the soul to form an immaterial "image" of an object rather than physically becoming like the object itself. They distinguish between the soul's inner imagination and the external senses' focus on the outside world.</summary>

sensation occurs, and it is necessary for this process to precede the actual act of sensing. For the power of sensing is not entirely separated from bodies; rather, in the very inclination of the soul—or its command over the instruments of the senses—it finds its essence and is required for the completion of the living being. Nor can it act without these instruments. Yet, this power does not move the instruments at the same time in the way that imagination, which is primarily excited, does. This is because sensation is widely extended and reaches out entirely toward the external objects of the senses, which require their constant presence. Therefore, things that can be imagined are not external, although they are (if I may say so) likenesses <note>original: "assimilamenta"</note> of an external thing. However, things perceived by the senses are truly external. Sensation occurs regarding these external things, not regarding the affections <note>original: "passiones"; in this context, it means the state of being physically acted upon by an object.</note> experienced by the instrument, even if the sense itself perceives the species <term>Species: In this philosophy, a 'species' is an immaterial form or mental image of an object that allows the soul to 'see' it without the object being physically inside the mind.</term>, which are in the bodies, through such affections.

### Chapter III.

The thing to be sensed moves the instrument of sense in a certain way—that is, the living spirit <note>The "spiritus" was thought to be a subtle, vapor-like substance in the body that carried sensory information to the brain.</note>. This motion is called a "passion" <note>original: "passio," meaning the spirit is being "acted upon" by the object.</note> because the spirit is moved by the body, and also an "action" because the spirit is alive; the efficacy of the life applied to the passion provides a continuous action from itself. <margin>Marsilio's [Commentary]</margin>

<margin>e)</margin> This kind of motion is similar to the objects, both because it is caused by them and because the continuous action of this motion is already excited toward the objects when it is applied by the life of the spirit. Such motion, because it is more a "passion" than an action, and is divisible by time and place, does not have the nature of a species, but rather of "motion." Therefore, it is not the sense itself, which acts indivisibly and suddenly, and by acting through a species, comprehends the object as a whole. It is clear that such motion is not sensation, since otherwise we would sense every time we are moved, and a more violent motion would not harm the sense. After the motion and the passion, it is necessary to arrive at some species through which sensation occurs; the sense reaches the species and therefore perceives through a species. This species is not in the instrument [the physical organ]. Otherwise, it would be a kind of motion and passion rather than a species, and it would be equally extended within the instrument. But one must move from that which is extended <note>Occupying physical space.</note> to the species, which, reduced to a minimum quantity, always relates to the innate reason of the soul, which has no quantity at all. Furthermore, the species itself is not in the "vestige of life" <note>The basic biological trace of life in the body.</note> that the soul impresses upon the instrument; for every action of this vestige is mixed with passion, and the same motion agitates both this vestige and the instrument together. But the species is free from passion and motion, for it is the end-point of motion. It does not, therefore, come from the vestige of life (which is truly an accidental property), but from the life which is like a certain substance—not in a life separated from the body, but in the animal life proceeding from the higher soul. This higher soul is separated or separable, and is a true and complete substance subsisting in itself. However, the life diffused from this soul through the body, although it is like a certain substance, is nevertheless a part of the animal being and is a kind of vital application of the soul to the body, divided along with the body and acting like a certain propagation <note>An extension or spreading out.</note> of the soul.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains that sensation is not merely a physical movement (passion) but an internal recognition of a "species" or mental form. He distinguishes between the physical impact on the body and the soul's higher ability to process that impact into an indivisible perception.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how the soul perceives external objects. It moves from the physical interaction of the sense organs (instruments) to the internal, mental act of judgment that defines true sensation.</meta>

# PSELLUS ON PRISCIANUS

<margin>P</margin> The instruments of the senses themselves are affected by sensible objects; this is not as if they were inanimate things, but is an affection <note>original: "passio"; in this context, the state of being physically acted upon or receiving an impression.</note> of a living body. For this reason, it is not entirely a passive experience, nor do all things happen solely from the outside. Rather, it also follows its own action; it is not first moved and then acts later. Indeed, it is not moved at all without acting at the same time, nor does it act unless it is also moved. Such motion in the instruments becomes similar to the forms <note>original: "speciebus"</note> that are perceived, since it was brought into the instrument both by those objects and according to a certain vital awakening of an appearance or impression toward them.

But this is not yet "sensation"—namely, this likeness brought into the sense organ to be sensed. This is because this impression is a passive affection rather than an active one; it is something corporeal, divisible, and extended in time, striving toward a form but not yet established in that form, but rather still in motion. Sensation, however, encompasses the beginning, middle, and end of the indivisible thing being sensed. It is a completed action and judgment, and it exists entirely and simultaneously in the present moment. It is seen to have already established itself according to the form of the sensible object. 

For this reason, sensation is not accomplished without some affection of the physical instrument; yet, this physical affection is not the sensation itself. This explains why we sometimes "suffer" an impression <note>experience a physical stimulus</note> while awake or asleep, yet we do not actually perceive it. It is necessary, therefore, that after the physical impression, the process is finally perfected into a form <term>Form: Translated from "species," meaning the immaterial mental image or "look" of a thing that the mind can recognize.</term> and defined. I mean a form similar to the thing to be sensed, for sensation is produced according to a perfected form, since it involves judgment. However, this form of the thing to be sensed is not placed "in" the instrument. For in the instrument, physical affection and motion usually occur. While the process is at this stage, it deals with division and the form does not yet exist; nor is it bound up in that trace of life which is granted to the instrument by the soul. For the vital action of this trace is also carried out through the physical impression. A motion occurs there for both the instrument and the shared life bestowed upon it. But the form itself, according to which sensation occurs, is placed in "life"—specifically, in life as it exists in action. Yet it is not separated, but exists in the animal life that completes the living being, and in its vital application, which is already divided around the bodies.

### Marsilio's Chapter 4.
### The form produced in the life of the animal is attached to the body; since it is co-extended with this life, it is not sufficient for the act of sensation, which is indivisible. In an indivisible moment, it grasps a sensible whole in a single stroke.

<margin>f</margin> The act of sensing therefore occurs through an indivisible form; and because it is an internal, permanent act, it occurs through an inward form, which is called the "exemplary reason" <term>Exemplary Reason: A "ratio exemplaris" is an internal blueprint or mental pattern that the soul uses to recognize and represent physical things.</term> for representing sensible things. -># ON THE SOUL<-

...is essential to the soul and lives by itself along with the soul, and does not belong solely to the composite <note>original: "compositi"; the union of the soul and the physical body</note>, although it communicates in some way with the body. It can, however, be separated from the body, and indeed is separate; otherwise, it could not act indivisibly <note>original: "individue"; acting as a unified whole rather than through physical parts</note>. For any species <note>original: "specie"; the specific form or appearance of a thing</note> of sensible things, there is one sensual reason <note>original: "ratio sensualis"; an internal formal principle or "formula" for a sensation</note> in the soul that represents all individuals. It represents to us now this thing, now that thing, insofar as it is excited by this or that form produced in the life proper to the body and the animal. This is what it means to sense: to bring forth into act the very reason of the sensible thing upon the presence of the form made in the life [of the body], whenever a sensible thing moves one of the instruments of sense. Note that such a reason and the act of sense and imagination are impartible <note>not composed of parts; indivisible</note>, and therefore the substance of the soul in which it exists is indivisible, and thus separated or separable from the body.

### PRISCIANUS

<margin>u</margin> **Y**et even this form <note>original: "species"</note> is not sufficient for sensation. For a form concerning the instrument [the sense organ], even if perfected according to the act, is divided around the body and is not converted into a single impartible thing; therefore, it is not cognitive. But truly, there is in the soul a certain reason <note>original: "ratio"</note> of sensible things prior to the act of sensing and grasped before the form; this reason lives according to itself and does not belong only to the composite. For this reason, it also acts indivisibly, and it is a certain power over particulars; nor is it occasionally in the soul as if it were some single, divided particular form. For it is a cognitive reason of sensible things consisting in the soul itself, not lying in the body. It is indeed one, but not like singular things; rather, it possesses one [reason] that encompasses many within itself and is accommodated to each of them. For by one reason of "white," the soul senses individual white things. Therefore, a reason of this kind must be set forth and brought out if sensation is to occur. It is brought forth, however, when excited toward the vital form as if toward its own and familiar one, and it is accommodated to this form as if to a likeness of an exterior form, acting together with it. For that which judges is the reason; it is a thought according to the sensual soul, and that very collection into one impartible thing in the substance is separate from bodies.

### Chapter five. New forms are not imprinted into the soul by sensible things; and when the soul is said to receive a form from things, it is understood that the soul brings forth into act the forms latent within itself upon the presence of those things.

### MARSILIUS

<margin>q</margin> **S**ince the act of cognition is intimate and vital, it appears to be brought forth by an internal form, just as shining comes from light and heating from heat. This internal form—that is, the exemplary reason <note>original: "ratio exemplaris"; a blueprint or formal pattern</note> of sensible things—belongs to the essence of the soul itself. From this essence, which possesses the true essential reasons of things, there depends a certain animal life: not the true essence, nor the true soul, but like an accident, or like a substance and a certain vivification hanging from the first [the soul] just as light hangs from a light...

...[surfa]ce, under which, while it hangs, there remains a trace of life, like a kind of heat. Life of this kind is the animal part produced by the soul, insofar as the soul reaches toward the body; it is produced by the soul through its own principles <note>original: "rationes"; these are internal "formulas" or formative powers within the soul</note>, both vegetative <note>relating to basic biological growth and nutrition</note> and sensory. And therefore, this life also seems, in a way, to possess these principles and senses, and the duty of nourishing the body. However, we should not say that there are two distinct powers of sensing involved in a single act of feeling. Rather, the power itself, which is folded within the soul, is unfolded through this life. Similarly, the principle lying hidden in the soul is sometimes unfolded through a specific form perfected in the life of the body. This "life" is what is called the "limit and act and perfection of an organic body having the potential for life" <note>This is a variation of Aristotle’s famous definition of the soul, here applied specifically to the vital spark that animates the physical organs</note>. Finally, in the instrument of sense [the physical organ], the likeness to the sensible object is imperfect; but it becomes perfect within the life [of the soul]. Sensation occurs through the production of an internal principle.

## PRISCIANUS

<margin>a</margin> The soul is therefore said to possess the form <note>original: "speciem"</note> of the thing to be sensed because it brings forth the internal principle of that thing. It does not do this by receiving some shape or figure from the object as if from a seal <note>A rejection of the Aristotelian idea that the soul is like wax receiving a seal's imprint; the soul is active, not passive</note>. For judgment and action exist internally and are vital. Therefore, the principle remains within and is essential to the soul, whereas the "life" which completes the animal depends on these essential principles while hanging from them. Indeed, that life exists according to a certain extension toward the body. This life is also sensory, and it is the limit and perfection of the animal. Because of this, the likeness of the thing being sensed is perfected in this life; however, in the physical instrument, the likeness is imperfect and mixed with "passion" <note>original: "passione"; here meaning a passive state of being acted upon by an external force</note> and action. Passion falls upon it from external things, but action proceeds from the life of the soul. Likewise, the form exists in the animal life, but judgment and thought consist in the very act of the internal principle.

External things affect the instrument of sense in a certain material way. But the life present there transfers this affection into an immaterial form, through which the soul is excited to bring forth the principle appropriate to that form.

## MARSILIO. Chapter 6.

<margin>p</margin> Through such a "bringing forth," the soul makes itself similar to the thing being sensed. Furthermore, it can make itself similar to opposites at the same time by bringing forth different internal principles. It could not, however, become similar to opposites if it became so by being passively acted upon <note>Because a physical object cannot be both hot and cold at the same spot simultaneously</note>. Again, if one part of the soul touched heat and another part touched cold, it could not compare these two to see how they agree or differ; for the judge must be the same person and must grasp both opposites to compare them. Therefore, the soul—in its own indivisible state—touches many contrary things at once. It is, therefore, indivisible. For this very indivisibility suffices for knowledge, and therefore also for life.

## PRISCIANUS

<margin>q</margin> In what way, then, does the soul become similar to the things it senses? Not by receiving anything from them, but because it acts according to their internal principle.

It specifically addresses a classic philosophical problem: how can a single, indivisible soul perceive multiple or even opposing sensations (like hot and cold) at the same time? The text argues that while the physical organ can be divided into parts to receive different signals, the soul remains a unified acting force that judges these signals from within.</meta>

<header>ON THE SOUL</header>
<sig>O ii</sig>
<page-num>4</page-num>

...it may act, namely through the impression or appearance of certain external species <note>original: "specierum"; in this context, these are the "forms" or mental images of objects that enter the senses</note>. In what way, then, the soul sometimes becomes like many things at once and even contrary things; for surely it cannot suffer <note>original: "pati"; to be "passive" or "acted upon" by something external</note> contraries at the same time. It is capable of acting, however. For sensation consists of action and judgment, not of any passion <note>the state of being passive or receiving a stimulus</note>. For sensation is produced according to a principle <note>original: "rationem"; an internal logic or formative power</note>, whereas the passion is located in the instrument <note>the physical sense organ, such as the eye or ear</note>. Since the instrument is a body and is divisible into parts, nothing prevents it from having many and even contrary things simultaneously through its different parts. But the reason <note>ratio</note>, as something indivisible, acts similarly while grasping differences and contraries simultaneously, however many they may be. For this reason, it rightly judges their diversity, since many things happen within a single indivisible unit.

### Chapter Seven. The sensory form which is produced in the primary life of the animal is produced by a principle innate to the soul as if from a primary cause; it is also produced by the life in which it exists as if by an instrument. A certain passion brought upon the instrument of sense by the sensible object provides the occasion for this effect.

->MARSILIUS<- <note>Refers to Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century philosopher and translator</note>

<margin>i</margin> The power of sensing itself is not in a state of "formable potentiality" toward external things, but toward bringing forth its own acts regarding external things. The soul becomes like the things to be sensed insofar as it brings forth their principles <note>rationes</note> from itself into action. The instrument of sense, however, becomes like them insofar as it is affected by them as a body and acts as a living thing in a manner congruent with them.

->PRISCIANUS<- <note>Refers to Priscian the Lydian, a 6th-century philosopher whose work Ficino is commenting upon</note>

<margin>q</margin> Therefore, when Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school</note> also says that sense becomes like the thing sensed according to forms and principles without matter, we shall admit it in such a way that the forms are not simply brought in from outside, but are established from internal principles in life according to the sensory act. Now, because sense reaches out toward external things and becomes like them, it is rightly called a certain "power," as if carrying out acts or actions. In the soul, the assimilation <note>the process of becoming like the object</note> occurs according to the act of reason; but in the instrument, it occurs both according to the passion brought in by the sensible thing and simultaneously according to the vital act or life-giving action.

### Chapter Eight. Because the instrument of sense is extended <note>meaning it has physical dimensions and takes up space</note>, it can suffer in one part from one contrary and in another part from another. But it cannot compare these with each other. The soul, however, being indivisible, if it were to suffer from contraries simultaneously, it would suffer entirely through the same part, which is impossible. Therefore, when it perceives contraries simultaneously, it does not suffer from them but rather acts upon them.

->MARSILIUS<-

It resolves the paradox of how we perceive conflicting sensations (like hot and cold) by attributing the reception to the body and the judgment to the unified soul.</summary>

In what way, then, does the instrument of sense suffer from the bitter and the
sweet at the same time? For perhaps it perceives this one with one part

that be the tongue or some spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; in medieval and Renaissance philosophy, this refers to a subtle substance or "pneuma" that carries sensory information through the body</note> within the tongue. Certainly, since such an
instrument is divisible, because it is a body, it is possible that it suffers similarly
in one part from this, and in another part from that. This is clearly seen in touch,
where one part can be heated and another cooled at the same time. The same applies to the sensory spirit
of hearing, since it is divisible. But the Principle <note>original: "Ratio"; the internal power of judgment</note>, as has already been said,
being as it were indivisible, is by no means prohibited from acting upon contraries at the same time. For it is impossible to suffer <note>to be passive/receive</note>
contraries according to the same part at the same time.

### Chapter ten: External things do not make the sense similar to themselves, and much less do they do so for rational thought; rather, the power of sensing makes itself similar through the production of its own principles. Thought does this much more so.

## BY MARSILIO <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>.

<margin>f</margin>
Just as the reason innate to the sense is stirred at the presence of sensory forms <note>original: "specierum"; the mental images or likenesses of objects</note>, so too does it then stir the power of thinking to produce the principle <note>original: "rationem"</note> of the essence of sensible things because of the kinship of qualities to that essence, <margin>when such qualities are perceived by the sense.</margin>

## BY PRISCIANUS <note>Priscianus Lydus, a 6th-century philosopher whose work Ficino translated and commented upon</note>.

<margin>e</margin>
Furthermore, if knowledge occurs according to a certain assimilation <note>the process of becoming similar to the object being known</note>, in what way does thought—which does not suffer <note>original: "patiens"; in a philosophical sense, this means to be passively acted upon by an external force</note> from the things to be sensed—become similar to them? Or if it does "suffer," what is the nature of this suffering? But surely, as we have said, the judgment of the senses is not produced according to a passive impression, much less is rational contemplation. Rather, it is produced according to action and the "birth" of principles. Indeed, the principle of sensible things is brought forth when the impression of the sensory organ is already perfected into a form <note>original: "speciem"</note> or defined as similar to the sensible object. And thus, such a principle is fitted to the sensible thing. But if the soul is stirred toward something fitting by some proportion, then surely the principle, as the judge of sensory qualities, awakens the soul's power to know the essence of those sensible things—quite familiarly, indeed, because of a certain kinship of such qualities to the essence itself from which they proceed.

## BY MARSILIO <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Neoplatonist philosopher and translator</note>:

<margin>a</margin> It belongs to the same sense to judge between opposites, such as hearing judging both sound and silence. If it were pure silence, the external sense would not perceive it; instead, the internal sense would do so through the memory of sound, noticing that it has encountered the opposite of sound. However, for the most part, silence is not pure. In those cases, the hearing exerts itself toward a very weak object, and while barely perceiving anything, it is said to "apprehend" silence, as if catching what remains missing of the sound. The sense judges a thing to be harmonious, friendly, and pleasant when it accords with something innate. But it judges a thing to be alien when it is discordant, during which time the sensory instrument is moved in a disturbed <note>original: "peruerse"; meaning in a way that deviates from its natural or healthy state</note> manner.

->BY PRISCIAN<- <note>Priscianus Lydus, a 6th-century philosopher; Ficino wrote a famous commentary on his paraphrase of Theophrastus</note>

<margin>P</margin> Therefore, since the instrument of sense is usually struck first and more strongly by proper sensibles <note>original: "propriis... sensibilibus"; qualities unique to one sense, like color for sight</note>, but by common sensibles <note>original: "communibus"; qualities like size or motion perceived by multiple senses</note> only as a consequence and more weakly, it is for this reason that any sense usually perceives its own proper objects under these same conditions. Sight, of course, perceives color first, but perceives magnitude and motion as a consequence. For this reason, common sensibles can seem to relate more to the soul, and to be known by the sense as if by accident. Yet certainly, as has been said, these common sensibles become known to the sense as a consequence, and are not grasped by thought alone. Furthermore, it is often asked how the eye perceives darkness and the ear perceives silence. The answer is that they do not so much "feel" as "consent" <note>original: "consentire"; here suggesting a reflexive awareness of the organ's own state</note>; the sense does not lean or fix itself upon such things, but rather, because action is inhibited during the very attempt to sense, the sense judges that something is lacking in them. And it apprehends what is distant and alien from the fact that the "reason" <note>original: "ratio"; the internal organizing principle or pattern</note> innate to itself does not harmonize with this object at all. Meanwhile, however, the instrument of sense is moved in a somewhat disturbed manner because of a "passion" <note>original: "passione"; a physical impression or "suffering" an effect</note> brought in by some sensible object.

### Chapter twelve. Since the soul is the mistress of the body, and therefore a far more excellent substance, the body is rightly created and arranged for its sake.

<margin>i</margin> In the order of divine providence, therefore, the soul is both prior to and distinct before the body. For the body receives as many instruments <note>i.e., organs</note> as may serve the soul, which already possesses its various powers. Since these are formal powers and are distinguished according to their species <note>original: "speciem"; the essential form or type</note>, such a distinction does not arise from matter. Therefore, one innermost sense <note>original: "sensus intimus"; often identified with the "common sense" that unites the five senses</note> derives the fruitfulness of its unity into five individual senses. To these five, instruments in the body are subsequently adapted.

<margin>h</margin> Thus far, we have treated the sense in general. Regarding the individual senses, however, such as sight, hearing, and the rest, we must first make this distinction: it is not, as some believe, that there is only one single sense which is divided into different types by the physical instruments that participate in it. For the diversity of the instruments does not come before the differences in the powers of the soul, nor does it have the authority to divide those powers. Rather, the sense itself is one within itself, and from its own nature it is distinguished into five in order to discern individual sensible things. Furthermore, the difference in the physical instruments followed after this distinction of the senses, being appropriately adapted to each. For the formal or specific division—the diversity within the user of the senses—precedes the material and instrumental division, as if relying on a greater authority <note>The author argues that the soul’s internal architecture dictates the body’s anatomy, not the other way around</note>.

### Chapter thirteen. The act of sensing is not brought about as if the sense naturally touches the sensible object, or the sensible object naturally forms the sense; rather, it occurs by a certain rational process in a spiritual manner.

->BY MARSILIO<- <note>Marsilio Ficino, 1433–1491, the Italian scholar who translated and commented on these Platonic and Aristotelian texts</note>

<margin>n</margin> Neither does sight emit from itself anything natural or corporeal by which it might touch color, as if using a proboscis <note>a trunk or snout; here meaning a physical probe extending from the eye</note>, nor does anything natural flow out from the color to be imprinted upon the sight. Nor, again, does a color, by its physical reality, color the air, and the air then color the sight. Species <note>original: "species"; the "form" or "mental image" of a thing, distinct from its physical matter</note> that are separated from matter—because they are entirely released from location and excluded from the limits of matter—are therefore able to act upon all things and to act equally across any distance. However, species determined within matter and place act according to the mode of their nature toward specific things, and only up to a certain distance; they are likewise received by undergoing a physical effect. 

There are, however, many actions of natural things belonging to the composite whole <note>the "composite" refers to the union of body and soul</note>, such as heating; but naturally, smell and taste affect nothing in this way. Yet, besides these actions, there are certain ones belonging to these "species," which are not so much attributed to the composite things as to the species themselves—specifically following the excellence and peculiar property of the species itself. These actions are, as it were, spiritual, and they extend further than the actions proper to the physical composite. They sometimes occur suddenly, yet only up to a certain distance, because these species are in matter and contained by place. Actions of this kind are not only found in the soul when it acts upon things, but also in the species of things as they extend themselves, in a way, toward the soul. Certainly, in such action and passion <note>original: "passione"; here meaning the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression</note>, the sense is formed. The soul, since it is a living and sensory form, acts upon those things offered to it in a vital and sensory manner; and because it is currently in a body, it operates only up to a certain distance.

<margin>u</margin> But what indeed is seeing, or hearing, or smelling? And are all the senses brought about through a certain medium? Just as vision occurs through the <term>transparent</term> <note>Latin: *diaphanum*; the medium, such as air or water, that allows light and color to pass through</note>—that is, the clear medium accessible to the eyes—or do certain senses rather touch the things to be sensed without any medium? For my part, I judge that vision is perfected neither by a reception from external things—as if the sense were "formed" by the objects of sense through a certain flow or "efflux" coming from them—nor according to an emission from the eyes, as if some physical body were sent out from the eye to touch the things to be sensed. Nor, indeed, do colors move the transparent medium as if they were physically shaping it, with the transparent then moving the sight in a similar way. Rather, the species themselves possess an effective power, through which each one acts upon that which is most exposed to an impression of this kind—not merely by touching, but also upon those things which are distant, provided there is a certain proportionate distance: one part being for the acting, and the other in turn for the suffering of the action. For since a natural species is corporeal, and is contained in something, and is circumscribed by a certain place, it does not act upon just anything placed anywhere. Instead, it acts only upon that which is distant according to a certain proportionate reason, measured both by the effective power of the agents and by the power of the recipients which is suited and exposed to this. And again, it is measured according to the proportion of the impression itself. Thus, the visible thing acts upon the instrument of sight from a certain interval, which is proportionate both to the one seeing...

### Chapter 14. How among the other senses, the most celestial alone uses light—a truly celestial thing—and must use it.

->MARSILIO<-

<margin>s</margin> Under the category of light are the *luminous* <note>things that emit light</note> and the *luminary* <note>original: *luminalia*; things that have a natural affinity for light or are receptive to it</note>. The first luminous thing is the celestial <note>the sun and stars</note>. The second is fiery. The third is found among composite things, which shine like fire <note>such as glowing minerals or certain organic matter</note>. The first luminary is the eye, which is especially radiant in animals that see at night. But other eyes, although less so, are nonetheless luminary. The second luminary is color, which is created from a certain dominance of light in naturally composite bodies. The third luminary is the *diaphanous*, which we can call the *transparent* <term>diaphanum: the medium, such as air or water, that allows light to pass through and connects the eye to the object</term>. Indeed, this transparency seems to be so easily passable for the incoming light that it is a kind of beginning of light, a supreme aptitude for receiving the fullness of the remaining light. Since, therefore, sight, color, and the transparent medium naturally possess something of light within themselves (though in a small amount), they rightly seem to strive toward a fuller light. By this, they pass from being "luminary" to being truly "luminous," and having attained a perfect degree in that category, they are joined to one another: specifically, color is joined with the eye through the transparent medium. Now, the necessary medium between the eye and color is not "air" simply (by which reasoning air, which is otherwise opaque, would not see similar things), but rather it is the transparent quality—that is, the "diaphanous"—which is passable by rays on all sides and is friendly to them, like a welcoming host and something naturally...

...something light-like <note>original: *luminale*; possessing the quality or essence of light</note>, which is indeed required. For the most part, it is so that the light, already imbued with this quality, may now illuminate the eye and the colors. Color is called the boundary of the transparent <term>diaphanum: a substance like air or water that is not visible itself but allows light and color to pass through it</term> in a bounded body in two main ways: first, by reason of the transparent; second, by reason of the object. You look at white snow; know therefore that this white color is the boundary of the transparent—namely, both of the intermediate air (for whiteness is at its boundary where it touches the snow) and of a certain transparency that we understand to be inherent in the snow itself. This whiteness appears in actuality not in just any part of this transparent substance, but only at the boundary—that is, always on the surface of the snow, however much you might cut into the snow. By these points, it is confirmed that color is something light-like.

->PRISCIAN<-

<margin>h</margin> These things are indeed common to hearing and sight alike, and to some other senses as well, if any other sense is not forced to touch its own proper sensible object. But in sight, the use of light is most excellent and unique, perfecting both sides: both the one who sees, so that they may see, and the visible object, so that it may be seen. For neither will the visible object itself act upon the seer without light, nor will the one intending to see act upon the visible object. For that which is visual within us is, in a way, naturally light-like; this is clearly shown by certain animals that first illuminate the things they need to see. For this reason, they can even see at night. Similarly, colors are in a way light-like, since they are considered to exist around the boundaries of the transparent parts of bounded bodies. For these reasons, therefore, both are rightly perfected by light; for since by their own nature they possess only a small amount of the light-like quality in terms of their perfect mutual action, they require external light in addition. Thus, the visual power itself is treated as something light-like, and colors as certain lights. This is surely indicated by their appearance; for colors are the boundaries of the transparent. But the transparent is (if I may put it this way) a certain aptitude for receiving light, or perhaps a trace of light so faint that it cannot yet complete the intermediate distance for vision. Yet this very interval is suited for vision, not merely as air or water or something else, but as a transparent medium already made perfect by the one illuminating it, and perfecting both that which sees and that which is seen.

### Chapter fifteen: Whether vision occurs through the emission of a ray from the eye, or through the reception of a certain species from the object. Also regarding three rules pertaining to the senses in general.

->**MARSILIO.**<-

Vision is an action that remains within the seer, just as shining and heating remain in fire. Therefore, if vision somehow occurs in the external object, there will also be something like the seeing vision itself there. By the presence of a certain virtual ray sent forth <note>original: *radii cuiusdam uirtualis emiffi*; a power or "virtue" rather than a physical beam</note>, vision also seems to occur around the visible object placed outside. This is partly because, otherwise, distance would not be easily judged. It is also because nothing "natural" <note>physical matter</note> from the thing to be seen comes to the eye, as seems to happen from other objects to other senses <note>such as odorous particles for the sense of smell</note>. It also happens that one might think something comes to the eye from the object in turn. For the eye suffers something from it; thus, sight is indeed contracted by black and scattered by white <term>congregatur / disgregatur: the physical contraction and expansion of the visual spirit when encountering dark or light colors</term>. Now it is dazzled by brightness. Such a passive affection is indeed perceived by the eye, but more on these elsewhere. 

There are three main rules handed down by Iamblichus <note>a 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> to be firmly held regarding every sense. First, something happens in the instrument of the sense. It must necessarily be affected from there in some way; this affection is both a "passion" <note>a passive receiving</note> brought in from external things—because this instrument is a body—and an "action" resulting in the instrument. Because it is a living thing, this kind of affection is made in some way similar to the thing being sensed. The second rule is that after this affection of the instrument (which is living in some way), there is a certain "species" <term>species: a non-physical image or form that represents the object</term> in a more spiritual manner within the animal's life itself, now better suited for the sense and still similar to the sensible object. The third rule is that at the presence of this species, a certain "reason" <note>original: *ratio*; a rational or formal principle</note> of the thing being sensed—which was previously hidden in the soul—is awakened. Once awakened, it aligns with the species, and through the species with the affection, and through the affection with the sensible object positioned outside. This awakening and alignment is what it means "to sense" in general.

->**PRISCIAN.**<-

A great variety, therefore, occurs in sight; for it seems to go forth outside. This is because it acts around the sensible object outside its own location, and yet it also receives something from the thing to be seen, because it clearly suffers something from that source. Now indeed, the transparent and the medium seem to pass through to both as if

...and perfecting [the sense] with light, and exhibiting a proportion through the interval. Let us also apply to these things whatever we have collectively considered regarding every sense: namely, the appearance of the sensible object itself, or the mark impressed upon the instrument of the sense. This occurs through a process of both undergoing an impression <note>original: *passionem*; the state of being acted upon by an external object</note> and a simultaneous action already established within the sense itself for perceiving the object through a certain likeness. Furthermore, let us understand such an appearance or impression as a completed form that resolves into a "species" <note>original: *speciem*; in this context, a philosophical term for the formal image or "likeness" of an object that travels to the mind</note> within the common life of the composite being <note>the unified entity of soul and body</note>. Let us also consider the innate reason of the soul, sprouting from the sensory soul and corresponding to such species, through which all judgment and thought occur. This is the method for contemplating each individual sense, which we should primarily adopt from Iamblichus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the soul's active role in perception</note> where he philosophizes about the soul. From his works, we have presently written these summaries, desiring to prescribe a certain formula for the exact contemplation of each sense. Indeed, our purpose now is not to pursue a highly distinct discussion of these matters, but to investigate the thoughts of Theophrastus. We aim to connect his ideas to the Aristotelian tradition if he has added anything to it, and to deal with whatever doubts he proposes to the best of our ability.

### Chapter sixteen: How a medium is necessary between the sensible object and the sense, and concerning the color of the diaphanous.

->**MARSILIO.**<-

The sensible object itself is excessively material, while the sense is remarkably spiritual. Thus, they do not come together by themselves to complete the act of perceiving; rather, there is need for a certain medium that is in some way spiritual to reconcile them with one another. In every sense, this medium involves a certain "species" <note>an image-form</note> like the one we described a little earlier. Regarding sight, however—as it is the most excellent sense—there is need for the diaphanous <term>diaphanous: the transparent medium, such as air or water, that allows light to pass through</term> and light beyond the species, through which the material may be thoroughly adapted to the spiritual. Where Aristotle says that the diaphanous is seen not through itself, but through an external color, Theophrastus questions whether it is correctly said that something becomes visible through an external color, or tastable through an external flavor. The answer is that Aristotle called light the "color" of a body that is luminous in itself; by communicating this light to it, the diaphanous becomes visible. There are those who think the diaphanous has its own color, but a very faint one. Otherwise, it would not be so easily permeated and shaped by external colors. Therefore, they say this imperfect color is perfected by the light of a luminous body through a perfect color; whereas those who deny the diaphanous has its own color...

# OF PRISCIAN.

<margin>f</margin>But let us now return to Theophrastus <note>a student of Aristotle and his successor at the Peripatetic school</note>. He himself also seems to think it unreasonable that no sense should touch its sensible object through its own power. He says it is strange, since all the senses are of the same genus, that they should not have a mutually common and similar condition. He brings up, moreover, this point regarding the **transparent** <note>original: *diaphano*; the medium (like air or water) through which light travels</note>, which might indeed disturb some because of its novelty: namely, in what way this visible thing is said not to exist through itself, but becomes manifest to the eyes because of a foreign color <note>original: *alienum colorem*; here referring to light as something added to the object</note>. This would be as if it were said that something "tastable" becomes so through a foreign flavor. Truly, this doubt is easily solved. Indeed, that foreign "color" is called light, proceeding as if from elsewhere—that is, from the source of illumination. For light is so familiar to things to be seen that it perfects them and brings them into act <note>original: *educat in actum*; a philosophical concept where a potentiality (the ability to be seen) becomes a reality</note>. For this reason, even if the transparent medium itself has its own color, it is nevertheless perfected by light just as the colors of other things are. For light does not take away the properties from anything; on the contrary, it leads them to their full expression. Or, as I said, if the transparent is by itself devoid of light, it is certainly perfected by light as if colored, and thus it emerges as something visible.

### Chapter seventeen: on the transparent and light.

## OF MARSILIO.

<margin>d</margin>Transparency, or perspicuity, is not a body <note>it is not a physical substance like a rock or water, but a quality</note>. Otherwise, it could not be infused into bodies without being scattered, nor is it some disposition brought upon other bodies by one body through a mode of "suffering" <note>original: *passionem*; a state of being acted upon</note>. Rather, it is a certain *species* and form in itself, just like light, color, and heat. Truly, the *species* <note>the formal, non-material essence</note> of forms do not flow primarily from physical matter—which is ineffective in its own right—but they are created and formally distinguished by the First Form, which is both uniform and "omniform" <note>containing all forms within itself</note>: that is, the Divine Mind. Moreover, Priscian posits this from the mind of Iamblichus <note>a major Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, just as Julian <note>Emperor Julian the Apostate, a follower of Iamblichus</note> asserts in his book *On the Sun* from the same school of thought. The transparent is found not only in ether, fire, air, water, and glass, but even in the earth itself and in all composite bodies. Indeed, a certain **intellectual soul** is infused into all these things. From this soul, therefore, insofar as it is a certain life, heat proceeds through all things (though it may be hidden); and insofar as it is intellectual, light is diffused through all things. Although it may be hidden in some places, the transparent is exhibited alongside light as the proper receptacle of light. Furthermore, Julian says (following the thought of Iamblichus and the Phoenicians) that light is a pure act extended through all things by the act of the Divine Intelligence. The transparent, however, is the vehicle for an act of this kind, and it is indeed incorpo- <note>The text breaks off here; the word is likely "incorporeal"</note>

### OF PRISCIAN.

<margin>¶ q</margin> What then is the nature of the diaphanous—that is, that which is clear and accessible to the eyes? For it is not enough to say that this quality exists in air, water, ether, and some solid things. It is necessary, he says, that the diaphanous be either a certain **passion** <note>original: *passionem*; a property or state that a substance "undergoes" or receives</note> or a disposition. For this is deep within the body; however, a body cannot be within another body in this way. But if it is a passion or a certain disposition, we shall investigate by what it is produced. Now, it seems to come from one or perhaps from several simple bodies. However, if this cannot happen—for these simple things, namely air and water, are themselves diaphanous—the Earth too is diaphanous through fire; indeed, all composite bodies are so, insofar as they are all colored. For color is the limit of the diaphanous. I assert, therefore, that the diaphanous is not a passion or a disposition brought into bodies by something else, but is a certain unifying **form** <note>original: *speciem*; the essential nature or "look" of a thing</note> of those things that are in the process of generation, for receiving the perfection of light. Likewise, it provides them with a certain aptitude for receiving light and for undergoing darkness, whether participating in one of these by essence, or both in turn, or both simultaneously through some mixture. Indeed, the diaphanous which is in fire has essential light. But the diaphanous which is in the earth has essential darkness. For which reason, just as fire is light-bringing, so the earth is darkness-bringing; for the darkness itself (as we might say) is not a privation of light, but is also itself an **act** <note>original: *actus*; a formal reality or state of being, rather than a mere void</note>. The diaphanous of the air and the water, in turn, loses both [light and dark] alternately: which indeed we are more properly accustomed to call the diaphanous. But the diaphanous that exists in composite bodies receives both through a mixture.

We ought not, therefore, to inquire from which of the simple bodies <note>the four elements: earth, air, fire, and water</note> the diaphanous arises. For **species** <term>species; here meaning philosophical "forms" or "essences" rather than biological categories</term> are produced neither from elements nor from bodies at all. Rather, the bodies themselves participate in these forms, and according to them, they obtain their own specific characters. Wherefore those things which do not claim a luminous form for themselves by their own essence, these need light in order to be seen. Fire and similarly shining things, however, by no means need this; since they are participants in a luminous form that is sufficient for this purpose through its very essence.

### Chapter XVIII. Of what thing light is the act. BY MARSILIO.

<margin>1</margin> Light, wherever it may be, is the **act** <note>original: *actus*; the active reality or fulfillment of a potentiality</note> of the diaphanous. But in a body that is naturally luminous, it is an act like a form and a certain quality proper to it. In a diaphanous body that is not naturally luminous, light is introduced, not as its own form or quality, or a true **passion** <note>original: *passio*; a philosophical term for a state of being acted upon or modified by an external force</note>, but as if it were a passion.

ON THEOPHRASTUS.

The question is asked: what is light? But we should rather ask about that which proceeds from a cause, which is indeed said to be the **act** <term>actus; the "actuality" or active realization of a potential</term> of the **diaphanous** <term>diaphanum; the transparent medium, like air or water, that allows light to travel</term> in the air, the water, and other things which alternately receive darkness and light.

### Chapter Nineteen. That light does not exist within the diaphanous medium as if it were a quality of it, but is present rather as the very act of the illuminator.

->**MARSILIO.**<-

<margin>e</margin> The Epicureans <note>followers of the Greek philosopher Epicurus who believed the world was made of physical atoms</note> think that light is a body. Most of the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note>, however, believe that it is certainly not a body—otherwise it would not penetrate other bodies so easily—but they want light to be a "passion" <note>an effect or impression made upon a substance</note> and a quality within the diaphanous things that receive it. Priscianus rejects this view as being foreign to the Platonists, whom he honors above all others. He therefore introduces the arguments of Iamblichus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> on these matters, which Iamblichus had himself received from Plotinus. A quality that comes into a body and is properly grasped by it, becoming its "form," possesses six conditions:

1.  **First:** It enters the parts of the body gradually.
2.  **Second:** It brings a "passion" to the subject and changes its natural disposition, beginning as an accidental change and ultimately becoming a substantial one.
3.  **Third:** It is propagated only up to a certain distance.
4.  **Fourth:** When the source that formed it departs, the quality remains in the subject for some time—just as heat remains in water once the fire has been moved away.
5.  **Fifth:** The quality itself moves when the body moves from place to place.
6.  **Sixth:** It can be tainted by the impurity of the body and be confused there, mixing with other qualities into a single composition.

Light, on the contrary, arrives suddenly; it does not change the nature of its subject; it is capable of propagating through an immense distance, so long as there is a medium present capable of receiving it. When the source that illuminates recedes, light leaves nothing of itself behind in the medium where it seemed to cling. It does not move when the air or water moves. It is not tainted when the diaphanous medium is tainted, but either remains pure in itself or departs instantly, always remaining continuous with the one who illuminates. Furthermore, multiple lights do not merge into one; this is apparent from the fact that if you walk toward two lamps, twin shadows will result. If you walk toward more lamps, there will likewise be more shadows. Similarly, if a large board with a hole in the middle is placed before three lamps, it will transmit three distinct lights through the hole to the opposite side. Finally, light is present in the diaphanous medium in a separable way, just as the intellectual soul is present in the body.

->**PRISCIAN.**<-

<margin>p</margin> Therefore, following Iamblichus, I judge that light is neither a body nor, as the Peripatetics think, a "passion" or quality of some body. For light does not have an "outpouring" <note>original: "effusuum," suggesting a physical leaking or spreading of substance</note> in the air. For when the air is moved, the light remains; and though the air may be changed in many different ways, the light departs from it by its own force into itself, and meanwhile preserves an unbreakable connection with its cause. Indeed, the whole presence of this light is received simultaneously through all things capable of receiving it...

happens suddenly—namely, in the presence of that which illuminates. And likewise, when it departs, the sudden failure of light—leaving no trace of itself behind—can serve as proof to us that light is not a **passion** <term>passio; here meaning a physical change or "suffering" undergone by a substance, like air being heated</term> of the air. For passions, such as heat, do not arrive suddenly; and once the fire is removed, the heat leaves at least some small trace of its form in the "patient" <note>the substance receiving the effect</note>. Nor does this luminous act ever truly become a part of the **diaphanous** <term>diaphanum; the transparent medium, like air</term>; rather, it brings it about that the diaphanous medium exists in a permanent state, while the light itself remains continuous with the source of illumination, moving with it in every direction. Let this, then, be a brief summary, lest we suspect that light is produced or received in something in the same way that effects are usually produced in other physical subjects.

### Chapter 20. On light again and the diaphanous.
### MARSILIO.

Since it is clear from the points above that light is something incorporeal and not mixed with physical things, we can conjecture three things from this. First, indeed, that the celestial body—the first receptacle of light—is ruled by an incorporeal life and **intelligence** <term>intelligentia; in Neoplatonism, a higher spiritual mind or angelic-like being</term>, from which it receives its light to pass on to others. For that which is incorporeal cannot be procreated by a body. Second, that the celestial body does not possess the kind of matter that would mix with other elements. Third, that light is the most powerful cause in action. For if it is not mixed with the things it acts upon, it acts more freely and without hindrance, being most powerful by its very nature. For this reason, marvelous actions proceed from it. Light does not flow out from a luminous source through a kind of "resolution" <note>original: *resolutionem*; a dissolving or physical shedding of particles</note>, like a scent from an apple, nor like heat from a fire (which becomes the property of the one receiving it and is not always continuous with the one giving it). Instead, it acts like a visual ray from the eye—if indeed vision occurs by the emission of rays—which is perhaps nothing other than the sight itself stretched out toward external things; or rather, it is the very act of sight acting at a distance, not leaving the one who sees, but remaining always continuous with the agent and unmixed with external things. It is capable of doing harm—as is seen in the **basilisk** <term>regulus; the legendary "king of serpents" whose gaze was said to be lethal</term>—and it is capable of doing good, as is established by instruction. If we say that light is the "visual rays" of the celestial eyes living within themselves, and that through such rays all things are seen...

After these things, Theophrastus asks in this way: if light is incorporeal, why does it happen through the presence of fire or any other body? Moreover, if darkness is seen without light, then light will not be the cause for all things to be seen. But indeed, as Theophrastus says, darkness is not visible. And therefore it does not completely lack light in order to be seen. Fire, therefore, to be perceived, does not need some act that is already diaphanous—that is, already illuminated. Since, however, it is necessary for there to be some medium (for vision does not happen by contact), therefore this medium must be diaphanous, lest by chance it be solid or resistant, and impede by its opaque and dark property the mutual action of luminous things between themselves—I mean, of the fire and the instrument of the senses.

It appears that sight is the most excellent of the senses, because it perceives more quickly, further, more broadly, and more distinctly than the others. For which reason, for the act of hearing and of the others, a material path, a sensible interval, and a suitable medium standing between are sufficient. ## PRISCIAN

<margin>c</margin> It happens (as Theophrastus says) that the cause of colors being seen is color itself, and simply that for any things to be visible, the cause is "the visible" <note>original: "uisibile"; the quality or category of being able to be seen</note>. Indeed, since light exists as color, it is the cause of the **transparent** <term>diaphanum; the medium, like air or water, through which light and color travel</term> and of the visible. He adds again that this is not absurd, but is also observed in other things; for taste, too, occurs through flavor. 

Perhaps, however, someone will say that flavor is the proper **sensible** <term>sensibile; a specific object of perception, like a sound or a smell</term> of taste, and sound is the proper sensible of hearing, and these two need absolutely no external thing by which the instrument <note>the sense organ</note> might be moved—unless perhaps one says that hearing needs a sounding object, just as the transparent medium needs color. 

But truly, sound is immediately sensible once the intermediary air has been traversed. We know that color requires an external illuminator if it is to be visible. This is perhaps a unique property of sight: namely, to require light. This is not because sight is less perfect than the other senses—which require no other external completion—but because it has a more excellent and more sublime action, for which a merely sensory power does not suffice. Instead, it requires a certain more divine **species** <term>species; here meaning a formal appearance or light-form that gives sight its power</term>. 

For just as our body does not need a soul in order to be heavy and to descend, but does need it for the very movement of progression and apprehension—on account of the excellence of motion surpassing the natural movement of the body—this motion made by the impulse of the **imagination** <note>the faculty that directs voluntary movement</note> is not therefore worse than natural motion, but better. Thus sight, more excellent than the others because it operates more excellently, employs another "perfector" <note>something that brings it to its final, perfect state; in this case, light</term>.

### Chapter 22. Sight, as the most perfect of the senses, and the visible, as the most perfect of sensible things, hold an order from the multitude to the one, which the other senses and remaining things to be sensed do not have.

## MARSILIO

<margin>n</margin> Neither are all tastes reduced to one taste through which they may taste, nor are all things tastable reduced to one "tastable" thing through which they may be tasted. It is similar with similar things. But visible things become visible through the "first visible," that is, light; and therefore all sights exist through the "first sight." 

Since, truly, those things which are divided among lower things are united among higher things, we can therefore conjecture that the first visible and the first sight are the same: that is, especially the light of the sun. Hence **Orpheus** <note>the mythical poet, often cited by Ficino as a source of ancient wisdom</note> calls the sun the "eye of the world." Similarly, all intellects are referred to the First Intellect, and all intelligible things to the First Intelligible. Indeed, the First Intellect and the First Intelligible are the same. Consequently, just as from that very center of the heavens—as many confirm—that is, the sun...

universal life is diffused through all things without any dissolution, rarefaction, or mixture of that life itself; similarly, light is diffused through all things from that source, which indeed, coming from the life of all things, becomes life-giving to all. And here is a marvelous order in this very genus of things visual and visible: they are reduced from a multitude into a single thing, from which they had previously proceeded. There is also a marvelous abundance of that first visible thing <note>original: "primi uifibilis"; referring to light itself as the primary object of sight</note>, so that by its power all things may be seen. Finally, there is a singular efficacy of sight, such that it perceives innumerable things through one; however, since the other senses and the remaining things to be sensed <note>the objects of perception</note> ought not to lack order entirely, it is likely that both the other senses and the other **sensibles** <term>sensibilia; objects capable of being perceived by the senses</term> are contained in the power of the first sight and the first visible thing, so that if they are not ordered by themselves, they are at least ordered through the order of that primary sense.

## PRISCIAN

<margin>d</margin> Someone might perhaps say that it is worth considering whether that which is bright, and light itself, is the primary visible object which, through itself, moves the eye and around which sight acts, needing no other external thing to complete the process. Colors, however, as if they were certain tiny lights, might not be able to be seen by themselves, but require the primary visible object <note>light</note> to immediately perfect them. But someone might say further: if this were so, light ought not to contribute to colors so that they are seen, but on the contrary, it should confound them. Just as a greater light usually overwhelms a smaller one, and among physical things, that which shines more occupies the place of that which shines less. Thus, under the sun, the light of a lamp <note>original: "lychni"; a portable lamp or candle</note> is hardly seen at all. However, the comparison of a greater thing to a smaller one is not the same as the comparison of a preceding thing to a following one. For color is not compared with the light of the sun as if it were simply a competing visible thing; nor is color visible at all without light. Therefore, color is compared to light as a "consequent visible" <note>a secondary object of sight</note> insofar as it is perfected by light and becomes visible through it. Light itself, however, is sufficient by its own nature to be seen. If a similar proportion is not found in the other senses—by which one thing is primarily audible or tastable and another is consequently so—this is certainly due to a certain richness, both of the first visible thing of all (which we say is light) in perfecting the other things to be seen, and of the power of seeing itself. For the power of sight perceives not only light, but also certain other things through the benefit of that light.

...are passions of the body.
