### Chapter 48. Confirmation of the above.

->MARSILIO'S<-

<margin>n</margin> Numenius, Plotinus, Porphyry, and Iamblichus <note>a list of major Neoplatonic philosophers who influenced Ficino’s thought</note> believe that the **sensory soul** is separable from the body. Priscian touches upon this here because of the present conjecture: that it possesses a single and indivisible faculty that performs very different actions simultaneously. I set aside the duty of growth and nutrition <note>original: *vegetationis officium*; the basic biological functions shared with plants</note>, and speak instead of the single **imagination** which imagines such diverse things at once. Through this, the soul is turned back into itself, where it notices the actions of the senses; through this, it acts in a certain way without the instrument of the body, since it perceives darkness, silence, and the <term>cessation</term> <note>original: *vacationem*; the state of a sense being "off" or inactive</note> of sensing. For then the instrument is not moved. Therefore, the sense does not move the imagination then; thus, the imagination acts as if it were in some way separated from the instrument. Here, therefore, this common sense flourishes in the soul as something eternal according to its form and power. And when the powers of the bodily instruments are applied to it—that is, produced within it—those powers were already flourishing within it beforehand, distinct by their formal nature and internal logic <note>original: *ratione*</note>, but not separated by location or by their own specific actions. Therefore, when the body fails, the senses do not entirely cease to be, but they cease to be unfolded [into the organs]. Remember that these things are told to us according to the **Platonists**.

->PRISCIAN’S<-

<margin>n</margin> Therefore, each individual sense in truth—but especially the common sense itself—will take notice of itself and its own action. For if any sense recognizes its action, it would also notice the absence of that action. If it records the cessation, it will simultaneously be at rest and yet active, as if perceiving itself. Does it not, then, rest insofar as it is divided and singular, and as far as it is in itself? Yet it acts meanwhile insofar as it remains detached from its own specific action and cessation. For this reason, it then acts according to the **common sense**, according to which each sense acts in this way—not by the logic by which they are individual and divided, but by the logic through which they are united by a single unity of all. Indeed, the duty of this faculty is to grasp the sensible objects of all the senses in the same [instant] without division, while it acts through internal logics <note>original: *rationes*</note> that differ from one another. For this reason, the judge itself remains one and indivisible in number, but is judged to be divisible insofar as it exercises different logics.

### PRISCIANUS.

After this, where Aristotle says that the voice is a harmony <note>original: *consonantia*; a musical sounding-together or agreement of sounds</note>. It must be understood that this occurs where it is already sensible in act, or placed in the sensible act—that is, while it is already being heard. But it is heard when both the voice and the hearing are in accord with each other and made one, while they are completely tempered together. For an excessive surplus of the thing to be sensed dissolves or destroys the action of the senses; but the sense itself consists in a certain commensuration <note>a state of being in proper proportion or measure</note>, and we say those objects are "soothing" which are tempered to the senses. Tell me then: when the sense does nothing, is it never placed in commensuration according to itself? Certainly, since the sense is not accustomed to act according to itself alone, but consists in a certain extension toward external things and in a certain relationship to the things to be sensed; when it is idle, it will not have an active or effective commensuration according to itself. It will only have commensuration according to its potential. For the potential itself pre-existed and is considered according to itself. But let us proceed next to those things which follow from another beginning, about to treat the remaining matters pertaining to the book.

# The interpretation by the Lydian philosopher Priscianus of Theophrastus's book *On Imagination and Intellect*, translated by Marsilio Ficino the Platonist and explained by him chapter by chapter.

## Chapter one.

<margin>1</margin> In the sense and the imagination, there are innate principles <note>original: *rationes*; here meaning formal patterns or mathematical ratios that allow the soul to recognize external objects</note> that are assimilative of sensible things. In the sense, these are provoked into action by the "passions" <note>the physical impressions or "undergoings"</note> of the instrument. In the imagination, however, they are provoked by the actions of the senses. Imagination <note>original: *phantasia*</note>, which is the medium between sense and reason, is a certain action within the sense. Iamblichus says of imagination: "Imagination is innate to all the powers of the soul. It shapes all things within itself, and carries forms over from some powers to others, and emulates the acts of all powers." Imagination does not receive forms from external things, but brings them forth from itself.

# ON THEOPHRASTUS: BY PRISCIANUS.

<margin>P</margin> Imagination, which Theophrastus discusses next following Aristotle, must be admitted from his books to be another power besides sense. Furthermore, it differs from opinion and every rational perception. Just as the sense is moved by sensible forms <note>original: *speciebus*; the mental images or patterns received through the senses</note> when vitally excited, and acts around them according to its own production of reasons, so too imagination is agitated by sensory forms, using these as its immediate subjects and acting around them. For this reason, this too is a corporeal life, and it does not act without physical instruments, since even the sensory forms by which it is moved are perfected from those impressions that appear in the instruments of the senses. The following teachings of Iamblichus <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized the soul's intermediate role</note> must be added to these: Imagination is innate to all the powers of the soul and shapes them all; it fashions likenesses of forms and appearances, and transmits the "visions" or impressions of some powers into others. Those which flash from the senses, it stirs into opinion; but those which come from the intellect, it offers to opinion in the second place. Within itself, it receives images from all, and through its own characteristic is specifically marked according to a process of assimilation, both in acting and in receiving. These images are assimilated and appear in intellectual or generic operations, or in those midway between the two. Indeed, imagination fashions and expresses all actions of the soul. It accommodates external things to internal ones, and imposes the impressions descending from the intellect upon the defects extended through the body. Since, therefore, imagination is in itself a power of assimilating other things to itself, it is deservedly joined to the other powers, preceding them and providing the beginnings for their actions. It is neither a passion <note>original: *passio*; here meaning a passive state of being acted upon</note> nor a motion, but an impassible and definite action. Nor is it shaped by receiving from the outside like wax; rather, it is stirred from within according to the production of assimilative reasons toward the manifestation of mental images <term>phantasmata: the mental "pictures" or appearances produced by the imagination</term>. Thus says Iamblichus.

### Chapter Two. BY MARSILIO.

<margin>i</margin> Imagination fashions the actions of reason under the condition of sensible things, and can bring forth mental images more broadly than the acts of the senses. Imagination agrees with sense because it perceives particulars. It surpasses sense because it produces images even when nothing is moving it. Imagination is like Proteus <note>a mythical sea-god capable of changing shape at will</note> or a chameleon.

### BY PRISCIANUS.

<margin>u</margin> But if imagination expresses other lives, as is found in Iamblichus, and fashions intellectual and rational actions themselves, in what way will that Aristotelian saying still be true—namely, that <margin>a</margin> imagination is agitated by sensory forms? Perhaps, even if all the more excellent actions...

--- Page 244 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of imagination (phantasia) from the previous page, specifically exploring how it operates independently of the physical senses. It includes a transition into Chapter Three, which features commentary from Marsilio Ficino alongside Priscianus’s summary of Theophrastus.</meta>

...mmodates and fashions all things, while at the same time it imagines according to sensory forms <note>original: *species*; the mental patterns or images received from the senses</note>, and through a certain formative condition, it likens them to itself; it is broken down and shaped according to a certain relation to sensible things. For this reason, it fashions more excellent actions by the way it is agitated by sensory forms. In what way, then, is imagination moved even when sensible things are not present? For even if imagination itself is moved by sensory things, and these are produced into action when sensory things are present or fail when they are absent—perhaps it is not moved in the same way that sight is usually moved only by present objects. Rather, once imagination has been moved, it can then awaken from within itself and produce mental images <note>original: *phantasmata*</note> according to a certain relation to the forms that originally moved it. Sometimes, indeed, it must be moved not just once or twice, but more often, so that it may offer up those things within itself that are similar to the things that moved it. Now this power, whether formative or formable and divisible, perhaps communicates with the sense. But in the faculty by which it produces mental images from itself—even if no moving causes are further present—it surpasses the sense. Again, because by its very condition it always refers to other things and is likened to different actions of the soul, it is naturally connected to all the powers of the soul; it is judged to be a defining power according to its assimilation or its capacity to be likened to the soul's own properties.

### Chapter Three.

<margin>f</margin>
->MARSILIO FICINO<-

Just as in the same substance of the soul, sense and imagination are formally different, so the same substance of the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; referring to 'pneuma', a subtle physical vapor believed to be the "vehicle" of the soul</note> is the instrument of imagination and sense according to different qualities. Likewise, from the actions of sense and imagination, certain marks representing them are imprinted in the spirit. Imagination has sensory forms for its objects, to which it refers its innate reasons. If the movements of reason and imagination produce manifest signs in the humors <note>the four primary bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note> and the solid body, how much more so in the spirit; through these things, it is known how demons <note>in this Neoplatonic context, 'demons' are intermediary spirits capable of perceiving these subtle physical changes</note> detect the thoughts of men. Regarding the same object, the sense can be truthful while the imagination is false, and vice versa. Once awakened, the imagination can proceed further even while the sense is at rest.

<margin>q</margin>
->PRISCIANUS<-

Meanwhile, Theophrastus asks where imagination should primarily be placed. For it should not be placed in the sensitive power itself, since even when the sense is truthful, imagination itself sometimes lies. Nor, again, is it in the physical instrument of the senses. For a "passion" <note>an impression or physical effect</note> made in the instrument occurs only when the sensible object is present. But mental images or "imaginaments" (for one may interpret *phantasia* as imagination)—I say these mental images occur even when the sensible object is absent. I assert, therefore, that imagination is another power besides sense, but very close to sense, and in a certain way it is moved by sense, using sensory forms as its subjects. From these, it is then awakened, and toward these mental images...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how imagination (phantasia) relates to the physical body and the "spirit," which acts as the soul's primary instrument. It concludes the commentary on the previous section and prepares to transition into Chapter Four.</meta>

->### ON THEOPHRASTUS<-

...referring back to mental images <note>original: *phantasmata*; the internal "apparitions" or pictures created by the mind</note>. But imagination varies these images in many ways based on what it receives from the senses, and once it has been moved toward forming an image, it searches out forms from within itself however it first began. I believe, furthermore, that the signs or impressions of the forms emerging from the boundaries of imagination can be received by the instrument of sensing <note>The "instrument" refers to the *spiritus*, a subtle, vapor-like substance that Renaissance thinkers believed connected the immaterial soul to the physical body</note>, just as formal and possible shapes testify, even if they do not indicate a separation from bodies. 

Indeed, often while the body is moved toward mental images and is affected by them, I believe that images appear in the instrument itself—not as something sensory, since they do not fall upon it from outside, nor as if we were changed by certain active physical bodies. Rather, they appear as if in a spirit receiving imaginative forms. This should not seem strange, since certain signs and marks of our rational action also descend into the body, which is clearly seen when the eyes and eyebrows are contracted during intense investigations <note>Ficino uses the physical reflex of squinting or frowning during hard thought as proof that the soul's internal activity affects the physical body</note>. Now, if these solid members of the body are affected according to the movements of the soul, much sooner must the instrument of the senses, being more vital, receive certain traces of life. 

In those beings where life is only sensory, the instrument is also only sensory; but in those where life is additionally imaginative and appetitive, or even rational, the instrument is likewise adapted to receive that kind of life. Therefore, the instrument will receive imaginative marks as an imaginative thing, even false ones if the imaginations happen to be false. And just as we sometimes sense true things while simultaneously being able to produce false imaginations about them, so consequently the spirit itself, insofar as it is sensory, receives true marks from the senses; but insofar as it is imaginative, it receives false ones from the senses but true ones from imagination. 

Consider when we see the sun to be a foot wide, but meanwhile imagine it to be much larger than the earth, compelled by geometric demonstration <note>This is a standard philosophical example: your eyes see the sun as a small disk (the sensory "truth"), but your mind knows it is massive (the rational/imaginative "truth")</note>. Yet there is no sense of the image itself in us, even though the image exists in the instrument of sense; rather, sense properly pertains to sensible things and depends on them, whereas mental images emerge from the imagination. 

Hence, it is not impossible for the underlying spirit to receive true and false appearances about the same things simultaneously, as happens in our view of the sun. It receives these through different powers and according to different forms of life. Nothing prevents a mental image and the act of sensing from occurring together in the same subject, even if they are opposites, as they are not of the same order or pairing, nor the work of the same power. Indeed, opinion and sense regarding the size of the sun are opposed to each other in the same person. This has been answered by reason; it has been stated further that the presence of sensible things is not always necessary for the imagination to be moved, but once it has been impressed and struggles in the birth of such a form, it is sufficient unto itself. Let us proceed to the rest.

# ON IMAGINATION AND INTELLECT

<margin>f i</margin> Our intellect is something proper to the soul; it is a certain form <note>original: *species*; here referring to a mental blueprint or intelligible pattern</note> and is intellect in its actual state. By its very essence, it contains within itself the forms of all things that can be understood. However, because it has declined from its primary source, it requires the nourishment <note>original: *fomentum*; literally "kindling" or "warmth," suggesting the intellect needs to be "re-ignited" by divine light</note> of that primary source for three purposes. First, so that it may be most sharp-sighted. Second, so that its forms may be most clear. Third, so that the intellect may be made one with those forms. Sensation is also a certain form and, according to its essence, it contains the "reasons" <note>original: *rationes*; the formative principles or logic of physical things</note> of sensible objects, which it brings forth when those objects move its instrument. The animal intellect <note>The "animal" intellect refers to the faculty of the soul (*anima*) that deals with the physical world, distinguished from the "divine" or "pure" intellect</note>, because of the soul's nature which leans toward things that are divisible and changeable, stands far apart from the unity and stability of the first intellect and of the primary intelligible things. Note here that throughout this text, the "agent intellect" <term>Agent Intellect: In medieval philosophy, the active power of the mind that "lights up" sensory data to turn it into abstract concepts.</term> within us is considered to be the first intellect. These ideas are similar to those found in Plato's *Republic*, where the light of the Good itself joins intelligible forms with the powers of the intellect. There are those who write letters on paper using onion juice, but these letters are not seen unless the paper is heated. The forms of things held by what is called the "possible intellect" <note>The "possible" or "passive" intellect is the mind's capacity to receive knowledge, like a blank slate</note> are like this: they come into view only through the presence of divine fire, just as colors are made visible by the light of the sun. Our intellect is not "in potential" <note>i.e., it doesn't just have the *potential* to become these things</note> so that it may *become* intellect and intelligible things, but rather it moves toward the ultimate perfection of understanding and of the things understood.

->THEOPHRASTUS, where he discusses the intellect later on, says:<-

We must not accept this entirely, nor in the same way. For it would be a matter of dispute to accept these things so simply—namely, that the intellect is a certain potentiality that is entirely subject, in the same way that material potentialities usually are. And having progressed a little further, he adds: Perhaps it will appear absurd if the intellect has the nature of matter in such a way that it is "nothing," but is potentially "all things." Therefore, it should not be explained in this way, nor should this be accepted similarly regarding every kind of intellect; rather, a distinction must be used. What then is this distinction, and of what kind? Matter, indeed, is not a "this something" <note>original: *hoc aliquid*; a translation of Aristotle’s *tode ti*, meaning a specific, individual, existing thing</note>; but if the intellect were not a "this something," what else would a "this something" be?

->Thus far the words of Theophrastus.<-

<margin>q</margin> Therefore, when the intellect is compared with nature according to a certain comparison of proportion, this must be understood: to the extent that one intellect is in a state of potentiality relative to another. For in this way, the animal intellect is compared to that which is always intellect in act and is separate; it is rightly said that all things are in potentiality. It is said that senses are matter—not properly, but by a certain metaphor—or that they are *like* matter. For matter is thought of as the last of all things, yet sense is not the last of all things in the same way matter is. For sense is a certain form, and it is said to contain the "reasons" of sensible things according to its essence. There is, however, another reason why sense is said to be "sensible things in potential": insofar as it is incited by them toward the beginning, and it requires them both to be present and to act upon its instrument for its own proper action. But the animal intellect is neither like matter, nor like sense. For it is a form and a comprehender of all forms according to its own essence. It also acts from itself and within itself, since it contains intelligible things because of its kinship with...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "animal intellect," explaining how it differs from the higher, "separate" intellect. It addresses the classical metaphor of the mind as a blank slate, clarifying that the mind is not empty like matter, but rather "potential" in the sense that it requires divine illumination to see the truths it already contains.</meta>

<header>ON THEOPHRASTUS</header>

...with the soul, and because of its essential relationship to the soul, and finally because of its inclination toward the divisible. Thus, it has fallen somewhat from that purely intellectual essence and action, which is entirely indivisible and united. Likewise, the "intelligible things" <note>original: *intelligibilia*; the concepts or truths grasped by the mind</note> within it seem to have declined from that first substance of intelligibles, which shines with its own light. In the same way, the continuity between the soul’s intellect and its concepts has been loosened. It is not entirely whole like the unity found in the "Separate Intellect" <note>The "Separate Intellect" refers to a higher, divine mind that exists independently of human bodies</note>, which is always active. For this reason, the human intellect needs a "perfector"—an intellect that is always in act—to reach fully indivisible knowledge. The concepts within it also need illumination from those higher, separate intelligibles so that they too may become perfect. This is why Aristotle says these concepts are like colors that need the sun's brightness <note>Aristotle famously compared the "Agent Intellect" to light, which makes potential colors (our thoughts) visible to the eye (the mind)</note>. Even the point where this intellect touches its own concepts is less indivisible than the perfect unity of the higher mind. Therefore, the soul's intellect is said to be "in potential" <term>In potential: Having the capacity to understand something, but not currently doing so—like a person who knows how to read but is currently sleeping</term> relative to the Separate Intellect. This is because the higher mind is purely indivisible and united with the highest and most perfect lights of truth. It is also called "in potential" because it is perfected by such a mind. Furthermore, when the intellect is called a "writing tablet devoid of letters" <note>original: *tabella litterarum expers*; the Latin equivalent of the Greek *tabula rasa*</note>, this should be understood as a comparison of proportions. It does not mean the intellect has no "forms" <note>original: *species*; the mental blueprints or patterns of things</note> at all. Just as the intellect itself is "in potential"—not in the sense that it isn't an intellect, but that it is the kind of intellect that must be perfected by the First Intellect—so too the concepts within it are indeed "intelligibles," but of the sort that must be illuminated by separate truths to be purely understood. This is why they are compared to colors. And this "tablet" is called "empty of letters" only in regards to receiving those perfect, higher forms. Therefore, Theophrastus rightly cries out that it is absurd to give the intellect a "material" nature, or to think that like matter it has nothing in act and is only potential. He forbids interpreting the teachings in that way. He further commands us to investigate how the intellect can be said to be "in potential" in another sense. But regarding how it is in potential for our present purposes, enough has been said; it has also been distinguished that not every intellect is in potential, but only this specific kind.

# ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

...it turns, and to that extent it turns toward the first intellect <note>The "first intellect" refers to the supreme, divine mind from which all truth originates</note> and its expectations. By this first intellect, the soul's mind and its own **species** <term>Species: In this context, mental "forms" or "concepts" that allow the mind to recognize things</term> are shaped, so that the mind itself becomes more perceptive and its concepts become more lucid. In this state, our intellect is as united as possible with them and is something **consubstantial** <note>original: *consubstantiale*; sharing the same essential nature or substance</note> with the soul. They say something similar regarding the **free act** by which angels turn toward themselves, and through themselves toward God; this is a sign that these species are innate, and that our intellect is naturally joined to the divine. This is because, when the intellect is turned toward itself, it finds all things and is perfected by the divine. **Note here and below** that our intellect is always coupled with the divine. External things do not form the sense, but the **spirit** does. The sense, however, leads the spirit toward such formations by drawing out from itself species or actions that conform to those external things. When we say the "possible intellect" is formed by the "agent intellect," we do not mean that it receives forms from outside, but rather that in the presence of the agent, it is more effectively coupled with its own internal forms. Thus, in the "possible intellect," there is no movement and no "passion" <note>original: *passio*; here meaning "suffering" or "undergoing" a change caused by an external force</note> in the proper sense of the word.

->OF PRISCIAN<-

After this, however, **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> wonders how either our intellect becomes "intelligible things" <note>original: *intelligibilia*; the abstract truths or concepts the mind grasps</note>, or how those intelligibles themselves are made, and what it means to "undergo" something there. For it is necessary that the intellect itself somehow both becomes the intelligibles and that a certain "passion" or undergoing occurs there—if, indeed, the intellect proceeds into action in the same way that the senses do. Nevertheless, it remains a question: what kind of "passion" can be brought from a corporeal nature into an incorporeal thing? Or what transformation occurs between these two, and whether the beginning of this process is given by the object, or rather by the intellect itself? Indeed, the intellect seems to "suffer" or be affected by the object, for of those things that undergo change, none undergoes it from itself. Yet it is also fitting for the principle of all things to belong to the intellect, and it is appropriate for the intellect to understand from itself. Nor is "knowing from oneself" attributed to the intellect in the same way it is to the senses, but rather in a more excellent manner. Thus far are the words of Theophrastus.

In the meantime, however, it becomes the intelligibles. Nor is it exactly like the intellect that is entirely "separate" <note>The "Separate Intellect" is the divine mind that exists independently of human bodies</note>, because its unity is, in a sense, "relaxed," as we have said. And so it is more fully adapted to the intelligibles. By this reasoning, it "undergoes" in a certain way when it has declined from that pure and utterly indivisible union of the "separate intelligibles." It is as if it has departed from that state because it was born together with the soul. Doubtless, it is perfected as one thing by another—both by the "intellect in act" <note>original: *intellectu secundum actum*; the mind when it is actively thinking/knowing</note> and by the intelligibles that are within it. Nevertheless, it also perfects itself, insofar as it "awakens" from within itself and accommodates itself to that active state of understanding, receiving perfection from that state through its own action. This is especially true because it has not entirely withdrawn from that active intellect. Although it "succumbs" to it, it is simultaneously joined to it, as something that is itself also an intellect. And for that reason, it is not distracted toward exterior things, but having entered into itself and turned toward itself, it is joined to itself as much as possible. Thus, finally, it is perfected by that intellect in act.

### ON THEOPHRASTUS

...is perfected by the intellect. Therefore, the mind undergoes experience in a different way than the senses do; it is not "affected" in the strict sense, but equivocally <note>original: *aequivoce*; meaning the word "affected" is being used in a special, non-standard way</note>. It acts rather than being acted upon, since through its own activity it receives perfections from higher realms, rather than receiving the things it understands from the outside. For here, the thing itself exists in a secondary degree, insofar as it is perfected while it is coupled with its own **intelligibles** <term>Intelligibles: Things that can only be understood by the mind, rather than perceived by the senses</term> and is simultaneously joined to higher things. This is because its own properties are not severed from those higher sources.

Hence, these intelligible things act upon the intellect in the same way that sensible things act upon the senses, with this one exception: intelligibles do not come from the outside to do their work. Indeed, they are never separated from the intellect. For this reason, there is a single, unified action for both: for the intellect regarding its concepts, and for the concepts regarding the intellect, insofar as they are not divided from one another. Rather, the intellect *is* those very things which are offered to be understood.

Furthermore, even in the case of the senses, "passion" <note>original: *passio*; in ancient philosophy, this refers to being "acted upon" by an external force, like a wax tablet being pressed by a seal</note> only happens to the physical organ. The primary sensing faculty is perfected by its own action; it does not receive movement from sensible things passively, but actively. Therefore, the intellect acts from itself to an even greater degree. It receives perfection from the things it understands not through "passion," but through action—if indeed it should even be said to "receive" at all, rather than to produce from within itself. For the intellect is perfected by starting from itself. 

In truth, "passion" properly happens only to things that are moved by something else, such as things incited from the outside. But in things that operate entirely from within and are active through and through, we cannot suspect any "passion," unless we use the term loosely. For the intellect—even that which is called the "potential intellect"—is essentially a certain **act** <term>Act: Latin *actus*; the state of being fully "real" or functioning, as opposed to just having the "potential" to function</term>, even if only in a secondary degree. This "act" is the opposite of "passion," and can never be affected passively.

Indeed, regarding incorporeal things that are separate or separable from the body, **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, known for his works on nature and the soul</note> says that neither "passion" nor change can occur. He notes that "passions" usually arise from external things, but the intellect is a primary principle and is self-originating. Thus, it may appear similar to something that "suffers" an experience, although in truth it suffers not at all. For if one excluded all "passion," he says, the intellect would be nothing. In this context, he clearly uses the word "passion" to name the perfection bestowed by the things the mind understands, because he thinks it necessary to keep the intellect entirely pure. 

Meanwhile, because the intellect is perfected by these concepts according to its own activity, he is using a more general name rather than the proper one when he calls it "passion." For the intellect (as Theophrastus says) is devoid of "passion," unless perhaps "passive" is defined differently than usual. It is not "passive" like something movable—for movement is always imperfect—but rather like an "action." These concepts differ, even if we must sometimes use the same words for them; such are the views of Theophrastus.

You see, therefore, that "passion" in the intellect is not understood as a defect, a transformation, or a movement caused by external things, but rather as a specific action belonging to the intellect itself. Again, he considers that one must be forgiven...

# ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> commands, however, that we define what "passion" <note>original: *passio*; in this context, it refers to the state of being "acted upon" or receiving an impression from outside</note> is in the mind. ### Chapter six.
->MARSILIO<-

<margin>d</margin> The intellect in the soul is twofold, and both are called "possible" <note>original: *possibilis*; the capacity of the mind to receive or become all things</note>. The first is an indivisible essence shared by the soul. The second is the power that reasons through discourse <note>logical, step-by-step thinking</note>, which is properly called the "soul." The first always understands in actuality, being formed by the divine mind; the second understands when it turns toward the first. It ceases to understand, however, when it turns away from there toward the senses; and in both, there is a proper and free act. Imagination (Phantasia) is sometimes called "intellect," for this is the final trace of intelligence. Because the rational soul is a particular kind of life, it acts in turns. At times it turns toward divine things, at other times toward fleeting things. Free will <term>Liberum arbitrium: The power of the mind to choose its own direction</term> exists in the intellect, both in the purely intellectual and the rational parts. The intellect, whether intellectual or rational—both of which are within us—begins its act from itself, nor does it have anything prior to itself; that is, according to time. If something else recently moved our intellect, which would otherwise be sluggish on its own, two absurdities would follow: first, something would be prior to this according to time; second, it would not have its own proper action.

->PRISCIANUS<-

<margin>q</margin> It is asked after this why our intellect does not always receive from the higher intellect, nor does it always seem to understand. But in truth, the intellect is always acting. The soul, however, does not always use the intellect that is always present to it, because it clearly turns toward bodies. It truly seems <margin>ne</margin> that Aristotle and Theophrastus <note>The superscript 9 is a common Latin abbreviation for "-us".</note> (as has already been said) sometimes call the entire rational life "intellect," where they extend the name of intellect even as far as the imagination. And so, not without reason, one might ask concerning the soul why it does not always understand. Surely understanding is never interrupted because it lacks the power to understand, but because the soul is distracted toward following things, toward bodies, and entirely outside of itself, due to the condition of a particular life acting in turns toward both. For the entire perfection of the soul consists in the clear return to itself and the turning toward the intellect. On the contrary, however, a fall from the intellect happens in the inclination toward bodies. Not only, indeed, does the intellect...

->ON THEOPHRASTUS<-

### Chapter seven. <margin>MARSILIO'S</margin>

<margin>i</margin> In our intellect, there are things to be understood <note>original: *intelligibilia*</note> that are known in the reason and are innate to us. But the higher intellect acts upon those through a certain eternal act; the soul, however, acts upon its own through a temporal <note>happening within time</note> action via the same action of the intellect—namely, through intelligence. At that point, the intellect itself is at its peak, and the things to be understood are at their peak, and vice versa. Therefore, the intellect is the very things it understands. Also, our intellect, according to its essence, is an "act" <note>it is inherently active rather than passive</note>. Therefore, in the intellect, "to be" is the same as "to act"; for that reason, it always understands. 

But in the soul—that is, in the rational power—essence is one thing and action another; therefore it does not always understand, nor does it always know. Just as our intellect is the "intelligibles," so the rational power is the "knowables" <term>Knowables: Things that can be known through logic or study, as opposed to direct spiritual intuition</term>, although the soul does not always have these in act <note>in a state of active use</note>, as the higher intellect does. Reason draws out the knowables into act through its own action, when the essence of the soul returns into itself. Where the soul is most indivisible, it is the intellect, and "to be" there is "to understand." Where it is no less indivisible, it has attached to it an action of reasoning distinct from its essence, as well as the power of discourse <note>discursive reasoning or step-by-step logic</note>. 

The essence of the soul is both stable and mobile, and its action is similar. Stable action accompanies the stable essence, and mobile action accompanies the mobile essence. The whole soul at once remains still and is moved; likewise, the mobile power revolves around the stable one. Likewise, in the permanent essence of the soul, a certain eternal action lies hidden. The attention of the soul is mostly turned toward things that can be imagined or sensed. But when it returns into itself, it finds the knowables in the rational power, through which it is finally joined to the things to be understood <note>the higher intelligibles</note>, which always flourish in the intellect, even in the animal soul <note>the part of the soul responsible for basic life and sensation</note>. The rational power returns to the intellect; it does not act upon all things at once, but in a certain succession because of its divisible nature. <margin>PRISCIAN'S</margin>

<margin>c</margin> Furthermore, we must ask what nature intends for itself, which Theophrastus subsequently introduces in this manner. For if, he says, the intellect in acting becomes the things themselves, and this is especially true of both, then certainly the things themselves will be the intellect. <meta>This page continues the discussion of how the soul relates to the intellect. The previous page ended by noting that while the higher intellect is always active, the human soul's rational power exists as an essence that is not always engaged in the act of understanding.</meta>

->ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT<-

of the intellect, they are at their peak when the intellect understands. For this reason, he <note>Likely referring to Theophrastus or Aristotle</note> just now said both: if, therefore, the intellect exists when the objects themselves exist, then surely the intellect will be the very objects that are understood. Is it then the case that when it understands nothing—since the object itself is not present to it—the intellect similarly will not exist? But surely that which is truly the intellect, and also that which is called the intellect in potentiality <note>original: *potentia* — the capacity or power to act</note> (namely, that shared by the soul), certainly understands, insofar as it is itself an "act" <note>original: *actus* — an active reality or state of being</note> by its very essence, though on a secondary level. However, in the individual soul itself, there is room for doubt, for the soul does not always understand.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But is the soul nothing at all before it understands? Or is it indeed something, but like a kind of "matter" <note>a passive substance or blank slate</note> which is only formed when it knows things falling upon it from the outside? On the contrary, the soul itself is indeed something even before it knows; and it does not begin from external things, but rather from itself. It produces the things that are to be known, finding the objects within itself insofar as it enters into its own being. Therefore, the soul is the objects themselves within itself before it even knows them.

Since, however, the soul is in a way divided by this reasoning—because it is clearly not an "act" according to its essence, but rather possesses the act of knowledge as something proceeding from its essence—it is certainly the case that just as the soul exists even when it is not actually knowing something, so too the things themselves exist within it; namely, not according to act and action, but rather through essence. For it is necessary to accept the things themselves within the soul in the same order as the soul itself; not indeed because these things are always being understood, but because the mind acts in a "knowable" way, and these knowable things are produced according to the action following and originating from the essence. 

Indeed, in the soul, neither "being" nor "acting" is simple and uniform; rather, one part is permanent and the other is mobile. While a mobile power proceeds around a permanent power, the whole soul is meanwhile weighed according to both; and for that reason, the soul both remains still and moves at the same time. At the same time, it also always acts according to a hidden action that is innate to its permanent essence, and according to a life that progresses outward and is changeable. When the soul turns itself entirely toward these subsequent and divisible things, it operates upon them, using "opinion" along with "sense." At that time, it is not turned toward those things which (if I may say so) are called "knowables" <note>original: *scibilia* — truths that can be known through the use of reason</note>, which are the things themselves within the soul. Much less is it then turned toward those things called "intellectibles" <note>original: *intelligibilia* — higher, divine truths understood by the pure intellect</note>, to which it is coupled through those very knowables as if by a single continuum or union. Now, however, when the soul recalls its produced (and sometimes progressed) life and action back toward those things that remain within itself, it does not act upon all things at once, but now upon these, then upon those, clearly because of its divisible nature.

<header>ON THEOPHRASTUS</header>

### Chapter eight.
->MARSILIO<-

Rational power <note>original: *potentia rationalis* — the human capacity for reasoning</note> is said to proceed into "act" <note>original: *in actum* — the state of being active or fully realized</note> not because it receives new forms—for it always possesses all of them—but because it now exercises those which it did not exercise before. Theophrastus <note>A student of Aristotle and a philosopher of the Peripatetic school</note> says that if the intellect were like "matter" <note>a passive, blank slate</note> simply in potentiality, it would undergo a certain essential change whenever it understood something by receiving new forms. This is absurd. What Theophrastus says regarding our intellectual intellect, Priscianus <note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century Neoplatonist</note> also applies in a certain way to the rational intellect; therefore, the latter neither receives new forms nor is it "moved" <note>changed or affected</note> here; it indeed receives nothing new, but rather moves within its own forms.

->PRISCIANUS<-

Therefore, when we say that potentiality and act exist in the soul, we understand this according to a shift, or certainly when that proceeding action—by which knowledge is held—is not present. In that case, we say that this permanent essence is "in potentiality" as the producer of such action; the soul then exists as the very things themselves, yet it does not act according to that proceeding action. Although it does not know all things at once, but rather some at one time and others at another, it is not for that reason "one thing" at one time and "another" at another. It is never "not the same," because it is not changed in every respect; instead, there is something in the soul that remains permanent meanwhile, and according to this very thing, the objects of knowledge have always remained in the soul. 

Theophrastus says it would be absurd if the intellect were "in potentiality" in such a way that nothing existed in "act," but once placed in "act," it became something else, and then something else again when it was not understanding itself. For in this way, because it would understand one thing after another, it would never be the same. But truly, a nature of that kind—indiscriminate and lacking order—would clearly refute those who thought that the intellect is indeed "all things in potentiality" but "nothing in act." First of all, when it was not understanding, it would be nothing. Secondly, even if it did understand other things, it would not have understood itself. It would be something else and not at all the same, but different at different times, and thus it would be perpetually changed. For this reason, he says, one must not understand "potentiality" and "act" in the intellect in the same way as in matter, but (as was said before) where he judged that these two must be placed according to a certain comparison of proportion. In no way should these be affirmed in the intellect as they are in matter.

### Chapter nine.
->MARSILIO<-

The intellect of a living being is not mixed with the body; therefore, it is not formed by the senses. The rational power, which is innate to this intellect, also does not receive new forms, but rather exercises its own forms through a certain succession.

<header>ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT</header>

The rational nature includes within the formal logic of its essence the forms of all knowable things. Although the Soul <note>original: *Anima*</note> may migrate from potentiality into act <note>the state of being fully active or realized</note>, it does not thereby become something else, because it does not put on a new form; rather, it displays a new action.

->OF PRISCIAN<- <note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote a famous commentary on the works of Theophrastus.</note>

**T**herefore, when he says the intellect is "this specific something," he adds this point: that the senses are not equal to it in this regard. For the sense—as he now argues—does not exist without the body, whereas the intellect is separated from the body. Because of this, the intellect does not require those things which proceed from the outside for its own perfection. Thus, even when the soul is in the process of knowing, nothing actually exists in the interim <note>as an external object</note>; all things exist according to an essential and permanent perfection, even if, meanwhile, the action itself—the production and application of that knowledge—should be absent or fail. Therefore, insofar as it relates to this action, the soul is then judged to be "in potentiality." Yet truly, because it is born together with all knowable things, when it has known something, and thus exists "in act," that which is known is not something different from the soul itself. Indeed, the soul determines its own essence there according to all knowable things. Nevertheless, it seems to "become" in a certain way; for it becomes individual things in the same way that a person is said to be "knowing in act." We say this happens when the soul is able to act according to its own nature. Certainly, it is even then in potentiality in a certain way, but not in the same way as when it had neither learned nor discovered the knowledge.

### Chapter ten.

->OF MARSILIO<- <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Italian Renaissance philosopher who translated and commented on these works.</note>

**I**n the intellect, nothing new is born; in the soul, at least, a new act and a "habit" <note>original: *habitus* — a stable disposition or state of having acquired knowledge</note> are born through action. For the intellectual nature is uniform and stable, but the nature of the soul <note>original: *natura animalis*</note>, in addition to these two traits, also possesses their opposites. For it is, moreover, multiform and mobile; indeed, motion pertains to the very definition and nature of the soul. The rational soul, because it is the "middle point" of things and is mobile by its own nature, therefore alternates between extremes, especially because it is a particular form of life. The rational power sometimes turns itself toward the intellect, and sometimes toward the senses.

->OF PRISCIAN<-

It seems, rather, that it is the habit, and this generation of the habit, which approaches the soul to complete its nature. The soul "becomes," therefore, in a certain way, because it is not as uniform and simple as we judge intellectual things to be, nor is it entirely stable like them; rather, it remains the same while simultaneously having an innate capacity for change, and toward...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the soul’s dual nature—how it can be both a single, unchanging essence and a changing source of various thoughts and actions. # ON THEOPHRASTUS

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

[The soul] plays both roles, since it is both at the center of things and has a life defined by motion. For this reason, it is sometimes carried toward ignorance, insofar as it leans toward the lower; and sometimes it is perfected by the gift of knowledge, insofar as it turns toward the higher. Therefore, it becomes imperfect at one time and perfect at another. Whenever it is ignorant, it is judged to be imperfect and is therefore said to be "in potentiality" <note>original: *in potentia*; the state of having the capacity for something without yet exercising it</note>, because even then it possesses the power of knowing. Whenever it truly knows, it is judged to be perfect. 

Then, indeed, insofar as it acts, it claims perfection for itself from the act itself. But insofar as it does not always act even when it knows something, it is even then judged to be in potentiality. This, however, is not the same condition as before it learned or discovered; for now it possesses the "habit" <note>original: *habitum*; a stable disposition or acquired skill, like knowing a language even when one is sleeping</note>, and it has perfected that power of its own which is accustomed to producing the acts of knowledge.

Therefore, when Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> asks in what way generation <note>the process of coming into being</note> occurs in the soul—whether of habit and power, or of essence—he should be understood to be asking this: whether a change occurs in the soul only according to its habit and power, or also according to its very essence <note>original: *essentiam*; the fundamental nature or "what-it-is" of a thing</note>.

->Chapter Eleven.<-
->MARSILIO.<- <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Florentine philosopher translating and commenting on this text.</note>

Our soul is also changeable in a certain way according to its essence. Otherwise, if its essence were entirely immutable <note>unchanging</note>, it would not produce actions so diverse and changeable that they tend toward opposites. Likewise, there is one soul in us in its essence. That which is in itself entirely immutable does not produce actions that are sometimes right and sometimes perverse. If there were two essences of souls in us, disconnected from each other, and one did not depend on the other, the living being would not be a single unit. The intellectual soul <note>original: *anima intellectualis*</note> would not be the ruler of the bodily life unless the latter depended upon the former. There is a single essence in which there is an intellectual and rational power, and a power that discourses <note>moves through a logical argument</note> in whatever way. He [Theophrastus] seems here to place the intellect, reason, and imagination in the same essence of the soul. Because of this union, this is a single living being, and the lower powers are referred back to a single principle in the soul. There is a single essence of the soul in each one of us, and this is simultaneously immutable and mutable; in whatever change of the soul occurs, that life which is its own and rational remains.

->PRISCIAN.<- <note>Priscian of Lydia, whose commentary Ficino is following.</note>

Since, therefore, habits and acts come from the essence, it is impossible to posit a certain essence that is entirely permanent, secreted from all change, and always holding itself in the same way, which nevertheless occasionally produces perfect and good actions, but at other times produces imperfect and perverse ones. For actions correspond to the essence; and therefore, just as the actions are, so also is the power...

...and we rightly conjecture that the appearance of the essence is the same. If anyone, however, were to devise a double essence within us, along with double powers and actions, and should think some are always perfect in themselves, while others are sometimes imperfect and sometimes perfect, then if he understands these as distinct, he will make one animal into many animals. Furthermore, he would entirely set aside the more excellent essence as if it were neither the ruler of life nor had anything in common with it—if indeed it is through the second essence that the alternation between the imperfect and the perfect is achieved, by which human life is defined.

We must avoid making our nature similar to a choir or some other multitude in this way; instead, let all things come together into one, and, having been fused into a single principle, let them breathe together in harmony. 

Regarding this "one," we shall immediately ask whether it is uniform, always immutable, and whole. For if that is admitted at the outset, it would follow that there is never any imperfection, or any depravity, or any passion in animals, whether according to their essence or their action. For actions follow essence. Nevertheless, we must not concede that this "one" is entirely changeable either; for life itself remains through all changes.

## Chapter Twelve.

### MARSILIO’S <note>Refers to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Italian Neoplatonic philosopher who translated and commented on these Greek texts.</note>

Our soul, because it is the mean <note>original: *media*; the bridge or middle point</note> between things that are entirely stable and those that are mobile, therefore possesses an essence that is both stable and mobile. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD)</note>, on the composition of the soul and the alternation of lives: in the soul there is a certain change not only according to its dispositions, but in a certain way even according to its essence, insofar as it varies the forms of the intellectual or rational fire—now living as a terrestrial man, then as an aerial one, and at other times as an ethereal one <note>Ancient philosophy often categorized beings by the element they inhabited: Earth (terrestrial), Lower Air (aerial), or the Upper Heavens (ethereal).</note>. Iamblichus, however, allows for the smallest possible amount.

### Chapter Thirteen.

-> BY MARSILIO <-

<margin>r</margin>
Immaterial things possess nothing in themselves unless it necessarily pertains to their essence. Material things, beyond essential traits, undergo many accidental ones. Our intellect knows both through **innate forms**, which represent immaterial things as if they were their kin, but material things as if they were their causes. Aristotle and Theophrastus [wrote] concerning things separated from matter and things joined to it. Iamblichus and Plutarch are commentators on Aristotle. The "possible intellect" <term>intellectus possibilis: the capacity of the human mind to receive and process new information</term> in us is twofold: one is primary and always in activity; the other is secondary, passing from potentiality into activity—that is, reason <note>original: *ratio*</note>. Reason, when it does not wander through the imagination and the senses, finds the innate "reasons" <term>rationes: the logical blueprints or principles of things</term> of things by turning toward itself. These innate reasons are the siblings of the "separated substances" <note>purely spiritual beings or intellects</note>, and they are either the causes of material things or are similar to those causes. The **agent intellect** <term>intellectus agens: the active power of the mind that "illuminates" thoughts and makes understanding possible</term>, seeing itself, beholds all things according to their cause.

-> BY PRISCIANUS <-

<margin>d</margin>
Next, Theophrastus, just as Aristotle does, posits two kinds of species: some indeed are immaterial, others truly material. And regarding species separated from matter, he says that "each thing itself" and "the being of that thing itself" are the same. When he says "its being," he designates the formal reason and the species; but when he says "each thing itself," he signifies the whole substance. In species existing without matter, he thinks the whole substance exists according to the formal reason and species alone. However, in material species, he wishes "each thing itself" to be one thing, and its "being" to be another. For "the good" is understood in the first sense according to both [matter and form] joined together, while the other is understood according to the species. Therefore, since the intellect which is called "potential" contemplates both kinds of species, Theophrastus inquires along with Aristotle how it contemplates both, and how it knows species existing in matter through a certain abstraction. ...[continues from previous]. Therefore, the legitimate interpreters of Aristotle—Iamblichus and Plutarch, born of Nestorius <note>referring to Plutarch of Athens, the Neoplatonist teacher of Syrianus and Proclus</note>—have distinguished these things more clearly. We must also comment briefly on these matters, judging the questions raised. I assert, therefore, that the intellect in potential <term>intellectus in potentia: the capacity of the human mind to receive and process information before it is actually engaged in thought</term>—both that which is shared by the soul and the rational power itself—whenever it uses reason purely and is not stretched toward external things alongside sensation and imagination <note>original: *phantasia*</note>, then it contemplates the immaterial forms and principles <note>original: *species rationesque*</note> implanted within itself. According to these very forms, it thinks both of things separated from matter and those distinct from matter. The former it contemplates according to a certain identity (if I may put it so) and a common union among immaterial forms; the latter, however, as though from that cause which they resemble. For just as that intellect in act <term>intellectus in actu: the mind when it is actively engaged in the process of thinking</term>, while it understands itself, knows all the things following beneath it—inasmuch as it is the things themselves by way of their cause—and apprehends the effects from such causes in a more excellent way than they exist in themselves; so too does the intellect in potential, at a subsequent level, perceive material things from those causes closest to it within itself. It contemplates the immaterial principles of material things that are implanted within it.

## Chapter Fourteen. MARSILIO'S [COMMENTARY].

Sensation knows only accidents <term>accidentia: properties like color, heat, or shape that can change without changing the identity of the object</term> and particulars. The intellect, however, knows universally; it likewise knows essential principles <note>original: *rationes essentiales*</note> and the accidents following from them, all through infinite principles. It knows immaterial things as if they were joined to these principles, but <margin>material things</margin> as if they were produced from them. The principles implanted in the soul look upon material things as causes, and upon immaterial things either as kin or as effects. Natural species <note>original: *species naturales*; the essential blueprints of things in nature</note>, although they do not exist truly outside of individuals, are nevertheless thought of without the individual accidents being thought of. Likewise, if reason thinks out mathematical figures without specific matter, it nevertheless knows that they can never exist without matter.

### BY PRISCIANUS.

The intellect indeed knows material things, but not in the same way as sense. For <margin>sense</margin> sense touches things as particulars according to their qualities—such as things being hot, or cold, or white, or something else of that same kind. The intellect of the rational life, however, knows essences according to the common species of material things. Will the intellect, therefore, not know that fire is hot? Certainly, all qualities and accidents proceed from each individual essence. On this account, the intellect—which has known the essence—also knows the accidents through the very principles of that essence, and knows them even more excellently than sense does. But to return to the proposal...

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

In this way, each soul perceives both kinds of forms: those that are material and those that are entirely independent of matter. Certainly—as has been said—it perceives both according to the principles <term>rationes: the inherent logical structures or "seeds of knowledge" implanted in the soul</term> belonging to the soul itself. However, it perceives immaterial things as if they were joined to the principles within it, or as being superior to them; whereas it perceives material things as if they were their effects, or as things known by "taking away" through abstraction <note>original: *abstractione*</note>. In a certain sense, these abstracted forms are the same as the material species, but they are thought out by us according to their own nature—that is, they are not thought of alongside matter. For they do not exist in a separate state, nor are they understood as if they claimed their own essence in a separate way. Rather, when we think of them together with matter, we call them "material." But when we recognize them as the forms alone—knowing all the while that they exist in matter and cannot exist otherwise—we are then perceiving them through abstraction.

## Chapter Fifteen.
->MARSILIO<-

The same intellectual power in us knows both immaterial and material things, and these latter it knows either universally or individually. It performs all of this through innate principles, which it uses toward immaterial things as if they were of the same origin <note>original: *germanis*</note>, or as if they were their effects; toward material things, however, it uses these principles as their causes.

->PRISCIANUS<-

Does the soul, therefore, judge material and immaterial things by some different power, or through a different mode? And similarly, does it judge those things found entirely in matter differently from those perceived through abstraction? Or is it rather the same power acting in a similar way? Perhaps both are true. For the same judge can distinguish between different things. Indeed, the intellectual faculty itself, while remaining the same and acting in the same way, accomplishes this: for according to its own principles, it acts in a certain sense as a different faculty, or at least as if it were in a different state. This is because it contemplates its own principles either as causes (when it thinks of material things through them) or as being joined to immaterial things, or as if they were produced by intellectual forms <note>original: *intellectualibus speciebus*</note>. And in this way, it contemplates through its own principles to such an extent that they have effectively become different or behave differently.

They are absolute and identical with the forms because there is no division, since they are forms and are truly intelligible because of their separation from matter. Therefore, these intellects are separate. It is necessary that material species exist in them, because...

...are imperfect, to be immaterial. Whatever is separated from matter immediately becomes intelligible, just as the intellect is. The intellect appears indivisible because it turns back into itself. Likewise, it is full of forms because, having turned back into itself, it finds all things. There are three orders of separate substances, and three of intellects. There are supermundane <term>supermundani: intellects existing beyond the physical universe</term> intellects who are solely contemplators. Then there are intellects that are indeed supermundane but serve as the rulers of celestial souls. Third, there are the mundane intellects—that is, the celestial souls. Similarly, there is both an active and a possible intellect <term>intellectus agens and possibilis: the "active" intellect which produces thought and the "possible" or "potential" intellect which receives it</term> within the rational soul. Thirdly, there is the rational power itself, which is also called "intellect." The rational soul, through the office of reason, testifies that it is also separate and full of forms, insofar as it freely begins its own act, gathers itself to itself, and in this way finds all things.

### PRISCIANUS

In every way, just as things themselves are separated from matter, so Aristotle and Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school</note> believe the conditions surrounding the intellect to be. Perhaps, therefore, their opinion should be explained in this way: just as material species <term>species: the mental forms or "images" of things</term> are separated from matter by thought alone, and thus are judged by a different faculty and in a different manner—as if they were grasped and discerned through thought alone—so too the species implanted in the potential intellect are separated by it through understanding alone. For, according to its essence, the intellect always exists together with these forms. This is so much the case that we may say the intellect is "in potentiality," and yet we perceive nothing in act, because we do so only through understanding. Either those words of Aristotle and Theophrastus mean this (for this is how Plutarch <note>Plutarch of Athens, a Neoplatonist philosopher who commented on Aristotle</note> explains it), or rather they mean what I shall add below.

Just as those things said to be "separated from matter" are in some cases truly separate (existing in an entirely different matter), while others are separate only through the understanding (such as things perceived by abstraction), so too are both kinds understood. Some are understood as truly separate, while others are understood as separate if they are disconnected by some thought, yet they subsist in no other way than—so to speak—materially. But perhaps we shall explain it better in this way: just as we arrange things that are entirely separate from matter, so it is fitting to arrange those things which pertain to the intellect. We should not perhaps assume that these processes happen according to thought alone, but that they occur properly and principally. Nor should we assume that just as those immaterial forms are truly separate from matter, so too the intellect is entirely segregated from matter so that it may be understood...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the intellect and its relationship to immaterial forms. It builds upon the previous argument that for the soul to understand the world, it must possess internal principles that are not bound by physical matter.</meta>

<header>ON THEOPHRASTUS</header>
<meta>catchword: enlightened (original: "illuminatus")</meta>

Truly, before and above material forms <term>species: here meaning the essential "forms" or "patterns" of things that give them their identity</term>, it is necessary for immaterial forms to exist and to subsist within themselves in an intelligible way (if I may put it that way). Indeed, because these forms are indivisible and are entirely filled with life and knowledge through their union, it is said that they possess neither a void of life nor ignorance by way of privation <term>privatio: the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</term>; for privation usually occurs only when there is a mixing with matter. Since, therefore, these forms are free from matter, they are immediately intellectual. It is clear that they exist in the intellect, and that the intellect itself is entirely free from matter, having received its essence along with these immaterial forms. This is because life and knowledge, which turn back upon themselves, are indivisible—especially since the intellect, by entering into itself, finds true beings.

However, among things that are truly separate from the parts of matter, there is a certain difference according to a descending order. Some are entirely indivisible; others exist with a certain unfolding <term>explicatio: the "unfolding" or manifestation of complex ideas into simpler, sequential thoughts</term>; and finally, others are intermediate between these, acting as indivisibles that merely determine the limits of what is unfolded. The intellect itself is arranged in this same way. At the first level is that which is called the "active intellect" <term>intellectus secundum actum: the intellect in its state of full, perfected operation</term>, which is entirely separate from matter. At the second level is the "potential intellect" <term>intellectus secundum potentiam: the "possible" intellect which has the capacity to receive knowledge</term>, which is designated as such and participated in by the soul, along with the rational soul itself. For although the rational soul functions through an "unfolding" of thought, it nevertheless gathers both itself and other things into a single indivisible point. This soul begins its work from within itself; it finds things within itself, and finds them to be true. It is therefore separate from matter and full of separate rational principles.

<margin>t</margin> Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was Aristotle's successor; here, his views on the soul are being analyzed</note> reminds us again in a very philosophical manner how we should properly understand this very point: that what we call "the thing understood" exists both in the intellect in potentiality <term>potentia: the capacity to be something</term> and in the intellect in a state of actuality <term>actus: the state of being fully realized or active</term>. ## Chapter Eighteen.

### FROM MARSILIO.

<margin>1</margin> When the **possible intellect** <term>intellectus possibilis: the part of the mind that is "open" to receiving knowledge</term> first exists, it is itself all the species <term>species: the essential mental forms or patterns of things</term> according to its essence; therefore, it does not receive them from the **agent intellect** <note>The "active" intellect which illuminates the mind, often associated with a divine light</note>. Instead, it possesses from eternity a perfect union with those species and of those species with one another. **Reason**, however, receives its union from the intellect within time. The possible intellect is said to be "empty of forms," as it were, because unless it is united with its forms by the agent, it behaves as if it did not possess them. For it does not see them unless it is perfectly united to them. Note here and below that the possible intellect takes its perfection from the agent through its own free and deliberate act, and thus perfects itself. The possible intellect is always coupled with the agent and is always formed in actuality. Reason is not always coupled with the intellect; similarly, reason is coupled to the intellect through its own proper and free act, and thereby perfects itself.

### Chapter Nineteen.
### Every form separated from matter is far from privation, motion, and division.

### FROM MARSILIO.

Because of the first <note>the first principle of form</note>, there resides within an "all-formed" life, which is also a master of intelligence; because of the second, it understands while remaining within itself, and therefore, by understanding itself as containing all forms, it understands all things. Because of the third, all forms exist there simultaneously within one another, and that which understands and that which is understood are entirely the same. 

When he <note>likely Plotinus or Theophrastus</note> says that corporeal things for the most part perceive themselves, he seems to exclude certain ones. For there are those who would have it that celestial bodies perceive themselves by their own light. A form separated from matter, since it is a perfect form—whether it is called "intelligible" <note>perceivable by the mind</note> or a "perfect intelligible"—is that which is united to the intellect. Similarly, if it is called "intellect," it is likewise perfect in the intellect. Such an intellect is one that is united to the object of its understanding. 

Our intellect always possesses a simple and stable intuition, but **reason** <term>ratio: the logical, step-by-step processing of the mind</term> possesses **discourse** <term>discursus: the process of moving from one premise to another to reach a conclusion</term>. Within reason is **science** <term>scientia: certain knowledge acquired through demonstration and logic</term>, which is knowledge acquired through this discourse. Reason, when it is about to know something, recalls its discourse to those internal principles <note>original: "rationes"</note> through which it knows things; while it knows them, it is said to possess the known things within itself. Indeed, Plotinus says that reason, through these innate principles, is all things according to potentiality. When it exercises a specific principle in "act," then the soul itself actually persuades the reason and effects this very thing. Reason, through its innate forms...

## PRISCIANUS.

After this, where Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school</note> explains Aristotle’s statement that separate and immaterial things are the same as the intellect, while in material things, each of the objects of thought exists only in a certain **potentiality** <term>potentiality: the capacity for something to exist or happen, which has not yet become a reality</term>. And he [Theophrastus] distinguishes such sayings point by point—noting that the mind is not present in these [material things]—directs them, and meanwhile expresses certain doubts. To help us grasp these points more clearly, we will first arrange Aristotle’s words point by point and very briefly. Since, he says, some things are in matter, while others are without matter—such as incorporeal and separate substances <note>original: "separatæque substantiæ"; in this context, these are "separate" from physical bodies, like souls or divine beings</note>—in separate things, the one who understands is the same as the thing understood. For the intellect is not stretched out toward external things, but remaining within itself, it understands the things themselves. Therefore, it is the same as the things it understands. 

Furthermore, since all immaterial things are indivisible and full of life and knowledge, they are undoubtedly considered to be intellectual in nature. For sensible things [objects of the senses], because of their material division, must be perceived by others, but for the most part, they cannot perceive themselves at all. But things entirely free of matter, being intelligible, differ from sensible things in this way: they are not torn away from the one who understands, nor are they perfected by external things. Instead, they are intelligible of themselves by a perfect principle. For this reason, they are also "understanding" things; and since they are **impartible** <term>impartible: indivisible; having no parts that can be separated</term>, they are united to the one who understands in an indivisible way. 

And since, moreover, they are entirely intelligible throughout their whole being, they are deservedly united to the intellect entirely throughout. They are not intelligible by accident, but according to their very essence. And they are perfect according to their essence; because they exist as perfect according to their own essence, they are undoubtedly the same as the objects of thought. And at the same time they are "understanding" things, so that through themselves they are both objects of thought and the most perfect understanding subjects. Accordingly, Aristotle also reminded us, by looking at knowledge itself, that in separate things, that which understands is the same as that which is understood. For **speculative knowledge** <term>speculative knowledge: from the Latin 'speculari' (to observe); theoretical or contemplative knowledge aimed at truth for its own sake</term>, he says, and that which is knowable in such a way, are the same thing. That is, knowledge not at all stretched out toward external things, but remaining
