If, therefore, knowledge and the knowable are the same, and even more so the one who understands and that which is understood are united, then certainly the intellect is judged to be the same as the things understood.

### Chapter Twenty.

<margin>¶</margin>That which is material is not intelligible of itself, but only insofar as it is set free from material conditions by the intellect. Therefore, it does not become intelligible to itself, but to the intellect that abstracts it. On the contrary, a thing separated from matter by its own nature is intelligible of itself, and to itself as an intelligible thing. In separate things, therefore, the intellect and the understood object concur in the same form. The intellect knows material things, not through them, but through their principles innate to the intelligence, as if through causes. According to Theophrastus and Aristotle, the intellect is immaterial, yet it is a certain power <note>original: "potentia"</note> over material things. This is explained in three ways: two actively, one as if passively. First, the intellect is the power productive of its own acts or actions regarding material things. Second, not by equality of nature, but by an overriding power, it knows material things through its own forms as if through causes. Third, it also knows material things insofar as it has been formed by the light of the **active intellect** <term>active intellect: the part of the mind that makes understanding possible by "lighting up" concepts, similar to how light makes colors visible</term>. Immaterial things are always naturally present to the intellect. Material things, however, become present insofar as they are resolved from matter by the intellect. Knowledge in act becomes the same as the thing known in act, even in the very discourse of reason. Much more so in the state of intelligence itself, the one understanding and the understood are the same. Indeed, the intellect itself, according to its essence, is those very forms which are understood by it.

# ON THEOPHRASTUS BY PRISCIANUS

The intellect knows immaterial things as if they were joined to itself. However, it perceives material things as inferior, insofar as it notices within itself the innate causes of those forms, as though they were the material causes. The **active intellect** <term>active intellect: the part of the mind that is always "on," providing the light of reason to make things understandable</term> is in no way created. The **first potential intellect** <term>potential intellect: the capacity of the soul to receive and store knowledge</term> within us is never in the process of becoming, but is always already made—that is, it is formed by the agent. The **second potential intellect** within us—that is, **reason**—is always becoming; that is, it is formed daily into **act** <term>act: the state of actually functioning or being real, as opposed to just being a possibility</term> through the higher intellect and its own discourse toward it, or at least it brings forth innate forms from idleness into action. This opinion regarding a triple intellect and a certain eternal act of intelligence within us is frequently approved by Plotinus and Iamblichus.

<margin>c</margin> Since these things are so, he <note>Theophrastus</note> rightly signified the same in the timely middle of the discussion with these words: "Why then," he asks, "do we not always understand? If indeed both the one who understands and that which is understood are within us—for they are both the same." We must therefore consider this as soon as possible with all our strength. In those things, then, which are separated from matter, the one who understands and that which is understood are the same, just as we said above. However, in those things which exist with matter, each of the knowable things exists in **potentiality**. For material things are not knowable in themselves, nor according to their essence, nor do they share the same rank as the intellect, nor are they known as if joined to it. How then are they said to be knowable according to potentiality?

For if they are such in potentiality, they will also eventually be knowable in act. They will indeed be such at some point, but perhaps not joined [to the intellect]; rather, they will be known according to their causes placed within the intellect. And since they possess the same property as their causes, they too are called "knowable," but knowable by a certain potentiality. This is because the one who understands them towers above them, and they are understood by him according to a superior cause; they are not knowable to themselves or by themselves. For they do not understand themselves. For this reason, he brings forward the following: "Therefore, the intellect is not present in them"—meaning in material things. For this reason, they are not knowable to themselves or by themselves, because these are material, while the intellect exists as immaterial. "For without matter," as he says, "the intellect of such things is itself potentiality."

Of these things, that which is said to be "without matter" shows the nature of the intellect to be completely devoid of matter. Moreover, the "intellect of material things" is potentiality—either as the cause of actions (as Plutarch <note>Plutarch of Athens, the Neoplatonist</note> explains it), or as understanding these things not as joined to it but by a certain more eminent condition. Because these things are contemplated from their cause, or the intellect in potentiality is itself the potentiality of such things, as if it were also understanding these things according to perfection from a higher source...

But when the intellect perceives the things within itself—not just as they are, but as the causes of material things—then the material things are also present to the intellect according to their cause. I would not affirm that these things were said about the intellect when considered as being "in act." For that intellect is not a potentiality, nor can it ever be "made."

# ON THEOPHRASTUS

[...casting away] the lusts of the body, which are all fleeting and falling, they set out with a common zeal and with the full fire of the mind to grasp and cultivate the one stable virtue of the soul. Our Plato, that master and leader of all philosophers, wished for the virtue of the soul to be called wisdom <term>wisdom: *sapientia* in Latin, which for Neoplatonists meant a deep, lived understanding of divine truths rather than just factual knowledge</term>. Indeed, he judged wisdom to be the knowledge of divine things. 

Furthermore, in his books on the Republic, he demonstrates that divine things can only become known to our mind by God illuminating us, just as the forms of bodies are seen by the eyes only when the sun illuminates those eyes. Therefore, God is that very same one whom we desire to see: He who illuminates the mind’s eye so that we may look upon Him, and who finally shows Himself to the brightened mind. By showing Himself, He delights us; God is likewise the way, the truth, and the life for us. 

He is the Way, because He turns us toward Himself with His rays, and leads and carries us away. He is the Truth, because He reveals Himself as true to us when we are turned toward Him. He is Life, finally, because He perpetually feeds and delights our soul—the contemplator of Himself—with that blessed vision. All who desire to taste the sweetest liquids of wisdom must thirst for this perennial fountain of all wisdom. All who desire to obtain the virtue of the soul must follow wisdom; thus it follows that all who set out to cultivate their soul are compelled to worship God <note>original: "Deum colere compellantur"; here *cultus* implies both cultivation of the mind and religious worship</note>. 

In earlier sections, we defined friends as those who strive toward virtue with a similar and equal zeal and cultivate their souls with mutual favor. The cultivation of the soul consists in virtue alone. Virtue is wisdom, wisdom is the knowledge of divine things, and the divine light grants us such knowledge. Therefore, the cultivation of the soul is the worship of God himself. 

Since friendship strives through the consensus of two people to cultivate the soul through virtue, it seems to be nothing other than the supreme harmony of two souls in worshiping God. However, all who worship God with a pious mind are loved by God. Therefore, there are not just two, but necessarily three friends always present: namely, two humans and one God. God, I say—Jupiter, the god of hospitality <note>original: "Iupiter hospitalis"</note>; Jupiter, the god of friendship <note>original: "Iupiter amicabilis"</note>; Jupiter, the savior of human life, whom Plato always worshipped and Socrates always honored. 

He is the leader of human life; He reconciles us into one; He is the unbreakable knot of friendship and its perpetual guardian. With this God as the reconciler, those ancient theologians whose memory we venerate are said to have entered into the holy bond of friendship with one another. ## The Book of Alcinous the Platonist philosopher, on the doctrine of Plato.

### Chapter one: what philosophy is, and what the philosophical nature is like.

This doctrine of the primary teachings of Plato is handed down as follows. Philosophy is the longing <term>longing: *appetitio*, suggesting a natural drive or hunger</term> for wisdom. Or, it is the release of the soul from the body, and a certain turning toward those things which are true and divine. Wisdom <note>original: "sapientia"</note> is the knowledge of divine and human things. A philosopher, moreover, is one who takes his name from philosophy, just as a musician does from music. And he who is to be a philosopher must be so constituted by nature itself that, first of all, he is apt and ready <note>The Latin text ends mid-word: "prō[mptus]"</note> for all kinds of disciplines...

## Chapter Second: The philosopher prefers contemplation to action.

Since there are two lives—namely the contemplative and the active—and the duty of the contemplative consists in the knowledge of truth, while the active consists in the performance of those things which reason dictates, the contemplative life is indeed to be honored. However, that life which is engaged in action is a handmaiden and a servant of necessary things. That this is so will be made clear from the following: Contemplation is the operation of the divine mind understanding; Action, however, is the operation of the rational soul completed through the body. For the soul, contemplating the divine and divine intelligence, is said to be affected in the best possible way. And this affection is called wisdom <note>original: *sapientia*</note>, which indeed ought to be called nothing other than a likeness to God. For this reason, an operation of this kind is primary and venerable, and to be sought after most of all, and is especially proper to man, as no obstacles stand in the way of it remaining in our power; it is also the cause of our proposed end. 

The active life and its actions, however, since they use the service of the body extensively, are frequently impeded, and those who live it desire to transfer those things which the contemplative life observes into the duties of character. For a man devoted to learning only then betakes himself to civil administration when he perceives it being poorly handled by other men, regarding military service, embassies, and the execution of judgments as if they were certain external aids; but the primary and greatest of all duties to be performed are establishing laws for the republic, prescribing order, and the discipline of those who must be educated...

### Chapter Three: The philosopher is occupied with three things: namely, the contemplation of things, moral action, and the art of discourse.

Plato certainly wished for the philosopher's study to be occupied with three principal areas: the speculation of things, the practice of virtues, and the consideration of speech. The knowledge of things is called **contemplative**; the study of morals is **active**; and the care of speech is **dialectical**. 

Dialectic is indeed distributed into many species: division, definition, induction, and reasoning <note>original: *ratiocinationem*</note>. This reasoning is further divided into **demonstration**, which is necessary reasoning; **ostension**, which is called probable reasoning; and the **rhetorical enthymeme**, that is, a cautious thought, which is called imperfect reasoning. Finally, there are **sophisms** <note>Arguments that seem true but are actually false or misleading.</note>, to which the legitimate philosopher will apply his effort, not because he approves of them as primary, but because he judges that they will occasionally be necessary to recognize. 

Furthermore, of that philosophy which is concerned with action, the first part cares for the morals of the man himself. The second governs the home, and the last protects the state; the first is called **moral**, the second **domestic**, and the third **civil**. 

Regarding that philosophy which is devoted to contemplation, one part investigates immobile and divine things and the primary causes of things, which we call **theology**. Another observes the movement of the stars, their circuits and heavenly revolutions, and the order of the world, which is named **natural knowledge**. This is followed by **mathematics**, which contains geometry and arithmetic. 

Since philosophy is distributed into these three principal species—contemplative, active, and dialectical—we must first treat dialectic itself, exploring what Plato thinks of it, and specifically concerning the faculty of judgment.

### Chapter Four: On the faculty of judgment, and the powers of the soul pertaining to judgment.

Since there is something that judges and something that is judged, it is necessary that something also arises from both, which we can properly call a judgment; thus, the faculty of judgment itself is named. More commonly, however, that which judges is also called the judgment. 

Furthermore, the "judging" element appears to be twofold: one is that *by which* <note>the agent</note> and the other is that *through which* <note>the instrument</note> something is judged. The former is our **intellect**, while the latter is a **natural organ**; it judges true things in the first place and false things in the second. This is nothing other than **natural reason**. If we wish to explain this even more clearly, the "judge" should be called the **philosopher**, by whom the things themselves are judged; the "judge" is likewise **reason**, through which the truth is also judged, which we have called the instrument.

# ALCINOUS

Reason is indeed twofold: one is utterly incomprehensible <note>Inaccessible to human minds</note> and true, while the other is infallible according to the knowledge of things. The first belongs to God; to man, not at all. The second is suitable for man. But this human reason is also twofold: one part looks toward **intelligible things** <note>Things understood by the mind alone, such as mathematical truths or the "Forms"</note>, and the other toward **sensible things** <note>Physical things perceived through the five senses</note>. The first is called **science** <note>original: *scientia*; meaning certain, demonstrative knowledge</note>, while the second is called **opinion**. The former possesses stability, since it deals with stable things; the latter deals with probability and imagination, as it tends toward things that are changeable. Regarding science (which concerns the intelligible) and opinion (which concerns the sensible), the principles are **intellection** <note>The act of the mind understanding</note> and **sensation**.

Sensation is surely an affection of the soul through the body, first announcing a passive power; afterwards, when the forms of things are impressed upon the soul through the organs of the senses, they remain so firm and indelible that they are preserved. This preservation is called **memory**. 

**Opinion** is the combination of memory and sensation. For when some sensible thing first meets us, a sensation is produced in us by it, and from that sensation comes memory. Then, when the same thing is presented to us again, we join our preceding memory with the following sensation, and in these instances we say, "**Socrates**," "**horse**," "**fire**," and other things of this kind. This is called "opinion" because we are joining preceding memory with a recent sensation. Whenever these things that are gathered together harmonize with each other, it is a **true opinion**; if they disagree, it is a **false opinion**. For if someone, while keeping the likeness of Socrates in his memory, should come across Plato and think—due to a certain similarity—that he has met Socrates again, and then receives the sensation of Plato as if it were from Socrates, applying it to his memory of Socrates, a false opinion results. 

Plato compares that medium in which sensation and memory occur to a **wax image** <note>A famous metaphor from Plato's *Theaetetus* where the mind is like a wax tablet that receives impressions</note>. But when the soul, reflecting on a concept formed through sensation and memory, looks back at these things as if looking at the sources from which they flowed, Plato calls this a "picture" and also a "phantasy." He calls **thought** the discourse and reasoning of the soul itself with itself; and he calls **speech** the flow of thought through the mouth joined with the articulated voice. 

**Intellection** is the primary operation of the intellect contemplating intelligible things. This also appears to be twofold. One occurs before the soul descends into the body, for then it contemplates the intelligible things themselves. The other occurs after the soul has been immersed in this body. Of these, the first is properly called "intellection," while the second, occurring while the soul is within the body, is called "natural intelligence"—a kind of intellection existing within the soul. Therefore, whenever we call intellection the principle of science, we do not mean the type we just proposed <note>i.e., natural intelligence</note>, but rather that which belongs to the soul when it is freed from the body, which, as we have said,

# ON THE DOCTRINE OF PLATO

...then it is called intellection, now it is named natural intelligence. And Plato calls this same intelligence <note>original: *intelligentiam*</note> sometimes simple science, sometimes the **wing of the soul**, and even **reminiscence** <note>The Platonic theory that learning is actually "recollecting" (anamnesis) knowledge the soul possessed before birth</note>. Finally, from these simple sciences, the natural reason inherent in the soul is composed. Since, therefore, there is both a knowing and an opining reason, as well as intellection and sensation, it is necessary that there also exist subjects for these to perceive, namely **intelligibles** <note>things understood by the mind</note> and **sensibles** <note>things perceived by the senses</note>. And because some intelligibles are primary, such as the **Ideas** <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes or "Forms" of things</note>, and some are secondary, such as the species inherent in matter which cannot be separated from it, intellection will also be twofold: one focused on primary things, the other on secondary. Again, even among sensible things, some are primary, such as qualities—like color or whiteness—and others are accidental, such as "the white thing" or "the colored thing." After these comes that which is a concrete whole made of these, such as fire; and in the same way, primary sensation is of primary things, while secondary sensation is of secondary things. Intellection judges primary intelligibles not without scientific reason <note>original: *scientifica ratione*; reason based on certain knowledge</note> through a certain comprehension and discourse. But scientific reason judges secondary intelligibles not without the help of opinative reason. The concrete whole, however, is judged by opinative reason not without sensation. And since the intelligible world is the primary intelligible, while the sensible world is a certain concrete whole, intellection judges the former with reason—that is, not without reason—while opinative reason judges the latter not without sensation. And since right reason consists of both contemplation and action, it does not discern the things subject to contemplation and the things subject to action in the same way. Moreover, in contemplation, it considers what is true and what is false; in action, it considers what is appropriate, what is foreign, what is to be done, and what is not. For from the fact that we have a natural intelligence of the beautiful and the good, by using reason and referring to these natural intelligences as if to predefined norms, we judge whether individual things are good or evil.

### Chapter Five: The element and duties of dialectic.

Plato maintains that the first element of the <term>dialectical faculty</term> <note>The art of logical discussion and the investigation of truth through classification and analysis</note> is to first consider the essence <note>the "what-ness"</note> of each thing, and afterwards to notice its accidents <note>non-essential characteristics</note>. It considers what each thing is, either by **dividing** and **defining** from higher concepts, or by **resolving** composite things back into their parts in reverse order. As for contingencies and things adjacent to essences, it considers them either from those things contained through **induction**, or from those containing them through **reasoning**. Thus, the members of dialectic are rightly said to be division, definition, resolution, induction, and reasoning. Furthermore, one type of **division** is the distribution of a genus into species; another is the distribution of a whole into parts, such as when we divide the soul into a rational part and a part lacking reason; and we further distribute this latter part into the powers of desire and anger. There is, moreover, the division of a word into its meanings, when...

# ALCINOUS

...the name **being** <note>original: *ens*; the most general category of existence</note> signifies many different things. To this is added the division of **accidents** <note>original: *accidentium*; properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, like the color of a shirt</note> into subjects: as when we say some goods concern the soul, others the body, and some concern external things. Nor is there a lack of a partition of accidents for subjects. For example, when we say some men are good, some are bad, and others are in the middle. Therefore, one must first use the **division of a genus into species** <note>a method of classification where a general group is broken down into specific types</note> whenever we wish to distinguish what each individual thing is. Moreover, this cannot be done without a **definition**, and a definition is constructed from a division in this way: first, it is necessary to grasp the **genus** <note>the broad category</note> of the thing to be defined, just as the genus of "man" is "animal." Then, one must divide it according to its nearest differences, descending all the way to the species: such as into "rational" and "irrational," and "mortal" and "immortal." Therefore, if these nearest differences are added to the genus, the definition of "man" will be established.

There are three species of **resolution** <note>original: *resolutionis*; also called "analysis," the process of tracing something back to its first principles</note>. One is the ascent from sensible things <note>things perceived by the senses</note> to the first **intelligibles** <note>things understood by the mind alone</note>. The second is the approach through demonstrated and sub-demonstrated things to those propositions which are indemonstrable and immediate. The last is from a hypothesis to principles that are not hypothesized at all. 

The first type is of this kind: as if we transcend from the beauty of bodies to the beauty of the soul, and from this to the beauty of moral duties, and then to the beauty found in laws, and finally to the source of beauty itself. In this way, ascending step by step, we may contemplate **Beauty itself** <note>Plato’s "Form of Beauty," the perfect archetype of all beautiful things</note> by its own nature. 

The second species of resolution occurs in this way: one must assume that which is sought, and consider the things that precede it, and demonstrate those by proceeding from later things to earlier ones until we arrive at the first and clearly granted principle. From there, beginning again, we return to the thing sought by the method of composition. For example, if someone asks whether the soul is immortal, they would first assume this very thing, inquiring whether it is always in motion, and then demonstrate that by further asking whether that which is always moved is moved by itself. One would then show this again by considering whether that which is moved by itself is the **principle of motion** <note>the original source that starts all other movement</note>. Finally, one would demonstrate this by inquiring whether the principle is **unbegotten** <note>original: *igenitum*; something that was never created and has no beginning</note>, which is indeed admitted by all as being clear. For that which is unbegotten is surely incorruptible. From this, as if from a manifest fact, one gathers the demonstration in this manner: the principle is unbegotten and incorruptible; the principle of motion is that which is moved by itself; that which is moved by itself is the soul. Therefore, the soul is incorruptible and unbegotten.

The resolution from hypothesis is of this kind: whoever investigates something should first assume it, then notice what follows from that assumption. <unclear>Afterward</unclear>, they must give an account of the hypothesis, <unclear>bringing forward</unclear> another hypothesis which <unclear>would prove</unclear> what had been previously assumed, and again...

### Chapter 6. Types of proposition, and of argumentation.

Of that kind of reason which we call a **proposition**, there are two species: **affirmation** and **negation**. An affirmation is this: "Socrates walks." A negation is this: "Socrates does not walk." Furthermore, among affirmations and negations, some are **universal** and some are **particular**. A particular affirmative is this: "Some pleasure is a good." A particular negative: "Some pleasure is not a good." A universal affirmative: "Every shameful thing is an evil." A universal negative: "No shameful thing is a good."

Among propositions, some are **predicative** <note>original: *praedicativae*; often called categorical propositions in modern logic</note> and some are **supposititious** <note>original: *supposititiuae*; referring to hypothetical or conditional propositions</note>. Predicative propositions are those that are simple, such as "All just things are good." Supposititious propositions are those that imply a consequence or a contradiction. 

**Plato** makes use of **reasoning** <note>original: *ratiocinationibus*; the formal structure of an argument, like a syllogism</note> both for refutation and for demonstration: refuting through questioning those things which are false, and demonstrating through teaching those things which are true. Reasoning is a form of speech in which, once certain things are established, a conclusion follows by necessity. Some forms of reasoning are predicative, some are supposititious, and others are a mixture of both. Predicative reasonings are those where both the assumptions and the conclusions are simple propositions. Supposititious reasonings are those made from supposititious propositions, and mixed ones are from both. 

Plato uses **demonstrative argumentations** in those dialogues that pertain to the explanation of doctrine. He uses **probable** and **apparent** arguments against the **Sophists** <note>professional teachers in Ancient Greece often criticized by Plato for prioritizing winning an argument over finding the truth</note>, and he uses **contentious** arguments against those who are properly called "litigious" <note>those who argue for the sake of conflict</note>, as in the *Euthydemus* and the *Hippias*.

Since there are three "figures" <note>patterns of syllogism</note> of predicative arguments: the **first** is that in which the common term is a predicate to one and a subject to the other. The **second** is that in which the common term is predicated of both. The **third** is that in which the common term is the subject for both. I call the "terms" the parts of the propositions; for example, in "Man is an animal," we call "man" and "animal" the terms. 

Plato usually disputes according to the first figure, though also according to the second and third figures. He argues according to the first figure in the *Alcibiades* in this way: "Just things are beautiful; beautiful things are good; therefore, just things are good." He argues according to the second figure in the *Parmenides* as follows: "That which has no parts is neither straight nor round. But..." <unclear>...u</unclear>

...whatever partakes of shape is either straight or round. Therefore, that which has no parts partakes of no shape, according to the third <note>This refers to the "third figure" of a syllogism, a technical arrangement of logic where the middle term is the subject of both premises.</note> in the same book. In the same way, in that book: What partakes of shape has a certain quality; what partakes of shape is finite; therefore, what has a certain quality is finite. Furthermore, one may find many **argumentations** that are constructed through **suppositions** <note>original: *suppositiones*; these are hypothetical or "if-then" arguments.</note> in Plato, especially such reasonings in the *Parmenides*. If the **One** <note>original: *ipsum unum*; a central concept in Platonic metaphysics representing ultimate unity.</note> itself has no parts, it has neither a beginning, nor an end, nor a middle. But if it has no beginning, middle, and end, it will have no limit. If it has no limit, it partakes of no shape. Therefore, if the One itself has no parts, it partakes of no shape. 

Indeed, according to the second figure of the hypothetical argumentation—which many call the third—in which the common term follows both extremes, he reasons in this manner: If the One has no parts, it is neither straight nor round. If it partakes of shape, it is either straight or round. Therefore, if it has no parts, it will not even partake of shape. 

Moreover, according to the third figure—which some wish to be the second—in which the common term precedes both [extremes], he argues in the *Phaedo* in a certain way: If, having acquired knowledge of the **Equal** <note>original: *ipsius aequalis*; referring to the Platonic "Form of Equality."</note> itself, we have never forgotten it, we surely know it. But if we have forgotten it, we are **recollecting** <note>original: *reminiscimur*; referring to Plato's theory that learning is actually the soul remembering knowledge it had before birth.</note>. 

Likewise, he uses **mixed argumentations**, which proceed by consequence, in this way: If the One is a whole and is finite—having a beginning, middle, and end—it also partakes of shape. The antecedent is true, therefore the consequent is true. In this way, the differences among those things that occur by consequence are considered. 

Therefore, when someone has diligently observed the powers of the mind and the various natures of men, as well as the different species of arguments, and then—having considered the opportunity of the moment—adapts the appropriate arguments to specific human emotions by which they may be moved, he will be the **perfect orator**. His <term>rhetoric</term> <note>the art of persuasive speaking</note> will rightly be called the science of speaking well. 

Let us now look more clearly at the snares of **sophisms** <note>original: *sophismatum*; deceptive or fallacious arguments used by the "Sophists" whom Plato often criticized.</note> and traps; we will perceive them as suggested by Plato in the *Euthydemus*. For there, one finds both the sophisms that arise from words and those that arise from the things themselves, as well as their solutions. 

But he also handed down the ten <term>categories</term> <note>original: *praedicamenta*; the fundamental ways in which things can be described (e.g., quality, quantity, relation), which Alcinous attributes to Plato though they are more famously systematized by Aristotle.</note>, both in the *Parmenides* itself and in other dialogues. Moreover, he included all the topics derived from **etymology** in the *Cratylus*. And without a doubt, our Plato stood out as a man to be admired above all others in **dividing** and **defining**—two things which most greatly attest to the power of <term>dialectic</term> <note>the philosophical method of investigation through dialogue and logic.</note>. The things handed down in the *Cratylus* aim at this: he discusses whether the use of names is by **nature** or by **convention**...

...[names] have their own [correctness]. It pleases him <note>Alcinous is referring to Plato's views in the dialogue *Cratylus*.</note> that the correctness of names is established by a certain convention. However, he does not believe this was done randomly or as chance provided, but rather that the convention itself followed the very nature of things. He considers the **correctness of names** to be nothing other than a naming that is in harmony with the nature of the thing itself. For not just any naming is sufficient for correctness, nor is nature alone or the first utterance of a voice, but rather a composition of both. Thus, all correctness of names is according to an assignment that fits the nature of things. If any name were applied to anything at random, it would not signify correctly—for example, if we were to give the name "horse" to a "man." Indeed, speaking is a kind of operation. For this reason, one does not speak correctly simply by speaking in any way one pleases, but only if one speaks as the nature of the things themselves requires. Since, indeed, the act of naming is a part of speech itself (just as a name is a part of an oration), naming correctly or incorrectly would not happen through just any assignment, but through a natural kinship of the name to the thing itself.

The one who signifies the nature of the thing through the name will be a correct **founder of names**. For a name is an <term>instrument</term> <note>original: *organum*; in this context, it means a tool for performing a specific task.</note> of a thing—not one that chance has offered, but one consistent with nature. And through this, in turn, we indicate things to ourselves and discern their nature. Thus it follows that a name is a certain indicating instrument that distinguishes the substance of each thing, just as the <term>weaver's comb</term> <note>original: *pecten*; a tool used by weavers to push the threads of the warp together.</note> distinguishes the web. Therefore, it will also pertain to the <term>dialectician</term> <note>A practitioner of dialectic, the highest form of philosophical reasoning and logical discussion.</note> to use names correctly, just as the weaver uses the comb, recognizing the specific work of that tool, even though the smith was the one who made it. In no different way, the dialectician will use a name as is fitting, which the founder of names has shaped. For truly, it is the smith's job to construct a **tiller**, but the duty of the **helmsman** to use it correctly. In the same manner, the institutor of names will establish names correctly only if he establishes them as if a dialectician were present, since the dialectician understands the natures of those things that lie hidden beneath the names. Let these things said about dialectics be sufficient.

### Chapter VII. The Distinction of Speculative Science.

The goal of the **mathematician** is to know nature in terms of planes and three-dimensional extensions, and to observe the motion and progressions of the heavenly bodies. And so, in a certain summary, the speculation of the mathematician...

...be proposed. These things were certainly undertaken by Plato to sharpen the **acumen of thought**, reaching into the soul and sharpening the mind’s edge for the intuition of **divine things**. That part of the mathematical faculty which looks toward numbers <note>arithmetic</note> provides no small power for perceiving divine things; indeed, it frees us from the error and ignorance that revolves around these **sensible things** <note>objects perceived by the physical senses rather than the mind</note>, offering help toward the knowledge of **essence** <term>essentia</term> <note>original: *essentia*; the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing that exists beyond the physical world.</note>, and renders a person ready for the struggle through their skill in the order and consequences of things.

**Geometry** also seems to contribute greatly to the understanding of the **Good** itself: provided that one does not pursue it for the sake of **mechanical measurement**, but uses it in such a way that, by its assistance, he may ascend to higher things, and does not dwell merely on measuring things that are born and perish. Furthermore, **stereometry**—that is, the dimension of solids—is extremely useful. For after the second increase <note>plane geometry/two dimensions</note>, there follows its consideration which takes up the third increase <note>solid geometry/three dimensions</note>. 

**Astronomy** is useful, moreover, as a kind of fourth discipline, through which we behold the motions of the heaven and the stars, and the author of day and night, and of months and years: from which, as if from a neighboring region, we track down the author of all these things; and from these disciplines, as if from certain benches, elements, and steps, we progress to higher things.

We must also learn **Music**, applying our hearing to it. For just as the eyes were fashioned for astronomy, so were the ears for **harmony**: certainly, while laboring in astronomy we are led from those things perceived by the eyes to the **invisible essence**; so too, by drinking in the harmony of voices with our ears, we gradually approach **intelligible things** <note>things that can only be grasped by the intellect, not the senses</note> from those things which are heard.

Therefore, unless we pursue the end of this mathematical grace, the curiosity for these things is surely deemed crippled, mindless, and of no value. For it is fitting to pass over immediately from those things perceived by the eyes and ears to those which **reason** alone discerns. For the consideration of the mathematicians is a kind of **prelude** to the contemplation of divine things. Indeed, **Arithmetic** and **Geometry**, and those who cultivate them, desire to see **essence** itself. Yet they dream about these things in a way, and they cannot see them in truth, being ignorant of the **principles** and those things which are constituted from principles. 

Nevertheless, they contribute to those things we have mentioned. And for that reason, Plato did not think that such disciplines should be called **sciences** <term>scientiae</term> <note>original: *scientias*; here meaning certain, absolute knowledge based on first principles.</note>. However, the faculty of **dialectic** rises from geometric suppositions to the **first principles**, which are not "supposed" <note>or "hypothesized"</note> at all. For this reason, he rightly called dialectic a **science**. But the disciplines of the mathematicians he called neither **opinion** (because they are clearer than sensible things) nor, on the other hand, **science** (because they are more obscure than the first intelligibles), but rather a "thought" <note>mediating</note> between the science of bodies and the...

### Chapter 7: On Prime Matter

<margin>p</margin> After these matters, let us briefly discuss the **principles** <note>the fundamental "first things" of reality</note> and those subjects pertaining to theology. We shall descend from prior things (as it now seems) to the generation of the world itself, and finally down to the birth of human beings. First, therefore, we must treat **matter**. Plato indeed names this the "receptacle of all things," the "nurse," the "mother," the "place," and the "subject." He asserts that it is grasped without the senses, being understood by a **bastard reasoning** <term>adulterina ratiocinatione</term> <note>original: *adulterina ratiocinatione*; a term from Plato's *Timaeus* describing how we "see" matter not with eyes or pure logic, but by a strange, indirect intuition.</note>. He maintains that the unique property of matter is to receive all generations and to cherish them like a nurse; likewise, it takes on all forms, though by its own nature it is void of all form, quality, and appearance. Furthermore, he compares it to a surface shaped by forms, yet asserts it participates in no shape or quality of its own. Indeed, the subject will not be properly prepared for the various impressions of forms unless it is entirely lacking in every quality it is meant to receive. For we see that those who seek to make sweet-smelling ointments from oil look for oil that is infected by no scent at all; and those who are about to impress shapes into either wax or clay first polish and smooth the material entirely until the former figures are erased. It is fitting, therefore, that **universal matter**, if it is to receive all forms, should have no nature of its own, but should be subjected to those forms without any quality or appearance. And since it is of this kind, it is neither a body nor is it incorporeal, but it is **body in potential** <note>original: *potentia corpus*</note>, just as bronze is a statue in potential, because by receiving the form, it becomes a statue.

### Chapter 8: On Ideas and the Efficient Cause

<margin>c</margin> Since matter holds the status of a certain principle, Plato introduces other principles besides matter: namely, the **exemplary principle** <note>the blueprint or model</note>, to which the **Ideas** themselves are referred; and the **paternal principle**, which pertains to God, the cause of all things. Now, an **Idea** is, in relation to God, the "thinking of God." In relation to the sensible world, it is the "model" <term>exemplar</term>; but in relation to itself, it is "essence" <term>essentia</term>. Moreover, whatever is produced by intelligence must necessarily be referred to something else, which will be the model for the work: just as if something were made by someone, such as an image from their own mind. The model is not entirely separate from the one who acts, just as every craftsman, conceiving the models of his crafts within himself, then unfolds their forms into matter. They define an **Idea** as an eternal exemplar of those things that occur according to nature. For to most of those who followed **Plato**, it was not at all pleasing that an Idea of artifacts exists—such as of a shield or a lyre; nor again of things against nature, such as fever or immoderate bile; nor of particulars, such as **Socrates** and **Plato**; nor even of any of those things that are imperfect, like dirt or chaff; nor of relations, such as "the greater" and "the exceeding." For Ideas are the eternal and self-perfect thoughts <note>original: *intellectiones*; the internal mental acts of the Divine Mind</note> of God. 

That Ideas exist, they prove thus: whether God is himself an intellect, or something intellectual, notions are present in him that are eternal and immobile. If this is so, Ideas exist. For if measure by itself lacks matter, it is necessary that it receive measures from something higher and completely absolute from matter. The premise is indeed true; therefore, the consequence is true; and if this is so, Ideas are certain measures existing without any mixture of matter. 

Furthermore, if the world is not such as it is by some reckless chance, it was made not only *from* something, but also *by* someone; and not only that, but also fabricated *toward* something. Truly, toward what was it produced? What else exists besides the Idea? From which it follows that Ideas themselves exist. Likewise, if the intellect differs from true opinion, the **intelligible** <term>intelligibile</term> <note>Things understood by the mind alone, as opposed to things perceived by the senses.</note> will also differ from the **opinable** <term>opinabile</term> <note>Things that are merely the subject of belief or sensory observation, which can be mistaken.</note>. If this is true, there will exist intelligibles differing from opinables, so that there are primary intelligibles just as there are primary sensibles. From which it is concluded that Ideas exist.

Next, we must speak of the third principle, which **Plato** declares is almost ineffable <note>Too great or sacred to be expressed in words.</note>. Nevertheless, let us attempt to demonstrate it in this way. If there are intelligibles, and these are neither sensibles nor cohering with them, but primary simple intelligibles exist [distinct from] primary intelligibles, just as there are primary sensibles. The premise is true; therefore, what follows is true. 

Certainly men, as they are occupied by the disturbance of the senses, whenever they decide to contemplate something intelligible, immediately fall back into the **imagination** <note>original: *phantasiam*; here meaning mental images of physical things</note> of some sensible thing, so that they frequently apply either magnitude, or figure, or color to that which is to be understood, so that they cannot understand it purely. ### ON FANTASY AND THE INTELLECT

...which is its cause, and which stands above all things, is surely God himself, the first existing being. He is the cause for the mind of the world <note>original: *mundi mens*; the cosmic intelligence that governs the universe</note> to always act, while he himself remains always immobile, much like the sun acts upon the eye when it is placed before it. And in this manner he moves things, because that which is desired <term>immobile</term> <note>This refers to the Aristotelian concept of the "Unmoved Mover" who attracts all things toward itself through love or desire without moving itself.</note> stirs the one who desires. In this way, the supreme mind leads the mind of the entire heaven. And since this first intellect is most beautiful, it is necessary that the most beautiful object of thought be subject to it; yet nothing is more beautiful than itself. Therefore, it always understands itself and its own notions. And this operation of its is the **Idea**. Furthermore, God himself is supreme, eternal, ineffable, perfect in himself, needing nothing, and always and everywhere absolutely perfect. He is the essence of Divinity, Truth, Harmony, and the Good. Nor indeed do I count these so as to separate them from one another, but rather I contemplate them all as one. 

Indeed, he is called **the Good** for this reason: that he fills all things with benefits according to the capacity of each, and is the cause of all goods. He is called **the Beautiful** because his very nature is fullness and all harmony. He is likewise called **Truth** because he is the principle of all truth, just as the sun is the father and source of all light; for he is the cause of all things, and he adorns the mind of the whole heaven and the soul of the world according to his own exemplar. For by the gift of his will, he has filled all things with himself, awakening the soul of the world and turning it toward himself, since he is the cause of its mind. And yet that mind, adorned by the benefit of the Father, further adorns the entire nature of this world. 

Moreover, God is called **Ineffable** <note>Beyond the power of words to describe.</note> and perceivable only by the mind, because there is no genus surrounding him, nor species, nor any difference, nor does any "accident" <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing can lose without ceasing to be itself; God is seen as having no such temporary or external qualities.</note> happen to him. For he is not evil (to say so would be a sin), nor even "good" in the sense that he exists by participating in some goodness. Neither does any "difference" happen to him, for that cannot occur according to his own nature. Nor is he a quality, for he is not a "type" of effect. Nor is he among forms, for he is not deprived of any quality pertaining to himself, nor is he a part of anything, nor a whole as if constituted of parts. He is neither the same as anything nor different, since nothing happens to him by which he could be distinguished from others; he neither moves nor is moved. 

Therefore, the **first way** of understanding him is through the "removal" <note>original: *ablationem*; also known as the *via negativa*, defining God by what He is not.</note> of all these things, just as we conceive of a point through removal: first considering a surface, then a line, and finally a point. The **second way** of understanding him is according to the principle of "proportion," in this manner: just as the sun is to sight and to the things that are seen—not being sight itself but providing the means for the eye to see and for objects to be seen—exactly the same proportion does the **First Intellect** have to the intelligence of the soul...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the nature of God as the First Intellect and introduces a new chapter on the nature of qualities. The text moves from God's role as the source of truth to a logical proof of his incorporeality (lack of a physical body).</meta>

->ALCINOUS<-

...is in them, and those things which are understood; for he himself is not the same thing as understanding. Rather, he extends the power of understanding to the soul so that it may understand, and to the **objects of thought** <term>intelligibilia</term> <note>original: *intelligibilia*; these are the abstract realities or "Ideas" that can only be grasped by the mind, not the senses</note> so that they may be understood, illuminating them with the truth that is within them. The third way of understanding is of this kind: someone, noticing the beauty present in physical bodies, turns toward the beauty of the soul, then toward that which is in **moral duties** <term>officiis</term> <note>original: *officiis*; refers to right actions and the obligations of a citizen or person</note> and laws, and finally toward the very fountain of beauty, above which he understands the Good itself, which is to be loved and sought after—like a light suddenly shining into the soul that has flown up to that height.

Truly, one recognizes that this light is God himself because of his excellence. One acknowledges him primarily as being without magnitude of quantity. For a part, and that from which something is built, always precedes that of which it is a part. For a plane comes before a body, and a line comes before a plane. Since he has no parts, he will be moved neither according to place nor according to change. For if he undergoes change, it must be changed either by himself or by someone else. If by another, that other would surely be stronger. If by himself, he would change either into something worse or something better. However, both are impossible. From all these things, it is clear that he is **incorporeal** <note>literally "without a body"</note>.

Moreover, from what follows, the same will become clear. If God were a body, he would consist of matter and **form** <term>specie</term> <note>original: *specie*; used here in the philosophical sense of the formal structure that combines with matter to create a physical thing</note>, because every body is a certain composition of matter together with form—which is seen as similar to the **Ideas** <note>original: *ideæ*; the eternal patterns of things</note> while it participates in them by some ineffable reason. It is absurd to think God is constituted of matter and form. For then he would be neither simple nor a first principle. Therefore, God is incorporeal. Furthermore, if he is a body, he consists of matter. Therefore, he is either fire, or air, or earth, or water, or something forged from these. But however it might be, he would by no means be a first principle, and matter itself would be prior to him, if indeed he were made of matter. Since these thoughts are wicked, it is necessary that God be incorporeal. For if he is a body, he can be destroyed, he is created, and he is subject to change. Yet none of these things apply to God.

### Chapter 11. Qualities are incorporeal.

Moreover, we shall show that **qualities** <note>The properties of things, like "redness" or "heat"</note> are incorporeal in this way. Every body is a **subject** <term>subiectum</term> <note>the underlying physical thing in which properties exist</note>, but a quality is by no means a subject, but rather an **accident** <term>accidens</term> <note>a property that can change or be removed without the thing itself ceasing to exist</note>. Therefore, a quality is not a body. No body is "in" a subject; every quality is in a subject. Therefore, a quality is not a body. Likewise, one quality is contrary to another quality. But no body, insofar as it is a body, is contrary to another body. Therefore, qualities are not bodies. Furthermore, it is most consistent with reason that just as matter is devoid of quality, so also quality should be devoid of matter. And if it lacks matter, it cannot be a body.

...[remains]. Indeed, if qualities were physical bodies, then two or three bodies would converge into the same place, which is far from reasonable. But if qualities are incorporeal, then the **Craftsman** <term>opifex</term> <note>original: *opifex*; a term used for God as the divine architect or "Demiurge" who shapes the universe</note> of those qualities is also incorporeal. Furthermore, nothing can be an active agent except for incorporeal things. This is because physical bodies are passive and in a state of flux; they do not always behave in the same way, nor do they persist in the same state. In instances where they might seem to produce an effect on something, they are found to be much more "passive" (acted upon) in that situation. Therefore, just as there is something that is entirely passive, it is necessary that something exists which is entirely active. We shall find that this active force is nothing other than the incorporeal. Thus, let the discourse concerning the principles of things—which is called **theology** <note>In this context, "theology" refers to the study of the highest, most abstract principles of reality and the nature of God</note>—reach its end here. For next, it seems we must descend into that discussion which is called **physics** <note>the study of the natural, physical world and its laws</note>.

### Chapter XII. Concerning causes, generation, elements, and the order of the world.

<margin>c</margin>
For all physical things which are created as distinct from one another according to nature, there must be certain pre-defined models, which are **Ideas** <term>ideae</term>. These things must be traced back to those sciences and definitions. For beyond individual men, it is proper to understand "Man" himself; and beyond individual horses, the "Horse" itself; and beyond all created living things, an "Immortal Living Being" which is unbegotten. Just as many images are pressed from a single seal, or many likenesses are made of one man, the **Idea** <term>idea</term> <note>referring to the Platonic "Form"—the perfect, eternal template of a thing</note> is the cause for all of them, ensuring they are of the same kind as the Idea itself. Therefore, it is necessary that this entire world—the most beautiful work of God—was fabricated by God in such a way that he looked toward a certain Idea as a model for this world during the fabrication. In doing so, through a certain marvelous providence and the highest standard (which is his own goodness), God prepared himself for the construction of this great machine. He created it, therefore, out of the whole of **matter** <term>materia</term>. Before the creation of the heavens, this matter was tossed about in a chaotic tumult; God brought it back from that deformed confusion into a beautiful order. He decorated its parts on all sides with fitting numbers and shapes, so that the world might be woven together in that proportion which fire and earth still maintain toward air and water. At that time, only the traces of these elements lay confused within the "receptacle," without reason or measure; they shook the matter, and were in turn shaken by the matter. God joined the world together from the four elements in their entirety—that is, from all the fire, air, water, and earth—leaving no part or power of them remaining outside. For he foresaw that the world was to be a physical body, perceptible by touch and sight. But without the presence of fire and earth, nothing can move the senses of touch or sight. For this reason, according to fitting logic, he constructed the world from fire and earth. However, because a certain bond was needed for both...

<meta>This page continues the "Physics" section of the treatise, specifically the "Timaeus"-influenced account of how the Craftsman (the Demiurge) structured the physical universe using mathematical ratios and geometric solids. ...to bind the extremes, a middle term was necessary. The **divine bond** <note>This refers to the mathematical concept of geometric proportion, which Plato's *Timaeus* describes as the most perfect bond for the elements</note> is that which occurs according to proportion, which makes both itself and the things being bound together into a single unit. Now, if the world were intended to be a flat plane, a single middle term would have been sufficient. However, it had to be spherical, and for that reason, it required two middle terms. For this cause, I say, air and water were placed between fire and earth according to the **harmony of proportion** <note>original: *proportionis consonantiam*; the idea that the four elements are linked by a ratio: Fire is to Air as Air is to Water, and so on</note>. Thus, as fire relates to air, so air relates to water; and as air relates to air, so water relates to earth. And again, as earth relates to water, so water relates to air; and as water relates to air, so air relates to fire. 

Furthermore, because the **Craftsman** <term>artifex</term> left nothing outside the world, He made it unique, matching it in number to its **Idea** <term>idea</term>, which is also unique. Moreover, neither disease nor old age could ever affect it, since nothing remains outside that could exert force upon it. Truly, it remains self-sufficient, in need of nothing, and preserved in safety. He gave it a **spherical shape** <note>In ancient philosophy, the sphere was considered the most perfect and "equal" shape, as every point on the surface is equidistant from the center</note>, as it is the most beautiful of all shapes, the most capacious, and the easiest to move. And since it had no need for hearing, sight, or the other senses, He added no sensory instruments at all for the purpose of feeling. He likewise commanded the other types of motion <note>i.e., linear motions like up/down, left/right, or forward/backward</note> to be far removed, and granted it only **circular motion** <note>original: *circuitū*; rotation on an axis was seen as the most "intellectual" motion because it stays in one place</note> as being proper to mind and wisdom.

### Chapter XIII. On the correspondence of shapes with the elements of the world and the world itself.

Since there are two things from which the world is constructed—namely, body and soul—the former is visible and subject to decay, while the latter is invisible and intangible; the power and constitution of each remains distinct. Indeed, the body of the world is compacted from fire, earth, water, and air. The Architect of the world, encompassing these four, gave them shape (having previously observed no order among the elements) using the **pyramid** <term>pyramide</term>, the **cube** <term>cubo</term>, the **octahedron** <note>a shape with eight faces</note>, and the **icosahedron** <note>a shape with twenty faces</note>. Upon the whole, however, he impressed the **dodecahedron** <note>a shape with twelve faces; in Platonic thought, this represents the zodiac or the heavens as a whole</note>. 

Insofar as matter took on the shape of the pyramid, **fire** shone forth. That shape is indeed sharp and better suited for cutting than the others, and it is composed of fewer triangles, making it the lightest of all shapes. Insofar as it took on the octahedron, it assumed the quality of **air**. When it first took the icosahedral shape, it was assigned the nature of **water**. Finally, he bestowed the cubic shape upon **earth**, which is the most solid and stable of all the elements. To the fabric of the universe itself, he applied the dodecahedron. 

Older than all these shapes is the nature of **planes** <term>planorum</term>, for planes precede solids. Of the nature of planes, there are two origins for right-angled figures: the **scalene** and the **isosceles** <note>original: *scalenus & isoceles*; refers to the two fundamental triangles—one with unequal sides and one with two equal sides—that Plato argues are the building blocks of the elements</note>. And the scalene is a triangle that has one...

...having one right angle, another of two-thirds <note>Specifically, a 60-degree angle, which is 2/3 of a 90-degree right angle</note>, and another of one-third <note>A 30-degree angle</note>. Thus, the **scalene triangle** <note>original: *scalinus triangulus*; Alcinous refers to the 30-60-90 triangle which Plato used to build the faces of the tetrahedron, octahedron, and icosahedron</note> becomes the element of the pyramid, the octahedron, and the icosahedron. Since the pyramid is composed of four equilateral triangles, each of which is distributed into six scalene triangles. Indeed, the octahedron figure is from eight similar [triangles], each of which is divided into six scalene triangles. The icosahedron figure is from twenty similarly. The **isosceles triangle**, however, is the element of the cubic figure; for four isosceles triangles meeting together complete a square. From six such squares, a cube is fashioned. But God himself assumed the **dodecahedron** figure for the construction of the universe; hence the twelve forms of living creatures are seen in the **zodiac circle** <note>The twelve signs of the zodiac correlate to the twelve faces of the dodecahedron, which was often associated with the quintessence or the shape of the heavens</note>, each of which is cut into thirty parts. Similarly, one may observe in the dodecahedron figure itself twelve pentagons, each divided into five triangles, such that each pentagon exists divided by six triangles; and in the whole dodecahedron, three hundred and sixty triangles are found, as many as there are portions in the zodiac. 

Matter, formed by God himself from these shapes, began to be moved—at first indeed by traces without order, but then it was reduced into order by God, with each thing tempered according to mutual proportion. Yet these elements do not remain separate in one place; they have an unceasing shaking <note>original: *concussionem*; referring to the "Receptacle" or chaotic motion of matter described in the *Timaeus*</note> both within themselves and which they bring into matter. For they are kept constricted by the circumference of the world, and are carried along, agitated by mutual alternating pulses, the thin parts indeed into the province of the solid ones. For this cause, no vacuum at all remains, and a perpetually persevering inequality provides the cause of the pulsing. For by these, matter is sought, and these in turn are sought by matter.

### Chapter 14. On the World Soul, Representation, and the Stars.

**From** bodies, therefore, he began to investigate the powers of the soul. For since the soul discerns individual things, he [Plato] rightly bestowed upon it the principle of all things: so that whatever it might encounter, recognizing it by a certain kinship, it might conform itself to those things. He applied its essence to this: Again, when he said there was a certain **intelligible and indivisible substance** <note>The "indivisible essence" refers to the realm of Forms/Ideas</note>, he also handed down another substance dispersed around bodies <note>The "divisible essence" refers to the material world</note>, perceiving that the soul, through intelligence, could perceive both substances. And because he knew that in those things which pertain to the intelligence, and also in those which pertain to sense, "the Same" and "the Other" <term>Idem et Alterum</term> exist, he established the soul from all of these. For either **like is known by like** (as the Pythagoreans prefer), or as the physicist **Heraclitus** <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535 – c. 475 BC), who emphasized change and the "unity of opposites"</note> says, the unlike is always known by the unlike. When Plato says the world was "born" <note>original: *genitum*; meaning created or generated</note>, it is by no means to be believed that he thought some time existed before the world; rather, it is because time is a duration through generation, indicating that its substance provides its own cause.

# ALCINOUS

Moreover, God does not create the **World Soul**, which has always existed, but rather adorns it. For this reason, he is sometimes said to "make" the soul, insofar as he awakens it and turns its mind toward himself—as if from a deep sleep—so that, looking toward those things understood by God and desiring divine notions, it might receive species and forms from them. 

Furthermore, it is clear that the world was gifted with both a soul and a mind by God himself. For since he wished it to be his finest work, he rightly made the world both living and intellectual. Indeed, a living work <note>original: *opificium uiuens*; Alcinous emphasizes that for the Platonists, the universe is a biological, sentient entity</note> is altogether more excellent than one that is not alive, and that which possesses a mind is superior to that which lacks one. Nor, perhaps, could mind be present in the world without a soul. 

And since the soul poured itself out from the center of the world to its furthest reaches, it embraced the entire body of the world in a circle, covering the universe and being shared with its individual particles. In this way, it connects the world by an indissoluble bond and preserves it unharmed. And that power of the soul which remained on the outside precedes its inner parts. The former indeed remained undivided <note>The outer sphere of the "Same," associated with the fixed stars</note>, while the interior portion was divided into seven circles <note>The spheres of the seven classical planets: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn</note>, distributed from the very beginning throughout by double and triple intervals <note>Alcinous refers to the harmonic proportions (1, 2, 4, 8 and 1, 3, 9, 27) described in Plato’s *Timaeus* used to "tune" the World Soul</note>. 

And that part which is contained by the undivided sphere remains akin to that which is the **Same**; whereas that which is dispersed is akin to that which, by contrast, is called the **Other**. For the motion of the heaven that encompasses all things, since it does not wander, is uniform and preserves a primary order. However, the progress of the lower bodies <note>The planets</note> is varied and changes with their risings and settings. Hence, it is called a certain "wandering" or "straying" <note>This is the etymological root of the word "planet," from the Greek *planētēs* (wanderer)</note>. 

The outermost circle runs to the right, from the east to the west. The interior portion, however, moves in the opposite direction to the left, revolving from the west to the east. Furthermore, God himself fashioned the stars and the constellations, including those which do not wander <note>The fixed stars</note>, for the adornment of the heaven and the night. The multitude of such stars is beyond counting. But those which wander are seven in number, created for the origin of number and time, and for the illumination of all things. 

**Time** is clearly the interval of the world's motion, serving as a kind of image of eternity <note>A direct reference to Plato's *Timaeus* 37d: "a moving image of eternity"</note>; for eternity is the measure of the state of the eternal world. Moreover, the power of the courses of the wandering stars is certainly not the same for all. For the **Sun** is the leader of all the rest, both illuminating and revealing all things to our eyes. Next, the **Moon** holds her rank for the sake of fertile power. The other planets each follow their own course according to their own specific proportion. The Moon completes a month in the span of a single circuit, running through her circle in that space of time; the Sun, however, completes a year—that is, a cycle of months—as it traverses the **zodiac circle**... <note>The text here is partially obscured by the staining mentioned in the header</note>... Each of the other stars is likewise carried along by its own circuit. And indeed, these circuits are not known to just any men, but only to the learned...

At last, from all these revolutions, a full number and period of time will be completed <note>This refers to the "Great Year" or Platonic Year, the moment when all celestial bodies return to their original relative positions</note>, when all the planets, reaching the same point, receive such an order that if a straight line were considered as a perpendicular from the highest circle down to the earth, the centers of all would be seen upon it. ### Chapter XV. On spirits and the elements.

There are also others, called **spirits** <note>original: *dæmones*; in the Platonic tradition, these are not "demons" in a modern sense, but intermediary beings between gods and humans</note>, inhabiting the individual elements, whom we might call "intelligible gods." Some are visible, while others escape the sharpness of our sight, dwelling in the ether, fire, air, and water, so that no part of the world should be left without a soul, or without a nature of an excellent living being. 

To these spirits, all earthly things and those beneath the moon are subject. For indeed, the God of the whole world is the author of gods and spirits, and by the gift of his divine will, this universe shall never hereafter be dissolved. However, his **sons** <note>The lesser created gods tasked with the generation of mortal things</note> preside over the other works, carrying out each task according to their father’s command and in imitation of him. From these spirits come the stirrings of divine frenzy and ecstasy, as well as dreams, oracles, and whatever occurs to mortals through prophecy. 

The Earth is situated in the middle of all things, held fast around the axis <note>original: *discordiam agitationemque*; likely a corruption or variant reading of the "axis" or "pole" of the universe</note> that stretches through the whole, acting as the guardian of day and night, the most ancient of all the gods within the heavens. And after the soul of the whole world itself, the Earth provides us with sweet nourishment; around her the heaven revolves, and she herself is also a kind of star. For this reason, she remains unmoved, because she is balanced in the center like those things which contain her. The **ether** <note>The "fifth element" or the purest upper atmosphere where the stars reside</note> has been allotted the outer province, divided into the spheres of the wandering and non-wandering stars. After these follows the air. In the center, however, the earth resides together with its moisture. <unclear>in a circle toward whatever is in it ...</unclear>

### Chapter XVI. The younger gods are the craftsmen of man. On the transmigration of the soul.

<margin>c</margin> When all these things had been fashioned, three classes of mortal living creatures remained: those that fly, those that swim, and those that walk. The **Maker of the world** <note>The Demiurge or supreme craftsman</note> entrusted the creation of these to his sons <note>The "junior gods" or celestial deities like the planets</note>. For if he himself had also begotten these, they would have been born immortal. They, therefore, borrowing particles from the primary matter—which they were to return after certain fixed cycles of time—fashioned the mortal kinds of living beings. But since the Father God was concerned for the human race as being more akin to the gods, both he and his children took care of them; the **Architect of all** himself sent down the souls of this race, equal in number to the stars. 

But when he had first placed each soul upon a related star as if upon a **chariot** <note>original: *uehiculo*; this refers to the "astral vehicle" or *ochema*, a subtle body that carries the soul down into the physical world</note>, he explained to them the laws of fate, like a lawgiver, so that he himself might remain free from blame for any future faults. He taught them that mortal disturbances would arise from the body: first, sensation; then pleasure and pain, fear and anger. Those who overcame these and did not allow themselves to be led away would live justly and finally return to their related star. But those overcome by injustice would, in a second birth, migrate into the life of a woman. And those who did not yet cease from wickedness would finally degenerate into the nature of beasts. There would only be an end to their labors when they had driven out the innate affections of the body and returned to their proper state.

### Chapter XVII. On the body, the limbs of man, and the powers of the soul.

<margin>d</margin> These younger gods first fashioned man from earth, fire, air, and water—borrowing certain portions from matter which they would one day return—and, binding them together with hidden links, they made one body out of all. And then they placed the more excellent part of the soul in the head, after they had prepared the brain like a cultivated field. Around the face, they arranged the organs that serve the senses. They also composed the marrow from smooth and straight **triangles** <note>In Platonic physics, the four elements are composed of microscopic geometric shapes; Alcinous explains that the finest of these form the marrow and seed</note> from which the elements had been born, to be the future origin of the generative seed. 

They fashioned bone from marrow and earth; after they had moistened these two repeatedly with fire and water. They made nerves from bone and flesh. Flesh was compacted from a certain salty and sharp fermentation <note>The author uses "fermentation" to describe the chemical-like thickening of elements into organic tissue</note>. They surrounded the marrow with bones, and for the sake of the joints of the bones, they added nerves. From this, the bending of the limbs and the nodes of the joints were produced by the service of the nerves. Finally, a covering was added to them through the flesh, which was provided both for protection against heat and for beauty, and for the use of the living creature. Furthermore, from these things, the internal organs were entwined: the stomach and the intestines coiled all around it. From above, indeed, from the...

<note>The following text describes the anatomy of the upper body and the digestive process as understood in the Platonic tradition, where physical structures are designed to house specific functions of the soul.</note>

...the mouth, the windpipe, and the passage of the throat, one indeed extending into the stomach, the other into the lungs. Food is certainly digested in the belly, ground down and softened by spirit <note>original: *spiritu*; here referring to *pneuma*, a vital air or gas believed to drive physiological processes</note> and heat together, and from there it flows into the whole body through its own specific transformations. Two veins erected around the spine wrap around the head in an opposing fashion where they meet one another, and from there they split into many branches. After the gods fashioned man and joined the soul, his mistress, to the body, they ordered **Reason**—the ruler of that soul—to inhabit the head. From this point, the origin of the marrow and the nerves is derived; when its various passions are disturbed, a "wandering of the mind" <note>mental alienation or madness</note> follows. For this reason, they fortified the citadel of the body, as if with certain guards, by placing the senses around the head. Indeed, in that place dwells the power that reasons, judges, and contemplates. But the parts of the soul moved by the passions they assigned to lower seats: the power of **Anger** to the heart, and the power of **Desire** to the belly and those parts around the navel, about which we shall discuss in later sections.

### Chapter . XVIII . On sight, light, and images in mirrors .

<margin>note</margin>
Furthermore, after they carved the light-bearing eyes into the face, they kindled a fiery light within them. Because this light was mild and somewhat dense, they considered it to be a sibling of the divine light. This light certainly emanates everywhere through the eyes, but it runs through the pupils more purely and abundantly. Indeed, when this internal light is mixed with and strengthened by an external brilliance of a similar kind, it provides the sense of seeing. Therefore, when those external lights depart at night, our internal ray—being now in shadowed light—no longer mingles with the nearby air. The result is that it withdraws into the interior, soothes and relaxes the internal movements, and softens the limbs with sleep; hence, once it has been drawn back, it closes the eyelids in rest. And if it induces a great deal of rest, a dreamless form of sleep creeps in. But if some stirrings still remain, frequent "phantasms" <note>images or visions</note> immediately encounter us; in this way, **Imagination** <term>Phantasia: the faculty of the mind that produces or perceives mental images</term>, whether true or false, is born through a direct path. After these things follow the images seen in mirrors or other translucent and smooth bodies, which result in no other way than through a "reverberation" <note>reflection</note>. Depending on whether the mirror is concave, convex, or oblong, different sights will appear to those looking; for the lights are reflected to other parts—repelled and diffused by a convex surface, but converging in a concave one. For this reason, in some mirrors the right and left appear reversed, in others they appear normally, and in some, the top is turned to the bottom and the bottom to the top.
