### Chapter . XVIII . On the remaining senses and their objects.

<margin>a.</margin> **Hearing** was indeed created for the perception of the voice, arising from a motion that begins around the head and extends all the way down to the liver. <note>Ancient physiology, following Plato's *Timaeus*, often linked sensory vibrations to the lower organs where the "desiring" part of the soul resides.</note> The **voice** itself penetrates through the ears, the brain, and the blood until it reaches the soul. A high-pitched voice is that which moves more swiftly; a low-pitched one moves more slowly. A loud voice is made of many parts, while a quiet one is made of few. Following this, the power of the **nostrils** follows, produced for the perception of smells. **Odor** is a certain condition that flows from the veins of the nose down to the regions of the navel; its types have no specific names, except for two very general ones. These are named as nothing other than "good odor" and "bad odor," which are also called by the names "pleasantness" and "nausea." Certainly, every odor is thicker than air but thinner than water. <note>This reflects the belief that smells are "half-formed" substances, like vapor or mist, existing in a state between liquid and gas.</note> Properly speaking, this kind of odor occurs in things that have not yet undergone a complete transformation, but consist of a certain combination of air and water, such as those made from smoke and mist; for it is through the alternation of these that the sense of smelling is achieved.

The gods then fashioned **Taste** as a judge of many different juices <note>original: *succorum*; referring to the liquid essences or "flavors" of things</note>, extending veins from the tongue to the seat of the heart, by which various liquids might be examined. Indeed, as these veins dilate and contract in different ways according to the arrival of the juices, they discern the variety of those flavors. There are seven differences in flavor: **sweet**, **sour**, **pungent**, **harsh**, **salty**, **piercing**, and **bitter**. The nature of the **sweet** is contrary to all the others, for it soothes and bathes the moisture absorbed by the tongue. The **sour** disturbs and scatters it. The **piercing** inflames and flies upward. That which vehemently wipes away and liquefies the moisture is called **bitter**, but that which cleanses more gently and softens is called **salty**. Among those flavors that block the passages of the tongue and contract them, those that do so more roughly are called **pungent** <note>original: *pontici*; a term often used for tart or astringent flavors like those of unripe fruit</note>, while those that do so more gently are called **harsh**.

Finally, the sense of **Touch** was created by the gods so that it might distinguish the hot and the cold, the soft and the hard, the light and the heavy, and the smooth and the rough. Indeed, bodies are said to be **yielding** when they receive a touch, and **resisting** when they do not yield at all. This occurs because of the foundations of the bodies themselves. For those which have broad, stable, and solid foundations are resisting, while those which, on the contrary, use a small foundation are yielding, soft, and slippery. That which is uneven and hard is surely **rough**; that which is level <unclear>likewise often</unclear> is **smooth**. Since, however, the sensations of **hot** and **cold** are entirely opposite, they are brought about by different causes. For that which cuts with the sharpness and velocity of its parts produces the sensation of heat; but the sensation of cold is produced by that which enters more sluggishly, so that while the thin parts are expelled, the thicker parts are forced to penetrate into their seats. Then, indeed, a shaking and trembling occurs, and this is the sensation born in the bodies. By stiffness <unclear>is produced that which is motion</unclear>

<header>ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT</header>

### Chapter XX. On the heavy and the light.

It is not fitting to define the **heavy** and the **light** by means of "upper" or "lower" locations; for nothing is truly "upward" or "downward" in itself. Since the heavens are entirely spherical and smoothed equally across their convex surface, it is not proper to designate one part as "above" and another as "below." Instead, we should say that **heavy** is that which is moved with difficulty into a location outside of its own nature, while **light** is that which is moved easily. Likewise, the heavy is that which is composed of many parts, and the light is that which is composed of very few.

### Chapter XXI. On respiration.

We breathe in the following manner. The vast amount of air surrounding us on all sides flows in through the mouth, the nostrils, and other hidden passages of the body. Once warmed, it strives to flow back out toward the external air that is its "kin." <note>This refers to the ancient principle that "like seeks like"—the air inside the body seeks to rejoin the atmosphere.</note> Moreover, from whichever part it flows out, it pushes the outermost air back toward the internal regions. In this way, through a never-ending cycle, inhalation and exhalation follow one another.

### Chapter XXII. On the causes of diseases.

<margin>r:</margin>
Plato taught that there are many causes of diseases. The first is an **excess or deficiency of the elements**, or their movement into regions of the body that do not suit their nature. The second is the **mutual corruption** of related substances—for instance, if blood, bile, or phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note> is formed from the breakdown of flesh. For he considers all these things to be nothing other than liquefaction and decay. Indeed, <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita," one of the four humors; here described as a byproduct of melting tissue</note> is the liquefaction of fresh flesh. Sweat and tears are a certain discharge and the remnants of this phlegm. When phlegm is expelled externally, it causes white skin infections. But when it is mixed internally with **black bile**, it produces the "falling sickness" <note>original: "morbum comitialem," known today as epilepsy</note>, which is called the **sacred disease**. Sharp and salty phlegm is the cause of those sufferings that occur through "flux" or discharge. <note>This likely refers to catarrh or respiratory discharge.</note> For it is inevitable that everyone burdened by both phlegm and bile will suffer in this way. Indeed, bile combined with phlegm generates numerous and varied diseases. Plato believes that a **continuous fever** happens through an excess of fire; a **daily fever** from an excess of air; a **tertian fever** <note>A fever that returns every third day, classically associated with malaria.</note> from water; and finally, a **quartan fever** from earth. From this point, taking our beginning from here, we must speak about the **soul**, even if we seem to be returning to the same subject.

### Chapter XXIII. On the three principal powers of the soul.

The gods who were the creators of the mortal race received the **immortal soul** from the first God and added to it two mortal parts (as we have said). But, so that the divine and immortal power of the soul would not be stained by mortal follies, they established its seat in the "citadel" of the body, as if it were the ruler of all. Indeed, they willed its dwelling-place to be the **head**, which is shaped in the same form as the universe was fashioned. <note>The sphere was considered the most perfect shape, mirroring the cosmos.</note> They placed the rest of the body beneath this as a sort of vehicle for those parts that serve the soul. They themselves...

...assigned specific provinces to the mortal portions of the soul. They placed **anger** <note>This refers to the "spirited" part of the soul, known as *thymos* in Greek.</note> in the region of the heart, while the seat of **desire** was set in the middle ground between the navel and the diaphragm. There, they bound that force like a wild and savage animal. They engineered the **lungs** for the sake of the heart; they are soft, airy, and hollow like a pipe, much like a sponge, so that the heart—lest it boil over with the heat of anger—might be cooled and soothed by some measure of refrigeration. The **liver** was created to both stir the soul’s desire and to calm it again, possessing both sweetness and bitterness. Furthermore, it was arranged so that the **divinations** <note>This refers to the ancient practice of hepatoscopy, or reading the liver, and the belief that the liver acts as a mirror for the mind during sleep.</note> that occur through dreams might shine upon it; for he <note>Referring to Plato.</note> believed that because of the liver's smoothness, density, and brightness, a force flowing from the mind reflects upon it. The **spleen** exists for the sake of the liver, to cleanse it and keep it shining, so that the corrosive impurities that flow around the liver during certain illnesses might drain away into the spleen.

### Chapter XXIV. On the distinction between the parts of the soul.

<margin>q</margin> That these three parts of the soul are separated into their own locations can be learned from what follows. First, things that are distinct by nature exist as separate entities. Now, that which possesses **reason** and that which is **subject to reason** <note>The irrational or emotional parts.</note> are distinct by nature; the former deals with things that can be understood by the intellect, while the latter deals with things that are painful or pleasant. Furthermore, reason belongs only to human beings, whereas the part that follows after disturbances <note>The passions.</note> is common to all other living creatures. Therefore, since the rational and irrational portions of the soul are distinct by nature, they must also be separated by location. Indeed, these two are often found to be in conflict with one another. However, nothing can fight against itself, nor can opposites be present in the same thing, in the same way, at the same time. We see this in the character of **Medea**, where anger fights against reason; she says, "I understand that the things I am about to do are evil, yet my anger overpowers my judgment." <note>original: "intelligo... quæ factura sum esse mala, ira tamen consilium superat." This is a common citation of Euripides' Medea to show the soul's internal conflict.</note> Likewise, in **Laius** <note>The father of Oedipus.</note> when he abducted **Chrysippus**, desire fought too much against reason, for he says: "Alas, this is a divine evil for men, when someone knows the good but does not practice it." <note>original: "Heu heu diuinum hoc hominibus malum, quando quis bonum nouit, sed minime utitur."</note> It is also clearly evident that the rational power is a distinct thing from the fact that the treatment for each is different: reason is cured by **instruction**, while the other part is cured by **habit** and **exercise**.

### Chapter XXV. On the immortality of the soul.

<margin>a</margin> Plato demonstrates that the soul is immortal through the following arguments. To whomever the soul is present, it brings **life**, as life is naturally inherent within it. However, that which provides life can never receive its opposite, which is **death**.

<meta>catchword: opposite (original: "traria")</meta>

The souls of other living beings perhaps exist in such a way, and he <note>Referring to Plato</note> calls that soul which participates in the same mixture "self-moving" by its very nature. This is because it possesses an innate life that is always operating according to its own essence. Therefore, anyone can assert, following the opinion of Plato, that rational souls are immortal. However, whether irrational souls <note>The souls of animals that lack human reason.</note> are also immortal appears to be an ambiguous matter. Yet it is probable that the souls of irrational creatures—since they are led solely by **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"; here meaning sensory impressions without the guidance of reason.</note> and are devoid of reasoning and judgment, neither using the intellect nor the collection of thoughts, nor the discernment of good and evil—are not of the same nature as our own souls, but are instead mortal and subject to decay. From the fact that our souls are rational, it follows that they enter into bodies from the outside, attaching themselves to fetuses that are already formed. They are able to transmigrate into many bodies, both human and otherwise, while always maintaining the same number. This occurs either by the will of the gods or because of a lack of self-control in life and a love for the body. Indeed, the body and the soul have a certain kinship between them, much like the relationship between fire and **bitumen** <note>A naturally occurring petroleum or tar; Alcinous uses this as a metaphor for a powerful, sticky attraction or bonding between two different substances.</note>. Furthermore, the souls of the gods have obtained the power of discernment, which can also be called the faculty of recognition. Besides this, they have a nature for undertaking actions, which we can call the "vigor of assistance." Finally, they possess a certain power by which they reconcile and govern. Although these qualities of nature are present in the souls of men, they are changed once they have entered into bodies. For the faculty of reconciling and governing is transformed into **temperance** <note>original: "inconcupiscentiam"; literally a lack of worldly desire or lust.</note>, while the vigor of undertaking actions is transformed into **spiritedness** <note>original: "iracundiam"; usually "anger," but in Platonic psychology, it refers to the "irascible" part of the soul that deals with courage and defense.</note>.

### Chapter .xxvi. On virtues and vices, and the distinctions between them

<sig>q</sig>
Since the soul is divided into three parts according to its rational and irrational powers, Plato considers it to be a consequence for man that he can never be **prudent** <note>original: "prudens"; possessing practical wisdom or foresight.</note> so long as he remains either fearful or intemperate. Therefore, the absolute virtues are inseparable from one another. In another sense, we also speak of "natural virtues," which are innate gifts and good inclinations; because of a certain similarity, they have acquired the same name as the "perfect virtues." For this reason, we sometimes call soldiers "brave," even though they may be unwise and reckless; in doing so, we are certainly not speaking of the perfect virtues, but of their natural dispositions. Truly, the absolute virtues never increase or decrease. Vices, however, can be intensified or even diminished. Indeed, one man may be more unwise or more unjust than another. Yet, not all vices necessarily follow one another, for there are **opposite**...

...certain opposites, which cannot come together in the same thing. So it is with ferocity against timidity, and prodigality against **avarice** <note>original: "auaritiam"; extreme greed for wealth or material gain.</note>. Nor can anyone be found who is stained by the marks of every vice, just as a body cannot be afflicted by all the corruptions of diseases at once. Moreover, a certain middle disposition must be accepted, which belongs neither to vice nor to virtue. For it is not necessary that all men be either good or wicked; for such people are those who have already reached perfection. Indeed, it is not easy to proceed from vice to virtue in a single step. For the extremes are distant from each other by a long interval.

Furthermore, some virtues are leaders <note>original: "principes"</note>, while others are attendants <note>original: "pedissequae"; literally 'foot-followers' or servants</note>. The leaders are those in the rational part of the soul, by which the other virtues are perfected. The attendants are those concerned with the part of the soul devoid of reason. These indeed perform honorable deeds, but not according to a reason inherent in them (for they have none). Instead, they act according to the norm imposed on them by **prudence** <note>original: "prudentia"; practical wisdom or the ability to govern oneself by use of reason.</note> through habit and exercise. And since neither science nor art exists in any part of the soul other than the rational, the virtues concerned with the irrational parts cannot be taught, because they are neither arts nor sciences. For they do not possess their own intelligence. 

Yet Prudence, which is a science, assigns to each its own, just as a pilot sometimes indicates to sailors things they have not seen. They follow; the same logic applies to the soldier and the leader of the army. Since evils are both intensified and relaxed, sins will by no means be equal, but some will be greater and others smaller. For this reason, lawmakers punish some things more mildly and others more harshly. And although the virtues themselves are certain "summits" <note>original: "summitales"; meaning they are the highest state of perfection.</note>, because they are perfect and compared to what is right, they are nevertheless called "middle states" <note>original: "mediocritates"; the Aristotelian and Platonic concept of the "Golden Mean."</note> in another way, because regarding each virtue (or at least most of them), two vices are seen on either side: one arising from excess, the other from deficiency. 

Just as regarding **liberality** <note>original: "liberalitatem"; the virtue of being generous with money or gifts.</note>, one sees avarice on one side and prodigality on the other. For in the passions, intemperance follows either because one goes beyond what is fitting, or because one does not reach it at all. Nor truly is he moderate who is not moved at all by his parents' rage, nor is he moderate who is carried away by the smallest of things. Likewise, he who feels no grief when his pious parents have died is senseless; but he who destroys himself with sorrow is unrestrained. But he who grieves in moderation is called moderate. And he who trembles at everything is fearful; he who fears nothing at all is fierce; but the brave man is he who maintains the middle ground <note>mediocritatem</note> between fearing and daring. The same logic applies to all other things. Since indeed the middle state in the passions is best, and the middle state is nothing other than the mean between excess and deficiency, for this reason such virtues...

ALCINOUS

...these are called the means <note>original: "mediocritates"; referring to the "Golden Mean," the virtuous middle ground between two extremes of excess and deficiency.</note>, because they render us moderately affected regarding human disturbances.

### Chapter 27. How virtue is indeed voluntary, but vice is involuntary.

Since indeed, if anything else exists within our power and is not coerced, virtue is of this kind above all. For it would not be judged worthy of praise if it occurred either by nature or by divine chance. It follows that virtue exists voluntarily, and does so through a certain burning, noble, and perpetual affection. From this fact—that virtue is voluntary—it is concluded that vice <note>original: "prauitatem"; depravity or moral crookedness.</note> is involuntary. For who would ever willingly choose the extreme evil to reside in the most excellent part of themselves <note>The "excellent part" refers to the rational mind or soul.</note>? But if someone falls into vice, he is initially inclined toward it not as if it were an evil, but rather as if it were a good. And if he rushes into evil, he is entirely deceived, acting so that he might avoid a greater evil by means of a lesser one; thus, he acts involuntarily. For it cannot happen that anyone turns toward evils with the intention of desiring them for their own sake, nor without being moved by some hope of good or fear of a greater evil.

For this reason, all the things that a wicked man does are involuntary. Since injustice is involuntary, acting unjustly is much more involuntary, to the degree that the actual practice of a vice is worse than just having the idle habit of it. And although crimes are involuntary, wicked men must nevertheless be punished. There must also be different kinds of punishments, just as the damages inflicted through injury differ. Furthermore, the involuntary state consists in a certain ignorance or disturbance. These can certainly be shaken off through reason, civic custom <note>original: "consuetudineque ciuili"; the habits formed by living in a well-ordered society.</note>, and personal diligence.

### Chapter 28. On injustice, and on the distinction of passions.

Injustice is such a great evil that it is far better to suffer an injury than to inflict one. To affect someone else with an injury is the work of a wicked man, while to be affected by an injury is a state of weakness. Both are indeed shameful. Yet, to inflict an injury is worse to the extent that it is more shameful. It is even worthwhile to submit oneself voluntarily to a judge when one has been unjust, just as a sick person commits themselves to a doctor. For every punishment is a kind of medicine for the soul that has gone astray. 

Since many virtues are concerned with the passions <term>affectus: the internal movements or emotions of the soul, such as anger, fear, or desire</term> and disturbances, these passions themselves now seem to require distinction. A passion is a movement of the soul without reason, arising on account of some perceived good or evil. It is called an "irrational movement" because neither judgments nor opinions are passions in themselves, but rather they are movements of the irrational parts of the soul. For these are motions in that part of the soul devoid of reason; and even if they are our own doing, they are nevertheless not entirely within our power. Often, therefore...

### ON IMAGINATION AND THE INTELLECT

<center>V iiii</center>

...involuntary movements of this sort arise within us, which run contrary to our will. For sometimes it happens that although we recognize that the things occurring are neither harsh nor sweet, nor to be sought after, nor even to be feared, we are nonetheless dragged along by them. We would certainly never endure this if our disturbances <note>original: "perturbationes"; in Platonic philosophy, these are the passions or emotions that "disturb" the calm of the rational soul.</note> were the same as our judgments. For we reject judgments when we refute them through deliberation—whether we do so properly or not. Furthermore, the definition includes the "sake of some good or evil." For a passion is not stirred by an indifferent encounter. Indeed, all disturbances are born from the fact that something *appears* to be either good or evil. If a good seems to be present, we are flooded with pleasure; if we desire it to be present in the future, we feel longing. Conversely, when an evil appears present, we grieve; when it is in the future, we fear.

The primary and simple affections <note>original: "affectus"; the basic ways the soul is "affected" by external things.</note> are two: namely, pleasure and pain. The others are composed of these as if from certain elements. We should not count fear and desire among them as if they were simple and primary. For one who fears is not entirely deprived of pleasure; indeed, if he utterly despaired of the repelling or lightening of evils, he would no longer fear; rather, afflicted by a sharper passion from that point, he would feel pain rather than fear. On the other hand, one who desires—since he hopes for the fulfillment of what he seeks—is in some way delighted. Yet, because he does not have certain hope, he is distressed. If, therefore, desire and fear are not simple, it will be granted without controversy that none of the remaining affections are simple either—such as anger, longing, emulation <note>original: "emulationem"; can mean jealousy, zeal, or the desire to equal another.</note>, and others of this sort. In these, pleasure and pain are observed as if within compounds. 

Furthermore, some disturbances are "wild," while others are "domestic." The domestic ones are those that exist in humans according to nature. As long as these maintain a middle ground <note>original: "modum"; the proper limit or "mean."</note>, they are necessary and proper to us. But when they are carried away beyond measure, they certainly fall into fault. Of this kind are pleasure, pain, anger, mercy, and shame <note>original: "uerecundia"; a sense of modesty or moral hesitation.</note>. For it is appropriate for humans to be delighted by things that happen according to nature, and to grieve at the contrary; and anger is indeed necessary for repelling and avenging injury. Mercy is characteristic of humanity and charity. Shame, moreover, provokes us to turn away from disgraceful things. 

But "wild" and beast-like disturbances are created contrary to human nature from a perversion of life and the worst habits. Of this kind are excessive laughter, exultation in the misfortunes of others, and hatred of the human race. Whether these are vehement and intense, or mild, or however they may be, they always wander astray and never attain any praiseworthy moderation <note>original: "mediocritatem"; the "Golden Mean" of virtue.</note>. Concerning pleasure and pain, Plato says this: that these disturbances are naturally excited in us from our very origin. Pain...

...indeed, [pain] happens to those who are moved contrary to nature, while pleasure happens to those who are restored to their own nature. For he <note>Referring to Plato, whose doctrines Alcinous is summarizing.</note> considers the natural state of man to be a middle ground between pleasure and pain, while one is moved by neither, a state in which we live for most of our time. He also teaches several kinds of pleasure: some through the body, some through the soul; some pleasures are mixed with pain, others are pure; some occur through memory based on hope, others are newly stirred up. Some are shameful and others honorable—the former arising from lack of self-control and injustice, while the latter arise from temperance or some other good, such as the joy perceived from the exercise of virtue. Therefore, since the nature of most pleasures is shameful, he considers that there is no room for debate as to whether pleasure can be a good simply and absolutely. For pleasure seems a thin and empty thing, whose nature is a handmaiden <note>original: "pedissequa"; a servant or follower. Alcinous argues pleasure follows an action rather than being a primary good in itself.</note> to another and follows after it, not sharing in its own primary substance. It also meets its opposite, being always mixed with pain—things which certainly would never happen if pleasure could be an absolute good and pain an absolute evil.

### Chapter 29. On Fate and Free Will.

<margin>d</margin> Concerning fate, Plato held views of this sort. Everything, he says, is *within* fate, yet not everything is *decreed* by fate. For he does not describe fate like those laws that say: "this man will do such things, this man will suffer such things." For then the progression would be infinite, since those who are born are infinite, and the things that then happen to them are innumerable. Furthermore, no freedom would remain, and praise and blame would be utterly abolished. Instead, he pronounces fate in this way: "Whatever soul chooses such a life and commits such acts, such consequences will follow." Therefore, the soul is free, and it is placed within its own judgment <note>original: "arbitrio"; the power of the soul to choose its own path.</note> whether to act or not to act, nor is it forced by anyone. However, that which follows the action will be fulfilled by fate itself. For example: from the fact that Paris will seize Helen—which will be within his own choice—it will follow that the Greeks will go to war over Helen. So too Apollo predicted to Laius <note>In Greek mythology, King Laius of Thebes was warned by the oracle of Apollo that his son would kill him. Alcinous uses this to show that the "choice" to have a child was Laius's, but the consequence was fated.</note> himself: "If you father a son, that child will slay you." In the law [of fate], both Laius and the fathering of a son are included together. By fate, however, it is established what follows from the fathering of the son. The nature of that which is "possible" falls between the false and the true; and for the soul, its free power is carried along in every direction according to its own undefined nature. But what is accomplished by our choosing is immediately either true or false. This differs greatly from that which is in "potential" <note>Potentiality refers to the capacity for something to happen, while "actuality" is the realization of that capacity.</note>—that is, what will at some point exist by habit <note>original: "habitu"; a settled disposition or state of being.</note> or by act. For "potential" signifies a certain faculty and fitness for things which have not yet been assigned their order...

...just as a boy is called a grammarian, a flute-player, or a craftsman in **potentiality** <term>potentiality: the capacity to become something before it is actually achieved</term>, he will be established in the **habit** <term>habit: a stable quality or learned disposition (Latin: habitus)</term> of one of these only once he has learned it and acquired that state. ### Chapter 30. On goods, the highest good, and virtues.

<margin>d</margin> Next, let us briefly touch upon what Plato decided regarding ethics. He believed that the most venerable and supreme good <margin>ri</margin> <note>original: "summum bonum"</note> could neither be found easily nor, once found, be safely revealed to just anyone. Therefore, he shared the contemplation of this highest good with only a very few people, and indeed those who were most familiar and properly chosen. 

However, if anyone carefully examines his books, they will find that he placed *our* good in the contemplation of that First Good itself. This good may be called both "God" and the "Primary Mind." For he intended that all things called "good" by men should be named so for the reason that they participate in some way in the First Good itself. Just as all things that are sweet or hot obtain their names through a certain participation in a "primary sweet" or "primary hot" thing. 

Of those things within us, only the mind and reason achieve a likeness to that Good. For this reason, our good is called by him something beautiful, venerable, divine, lovable, well-proportioned, and "blessedness" <note>original: "beatitudo"</note>. 

However, of those things commonly called "goods"—such as health, beauty, strength, as well as wealth and honors—none of them is a good at all unless it is used with virtue. For if these are separated from virtue itself, they perhaps hold only the "matter" of a good, and for those who use them badly, they are undoubtedly evils. Indeed, Plato never calls these "mortal goods." 

Truly, he holds that blessedness is found not in [ordinary] good men, but in the divine and the holy. Therefore, he proclaims that the souls of legitimate philosophers are filled with certain wonderful and divine goods. And after the death of the mortal body, they feast upon divine banquets and circle the "field of truth" <note>A reference to Plato's *Phaedrus*, describing the place where the soul perceives true reality.</note> together with the gods. They deserve this most of all because throughout their whole lives they burned with a desire for divine knowledge and cherished it above all other things as something most precious. By its gift, the eye of their mind is awakened and—once blinded but now living again—is more precious than countless physical eyes, making them masters of the whole of rational nature. For indeed...

# ALCINOVS

...comparing [ignorant] men to those who have spent their entire lives in a certain subterranean cave, where they have never looked upon the bright light of the sun, but only at the small and empty shadows of those bodies that we see above the earth. While they looked at these, they would have thought they were seeing true bodies. For just as it is natural for these people, if they ever emerge from the darkness into the light, to criticize all that they had seen before—and themselves much more—as having been completely deceived, so also is it reasonable that those who turn from the darkness of this life toward divine things should despise what they once valued most, and love only the blessed contemplation of divine things. 

From these points, it follows to say that the only good itself consists in the knowledge of the First <term>First Good: The ultimate source of all value and reality in Platonism, often identified with God</term>, which is also the Beautiful. This is shown through all of Plato’s books, yet it is always asserted according to its own participation <term>participation: the Platonic idea that earthly things "participate" in or mirror the perfect Forms</term>. In the first book of the *Laws*, he speaks in this way: "There are indeed two kinds of goods: those that are human, and those that are divine" <note>original: "Duo quidem bona sunt, humana uidelicet, atque diuina"</note>, and so on. But if something is possessed without virtue and is devoid of the essence of the First Good, it is further called a "good" only by the ignorant; yet in the *Euthydemus*, Plato testifies that such a thing is actually a great evil to the one who possesses it.

That he thinks virtues should be chosen for their own sake is clear from the fact that he considers only the beautiful and honorable to be "good." This is demonstrated in many of his dialogues, but especially in those he published *On the Republic*. For this reason, he considers the human who has attained the knowledge of God <note>original: "dei scientiam"</note> to be the most happy and most blessed. However, he does not call such a man blessed because of the honors that follow such a man, nor for the sake of any other reward; rather, even if he is hidden from all people, and even if those things commonly thought to be evils—infamy, exile, and death—befall him, he will nonetheless be blessed. 

On the other hand, he does not think a man without the knowledge of God is any more blessed by possessing all the things the common people proclaim as "goods": riches, kingdoms, health, strength, and beauty. To all these things he introduced a consequent and harmonious end: that is, to become like God <note>original: "dei similem fieri"</note>, as far as the human race is able to achieve it. He attempts to establish this in various ways. Sometimes he says the "likeness to God" is to be wise, just, and holy, as he declares in the *Theaetetus*. For this reason, he warns that one must strive to flee from here to divine things as quickly as possible. But the "flight" is the likeness to God; and the likeness to God is to become wise, just, and holy. Sometimes he also demonstrates that we are able to become like God through justice alone, as in the last book of the *Republic*. For he says that no one is ever neglected by God who strives to become just, and through the duty of virtue itself, to make himself as much like God as possible. In the *Phaedo*, however, he asserts that the likeness to God is acquired through temperance and justice in this way: "Are they not blessed and holy, and in the best...

Justice always follows him as the punisher <note>original: "iudicium... index"</note> of those who have turned away from divine law." He who would be happy submits to this justice calmly <unclear>n</unclear>, obeying with mildness and modesty. Therefore, the end will be in harmony with the principle: to be made like God—namely, the celestial God, or without a doubt the super-celestial God <note>The "super-celestial God" refers to the highest principle or the One, which transcends even the heavens</note>, who does not possess virtue as such, but is more excellent than virtue. For this reason, someone might rightly call <gloss>misery (original: kakodaimonia)</gloss> the depravity of the <term>daemon: a person's inner spirit or guiding genius</term>, while <gloss>happiness (original: eudaimonia)</gloss>, which is to say blessedness, is the good state of the daemon. We shall finally approach that very likeness of God if we utilize a suitable nature, with morals, a way of life, and perceptions according to law and reason—and especially through teaching and doctrine—so that we may live always as those who are far removed from human affairs and devoted to divine contemplations. The preliminary cleansings and, as it were, the purifications of the inner daemon—if there should be a need for greater atonements—will be the mathematical disciplines themselves: music, arithmetic, astronomy, and geometry. Care of the body must also be maintained through gymnastics, by which the body is made more ready for the works of both peace and war.

->Chapter XXXI. The definition of virtue, and its distinction.<-

<margin>V</margin> Since virtue is a certain divine treasure, it is a perfected and excellent state of the soul, making a person orderly, harmonious, and stable in both action and speech, toward oneself and toward others alike. Now, among the virtues, some concern the rational part of the soul, and others concern the part devoid of reason. For since the nature of the rational part is one thing, that of the power of anger <note>the irascible part</note> is another, and that of the power of desire <note>the concupiscible part</note> is yet another, the perfections of these parts must also be different. Hence, prudence belongs to the first, fortitude to the second, and temperance to the last. Prudence is the science of things good, evil, and indifferent. Temperance is the order concerning pleasures and lusts, making them obedient to reason. When we attribute "order" and "obedience" to temperance, we wish it to be understood that it is a power by which our desires become the servants of their natural master <note>the "natural master" here is Reason</note>. <margin>Justice</margin>
Justice is a certain consensus of all the parts of the soul; indeed, it is a certain power through which the three powers of the soul <note>The Platonic soul is divided into the rational, the spirited (emotions/will), and the appetitive (desires).</note> harmonize with one another, and each performs its own function according to its dignity. Thus, justice is a certain common and integral perfection of these three virtues: prudence, fortitude, and temperance. It exists while reason leads and commands, and the remaining parts remain subject and obedient to the superior part, each according to the office of its nature. For this reason, it must be thought that the virtues follow one another in a certain connection. 
<margin>Fortitude</margin>
For Fortitude, since it is the preservation of a legitimate institution, will be the preserver of right reason. Moreover, right reason proceeds from 
<margin>Prudence</margin>
Prudence. Furthermore, Prudence consists with Fortitude, for it is indeed the knowledge of goods; and no one can discern the good while they are blinded by fearfulness and the disturbances that follow it. And in the same way, the prudent man has no commerce with intemperance. Generally, whoever, stirred by disturbance, does anything contrary to reason, always goes astray because of ignorance. Prudence truly administers personal affairs, household affairs, and the commonwealth. And insofar as it governs the commonwealth, it is called civil science <note>political science</note>, which has two duties: to establish laws, and to execute those that have been established. 
<margin>Legislative <note>original: νομοθετική (nomothetikē)</note></margin>

<margin>Judicial <note>original: δικαστική (dikastikē)</note></margin>
Judicial. Finally, civil expertise considers those things which pertain to peace and those which pertain to war; and in this matter, among many other things, it especially considers whether war should be entered upon or rather refused.

### Chapter 32. On Friendship.

<margin>Friendship</margin>
Friendship, properly speaking, is nothing other than mutual benevolence. This indeed exists when each person desires the good for the other just as much as for himself; which equality is preserved in no other way than through a similarity of character. For the like is a friend to the like and to the moderate. But the intemperate can agree neither with each other nor with the moderate. Others are also spoken of as "friendships," and yet they are not true friendships, though they are colored in some way by virtue. Of this kind is the natural benevolence of parents toward children and of kinsmen toward each other, as well as those which are called civil and rhetorical. For these do not always have a reciprocity of benevolence. Furthermore, a certain species of friendship is amatory affection <note>love/eros</note>. Honorable love belongs to a noble soul; shameful love to an abject soul; and the middle love to the middle soul. Indeed, just as there are three dispositions of the rational soul—namely, good, bad, and middle—so there are three amatory effects, differing from one another in species. That there are three loves is declared by their diverse ends. The shameful love indeed seeks only the pleasure <note>original catchword: "ptatem" from "voluptatem"</note> of the body...

...follows pleasure. And therefore, it is a passion of beasts. The noble lover, however, looks only to the soul, being ready for the duties of virtue. The middle type of lover delights in both: the beauty of the body as well as the beauty of the soul. Since the movement of love is distributed into the three forms <note>original: "ideas"</note> we have mentioned, the love of a good man, being free from passion, is in a certain sense artful <note>original: "artificiosus"; meaning guided by skill or a systematic method rather than raw impulse</note>. Thus, it resides even in the irrational part of the soul, and its thoughts are of this kind: to discern who is worthy of goodwill because of their soulful gifts, and to win them over. Then, if the thoughts and desires of the one he loves are noble and are carried toward the good with a certain fervor of spirit, he praises and approves of them. But if they are the opposite, he will neither flatter that person nor soothe them with sweet words and compliance; instead, he will deter them and teach them that they must by no means live in such a way, so long as they remain as they are. He will always promise and provide those things by which the one he loves, having been trained, may turn out to be of the best harvest. The final goal of this process is that friendship may be created out of love.

### Chapter .xxxiii. On the types of the state

<margin>r</margin>He says that certain forms of the state <note>original: "rerum publicarum"; the commonwealth or republic</note> must be presupposed, which he handed down in his books on the Republic. In these, he described the first form as concordant and the second as discordant, inquiring into what their excellences were and in what manner they were established. There is also in his work a form of the state that mirrors the division of the soul, divided into three members: the guardians, the helpers, and the artisans. To the first group, he assigns deliberation and leadership. To the second, defense whenever it is needed; these he compares to the "spirited" part of the soul <note>original: "iracundiae"; the *thymos* or emotional seat of anger and courage</note>, as if they were bringing aid to reason. To the last group, he assigns the arts and other services. He considers that the leaders must be philosophers, and that they ought to be dedicated to the contemplation of the Good itself. For only in this way will they govern all things rightly; indeed, the human race will never cease from evils unless either philosophers rule, or those who rule, by some divine lot, truly philosophize. For the state is administered best and with justice when each individual portion of the city performs its own duty: the leaders of the people consult and decree, the military follows and protects them, and the rest willingly obey their superiors. He introduced several species of the state: the first is the rule of the best <note>Aristocracy</note>, when the most excellent men are in charge; the second is the ambitious rule <note>Timocracy</note>, in which men inflated with pride dominate; the third is the popular rule <note>Democracy</note>.

...the fourth, the power of the few <term>Oligarchy: A system where power rests with a small, typically wealthy, elite</term>. The last is the tyrannical form, which is the worst of all. He also describes other states based on various suppositions, such as the one established in his books on the *Laws*, and the one resulting from the amendments found in his *Letters*. He applies these to those cities which were described as "ailing" in the book of the *Laws*, which have already secured a distinct territory and people chosen from every age. Thus, according to the differences of their natures and regions, they are shown to require their own specific training regarding imports, exports, and weaponry. For those who border the sea will apply themselves to navigation and engage in naval battles. Those who live inland will be better suited for infantry combat; those who inhabit the mountains will use lighter armor, while those on the coasts will use heavier. Some of these will also practice cavalry combat.

<margin>1.</margin> In this particular state, he certainly does not establish women in common <note>Referring to the "Second Best State" in Plato's *Laws*, which allows for private families, unlike the "Ideal State" in the *Republic*</note>. Therefore, the civil faculty is a virtue that is at once contemplative and active; it chooses and proposes to make a state good and blessed, and is most consistent with itself. Its specific role is also to command, which is why all military arts are subject to it.

### Chapter 34. On the Sophist.

Thus far it has been stated what kind of man the philosopher is. The **Sophist**, however, differs from the philosopher both in *method* and in *subject matter*. In method, because he pursues the wages of young men, and prefers to *seem* good and famous rather than to *be* so. In subject matter, because the philosopher is concerned with those things which are always the same and remain in the same state <note>original: "circa illa, quae semper eadem sunt" — referring to the eternal Forms</note>. The Sophist, on the other hand, struggles and labors regarding that which "is least," fleeing into a province that can hardly be seen due to its darkness. For "that which is not" <note>original: "id quod non est"</note> is by no means opposed as a direct contrary to "that which is." For absolute non-existence neither exists, nor shares in any substance, nor can it even be understood. If anyone were forced to utter or think of this absolute nothingness, he would go astray and vacillate, because he would be at war with himself and lack confidence. But "that which is not," insofar as it is heard spoken, is not a bare negation of being itself, but carries a certain suspicion and insinuation of the *Other* <note>Alcinous is summarizing Plato's *Sophist*, where "non-being" is defined as "Difference" rather than "Nothingness"</note>, which in some way accompanies that which is. Unless things also participated in "that which is not," they would by no means be distinguished from one another. Now, however, as many things as there are, they exist in just as many ways as "that which is not" is pronounced. For "that which is not" is simply not one specific thing among those that exist.

### Finally, on the Epilogues.

Let these things suffice for an introduction to the Platonic discipline. Some of these have been treated in their proper order; others, without a fixed order, have been introduced here and there. Nevertheless, they have been handed down in such a way that by following these tracks, one may also hunt down the remaining meanings of Plato.

-> THE END OF ALCINOUS. <-

# ¶ The Book of Speusippus, disciple of Plato, on the Definitions of Plato.

¶ **Everlasting**: that which exists through all time; it existed before, it exists now, and it is subject to no decay. ¶ **God**: a living being, immortal and self-sufficient for happiness by his own nature; an everlasting essence and the cause of goodness itself. ¶ **Generation** <note>original: *Generatio*; in this context, the process of "coming into being"</note>: a movement toward essence, the receiving of essence, or the process of entering into existence. ¶ **The Sun**: a celestial fire which alone can be seen by the same observers from its rising to its setting; an everlasting living being, an ensouled star, active by day, and the greatest of its kind. ¶ **Time**: the motion of the sun and the measure of progression. ¶ **Day**: the sun's journey from its rising to its setting; a light contrary to night. ¶ **Dawn**: the beginning of the day, the first light from the sun. ¶ **Midday**: the time in which the shadows of bodies are at their shortest. ¶ **Sunset**: the end of the day. ¶ **Night**: a shadow contrary to day; the deprivation of the sun. ¶ **Fortune**: a movement from the hidden to the hidden, occurring by some chance, and the cause of a successful outcome. ¶ **Old Age**: the decline of life brought about by time. ¶ **Wind**: the agitation of the air around the earth. ¶ **Air**: an element whose every change of place is according to nature. ¶ **Heaven** <note>original: *Caelum*; referring here to the physical sky or cosmos</note>: a body encompassing all bodies except for the highest air. ¶ **The Soul**: that which moves itself, and the cause of vital movement in living beings. ¶ **Power** <note>original: *Potentia*; here meaning potentiality or the capacity to act</note>: that which is effective of its own accord. ¶ **Sight**: a state or habit by which bodies are distinguished. ¶ **Bone**: marrow solidified by heat. ¶ **Element**: that from which things are composed and into which composite things are dissolved. ¶ **Virtue**: the best disposition or habit of a mortal living being, praiseworthy in itself; the state according to which that which possesses it is called "good." ¶ **Fellowship** <note>original: *Communio*</note>: a just institution of laws, by which that which is endowed with it is called upright; a state that provides harmony. ¶ **Prudence** <note>original: *Prudentia*; translating the Greek *phronesis* or practical wisdom</note>: a power that leads of itself toward human happiness; the knowledge of good and evil, providing a fortunate disposition by which we judge what should be done and what should not. ¶ **Justice**: the soul's agreement with itself and the mutual order of its parts; a state that distributes to each according to their worth; a state by which one who is always endowed with it chooses what seems just; a state obedient to the laws of life; a communicative equality; a state that always obeys right laws. ¶ **Temperance**: the soul's moderation regarding natural desires and pleasures; the soul's composition and order toward natural pleasures and pains; the soul's voluntary harmony in commanding and obeying; the rational activity of those things that are according to nature; the soul's conduct regarding things honorable and shameful; a state by which proper things are cho[sen]... <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

¶ **Courage** <note>original: *Fortitudo*</note>: an undaunted habit of the soul; military daring; skill in those things which pertain to war; constancy of mind against those things which usually cause terror. ¶ **Self-sufficiency** <note>original: *Sufficientia*</note>: the perfect possession of goods; a habit by which each person becomes master of himself.

¶ **Equity** <note>original: *Aequitas*</note>: a relaxation of what is strictly just or advantageous <note>In a legal sense, equity is the application of fairness where a strict law might be too harsh</note>. ¶ **Gentleness** <note>original: *Manſuetudo*</note>: a constitution of the soul that remains immovable against the impulse of anger; a moderate tempering of the soul.

¶ **Happiness** <note>original: *Beatitudo*</note>: a good accumulated from all good things; a power sufficient in itself for living well; perfection according to virtue; a sufficient convenience of life.

¶ **Magnificence** <note>original: *Magnificentia*</note>: an estimation according to right and honorable reason.

¶ **Frugality** <note>original: *Frugalitas*</note>: the simplicity of a rational life, and the pursuit of good character.

¶ **Goodness** <note>original: *Bonitas*</note>: a disposition by which we choose the best things.

¶ **Magnanimity** <note>original: *Magnanimitas*</note>: the moderate use of life’s occurrences; refined conversation with people. Magnificence of the soul joined with reason.

¶ **Philanthropy** <note>original: *Φιλανθρωπια*; literally, "love of humanity"</note>: that is, humanity; a disposition of friendship that wins people over; a habit beneficial to people; the returning of thanks. Beneficial gratitude.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical explorations of Porphyry, a 3rd-century Neoplatonist. The text focuses on the distinction between the physical "composite" (body and soul) and the eternal "simple" essence (the soul or intellect itself).</meta>

### PORPHYRY:

For the alteration that is present in a thing does not happen from just anything. Therefore, matter does not suffer <note>original: *patitur*; in this philosophical context, "suffering" or "passion" refers to the capacity of a thing to be acted upon or changed by an external force</note>. For matter, according to itself, is devoid of quality. Nor do the forms themselves suffer, which enter into it and subsequently leave it. Rather, this "passion" or change occurs around the composite <note>The "composite" is the physical object or body made of both matter and form</note>, and its being consists in that composition. For the composite appears to persist in its existence despite the conflicting forces and qualities of the things entering and leaving it. For this reason, those things whose life comes from external sources—and not from themselves—must certainly undergo both living and not living as "passions." But for those things whose existence consists in life, it is necessary that they remain according to life, just as it is proper for a state of "life-emptiness" <note>referring to inanimate matter</note> to not "suffer" life insofar as it is a void of life. 

And so, just as it happens to the composite of matter and form—that is, the body—to be changed and to suffer, yet this does not happen to the matter itself; so also living and perishing is perceived in the composite of soul and body, yet this does not happen to the soul. For the soul is not something fused together from "life" and "non-life," but consists of life alone, seeing as it is a simple essence <term>Simple essence: a fundamental reality that cannot be broken down into smaller parts or different substances</term>, and the very definition of the soul is a nature that moves itself.

->Every intellect is all-formed.<-

Intellectual essence is so similar in its parts that even in any particular intellect, all beings are present as one, and that one is the intellect. But in the universal intellect <note>The "Universal Intellect" (Nous) is the divine realm of Ideas in Neoplatonic thought</note>, even particular beings exist in a universal manner. In a particular intellect, however, even universal things exist together with particulars in a certain particular condition.

->The soul does not die because its essence is life.<-

Concerning the essence whose being consists in life, and whose "passion" is life: certain things are surely so. Death is found within some kind of life, not in a total privation of life all at once. For neither is "passion" or life entirely absent there toward non-living; rather, it is there that bereavement <note>original: *orbitas*, meaning a loss or deprivation</note> happens.

->Every incorporeal life remains immortal, however it may change.<-

In the case of incorporeal beings <note>Things without physical bodies, like souls or divine minds</note>, their progressions are achieved while their prior states remain firm within themselves, losing nothing of themselves. They do not change their substance in order to provide for inferior things. Therefore, the things that exist because of them do not exist through any loss or transformation of the source. Nor indeed are they produced through the process of generation, destruction, or change. Therefore, they are unbegotten and incorruptible; and they are unbegotten and incorruptible because they are produced according to this very principle.

->How that which is above the intellect should be understood.<-

Concerning that which is higher than the mind <note>Porphyry refers here to "The One," the absolute source of all existence which transcends even thought</note>: many things are said through the intelligence. Yet, these things are desired through a certain "void of intelligence" <note>A state of mystical unknowing or silence</note> that is better than intelligence itself.

***

<summary>Porphyry argues that while the physical body (a composite) undergoes change and death, the soul—as a simple, self-moving essence—is inherently life and remains immortal. He further describes how the Intellect contains all forms of existence and how the ultimate source (The One) transcends even intellectual understanding.</summary>

¶ **Ferocity** is an excess of boldness, not fearing the things that ought to be feared.

### The Golden Words of the Philosophy of Pythagoras.

First, honor the immortal gods, as the laws command; respect your oath, 
<margin>1</margin> then the blessed heroes. Afterward, honor the terrestrial spirits <note>original: *demones*; in the Pythagorean tradition, these are protective intermediary spirits, not "demons" in the modern sense</note>. Observe those things established by law. Honor your parents and your kin. From among other men, make him your friend who is most excellent in virtue. Yield to mild words and useful deeds. Do not turn against your friend for a slight error; bear it as long as you are able. For power dwells near necessity. Consider these things well. Abstain from these: first, the belly, then sleep <note>original: *sonō*; likely a variant or error for *somno* (sleep), which is standard in the Golden Verses</note>, and luxury and anger. Commit nothing shameful, neither in the presence of others nor by yourself. Above all, respect yourself. Practice justice, both in word and deed. Accustom yourself to doing nothing without reason. Know that death is ordained by fate for all. Learn to accumulate money in season, and again, when the situation requires, to spend it. As for those adversities which befall men by chance, bear whatever lot you have without disturbance. It is right to seek a remedy as much as you can. Know that fortune does not bring many such adversities to good men. Many and various discourses, partly good and partly evil, are spread among the common people; do not let these move you, nor allow yourself to be constrained by them. If something false is said, bear it with moderation. Completely fulfill what I now tell you. Let no one, by either deed or word, lead you to do that which is not best for you. Deliberate before a deed, lest you act rashly. For it is the mark of a wretched man to say or do something rashly. Do not do those things which may eventually cause you to repent. Do not do what you do not know, but learn as much as is necessary. And thus you will lead a most pleasant life. Do not neglect the health of your body, but apply measure to food, drink, and exercise—indeed, I mean that measure which will cause you no distress. Accustom yourself to a way of life that is pure and without luxuries. Avoid those things which stir up envy. Do not squander your wealth at the wrong time, nor be ungenerous; for moderation <note>original: *mediocritas*; referring to the "Golden Mean" or the ideal middle path</note> is best in all things. Do not do things that might harm you. Consider before the deed. Do not surrender yourself to soft sleep until you have reviewed your daily works three times in your mind,

### The Golden Words of the Philosophy of Pythagoras

Because what has been done has passed, and what should have been done was omitted; beginning from the first, run through the rest. When you have done something shameful, <term>chastise yourself</term><note>original: *te ipsum crucia*; literally "torment yourself," here meaning to feel a healthy remorse that leads to correction</note>. But when you have accomplished good things, congratulate yourself. You must practice these things, meditate on these things, and love these things: these will set you in the footsteps of divine virtue; by him who delivered to our soul the <term>fourfold fountain</term><note>This refers to the *Tetractys*, a sacred Pythagorean symbol consisting of ten dots arranged in a triangle (1+2+3+4), representing the source of all nature and the divine</note> of ever-flowing nature. Go out to your work, having prayed to the gods. For if you hold to these things, you will know the condition of the immortal gods and mortal men, by which all things proceed and are contained. You will know, as far as is divine law, that nature is similar in all things. Then it may happen that you do not hope for things that should not be hoped for, nor shall anything be hidden from you. You will know that men are wretched by the cause of their own evils. They neither see nor hear the good things that are near them. Indeed, very few understand the release from evils. Such a fate harms the minds of men, who are carried from some things to others by certain revolutions, subject to infinite evils. A hidden, deadly discord within hurts them; avoid it by yielding, and after it has come, do not increase it. O Father Jupiter, either free men from evils, or show them what <term>spirit</term><note>original: *daemon*; in this context, a guiding personal genius or destiny</note> they follow. But be of good confidence, since a divine race is in men; for to these, sacred nature, bringing forth all things, demonstrates them. If any of these things are revealed to you, you will abstain from those things which I command you to abstain from. And if you apply this medicine, you will free your soul from these labors. But abstain from those mortal things which we mentioned above in the purification and release of the soul. Consider each thing with right judgment. Then set the best opinion before you as a charioteer.

->¶ The Preface of Marsilio Ficino of Florence to the translation of the book by Xenocrates the Platonist, "On Death," to the most illustrious man Piero de' Medici.<-

Cosimo, the glory of Italy, O Piero de' Medici—happy both in his great deeds and in having such a son as you—acquired for himself wonderful glory, not only through human prudence but also through divine wisdom. He spent no part of his life, even in his most important business affairs, without the company of the <term>Muses</term><note>The nine Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences; here implying intellectual and cultural pursuits.</note>. Especially in his old age, he surrendered himself entirely to the study of philosophy and sacred letters. So that he might be initiated into the first mysteries of philosophy, he desired that several books of Aristotle be translated by <term>Johannes Argyropoulos</term><note>A major Greek scholar and refugee who helped spark the revival of Greek learning in 15th-century Italy.</note>, a most learned man, and he read them with the greatest diligence. Then, so that the innermost secrets of wisdom itself would not be lacking to him, he ordered that eleven books of the divine Plato and one book of <term>Hermes</term><note>original: *mercurii*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus and the *Corpus Hermeticum*, which Ficino translated before finishing Plato.</note> be translated by us from the Greek language into Latin. In these, all the precepts for life, all the principles of nature, and all the sacred mysteries of divine things and kings are revealed. Cosimo read all these accurately and understood them completely. And when he had already finished reading Plato's book on the <term>One Principle of all things</term><note>original: *de uno regz̄ oium pricipio*; referring to the Neoplatonic concept of "The One."</note> and on the Highest Good, then on the twelfth day—as if about to return to that very Principle and to the enjoyment of that Good—he was called back from this <term>shadow of life</term><note>original: *uitæ umbra*; a Platonic metaphor for the physical world as a mere shadow of the higher, spiritual reality.</note> and approached the light above. Both his fatherland and the <term>Academy</term><note>The Platonic Academy of Florence, an informal circle of scholars sponsored by the Medici.</note> would deeply mourn his passing, had Piero not been so very like his father; in whose prudence and piety the fatherland may strengthen its hope and the Academy may find rest. On the twentieth day before his pure spirit was released from the bonds of the body, the sun now...

<meta>This page transitions from the cryptic "Pythagorean Symbols" to a personal letter and translation by the Renaissance philosopher Marsilio Ficino. It completes the thought regarding the "setting" of Cosimo de' Medici’s life and introduces a dialogue on death attributed to Xenocrates.</meta>

As his life was setting <note>original: *occidente*; referring to the final days of Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino’s patron</note>, he began to lament the misery of this life. Indeed, he spoke so forcefully against the errors of mortals that he claimed death was a kind of gain. At that time, he discussed the contempt of this life both acutely and at great length, as one who was already aspiring to heavenly happiness. When he had finished speaking, I said these same things: "Cosimo, Xenocrates—a holy man and a beloved disciple of our Plato—treated these matters in his book on death." Then he said, "Marsilio, bring into Latin those things which Xenocrates discusses in Greek." I brought them <note>likely meaning he brought the Greek manuscript to show him</note>. He approved. He ordered them to be translated. I translated them, and I have dedicated the work to your name <note>referring to Piero de' Medici, Cosimo's son</note>. Thus, when you read this brief but most precious little work, you may reflect on how much should be hoped for in this life, and how much one's own death, or that of parents or children, ought to be mourned. Therefore, read these things happily, O pillar of the Academy. And live long, so that we may not feel ourselves to be lacking Cosimo.

## The Book on Death by the Platonic philosopher Xenocrates, translated from the Greek language into Latin by Marsilio Ficino the Florentine, for the most illustrious man, Piero de' Medici. <note>While attributed here to Xenocrates, this dialogue, known as the *Axiochus*, is now considered a "pseudo-Platonic" work written by an unknown author in the 1st century BCE.</note>

### Socrates, Clinias, Axiochus

When I was setting out for the <term>Cynosarges</term> <note>original: *cynosargem*; a public gymnasium outside the walls of Athens</note>, and had already reached the <term>Ilissus</term> <note>original: *ilisso*; a river in Athens</note>, I heard the voice of someone calling me by name. Turning around, I saw Clinias, the son of Axiochus, running toward the <term>Callirhoe</term> spring <note>original: *fontem calliroem*; a famous natural spring in Athens</note>. With him were Damon the musician and Charmides, the son of Glaucon; the former was his teacher of music, while the latter was joined to him by a certain mutual goodwill. It seemed right to me to turn back and meet them, so that we might come together more quickly and easily. 

"Socrates," Clinias said with tears, "the present time demands that you show us that wisdom which you always preach. For my father has been struck by a sudden and intolerable illness, and he is near death; he seems to take it hard, even though in the past he used to mock those who feared death as if they were terrified by the faces of <term>masks</term> <note>original: *laruarum*; referring to theatrical masks or frightening ghosts</note>. Come, I beseech you, and rebuke him as you usually do, so that he may bear this necessity easily. Join us, then, and together with the others, perform this pious work." 

**Socrates:** "Honorable Clinias, your wish will be fulfilled as far as it lies in me, especially since the work you request is holy. Let us hasten then; if things are as you say, we must hurry."

**Clinias:** "As soon as he sees you, Socrates, he will recover. Indeed, it has often happened that he would somehow come to his senses." 

So we proceeded to him through the <term>Peritonian</term> fields <note>original: *peritonios agros*</note> along the walls. For he lived near the gates, toward the <term>Amazonian column</term>. We found him physically sound and robust in body, but weak in spirit and greatly in need of consolation; he was breathing heavily and drawing sighs, with many tears and the striking of his palms together.

## Xenocrates the Platonist

When I had seen these things, I said: "What is this, O Axiochus? Where now is that former and vaunted steadfastness of yours? Where are the perpetual praises of the virtues? Where is the wonderful greatness and boldness of your soul? For like a cowardly wrestler <note>original: *luctator ignavus*; a common philosophical metaphor comparing life's trials to athletic contests</note> who appears noble in the gymnasiums, you have succumbed in the actual matches. You do not consider the order of nature itself, even though you are such a great man, imbued with so many disciplines, and, if nothing else, at least an Athenian. Do you not hold to that common and well-worn maxim, which says that this life is a kind of journey <note>original: *peregrinationem quandam*; the idea that life is a temporary stay in a foreign land</note>, and that we, traveling properly and with an equal mind, ought to approach what is owed and necessary with a joyful rather than an ailing mind? This softness is not suited to a mature age, but to an infant." 

**Axiochus:** "These things, O Socrates, seem to be spoken rightly. But I know not how, when the danger looms, those very speeches about endurance, once so abundant, secretly vanish and are neglected. A certain conflicting fear arises, shaking the soul from every side. Alas! I shall be deprived of this light and these goods. I shall lie in darkness, deprived of taste and sight, and I shall rot. I shall be turned into worms and wild beasts." 

**Socrates:** "You join things together, O Axiochus, without the examination of reason; you confuse the loss of sensation with sensation itself, and you contradict yourself both in your speaking and in your grieving. You do not notice that you complain about the loss of sensation while simultaneously mourning over decay and the loss of goods, as if you were about to pass into another life, rather than migrating into a total lack of sensation—a lack, I say, such as preceded your birth. For just as nothing bad happened to you during the era of the republic of Draco or Cleisthenes <note>Draco (7th c. BCE) and Cleisthenes (6th c. BCE) were famous Athenian lawgivers; Socrates argues that because Axiochus did not exist then, he could not suffer, just as he will not exist to suffer after death</note>—for you did not exist as one to whom evil could happen—so after death, nothing will be against you; for you will not exist as one to whom evil might happen. Therefore, push away all such nonsense from yourself. Consider this: that when that which was composed is dissolved, and the soul departs to its own proper place, this which remains—the earthy and irrational body—is in no way the 'man.' For we are the soul, an immortal being <note>original: *animal*; in the sense of a 'living thing' or 'animated being'</note> shut in a mortal dwelling. Nature constructed this shelter for us for the purpose of suffering. Its pleasures are counterfeit, fleeting, and mixed with many troubles; its pains, however, are unmixed, long-lasting, and void of sweetness. Then there are the swellings of bile and phlegm <note>original: *pituita*; references to the 'four humors' believed to govern health and temperament in ancient medicine</note>, and diseases of the senses, as well as the decay of the internal organs. The soul necessarily suffers along with these, diffused through every passage so that it may bind each part. Thus it follows that it now longs for the celestial and kindred ether, and thirsts for the life and the heavenly choir. For the loss of this life is a transition from evil to good." 

**Axiochus:** "Since you judge this life to be evil, O Socrates, why do you remain in it? Especially since you meditate on these things most of all, act as a caretaker for others, and excel the rest in mind?" 

**Socrates:** "Axiochus, you are not a very true witness to me. For you think..."

<summary>In this dialogue, Socrates comforts the dying Axiochus by arguing that death is merely the soul's release from a burdensome, suffering body and that, since the self ceases to exist as a sensory being, there is no one left to experience the "evils" of death.</summary>

# On Death

Indeed, the Athenian people believe—ever since I became a searcher of things—that I know something. However, I would prefer to understand those common matters, so that I do not merely possess skill in superfluous ones. Those things we have just discussed are the declamations of the wise Prodicus <note>Prodicus of Ceos (c. 465–395 BC) was a contemporary of Socrates known for his linguistic precision and his lectures on the burdens of life.</note>; some were bought for two-thirds [of an obol], some for two drachmas, and some for four <note>Prodicus famously charged different fees for his lectures; the "fifty-drachma" lecture was his most prestigious, while cheaper versions were available to the general public.</note>. Truly, that man teaches no one for free. He always has that saying of Epicharmus <note>Epicharmus was a Greek comic playwright and Pythagorean philosopher.</note> in his mouth: "Hand washes hand; give something, and receive something in return." In recent days, he brought so many arguments against life that it was nearly enough to make me end my own life; and from that time, O Axiochus, my soul dies continually.

**Axiochus:** What then are the things he said, Socrates?

**Socrates:** I shall recount everything that remains in my memory. For he asked: "What part of life is not full of evils?" Does not the infant, having just been born, immediately lament? Does it not begin life with sorrow? No pain is absent. Whether because of lack, or cold, or heat, or a blow, it cries. It cannot yet explain in words what it suffers; instead, it weeps and cries out, and this alone is its voice, a sign of its distress.

When it has completed its seventh year, it is burdened with many more labors. For then arise the pedagogues <note>Tutors or attendants, usually slaves, who supervised a boy's conduct and accompanied him to school.</note>, the grammarians, and the physical trainers; they rule over the child no differently than tyrants. When he has grown a little older, the censors, arithmeticians, geometricians, and distributors are in charge, along with countless other masters.

Once he becomes a youth <note>original: *ephæbum*; the ephebe was a young man aged 18–20 undergoing military and civic training.</note>, fear surrounds and enslaves him; the Lyceum, the Academy, the governance of the gymnasium, the rods of authority, and an immoderate amount of evils suddenly rush upon him. All the distress of the young man is held under the censors of morals and the chosen council of the Areopagites <note>The Areopagus was the high court of Athens, which at various times held oversight over the education and behavior of citizens.</note>.

When he is finally released from their dictates, cares and anxieties creep in, as he debates which path of life he ought to enter. This is so difficult that, in comparison to the following labors, those preceding ones seem light and to be feared only by infants. Campaigns of war, wounds, and frequent struggles arise.

At last, old age itself creeps in secretly, into which flows every foul and incurable evil of nature. Unless one immediately 
<margin>+</margin> restores his life like a debt, nature—acting like a moneylender—insists and demands her collateral. From this man, sight is taken; from that one, hearing; from another, both. If one resists, nature dissolves, infects, mutilates, and cuts him off. Some live even to extreme old age, but they become "twice-children," decrepit in mind.

For this reason, the God who provides for human affairs recalls those whom He loves quickly to Himself from this life. Thus, when Agamedes and Trophonius <note>Legendary architects who built the temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note> had built a temple for the Pythian god and prayed for whatever might be best for them, they were immediately weighed down by sleep and never rose again. The same also happened to the priests of Argive Juno <note>This refers to the story of Cleobis and Biton, the sons of a priestess of Hera (Juno) at Argos.</note>, when their mother asked Juno for some reward for her sons' piety. For when the oxen were slow, they themselves went under the yoke and transported their mother to the temple...

<meta>The previous page concluded with Socrates recounting the childhood miseries of cold, heat, and hunger.
