### Xenocrates the Platonist

Truly. And when they had made a vow to the god, they departed from life in the night. It would be tedious to recount the opinions of the poets, who deplore the calamities of human life in their divine poems. I shall mention one most famous poet <note>Socrates is likely quoting Homer’s *Iliad* (24.525–526), a common reference in Greek philosophical discussions on the nature of suffering.</note> saying: "The gods have ordained that miserable mortals should live in perpetual sorrow. Nor is there anything on earth more wretched than man." And so they say that Amphiaraus <note>A legendary seer and hero who was swallowed by the earth; in some traditions, this was seen as a divine mercy to spare him from old age or defeat.</note> was loved with a supreme affection by Jove <note>original: "Ioue" (Jupiter/Zeus)</note> and Apollo, yet he did not reach old age. What, moreover, would you think of him who commands that one should mourn the misery of their own life at birth? But I shall stop now, lest I seem to wander further than what was proposed. 

Who, then, would not complain greatly about the pursuit and the craft he has chosen? Let us run through the hired and mechanical laborers, working from night to night, and scarcely acquiring those things which are necessary for sustenance; they live complaining, and fill their nightly vigils with weeping and tears. What shall I say of sailors? To how many dangers are they subjected? Rightly indeed did Bias <note>Bias of Priene (6th century BC), one of the Seven Sages of Greece, famously remarked that those at sea are neither among the living nor the dead.</note> say that a sailor is counted neither among the dead nor among the living; for as a creature of the earth, yet a sharer of both and a doubtful life, he plunges himself into the water, entirely subject to fortune. 

But agriculture is sweet. So be it—but does it not, as they say, always find some occasion for sadness like an ulcer? Now indeed the farmer blames the drought and groans; now the rains; now the heat and scorching; now the worms; now the heat, now the untimely cold. 

Truly, the devotion to the republic <note>original: "rei p." (rei publicae), referring here to the life of a politician or statesman.</note>—to pass over much—by how many evils and hardships is it tortured! It possesses a joy that is as fickle, swollen, deceitful, and turbulent as phlegm or seething bile. But its loss is grim, and worse than a thousand deaths. Who, moreover, can be happy while he lives at the whim of the crowd, is mocked and hissed off stage, as if he were some game and a tale for the common people—shaken, hissed at, fined, miserable, and ruined? 

Where now, O civic Axioche <note>This likely addresses Axiochus directly or refers to a known associate; the text mentions Miltiades, the hero of Marathon, who ended his life in disgrace and prison.</note>, is Miltiades? Where is Themistocles? Where is Ephialtes? Where are the remaining leaders? I have never gasped for these things. For it does not seem to me honorable to perform the duties of a magistrate among a senseless people. What of those who—on the day after the trial of Theramenes and Callixenus <note>Theramenes and Callixenus were instrumental in the illegal collective trial and execution of the Athenian generals after the Battle of Arginusae (406 BC). Socrates was famously the only member of the presiding committee to vote against the illegal procedure.</note>—acting as presiding officers and subduing the accusers, condemned the men to an indiscriminate death? You, along with Euryptolemus, resisted the three thousand in the assembly when they were in a tomb-like frenzy.

**Axiochus:** You speak the truth, O Socrates. And indeed, from that time until this very day, I have avoided the tribunal; nor has anything seemed more difficult or harsh than the governing of the state. This is clear to those who themselves handle civil affairs. But you speak of these things as if looking at them from a distance, from some watchtower. We certainly understand those things more sharply, as we are engaged in the work itself. For the people, O friend Socrates, are ungrateful, irritable, hostile, cruel, envious, and unrefined...

<summary>Socrates argues that all human endeavors—from manual labor and seafaring to farming and high-stakes Athenian politics—are inherently miserable and subject to the whims of fortune or the fickle crowd. Axiochus agrees, noting that while Socrates observes these hardships from a philosophical distance, those in public life experience the cruelty of the populace firsthand.</summary>

**Socrates:** Since, O Axiochus, you judge the liberal discipline <note>Socrates refers to the "liberal arts" or intellectual pursuits, which he ironically notes Axiochus now finds as repellent as manual labor.</note> to be avoided above all others, what must be thought of the rest? **Axiochus:** By what reasoning, Socrates? 

**Socrates:** Because death is not present for the living, and those who have died no longer exist. Therefore, it is not around you now, for you are not yet dead. Nor, if you should pass away, will it be around you. For you will not be. Therefore, it would be a vain grief if Axiochus were to mourn that which is not around Axiochus, nor will be in the future. For you would be doing just as if you feared the horrors of Scylla or the Centaurs <note>Mythological monsters; Socrates uses them as examples of things that do not exist in reality and therefore cannot harm a person.</note>. For that which is fearful and horrible happens to those who exist; but for those who do not exist, there is nothing to be terrified of. 

**Axiochus:** You indeed gather these things from that shallow loquacity <note>original: "loquacitate"; referring to the clever, fast-talking style of the Sophists that prioritized style over substance.</note> which is now common everywhere; for from that comes this abundance of empty words, composed for the sake of young men. For a wavering mind does not understand the ornament of words, nor does it reach the "colors" of oratory <note>The "colors" (colores) of rhetoric are the artistic flourishes and stylistic devices used to embellish an argument.</note>. If it hears the pomp and splendor of speech, it neglects it, and it is far from the truth; it by no means endures the traps of sophisms <note>Clever but fallacious arguments used by some teachers to "win" a debate rather than find the truth.</note>. It only attends to those things which can strike and penetrate the soul entirely. 

**Socrates:** Without reason, Axiochus, you join the sensation of evils with the deprivation of goods, and it escapes you that you will be dead. Clearly, the person who is deprived of goods is afflicted by the contrary suffering of evils. But he who does not exist does not even notice the deprivation itself. In what way, therefore, where the knowledge of things afflicting is absent, can there be affliction? For in the beginning, unless through ignorance you supposed some sense to remain, you would not dread death. 

But now you overturn yourself, fearing lest you lose your soul. To loss you assign the soul. You fear lest you be deprived of sense, and you think that non-existing sense is grasped by sense—even though there are many and noble discourses on the immortality of the soul. For mortal nature would not have risen to such excellence as to despise the violence of savage beasts, cross the sea, build cities, prescribe the order of the state, look up to heaven, and measure the circuits of the stars, and observe the progress of the sun and moon, their risings and settings, and furthermore their eclipses and swift midday returns, and the double turnings of the Pleiades <note>A prominent star cluster; their movement was used by ancient farmers and sailors to mark the change of seasons.</note>, and winter and summer alike: the blasts of the winds, and the force of the rains, the flashing cast of the lightning-fire <note>original: "presteris"; a term for a fiery whirlwind or a specific type of lightning bolt.</note>, and finally wondrously fix the passions of the world in eternity, unless some divine spirit was within the soul, through which...

# ¶ The Book on Pleasure, by Marsilio Ficino of Florence while still a youth, addressed to Antonio Canisiano, a citizen of Florence. Prologue.

### THREE MODES OF DISCOURSE.

<margin>m</margin>I remember when I was together with you at your estate in Campoli; as we were led along both by the singular beauty of that region and the sweetness of the various fruits in which that villa especially abounds, we happened upon a discussion concerning pleasure. You requested then that as soon as I had the leisure, I should commit this discussion to writing. Therefore, I have composed this little work on pleasure for you with the greatest pleasure myself, as soon as I returned to Figline <note>original: "Figinum", the Latin name for Figline Valdarno, Ficino's birthplace near Florence.</note>. ¶ There are truly three modes of discourse among philosophers—to begin from this point specifically—one by which we defend and approve a certain fixed side of a question through argument, as the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were followers of Aristotle, known for walking about while teaching.</note> and Stoics <note>The Stoics were a school of philosophy that emphasized virtue, reason, and emotional self-control.</note> have done. The second is that in which, a question having been proposed, we bring forth various opinions and reasons regarding what is sought, so that after many views have been presented and compared in turn, we may choose which of them appears more probable and likely; this was the method used by the Academics <note>The "Academics" refers to the school of Plato's Academy, particularly in its later phases when it favored weighing multiple arguments rather than dogmatic assertion.</note> and nearly all the Socratics. The third kind is most characteristic of the Skeptics, who, since they think all things are indifferent and hold nothing certain or even probable to follow—for they confuse and mix together those things which are separated and distinct by the order of nature—are rejected by all the more excellent philosophers. 

¶ I have therefore decided at this time to adopt the method of the Academics and Socratics in this discussion from among them all. For indeed Plato, whom we follow and venerate as if he were a god among philosophers, forbids those who are still of a tender age from offering their own opinion on any matter, lest—as often happens among the young—what we have most approved of in our early years must later be revoked and turned toward a contrary opinion in our more mature age and weightier judgment. Therefore, I judged it better to run through the opinions of other philosophers on pleasure in a brief discourse than to express my own, so that I might not shamelessly assert anything against what is taught by our Plato, and so that I might satisfy your will, which I know to be most ardent in the study of philosophy. But so much for this; let us now come to the opinions of the philosophers.

<summary>In this preface, a young Marsilio Ficino introduces his treatise on pleasure to his friend Antonio Canisiano, explaining that he will use the Academic method of comparing different schools of thought rather than asserting his own youthful opinion.</summary>

### ¶ Chapter 1. On the parts of the soul.
### ¶ Also on gladness, joy, and pleasure, according to Plato.

PLATO therefore (to begin with the prince of philosophers) when he had divided the soul into two parts—namely, the mind and the senses—attributed gladness and joy to the mind, and pleasure to the senses. However, he thinks these first two differ from each other in that all joy is worthy of praise, while gladness is partly to be praised and partly to be censured. For he defines gladness <note>original: "lætitiam"</note> as a certain elevation of the mind in the possession of some good, which can either exceed or maintain a sense of moderation. Joy <note>original: "gaudium"</note>, however, is that very delight which is received from contemplation or from some other use of the virtues.

And so he himself says in the *Phaedrus* <note>Plato’s dialogue *Phaedrus* deals with the soul, love, and the afterlife.</note>, when he was speaking of that first and true life which the soul enjoys in the heavenly dwellings: "it is nourished by the contemplation of truth, and rejoices." For this reason, he frequently calls joy the "nourishment of the mind." Indeed, he wishes truth itself to be like a field, while the contemplation of that truth is like the crops. Then the nourishment taken from these two is the joy by which the mind thoroughly enjoys the contemplation of truth. 

Wherefore the same Plato, in that same *Phaedrus*, was disputing about that darkness into which the soul has been depressed and submerged from the highest and true light. He says there: "much effort is required to gaze upon the plain of truth," for the fitting food of the soul arises from that place, and the nature of the wings—by which the soul is elevated—is nourished by this. Plato calls those things "wings" by which the mind flies back to the heights from which it had descended due to the contemplation of earthly things. 

Since the soul can achieve this through two virtues—namely, the contemplative and the moral—Plato understands these virtues (as I interpret it) to be the "wings" of the soul itself. These wings it recovers through the contemplation of truth and divine things, just as it had lost them through the desire for these earthly things. When the soul has flown back to the higher realms with its wings recovered through the exercise of both natural and moral philosophy, he believes two rewards are returned to the soul upon its arrival. One is the contemplation of divinity; the other is a certain perfect and absolute joy, which the soul enjoys in that very knowledge of God. 

Plato calls the former "ambrosia" and the latter "nectar" in the *Phaedrus* with these words: "The soul that has truly gazed upon these things and been nourished by them, entering again, returns to its home within heaven. But when the charioteer has returned, standing the horses at the manger, he sets before them ambrosia, and nectar to drink upon it." In the manner of Pythagoras <note>Pythagoras was an earlier Greek philosopher who influenced Plato; the image of the soul as a charioteer is a famous Platonic allegory.</note>, he calls Reason the "charioteer," while the "horses" are the other parts and natures of the soul which Reason leads. The rest...

### ¶ Chapter 2. What pleasure is, and that it is not a good in itself, for many reasons, according to Plato.

<margin>u</margin>
Plato maintains that pleasure <note>original: "voluptatem"</note> is a certain sweet motion in the senses, which arises from the fulfillment of a lack <note>original: "indigentiae repletione"</note>. For he says that lack and its fulfillment are in a way 
<margin>in a way</margin>

Although he has demonstrated this with many very true arguments, this one is the first and most powerful of all: ¶ Just as by the presence of heat, those things to which heat comes are made hot, so also by the presence of that which is good, all things to which goodness itself is present become good. However, no one is made better by the possession of pleasure. For pleasure exists even in beasts—and to a greater degree than in humans—yet they are not only not better than humans, they are not even good at all. Furthermore, women and children, and finally fools and all the lazy, pursue pleasure and embrace it with all their strength, even much more than men who are good and of excellent character. And yet it would be absurd if that which is good were more suited to the wicked and the lazy than to honest and excellent men. ¶ Nor can opposites be mixed with one another, as he thinks. Yet pleasure is undoubtedly found even where there are evils, since it is not lacking in the wicked and the unjust. Therefore, in no way is it a good; for it associates with that which is evil. But the good, because they are opposites, can in no way unite with the evil. ¶ Add to this what is said by Socrates in the *Gorgias* <note>A Platonic dialogue discussing the nature of justice and rhetoric.</note>: that good and evil are never found at the same time in the same person. Yet the same person is often affected by pain and pleasure at one and the same time. For indeed all lack is painful, and every fulfillment of it is pleasurable to the senses. Now, he calls thirst a lack of nature, but drinking its fulfillment. Therefore, the former is troublesome, while the latter—drinking—is pleasant.

¶ Moreover, since every good ought to be stable and permanent, who would say that pleasure, which has no stability, is a good? Yet it cannot be denied, if one considers its definition, that pleasure is unstable and uncertain; for, as we mentioned above, it was called a "motion" in its very definition. Nothing is more contrary to stability than motion, nor is there anyone who has tasted any bodily pleasure who does not know how fragile it is, how brief, with what speed it slips and flows away, and how quickly it turns into its opposite. Furthermore, what is good can never be contrary to another good. Since pleasure hinders many of the greatest goods, who could doubt that it is contrary to the good? For pleasures block prudence, pour darkness into the mind, corrupt judgment, and with their charms and enticements—like certain harlots—they lure and ensnare the minds of men, prostrating the entire nature of man in the mud and filth of vices and crimes. For divinely, <term>Plato</term> <note>A foundational Greek philosopher whose works often contrast physical sensation with intellectual truth.</note> says in his letter to <term>Dionysius</term> <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse, to whom several of Plato's letters are addressed.</note> that pleasure brings detriment to men, giving birth to ignorance, restlessness, folly, and insolence.

¶ Moreover, there is no good that is not worthy of either praise or veneration. Yet no one of sound mind praises pleasure, nor is anyone judged worthy of honor and glory because they enjoy the greatest pleasures. But rather, the person who is truly worthy is the one who scorns and neglects them with a high and unconquered spirit.

...nor do they look back at the breezes, enclosed as they are in darkness and a blind prison <note>A common Platonic metaphor for the physical body imprisoning the soul.</note>, whereby it is brought about that only those things seem to be truly ours and to exist within us which have proceeded from the soul and reason. Everything else, however, arises from fortune or from that prison hostile to us, and is not so much ours as it belongs to the body and to luck. Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), an influential Roman scholar and writer.</note> rightly says: "No one should call 'his own' that which is outside of himself." Therefore, since pleasure is innate and implanted in the body and the senses, anyone who counts it among our [true] goods will undoubtedly seem to be insane. 

Add to this, if you please, what Socrates says in Plato’s *Gorgias*: that all goods of the soul proceed from art <note>original: "arte," here meaning a systematic skill or craft</note>, rectitude, order, and choice <note>original: "electione"</note>. Indeed, the entire discipline of moral philosophers agrees on this point: that the whole power of virtue and of the soul’s goods consists in choice. But who would say that pleasure proceeds from choice? Is it not true that for those things which fall under choice, counsel and deliberation must first have taken place? For nothing is chosen unless it has been previously considered and judged. Yet no one deliberates in order to have pleasure within himself; for it is innate <note>original: "ingenita"</note> in us. For this reason, Socrates thinks there are two "ideas" <note>ideals or ruling principles</note> in each of us which we follow wherever they lead: one is the pursuit of the best opinion; the other is the desire for pleasures. He calls the former an acquired idea, but the latter an innate one. 

Therefore, pleasure follows neither art, nor reason, nor any order at all. Instead, it is excited in us by a sudden and reckless impulse of nature and the senses, rather than by any certain judgment or counsel. It flatters the senses, soothes and tickles the body with a certain ruinous sweetness, softens <note>original: "effœminat," literally "renders womanish" or "weakens"</note> the soul, and removes the mind and reason from their proper state.

¶ Furthermore, such is the nature of all [true] goods that while they are still in the future, they raise a person’s hope; but when they are present, they make the possessor’s soul tranquil and quiet. They make him content with what is present and satisfy him with their possession, so that he lacks nothing further, seeks nothing, and desires nothing, as if he possessed that one thing which is by its nature sufficient and perfect. Even if someone who enjoys the possession of some good does desire something further, he nevertheless seems to be entirely free from anxiety and trouble. 

Future pleasures, however, affect the senses with an intolerable heat of desire; they inflame them with care, burden the soul with anxiety, and (to put it briefly) drive it into a certain madness and rage. When someone finally embraces those present pleasures for which they had burned with desire, those pleasures immediately bring fear and suspicion along with them. They blind us while we enjoy them and reduce us to the savagery of wild beasts. Nor while being drained—nay, (to speak more <unclear>truly</unclear>) nor yet

This makes that saying of Socrates in the *Phaedo* very true: that pain and pleasure are both connected to the same head, and that nature has joined their summits into one. For this reason, it happens that whenever one of them is present to someone, the other follows afterward. From this, the fires of desire arise again, and the more greedily pleasures are drained, the more numerous and fertile the seeds and sprouts of lust spring back. This is why (in my opinion) the poets portray Tityus in the underworld <note>Tityus was a giant in Greek mythology punished in Tartarus for attempting to rape Leto.</note>, 

> Whose body is stretched out across 
> Nine whole acres, and a monstrous vulture with a hooked beak 
> Pecking at his immortal liver and his vitals 
> Fruitful for punishment, searches for its feast; it dwells deep 
> Within his chest, and no rest is given to his fibers as they are born anew. 
<note>original: A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book VI, lines 595-598, used here to symbolize the endless cycle of desire and the pain it causes.</note>

For this reason, the divine Archytas of Tarentum <note>A mathematician and Pythagorean philosopher, a contemporary of Plato.</note> and Plato held that a soul of this kind is like a leaky jar, because of the insatiable and infinite abyss of wanting, which can be filled by no pleasures. Epicharmus the Pythagorean and Socrates compared the lustful soul not only to a broken jar, but even to the Euripus <note>The Euripus Strait in Greece is famous for its powerful and unpredictable currents that reverse direction many times a day.</note>. For just as the water in the Euripus flows and ebbs, and is tossed up and down, so too in a soul of this kind: now desire or pleasure enters, now it ceases and flows away, and then it is born again and flows back. One moment the lustful soul rejoices and hopes, and is raised upward, as it were; the next moment it grieves, despairs, fears, is anxious, and falls downward. At one time it wants a thing, then it does not; indeed, even at the same time, reason wants one thing while the senses <unclear>afflict</unclear> <note>The Latin 'affigent' is likely 'afficiant' (affect) or 'affigant' (fasten/attach).</note> another. Thus it happens that such a soul not only directs itself now to this and now to that, but is even pulled apart at the same moment into contrary passions and differing opinions. 

Therefore, Socrates used to say he would rather that his lyre be out of tune, or the choir he led, and that many other men should contradict him, than that he himself, being one, should be at odds and out of harmony with himself. From this, Pythagoras reasonably calls virtue a certain kind of harmony. 

¶ Next follow Plato’s remaining three arguments against pleasure. Indeed, he judges that the natures of good and evil are contrary, such that we achieve the good only with difficulty. In the case of evil, however, we slip down easily as if on a slippery path; therefore, evil things grow in such a way that it would be necessary for the entire nature of good things to be utterly destroyed and uprooted, unless nature had applied a most suitable remedy to this so destructive a plague. It is so established that individual goods, because of their great kinship with nature, limit themselves...

...they strive for it. They tend toward a single point, and are not separated from one another by any means, but come together in a kind of fusion. To whomsoever any one of these is present, no good thing can be missing. Virtues follow one another with such a strong connection <note>This refers to the classical doctrine of the "Unity of Virtue," suggesting that the virtues are so interdependent that one cannot truly possess one (like courage) without possessing them all (like wisdom and temperance).</note> that whoever has attained one already enjoys the possession of all virtues. Therefore, against the labors and difficulties of attaining goods, God seems to have set their union and coupling as a reward.

But truly, evils disagree and dissent among themselves, and in no way can they come together or be mixed. And Aristotle rightly says that evil destroys itself <note>original: "malum se ipsum corrumpit" — a reference to the *Nicomachean Ethics*, where Aristotle argues that vice is inconsistent and self-defeating.</note>; for if it were complete in every respect, it would be intolerable. Nor do extravagance and greed, or boldness and fear, ever meet in the same person; and in the same way, no other extremes of vice are connected to each other, since they are fundamentally opposed. Therefore, nature seems to have applied an excellent remedy against the tendency toward wrongdoing: that he who is more prone to a fall still cannot slip into every part of the abyss, whereas he who ascends with the greatest difficulty necessarily reaches the whole and complete summit. 

Since, therefore, this is the condition of evils and goods, it is concluded by necessary logic that those things which do not follow one another cannot be "goods." Pleasures, far from coming together, seem in a way to clash with one another and more often than not bring about hindrance. For while one of the bodily senses is moved by the greatest sweetness, the rest of them hardly perceive the joy of the things then offered to them. It also happens that one person feels more and greater pleasures than another, nor are all living beings delighted equally. Virtues, however, and all goods whatsoever, are so coupled together for the reason I mentioned a moment ago, that they are all present to the same person at once, and no more of these can be present to one person than to another. Since it is clear that the nature of goods and pleasures is different, surely no one—except one who is too much a friend to it—would call bodily pleasure "good."

¶ Then another argument of Plato proves that it is a property of goods to tend toward the common utility and well-being of the human race. But he says that pleasure produces its own particular lust and love <note>term: libido (lust) — used here to denote a narrow, selfish desire as opposed to a communal good.</note>; and whoever is subject to it always focuses only on his own desire, and has no care for anyone else, provided he may more watchfully obey his own whirlpool <note>original: "uoragini" — literally a whirlpool or abyss, used metaphorically for insatiable greed.</note> of greed. Everything he does, he relates back to that sweetness and joy perceived by the senses. 

¶ The final reasoning of the Platonists is that by which they claim that the good and the end <note>The "end" (finis) refers to the *summum bonum*, the ultimate goal or purpose of human life.</note> are exactly the same...

...they say an "end" <note>original: "finem" — in classical philosophy, the *telos* or ultimate purpose of an action.</note> is that toward which an appetite is referred as its ultimate point. Therefore, since man's natural appetite <term>appetitio|The natural inclination or drive toward something perceived as desirable.</term> desires pleasure only for the sake of something else, who of sound mind would think that this is an end, or a good at all? Indeed, for this reason they believe nature has given living beings this kind of sweet perception so that they might acquire and prepare those things necessary for living. For a living thing requires two main things: to reject and repel what can harm it, and to take and adopt what is beneficial. 

Since repelling the former and pursuing the latter is laborious and difficult, nature has woven a certain pleasure into every such action, lest living things be too slow to provide what they need because of that very difficulty. Thus, enticed and thoroughly captured by this sweetness—like a bait—they neither flee from any dangers or labor, nor perceive the difficulty of procuring food, and they are more ready to provide the necessities of life. 

That pleasure was given to us by nature for these reasons is demonstrated by this sign: all living creatures, when they expel what is superfluous from the body or take in what is necessary, are moved by this sweetness we have often mentioned; and those who do this more actively also perceive greater delight. But once they have fully satisfied nature’s need <term>indigentia|A state of lack or biological necessity, such as hunger or thirst.</term>, they feel no further pleasure. But we see them moved as long as they are filling a need, as if nature directed the pleasure of the senses toward attaining life's necessities and filling a void. 

Therefore, pleasure was handed down for the sake of both preserving life and propagating the species; it should not be sought for its own sake, nor is it an end, and for that reason, as we have often shown, it ought not even to be called a "good." 

¶ **Archytas the Pythagorean** <note>Archytas of Tarentum (c. 435–360 BC), a mathematician and statesman who believed that the mind is ruined by the pursuit of pleasure.</note> also used this argument against bodily pleasure: that causes and the things that follow from those causes must always be related. And so he thinks no one should doubt that something from which so many evils follow cannot be a good. It is clear that for the sake of pleasure <term>Voluptas|Sensual or bodily pleasure, often contrasted with intellectual joy or virtue.</term>, all poisonous disturbances of the soul, adulteries, debaucheries, homicides, thefts, dissensions, and finally all crimes are born. 

From these things it follows (as he believes) that pleasure seems not only not a good, but a certain greatest and detestable evil. By the same reasoning, **Antisthenes the Socratic** <note>Antisthenes (c. 445–365 BC), a student of Socrates often credited as the founder of the Cynic school; he famously said he would "rather be mad than feel pleasure."</note> proves that bodily pleasure is the extreme and highest of evils <term>summum malum|The "highest evil," the opposite of the "summum bonum" or highest good.</term>. Because what is the cause and origin of all evils can deservedly be judged the worst of all things; and since all sins proceed from ignorance, and nothing can be equally...

¶ Furthermore, **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure perceived as a "thrice-great" Egyptian sage, believed to be the author of the Hermetic Corpus, which blended philosophy, religion, and magic.</note>, the wisest of all the Egyptians, attempts to uproot this nefarious stain from the souls of men by two primary arguments. For he judges that to be good for anyone which either contains the thing itself within its own nature, or leads to a better result. 

We see that the virtues of the first kind are those placed in action. For it is their specific property to render the soul free and tranquil from all the tumult of disturbances. Indeed, the removal of disturbances and a certain serenity of mind exists as the proper and natural quality of each soul. It is established that virtues of the second kind are those engaged in **contemplation**. Truly, since they raise and exalt the soul through the study and understanding of divine things somewhat above human nature, they allow it to appear to approach as closely as possible to the life of God, which consists solely in contemplation. 

It is clear, however, that the condition of pleasure is contrary to both. For it agitates the soul with countless burning passions as if with Furies, so that it is far from that tranquility which nature so greatly requires. And since the human race holds a middle position between God and the beasts, and for that reason seems to participate in both, **Trismegistus** thinks it is possible to migrate or be converted into either one. For indeed, he who primarily uses his mind truly leads the most blessed life of the immortal gods, but he who uses his body and senses leads the life of beasts. 

Therefore, since the use of pleasure exists in the body and senses, he who is most dedicated to this not only fails to ascend to those things which are better and more divine, but does not even retain the status and dignity of his own nature; he slips, as it were, from soul to body, from mind to senses, and from man to beast. 

Divinely, in the works of **Plato**, **Socrates** says in the *Phaedo*: 

> pleasure, holding as it were a nail, fastens and joins the soul to the body, and brings it about that the soul, infected by the bodily appearance, thinks those things are true which the body suggests. <note>original: "quasi clauum tenens animum corpori affigit" — This is a reference to *Phaedo* 83d, where Socrates explains that every pleasure or pain acts like a "rivet" or "nail," pinning the soul to the physical world and making it believe the material world is the only reality.</note> 

For when the soul is moved by the same things and feels the same things as the body, it is forced (I think) to become of the same habits and the same nourishment.

...and should be called good things insofar as they imitate the highest good. That the highest good is God—whoever doubts this understands nothing at all. From this, all virtues, which are most closely related to God, are judged not undeservedly to be perfect and best. Indeed, tranquility and the knowledge of truth (as Plato also argues) are most characteristic of divinity. Therefore, no one can doubt that both kinds of virtues make men kindred to the immortal God. But what kinship can there be between pleasure and divinity? ### Chapter III. Objections of the Peripatetics against the Platonic definition of pleasure.

This, then, is the divine opinion of Plato concerning pleasure, in which **Hermes Trismegistus**, all the **Pythagoreans**, and all the more excellent **Socratic** followers agree without any doubt. But the **Peripatetics** <note>A school of philosophers who followed the teachings of Aristotle; they were known as "Peripatetics" (Walkers) because they often discussed philosophy while walking in the gardens of the Lyceum in Athens.</note>—men who are certainly sharp, but in this matter perhaps more devoted to dispute than to truth—strive to subvert and deprave such an excellent and divine opinion of Plato with certain subtleties of their own. 

¶ There are three points in which they attempt to criticize the Platonists. First, that Plato, in defining pleasure, called it a <term>motion</term> <note>Plato often defined pleasure as a "restoration" or a "motion" toward a natural state.</note>. For they say that every motion is either fast or slow, yet no pleasure can be called fast or slow. Rather, it must be called either brief or long-lasting; nor can any motion exist as a whole all at once. Instead, one part of a motion always succeeds another part, so that as one fails, another is born, and no two parts of a motion can wait for each other. Pleasure, on the contrary, becomes a whole all at once, and all its parts in turn (as it were...

(as I might have said) remain. For when the soul knows it enjoys the possession of some good, they think it immediately perceives pleasure. Thus, it follows that pleasure of the soul follows cognition and perception; and just as the perception of that which seems good (being an object presented from the outside) is entirely completed in a single point of time, so too is pleasure—which follows such an apprehension—perfected in a single point of time. Things that happen in this way occur all at once and equally, consisting in a certain indivisible and simple nature. From these points, they wish to conclude that pleasure is born in the senses at a simple point in time, and from its very first beginning, it exists as something whole and perfect, requiring no further part to make it more complete; from this, it follows that pleasure cannot be a **motion** <note>original: "motus" — in ancient philosophy, a "motion" or process is something incomplete until it reaches its end; the Peripatetics argue pleasure is a complete state, not a process.</note>.

Next, they reprove Plato for calling pleasure the "filling of a deficiency" <note>original: "repletionem indigentiæ" — Plato's theory that pleasure is the process of returning to a natural state of balance, like eating when hungry.</note>. They think this is false because pleasure resides in the soul, whereas "filling" occurs in the body. Nor do they agree that every pleasure is of such a kind that it matches the filling of a deficiency. For instance, the pleasures perceived by the eyes, ears, and nostrils from shapes, sounds, and smells do not fill any prior lack. Furthermore, they argue there is a certain ineffable pleasure in contemplation which fills nothing that was missing. Indeed, that pleasure is proper to the mind, and the mind truly neither needs any physical support nor can it be "filled" in any literal sense. For being filled—and conversely, being emptied—is something that happens to bodies, which can be full or vacant. But since the soul is simple and incorporeal, such things can in no way happen to it.

In the third place, they argue against the claim that Plato said no pleasures were good, and that most were bad. On the contrary, they [the Peripatetics] consider very many pleasures to be excellent and most worthy of praise, specifically those undertaken from honorable actions. For actions of this kind seem most pleasant, and the pleasure inherent in them is the best and purest.

### Chapter 4. Responses to the objections.

<margin>h</margin> These are the arguments of the **Peripatetics** <note>original: "peripateticorum" — the followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught.</note>, which I would distrust my ability to answer, were it not for the fact that the very man they are fighting against [Plato] defends himself (as the saying goes) by his own martial skill. Therefore, regarding the first argument—by which they conclude that pleasure can by no means be a motion—even if it happens to be true, it has no force against the Platonists. For Plato himself taught that there are two kinds of motion: one of bodies and another of souls. The motion of those bodies follows the nature of the body, since it cannot be gathered into an indivisible and simple state. Rather, it is necessary for one part of it to lie outside of another part; otherwise, it would lack division.

it is necessary; however, that which remains undivided has already stripped away the nature of the body. For this reason, since every body is extended and divisible, it is necessary that whenever it acts or is acted upon, or is moved from one place to another, the closer and forward parts must suffer, act, or be turned before the rest. Thus, all motion of bodies requires a span of time and is stretched out in a certain succession from what is first to what is later. The soul, however, is indivisible and simple, having no internal distinction or distance between parts. Therefore, the motion of the soul is indivisible and simple, and is completed entirely at once in a single point of time. Whence **Thales of Miletus** <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece, often considered the first philosopher.</note> said that nothing is faster than the soul. Since, therefore, pleasure was defined in **Plato** <note>Specifically referring to arguments found in the *Philebus* or *Laws*.</note> not as a motion of the body, but of the soul, nothing surely prevents it from being a motion and also existing entirely at once—especially since in the Platonic books, "motion" signifies not only flux and succession (as the **Peripatetics** <note>term: Peripatetics | Followers of Aristotle, who defined motion as a gradual process toward a goal.</note> maintain) but also every operation and act.

¶ Next, regarding their claim that Plato called pleasure the "filling of a deficiency" and deficiency "pain," this may perhaps seem less than true. For he himself in the **Gorgias** <note>A Socratic dialogue by Plato focusing on rhetoric and ethics.</note> maintains that pleasure consists in the act of filling. Truly, no one—except those most unlike Plato—would say that pleasure consists in "pleasure itself," or that any of those things which occur by nature consist in themselves. Furthermore, in the same book he says that "filling" is pleasurable, while "deficiency" is mostly painful. But who speaks so foolishly as to call pleasure "pleasurable" or pain "painful"? Who likewise would say "beautiful beauty" or "just justice"? In the same way, Plato would not have called pleasure "pleasurable" nor pain "painful." He did not, therefore, intend for pain to be deficiency, nor for pleasure to be the filling. Moreover, he says that pleasure is produced *from* filling, and pain *from* lack. He himself, however, believes that nothing can be produced from itself. In what way then will pleasure, if it were the "filling," be produced from that very "filling"? Or how will pain, if it were "lack," be born from "lack"? Indeed, even he himself in the **Timaeus** <note>Plato's dialogue on the nature of the physical world and human biology.</note> places pleasure in the senses and calls it a motion and an affection. Such a great man would never say that an affection or a sensory motion is a "filling." But if anyone should read in the *Gorgias* that pleasure is the filling of the body, let him consider that passage more attentively; he will eventually find that Plato does not feel this way himself, but that it is the opinion of **Callicles** <note>A character in the *Gorgias* who represents the "might makes right" philosophy and the pursuit of raw hedonism.</note>, a most pleasure-seeking man, against whom **Socrates** disputes most sharply.

¶ Truly, the Peripatetics grant us this. Nevertheless, some deny that every pleasure is created from the filling of a deficiency; especially since that pleasure which contemplation brings to us, and which remains in the mind...

it consists; it does not arise from the filling of any lack <note>original: *indigentiæ repletione*</note>. Even though I could show more clearly than light itself that the delight of the mind, which is captured from contemplation, also takes its origin from that very filling, let us nevertheless grant this to them, lest we seem perhaps too contentious. Let it be exactly as they wish. What then? Did not **Plato** (as we also said above) place pleasure in the senses and joy in the mind? If the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics | The followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, known for their focus on empirical observation and systematic logic.</term> also place pleasure in the mind, what is that to us? For Plato does not hold this view. Therefore, what is perceived in contemplation we call not "pleasure," but "joy" <note>original: *gaudium*</note>. If this joy is born less from a "filling," it is nothing against Plato; for he said that not joy, which is in the mind, but pleasure, which resides in the senses, is created from a filling.

But **Aristotle** presses more sharply in the tenth book of his *Ethics* <note>Referring to the *Nicomachean Ethics*, where Aristotle critiques the Platonic view that pleasure is a process of restoration.</note>, proving that even that pleasure which occurs in the senses does not always proceed from the filling of a lack. For he holds this to be true in the senses of touch and taste. But in those pleasures which we take from smells, forms, and sounds, it happens in no way. For he who rejoices in sounds or forms is not "filled" in any way by these very things in which he delights, nor did he lack them beforehand. And indeed, although these arguments might perhaps seem plausible, they are not such that they can detract from Plato in any part. For those words of Plato, in which he says pleasure is born from the filling of a lack, we can interpret (as it seems) in two ways.

For these two, "lack" <note>original: *egestas*</note> and "appetite" <note>original: *appetitio*</note>, are so connected to each other that one cannot be separated from the other. For we desire those things which we lack, nor do we desire anything that we did not lack before the desire arose; nor is anyone in a state of lack who does not desire, nor does anyone ever desire who does not lack. Thus it happens that both seem to be so joined together that one always accompanies the other. Therefore, among all the more excellent philosophers, this is the custom: they frequently signify "appetite" by the name of "lack," and in the same way they wish "lack" to be understood by the name of "appetite." Whence **Cicero** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and philosopher who translated Greek thought for a Latin audience.</note> rightly said, "He does not lack, who does not desire." **Socrates** also denied that he lacked our wealth and luxuries, which others strive for most ardently, because he did not desire them at all. **Epicurus** <note>The philosopher of the Garden, who taught that true pleasure is found in the absence of bodily pain and mental trouble.</note> used to say that it was not the one who had little who lacked, but the one who desired more. And so, if anyone wishes to drive away "lack," one must not add to their money, but rather subtract from their desire. In the same way, ~~when Plato spoke of the filling of a lack, he wanted it to be understood as the filling of appetite.~~ <note>The scribe appears to have struck through this line, likely as a correction to the phrasing that follows.</note> For "desire" <note>original: *concupiscentia*</note> is filled when it attains that which it wanted. ...we say. This is how we interpret **Plato**: The filling of a deficiency <note>original: *indigentiæ repletio*</note> exists as the cause of pleasure. This occurs when a desire, which is in need—and which we call a "deficiency"—has attained that which it longed for, enjoys its presence, and is, as it were, filled. That motion is immediately born in the senses, which we call sweetness, delight, and pleasure. Hence the **Delian epigram** <note>A famous inscription from the Letoon at Delos, also quoted by Aristotle, which ranks justice as most noble, health as best, but "to obtain what one loves" as most pleasant.</note> says that the most pleasant thing is to possess the thing loved. Moreover, this interpretation applies to all the senses: when they have attained the very thing for which a desire preceded, they are soothed by an ineffable pleasure. 

And this is the first way of responding, by which the **Platonists** may escape the snares <note>original: *laqueos*; referring to the logical traps or arguments used by Aristotle's school.</note> of the **Peripatetics**. And if perhaps this interpretation seems too harsh to anyone, come, let us attempt another, lest our side seem to have succumbed to the arrows of those others. What else is it to "fill a deficiency" but to attain that which you lack? But what do we lack, if not those things which can either protect our health while it is present, restore it if it is lost, or bring us some other utility in some other way? Indeed, we are humans. 

However, a **Human** <term>Man/Human | Latin *Homo*. The author is exploring the ontological definition of what constitutes a human being.</term> is—as the **Peripatetics** and **Stoics** <term>Stoics | A school of Hellenistic philosophy that taught that virtue is the only good and that humans should live in accordance with reason and nature.</term> believe—that which consists of a rational soul and a body. The **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists**, differing slightly from the others, think that a human is a certain divine mind <note>original: *divinam quandam mentem*</note> bound by earthly chains. Thus, among the other philosophers, the soul has the nature and name of a "part" of the human, but among the Platonists, our soul is the entire human. 

For this reason, when **Socrates** was asked by **Crito** how he ordered himself to be buried, he replied: "However you like, provided you can catch me and I do not escape you" <note>A famous scene from Plato's *Phaedo*, where Socrates argues that his true self is his soul, not the body being left behind.</note>. And the same Socrates, disputing with **Alcibiades** in **Plato's** writings, proves by many arguments that a human is nothing other than the soul. The body, however, is not the human, but belongs to the human. External things, moreover, do not belong to the human, but to fortune. Yet he does not call our soul "human" always and everywhere; rather, as long as it leads its life in the celestial seats, it is called now a "god" and now a "**divine spirit**" <note>original: *daemon*; in the Greek sense of a *daimon* or intermediary spirit, not a malevolent demon.</note> by the Platonists. 

But when it is shut within earthly dwellings, it receives the name of "humanity" from the very nature of the ground <note>original: *humus*; a common Latin etymological play: *homo* (man) comes from *humus* (earth/ground).</note> in which it is submerged. Thus **Origen** the Platonist <note>Likely referring to Origen the Pagan, a contemporary of Plotinus, rather than the Christian Father Origen, though the two were often confused in the Renaissance.</note>, a most noble man, used to assert that a human could be transformed into a divine spirit or a god, and sometimes even migrate into beasts. **Seneca** likewise, a great student of Plato, called our soul a god guesting in a human body. But all these men, and **Plato** himself, imitated **Heraclitus**, **Empedocles**, and **Pythagoras**. For Pythagoras asserts that our soul is transferred from a human into a god with these verses:

> Having laid down the body, when you go free to the high air,
> You shall escape being human, made a god of the nourishing heavens.

Since therefore (to return to our purpose) man, according to the opinion of the **Aristotelians** <note>The followers of Aristotle, often called Peripatetics.</note>, consists of a rational soul and a body; but as **Plato** wishes, man is a certain divine soul that makes use of the service of an earthly body; it follows that we must surely undertake the care of two things, namely the soul and the body. Of the soul indeed (as he commands) for its own sake alone; but all care of the body ought to be referred to the soul, just as a servant is referred to a master. 

Therefore, there are two kinds of things we need. For we lack those things that will be beneficial to the soul, and those that will be beneficial to the body. Now, those things benefit the body which either restore or preserve life, health, strength, form, or its own specific nature. To the soul, however, all those things are suited which contribute anything toward the best character or toward the knowledge of things. Add to these those things which, above others, benefit both soul and body, which seem similar and akin to either one. For like things (as it is said) are preserved by like things, and each thing seeks its own well-being. These, then, are the things people need. Wherefore, when these things are present, or at least those which have a certain appearance and likeness of them, we are affected by pleasure. If indeed those things which seem good to us are present, they bring pleasure. From which it happens that an opinion <note>original: *opinio*; in the Stoic sense, this refers to a value judgment or mental assent.</note> precedes pleasure, for as it pleases the **Stoics**, nothing can be pleasant to anyone unless each person has judged it to be akin to himself and good.

Since, however, the pleasure of the body is perceived by the senses, and since there are five types of these, there will similarly be five kinds of pleasures: one is perceived by touching, another by tasting; odors provide another, while the ears and eyes supply the remaining ones. And these senses relate to each other in such a way that they maintain a certain order, both of place and of nature. For the eyes are the purest and, as the Platonic **Timaeus** <note>The narrator of Plato’s dialogue *Timaeus*, which discusses the creation of the universe and the human body.</note> argues and proves, are akin to the nature of fire and light. The ears hold the second rank in order of purity and are compared to air. The nostrils then possess the third degree of thinness <note>original: *tenuitatis*; referring to the refinement or "subtlety" of the element.</note> and, being composed of a somewhat thicker nature, hold the middle ground between air and water. Next, the organ of tasting is thicker and most similar to the nature of water. Finally, those parts with which we touch are assigned to the lowest degree of refinement; for these approach more closely to the nature of the physical body and are assigned to the thickness of earth. 

You see these five senses arranged step by step, relating to each other in such a way that those placed in the higher part of the body also obtain a superior rank of purity, and some are akin to different things than others. ## ON PLEASURE ##

When denser bodies are brought near, endowed with the same nature of moisture and heat as the sense itself is affected by, the sense then exults and rejoices in a way at the presence of these bodies because they are kindred to it, because they share the same nature, and because they preserve its own particular composition and quality; thus, it is entirely bathed in sweetness. Taste, truly, is refreshed by more liquid bodies (as is evident). For it is delighted by those flavors which have the nature of a ripened and well-prepared moisture <note>original: *humoris decocti, maturiq;*; referring to the ancient idea that flavors are produced by the "cooking" or ripening of fluids within plants.</note>. Indeed, since taste itself (as the **Platonists** <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato.</note> believe) is composed in that same proportion, it follows that when a similar and, as it were, "familiar" substance approaches, it rests most sweetly with it. Furthermore, the power of smelling is most refreshed by those odors which are a mixture of the natures of water and air, as is perceived in fruits and flowers; for the sense of smell itself was allotted this same nature from its origin. 

In addition, the ears are delighted by sounds of the kind that are fashioned from the purest air and from the same harmony in which the ears themselves consist; and so we see that, due to the diversity of their natures, some people are delighted by softer harmonies, others by more forceful ones, some by deeper sounds, and others by clearer ones. To the eyes, however, because they are most familiar with light, those things seem most pleasing whose nature is tempered by a light very similar to their own. Truly, such things are all those which result from the most beautiful blending of colors, all of which originate from light. 

And we do not only need these things, which we drink in through the senses, for the sake of increasing life and restoring our nature, but also for achieving the skill of the mind. From this it follows that the senses, for two reasons, require those excellent things which are offered from the outside: first, because they are kindred and similar to themselves—for it is necessary for individual things to be preserved and perfected by things similar to them—and second, because they are able to instruct us toward the knowledge of things and arts, which is the thing we most greatly desire. Therefore, as often as those things of which we have spoken are offered to the senses and admitted deep within for our enjoyment, that deficiency of the senses—which previously gave birth to desire—is filled. And that pleasure which we seek happens because of this replenishment of deficiency. This, then, is the second interpretation of the **Platonic** definition, which I believe no one, provided they are of sound mind, will find fault with. Therefore, enough on these matters for now; let us proceed to the rest.

### Chapter 5. Various opinions on what pleasure is. The first opinion: Aristotle’s.

<margin>a</margin> Now **Aristotle**, to come to his opinion, uses the term *pleasure* more broadly; by that name he wishes to signify not only that delight which clings to the senses, but also that which resides in the mind. Yet what pleasure itself actually is, he seems to hint at rather than explicitly define. Nevertheless, what he disputes concerning this in the seventh and tenth books of the *Ethics* <note>Referring to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, the foundational text for Western moral philosophy.</note>, we can interpret in the following way. 

There are (to use Aristotle’s words) three powers of the soul. One of these is common to us and to plants, which they call the *vegetative power* <note>original: *uegetandi uim*; the faculty responsible for basic biological life.</note>. Its duties are three: to nourish its own body, to grow, and finally to produce another like itself outside of itself. The second nature of the soul he calls the *sensitive power* <note>original: *sentiendi uim*</note>, which exists in us and is common to all other animals as well. Of the senses, some are internal and others are external. The external ones—which are more relevant to our purpose—are five in number, well known by the common division. 

The third power of the soul belongs only to humans out of all the types of mortal living beings, and this he calls the *intellect* <note>original: *intellectum*</note> and the *mind*. To these he adds the power of movement; but since it has no bearing on our purpose, let us set it aside. Concerning the first nature of the soul, which belongs to plants, the ancient philosophers held various opinions. Indeed, **Plato** thinks that the souls of trees and herbs possess a certain silent appetite, which he calls the "striving of nature." **Empedocles** claimed that not only a natural inclination, but even *sensation* is present in plants. **Anaxagoras**, moreover, and **Democritus** believe that they are affected by pleasure and pain; they judge them to have the power not only of sensing, but also of thinking and understanding. But **Aristotle** considers them to be endowed with neither reason nor any sense at all, nor to be participants in any pleasure. Thus it follows that this power of nourishing and growing [contributes] nothing to Aristotle's [opinion] on pleasure...

...may contribute his opinion. The remaining powers of the soul, therefore, to which he attributes pleasure, are two, one of which (to use his own words) he calls **intellect**, and the other **sense**; and to these he assigns their actions, which he calls cognitions <note>In this context, *cognitiones* refers to any act of knowing or perceiving, whether through the mind or the physical senses.</note>. Thus, he wishes the operation of the intellect or—to speak in Latin—of the mind and reason, to be called intelligence, thought, and contemplation. Regarding the senses, he calls the act of sight **vision**, hearing **audition**, smell **olfaction**, taste **gustation**, and finally touch **tact**. 

In this system, sight itself is the power and nature of the soul by which a person is able to see, whereas vision is the action itself—that is, the act of seeing. The same logic applies to the other senses. Aristotle argues that vision (to follow one example for them all) has two principal origins or causes from which it arises: namely, the sight itself in which the power resides, and furthermore the external thing being perceived, by which the sight is stimulated to see. Aristotle calls sight a power and capability of the soul, while the thing perceived is the **object**. He states that "perfect vision" occurs when both the power of the soul is in its best possible state and the object to be perceived is, by its own nature, excellent and in harmony with the soul's nature. 

If either of these is lacking, the vision will be imperfect; but when both occur together, the vision is perfect. Furthermore, whatever vision is perfect is also pleasant <note>original: *iocundam*</note>; that which is more perfect is more pleasant, and the most perfect is the most delightful. Therefore (to repeat the same point), because vision is perfect, it is pleasant; thus, the "perfection" of vision appears to be a certain delight. Conversely, the delight of vision is its very perfection. Since delight and pleasure <note>original: *uoluptas*</note> signify the same thing in this context, he concludes that pleasure is the perfection of vision. What has been said of sight, we wish to be understood of the other senses and of the mind itself. For in all of them, there is a proper operation: in hearing, audition; in smell, olfaction; and so on for the rest. 

Therefore, according to the common definition found in **Aristotle**, pleasure is nothing other than a certain perfection of the soul's operation, which is the same as the perfection of cognition. Since pleasure resides in all the senses, the pleasure of sight will be the perfection of vision, that of hearing the perfection of audition, that of taste the perfection of gustation, and so on, such that each pleasure is the perfection of its own specific operation. Now, in **Aristotle's** view, perfection is twofold: one is primary, and the other is annexed <note>Also known as "accidental" or "attendant" perfection.</note>. The primary perfection is that which exists as a part of the nature it perfects, such as the human soul; for the soul is the perfection of a human being and a part of the human substance. We call "annexed" perfection that which, while not being a part of the substance, nevertheless follows or accompanies the substance itself, and as it were...

...is joined and attached to the nature of the thing itself which it perfects, in the same way that **beauty** <note>original: *pulchritudo*</note> is joined to the bloom of youth. For beauty is not youth itself, nor is it any part of youth, but it follows upon youth, adorns it, and makes it perfect. Since, therefore, pleasure is the perfection of that activity which consists in the senses or the mind, what kind of perfection will this be? Will it be a "primary" perfection? <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, a "primary perfection" refers to the mere capacity or state of being (like having the sense of sight), whereas "secondary perfection" refers to the actual exercise of that capacity (the act of seeing).</note> Certainly, Aristotle will deny this. For the pleasure produced by sight is neither the vision itself, nor any part of the vision. Therefore, pleasure in sight will be a certain perfection annexed and joined to the vision. 

For even if it is implicit within the act of vision itself, it is nevertheless not any part of the vision, nor is it the vision in its entirety. Otherwise, vision—which I have mentioned so often now—could in no way occur without pleasure. Rather, pleasure arises from the vision itself and follows it like a companion; it mixes with it, clings to it, adorns it, and makes it perfect. Indeed, everyone performs an action more diligently and more perfectly when it brings them delight. This is surely so well-known that it seems to require no proof. For this reason, it is not without logic that pleasure is defined as a certain "added perfection" to the operation it belongs to, such as contemplation, vision, hearing, and all the rest. 

If the activity is **noble** <note>original: *honesta*</note>, Aristotle calls the pleasure itself noble; if it is base, the pleasure is base; but if it is intermediate, the pleasure is likewise intermediate. In this matter, Aristotle differs from most of the ancient philosophers. 

¶ For some have thought that pleasure is a nature imposed upon the senses by a certain thing that suits us, just as the sweet taste of honey is absorbed by the tongue. Others, however, define pleasure as the **perception** of a fitting thing. For example, when the sweetness of a liquid is applied to the sense of taste, they did not call the sweetness itself, nor the liquid, nor the taste "pleasure," but rather the act of tasting itself—that is, the perception of the sweetness. This is the opinion that **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to European Scholasticism.</note> seems to approve of. 

Some, however, did not even want the perception of the sweet liquid to be pleasure, but rather that judgment of the mind which follows the first sensory apprehension (which most call **imagination** <note>original: *phantasia*; in this context, it refers to the mental representation of a sensory object before it is intellectually judged.</note>). They argue that, first, the sense knows that the taste is sweet; afterward, it judges that the taste is good and should be embraced. Most of them believe that it is this very judgment that is signified by the name of "pleasure." 

Nor were there lacking those who called neither the sweet quality imposed on the senses, nor the perception of that quality, nor the judgment "pleasure," but rather a certain commotion of the body and sense which follows the perception and judgment—such as a certain liquefaction <note>A common medieval term for the "melting" or softening of the spirit when experiencing joy.</note>, an outpouring, elation, exultation, wantonness, and similar things. ### Chapter VI. The Opinions of the Peripatetics on Pleasure.

<margin>a</margin> Aristotle, however, seems to call none of these things pleasure. Rather, he views it as a certain perfection of the act of apprehension itself. For instance, if the first perception is of sweetness, another thing is born from this as a kind of companion and attached perfection—and this is pleasure itself. But as to what this kind of "perfection" is which he calls pleasure, he never (it seems) explained it sufficiently. However, the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were the followers of Aristotle, named after the *peripatos* or covered walkway in the Lyceum where they held their discussions.</note>, who descended from Aristotle, wanted to explain and bring to light what had been expressed obscurely by their leader, and so they were divided into different opinions. Some placed pleasure in the senses, while others placed it in the "appetite" <note>In this context, "appetite" (*appetitus*) refers to the faculty of desire or the soul's leaning toward something it perceives as good, not just hunger.</note> that follows the senses. And those who placed it in the senses interpreted Aristotle in various ways. 

Indeed, some believe there are two perceptions in the senses. The first seems to proceed and flow into the soul from those things offered from the outside. The second, proceeding more from the soul itself, extends toward those external things. For first, the soul perceives sweetness—for example—which seems to arise from the pleasantness of the object itself. Then, it considers that it has obtained that sweetness, and that it perceives, holds, and enjoys it. They believed that this second perception of the soul—whether called thought, meditation, or awareness—was what Aristotle called pleasure. Thus, pleasure is that very consideration by which one thinks about enjoying present goods. 

¶ Some think it is not the sense itself, but that when the soul notices it has obtained sweetness, it is lifted up and, as it were, raised, conceiving and carrying a certain cheerfulness <note>original: *hilaritatem*</note> within itself; and they judge this to be what Aristotle called pleasure. Therefore, pleasure is the elevation or the cheerfulness of the soul that has already attained the good it desired. 

¶ But those who placed pleasure in that part of the soul by which we desire <note>original: *appetimus*</note> think there are two properties of the appetite. One is that we are moved and inclined toward those goods which are far from us and which we have not yet obtained. The other consists in that which we have already attained and secured. They call the first "desire" <note>original: *cupiditatem*</note> and the second "rest" <note>original: *quietem*</note>. They claim the first is full of trouble, worry, care, and anxiety; but the second is infused with an inexpressible sweetness. They say this is what the leader of the Peripatetics calls pleasure, so that pleasure is said to be nothing other than a certain limit or "rest" of the appetite in a good it has already secured. Hence Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher known for "On the Nature of Things."</note> says: "The rest of men and the pleasure of the gods." <note>original: *requies hominum divumque voluptas*</note> 

¶ However, as to what this "rest" itself is, they do not all [agree] in the same way...

...explained. For some define this very cessation, and a kind of rest <note>original: *quietem*</note> from seeking, as the end of desire. For they say that the **appetite** <note>In this philosophical context, "appetite" (*appetitus*) refers to the soul’s natural leaning or desire toward something it perceives as good.</note>, once it has attained the good it desired, ceases from seeking. Therefore, it is free from care and anxiety; this freedom is rest itself, and was called "pleasure" by Aristotle. Thus, as these people define it, pleasure is the freedom from all the worry and anxiety of seeking once the desired good has been acquired.

¶ However, some **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> added something else to this freedom from care. For they believe that to lack all distress is not yet to possess the full and perfect nature of pleasure. Rather, it becomes complete and absolute if, in that very state, all appetite rests in such a way that it not only seeks nothing further, but clings to this good which it enjoys with all its nerves and strength. It **assents** <note>original: *assentiatur*; a formal agreement or "yes" from the soul to its current state.</note> within itself that this is enough, and it is poured out deeply into that good. Therefore, as these men judge, pleasure is the **assent** and the **diffusion** of the appetite into the good which it possesses. This is why, in the midst of pleasures, the whole body seems to *melt* and *flow away*, since every power and movement of the mind and body is inclined toward that which is presented from the outside, and is completely carried away. Indeed, such a diffusion must exist not only in the limbs and parts of the body, but also in the appetite and nature of the soul. For the body is not poured out into anything except by the impulse of the appetite and the power of the soul. For this reason, it is necessary that the appetite and the soul themselves be diffused, and most greedily fixed and clinging to that which seems to agree with their own nature. Every such effort of the soul and appetite—to couple, cling, and be fixed to the good already possessed—contains pleasure. According to these men, pleasure seems to be nothing other than to assent to, cling to, and be fixed to a present good, and to flow into it and be deeply poured out. You should understand these things as happening in the soul, specifically in that part of the soul called the "power of appetite." For a movement of this kind is also found in the heat, blood, **spirits** <note>In ancient medicine, "spirits" (*spiritus*) were subtle vapors or fluids that acted as the messengers between the soul and the body.</note>, and the whole body; yet this is neither pleasure itself nor any part of pleasure. Rather, from that diffusion and assent which is in the soul (which they call pleasure), that liquefaction and pouring out of the body proceed as if they were certain "traces" of an internal pleasure. For just as these things appear in the body, such is the existence of pleasure in the soul.

This, then, is the opinion of the Peripatetics concerning the definition of pleasure. I myself judge that it does not differ even in the smallest part from the view of Plato...

Plato, however, calls that which happens in the senses "**pleasure**" <note>original: *voluptas*</note>, while that which is in the mind he calls "**joy**" <note>original: *gaudium*</note>. Indeed, at times Plato himself confuses the names of pleasure and joy, using both terms to signify each state. Therefore, they differ in name either not at all, or barely and in the smallest degree; that they agree in the actual matter can be attested by several of Plato’s books, as well as by many **Platonists** who are by no means philosophers to be looked down upon. For **Apuleius, Calcidius, Contius,** and **Ptolemaeus**, noble Platonists, interpret Plato’s opinion—which was placed in very obscure words in the *Timaeus*—in the manner that I will briefly report. 

They say that by **sensation** <note>original: *sensus*</note>, Plato certainly meant the first perception of the soul, which is born from the actual **passion** <note>In this philosophical context, *passio* (passion) does not mean "emotion," but rather the state of "undergoing" or being affected by an external force.</note> of the body. For they say that certain "species" <note>The "forms" or "images" of things.</note> of all things that are to be known flow toward us, are drawn in through the openings of the senses, and are imprinted and sealed upon the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*; in early science and philosophy, "spirits" were thought to be a very thin, vapor-like substance in the brain's ventricles that carried sensory information to the soul.</note> that resides in the ventricles of the brain. These types of "species," shaped within the spirit—which is itself a very thin and transparent body—strike the soul and cause it to gaze upon and perceive those same external objects of which these are the images. We see that this perception of the soul is born from the actual passion and impulse of the body. Since the spirit is moved by external bodies, it strikes the soul with a similar image and forms it. Therefore, since a perception of this kind is born from the impulse of the spirit, it follows that it proceeds from a passion of the body—that is, from a pulse and a motion. 

This was echoed by **Aurelius Augustine**, a good Platonist, in his book titled *On the Magnitude of the Soul*. <margin>scribal mark</margin> "Sensation," he says, "is a passion of the body which, in itself, is not hidden from the soul." <note>original: *Sensus est passio corporis per se ipsam non latens animam.*</note> That is to say, through the very form of the body drawn in by the senses, the passion of the body is also perceived through a certain primary and proper image. From this it follows that we perceive through a twofold passion of the body. For by the impulse of the brain and the spirit, we apprehend the passions of external bodies. 

But the Platonists divide that passion which our own body receives from the outside into two parts: one of these soothes and softens the body, not so much striking the limbs and organs as stroking and tickling them; the other, however, agitates them more roughly and harshly. When the soul **assents** <note>Gives its internal agreement.</note> to that first motion of the body, whose nature is to soothe, **pleasure** is created. When it recoils from and rejects the other motion, which we call "harsh," they say **pain** is brought about.
