...finds rest. For this reason, **Aurelius Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose Christian theology was deeply influenced by Platonic philosophy.</note> defines pleasure as "the union of the appetite itself with the thing it has loved." <note>original: "uoluptatem definit appetionis ipsius cum eo, quod amauerit unionem"</note> Did not the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they often discussed philosophy while walking (*peripateo*) in the walkways of the Lyceum in Athens.</note> also define pleasure above as the mind finding rest, being suffused with light, and being intimately joined? What reason remains, then, why the Platonists and Peripatetics should not be said to be at one regarding pleasure, thinking and speaking the same thing? In what else do they differ, except that the former say the mind "assents," while the latter say it "rests" and "stops"? Indeed, they differ in nothing on this account; for the mind never rests unless it assents, nor does it truly assent unless it also rests.

### Chapter 8. How the Peripatetics divide pleasure, and on the powers of the soul.

<margin>q</margin> I believe it has now been sufficiently declared what the **Platonists** and **Peripatetics** have handed down concerning the definition of pleasure, and how the arguments of both coincide. Let us now examine what the Peripatetics thought regarding the division of pleasure. The Peripatetics believe that the whole nature of man consists of soul and body. As it pertains to our current question, they believe the soul is distributed into two parts: namely, the **mind** <note>original: *mens*</note> and the **sense** <note>original: *sensus*</note>. In turn, they hold that the mind possesses a twin power and nature. One of these is occupied with the investigation of truth, while the other is occupied with deliberation and action; the former they call the **contemplative intellect**, and the latter the **active intellect**. They say it is the property of the contemplative intellect to seek out the causes, characteristics, and developments of those things contained within the order of nature, being content with the contemplation of truth alone. However, they wish it to be said that the work of the active intellect is to discern, through deliberation, what things should be sought or avoided. 

Regarding the senses, they call some "internal" and others "external." The internal senses—as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a medieval Andalusian philosopher known as "The Commentator" for his influential work on Aristotle.</note>, the most acute of the Peripatetic interpreters, maintains—are divided into four species. The first of these collects and perceives all images that are drawn in through the five external senses; for this reason, they call it the **common sense**. Next, they named a second power the **imagination** <note>original: *uis imaginandi*</note>, whose duty is—since it produces no images itself—to retain those images which were received from the primary senses and bring them to the third nature of sensing, which they call **phantasy** <note>original: *phantasia*</note>, or the power of estimation and thought. They judge its work to be that, having received these images, it judges and perceives what or of what kind the thing is to which those images belong. Those very things which it has distinguished, joined, or conceived by judging, it commends to be preserved in the final part of the brain and the sensory faculty itself, which they call **memory**. As for those external senses...

...the others <note>The text likely refers to the "internal" or "lower" faculties following the description of the mind on the previous page.</note> which are more relevant to our inquiry, they divide into five species known to all. They consider these to be arranged in such a way that those occupying a higher position in the body are purer and simpler, while the remaining ones are coarser. Therefore, sight appears purer than hearing, hearing purer than smell, the power of smelling purer than taste, and finally, taste purer than touch. For light and colors pertain to sight; sounds to the ears; odors to the nostrils; flavors to taste; while solidity, softness, heat, and cold pertain to the power of touch. 

Consequently, just as light and color are purer than sound, sound purer than odors, and odors purer than flavor—and just as flavors are purer than those things subject to touch—so too sight excels hearing, hearing excels the sense of the nostrils, this sense excels taste, and taste finally excels touch in purity and dignity. To these five powers of sensing, five corresponding organs and substrates in the body—what they call "foundations"—are assigned. These seem to be nothing other than certain **affections** <note>term: *affectiones* - here referring to the way the body is "affected" or disposed to receive sensory input.</note> of the body, which some call "dispositions," others "qualities," and some "complexions" <note>term: *complexiones* - the specific balance of the four elements and humors in a particular part of the body.</note>. These arise in various parts of the body through the diverse mixing of the elements and serve as the foundations for the various senses. For there is one affection of the body by which the power of seeing is sustained and flourishes, and another by which hearing does, and the same judgment must be made concerning all the rest. 

In addition to these five affections or substrates, five corresponding instruments—the more solid members of the body—were devised and established as "vessels," so to speak, in which both the senses and the affections themselves might reside. For the eyes, like small vessels, receive the affection and the power of seeing; and the other members of the body, as is evident, are assigned to the other qualities and senses in a certain fixed order. Furthermore, certain innate movements are born in these members and instruments, which seem to demonstrate the innermost state of each faculty. Thus, in the midst of disturbances of the mind, we see the body now redden, now turn pale; at one moment it contracts and grows rigid, while at another it flows abroad and seems to almost melt away.

¶ Aristotle thinks that pleasure pertains to all these things we have now listed in a long sequence in such a way that a certain perfect and absolute pleasure exists in that mind which he calls **contemplative**. <note>term: *contemplatiuam* - the part of the intellect dedicated to pure thought and the study of eternal truths, as opposed to practical action.</note> It then degenerates by degrees in the other parts of man. For he believes that for seven reasons, that first pleasure is seen to be more perfect than the other kind of pleasure which is placed in the **active mind**. <note>term: *actiua mente* - the practical intellect used for moral action and navigating the world.</note> ¶ For every [pleasure] which [arises] from the investigation of truth...

# BOOK

Pleasure undertaken through investigation and contemplation is honorable and most worthy of praise. However, when the other part of the mind deliberates on what should be done or avoided, and rejoices in the choice of such things, not all that pleasure is typically praised. That which arises from plans and actions that oppose the best laws is rightly condemned—for instance, if the mind should rejoice in a plan undertaken against the safety of one's country or parents, or against what is right. When the mind is delighted by honorable actions, that pleasure is honorable; but when it deals with neutral matters, that pleasure too is neutral. Thus it follows that in the first part of the mind <note>This refers to the theoretical or contemplative intellect.</note>, only one kind of joy exists, and that is worthy of praise. In the other part <note>The practical or active intellect, which governs our daily conduct.</note>, however, three kinds are found (as we have said): the honorable, the shameful, and the neutral.

¶ That reasoning which Aristotle <note>The text refers to him as "he" in the tenth [book] on morals.</note> uses in his tenth book on ethics <note>original: *in decimo de moribus* — a reference to Book X of Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, where he discusses the supremacy of the contemplative life.</note> is of no small value to our subject. He says that we are able to engage in contemplation longer than we can perform any other kind of action. Since the search for truth is more firm and stable than any duty of action, it follows that the pleasure arising from it must also be more stable and perfect.

¶ Furthermore, the life and contemplation of the wise person <note>term: *sapientis* — referring to the philosopher or person who has attained intellectual virtue.</note> requires fewer things than the civic life does. Therefore, since that pleasure is content with few and minimal things, it will undoubtedly be more self-sufficient and be judged as more perfect.

¶ Moreover, that part of the mind to which we attribute the contemplation of nature is—as no one would deny—more perfect than the other; for that reason, it brings a pleasure more excellent than all others.

¶ Since the movement and agitation of the active mind is directed toward something else—either to be chosen or rejected—while the contemplation of the primary mind is content within itself and desires nothing at all besides itself, it is established by necessary logic that the pleasure proper to contemplation is desired for its own sake alone. The other kind of pleasure, however, seeks something besides itself as an end; therefore, that first kind must be judged as far more excellent.

¶ Added to this is the fact that the primary and more perfect part of anything acts as a substitute and name for the whole. From this it follows that, although each human being is composed of many parts, the part assigned to contemplation—because it excels the others in dignity—encompasses almost the entire nature of man. As Aristotle says, a human being *is* primarily this part. For this reason, its action is especially suited to us and contains an ineffable pleasure; for those things which are more closely related to our nature typically bring the greatest pleasure.

¶ Indeed, Aristotle's final argument <note>original: "Postrema uero Aristotelis argumentatio" — likely referring to the conclusion of Book X of the Nicomachean Ethics.</note> proves that the specific activity of the immortal gods consists in contemplation alone. Therefore, nothing in us—except for the primary mind (as we have said) and contemplation, and the pleasure arising from it—appears to be akin to God. If pleasure of this kind is the most divine, because it alone is fitting for the immortal gods, it will rightly be judged superior to all other pleasures.

¶ Aristotle used these arguments to rank the pleasure of contemplation above that which is perceived through action. However, we shall now come to those pleasures which, as it were, titillate the senses and flow into them and glide over them with a certain sweetness. We find that these are divided by Aristotle into two species: some are natural, while others are seen to be against nature. He calls those "natural" which, because they restore our nature, are sought after by all or most people. He divides these further into two equal groups: some are equally common to all living creatures, while others are, in a sense, specific and innate to individual species according to their diverse natures. For the fact that all creatures seek food, drink, and the use of <term>Venus</term><note>A classical reference to sexual intercourse, named after the goddess of love.</note> is characteristic of a common and natural desire and pleasure. But the fact that individual species are variously delighted by specific things according to their different natures—and that some things are more pleasing to some than to others—belongs to a natural but specific pleasure. For since that which fits one's nature seems pleasurable to each, and since the dispositions and natures of various living creatures differ, it is necessary that those things which are fitting also differ among different animals. And for this reason, a certain and, as it were, specific desire and pleasure (as Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535 – c. 475 BCE). The author refers to the fragment: "Donkeys would choose chaff rather than gold," illustrating that different creatures value different things.</note> says) belongs to individual living beings. For what is suited to its own nature delights each one; "his own pleasure draws each." <note>original: "trahit sua quenque uoluptas" — a famous line from Virgil's Eclogues (2.65).</note> These are what he calls natural pleasures. On the other hand, he maintains that those pleasures which almost the entire human race abhors are "against nature." He divides these into three types: some arise from a shameful and corrupt nature, others from the worst habits, and some from diseases and unfortunate circumstances. Aristotle writes that it has happened through a perversion of nature that a certain woman would most passionately strive to cut open the wombs of pregnant women and devour the children, or what they report about certain wild tribes around the <term>Pontus</term><note>The Black Sea region, which ancient Greeks and Romans often depicted as a land of "uncivilized" or "monstrous" peoples.</note>. For some are delighted by raw meat, and others by human flesh. Some are said to trade their newborn children to be eaten at banquets. The <term>Troglodytes</term><note>Literally "cave-dwellers." Ancient writers often attributed strange dietary habits to these groups.</note>, moreover, feed on the flesh of serpents. ¶ From those things we have enumerated thus far, there appear to be three types of pleasures according to <term>Aristotle</term>. The first consists in **contemplation**; the second is found in **deliberation and action**. Both of these reside in the mind, though (as we have said) in different ways. We placed the third type in the **senses**, and this we divided into two species: the *natural* and the *against nature*. Of the natural pleasures, we call one "common" and the other "specific." Furthermore, of the bestial pleasures, we find that one arises from a corrupt and shameful nature, another from a wicked habit, and a third from disease. 

Therefore, the first pleasure—which is born from contemplation—he calls **divine**, because it is most like God; it belongs to us not insofar as we are merely human, but insofar as we are like the gods. However, the pleasure belonging to the active mind he calls **honorable** <note>original: "honestam" — referring to moral beauty and noble virtue.</note>, though not divine. For honor is not divinity itself, but rather a perfect likeness and image of divinity. Thus, the second level of mind and pleasure is a step down from the first, because divinity is granted to the first, while only the *likeness* of divinity is granted to the second. 

As for those pleasures which charm the body, they can no longer participate in divinity, and they share no more in honor. This is because honor exists as the grace, beauty, and ornament of the mind alone. Indeed, this ornament and the harmony of all parts is called "honor" in the disposition of the mind, "moderation" in the emotions, "modesty" in actions, and "order" in works. In the body, this same harmony is called "form" or "beauty" by many <term>Platonists</term> <note>Followers of Plato who emphasized the relationship between physical beauty and spiritual truth.</note>. For those sensory pleasures that obey the laws of the mind and reason, and for that reason become moderate, seem by this very moderation to imitate the nature of the honorable and the becoming. ...[they] do not only flatter the ears and eyes, but they also move the mind and reason by those very traces of reason which they contain within themselves. ¶ But indeed, odors, flavors, heat, and cold, and other such things that pertain to smell, taste, and touch, seem to possess or display neither harmony, nor proportion, nor order—and much less any similarity to reason. Therefore, they merely soothe the senses and the physical nature of the body, but they do not agree with the mind at all, or only barely. For this reason, the pleasures that proceed from these possess nothing of reason or dignity, nor do they offer any "food" <note>original: "pabulum"</note> (so to speak) to the mind.

¶ To those things about which the **Peripatetics** <term>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy</term> were disputing a little while ago, it is added that the power of sensing is more common to a greater number of living creatures the coarser it is. Hence, the power of seeing or hearing is not granted by nature to all. More have the power of smelling, and perhaps all have the power of tasting. Finally, no one would doubt that touch is present in all animals. In the same way, the pleasures of these senses are ranked: some are judged more common and viler than others. Indeed, it is established that of all of them, those located in taste and touch are the most common and viler; for this reason, **Aristotle** says they are bestial <note>original: "ferinas"</note>, servile, and absurd. **Plato** calls them most incontinent and furious. **Hippocrates**, however (as we said above), judged one of them <note>Likely referring to sexual pleasure, a form of touch</note> to be similar to the **comitial disease** <term>The historical term for epilepsy, so called because a seizure was seen as a bad omen that would stop the "comitia" or public assemblies in Rome</term>. Nor is it of little weight that almost all who philosophize about morals want those who exceed the limit in these two pleasures to be called incontinent or intemperate. But regarding the remaining pleasures, because they are much more noble <note>original: "liberales," meaning befitting a free person</note>, they have posited neither incontinence nor intemperance.

¶ Thus far, we have recounted three things to which pleasure is attributed: namely the contemplative mind, the active mind, and the senses. But indeed, after the powers of sensing, the affections themselves and the members of the body that lie beneath the senses are arranged; while these perceive neither delight nor annoyance by themselves, they are nevertheless subjected to those very bodily movements and excitations by which either pleasantness or pain is brought to the senses. Whence it happens that the members themselves also seem to hold certain traces of inward pleasure. And this very agitation of the viscera and parts of the body, which within...

Nor is the pleasure of the mind anything else but that very perfect and pleasing assent by which the will rests deeply in that which the mind considers, as if in something familiar and its own.

### Chapter ten. The opinions of the Stoics and others regarding pleasure and all the emotions.

These things, then, should be sufficient regarding the opinion of Aristotle. Let us turn to the **Stoics** <term>a school of philosophy founded in Athens that taught that virtue is the only good and that humans should master their emotions through reason</term>. The Stoics, whose leader was **Zeno** <term>Zeno of Citium (c. 334–262 BCE), the founder of the Stoic school</term>, define joy no differently than **Plato** <term>the influential Greek philosopher and teacher of Aristotle</term> does; but they often confuse the names of pleasure and gladness with one another, and designate the same thing by either name in their arguments. For when we are moved in such a way that we are in some state of "good," they think this happens in two ways. For when the soul is moved by reason, calmly and constantly, they want that to be called "joy" <note>original: "gaudium"</note>. But when it exults excessively and emptily, they call it "wanton gladness" <note>original: "laetitiam gestientem"</note> and "pleasure" <note>original: "uoluptatem"</note>. This they define as an irrational elation of the soul that believes it is enjoying some great good. However, **Cicero** <term>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman orator and philosopher who translated Greek concepts for a Latin audience</term>, in the second book of *On Ends* <note>original: "De Finibus [Bonorum et Malorum]"</note>, wants us to use these names in Latin such that "joy" and "gladness" reside in the mind alone, whereas "pleasure," although it is primarily attributed to the senses, can also be transferred to the mind. He states that "gladness" is an elation of the mind thinking it enjoys a great good, while "joy" is a rational elation of the mind; "pleasure" is that sweetness perceived by the senses, which can also be transferred to the mind—and that in the mind, it is always to be censured.

<summary>This page concludes the Aristotelian definition of mental pleasure as the will's rest in a familiar thought and introduces Stoic and Ciceronian distinctions between rational joy and irrational sensory pleasure.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Stoics, Zeno, Cicero, joy (gaudium), gladness (laetitia), pleasure (uoluptas), philosophy of mind, ethics, Latin terminology</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the general Stoic and Ciceronian definitions of pleasure to a technical Aristotelian critique. It builds on the previous page's distinction between the parts of the mind (thinking, remembering, willing) by analyzing how different schools of thought categorize the "motions" of the soul.</meta>

<header>BOOK</header>
<meta>catchword: Then</meta>

He <note>Referring to Cicero</note> says these things when he disputes about philosophy, and when he expresses the difference between these matters. In other places, however, he frequently uses the name of **pleasure** <note>original: "uoluptatis"</note> to represent both **joy** <note>original: "gaudio"; often referring to a calm, rational state of mind</note> and **gladness** <note>original: "lætitia"; often referring to an exuberant or outward display of delight</note>. ¶ **Aristotle**, however, appears to disagree greatly with Cicero and the **Stoics** <term>a school of philosophy that taught that virtue is the highest good and that emotions should be governed by reason</term>, as he does not wish either joy or any pleasure to be called "gladness." For when he enumerated the **emotions** <note>original: "affectus"; literally "affections" or states of being affected by something</note> in that work which is titled the second book on morals <note>The *Nicomachean Ethics*, Book II</note>, he included "gladness" among them. He then added that those are emotions which pleasure or distress follows. From this it follows that, according to Aristotle, pleasure cannot be an emotion; otherwise, what he had said shortly before would necessarily be false. For since pleasure cannot follow itself, anyone who calls it an emotion will seem to deny Aristotle's position—that pleasure follows all emotions. Furthermore, since in that same second book he called emotions "motions of the soul," but in the tenth volume of that same work he demonstrates that pleasure is by no means to be called a "motion," who does not understand that Aristotle utterly denied that pleasure is an emotion? Since, therefore, in his opinion pleasure is neither a motion nor an emotion, while he held that gladness *is* an emotion, it is concluded by necessary reasoning that pleasure and gladness differ greatly from one another. 

Nor indeed among the **Peripatetics** <term>followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, so named because they walked about (peripateticos) while teaching</term> is gladness the kind of thing that is present in the soul while it enjoys a present good. For no one among the Peripatetics doubts that gladness is a motion of the soul. And indeed, since emotions are defined by them as certain "passions of the appetite"—and in their opinion "passion" exists as a flow and a movement—they will be motions. Therefore, gladness, being an emotion, will necessarily be seen as a motion. However, once the soul has attained what it had desired, it is no longer moved; rather, all the agitation of seeking ceases, and it rests most sweetly in the good it has acquired. On account of this, while the soul enjoys the good, one must remove from the appetite all those emotions that are occupied with the very thing that has been acquired. Therefore, we shall also remove "gladness" from the soul when it enjoys some good. 

¶ Someone might perhaps ask: what then is "gladness," if it is neither pleasure nor joy, nor consists in the appetite while it enjoys a present good? And if this has not been sufficiently explained by the Aristotelians, I believe I shall interpret Aristotle in this manner without any absurdity: When something that appears good is presented to us, the mind first judges that it ought to be seized; then the appetite is inclined toward that very thing which was judged. This we call **desire** or **lust**.

<summary>This page analyzes Aristotle's technical distinction between pleasure and gladness, arguing that while gladness is an active "motion" or emotion of the soul, true pleasure is the state of rest and enjoyment that follows after a goal is achieved.</summary>

<header>ON PLEASURE</header>
->y<-

# ON PLEASURE

Next, the mind itself inquires within whether it can easily obtain what it desires; this inquiry we call "care" or "solicitude." If the mind discovers it is less able to achieve its goal, then this very opinion is called "diffidence" <note>A lack of self-confidence or trust in the outcome</note>, which is followed by "despair." This occurs when the mind no longer expects to easily enjoy that which it desires. From this arises "sadness" <note>original: "tristitia"</note>—that is, a depression and casting down of a despairing and diffident mind. However, those who take care to speak Latin properly apply this term to the expression of the face no less than to the state of the mind.

But if someone believes they will easily obtain what they desire, this very faith is called "confidence." "Hope" then follows confidence—that is, a firm and easy expectation of a future good. From this is born "gladness" <note>original: "laetitia"</note>, a certain lifting up and elation of the mind, which hopes that it will possess what it sought without any doubt. Indeed, certain confidence, very firm hope, and a powerful consideration of the thing we hope for represents the object of our quest to the mind in such a way that it is not far from appearing entirely present. 

The result is that something very similar to pleasure is born from this hope and thought. I believe that **Aristotle** himself called this gladness a certain "image" and "appearance" of future pleasure. **Lucretius** the **Epicurean** <term>a follower of Epicurus, who taught that pleasure, defined as the absence of pain and fear, is the highest good</term> called this the "drop of Venus" <note>original: "guttam ueneris"; a metaphor for the first spark of sexual desire or the initial physical sensation of love</note>, because it is a meager and light perception of the beloved thing. True "pleasure," however, is the perfected and absolute enjoyment of the desired thing (to speak in **Platonic** terms). For this reason, the same Lucretius, when speaking of this first "drop of Venus" in the fourth book of his work *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: "De natura rerum"</note>, says:

> For silent desire foretells pleasure.
> From this comes our "Venus"; from this comes the name of "love."
> From this, that drop of Venus's sweetness first
> Distilled into your heart, and there followed a burning care.

That is to say, when desire itself (which we call "venereal love") is "silent"—meaning it is still hidden and considering itself with an internal motion (so to speak)—it feels in advance and, as it were, "pre-tastes" future pleasure because of hope and confidence. In that moment, that first "drop of Venus" arises, which we call "gladness." 

Therefore, let it be held among the **Peripatetics** <term>the followers of Aristotle, named for the "colonnades" (peripatoi) where they walked and talked</term> that gladness is a certain sweet pre-sensation of future pleasure born from hope itself. Just as pleasure is in the appetite while it enjoys, so gladness is in that same appetite while it hopes. And this is the controversy concerning these names—"gladness" <note>original: "laetitia"</note>, "joy" <note>original: "gaudio"</note>, and "pleasure" <note>original: "uoluptate"</note>—among **Plato**, **Aristotle**, **Zeno** <note>the founder of Stoicism</note>, and **Marcus Tullius** <note>Cicero</note>. ¶ But let them use their own names as they please; let us return to the **Stoics**.

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of the soul's movements, moving from the general concepts of hope and confidence discussed on the previous page into a formal Stoic taxonomy of the four primary "disturbances" or passions of the mind.</meta>

# BOOK

Now, a **disturbance** <term>original: *perturbatio*; the Stoic term for an irrational or excessive emotion that "disturbs" the soul's natural calm</term> is (as the **Stoics** <note>A school of philosophy that taught that virtue is the only good and that we should remain indifferent to external circumstances</note> hold) a commotion of the soul turned away from **right reason** and contrary to nature, and they believe it is born from an **opinion** <note>An internal judgment or belief that something is "good" or "bad"</note>. For as soon as the appearance of something is presented to it, the mind judges it to be either a destructive evil or a good. From this opinion, four disturbances of the mind proceed. For the things that are presented to us—whether they be truly bad or good—seem to be either in the future or in the present. If the mind thinks that certain <margin>I</margin> evils are coming in the future, it immediately tries to turn away from them. If this turning away happens in accordance with reason, it is called **caution**, and this is neither a disturbance nor foreign to the mind of a **wise person** <note>The Stoic ideal of a person who lives in perfect accordance with reason</note>. However, that which happens without reason, and with a lowly and broken investigation, is called **fear**. Indeed, **fear** is a turning away that is averse to reason, or a worried expectation of a future evil. But when that which seems to be an evil is already imminent and affects the mind in the present, that disturbance arises which they call either **distress** <note>original: *aegritudo*</note> or **pain**. Distress is a contraction of the mind that opposes reason; however, in a wise person, there is no such affection caused by a present evil.

But when the appearance of something that seems to be a future good is offered, the very opinion of it (to speak like a Stoic) impels one toward obtaining it. When this is done steadily and prudently, we call such a desire the **will** <note>original: *uoluntas*</note>; they believe this exists only in the wise person and should in no way be called a "disturbance." They define it thus: **will** is that which desires something with reason. However, that which is incited in opposition to reason, and more violently, is **lust** <note>original: *libido*</note> or unbridled desire, which is found in all <margin>I</margin> fools. Furthermore, when we are moved in such a way as to enjoy some good, it happens in two ways. For either the mind is moved with weight and tranquility, and they call this **joy** <note>original: *gaudium*</note>. But when it exults lightly and excessively, then they call it **restless gladness** and **pleasure**. When they define this as an irrational and exultant elation of a mind that thinks it is enjoying a great good, they agree with those **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who met in the "Peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum in Athens</note> whose opinion I mentioned earlier when we were speaking of **Aristotle**. For both schools agree on this: that pleasure is an elation of the mind itself, which judges that it has attained some greatest good.

¶ The Stoics, moreover, divide pleasure into many parts. For they held that there are five parts in the senses and four in the mind, while the mind agrees with the senses. Those things which move the senses do not have distinct or proper names among the Stoics, except for that which is perceived by hearing; this they call **delight** <note>original: *delectatio*</note>, and they define it as follows: **Delight** is a pleasure that charms the mind with the sweetness of hearing, while the others entice the remaining senses.

It also explores the sensory and mental divisions of pleasure, noting the specific term for auditory delight.</summary>

# ON PLEASURE

In truth, besides those pleasures by which the body is affected, four others have been discovered which are also found in the mind after it has been corrupted by **desire** <note>original: *appetitione*; the reaching out of the soul toward a perceived good</note>. These are **delight**, **effusion**, **vaunting**, and **malevolence**. 

**Delight** <term>original: *oblectatio*; a softening of the mind's resolve</term> is an inclination of the soul toward a pleasure that softens it. I do not think this is anything other than the very softness of the mind and its assent, by which it most willingly joins itself to that sweetness which the senses offer; it agrees with it, obeys it, and submits to it. 

**Effusion** <term>original: *effusio*; literally a "pouring out"</term> they define as the loosening and dissolving of the soul's virtue. For the mind is not only inclined and drawn by a certain softness to obey the pleasures of the senses (which we said happens through delight), but what is more, the entire force and intention of our mind melts away and flows apart in the sweetness of a present good. It carries itself toward the enjoyment of that thing and spreads itself out deep within. This, I believe, is what the **Stoics** call effusion. 

Next follows **vaunting** <term>original: *iactatio*; a "tossing" or "boasting"</term>, which is a leaping pleasure that carries itself forward quite insolently. This too is a disease of the mind, when it exults in the possession of what appears to be a "good" and glories in it vainly. 

**Malevolence** <term>original: *maliuolentia*; malice</term> is pleasure derived from the misfortune of another without any advantage to oneself. For when someone feels pleasure at another's misfortune for the sake of their own profit, it seems to be a case of "benevolence" toward oneself rather than malevolence toward others. Therefore, that phrase—**without any advantage to oneself**—was rightly added to the definition.

### Chapter 11. The Cyrenaics on Pleasure, and how it is the Ultimate Goal.

<warning>A dark horizontal ink mark obscures portions of the final paragraph, specifically the lines regarding natural instinct and rational judgment.</warning>

Let these things said regarding the opinion of the Stoics suffice. Let us now hear the **Cyrenaic** <note>A school of Greek philosophy founded in the 4th century BCE, known for their radical "hedonism" or belief that pleasure is the highest good</note> philosophers, who followed from **Aristippus** <note>A pupil of Socrates and the founder of the Cyrenaic school</note>, the disciple of Socrates. The Cyrenaics proposed two "disturbances": pain and pleasure. They called pleasure a **smooth motion** <note>original: *lenem motum*</note> and pain a **rough motion** <note>original: *motum asperum*</note>. They claimed that one pleasure does not differ from another, nor does one soothe more than another. All living creatures seek out pleasure and reject pain. 

By pleasure, they mean the pleasure of the body, which they say is the **ultimate goal** <term>original: *finis*; the "end" or purpose of human life</term>. They do not mean the kind of pleasure that consists of a stable state or the mere absence of pain, or which acts as a rest from disturbance—which is the kind **Epicurus** <note>A later philosopher who defined the highest pleasure as "ataraxia" or freedom from fear and bodily pain</note> accepted and established as the goal. They believe the evidence that pleasure is our goal is that nature reconciles us to it from the time we are children, even without the **judgment of reason**. When the mind's judgment has been neither corrupted by habit nor shaped by opinion, we seem to consider pleasure the **highest good** <term>original: *summum bonum*</term> by the instinct of nature alone. And when we enjoy it, we seek nothing else besides it, as if...

<summary>The author concludes the Stoic definitions of mental pleasures (delight, effusion, boasting, and malice) before introducing the Cyrenaic school, which argues that bodily pleasure is the natural and ultimate goal of life.</summary>
<keywords>Stoicism, Cyrenaics, Aristippus, Epicurus, pleasure, highest good, mental disturbances, ethics</keywords>

--- Page 355 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Cyrenaic school of philosophy, specifically their belief that pleasure is the only inherent good and their disagreement with Epicurus regarding the definition of pleasure as the mere absence of pain.</meta>

...of all **pains** <note>original: *dolorum*; completing the word from the previous page</note>, the ultimate, the extreme, the highest, and the end exists, nor is there anything which we naturally flee as much as pain. Therefore, we seek **pleasure** <term>original: *voluptas*; the central focus of this school of thought</term> most of all. Furthermore, they hold that pleasure is good even if it comes from the most shameful things; for even if the source is foul, pleasure itself is still to be chosen for its own sake and considered a good. Furthermore, that removal of pain which **Epicurus** <note>The famous philosopher (341–270 BCE) who defined the highest pleasure as 'ataraxia' or the absence of pain and trouble</note> defends does not seem to them to be pleasure, nor is the deprivation of pleasure pain. For they believe both states are constituted in **motion** <note>original: *motu* (OCR reads *metu*); the Cyrenaics believed pleasure was a "smooth motion" and pain a "rough motion"</note>. Nor, however, are pleasures only of the body, but also of the mind, which are perceived, namely, from the memory of past things, the hope of future goods, or the study of the sciences. Yet, they believe bodily pleasures are far more excellent than those of the mind, and bodily pains are worse than those of the mind. Virtue, indeed, and absolutely everything else besides pleasure, is a good and to be sought only for its sake. And whatever things appear to be "evils" are seen as such because they cause pain, and thus should be avoided. Only pleasure is truly good and desirable for itself, while pain is evil for its own sake and to be rejected. They also believe that pleasure and pain happen through the mind's assent and **sympathy** <term>original: *compassione*; literally "suffering with," meaning the mind experiences what the body feels</term> toward the body. For the body is agitated by various and diverse motions. If these are gentle and sweet, the mind assents, and that is pleasure. But if the body is struck by a harsher **suffering** <note>original: *passione*; a passive state of being acted upon</note>, the mind contracts and suffers with it, and this is pain. For this reason, in this definition of pain and pleasure, they agree with most of the **Platonists** and **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on empirical observation and ethics</note>. However, they disagree in several other matters, as can be clear from what we have reported, and furthermore, because they thought nothing was inherently pleasant or unpleasant; rather, some people rejoice and others are distressed by any given thing, whether due to its novelty, variety, or the point of satiety.

### Chapter XII. The opinion of Eudoxus that pleasure is the highest good.

<margin>c</margin>The opinion of **Eudoxus** <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 390–337 BCE), a mathematician and astronomer who was a student of Archytas and Plato</note>, a pupil of Archytas, is nearly the same. For he proves that pleasure is the **highest good** <term>original: *summum bonum*; the ultimate goal of human life</term> by the reasons I shall set forth. 
He says that what is sought after appears to be a good; that which is sought after more is a better good; and finally, that which is sought most of all, no one would doubt is the greatest and highest good. He believes it is clear from two points that pleasure is sought above all others. For there is nothing among all things which living beings desire more vehemently or ardently than pleasure, nor is there any good besides it that is sought by everyone. Indeed, not only humans, but all other animals, and even infants immediately after they are born, and thereafter the young and the old, strive for pleasure. But nothing of the rest...

<note>original: *DE VOLUPTATE*</note>

->171<-

4

...it can be found among other goods that pleasure is desired by all of them. Likewise, no one, however unlearned, would deny that whatever is most in accordance with nature is the highest good. That **pleasure** <note>original: *uoluptatem*</note> most especially agrees with nature will be clear from this: that all living creatures are born of it, and it is so necessary for generation itself that many of the ancient philosophers even argued that plants come together through a mixture of both sexes and give birth through pleasure, sending forth their shoots. Furthermore, living things desire it immediately upon being brought into the light, even before they desire anything else or are able to choose what they seek through any deliberation. Beyond this, we are nourished, educated, and increased by the allurements of pleasure from our very nurse’s milk and throughout our whole lives; we are instructed by its delights, and we live our lives in its lap. This pleasure is innate to all our senses, and all the necessary duties of life are performed with it acting as a bait <note>original: *esca*; literally "food" or "bait," implying that pleasure is the lure that ensures biological functions are carried out</note>. For we do not expel what is poisonous, nor do we pursue what is useful, without pleasure. Therefore, it seems to be most in agreement with nature and most familiar to our race, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE). He discussed pleasure extensively in the *Nicomachean Ethics*, noting that it perfects activities.</note> says.

¶ Furthermore, a good is to be considered more divine the more widely it extends; and since pleasure belongs to all living creatures and is mixed into all goods, who could doubt that it is the most widely accessible and diffused everywhere? Indeed, there is no single virtue that is present in all other virtues, or that naturally suits all animals. Pleasure, however, is mixed into all virtues, and no virtue at all can be found without pleasure. Yet pleasure itself is found in many things without virtue, nor can there be any possession of a good without pleasure. From these points, it is concluded that it is infused into all goods, and for that reason, it stands as the most ample and the best.

¶ Moreover, there is nothing besides pleasure that we do not look for for the sake of something else. On the contrary—and this seems even more significant—we desire all other things for the sake of pleasure itself. For we do not strive for what is good for any other reason than that we may finally enjoy it once it is acquired, if that is in any way possible. Therefore, for the sake of **enjoyment** <note>original: *fruitionis*</note> (if I may put it that way), all goods are sought out. Pleasure, however, since it is nothing other than a certain most sweet enjoyment of a good already acquired—who would deny that other goods are desired for its sake? There is no one who seeks any good except to obtain it to the best of their ability, and they do not wish to obtain it except to possess it and to rest most sweetly within it. That sweet **rest** <note>original: *quies*; a reference to the philosophical idea of 'pleasure in stability' or 'katastematic pleasure'</note>, or that sweetness of rest, by which we fully enjoy a good we have already obtained, has been named "pleasure" by almost all who philosophize, and it is for its sake, as we have proved...

...all good things are desired, and pleasure can never happen for anyone unless they have first attained the good they desired. Thus, it happens that pleasure follows the attainment of goods. Since that which necessarily follows another thing also exists as its end, it is necessary that pleasure truly exists as that end for the sake of which we seek all goods. There are, therefore, two primary points in the dispute of <term>Aristippus</term> <note>A pupil of Socrates and founder of the Cyrenaic school, which taught that the goal of life is to seek pleasure, specifically physical pleasure.</note> and <term>Eudoxus</term> <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus, a student of Plato who argued that pleasure is the supreme good because all creatures seek it.</note>: namely, that bodily pleasure is more powerful than that of the mind, and that all happiness consists in that sweet movement of the body itself.

### Chapter 13. Aristotle’s arguments against Aristippus and Eudoxus regarding pleasure, proving that the pleasure of the mind is more powerful than the pleasure of the body.

<margin>a</margin>
Aristotle weaves together the truest and most approved arguments against both of these opinions. Among the first, he demonstrates through many reasons that the pleasure of the soul is more powerful than that of the body.

¶ For of all bodily pleasures, those perceived by touch and taste are the most intense. Indeed, the nature of these is such that without a sense of <term>lack</term> <note>original: *indigentia*; refers to a state of physical need or deficiency, like hunger.</note>, they can hardly, or not at all, move the body. Hence, Socrates used to say that the seasoning for food was hunger, and for drink, thirst. Since every lack is an enemy to nature, it brings pain. And since pleasures of this kind cannot occur without such a lack, they must always be partakers of pain. For this reason, they are considered neither complete nor pure, especially since they give birth to regret, satiety, and disease. The pleasure of the mind, however, has no sense of want mixed into it at all; for that reason, it neither partakes of pain, nor does it affect the mind with any satiety or trouble.

¶ What of the fact that the delights of the senses, the more intensely and greedily they are drunk in, the more quickly they fall back into their opposite? <note>A reference to the philosophical idea that over-indulgence leads to its opposite, such as disgust or physical illness.</note> The joy of the mind, however, the more it is sought, the greater and more perfect it is held to be.

¶ Furthermore, there are two causes—or, as it were, principles—of pleasure: namely, the power of the soul itself which receives such motion, and additionally, that which is presented to us from the outside. They call the former the *subject* of pleasure and the latter the *object*. For the subject of vital bodily pleasure is the sense, while the object is the quality and nature of the body, which the forms perceived by the senses provide. However, for that joy which the soul enjoys, the subject is the mind, and the object is truth—an incorporeal, simple, absolute, and eternal thing. Therefore, just as the principles of this pleasure are more divine than those of the former, so this pleasure is more perfect than that one.

¶ And (as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on philosophy were essential to the Latin West. He often distinguished between the external senses and the internal intellect.</note> argues) the senses touch only the surfaces or certain properties of things from the outside...

[they are] not joined with the things themselves, but rather with their **images** <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, "images" or "phantasms" are the sensory representations of objects, rather than the objects themselves.</note>. The mind, however, looks into the innermost and absolute nature of that which is the object, and thus is joined with that which it considers. This happens so that either one single thing is formed out of two—as <term>Averroes</term> <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher (Ibn Rushd) known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle; he argued for a "unity of the intellect."</note> maintains—or they cohere in an indissoluble connection—as <term>Aurelius Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, a pivotal Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> says. Through this comprehension and union, a much greater pleasure reaches the mind than the senses, which are unable to achieve such a state.

¶ Add to this that the nature of the mind always exists as one and the same, and for that reason, it is always similar to itself and consistent. From this it follows that the same thing is always pleasant to it, and the same pleasure is ever-present. The nature of the body, however, either never remains in the same state (as <term>Heraclitus</term> <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher famous for the idea that "everything flows" and that one cannot step into the same river twice.</note> and **Plato** hold) or is quickly shifted into many different conditions (as **Aristotle** thinks), and its quality varies from one moment to the next. For this reason, the same thing does not suit the body at all times. That which now seems to agree with its nature will immediately, or certainly shortly thereafter, disagree and be at odds; thus, the same thing is not always pleasurable to it. By these facts, it is understood that the pleasure of the mind is certain and stable, while that of the body is brief, fleeting, and fragile.

¶ Likewise, the senses are moved only by the sweetness of present things, nor do they receive pleasure from anything except physical objects. The mind, however, is similarly delighted by the **memory** of the past, the **hope** for the future, and the **contemplation** of the present. It can rejoice not only in those things that lack a body, but even in the knowledge of bodies themselves.

¶ And since the soul is the most excellent part of a human being, no one can doubt that whatever is in harmony with the mind ought to be judged more related and similar to a person than that which suits the senses. Furthermore, that which is most related to a thing is undoubtedly the most pleasant; from this, it is understood that the joy of the soul is greater and more excellent than the sweetness of the body.

¶ Added to this is the fact that the soul is indivisible and simple. The knowledge of truth is likewise indivisible. Therefore, since the pleasure of the mind flows from these two as if from certain causes, it will appear simple; it cannot become lesser or greater than itself, since its principles do not admit of any such variety. The senses, however, are disseminated and distributed through the limbs. For that reason, they are composed of a manifold variety. The objects of the senses also seem to be nothing other than certain forms and qualities of bodies which arise from a certain harmony of their parts, such as shapes, colors, sounds, smells, and other things of this sort. When that very proportion of bodies, by which the senses are moved, is harmonious and similar to the proportion of the senses themselves, the senses adopt it as something proper, familiar, and good, [finding] pleasure...

One can observe this in songs and sounds; for at the same moment of time (if I may say so), the very same delight perceived from the same song is made stronger or weaker as the voices are produced now more sweetly, now more discordantly <note>The author uses the analogy of music to show how physical pleasure fluctuates based on the quality of the stimulus, unlike intellectual truth which is constant.</note>.

¶ Indeed, Aristotle's final argument on this point is clear: those things which are sought for their own sake, he says, are seen to be better than those sought for the sake of something else. But the joy of the mind is loved for its own sake, which is most clearly shown by the fact that the mind and its motion far excel all other things within us in dignity. From this it follows that there is nothing in us to which those things could be referred as if to some end; and by the same reasoning, we do not desire the pleasure that dwells in them for the sake of anything else.

¶ However, we desire the pleasure of the body for three main reasons. The first of these is the mind; the second is the lack <note>original: *indigentia*; refers to biological needs like hunger or thirst</note> of nature; the last is internal and perpetual pain. For since nature has directed lesser things toward those that are more powerful, so that there might be a certain inexplicable order of things and a perfect connection of the parts among themselves, it is necessary that the senses of the body and their motions also be referred to the mind as if to a mistress and queen.

¶ Next (as we also said above), nature implanted such intense pleasure in the senses for this reason: so that we might be made more inclined by these allurements to acquire the things necessary for life. This is most evident from the fact that as long as we admit into the body what nature lacks, we are moved by this kind of sweetness. But after all the needs of nature are filled, not only do we taste no further pleasure, but what is more, we are affected either by regret or by satiety. I believe nature established this for the reason that, just as we are enticed by pleasure to drive away lack, so we are deterred by regret and satiety, lest we harm nature by admitting more than is necessary.

For not only manifest pains occur, but also certain hidden and intermediate ones. Violent movements brought in from the outside cause manifest pain. Natural agitations, however, which occur within, cause a silent and intermediate pain. He believes that perpetual <term>natural spirits</term> <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle substances that flowed through the nerves and arteries to facilitate movement and sensation.</note>, and motions of the senses and the mind, are within us. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of bodily pleasure as a remedy for biological lack or pain. <center>& iii</center>

Furthermore, [nature] pours humors and spirit <note>In this context, *spiritus* refers to the "vital spirits," a refined substance thought to circulate through the nerves and arteries to animate the body.</note> from the limbs of the body itself to other limbs in an alternating and perpetual motion. It then uses the instruments of the body for perceiving, and the senses for contemplating. It seems reasonable, truly, that these movements—so great, so varied, and so perpetual—weary nature and afflict it with a certain hidden pain (if I may call it that), which we notice less for the reason that we endure this pain from our first birth until our final day. Therefore, long-standing habit makes it somehow familiar to the senses and dissolves the mind’s focus on it. 

Moreover, it has been established by nature itself, the artisan and teacher of things, so that what that long-standing habit has erased from our awareness might be stirred by a certain necessary and blind instinct, lest the living creature <note>original: *animal*</note> perish through such neglect. By this instinct, almost all things are compelled to desire bodily pleasure as a medicine, as it were, opposed to this internal pain. For this reason, even those to whom no manifest lack occurs still strive for pleasure because of this innate and blind deficiency <note>original: *indigentia*</note>. Thus it happens that the saying of Plato—which we discussed above—is most true: namely, that all pleasure proceeds from the filling of a lack. For those in whom no open lack appears, an internal and hidden one can never be absent so long as they live.

And this very innate deficiency we spoke of happens especially to the young and to those of a melancholic temperament. To the young, certainly, because they are stirred by many and violent motions due to the necessity of growing and perfecting the body. It follows that they require a greater medicine, and for this reason, they pursue pleasures most of all. 

But for those in whom black bile <note>original: *atra bilis*</note>—which the Greeks call <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: *μελαγχολίαν* (melancholian)</note>—dominates, the body (as the philosopher says) is continually consumed and gnawed away because of the intense dryness of that humor. Because of this, they too greatly indulge in pleasures. Therefore, the young and the melancholic are usually the most <term>incontinent</term> <note>In early modern philosophy, "incontinence" refers to a lack of self-control or the inability to resist physical impulses.</note> and intemperate of all.

¶ Intermediate pain, however, can be called hunger, thirst, and any other bodily desire. For this pain is not entirely hidden, nor does it torture the body with an open or more violent motion. Hence it is not undeservedly named "intermediate," for the sake of driving which away—as everyone sees—we seek pleasures.

<margin>1</margin>
We have already declared at length the opinion of Aristotle, who judges that pleasure of the mind is superior to the sweetness of the body. Now there remains another disputation of Aristotle against Eudoxus <note>A student of Plato who argued that pleasure is the supreme good because all creatures seek it.</note> and the Cyrenaics <note>A school of philosophy founded by Aristippus of Cyrene, which held that immediate physical pleasure is the only absolute good.</note>, in which he demonstrates that bodily pleasure can in no way be the highest good <note>original: *summum bonum*</note>. Indeed, by the authority of all philosophers, the highest good must be of such a kind that there is nothing better beyond it, nor is it referred to any other thing. Bodily pleasure, however, is much inferior to the joy of the mind (as we showed just before), and it is desired for the sake of the mind's joy and the other things we have mentioned. Furthermore, that which is the highest good in itself ought always and for everyone to appear as a good to be desired, and it should be approved in all its parts. Yet, not every bodily delight is sought always, nor by everyone. For what often provides pleasure to one person usually provides annoyance to another; things that are pleasing to children seem troublesome to men; and what we crave while we are sober, we later feel nauseous even at the sight of once we have become full. 

To this we also add that it is the nature of the highest good that whatever we do, we choose it for its own sake, as if compelled by necessity. Yet there are many most laborious tasks and certain duties full of danger which, even if we know for certain they will bring us no bodily pleasure, we do not hesitate to undertake for the sake of honor, or virtue <note>original: *honestas*</note>, or the joy of the mind. Indeed, many of the bravest and wisest men have delivered themselves to certain death for the sake of virtue, for their country, or for their parents. If anyone should say that they did these things because they were ensnared by bodily sweetness or inflamed by lust, or that in their judgment they preferred the opinion of the common crowd and of beasts to their own power of reason, that person must surely be judged the most foolish of all. 

Moreover, anyone at all, even the most abject person, can enjoy bodily pleasures no less than the best man. But no one would say that happiness <note>original: *felicitas*</note> belongs to the abject. Nor is it reasonable to assert that the lowliest and half-dead wretches are as blessed as great and wise men. 

Likewise, the highest good of any nature ought to be specific to it; but since bodily pleasure is shared even with the lowliest living creatures, it should in no way be judged the highest good of man. 

Or would you truly call that the highest good which does not even seem to be a good? I believe our Plato has already sufficiently declared above how shameful, how wretched, and how pestilential this elation of the senses is.

[vo]luptas <note>The word begins on the previous page as *uoluptas* (pleasure).</note> of the body may be sought by everyone, this seems to the followers of Aristotle to have little weight in proving what they [the opponents] contend. For Aristotle thinks that there are various dispositions of different bodies. Therefore, those things which are related to these natures, and which produce pleasure because of that very relationship, differ greatly among themselves. From this it is understood that various and quite different pleasures fall to different living creatures. Indeed, if you were to run through all the pleasures of the body, you would find none that is ultimately and exceedingly desired by all. The mind, however, is established to be either one in all people, or at the very least, most similar. And therefore, that which is characteristic of the mind seems characteristic and innate to all who use a mind. But the characteristic of the mind is the investigation and knowledge of truth. It is clear, then, that this is agreeable to all people, and for that reason, it is to be desired. Wherefore all men (as Aristotle says) naturally desire knowledge <note>A reference to the famous opening line of Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*: "All men by nature desire to know."</note>. Moreover, that which is sought usually produces distress if it is absent, but pleasure if it is present. Therefore, for all men there is one thing innate by nature, one thing to be sought by all, and finally one thing that is most delightful. And yet, all of this consists in the contemplation of truth. This is the food <note>original: *pabulum*</note> of the mind (as Plato says), and it fills the soul with a certain ineffable pleasure. Thus, while some bodily pleasures are sought by some and others by others, the joy of the mind is one and the same, loved by all.

### Chapter XV. Why humans are prone to the pleasure of the body.

<margin>a.</margin> And yet someone might perhaps ask why nearly countless men are more inclined toward the pleasures of the body. Therefore, from our earliest years, when we use only our senses—which can achieve neither the nature of truth nor its joy—we follow that which charms the senses, being deceived by this similarity, and we embrace it eagerly in place of that pleasure toward which the primary intention of nature is directed. But when we have grown to maturity, and we begin to perceive the truth and taste its joy as if the eyes of the soul <note>A common Platonic and Aristotelian metaphor for the faculty of reason (intellect).</note> have been awakened, even then many continue in the course of their past life even until old age. For they have long been accustomed to trusting the senses and obeying their habits, and that very habit has now driven its roots so deep and wide that it is impossible, or certainly most difficult, to extirpate them now that they are solid and very deep. Cicero describes this most elegantly in the third book of his *Tusculan Disputations* with these words: "Nature," he says, "gave us small sparks <note>original: *igniculos*. Cicero uses this term to describe the innate "little fires" of reason or virtue we are born with.</note>, which we so quickly extinguish with corrupt habits and depraved opinions that the light of nature nowhere appears. For there are seeds of virtue innate in our characters, and if they were allowed to grow to maturity, nature herself would lead us to a blessed life. But now, as soon as we are brought into the light and raised, we live in constant depravity and the greatest perversity of opinions, so that we seem to have sucked in error with our nurse's very milk. When we are then returned to our parents and handed over to teachers, we are so imbued with various errors that nature itself gives way to vanity and entrenched opinion." Thus says Cicero. 

To return to the proposal: pleasure is various and uncertain according to the diversity of men, but a single joy of the mind is sought by all through nature. Since these two things—namely, the contemplation of truth and the pleasure derived from it—reside in the mind, and since the nature of the highest good seems to consist of these, the ancient philosophers doubted which of them was more excellent and preferable for happiness. For Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and the "Hermetic" tradition.</note>, and Theodorus (the disciple of Dionysius the Dialectician), Democritus, Pyrrho, Eurilochus, Philotimon, Phliasius, Nausiphanes, Theius, Epicurus, Origen, Avicenna, and Al-Ghazali <note>The author bridges Greek, Christian, and Islamic philosophy here, showing the breadth of the debate.</note> seem to judge that the principal part of the nature of happiness is the joy that accompanies contemplation. On the other hand, Thales, Bias, Anaxagoras, Socrates, Euclid of Megara, Aristotle, Herillus of Chalcedon, and Averroes prefer contemplation itself. This debate and controversy has flourished even into our own age and is discussed among Christian theologians as well. But more on this elsewhere. For now, it will suffice to have noted how Aristotle differs primarily from Eudoxus and Aristippus in two ways (as we declared above).

Indeed, he thinks the highest good is the joy of the mind, and the highest evil is the mind's distress; he believes the former consists of prudence, and the latter of imprudence. Furthermore, the goods by which we attain happiness are prudence and justice. Evils, conversely, are the opposite habits, while pleasure and pain—as the Stoics also believe—are indifferent.

### Chapter. XVII. What the Epicureans hold regarding the first principles of things, Pleasure, the emotions, and morals.

<margin>a</margin>
<margin><image-desc>A handwritten scribble, possibly a question mark or a correction mark, appears in the right margin.</image-desc></margin>
The Epicureans, however, establish the name of pleasure as a kind of genus, of which they think there are two species: they believe one pleasure consists in motion, and the other in a state of rest. That which is placed in motion they divide in two. One, indeed, is in the mind, the other in the senses. The former they usually call joy, and the latter they call delight. They define joy as a sweet commotion of the mind, enjoying that which it had sought. Delight, however, they define as a pleasant motion by which the senses open wide and overflow. They teach that this very pleasantness, which is placed in motion, arises in the following way. They say that the first principles of all things that exist are certain very small and entirely indivisible bodies, which they call <term>atoms</term> <note>original: *ἀτόμους*. From the Greek meaning "uncuttable" or "indivisible."</note> because they cannot be cut; and that these differ from one another in size and shape, so that some of these "seeds" are larger, others more minute; some are round and smooth, others are curved, hooked, and rough. All of these fly through the immense void in perpetual motions, striking one another, and clinging together by fortuitous collisions to constitute whatever exists in the nature of things. By the coming together of these, they believe three principal kinds of things are made. Some are formed from these atoms which are round, minute, and smooth; others by larger...

They <note>The Epicureans.</note> maintain that our body and our soul are composed of these same seeds, yet with this difference: that the body is filled with larger and thicker ones, while the soul is composed of tiny, smooth, and round ones. Furthermore, they claim that there is a void mixed into all bodies and natures, which they call passages and pores <note>original: *meatus porosque*</note>. Through these, it is brought about that bodies can receive one another and, as it were, drink them in. 

When, therefore, those primary types of seeds are presented to us—because, as we have said, they are the smallest that exist—they penetrate the body and the soul from all sides without causing any harm. Because they are round and smooth, and thus akin to the nature of the soul, they immediately soothe it and charm the senses. They believe that sweet fruits, the liquids of honey and milk, songs, the sweetest scents, and other things of this kind belong to this class. Because the seeds from which the soul is woven <note>The Epicureans believed the soul was a physical entity made of exceptionally fine atoms.</note> are touched by these smooth and charming little bodies, they indeed assent to this sweet movement. They spread themselves with a great eagerness into those little bodies drawn in through the senses and passages; they cling pleasantly, join firmly, and embrace most sweetly. They consider this very assent, outpouring, joining, and embracing to be <term>pleasure in motion</term> <note>original: *uoluptatem in motu positam*. This refers to "kinetic pleasure," the pleasure felt during the process of satisfying a desire or stimulating a sense, as opposed to "katastematic pleasure," which is the state of being free from pain.</note>. 

Conversely, however, it happens that when that third kind of body—which is constructed of rough and heavy seeds—is brought to the senses, a different effect occurs. Because the elements of which they consist are large, they are thrust with difficulty into the openings of the body and soul; with a certain force, they strike, break through, and pull apart the little bodies of the soul. Because they are rough and hooked, they bite the soul sharply in a way and prick the body. They judge such things to be wormwood <note>A notoriously bitter herb.</note>, bile, and unpleasant colors, sounds, and scents—all other things, in short, which touch the senses with some roughness or bitterness. Indeed, by the seeds of these things, the first-principles of the soul are stirred and pulled apart; they shudder, flee, and quickly contract themselves. They define such dispersion and contraction as pain following movement. 

The noble Epicurean Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher whose work *De Rerum Natura* is the primary source for Epicurean physics.</note> expresses these things in the second book of *On the Nature of Things* in these verses:

> So that you may easily recognize that those things
> Which can touch the senses pleasantly are made of smooth and round [atoms].
> But on the contrary, those which appear hooked and rough:
> These are held bound to one another by more hooked ties,
> And for that reason are accustomed to tear open the paths
> To our senses and break through the body by their entry.

<summary>This page explains the Epicurean physical theory of sensation, arguing that pleasure is caused by smooth, round atoms soothing the soul, while pain is caused by rough, hooked atoms tearing at it. It concludes with a supporting quotation from the Roman poet Lucretius.</summary>

# ON PLEASURE

Likewise, in the same book, these words appear:

> Moreover, since pain occurs when the material
> bodies, disturbed by some force throughout the living flesh and limbs,
> tremble within their internal seats;
> and when they return to their place, a soothing pleasure arises.
> <note>original: "Præterea quoniam dolor est..." — This is a quote from Lucretius’s *De Rerum Natura* (On the Nature of Things), Book 2, lines 963–966.</note>

But in truth, those things which are composed of certain intermediate elements are divided into several kinds. For some closely approach smooth and charming bodies; others rather approach those which are harsh to the senses; while some stand at an almost equal distance from both. The first kind, by a certain silent motion, entice the soul toward pleasure; the second seem to incite it toward sadness and pain gradually and hiddenly. However, those which are called **indifferent** produce an ambiguous and doubtful motion. For this reason, the mind grows sluggish and numb under their impulse, and is not aroused to action unless some new motion is added. 

Nor indeed do I think it should be passed over in silence that between those things which are entirely smooth and round, and those moreover which are completely hooked and rough, a certain middle genus of bodies is interposed. This consists of those atoms which are neither entirely round nor bent and hooked, but stand out with certain tiny and soft angles. They maintain that certain wines and fruits—which are moderately tempered with a wild, tart, and (as they say) sharp flavor—are of this kind. These do not soothe the mind, nor do they scatter it, and they do not force it to become any more languid; rather, they prick it lightly and moderately, and, as it were, <term>titillate</term> <note>The Epicurean concept of "titillatio" refers to a mild sensory stimulation that provides pleasure without the intensity of "kinetic" pleasure.</note> it, and produce pleasure.

This entire concept is understood from these verses of Lucretius:

> There are also things which are now rightly thought neither to be smooth,
> nor entirely hooked with bent points,
> but rather with small angles that project a little, and which
> can tickle the senses rather than hurt them.
> Of this kind are wine-lees and the flavors of wine.
> <note>original: "Sunt etiam quæ iam nec leuia..." — Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book 2, lines 422–425.</note>

From this it follows that there are three species of pleasures among those that follow motion in the senses: one is a certain affection toward softness, which they call **enticement**; the second is a smooth and sweet **commotion**; the last, truly, is a certain small stinging and (as they say) like an itching and tickling. **Epicurus** also uses another division of pleasures: for he says some are **natural and necessary**, such as those which settle pain and the intense craving of nature through food, drink, and all other things to which the violent motion of nature impels us. Others are **natural but not necessary**, which are of the kind that only vary delight, but do not...

# BOOK

...remove pains, nor do they increase pleasure. Indeed, once the needs of nature are satisfied and the pain that follows from those needs is removed, Epicurus believes that the highest bodily pleasure is reached. This means that pleasure can afterwards be varied and distinguished, but it cannot be increased or amplified. Therefore, in this second category, the Epicureans place those pleasures which are perceived through various seasonings and the exquisite delights of banquets.

Then, he adds a third kind of pleasures: those that are neither natural nor necessary. Examples include pleasures derived from spectacles of external things that pertain neither to one’s sustenance nor to skill, and all those pleasures taken from the immense accumulation of riches and wealth. 

The logic of all these pleasures is as follows: the desire for those that are **necessary** can be satisfied without much labor or expense. Nor do the cravings for **natural** pleasures require much, because nature herself keeps the riches with which she is content ready at hand, limited, and easy to obtain. However, for **empty cravings**—which seek pleasures that are neither natural nor necessary—no limit or end (as he believes) can be found. 

Hence, Epicurus says: "If you live according to nature, you will never be poor; if you live according to opinion <note>original: "si ad opinionem" — meaning living according to social expectations or false beliefs about what one needs.</note>, you will never be rich." Indeed, nature herself enriches the wise man, for her riches are easily obtained. Nor indeed are the pleasures perceived from the simplest and most humble food any less than those from the most exquisite feasts. For nature is content with a few, minimal things.

¶ Nor does Epicurus only pursue that pleasure which moves our nature with some sweetness—of which we have now said enough—but he considers that greatest pleasure to be the one perceived when all pain is removed. He calls this a **static pleasure** <term>static pleasure: original "in statu posita," referring to *katastematic* pleasure, which is the stable state of being without pain, as opposed to "kinetic" pleasure which comes from active stimulation.</term>. 

While the Cyrenaics <note>A rival school of philosophy founded by Aristippus of Cyrene, who argued that pleasure is only found in active, "moving" sensations and denied that the absence of pain was a pleasure in itself.</note> had argued to the contrary, Epicurus teaches that this state ought to be called pleasure. He argues that since we are deprived of pain, we rejoice in that very liberation and the absence of all distress. Now, everything in which we rejoice is pleasure, just as everything by which we are offended is pain. Therefore, the removal of all pain is rightly named pleasure. For just as when hunger and thirst are driven away by food and drink, the very removal of the distress brings the attainment of pleasure, so in every matter, the removal of pain brings about a succession of pleasure. 

Consequently, it did not please Epicurus that there should be some "middle ground" between pain and pleasure. For that very state which seems to some to be a middle ground—when we lack all pain—is not only a pleasure but even the highest pleasure. For whoever is aware of their own condition must necessarily be either in a state of pain or in a state of pleasure. Furthermore, they divide this **static pleasure** into two parts: they place one in the soul and the other in the body; the latter they call **indolence** <term>indolence: from the Latin *indolentia*, literally "freedom from pain." In this philosophical context, it does not mean laziness, but the physical state of being untroubled by bodily suffering.</term>...
