-># ON PLEASURE<-

...absence of pain <note>original: "indolentiam"</note>. That, indeed, they call tranquility. Now (as they see it), in the body, "absence of pain" is the removal of all pain. "Tranquility" <note>original: "tranquillitas"</note>, however, is a certain peaceful and constant freedom of the mind from all disturbance. Sometimes, indeed, they embrace both types of pleasure under a single name, calling it absolute and complete tranquility. Thus it happens that tranquility is twofold: one pertains to the mind alone, and the other to the whole man; it is this latter one that is entirely perfect and absolute.

### Chapter 18. Moderation in pleasures, and that happiness lies not in stimulated pleasure, but in tranquility according to Epicurus and Democritus.

Furthermore, every pleasure is good by its very nature and is to be sought, yet it must sometimes be avoided for the sake of something else. For those pleasures which are undertaken from immoderate and shameful actions ought to be avoided for this reason: they are very brief and fragile, and they bring with them repentance, care, anxiety, and pain. Likewise, all pains are to be avoided for their own sake, yet they should be undertaken for the sake of something else when, being light and very brief, they are likely to provide us with certain great pleasures and advantages. And even if all pleasures are good, a blessed life is not situated in all of them. For that pleasure which occurs through motion <note>Epicurus distinguished between "kinetic" pleasure (active stimulation of the senses) and "static" pleasure (the state of being free from pain or hunger).</note> is not sufficient in itself for a blessed life, nor is it entirely necessary for living blessedly for its own sake. Rather, they consider that absolute tranquility, which contains peaceful rest of the mind and the body's absence of pain, to be the highest good of all. ¶ For in these two things the entire nature of man—namely of the body and the mind equally—is made perfect, and this is the state to which all labors are referred. Indeed, men undergo all labors so that they might afterwards be able to exist in leisure and rest, and they pursue those pleasures which we have categorized as "in motion" so that they might drive away pains and satisfy the needs of nature. They drive away pain and satisfy need so that we may be released and free from all pain that arises from the "poverty of nature" <note>A term for natural lack, such as hunger, thirst, or cold.</note>. And this is that "absence of pain" <note>original: "indolentia"</note> which they want to be understood as a stable state, and which they judge to constitute one part of happiness. The other part is governed by tranquility of the mind, for the sake of which all virtues are sought. In fact, since the virtues desire nothing else but to free the mind from every disturbance, that very state is tranquility itself; for this reason they maintain that all virtues were sought for the sake of tranquility itself, and much more so all other human actions.

# BOOK

...while other human goods belong either specifically to the mind or to the body.
<margin>i</margin> Alone among all things, that absolute and perfect tranquility <note>original: "tranquillitas"</note> encompasses the whole of human nature. And therefore, it ought to be judged deservedly the most excellent of all goods. 

¶ In addition to this, it is of no small weight that it is confirmed by the authority of all philosophers: namely, that the "highest" <term>summum bonum; the supreme good that provides the ultimate motivation for human action</term> is seen as that to which nothing further can be added. But what, indeed, will you add to tranquility? Will you do so? Not unless something is lacking in it. But if any good were missing, it is necessary that the person who lacks it should desire it. He, however, who desires, can in no way be tranquil. Where, therefore, there is tranquility, there is no desire. Where, indeed, nothing is desired, there is no want. Where there is no lack, there finally is a perfect state, an abundance of things to be sought, and an absolute collection of all goods. Where, then, there is tranquility, there are all good things. Where all things are, there is also tranquility. By which it is understood that nothing is missing from it, nothing at all can be added, and it contains within itself the nature and reason of all goods. And therefore, it is a perfect and ultimate good, toward which every natural desire is directed. 

¶ Since goods are many, happiness is either one specific thing among them, or all of them gathered together, or rather a certain thing which is formed from the accumulated possession of all other goods. But any good separated from the rest, since many other things can be added to it, can in no way be seen as the highest good. Nor even all of them collected together. For happiness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note> exists as a certain ultimate and final end of human life. Moreover, an ultimate end must be one and simple. For this reason, the highest good will be that which results from the accumulation of all other things. This, indeed, can be nothing besides tranquility. For the nature of goods is twofold: for they both fill the soul and free it from all distress. Such a fulfillment and liberation is, without a doubt, tranquility itself.

¶ Since this follows the possession of all other goods, it follows that it is the end and ultimate goal of them all, and for that reason, it is deservedly seen as the highest. For the soul never rests unless it has attained all goods. Now, rest and tranquility are one and the same thing. Therefore, it succeeds the possession of other goods. Thus, all goods seem to be sought for its sake, as if this were the ultimate and best end to be sought by all. On account of this, Epicurus judges that a blessed life consists in tranquility of soul; indeed, in that tranquility which encompasses both the soul and the body's freedom from pain <note>original: "indolentiam," referring to the Greek concept of aponia</note>, it is most blessed. 

¶ But lest I seem to assert from my own self those things which have been reported concerning Epicurus, first

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of the "highest good," specifically focusing on the Epicurean definition of pleasure. ### ON PLEASURE

Epicurus himself testifies in his own words that pleasure, which accompanies motion <note>This refers to "kinetic" or active pleasure, such as the act of eating, which Epicurus viewed as secondary to the stable state of being satisfied.</note>, is not the supreme good. In his letter to Menoeceus <note>A famous summary of Epicurean ethics addressed to one of his students.</note>, he says: "When we say that pleasure is the end, we do not mean the pleasures of the dissolute or those found in the sense of taste—as some who are ignorant or who disagree with our views believe—but rather we mean not suffering in the body and being tranquil in the soul, free from disturbance." <note>original: "non dolere corpore, animoque tranquillum esse, & perturbatione uacare"</note>. He explains that neither constant banquets and drinking bouts, nor the company of youths and women, nor the consumption of fish and other luxuries offered by a costly table, produce a sweet life. Instead, it is produced by sober reasoning, which examines the causes for why every thing should be chosen or avoided, and which expels those opinions through which the greatest turmoil occupies the soul.

In the same letter, he also states: "The absence of pain and disturbance are constant pleasures <note>Also called "static" or "catastematic" pleasures; the state of being free from need.</note>; whereas joy and gladness are considered actions involving motion." The highest pleasure is the privation of pain. Furthermore, the pleasures of the mind are greater than those of the body; for the flesh is bathed only in present sweetness, while the mind rejoices in the contemplation of things past, present, and future. In the same letter, he adds: "It is not possible to live pleasantly unless one lives prudently, honorably, and justly; nor can one live prudently, honorably, and justly without living pleasantly." 

From these passages, Epicurus shows that the highest good consists neither in active pleasures nor in those derived from shameful actions. Instead, these two—namely, the absence of bodily pain and tranquility of the mind—constitute the most blessed life. Lucretius the Epicurean <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), the Roman poet who popularized Epicureanism in his epic poem *De Rerum Natura*.</note> testifies to the same in the second book of *On the Nature of Things*. While condemning the empty desires and luxurious delights of men, he says:

> O wretched minds of men, O blinded hearts!
> In what darkness of life, and in what great perils
> Is this span of time passed, however long it be!
> Do you not see that nature barks for nothing else
> But that pain be absent and separated from the body,
> and that the mind may enjoy a pleasant sense,
> removed from care and fear?
> <note>original: "O miseras hominum mentes, o pectora cæca..."</note>

Here, therefore, by rebuking the luxury of men, he calls them blind and wretched because they burden themselves with every kind of trouble and do not see what nature desires as the supreme end and good. He himself explains what that is, saying that nature seeks this: that pain be absent from the body—which signifies that <term>indolentia; a technical term meaning the complete absence of physical pain</term> of which we spoke—and that care and fear be removed. By these words, he surely intends for tranquility of mind to be understood, so that one might enjoy the benefit of these two gifts, and a sense of joy...

...and in the mind, as if to say that the highest joy of both body and soul consists in these. Therefore, since the most blessed life consists in these two things—namely, the absence of pain <note>original: "indolentia"; this refers to the Greek *aponia*, the state of having no physical suffering.</note> and the tranquility of the mind <note>original: "animi tranquillitate"; corresponding to the Greek *ataraxia*.</note>—these testimonies of Epicurus and Lucretius ought to be sufficient. But indeed, as evidence that he in whom there is tranquility of mind remains blessed even if the limbs of his body are tortured, Epicurus himself is a witness. In a letter to Metrodorus <note>A close disciple of Epicurus.</note>, he says that he who is once wise cannot pass into the opposite state, nor can he err by yielding to disturbances; and even if he is tortured or racked, the wise man will nonetheless be happy. Also in that letter which he wrote to Hermachus <note>Epicurus's successor as head of the Garden.</note> while dying, he said: "While we were spending the blessed and also the final day of our life, we were writing these things; such great pains of the bladder and intestines were present that nothing could be added to their severity. Yet the joy of mind, which I took from the memory of our reasonings and discoveries, was compensated against all these." In these words, he says he spends a blessed day while being tortured by the greatest pains. The same is said to have been the opinion of Leucippus, Democritus, and Theodorus: that happiness lies in the tranquility of the mind. But if the absence of pain in the body is added to this, then in this state of mind and body, absolute and perfect happiness consists.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on the works of Theophrastus, specifically regarding his treatise on the senses. ### ON THEOPHRASTUS

<margin>n</margin> According to general reasoning, regarding the nature of flavors—specifically the sweet and similarly the bitter—when the bitter and the sweet touch the tongue at the same time, the tongue is then affected by both through different parts. Meanwhile, the sense, contained by a common principle, acts upon both equally through different ratios <note>original: "rationes"; here referring to the proportional relationships or "logoi" that define different qualities.</note>.
->PRISCIAN<- <note>Likely Priscian of Lydia, a Neoplatonist who wrote "Paraphrase on Theophrastus' On Sense Perception."</note>

<margin>q</margin> In what way, then, is the instrument of sense affected by the bitter and the sweet at the same time? For it is perhaps not only specific parts of the tongue that perceive this quality or that one. The same thing happens similarly with hearing. If, therefore, it is permitted to distinguish hearing, and even the instrument of taste—whether that be the tongue or some spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; in ancient and Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to communicate sensations to the brain.</note> within the tongue—certainly, since such an instrument is divisible because it is a body, it is possible that it is affected by this quality in one part and by that quality in another. This is clearly evident in touch, for it is possible for one part to grow warm while another grows cold at the same time. Similarly, the spirit of sense (or hearing) can be affected, since it is divisible. But Reason <note>original: "Ratio"</note>, as has already been said, being as it were indivisible, is by no means prohibited from acting upon opposites simultaneously. However, it is impossible for the same thing to be affected <note>original: "Pati"; to undergo a change or receive an impression.</note> by opposites in exactly the same respect.

Chapter nine. All sensible things act in some way upon the instrument of sense; but heat, cold, and similar qualities—as well as flavors and the like, which are highly material—inflict a sharper passion <note>The "passion" here refers to a physical "suffering" or intense impression made upon the organ.</note>. However, form, figure <note>shape</note>, number, and motion, being more formal things, bring about a milder passion.
->MARSILIO<- <note>Marsilio Ficino, the influential Renaissance scholar who translated these Greek philosophical texts into Latin.</note>

<margin>p</margin> Furthermore, the *proper sensibles* <note>original: "propria... sensibilia"; qualities that can only be perceived by one specific sense, like color for the eyes.</note> of each individual sense are offered more clearly to the senses, such as color to sight, voice to hearing, heat to touch, and the like. But *common sensibles* <note>original: "communia"; qualities like size or movement that can be perceived by multiple senses (e.g., you can see movement and also feel it).</note> creep in more hiddenly and consequently, such as figure, motion, etc. There are those who think that number and motion are so "formal" <note>abstract or structural</note> and so far removed from matter that they do not suit the senses at all, and therefore are apprehended only by rational thought when it is appropriately stirred toward them through the sense—just as the essence of sensible things is apprehended by thought, not by sense. But the common opinion is that number and motion belong not only to thought, but also in some way to sense.
->PRISCIAN<-

<margin>c</margin> Heat, indeed, as a natural power, can act in some way upon the instrument of the senses. But how can form, figure, motion, and number render the sense similar to themselves by some action? We say, surely, that these too have something effective within them. However, they act "more formally," whereas heat and its related qualities act (if I may say so) "more corporally"—and therefore more sharply and with a certain more vehement passion. To say also

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how the human soul perceives the world. It specifically addresses the "common sensibles"—qualities like number and time that aren't limited to just one sense—and argues that the soul is active, not passive, when it perceives.</meta>

<page-num>44</page-num>
->**ON THE SOUL**<-

It is also permitted for the specific objects <note>original: "sensibilibus... propria"</note> of each individual sense to exert their own action and command respect, whereas the "common" attributes <note>Known as "common sensibles," these are properties like shape, number, and motion that can be perceived by more than one sense (e.g., you can both see and feel a square).</note> involve a certain relaxation. Indeed, the former are more immediate and superior, and are not measured by the sense in the same way, yet they are similar to the senses. These common attributes also exist and do not arise solely from rational reflection. And yet, this reflection, having turned back toward certain things from the senses, thinks of them according to its own nature, even when they have not yet been measured by any sense or when it contemplates the essence or substance of these sensible objects. Furthermore, if sense perceives time and number hardly at all, then rational thought will also recognize these, having been prompted by sensible things.

**Chapter Ten: External things do not make the sense like themselves, and much less do they do so to rational thought. Instead, the power of sensing makes itself similar to them through the production of its own internal principles. Thought does this to an even greater degree.**

### MARCIANUS SILIUS <note>Likely a reference to a commentator on the Aristotelian tradition.</note>

Just as the reason <term>ratio: internal principles or logical structures of the mind</term> innate to the sense is stirred by the presence of sensible forms, so it then stirs the power of thinking to produce the "reason of the essence" of sensible things. This occurs because of the kinship between the qualities perceived and that essence, specifically when such qualities are grasped by the sense.

### PRISCIAN <note>Priscian of Lydia, a 6th-century philosopher who sought to harmonize Aristotle's theories with Neoplatonism.</note>

Furthermore, if knowledge exists according to a certain "becoming like" the object <note>original: "assimilationem"</note>, in what way does thought—which does not suffer <term>passion: in this context, the state of being acted upon by an external force</term> from the things being sensed—become similar to them? If it does suffer, what kind of suffering is this? But surely it is not according to "passion" (as we have said) that either a sensory judgment or a rational reflection occurs. Rather, it occurs according to **action** and the **birth of internal principles**. Indeed, the "reason" of sensible things is brought forth when the "passion" of the sensory organ is fully realized into a form, or is defined by sensible things. In this way, such a "reason" is made to fit the sensible objects. For if it is stirred to a proportion with something fitting, the judging reason undoubtedly awakens the power of the soul regarding sensible qualities, being a knower of the essence of sensible things—certainly in a familiar way, because of a certain kinship of that kind of quality to the essence itself from which it proceeds.

**Chapter Eleven: Common sensible objects are apprehended not only by thought, but also by sense; and that follows naturally, for the primary and most specific things are known first because of their greater kinship.**
